c: In 1918, with the war thinning rosters, Ed Barrow put his ace pitcher in the everyday lineup. For about ten weeks Ruth pitched every fourth day and played the outfield or first base in between, leading Boston to the pennant. His World Series streak of 29⅔ scoreless innings, which included a 14-inning win in 1916, was one of the records he was proudest of.

In 1920, his first year in New York, he hit 54 home runs, more than 14 of the other 15 major-league teams. The runner-up in the AL had 19. His .847 slugging average stood until Barry Bonds broke it in 2001.

The 'Bellyache Heard 'Round the World' in 1925: he collapsed on a spring tour, a paper ran a photo with 12 hot dogs drawn on his stomach, and he needed surgery. After a terrible season he spent the winter at Artie McGovern's gym, dropped 44 pounds, and then averaged 50 home runs a year from 1926 to 1931.

The called shot, Wrigley Field, 1932 World Series: under heavy heckling from the Cubs' bench he held up fingers and gestured, then hit Charlie Root's 2–2 pitch to deep center. Only one writer reported a 'called' homer that day. Root said Ruth would have ended up on his backside if he'd pointed. Asked whether he really had, Ruth said, "It's in the papers, isn't it?"

His last great day came as a 40-year-old Boston Brave: three home runs at Forbes Field on May 25, 1935. The last of them, number 714, cleared the right-field roof, the longest home run ever hit in that park.

No team would hire him to manage. Of the Hall of Fame's first five, he was the only one never offered a managing job. Ed Barrow's explanation: "How can he manage other men when he can't even manage himself?"
Jack Dunn signed him to the minor-league Orioles in February 1914 and, short on cash that summer, sold him to the Red Sox.

In 1915 a broken toe, from kicking the bench after an intentional walk, kept him out of the rotation for two weeks; he'd also been slumping from carousing with Dutch Leonard. That fall he pitched all 14 innings of Game 2 of the World Series to beat Brooklyn 2-1.
His World Series pitching added up to 29⅔ straight scoreless innings, a record he was proudest of; Whitey Ford broke it in the 1960s.
Before 1919 he held out for double his salary and threatened to become a boxer. His curfew violations drew suspensions, and after the season Harry Frazee sold him to the Yankees.

After the 1921 World Series he barnstormed against a standing rule, and Commissioner Landis suspended him for six weeks and fined him his whole Series share, $3,362. In 1922 he jumped into the stands after a heckler, was fined and stripped of the captaincy, and was suspended for an obscene tirade at umpire Bill Dinneen.
The 1926 World Series ended with Ruth thrown out trying to steal second in Game 7.

Brooklyn hired him as first-base coach in 1938, but made clear he wouldn't be considered as manager. He left after the season and never worked in baseball again; radio networks didn't want him either, and a 1946 letter to the Yankees got a rejection.
p: At seven his parents had a court declare him 'incorrigible' and sent him to St. Mary's Industrial School in Baltimore. There Brother Matthias taught him to hit, and Ruth called him "the father I needed and the greatest man I've ever known."

In Boston he bused orphans out to his Sudbury farm for picnics and ball games, and came to Fenway on Saturday mornings to help the teenage vendors bag peanuts, racing them and then leaving a $20 bill on the table.
In 1934, getting a passport for the tour of Japan, he learned he had been born on February 6, 1895. He had always believed it was February 7, 1894, so he was a year younger than he thought.

His first wife, Helen, died in a 1929 house fire while living with another man. They had never divorced, and Ruth wept uncontrollably at the funeral. He married Claire Hodgson that April, and on the next day's Opening Day he homered and tipped his cap to her.
Cancer wasted him in his last two years. He made a final trip to Yankee Stadium on June 13, 1948, when his number 3 was retired, and died two months later at 53.
His father ran a saloon in Baltimore, where young George stole from the till and drained old beer glasses. His mother died when he was 12.

He married Helen Woodford, a Boston waitress, as a teenager in 1914. They adopted a daughter, Dorothy, in 1921. Dorothy later claimed she was really Ruth's biological child by a mistress, Juanita Jennings.
He married Claire Hodgson in April 1929, three months after Helen's death.
His daughter Julia and granddaughter said being passed over as a manager sent him into a severe depression.

c: In spring 1992 Dodgers executive Fred Claire said, "I won't trade Pedro Martínez, I don't care who they offer." Two years later he traded him to Montreal for Delino DeShields, partly because the Dodgers doubted a pitcher under 160 pounds could start.

On April 13, 1994, Reggie Sanders charged the mound after a Martínez pitch hit him in the eighth inning. Even the Reds doubted it was on purpose, because Martínez had a perfect game going at the time. Montreal writers called him 'Señor Plunk' that year.

On June 3, 1995, in San Diego, he became only the second pitcher ever to take a perfect game into extra innings. He was perfect through nine with the score 0–0. Bip Roberts doubled to lead off the 10th, after Montreal had scored in the top half.
After becoming the first Dominican to win a Cy Young, in 1997, he gave the trophy to Juan Marichal, who he felt should have won one. Marichal was deeply touched and gave it back.
Game 5 of the 1999 ALDS in Cleveland: his back was too sore to start, but he came out of the bullpen in a tied slugfest and threw six no-hit innings. He struck out Omar Vizquel to end the series.
In 2000, at the height of the offensive boom, he posted a 1.74 ERA when the league ERA was 4.91. Opponents had a .213 on-base percentage against him, the lowest in 100 years.
After the 2004 World Series sweep he dedicated the win to Montreal, which was losing its team: "My heart and my ring is with them, too."
He tagged along with Ramón to the Dodgers' academy at 13, and Ralph Avila signed him at 16 in 1988.
At Great Falls, coach Guy Conti taught him a circle changeup he had learned from Johnny Podres and helped him with English. Pedro called him his "white daddy."
Tommy Lasorda thought he was too small to start and used him mostly in relief, though Ramón said Pedro was the better pitcher.
In 1993 he and Ramón pitched in the same game, the first brothers to do it for one team since 1979.
In 1994 he led the league with 11 hit batters, was ejected from 12 games and got into three fights.
After his Cy Young the Expos traded him, a year before free agency. He signed with Boston for six years and $75 million, the most for any pitcher at the time.

A rotator cuff tear cost him most of 2001. In the 2003 ALCS he hit Karim Garcia, and 72-year-old Yankees coach Don Zimmer charged him; Martínez threw him to the ground. Zimmer later said it was his fault. In the deciding game Grady Little left him in to blow the lead and was fired.

Boston offered three years and $40.5 million because of his shoulder. The Mets gave him four years and $53 million. A torn rotator cuff and calf in 2006 kept him out of the Mets' postseason; cameras caught him apparently crying in the dugout.
The Phillies signed him for $1 million in July 2009. His last game was Game 6 of that World Series, with Philadelphia down three games to two.
Since 2013 he has been a postseason analyst for TBS, and since 2015 for MLB Network. His autobiography, Pedro, came out in 2015.
p: He grew up in a tin-roofed house with dirt floors in Manoguayabo. Too poor for baseballs, the Martínez boys used sticks for bats and their sisters' dolls for balls, ripping the heads off to the girls' horror.
His father Paolino was a fine pitcher in the 1950s whom the Alous thought was major-league caliber. The Giants invited him to a tryout, but he had no cleats and couldn't go.
Pedro tagged along at 13 when his brother Ramón went to the Dodgers' Dominican academy, and scout Ralph Avila clocked him at 80 mph. "Everything I am I learned from Ramón," he said.
He met his wife, Carolina Cruz, through his own foundation; she went to Boston College on one of its scholarships. Together they run the foundation in Santo Domingo, which built a three-story school.
He was the fifth of six children. When his parents divorced, Ramón, then 13, became the head of the household.
His mother washed clothes for wealthy families, and his father worked odd jobs. Pedro later worked as a mechanic.
His son Pedro Jr. signed with the Tigers in 2017. He also has sons Pedro Isaías and Enyol and a daughter, Nayla. He became a U.S. citizen in 2006.

c: The Giants drafted him out of high school in 1982 and offered $70,000. His father, Bobby, asked for $5,000 more, the Giants said no thanks, and Barry went to Arizona State. There he set a College World Series record with hits in seven straight at-bats.

When Pittsburgh's Andy Van Slyke won a Gold Glove in 1988, Bonds said, "Next year I'm gonna win me one of these." It took two years, then he won eight in nine seasons. Van Slyke said that once Bonds decided to be a good outfielder, "he willed himself to become great."
On May 28, 1998, Buck Showalter had him intentionally walked with the bases loaded, protecting a two-run lead in the ninth. It was the first time that had happened since 1944.

In 2001 Houston pitched around him for a whole series, to its own fans' anger, until he tied McGwire's 70 in the ninth inning of the last game. The next night he hit 71 and 72 off Chan Ho Park, and finished with 73.
In 2004 he was walked intentionally 120 times. That's nearly double the record of 68 he had set two years earlier, which itself had blown past Willie McCovey's 45.
In his only World Series, in 2002, he hit .471 with four home runs and a record 13 walks, seven of them intentional. The Giants blew a 5–0 lead in Game 6 and lost the Series.
His aunt Rosie ran hurdles in the 1964 Olympics, and his uncle Robert was drafted by both the NFL and AFL.

At Arizona State he set a College World Series record with hits in seven straight at-bats. Coach Jim Brock called him "rude, inconsiderate and self-centered." Pittsburgh took him in the first round in 1985 with a $150,000 bonus.

He hit .191 in Pittsburgh's three straight NLCS losses, 1990–92. The 1992 series ended with Sid Bream scoring just ahead of Bonds's throw from left. He then signed with the Giants for six years and $43 million, the biggest contract in baseball.
He tore a triceps in early 1999 and missed a third of the season. Knee problems led to several surgeries over the winter of 2004–05.

His trainer since 2000, Greg Anderson of BALCO, was indicted in 2003 for supplying steroids to athletes. Bonds testified he thought the substances were flaxseed oil and rubbing balm. His girlfriend Kimberly Bell later said she had seen him use steroids.
Indicted in 2007, he was convicted in 2011 of obstruction of justice for an evasive answer and sentenced to 30 days of house arrest. The conviction was overturned in 2015.
Nobody signed him after 2007. He came back to the Giants as a spring hitting instructor in 2014, and in 2026 joined Netflix's baseball broadcasts.
p: His father's Giants teammate Willie Mays was his godfather. As a boy in the Candlestick clubhouse he had to choke up on a bat too heavy for him, and he kept choking up for the rest of his life.
A scout in high school wrote 'Asshole' under Attitude/Personality. At Arizona State his coach let the team vote on whether to keep him, and almost everyone voted no.
Having watched the press build up his father and then tear him down over his drinking, Barry kept reporters away for his whole career, telling them "tomorrow" for interviews that never happened.
When he arrived in San Francisco he was given Mays's retired number 24. After an outcry he switched to 25, which the Giants retired for him in 2018.

His parents grew up next door to each other and married at 17. While Bobby played in the minors, Barry grew up in Riverside with his mother and two younger brothers, often one of the few Black children around.

He married Sun, from Sweden, in Las Vegas in 1988. They divorced in 1994, and the courts upheld the prenuptial agreement she had signed waiving any share of his earnings, which led to changes in California law.

From 1994 to 2003 he had a relationship with Kimberly Bell. In 1998 he married Liz Watson in front of 240 guests at the Ritz-Carlton. They had a daughter, Aisha, separated several times, and later divorced.
In 2010 his son Nikolai, who had sat beside him in the Giants dugout as a batboy, was charged with misdemeanors after a confrontation with his mother.

c: Detroit bought him from Augusta for $700 in August 1905, just weeks after his father's death. "In my grief, it didn't matter much… I only thought, Father won't know it."
As a rookie his Tiger teammates smashed his bats, nailed his cleats to the floor and knotted his clothes. "These old-timers turned me into a snarling wildcat," he said later.

The 1910 batting race: Cobb sat out the last two games, and the Browns played their third baseman back so Nap Lajoie could bunt his way to an 8-for-8 doubleheader. Cobb kept the title anyway, thanks partly to a game that was counted twice.

In May 1912 he went into the Hilltop Park stands and beat a heckler who had lost most of both hands. When he was suspended, his teammates, who didn't like him, went on strike. For one game Detroit fielded a team of semipros.
On the bases he kicked the bag, which everyone took for a habit. He was really nudging it a few inches toward the next base in case he decided to steal.

In 1926 Dutch Leonard accused Cobb and Tris Speaker of fixing a 1919 game. Commissioner Landis cleared both: "By no decent system of justice could such finding be made." Cobb then played two last seasons for Connie Mack.

The Augusta Tourists released him after two days. He joined a semipro team in Anniston, Alabama, for $50 a month and sent postcards praising himself under fake names to Atlanta sports editor Grantland Rice.
Detroit trained in Augusta in exchange for the right to buy one Augusta player later, and that player was Cobb.
He played in three World Series, all losses: twice to the Cubs and once to the Pirates.

He fought George Stanfield, a Black hotel night watchman in Cleveland, and fled town to avoid an arrest warrant for attempted murder; Stanfield sued. In 1908 he was arrested for assaulting a Black driver in a road-rage incident, and in 1924 he beat a Black ticket taker at Shibe Park. Each time he said the man had "insulted" him.
After a disputed play in Philadelphia, he got death threats when the Tigers went back there. Later he called segregation a "lousy rule" in a letter to Al Stump.

Near-yearly holdouts and the Federal League war made him the game's highest-paid player. He became Detroit's player-manager in 1921 and abruptly quit in November 1926. When the fixing charge came, he threatened to sue and got politicians to call for an investigation of baseball.
p: His father, a state senator and teacher, wanted him to be a lawyer or doctor. When Ty left for pro ball he told him: "Don't come home a failure."

In August 1905 his mother shot and killed his father, who had come back at night suspecting her of infidelity. She was tried for manslaughter and acquitted. Late in life Cobb said he played so hard "for my father… I knew he was watching me."
He got rich investing in Coca-Cola and General Motors and left an estate of about $12 million. He gave $100,000 to build a hospital in Royston and endowed scholarships for needy Georgia students.

Publicly he said he had no regrets, but near the end he told the comedian Joe E. Brown that he had played hard and lived hard and had no friends to show for it. Only a handful of baseball people came to his funeral.
His mother was 15 when she married his father. His brother Paul played nine years in the minors.
His father was killed with a pistol he had bought for her. She was released on a $7,000 bond.

He and Charlie Cobb had three sons and two daughters. She filed for divorce several times, and they finally divorced in 1947 after 39 years. He married Frances Fairbairn in 1949 and divorced again by 1956.

He expected his sons to be star athletes. When Ty Jr. failed at Princeton, Cobb went to campus and beat him with a whip. Ty Jr. was arrested twice for drunkenness at Yale, and his father cut him off for good. He became a doctor and died of a brain tumor at 42, still estranged.
His health failed in the late 1950s and he became an alcoholic. He died of prostate cancer in Atlanta in 1961.

c: Umpires came to trust his eye so much that more than one catcher complaining about a ball was told, "If Mr. Williams didn't swing at it, it wasn't a strike." At 20 he said all he wanted was for people to say, 'There goes the greatest hitter that ever lived.'
He hit .406 in 1941 even though sacrifice flies counted as at-bats then. His .553 on-base percentage that year wasn't topped for the rest of the century.
He lost the 1949 batting title, and with it a third Triple Crown, to George Kell by one ten-thousandth of a point.

Recalled to the Marines at 33 for Korea, he flew 39 combat missions, several as John Glenn's wingman. On his third mission his jet was hit and crash-landed and burned. He was back in the air at 8:08 the next morning.
In 1957, turning 39, he hit .388. Six more hits would have made it .400 again.
After a bad 1959 he came back for one more year but insisted on a 30 percent pay cut, saying he hadn't earned his salary. He homered in the last at-bat of his career in 1960.
He was a star pitcher at Hoover High and signed with the San Diego Padres while still in school. Sent to Minneapolis for a year, he won the American Association Triple Crown.
He refused an interview with columnist Bill Cunningham because the writer had been drinking. Writers like Dave Egan went after him, and some called him "Terrible Ted" and "the Splendid Spitter."

As his mother's only support he was exempt from the draft in 1942, and some questioned his courage for playing that season to pay off an annuity he'd bought her. He then joined the Navy's flight program.
He hurt his elbow in an exhibition before the 1946 World Series and hit poorly as Boston lost to the Cardinals in seven.
In Korea, ear infections twice put him in sick bay, and he was sent home in time to be an honored guest at the 1953 All-Star Game.

He broke his collarbone in 1954 spring training and fell 14 at-bats short of qualifying for the batting title he would have won at .345. After the season he "retired," apparently as a move in his divorce, and didn't return until May 1955.

He managed the Senators and Rangers from 1969 to 1972 and was Manager of the Year in his first season. He ran a baseball camp in Lakeville, Massachusetts, and taught hitting at Red Sox spring training.
p: His mother, May Venzor, was a Mexican-American Salvation Army evangelist, and he and his brother cringed when she took them to street-corner revivals. He later wrote that with his mother's name he would have run into the prejudices of Southern California in those days.

He swore he would never tip his cap to Fenway's fickle fans, and he never did. He admitted to "rabbit ears," hearing the one heckler over hundreds cheering. Yet he never argued with an umpire and was never thrown out of a game.

For years he was the face of the Jimmy Fund, Boston's children's cancer charity. The day he left town after retiring, he skipped any farewell dinners and quietly went to visit a child dying of leukemia.

In his 1966 Hall of Fame speech, which he wrote by hand the night before, he called for the Hall to honor the Negro League stars kept out of the majors. When the Red Sox finally integrated in 1959, he chose Pumpsie Green as his throwing partner.
"Yeah, I guess I was a great hitter, but I was a lousy husband and a crummy father," he told his SABR biographer, out of the blue, in the late 1990s.
His father was a photographer and former cavalryman. His parents weren't happily married and were often away, leaving Ted and his brother Danny to fend for themselves. They later divorced.

He married Doris Soule, his hunting guide's daughter, in 1944. Their daughter Bobby-Jo was born in 1948 while he was fishing in Florida. He married model Lee Howard in 1961 and divorced in 1967, then married Dolores Wettach, a former Miss Vermont, in 1968; they had John-Henry and Claudia.
He lived with Louise Kaufman for 20 years until she died in 1993. He kept a picture of Richard Nixon on his desk as Senators manager. His brother Danny and his son John-Henry both died of leukemia.

In his last years John-Henry ran his career and made him a fixture at card shows. When he died in 2002, John-Henry and Claudia had him cryonically frozen, though his will asked for cremation, and Bobby-Jo sued.

c: At 17 he faced Satchel Paige for the first time and doubled. Paige walked over to him at second and said, "That's it, kid." Mays went whoosh, whoosh, whoosh his next three times up.

In 1951 he was called up from Minneapolis while he was at the movies; the house lights came up and the manager asked Willie Mays to report to his hotel. He told Durocher he couldn't hit big-league pitching. Durocher asked what he was hitting. ".477." Then, "Do you think you can hit .250 for me?"

He started 1-for-26 and sat crying at his locker. Durocher told him, "As long as I'm the manager of the Giants, you are my center fielder," and told him to hitch up his pants. Mays then went 14-for-33.

The Catch, 1954 World Series Game 1: with two on and the game tied in the eighth, Vic Wertz drove one to the deepest part of the Polo Grounds. Mays caught it over his shoulder on the run, then whirled and threw. Mays himself thought a diving catch at Ebbets Field in 1952 was better; he knocked himself out on the wall.

He won the 1954 batting title on the last day. Going in, three hitters were separated by four ten-thousandths of a point: teammate Don Mueller .3426, Duke Snider .3425, Mays .3422. He went 3-for-4 and finished at .345.

As he left the Giants in 1955, Durocher pulled him into a small bathroom off the dugout and told him he was the best player he'd ever seen. "But you won't be here to help me," Mays said. "Willie Mays don't need help from anybody," Durocher answered, and kissed him on the cheek.
In 1947 he played briefly for the Chattanooga Choo-Choos, a farm team for the Birmingham Black Barons. His father introduced him to Black Barons manager Piper Davis when he turned 16.
His 11th-inning, bases-loaded single won Game 1 of the 1948 Negro American League playoffs against Kansas City. The Black Barons then lost the last Negro World Series to the Homestead Grays.

Roy Campanella begged the Dodgers to scout him, but Wid Matthews reported that "the kid can't hit the curveball." Giants scout Eddie Montague came to see first baseman Alonzo Perry, saw Mays instead, and signed him in the family's house for a $4,000 bonus and $250 a month. His father signed too, since Willie was a minor.
Monte Irvin was his rookie roommate and protector. He babysat Durocher's six-year-old son, Chris.

The Giants were losing money, so in 1972 he took a two-year, $330,000 contract instead of the 10-year deal he wanted. Mets owner Joan Payson traded for him and promised to retire his number, which the Mets finally did in 2022.

In 1976 the Mets canceled his 10-year contract, which still had six years at $50,000 to go. When he took a greeter's job at an Atlantic City casino in 1979, Bowie Kuhn banned him from baseball, even though he couldn't bet there and the casino didn't take sports bets.

Sudden collapses sent him to the hospital several times during his career. At the 1985 Pittsburgh drug trials John Milner testified that Mays kept liquid amphetamine in his Shea Stadium locker. Milner never saw him use it, and Mays denied it.
p: As a rookie he lived in a Harlem rooming house near the Polo Grounds and played stickball in the street with neighborhood kids at 9 a.m., then took them for sodas. On August 30, 1951, he hit two home runs against the Pirates and then homered in a stickball game that evening.

In Hagerstown in 1950, the first Black player in the Interstate League stayed in a Blacks-only hotel. Late that first night three white teammates climbed in through his window and slept on his floor until morning.

Home in Birmingham after winning Rookie of the Year, he sat down at the Woolworth counter where his Aunt Ernestine worked. "Junior, you know colored can't sit down at the counter in here," she told him.

In San Francisco in late 1957, neighbors pressured a seller to back out of selling him a house. The mayor apologized, and soon after they moved in someone threw a brick through a window. "They cheer Khrushchev and boo Mays," one columnist wrote.
Wilt Chamberlain gave him Mae Allen's phone number in 1961, and they married years later. When she developed Alzheimer's, Mays cared for her until her death in 2013.

His father, Cat, worked in the Westfield steel mills, and his mother, Anna, was a high school track and basketball star. She died in 1953 giving birth to her 11th child, long after she and Cat had split.
His parents never married and separated when he was 3. His father also worked as a railway porter.
In 1956 he became the third husband of Marghuerite Wendell Chapman. They adopted a five-day-old boy, Michael, in 1959, separated in 1962 and divorced in 1963, and she got Michael most of the time.
He was a special assistant with the Giants from 1986, signed a lifetime contract in 1993, and helped drum up support for Pac Bell Park.

c: How he joined the Homestead Grays, on July 25, 1930, may be legend. In a night game under the Kansas City Monarchs' dim portable lights, the Grays' catcher lost a pitch and broke a finger. Owner Cum Posey called the 18-year-old Gibson out of the stands to finish the game.

One drive in a 1937 Negro National League game at Yankee Stadium was said to hit the wall in front of the elevated tracks, about 580 feet out. A Chicago player swore another, in 1934, left the park entirely. Gibson himself always said he'd only reached the bullpen.
In Mexico in 1941 he hit .374 with 33 home runs and 124 RBIs in 94 games, with 75 walks and only 25 strikeouts. He nearly outhomered the league's second- and third-best hitters combined.

In 1943, while hiding a brain-tumor diagnosis (the papers called it a nervous breakdown), he hit .486. Playing part of the Grays' home schedule at Griffith Stadium, he hit more home runs over its left- and center-field walls than the whole American League did that year.

Walter Johnson said any big-league club would pay $200,000 for him: "He hits the ball a mile. He catches so easy he might as well be in a rocking chair. Throws like a rifle. Too bad this Gibson is a colored fellow."
His first uniformed team, at 16, was sponsored by Gimbels department store, which gave him a job as an elevator operator to keep him on it. Honus Wagner donated uniforms to his sandlot league.
On September 27, 1930, in a playoff game at Yankee Stadium, he hit a homer estimated at 430 to 460 feet into the left-field bleachers.
He played winter ball in Puerto Rico for Santurce for a reported $250 a month. Back home, the cash-strapped Crawfords had to sell him back to the Grays for $2,500 and two players.
He was the first manager of Santurce, one of Puerto Rico's most storied clubs.
He spent 10 days in a Pittsburgh hospital and was diagnosed with a brain tumor, which he kept from the public. He was reportedly relying more and more on alcohol and marijuana.
In 1944 he was held for mental observation at Gallinger Hospital in Washington.
Larry Doby thought he was the best Black player in 1945 and 1946, better than Jackie Robinson.
p: His father left a Georgia sharecropping life for a Pittsburgh steel job in 1923 and brought the family north three years later. Josh quit school at 15 to work at an airbrake plant. The Gimbels department store gave him an elevator job so he could keep playing on its team.

His wife, Helen, died in childbirth with twins in August 1930, when he was 18; he got to the hospital minutes before she died. Feeling unfit to raise them alone, he left the babies with her parents, and some say he never recovered from the loss.

"Next to hitting, I think he liked eating ice cream more than anything else in the world," said Ted Page. Monte Irvin said that for all the attention in hotels and bars, Josh never got a swelled head.

He died in January 1947 at 35, three months before Jackie Robinson's debut. His son hated the story that he died of a broken heart: "He was the last guy to brood about something he couldn't do nothin' about."
He was the oldest of three children. He studied to be an electrician in vocational school, and at 15 dropped out to work at an airbrake plant.

He met Helen Mason in 1928, and they married in March 1929, a month after she learned she was pregnant. The pregnancy aggravated an undiagnosed kidney condition, and one of her kidneys had ruptured by the time she reached the hospital.
His father, Mark, died in 1943, the year of his illness.
He died of a stroke in January 1947 and lay in an unmarked grave in Pittsburgh until 1975. Josh Jr. played for the Grays and helped start the Josh Gibson Foundation.

c: The nickname came from a 1988 batting-practice collision. The 6-foot-10 rookie ran head-first into Tim Raines, who said, "Damn! You're a big unit!"

Early in his career he was so wild that he led the majors in walks three straight years, and twice walked 10 in four innings. He credited a late-1992 session with Nolan Ryan and pitching coach Tom House with turning him around.

At the 1993 All-Star Game he threw a fastball over John Kruk's head. In 1997, facing Larry Walker, he did it again. Walker turned his helmet around and switched to the right side of the plate for a pitch.
In the 2001 World Series he threw a three-hit shutout in Game 2, won Game 6, and then came out of the bullpen the next night to win Game 7 against the Yankees.
On May 18, 2004, at 40, he threw a perfect game against Atlanta with 13 strikeouts. He was the oldest pitcher ever to do it.
He called his slider 'Mr. Snappy'. It came in in the low 90s and broke so late that right-handed hitters swung at pitches nearly hitting their back foot.
At USC he walked 104 batters in 1985, a school record. Montreal took him in the second round. In the minors he punched a bat rack in frustration and broke a bone in his non-throwing hand.
In May 1989 Montreal traded him to Seattle with Gene Harris and Brian Holman for Mark Langston. MLB.com later called it the biggest trade in Mariners history.
His father died of an aortic aneurysm on Christmas Day 1992, while Randy was on his way to see him. He told his mother he might quit, and she talked him out of it.
In 1993 Seattle nearly traded him to Toronto, and the Yankees tried to get him, but the Mariners gave him four years and $20.25 million.

A back injury cost him most of 1996. Upset that Seattle wouldn't extend him, he was traded to Houston in July 1998 for Freddy García, Carlos Guillén and John Halama. He signed with Arizona for four years and $52.4 million.

In a 2001 spring training game his fastball hit and killed a dove in midair. That July, after a game was stopped by electrical explosions, he came in the next day and struck out 16 in seven innings of relief.
Arizona traded him to the Yankees in January 2005. He struggled in two ALDS starts, and in January 2007 they traded him back so he could be near his family after his brother's death.
p: As a junior at Livermore High he was cut from the basketball team for failing to run a six-minute mile. As a senior he threw a perfect game in his last start.
When Montreal sent him down in 1989 he said, "I'm too old to cry, but that's what I feel like doing." He had been looking forward to pitching in front of his family on an upcoming West Coast trip.
When the Diamondbacks retired his number in 2015 they gave the lifelong drummer a replica of the drum kit Neil Peart used on Rush's 30th-anniversary tour. He has since photographed a Rush tour.
He has made more than 40 USO trips to visit troops.
He has a daughter born in 1989 from an earlier relationship, and four children with his wife. He lives in Paradise Valley, Arizona, and supports efforts to fight homelessness.

c: At 17 he was a skinny, weak-hitting shortstop who made 45 errors in Class D and begged, "Won't somebody teach me how to hit?" The Cardinals' only scout liked how he fielded bad hops so much that he bought him new spikes and a glove with his own money.

After his 1915 call-up Miller Huggins told him, "Kid, you're a little light… I think I'll farm you out." Hornsby took it literally. He spent the winter on his uncle's Texas farm eating steak and fried chicken and drinking all the milk he could, and came back 30 pounds heavier.
In 1924 he hit .424, the best average of the modern era. He was held hitless in only 24 of 143 games and never more than two in a row. In August he hit .509.

As player-manager he won the 1926 World Series and made the last play himself: Babe Ruth, trying to steal with two outs in the ninth of Game 7, was thrown out at second, and Hornsby made the tag. He called it the biggest thrill of his career. The Cardinals traded him two months later.
Near the end of the 1928 batting race, Paul Waner said, "Well, Rog. It looks like you're gonna beat me." Hornsby scowled: "You didn't doubt for a minute that I would, did you?"
Asked what he did in the offseason, he said, "I stare out the window and wait for spring."

A Texas League club, the Steers, signed him and cut him two weeks into the season without his getting off the bench. He took a bus to Hugo, Oklahoma, made the Class D team for $75 a month, and was sold to Denison for $125 when Hugo folded. The Cardinals bought him for $600.
In 1918 he loudly said he'd never play for manager Hendricks again, then took a war job at a shipyard in Wilmington, Delaware.

In 1923 the Cardinals said he was faking an injury, fined him $500 and suspended him. Branch Rickey, usually mild, twice charged and swung at him after a game. Brooklyn offered $275,000 for him that winter, and Sam Breadon said no.
In 1924 he hit .486 in July and August and .509 in August alone. He beat Bo McMillin, his old high school teammate and a pro football star, in a footrace at Sportsman's Park.

Gambling losses kept him from retiring. He managed in the minors, in Mexico for Veracruz, and in the Texas League. Commissioner Landis was rumored to have blackballed him from the majors over his gambling.
Most of his players disliked him because he wanted them to live the way he did. By one account he lost a managing job for placing a bet during a game.
p: At 16 he answered a newspaper ad and toured North Texas with the Boston Bloomer Girls, a traveling women's team. He had to wear a wig and bloomers and pass as a girl.

He never drank or smoked and slept 12 hours a night. He wouldn't read anything but the sports pages or go to the movies, to save his eyes. He sat in hotel lobbies for hours just watching people. He tried golf once, shot 39 for nine holes, and never played again.
His mother died just before the 1926 World Series. She had asked that nothing keep him from playing, so the funeral waited until the Series was over.

Gambling on horses followed him all his life. A bookie's suit claiming he owed more than $70,000 helped get him shipped out of New York, and he lost so much that he couldn't afford to retire when his playing days ended.
He was the youngest child. His father died when he was 2. He played on Swift & Company's team as a boy and left high school to work full-time at Swift.

He married Sarah Martin, whom he met in Denison, in 1918, and they had a son, Rogers Jr. In 1922 he began seeing Jeannette Pennington Hine, a married woman. Her husband sued him for alienation of affection and Sarah sued for divorce. He paid Sarah $25,000 to publicly clear him of the affair.
He married Jeannette in 1924, and they had a son, Billy, who played in the minors. Rogers Jr. died in a plane crash in 1949.

He and Jeannette separated in 1944. He then lived with Bernadette Harris, his "personal good friend and secretary," who killed herself by jumping from a third-floor window in 1953. After Jeannette died he married Marjorie Porter in 1957. He died of a heart attack in 1963.

c: Yankee scout Tom Greenwade came to Baxter Springs to look at a teammate. The 16-year-old shortstop hit two home runs, one from each side, and both landed in a creek beyond the fence.

Sent down to Kansas City in 1951, he called home saying he wanted to quit. His father drove up, started packing his bag and said, "I thought I raised a man, not a coward!" Mickey broke down and stayed. He hit .361 and was back in New York within weeks, now wearing number 7.

In the 1951 World Series he pulled up on a fly ball when DiMaggio called for it, caught his spikes on a drain cover and tore up his knee. Helping him into a cab, his father collapsed. They shared a hospital room for the rest of the Series. Mickey needed surgery; his father had Hodgkin's disease and was dead within months.

On April 17, 1953, at Griffith Stadium, he hit a ball off Chuck Stobbs that clipped the 'Mr. Boh' beer sign behind the left-field bleachers and landed beyond the houses across Fifth Street. Estimates ranged from 540 to 565 feet.

In September 1968, with the pennant clinched, Denny McLain grooved two pitches for him and then shouted, "Where the hell do you want it?" Mantle pointed and hit the next one for his 535th home run, passing Jimmie Foxx.

On May 22, 1963, he hit a Bill Fischer fastball off the right-field facade at Yankee Stadium, two feet from the top. He called it the hardest ball he ever hit. Fischer said it was still rising "like a jet taking off."
Greenwade signed him the spring he graduated from high school, with a $1,100 bonus and $400 for the rest of the season, for the Class D team in Independence, Kansas.
When he came back from Kansas City in 1951 he was given No. 7, which he wore for the next 18 years.

A former medical director of the NFL players' union later guessed that he tore his ACL in the 1951 Series and played the rest of his career without it properly fixed. The 1953 surgery took out torn cartilage but left the knee unstable, and teammates saw his gait change and his speed fade. A shoulder injury in the 1957 Series made hitting left-handed harder for the rest of his career.
A hamstring pull limited him to three games of the 1955 World Series. George Weiss nearly doubled his salary for 1956, from $17,000 to $33,000.
He retired third on the all-time home run list with 536. He coached first base and hitting for the Yankees for a few weeks in 1970, hated it, and quit.

In 1983 he took a job as a greeter at the Claridge casino in Atlantic City, and Bowie Kuhn suspended him from baseball, as he had Willie Mays. Mantle called the rule "stupid." Both were later reinstated.
p: His father named him after Mickey Cochrane without knowing Cochrane's real name was Gordon. "I would have hated to be named Gordon," Mantle said.
At 14 a football kick led to osteomyelitis, and doctors wanted to amputate his leg. His parents took him to Oklahoma City, where a new drug, penicillin, saved it.
Cancer killed his father, his grandfather and two uncles young, and he was sure he would die young too. He said that fear drove much of his drinking.
He brought old teammates along to card shows, where they made good money just sitting beside him. Late in life he made more from signing baseballs than he ever had hitting them.
Sober after the Betty Ford clinic in 1993 and dying of liver cancer in 1995, he told fans who had looked up to him: "This is a role model: Don't be like me."
His father, Mutt, was a former semipro player who worked in the lead and zinc mines. His uncle, his grandfather and other relatives all died of cancer in their 40s or younger.

He married Merlyn Johnson in December 1951. He said he did it not out of love but because his dying father told him to. They had four sons: Mickey Jr., David, Billy, named for Billy Martin, and Danny.

The press kept quiet about his cheating, but he didn't hide it: he brought his mistress to his 1969 retirement ceremony along with his wife. He and Merlyn separated in 1980 and never divorced, and they made peace before he died. His last decade he lived with his agent, Greer Johnson, and his family later sued to stop her auctioning his things.
His Country Cookin' restaurant chain failed. His Mickey Mantle's Restaurant & Sports Bar in New York, opened in 1988, was a success.

He had cirrhosis, hepatitis C and liver cancer, and his one-day wait for a transplant in 1995 drew charges of favoritism. The cancer spread quickly, and he died that August at 63, with Merlyn and David at his side.

c: In 1907, pitching semipro ball in Weiser, Idaho, he threw 77 straight scoreless innings, including back-to-back no-hitters. Before he'd sign with Washington he wired his parents for permission and demanded a train ticket home in case he failed. Weiser fans offered to set him up with a cigar store if he stayed.
Over Labor Day weekend 1908 the Senators' staff was in shambles, so he started three games in four days in New York. He shut out the Highlanders all three times, on six, four and two hits.
His teams were so weak that he holds the records for both 1–0 wins (38) and 1–0 losses (26). In 1910–19 Washington was 265–143 when he got the decision and 490–594 when anyone else did.

Game 7 of the 1924 World Series: Bucky Harris brought him in for the ninth of a tied game. "You're the best we've got, Walter. We've got to win or lose with you." He held the Giants for four innings, twice striking out George Kelly after an intentional walk. Washington won its only title in the 12th when a grounder hit a pebble and bounced over the third baseman's head.
In 1925 he hit .433, a record for a pitcher.
Ring Lardner on his sidearm fastball: "He's got a gun concealed on his person. They can't tell me he throws them balls with his arm."
Working on the farm and in the oil fields built his 6-foot-1 frame. A former teammate got him a job with Tacoma in 1906, but he was released after one exhibition.
In Weiser he also worked for the telephone company. Catcher-scout Cliff Blankenship signed him for Washington in July 1907, at 19.
Weiser fans offered to set him up with a cigar store on the town square if he stayed.
He didn't develop a good curve until around 1913. In 1918 the government's "work or fight" order ended the season on Labor Day with the Senators four games out.
In 1920 a bad cold, a sore arm and pulled leg muscles ended his streak of 20-win seasons.
He lost Game 1 of the 1924 Series 4–3 in 12 innings and Game 5 before his relief win in Game 7. In 1925 he won two early games and then lost Game 7.

After the 1924 Series he tried and failed to buy a Pacific Coast League team. He managed Newark for a year, then the Senators from 1929 to 1932 and Cleveland from 1933 to 1935, where the local press attacked him constantly.
Ty Cobb figured out that the good-hearted Johnson was privately afraid of seriously hurting a batter, and used it against him.
He was called "Barney" after racer Barney Oldfield, because he once got out of a speeding ticket when a teammate told the officer he was Oldfield.
p: Leaving Weiser at 19, he had tears in his eyes at the depot. "You know how you are at 19. You want to see things."
He met Hazel Roberts, daughter of Nevada's congressman, in 1913, and their romance became the talk of Washington society. The Senate chaplain married them in June 1914.
1921 brought his father's death in July and the death of his two-year-old daughter, Elinor, from influenza in December. He and Hazel sold their Kansas farm and moved east.

Hazel died in August 1930 at 36, apparently worn out by a cross-country drive in a record heat wave. A melancholy settled over the rest of his life. He later served as a county commissioner and ran for Congress as a Republican, and lost.
Ty Cobb, of all people, was a good friend, and often brought the Johnson children gifts when he visited.
He was the second of six children. Drought forced his father off their 160-acre Kansas farm, and the family moved to Humboldt and later to California, around Olinda.
He was never in a brawl and didn't go to saloons. He and Hazel had six children, five of whom lived to adulthood.
He was a Montgomery County commissioner, the Senators' radio announcer in 1939, and a Republican candidate for Congress, but lost.
He died of a brain tumor in 1946, at 59, and was buried next to Hazel in Rockville, Maryland. In 2024 one of his jerseys sold for $2.01 million.

c: Two weeks before he turned 12 he was sent to the Alabama reform school for stealing and skipping school. Coach Edward Byrd taught him the high leg kick and the long reach toward the batter. "You might say I traded five years of freedom to learn how to pitch."

He kept his own records in a notebook: more than 2,500 games, about 2,000 wins, 250 teams, and his own share of the gate. His count of no-hitters ran from 20 to 100 to "so many… I disremember the number."

Cleveland signed him on his 42nd birthday in July 1948. He went 6–1 with a 2.48 ERA for the pennant winner, and some writers voted for him as Rookie of the Year. He said he would have turned it down, since he "wasn't sure what year the gentlemen had in mind."

In 1965, at 59, he started for the Kansas City A's and shut out the Red Sox for three innings on 28 pitches. The only hit was a double by Carl Yastrzemski, whose father had faced Paige in a semipro game on Long Island a generation earlier.
On barnstorming tours he would sometimes call in his infielders, have them sit down behind him, and strike out the side.
The Chattanooga White Sox paid his mother a $200 advance in 1926, and in 1927 sold him to the Birmingham Black Barons.

After his fastball hit a St. Louis Stars batter on the hand, the man charged the mound and threw his bat, hitting Paige above the hip as he ran for the dugout. Police were called, and the paper called it a "Near Riot."
In Cuba he was homesick, hated the food and couldn't drink because of the gambling on games, and went 6–5.
Playing for a team in Bismarck, North Dakota, he went 35–2 over two seasons. He claimed he never hit below .300 in a season; he actually hit .218 in the Negro leagues and .097 in the majors.
He was 28–31 in the majors, with Cleveland, the St. Louis Browns and Kansas City.
In 1948 he became the first Negro league player to pitch in a World Series, and the Indians won it.
After his playing days he was an assistant trainer and, in 1973, pitching coach for the Tulsa Oilers.
p: The nickname came from his job at Mobile's train station. He rigged a pole and rope so he could carry four bags at once, and another boy yelled, "You look like a walking satchel tree." (A childhood friend told a less flattering version.)
His family changed the spelling of Page to Paige. His mother said Page looked too much like a page in a book. Satchel said they added the "i" to sound more high-tone.
His first wife served him divorce papers as he walked onto the field at Wrigley Field.
He played a cavalry sergeant opposite Robert Mitchum in the 1959 western The Wonderful Country.

At his last public appearance, in June 1982, Kansas City named a run-down ballpark for him. On oxygen in a wheelchair, he said, "I've been in Kansas City 46 years and I can walk down the street and people don't know me." He died three days later during a power outage, and a fallen tree delayed the paramedics.
He was born at home with a midwife. His mother, Lula, was a washerwoman with six children already. As a boy he collected empty bottles in the alleys and stole suitcases at the train station.
He was released from reform school in December 1923. The family changed the spelling to Paige around the time his father died.

He married Janet Howard in 1934, and they separated a few years later. In 1940 in Puerto Rico he married Lucy Figueroa, but he wasn't divorced yet, so it wasn't legal. His divorce from Janet was finalized in 1943 for $1,500 plus her lawyer's fees.
In 1946 or 1947 he married LaHoma Brown. They raised seven children in Kansas City, plus her daughter from an earlier marriage.
A few days after his last public appearance the power went out at his house. His daughters called paramedics, who were held up by a fallen tree, and he died of a heart attack.
Louis Gossett Jr. played him in the 1981 TV movie Don't Look Back.

c: Louisville's owner and manager weren't impressed by the bow-legged, barrel-chested kid Ed Barrow pushed on them in 1897. Club secretary Harry Pulliam talked them into it anyway.

He played every position but catcher before settling at shortstop in 1903, and he only took it because Fred Clarke had Tommy Leach talk him into swapping. In two stints on the mound he allowed no earned runs, which gives him the lowest ERA of anyone in the Hall of Fame: 0.00.

He hollowed out his small glove, cutting a hole in the palm and pulling out the stuffing. When Clarke complained that he took his time throwing to first on close plays, Wagner said he'd change when he stopped throwing runners out.

The 1903 Series haunted him: 1-for-14 in the last four games, six errors, and the final out on a called third strike. Boston writers hinted he was 'yellow'. He made up for it in 1909, outhitting Ty Cobb and stealing six bases to win the World Series.

The story of him bloodying Cobb's mouth with a tag in the 1909 Series is probably folklore: the throw was low and late, and a month later Wagner went hunting with Cobb in Georgia. Wagner never said it happened and never said it didn't.
In 1911 he won the batting title by a point, .334 to .333. It took a successful Cubs protest that wiped out a game in which he'd gone hitless.
Three of his brothers also played professionally. His mother called him Hans, which became Honus.
In 1902 Pittsburgh moved him to right field when Wid Conroy took over at short, but Conroy turned out to be an American League spy and was released.
He hated spring training and often held out to avoid it. After he talked of taking a year off, Barney Dreyfuss doubled his salary to $10,000, the most in the game for several years.

In 1910 he slumped and fielded lazily. The Pirates blamed an injury, a cold or a slump, but the open secret was his out-of-control drinking. He was ejected and suspended several times and had ugly run-ins with teammates, and Fred Clarke had a long talk with him after the season.
In 1915 he became the oldest player to hit a grand slam, a record that lasted 70 years. He was briefly interim manager of the Pirates, went 1–4, and told Dreyfuss the job wasn't for him.
He coached the Pirates for years and helped at Carnegie Tech in baseball and basketball. He wore No. 14 as a coach before switching to the No. 33 the team later retired.
p: He quit school at 12 to work in the coal mines with his father and brothers, and trained as a barber before baseball took over.

He stopped the famous T206 card in 1910. He didn't want kids buying cigarettes to get his picture, and he sent the club secretary a check for the $10 he would have made on the deal. Because so few got out, it became the most valuable card ever.
He married Bessie Smith on the last day of 1916. Their first child was stillborn. He called his two daughters "my boys" and taught them to play ball.

Broke in the Depression, he was rescued by a coaching job with the Pirates in 1933. He turned Arky Vaughan into a shortstop and told tall tales, like the grounder he scooped up along with a rabbit and threw to first, nipping the runner by a "hare".
At the unveiling of his statue outside Forbes Field in April 1955 he was too weak to get out of the car. He waved and left before the ceremony ended, and died that December.
He was one of nine children of German immigrants in western Pennsylvania coal country.

His sporting-goods store struggled because he had little business sense and some bad partners, though a store with his name ran in downtown Pittsburgh for 93 years. He ran for Allegheny County sheriff in 1928 and lost, and became a deputy sheriff in 1942.
His daughter Betty married Harry Blair, and their daughter Leslie Ann, his only grandchild, called him "Buck Jay." He read to her and slipped her Hershey bars.
He died in his Carnegie home in December 1955, less than an hour after Betty's birthday ended.

c: His first big-league manager, Solly Hemus, told him he'd never make it, used him rarely, and kept calling him Bridges after a different Black pitcher. When Johnny Keane replaced Hemus in July 1961, Gibson called it Independence Day for the Cardinals' Black players.

In Game 7 of the 1964 World Series Keane left an exhausted Gibson in to finish the Yankees. "I was committed to this fellow's heart," he explained. In the clubhouse he told Gibson, "Hoot, you're on your way. Nothing can stop you now."

After catching him in the 1965 All-Star Game, Joe Torre complimented him in the shower. Gibson didn't say a word; he showered, dressed and left. He wouldn't fraternize with opponents even as All-Star teammates.
In 1968 he posted a 1.12 ERA with 13 shutouts and struck out 17 Tigers in Game 1 of the World Series, still a Series record. Baseball lowered the mound the next year.
He threw his only no-hitter on August 14, 1971, at Pittsburgh. In 1974 he became the first National League pitcher to reach 3,000 strikeouts.

Cardinals scout Runt Marr offered him a small contract out of high school, but his brother Josh insisted on college. At Creighton his baseball coach was future NBA coach Bill Fitch, and he caught, pitched and played third and the outfield.
He signed with the Cardinals for a $3,000 bonus on the condition that he could tour with the Globetrotters after the season.
Solly Hemus once told the team he had called a Pirates pitcher a "black son-of-a-bitch," which settled any doubt about his attitude toward his Black players.

A broken ankle in batting practice cut one season short. On July 15, 1967, a line drive broke his leg; he pitched to three more batters before it snapped. He came back and won three complete games in the 1967 World Series, and was Series MVP again.

After he retired the Cardinals offered him a vague job that was never approved, and never offered another. Joe Torre hired him as an "attitude coach" with the Mets in 1981 and as pitching coach with the Braves and later the Cardinals.
p: His father died of tuberculosis before he was born. He had rickets as a child and was raised in an Omaha housing project, and his brother Josh, 15 years older, was his coach, teacher and father figure.

He wasn't allowed to try out for his high-school baseball team as a junior. He learned later that the coach didn't allow Black players. Indiana turned down his basketball application because it 'already had its quota of Negroes'. He went to Creighton instead, where his basketball number is retired.
The Harlem Globetrotters recruited him the day after his wedding, and he toured with them for four months before choosing baseball.

As a young Cardinal, Tim McCarver of Memphis got on the team bus with an ice-cream cone, and Gibson asked for a lick. McCarver fumbled and said he'd save him some. Gibson's aim was to make white teammates face their prejudices. The two became good friends.

His eyesight was so bad that McCarver painted his fingernails so Gibson could see the signs; he never pitched in glasses. He lived in Omaha all his career, partly because housing discrimination made it so hard to buy a home in St. Louis.
He was the youngest of seven. His mother worked in a laundry and cleaned houses.
He was named Pack after his father, who died three months before he was born, but he disliked the name and later legally dropped it.
He had two children, Ray and Annette, with his first wife, Charline, and a son, Christopher, with his second wife, Wendy.
He stayed in Omaha partly because housing discrimination made it hard for him to buy a house in St. Louis. He ran Gibson's Spirits and Sustenance, sometimes working 12-hour days.
In 2002 he got into a fistfight at a gas station after a road-rage incident, and both men were cited for third-degree assault.
He was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in 2019 and died in hospice in October 2020, at 84.

c: At 5-foot-7 and 140 pounds, he was the star of his Oakland high school team, but scouts came to see the pitcher. Nobody offered him a bonus or even a college scholarship. Houston finally signed him out of junior college for $3,000.

In his first game in Durham in 1963, the only Black player on the team, he could hear the slurs from the stands during warm-ups. Billy Goodman sent him up to pinch-hit in the ninth, and he hit a game-winning home run. He nearly quit soon after, but couldn't face telling his father.
Nellie Fox, an Astros teammate, told him to flap his back elbow like a chicken to keep it up. The flap became his trademark.

In April 1975 he slowed up on purpose going into third on a wild pitch to draw a throw. It went into left field and he scored the winning run. He told reporters, "I was hoping Hill would do just what he did." The Giants were furious.
He won the 1975 World Series with a single in the ninth inning of Game 7, and won a second straight MVP in 1976. Sparky Anderson called him the smartest player he ever coached.
He enrolled at Oakland City College in 1961. Houston's Bill Wight signed him in November 1962 for $500 a month and a $3,000 bonus.
In Winston-Salem he couldn't stay in his white teammates' motel and saw Black fans fenced into a cage-like section in right field. Billy Goodman also taught him not to swing at the first pitch.
A torn knee ligament cost him all but 10 games of 1968.
Even after his World Series titles and MVPs with the Reds, he said his debut for Houston was the highlight of his career.

In November 1971 Houston traded him, Cesar Geronimo, Jack Billingham, Ed Armbrister and Denis Menke to Cincinnati for Lee May, Tommy Helms and Jimmy Stewart. Sparky Anderson gave him the locker next to Pete Rose.
He hit .125 in the 1972 World Series loss to Oakland, and went 2-for-20 when the Mets upset the Reds in the 1973 NLCS.

He went back to Houston as a free agent in 1980 and helped the Astros win the West, then played for the Giants and the "Wheeze Kids" Phillies. His homer in Game 1 of the 1983 World Series made him the second-oldest player to hit one in a Series.
He broadcast for the Reds, Giants, ABC, NBC and ESPN, and was vice chairman of the Hall of Fame's board from 2000 until his death.
p: He believed Houston manager Harry Walker, who called him a troublemaker, was a racist. Walker had him traded to Cincinnati in 1971, a trade Morgan hated at first and which made his career.
In 1990 he finished his college degree at Cal State Hayward, keeping a promise he had made to his mother 27 years earlier.
In 1988 undercover police at LAX took him for a drug courier and threw him to the floor. "I was just another black man," he wrote. He sued the LAPD and won a settlement.
After his playing days he ran Wendy's franchises and a Coors distributorship, and spent 21 years calling Sunday Night Baseball with Jon Miller. He was an ardent jazz fan.
He was the oldest of six. When he was 5 the family moved to Oakland, where his father and several relatives worked for Pacific Tire and Rubber.
He married his high school girlfriend, Gloria Stewart, in 1967, and they settled in Houston. Their second daughter, Angela, was on the way when he was traded.
He and Gloria divorced in the 1980s, and he married Theresa Behymer in 1990.
In 2015 he was diagnosed with myelodysplastic syndrome, which became leukemia, and one of his daughters gave him a bone marrow transplant. He died at home in Danville, California, in 2020.

c: He wanted to go straight from high school to the majors. Nippon-Ham drafted him anyway and won him over by promising he could both pitch and hit. The Dodgers, his favorite MLB team, wouldn't.

His first spring training in 2018 was a disaster, with a 27.00 ERA against big leaguers and a .125 average, and many writers said he belonged in Triple-A. In his second start he took a perfect game into the seventh inning and struck out 12. He won Rookie of the Year.
In the 2023 World Baseball Classic final he came in to close and struck out his Angels teammate Mike Trout on a full-count slider to win the title for Japan.
On August 23, 2024, he stole a base and then hit his first walk-off homer, a grand slam, to reach 40 home runs and 40 steals faster than anyone ever had. He finished at 50–50.
In Game 4 of the 2025 NLCS he hit three home runs and threw six shutout innings with 10 strikeouts.
The Dodgers were thought to be his preferred team out of high school, but they wouldn't let him both pitch and hit. Nippon-Ham gave him Yu Darvish's old No. 11.
As an 18-year-old rookie he sprained an ankle and broke a cheekbone.

In his second big-league start, in April 2018, he took a perfect game into the seventh and struck out 12. That June he sprained his elbow ligament and was treated with platelet-rich plasma and stem-cell injections.
He came back from Tommy John surgery as a hitter in May 2019, then needed knee surgery that September. The injuries of 2019 and 2020 left him feeling "frustrated" and "useless."

After a second elbow surgery in September 2023, he signed with the Dodgers for 10 years and $700 million, then the biggest contract in pro sports. He couldn't pitch in 2024, but became the first 50–50 player and won the World Series in his first postseason.
His endorsements were estimated at $100 million in 2025, and he's an ambassador for about 20 companies.
p: His mother was a national-level badminton player and his father played industrial-league ball and coached him. As a seventh-grader he recorded all but one of the 18 outs in a regional championship game.
At Hanamaki Higashi, players lived on campus and went home six days a year. His coach assigned him to clean toilets to teach him humility.

His dog Dekopin ("Decoy") got an honorary visa from the U.S. embassy in Tokyo. When he announced his marriage in 2024 he said only that his wife was "a normal Japanese woman" before revealing it was former basketball player Mamiko Tanaka.
In 2024 his longtime interpreter and friend Ippei Mizuhara was found to have taken millions from Ohtani's account to pay gambling debts.
He is the youngest of three. His father worked at a car plant. His high school coach said he swam fast enough to have gone to the Olympics.
In Japan he lived in the team dormitory for five years and his parents handled his money.

His wife is Mamiko Tanaka, a former professional basketball player. Their daughter was born in April 2025, and a second child in June 2026. He bought a $7.85 million house through an LLC named after his dog.

Mizuhara, who had known him since he was 18, was his interpreter, confidant, conditioning coach and throwing partner. He stole more than $16 million by impersonating Ohtani with the bank and also bought $325,000 in baseball cards on his account. He pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to 57 months and ordered to repay $17 million.

c: Connie Mack had him debut in 1906 under the name "Eddie T. Sullivan" to protect his Columbia eligibility. He got a bunt single off Ed Walsh in his first at-bat. Columbia ruled him ineligible anyway, for semipro games, and made him an undergraduate assistant coach instead.
He believed a runner steals off the pitcher, not the catcher. He studied pitchers' feet and hips rather than their hands, and stole 741 bases without being especially fast.

In 1912 a hard tag by Collins broke Chick Gandil's nose, and Gandil spent years trying to get even. Later they were White Sox teammates, and Gandil's grudge helped split the 1919 club before the World Series fix.

He scored the run that won the 1917 World Series by dashing home in a rundown when nobody covered the plate, with Heinie Zimmerman chasing him in vain. "In a World's Series game, when you see a base uncovered you run for it."

As captain of the 1919 White Sox he said the club "pulled apart rather than together," yet called it the greatest collection of players ever assembled. His accounts of what he knew about the fix changed over the years.
Before signing he got Connie Mack's written promise that he wouldn't be sent to the minors without his consent. John McGraw had heard of him but didn't offer a tryout.
Columbia made him an undergraduate assistant coach for 1907.
He wrote magazine articles, and some A's players complained that other teams used them to fix the weaknesses he pointed out.
He hit .421 in the 1913 World Series. Chicago paid him $15,000 a year plus a $10,000 bonus, and by 1919 he still made more than double any teammate.

After the 1914 upset, Mack offered him a five-year guaranteed deal, the longest ever offered, but then sold him to the White Sox for $50,000, the most ever paid for a player and the first sale of a reigning MVP.
Players resented owner Comiskey's stinginess and Collins's privileged status, and Chick Gandil turned that against him.

In 1920 a gamblers' paper quoted him as saying he knew from the first inning of the 1919 Series that games were being thrown, and that he told Comiskey, which Comiskey always denied. He later changed his story.
He hit .226 in the 1919 Series but was never accused of being in on it.
He managed the White Sox from 1924 to 1926 and was fired and released two days apart. He finished in Philadelphia, mostly coaching, and played his last game at 43.
He won six World Series, though he didn't play in the last two. As Red Sox GM for 15 years he signed Joe Cronin, Ted Williams and Bobby Doerr.
p: Despite the Ivy League polish he was deeply superstitious. He parked his gum on his cap button until he had two strikes, went out of his way to avoid black cats, counted hairpins as base hits, and liked to have someone spit on his cap before a game.
Connie Mack introduced him to his wife, Mabel Doane, and the two men bet on who would marry first. Mack won by a week.
As Red Sox general manager he signed Bobby Doerr and Ted Williams on one California trip. He also oversaw the sham 1945 tryout of Jackie Robinson, and Boston became the last team to integrate.
His father was a railroad freight agent. At 135 pounds he quarterbacked Columbia's freshman team and one varsity season before the school dropped football.
His World War I service was mostly drilling and guard duty at the Philadelphia Navy Yard, and he was discharged in time for 1919 spring training.
Mabel died in 1943. Their son Eddie Jr. played outfield for Yale and briefly for the A's, and later worked for the Phillies.
He died of a heart condition in Boston in 1951, at 63, and the Red Sox hung a plaque in his honor outside Fenway.

c: In his first big-league at-bat, August 13, 2016, he homered. So had Tyler Austin, the batter before him, also in his debut. It was the first time two teammates had done that in the same game.
Through his 2017 rookie season he kept a note on his phone reading ".179", his average in 2016, and looked at it every day.

Before 2022 he turned down a seven-year, $213.5 million extension and bet on himself with a one-year deal. He broke Roger Maris's American League record with 62 home runs, won the MVP, and signed for nine years and $360 million.
In June 2023 he crashed through a closed gate in the outfield wall at Dodger Stadium making a catch, sprained his toe, and missed 42 games.
He hit .500 with seven homers to win his high school league's Triple Crown, and went 6–0 with a 0.88 ERA on the mound.
The Yankees took him 32nd in 2013 with a pick they got for losing Nick Swisher, and gave him a $1.8 million bonus. He tore a quadriceps muscle in a baserunning drill and missed all of 2013.

As a rookie in 2017 he broke DiMaggio's Yankees rookie record with his 30th homer, struck out in 33 straight games, set an ALDS record with 16 strikeouts and a postseason record with 27, and had shoulder surgery afterward.
In 2018 he fractured a bone in his wrist and missed nearly two months. In 2020 he had a stress fracture in his ribs and strained his calf twice.

He hit .063 as Houston swept the Yankees in the 2022 ALCS. That winter he turned down the Padres and Giants to re-sign for nine years and $360 million, then a free-agent record, and was named captain.

In his first World Series, in 2024, he went 1-for-12 in the first three games. In Game 5 he hit his first Series homer, but a string of defensive mistakes, including his first error of the year, let a 5–0 lead slip away, and the Yankees lost the Series.
p: He was adopted the day after he was born by two Linden, California, teachers. In high school he was league MVP in baseball, football and basketball, and Notre Dame, Stanford and UCLA recruited him as a tight end.
Before every home game he tosses 40 sunflower seeds onto the grass behind the plate, one for each man on the extended roster, and says a private prayer.
He married his high school classmate, who also went to Fresno State with him, in Maui in 2021. His mother runs his All Rise Foundation.
He won the Roberto Clemente Award in 2023. He and his wife had their first child in January 2025.

c: Boston didn't even send him a 1908 contract. He begged John McGraw for a chance twice, then paid his own way to the Red Sox camp in Little Rock. The Red Sox left him there as payment for the use of the field, with the right to buy him back for $500. He led the league and they did.

As a rookie, Cy Young hit him fly balls to teach him to judge direction and distance. He played so shallow that he made two unassisted double plays at second base in April 1918. "I could save more games by cutting off some of those singles than I would lose by having an occasional extra-base hit go over my head."
In the deciding game of the 1912 World Series his easy foul pop fell untouched between the Giants' Fred Merkle and Chief Meyers. Given another chance in the 10th inning, he singled in the tying run.

After the 1915 title the Red Sox president tried to cut his salary in half. When he held out he was traded to Cleveland. His first time back at Fenway in an Indians uniform, he headed to the Red Sox dugout at the end of an inning.
He took over as player-manager and won the 1920 World Series after shortstop Ray Chapman was killed by a pitch. He was one of the first managers to platoon heavily.
Asked in 1939 whether DiMaggio was his successor: "HIM? I could name 15 better outfielders!" In 1947 Bill Veeck brought him back to teach Larry Doby to play center field.
In 1906 he wrote to several pro teams for a tryout and signed with Cleburne of the Texas League for $50 a month. The Red Sox bought him after 1907.

After spring training in 1908 Boston gave his contract to Little Rock as rent for the training field, with the right to buy him back for $500. Pittsburgh, Brooklyn, Washington and the Giants all showed interest, but Little Rock sold him back to Boston.
His nickname "Spoke" came from his teammate and rival Bill Carrigan, who yelled "Speaker spoke!" when he got a hit.

In 1914 the Red Sox raised his pay to about $18,000, more than Ty Cobb made, to keep him from taking the Federal League's offer of $100,000 for three years. After the 1915 title they tried to halve it, and when he held out they traded him to Cleveland for two players and $55,000.
After the 1926 season Dutch Leonard accused him and Cobb of fixing a game in 1919. Landis cleared them both, but Ban Johnson, who believed they were guilty, had already persuaded both to resign.
He played for Washington in 1927, then managed Newark in 1929 and 1930. He broadcast for the Cubs and White Sox and was a part owner and manager of the Kansas City Blues, which didn't pay off.
p: He was a natural right-hander but taught himself to throw left-handed after breaking his right arm twice when thrown from a bronco. He could bulldog a steer, and he taught Will Rogers to use a lariat.
His mother opposed his going to the major leagues, saying they reminded her of slavery. For years afterward she asked why he hadn't stayed home.

The Red Sox clubhouse split along religious lines, with Speaker among the Protestants against the Irish Catholics, and he brawled with catcher Bill Carrigan. Writer Fred Lieb said Speaker once told him he had joined the Ku Klux Klan.

He died of a heart attack in 1958 while pulling his boat onto the dock after an afternoon of fishing. Afterward Cobb said, "I never let him know how much I admired him when we were playing against each other."
His father, whose two older brothers fought for the Confederacy, was in the dry-goods business and died when Tris was 10. He taught Will Rogers to use a lariat.
The Red Sox clubhouse split by religion, and he often wasn't speaking to Duffy Lewis, an Irish Catholic. He never forgave Babe Ruth for crossing his friend Joe Wood.
Writer Fred Lieb said Speaker once told him he belonged to the Ku Klux Klan. The Klan's national leader, Hiram Evans, lived near him in Hubbard.

In 2008 Marvin Miller argued that Speaker should be removed from the Hall of Fame over his alleged Klan membership. Bill James didn't dispute the claim, but noted the 1920s Klan had pulled in hundreds of thousands of men.
In 1925 he married Mary Frances Cuddihy of Buffalo. They kept boxes at League Park and Municipal Stadium in Cleveland.
In 1937 he fractured his skull and broke his left arm in a 16-foot fall from a second-story porch at his home. He later had a near-fatal perforated intestine and a heart ailment in 1954.

Later he sold wholesale liquor and was a state sales rep for a steel company. He was credited with reforming Cleveland boxing, bringing in new officials, guarding against fixes and making sure fighters got paid rather than their managers. He helped found the city's Society for Crippled Children.

c: His minor-league manager Tom Trebelhorn sat up nights watching film of Lou Brock and Ty Cobb with him and let him run whenever he liked. In Class A in 1977 he stole 95 bases.
Most base stealers study a pitcher's pickoff move. Henderson studied the move to the plate, so he could tell the instant the pitcher committed.

When Dave Henderson joined him in Oakland, both answered to "Hendu." Dave proposed that whoever homered first got the name. Rickey hit a leadoff homer in his next at-bat and circled the bases yelling "I'm Hendu! I'm Hendu!"
In the 1989 World Series, with Rickey on first, Giants catcher Terry Kennedy muttered, "Go ahead and steal it. You're going to take it anyway." He did, and Kennedy dropped the ball.

His "greatest of all time" line after breaking Brock's record in 1991, borrowed from his idol Muhammad Ali, was taken as arrogance. He later said Brock had gone over the speech with him and helped write it.

At 44 he played for the independent Newark Bears for $3,000 to get one more shot. The Dodgers signed him that July, and he scored his 2,295th and last run after being hit by a pitch in his final plate appearance.
Oakland scout Jim Guinn called him the best prospect in the Alameda County and Oakland leagues.
The A's won the West in 1981 and beat Kansas City, but the Yankees swept them in the ALCS. In December 1984 Oakland traded him to the Yankees, and he signed for five years and $8.6 million.
A hamstring injury cost him 67 games in 1987, the only year from 1980 to 1991 he didn't lead the league in steals.
The Yankees traded him back to Oakland in June 1989, and he was ALCS MVP with eight steals against Toronto. In 1990 the A's were heavy favorites and got swept by the Reds.

He was so proud of a $1 million signing bonus check that he framed it instead of cashing it, losing months of interest. He saved his road meal money in a box, and when his kids did well in school they got to pick an envelope.

The Mets released him in May 2000, after reports that he had been playing cards in the clubhouse with Bobby Bonilla during their 1999 NLCS elimination. He denied it. GM Steve Phillips: "It's addition by subtraction."
At 46 he played for the San Diego Surf Dawgs of the independent Golden League and helped them win the title.
p: He was born on Christmas Day 1958 in the back seat of an Oldsmobile on the way to the hospital. "I was already fast. I couldn't wait." He was named after Ricky Nelson.

Football was his first love; as an Oakland high school running back he was rated with Ronnie Lott among the best in the country. He let his mother choose between a football scholarship and pro baseball. She chose baseball.
On talking about himself in the third person: "Rickey says it when Rickey doesn't do what Rickey needs to be doing… Rickey's just scolding himself."
He batted right-handed and threw left-handed, a rare combination. He's by far the most successful of the few position players who did.
He was born Rickey Henley. His father left home and died in a car crash 10 years later, and when his mother married Paul Henderson the family took his name.
His stepfather worked for General Motors, and his mother was a registered nurse.
He married his high school sweetheart, Pamela Palmer, in 1983. They had three daughters, Angela, Adrianna and Alexis.
He had asthma and sinus problems, and died of pneumonia in December 2024, five days before his 66th birthday.

c: At 29 he had pitched nine pro seasons on a sore arm without a single big-league win. In a 1920 poker game in New Orleans he banged his elbow on the table while raking in a pot. The doctor who treated it found the old injury no one else had, and after the operation he could throw without pain.

Brooklyn only wanted catcher Hank DeBerry, and owner Charles Ebbets refused to take Vance too. DeBerry said he wouldn't go without him: "if he looks good down here, it's because Vance makes him look good." At 31 Vance began a run of seven straight strikeout titles.
In 1924 he went 28–6 with 262 strikeouts, won 15 straight, and was named MVP. The league paid him $1,000 in gold coins instead of a trophy.

He pitched in a tattered sweatshirt with the right sleeve slit into strips that flapped as the ball came out. John McGraw protested, but nothing in the rulebook banned a ragged shirt. "This is my lucky shirt… I ain't even washed it."
He was the runner on second in Brooklyn's famous 'three men on third' play in 1926. He was the one ruled safe, since he got there first.

He broke in with the York Prohibitionists of the Nebraska State League in 1912. Pittsburgh bought him in 1915, but his arm hurt so much that "I no longer could throw hard, and it hurt like the dickens every time I threw."
After the poker-game injury, a doctor finally found the underlying problem that every other doctor had missed.
Opponents accused him of slitting his sleeve with a razor blade into narrow strips. He led the league for the last time in 1930, in ERA and shutouts.

The Dodgers traded him to the Cardinals, and at 42 he won only six games. Cincinnati claimed him on waivers, but he went back to St. Louis and finally pitched in a World Series that fall. Released in spring 1935, he finished with Brooklyn.
p: As president of the Daffiness Boys' "4 for 0 Club" he wrote its bylaws ("Raise all the hell you want but don't get caught") and expelled Jesse Petty for getting caught. When Petty submitted an apology a sportswriter had written for him, Vance held a hearing and told him: "There are words in this letter that you can't spell."
