He and Burleigh Grimes once led teammates, in pillowcase hoods and claiming to be the Ku Klux Klan, through the Braves' sleeping car on an overnight train, dragging players out of bed until catcher Mickey O'Neil gave up his signs.
He learned he had made the Hall of Fame in 1955 when a Florida highway patrolman flagged down his car to tell him a photographer was waiting at his house.
He was born in Iowa, the fifth child of a farmer, and grew up near the Kansas line in Nebraska.
He married Edythe Carmony, the daughter of a Hastings railroad man. Their son, Bob, was born in 1918, and a daughter a few years later.
He died of a heart attack in Homosassa Springs in 1961, two weeks before his 70th birthday. He had been sick for months but was thought to be doing well.

c: He threw too softly in high school to interest scouts. At San Jacinto junior college, coach Wayne Graham taught him to finish hard on every pitch and turned him into a power pitcher. Then he left for Texas without telling Graham.
He won the 1983 College World Series final for Texas. Days earlier the Red Sox had drafted him: "As far as I was concerned, Boston was a foreign country."
In 1986, after Hank Aaron said pitchers shouldn't win the MVP, Clemens said, "I wish he was still playing. I'd probably crack his head open to show him how valuable I was."
In 1986 he struck out 20 batters in a nine-inning game, a major-league record, on his way to the Cy Young and MVP.

His last big-league start, in October 2007, came against Cleveland, the team he had debuted against in 1984. He limped off with a hamstring injury in the third inning, but struck out the last batter he faced.
He worked out for the Mets' Joe Torre and Bob Gibson at the Astrodome, but Texas coach Cliff Gustafson came calling and he went to Austin.
In 1992 he reported eight days late to spring training, straining things with the Red Sox.
After the 1996 season he left Boston as a free agent and signed with Toronto. Before 1999 the Blue Jays traded him to the Yankees.

His Toronto manager, Cito Gaston, said: "It's all about him, nobody else but him." After 1997 the Blue Jays hired trainer Brian McNamee, who later said he injected Clemens with the steroid Winstrol in 1998.

In 2000 he knocked down Alex Rodriguez in the ALCS, and Lou Piniella called him a "headhunter." He had beaned Mike Piazza that season and then threw a broken bat in Piazza's direction in the World Series.
In 2004 he came out of retirement to join Andy Pettitte on his hometown Astros. His 2007 Yankees contract let him skip road trips when he wasn't pitching to be with his family.

He sued McNamee for defamation and told 60 Minutes the injections were vitamin B12 and lidocaine. At his own press conference he said, "I don't give a rat's ass about the Hall of Fame," and stormed out. McNamee countersued and in 2015 got a settlement from Clemens's insurer.
In August 2010 he was indicted for making false statements to Congress. His first trial ended in a mistrial, and in June 2012 he was acquitted on all charges. He never tested positive.
In 2012, at 50, he pitched for the independent Sugar Land Skeeters, with his son Koby catching, and threw 88 mph.
p: His parents separated when he was an infant, and his stepfather, Woody Booher, whom he considered his father, died when Roger was a boy. He said the only time he envied other players was seeing them in the clubhouse with their fathers.
His older brother Randy, whom he idolized, taught him that you're either a winner or a failure. Roger moved from Ohio to Texas at 15 to live with him.
He named his four sons Koby, Kory, Kacy and Kody, all with a K for the strikeout. Kody reached the majors in 2022 and as a position player pitching struck out Shohei Ohtani.
Named in the 2007 Mitchell Report, he told Congress that Andy Pettitte had "misremembered" their conversation about human growth hormone. He was indicted for lying to Congress and acquitted in 2012.
His mother left his father when Roger was 5 months old, and he says he spoke to his father only once, at 10. His mother worked several jobs to support her children.

He married Debbie Godfrey in November 1984. She once posed in a bikini with him for a Sports Illustrated feature on athletes and their wives, and blamed Red Sox fans' attitude for the team's World Series drought.

In 2008 the Daily News reported a long relationship with country singer Mindy McCready that it said began when she was 15. His lawyer called her a "close family friend." She later said the affair lasted more than a decade and ended when he wouldn't leave his wife, but that they met when she was 16 and it became sexual years later.
The papers also reported relationships with Paulette Daly, golfer John Daly's ex-wife, who didn't deny it was romantic and included money, and with at least three other women.

c: At 17 he got into pro ball because his brother Vince, then with the San Francisco Seals, talked the manager into trying him at shortstop. His erratic arm moved him to the outfield. In 1933, his first full year, he hit in 61 straight games, a Pacific Coast League record.
A knee injury in 1934 scared off most teams. The Yankees bought him on condition that he stay with the Seals one more year to prove he was healthy. He hit .398.

The 56-game streak in 1941 began when the Yankees were in fourth place and he had hit .194 over his previous 20 games. Radio programs broke in with DiMaggio bulletins. It ended in Cleveland before 67,468 fans on two great plays by Ken Keltner. He then hit in the next 16. He struck out five times during the streak.
When Al Gionfriddo robbed him at the bullpen gate in Game 6 of the 1947 World Series, the famously stoic DiMaggio kicked the dirt near second base, one of the few times he showed emotion in public.

He missed the first 65 games of 1949 with a bone spur, then rejoined the team at Fenway and hit four home runs in a three-game sweep. Weak from pneumonia at season's end, he took himself out of the pennant-deciding game when his legs couldn't catch up to a fly ball.
He retired at 36: "If I can't do it right, I don't want to play any longer."
He dropped out of Galileo High School and worked odd jobs. "Getting a daily hit became more important to me than eating, drinking, or sleeping."
The Seals signed him in 1933 for $225 a month.
He tore ligaments in his right knee stepping out of a jitney in 1934. Yankees scout Bill Essick kept pushing his bosses to take another look.
The Yankees paid $25,000 and five players for him.

In 1943 he enlisted in the Army Air Forces. Paid $21 a month, he spent most of the war playing ball, ate so well he gained 10 pounds, and mostly tanned and drank on the beach in Hawaii. Embarrassed, he asked for combat duty and was refused. Ulcers got him a medical discharge in 1945.
The Yankees won nine World Series in his 13 seasons, losing only once in 10 trips. Against the Dodgers in 1947 he hit two homers, including one that won Game 5 2–1.
The AP named his 1949 return from heel surgery the comeback of the year.
In 1951 age and injuries held him to 116 games and a .263 average, the worst of his career.
p: The son of a Sicilian fisherman, he had no interest in the fishing boat. His mother named him Giuseppe after his father, hoping he'd be her last child; he was the eighth of nine.

A 1939 Life magazine cover story praised him for slicking his hair with water instead of olive oil and for never reeking of garlic. Italian-Americans adopted him as their hero, and the invitations from Italian clubs came almost daily.

His 1954 marriage to Marilyn Monroe lasted nine months. He hoped to remarry her for the rest of his life. When she died in 1962 he took charge of her funeral and had roses placed at her crypt twice a week.
A heavy smoker, he died of lung cancer in 1999. His lawyer said his last words were "I'll finally get to see Marilyn."

In 1981 he babysat a stranger's daughter at the San Francisco airport so geneticist Mary-Claire King could make her flight. She went on to win the grant that led to her discovery of the BRCA1 breast-cancer gene.
After Pearl Harbor his parents were classified as "enemy aliens." His father was barred from San Francisco Bay, where he had fished for decades, and his boat was seized.
He met actress Dorothy Arnold on the set of Manhattan Merry-Go-Round, where he had a bit part. She wanted him home being a father and husband, and they divorced in 1944; she got custody of Joe Jr.

His marriage to Marilyn Monroe was troubled from the start by his jealousy, his controlling behavior and his physical abuse of her. After the skirt-blowing scene for The Seven Year Itch they had a violent fight, and she filed for divorce that October.
He came back into her life as her marriage to Arthur Miller ended. In one of her last interviews she said, "We have a better understanding than we've ever had."
He was the face of Mr. Coffee for over 20 years, though ulcers kept him from drinking much coffee, and he preferred Sanka. He also did commercials for the Bowery Savings Bank from 1972 to 1992.
He raised more than $4 million for the Joe DiMaggio Children's Hospital in Hollywood, Florida. His son died five months after him, in 1999.

c: His father coached him obsessively; he learned the overhand curve he'd dominate with at age 7. At Lynchburg in 1983 he struck out 300 batters in 191 innings.
After his second big-league start, a pounding at Wrigley Field, he told his father he "may not be ready yet." He struck out 276 as a 19-year-old and was Rookie of the Year.
In 1985 he went 24–4 with a 1.53 ERA and 268 strikeouts, at one point winning 18 of 19 decisions. Nike put his likeness up in Times Square.
After the Mets won the 1986 World Series he stayed up doing cocaine until sunrise and missed the victory parade.
On Opening Day 1994 Tuffy Rhodes hit three home runs off him. He kicked a bat rack and broke his toe, and during the rehab assignment he started using cocaine again.
After a season-long suspension, he signed with the Yankees and on May 14, 1996, threw a no-hitter against Seattle.
The Mets took him fifth overall in 1982 with an $85,000 bonus. Pitching coach John Cumberland taught him to set up hitters by pitching inside. He became a frequent drinker at Lynchburg.
Called up for the 1983 Triple-A playoffs, he won the deciding game of the International League finals and then the Triple-A World Series for Tidewater under Davey Johnson.
He first tried cocaine at home in Tampa after the 1985 season, and fell deeper in 1986 amid the Mets' party atmosphere.
He had a 1.06 ERA in the 1986 NLCS, but went 0–4 in nine postseason starts over his career.
He failed a cocaine test in spring 1987 and went into the Smithers rehab center to avoid a suspension. He kept drinking that season.

After his 1994 relapse he was suspended and went to the Betty Ford Center, but used cocaine again two days after leaving, including in his room while his wife and children were home. He failed another test and was suspended for all of 1995.
He started a 1997 Division Series game for the Yankees, signed with Cleveland, and retired in spring 2001 before the Yankees could release him.
After retiring he worked in the Yankees' front office and was the go-between when they signed his nephew, Gary Sheffield.
p: At 5 he was there, playing with a cousin, when his sister's husband shot her five times.
In December 1986 Tampa police beat him during an arrest. A report clearing the officers helped spark the 1987 Tampa riots.

His addiction followed him long after baseball: arrests, a year in a Florida state prison in 2006, and an appearance on Celebrity Rehab. "I'll always be a Met at heart," he said, and in 2024 the Mets retired his number 16.

His father, who had a third-grade education, worked for Cargill and coached youth baseball. His mother worked in a nursing home and a pool hall. He grew up around his father's heavy drinking, adultery and violence.
The December 1986 arrest came after police stopped his Corvette with Gary Sheffield and Vance Lovelace in it. He was charged with resisting arrest with violence and battery on an officer.

He was arrested for drunk driving in 2002 and for driving on a suspended license in 2003. In March 2005 he was arrested for punching his girlfriend after she threw a phone at his head, and he left the Yankees.
In 2006 he showed up to meet his probation officer high on cocaine and chose prison over more probation, serving almost seven months.
In 2010 he left the scene of a crash in New Jersey under the influence with a child in the car, and pleaded guilty to child endangerment. In 2019 he was arrested again for cocaine possession.

c: He signed with the Cardinals as a pitcher at 16, before his senior year of high school. In August 1940, playing center field between starts in Daytona Beach, he tried a somersault catch, caught his spikes, landed on his shoulder and was finished as a pitcher. Manager Dick Kerr and Branch Rickey made him an outfielder.
Ted Lyons said his corkscrew stance looked like a kid peeking around a corner to see if the cops were coming. Teammate Harry Walker said he'd never last in the majors with it.
On May 2, 1954, he hit five home runs in a doubleheader against the Giants. In the stands was eight-year-old Nate Colbert, who matched the record for the Padres in 1972.

He pitched once in the majors, to one batter, in 1952: Frank Baumholtz, his nearest rival in the batting race. Baumholtz switched sides of the plate and reached on an error, which Musial insisted was a clean hit.

He finished with 1,815 hits at home and 1,815 on the road. On September 10, 1963, after staying up all night for the birth of his first grandchild, he homered in his first at-bat, the first grandfather to homer in the majors.
The Cardinals signed him after a 1937 workout, but didn't file the contract until June 1938, which kept him eligible for high school sports. He led Donora's basketball team to the playoffs.

The story that he turned down a Pitt basketball scholarship, with his mother telling his father "this is America," is probably more legend than fact. He had already signed with the Cardinals' Monessen club on September 29, 1937, which would have made him ineligible anyway.
On his Donora High team was Buddy Griffey, the father of Ken Griffey Sr. and grandfather of Ken Griffey Jr.

Albany sold his contract to Asheville, and though his pay rose to $100 a month he felt he was never given a chance there. In Daytona Beach his manager was Dick Kerr, who had won two games for the 1919 White Sox while his teammates were throwing the Series.

He enlisted in the Navy in January 1945. In Hawaii he ran a launch bringing in crews of damaged ships at Pearl Harbor and played ball every afternoon, and he got emergency leave in 1946 to see his ailing father.
His streak of 895 straight games ended on August 22, when he tore a muscle and chipped a bone swinging at a pitch in Pittsburgh.
p: His mother made 'baseballs' out of old socks for him to throw. The story goes that when his father, a Polish immigrant mill worker, wanted Stan to take a basketball scholarship to Pitt, his mother said, "Lukasz, this is America, and he has the right not to go to college."
His minor-league manager Dick Kerr and his wife stood up at Stan and Lil's wedding in Daytona Beach in 1940, and Stan named his first son Richard after Kerr. He and Lil were married almost 72 years.
He played the harmonica at Hall of Fame inductions and charity events, appeared on Hee Haw, and recorded 18 songs to go with a harmonica instruction booklet.

He joined SABR and listed his area of expertise as "Hitting a Baseball!" As general manager in 1967 he won the World Series in his only year on the job, then quit: "I have a darn good job, but please don't ask me what I do."

His father, Lukasz, a Polish immigrant, married 16-year-old Mary Lancos in 1913; she gave her age as 21 to avoid needing her parents' permission. His father drank, and Stan was the only one of six children to finish high school.
He met Lil Labash, a Donora grocer's daughter, when both were 15. They had four children and were married almost 72 years, until she died in 2012.
He sometimes worked in Lil's father's grocery store, where he could grab a quick bite.
In 1949 he opened Stan Musial & Biggie's restaurant with his friend Biggie Garagnani, and they later owned other restaurants and the Ivanhoe Hotel in Miami Beach.

He campaigned for John F. Kennedy, who gave him a PT-109 pin, and Lyndon Johnson made him his physical fitness adviser in 1964. In 1987 he gave $50,000 worth of sports equipment to Poland's baseball association.
He died in January 2013, at 92, the same day as Earl Weaver. He lay in state in the Cathedral Basilica wearing his red Cardinals blazer, with a harmonica in his pocket.

c: He went to the University of Cincinnati on a basketball scholarship and joined the baseball team because it needed pitchers. He struck out 16 and then 18, a school record. At his Giants tryout he forgot his glove and had to borrow Johnny Antonelli's.

To make room for the bonus-baby rookie in 1955, the Dodgers sent down Tommy Lasorda. "It took the greatest left-handed pitcher in baseball history to get me off that Brooklyn club, and I still think they made a mistake."
Barely used and wild, he told Carl Erskine in 1958 that he was going to quit and buy into a radio station. He gave it one more year.
He threw the last pitch ever by a Brooklyn Dodger in 1957, striking out Willie Jones on three pitches.
He sat out Game 1 of the 1965 World Series because it fell on Yom Kippur.
He retired at 30 rather than risk losing the use of his arthritic elbow: "I don't regret one minute of the last twelve years, but I think I would regret one year that was too many."

He grew up with his mother's parents in Brooklyn. Milt Laurie, a newspaper deliveryman and sandlot coach, spotted him in the Ice Cream League even though he walked nine in two innings, and invited him to join his team.
One of his youth teams was captained by Fred Wilpon, his childhood friend and the future owner of the Mets.
At Cincinnati he averaged 9.7 points a game for Ed Jucker, who thought he could have played pro basketball.

The Yankees sent a Jewish scout to see him, which offended his family. The Dodgers offered a $14,000 bonus and $6,000 salary. Branch Rickey's Pirates offered $5,000 more, but he signed with Brooklyn in December 1954.
He left Cincinnati to take architecture classes at Columbia, then dropped out because of baseball and six months of military service between seasons.
The Dodgers won the 1955 Series without using him, and he got a full share. He took night classes at Columbia during the Series, and in 1956 was on the postseason roster but again didn't pitch.
After retiring he signed a 10-year, $1 million contract with NBC for the Game of the Week. He was uncomfortable on the air and quit after six years.

As a Dodgers minor-league pitching coach from 1979 to 1990 he worked with Orel Hershiser and Pedro Martínez, learning a splitter from Roger Craig so he could teach it. He quit, reportedly because of friction with Tommy Lasorda.

In 2002 the New York Post falsely implied he cooperated with a biography only because the author threatened to reveal he was gay. The Post retracted it, and Koufax cut ties with the Dodgers, whom Rupert Murdoch also owned, until Murdoch sold the team in 2004.
p: He was born Sanford Braun. His parents divorced when he was 3, and at 9 he took the name of his stepfather, Irving Koufax, who told him baseball was a waste of money until he watched him pitch and bought him new spikes.

On a stalled team bus in 1955, coach Billy Herman grumbled, "you can give this town back to the Jews." The bus went silent until the 19-year-old Koufax said softly, "Now Billy, you know we already have it."
When she heard he was writing an autobiography, his mother asked for an early copy so she could learn about her son. "You never told me anything." His friends called him The Ghost.

After retiring he lived on a Maine farm, got his golf handicap down to six, and dabbled in carpentry, electronics and gourmet cooking. "It's hard not to miss the one thing in your life you've done very well."
His mother worked as a bookkeeper at Camp Chi-Wan-Da, where he spent his summers and later worked as a waiter and counselor. His grandfather, a socialist immigrant, took him to the Yiddish theater.

He smoked as a player but wouldn't endorse cigarettes or be photographed smoking, and refused liquor ads too. In 1962 he invested in the Tropicana Motel in West Hollywood and started KNJO, an early stereo FM station.

In 1969 he married Anne Widmark, Richard Widmark's daughter; they divorced in 1982. He was married to personal trainer Kimberly Francis from 1985 to 1998, and married Jane Clarke in 2008. He has no children of his own.
He lost money in Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme on Fred Wilpon's advice, but still offered to testify for Wilpon.
In 2012 he revealed he had been diagnosed with cancer in 2010: "Today, I'm a survivor."

c: He hit .179 with one home run as a high school senior and made Ohio University's team as a walk-on. Coach Bob Wren had him give up switch-hitting, and he became a two-time All-American. The Phillies took him one pick after the Royals took George Brett.

After hitting .196 as a rookie, he played winter ball for Phillies coach Bobby Wine, who told him not to swing so hard. When Danny Ozark tried to change his stance again in 1974 spring training, Schmidt said he'd rather go back to the minors. He led the majors in home runs that year.
On June 10, 1974, he hit what looked like a sure home run in the Astrodome, but it struck a speaker hanging 117 feet up and fell for a single. The next day the speaker was raised 56 feet.

On April 17, 1976, at Wrigley Field, with the Phillies down 12–1, he hit four straight home runs, the last in the 10th inning, and they won 18–16. "There isn't a lot of tension in an at-bat when you've already hit three!"

In May 1989 he booted an easy grounder in San Francisco, and the next batter hit a grand slam. That's when he knew. He retired in tears: "Some 18 years ago, I left Dayton, Ohio, with two very bad knees and a dream to become a major league baseball player. I thank God that the dream came true."
Two knee surgeries ended his football and basketball at Fairview High. He played youth sports against Steve Yeager, who he said was "the greatest athlete I ever saw."
In 1970 he led Ohio University to the College World Series and was the All-America shortstop.

Scout Tony Lucadello, who had followed him since high school, wanted him in the first round in 1971. The Phillies took him in the second, one pick after the Royals took George Brett. He signed for $32,500 and bought a Corvette Stingray.
The Phillies' Owens and farm director Dallas Green wanted to send him back to the minors as a rookie. Danny Ozark kept him, but Ozark's hitting tips shook him, and he ended 1973 on an 0-for-26 slump.
In 1977 he signed for $561,500 a year, then the most ever paid a ballplayer and the first salary over $500,000.
When Pittsburgh's Bruce Kison challenged him to a fight, he accepted, and Ed Ott tackled him in the brawl and broke his finger. It hurt his swing for the rest of the season.
He had hit .191 in the postseason with no home runs before the 1980 World Series. Against Kansas City he hit two homers, drove in seven and was Series MVP.
After the 1980 Series he and four teammates were contestants on Family Feud for a week.
He hit .467 in the 1983 NLCS win over the Dodgers.
Pete Rose said: "To have his body, I'd trade him mine and my wife's, and I'd throw in some cash."
p: At 5 he climbed a backyard tree and grabbed a wire carrying 4,000 volts. His heart stopped. Falling through the branches and hitting the ground started it again, and he escaped with burn marks on his legs.
His family ran a swim club and drive-in in Dayton. "The family business was swimming pools and ice cream," he said.

When the Phillies clinched in 1976 he celebrated apart from most of the team with his closest friends, Dick Allen, Dave Cash and Garry Maddox. "It happened that my best friends on the Phillies were Black."
Booed for years in Philadelphia, he opened his 1995 Hall of Fame speech by making peace: "If I had to do it all over again, I'd do it in Philadelphia. The only thing I'd change would be me."
His mother's great-grandfather started the family's chain of Ohio aquatic clubs in 1865. His older sister Sally and her husband ran the pool and Jack's Drive-In until 2009.
He married Donna Wightman in February 1974, and they had two children.
In 2005 he told Bob Costas that if he had played in the steroid era, "I would have taken steroids."
In 2014 he revealed he had had stage 3 melanoma the year before, and was cancer-free.

c: He was driving a horse-drawn cab for $7.50 a week, 'the Slugging Cabby,' when Fall River offered him $500 for the season. His answer became his motto: "I'm out for the stuff."

In 1900 he found out the Phillies were paying Ed Delahanty $400 more, despite promising them equal pay. "I saw the checks." He jumped to the new American League and hit .426 in 1901, still the highest average of the 20th century.

A Pennsylvania court barred him from playing for anyone but the Phillies in that state, so Cleveland signed him and he simply skipped every game in Philadelphia. The club became so identified with him that it was renamed the Naps, the only team ever named for an active player.

On the last day of 1910 the Browns played their third baseman deep so he could beat Ty Cobb for the batting title and a new Chalmers car, and he dropped seven bunt singles. Cobb was declared the winner anyway. Both got cars, and Lajoie, who believed he had won, didn't want to accept his.
He swung so hard that three times in 1899 he literally tore the cover off the ball.
He played semipro ball in Woonsocket under the name "Sandy" because his parents didn't approve. At Fall River, the owner turned down $500 from Pittsburgh for him.
In August 1896 Fall River sold him and Phil Geier to the Phillies for $1,500.
A collision with Harry Steinfeldt limited him to 77 games in 1899, but he hit .378. In 1900 he broke his thumb in a fistfight with teammate Elmer Flick and missed five weeks.
In April 1900 Brooklyn's Ned Hanlon publicly offered the Phillies $10,000 for him, and they said no.
In 1904 he was suspended for throwing tobacco juice in umpire Frank Dwyer's eye. After one ejection he refused to leave the bench, and police had to escort him out of the park.
With the league's best hitter skipping every game in Philadelphia, the A's won the 1902 pennant, partly on a gap between their home and road records that is still the second-largest ever.
He managed Cleveland until midway through 1909, when he quit with the team losing.

In 1910 the Browns' manager, O'Connor, was fired for letting him bunt seven straight hits, and eight of Cobb's own Tigers teammates wired Lajoie their congratulations. Ban Johnson still gave Cobb the title. Chalmers gave them both cars, and Lajoie didn't want his, but his wife made him take it.
The A's bought him after 1914, reuniting him with Connie Mack. He became player-manager of Toronto in 1917 and Indianapolis in 1918.
Brooklyn signed him for $3,000 in March 1918, but the contract was voided and he was "well pleased."
p: His father died when he was 6, and after eight months of school he went to work sweeping a textile mill at 10. His mother disapproved of baseball, so teammates called him 'Sandy' to hide that he was playing.
In 1905 the blue dye in his socks poisoned a spike wound and his leg nearly had to be amputated. Teams were then required to wear sanitary white socks.
He once threw chewing tobacco in an umpire's eye. Another time, angry that the umpire put a blackened ball in play, he threw it over the grandstand, and Cleveland had to forfeit.
At 43 he offered his services to the World War I draft board. They declined, with thanks. He later ran for sheriff of Cuyahoga County as a Republican and lost.
He was the youngest of eight surviving children. His father, a teamster and laborer, died in 1881.
In 1906 he married Myrtle Smith, a divorcée. They lived on a 20-acre farm in South Euclid, outside Cleveland, until moving to Mentor in 1939.
After baseball he dabbled in a rubber company, sold truck tires, and set up a small brass manufacturing company, more to keep busy than for the money. Myrtle died of cancer.
He fell and broke his arm in the fall of 1958, and died of pneumonia in Daytona Beach the next February, at 84.

c: The Braves signed him out of USC in 1966, but the commissioner voided the contract because USC's season had started. Teams willing to match the offer went into a hat. The Indians, Phillies and Mets entered, and the Mets' name was drawn.
In his first All-Star Game, as a rookie in 1967, he pitched the bottom of the 15th and closed it out. Hank Aaron, his boyhood hero, told him, "You've got a nice pitch, kid."

The "imperfect game," July 9, 1969, against the first-place Cubs at Shea: he retired the first 25. With one out in the ninth, rookie Jimmy Qualls, the one hitter who had been hitting him hard, lined a single to left.
Earl Weaver, managing in the minors, saw his pro debut and phoned Baltimore's general manager to say the Orioles should give up a piece of the franchise to get him.
He won his 300th game for the White Sox on August 4, 1985, at Yankee Stadium on Phil Rizzuto Day.
After high school he took classes at Fresno City College and worked in the raisin business. Scouts noticed after his second year, when he won 11 straight.
He was an All-City basketball player. Rod Dedeaux gave him a USC scholarship after he won a national tournament game and hit a grand slam in it.

The NCAA ruled him ineligible after his signing with the Braves was voided, so his father complained to the commissioner and threatened to sue. Eckert ruled that other teams could match the Braves' offer.
The Indians, Phillies and Mets made offers, and the Mets signed him for $10,000 more than the Braves had offered.
Braves owner Bill Bartholomay, whose team went 0–4 against him in 1967, said, "I get sick every time I watch him pitch."
He started the 1969 imperfect game with a sore shoulder. He started Game 1 of the first NLCS and won 9–5, then lost Game 1 of the World Series to Mike Cuellar before the Mets beat Baltimore.

In 1977 board chairman M. Donald Grant refused to renegotiate his contract. After Seaver worked out an extension with owner Lorinda de Roulet, Daily News columnist Young wrote that Seaver's wife was pushing him because she envied Nolan Ryan's salary. Seaver demanded a trade.
On June 15, 1977, the Mets traded him to Cincinnati for Pat Zachry, Steve Henderson, Doug Flynn and Dan Norman. That night became known as the Midnight Massacre, and it drove fans away from Shea.
p: At the Bing Crosby Pro-Am, his father asked Ralph Kiner for an autograph for his son, who wanted to be a ballplayer. Kiner signed a school photo: "To Tom, work hard and good luck." Years later Kiner called Seaver the driving force of the 1969 Mets.
After high school he joined the Marine Corps Reserve, serving six months of active duty before enrolling at Fresno City College.
He opposed the Vietnam War and spoke out against it in the run-up to the 1969 World Series.

He retired to California and planted a vineyard in Calistoga; his two cabernets were called "Nancy's Fancy" and "GTS." Each year he, Bob Gibson, Sandy Koufax and Steve Carlton shared a bottle at dinner during the Hall of Fame induction.
His father, Charles, was an executive with a raisin packer that shipped across the country. His mother, Betty, was a homemaker.
He married his high school sweetheart, Nancy McIntyre, in Jacksonville in June 1966, during his first minor-league season. They had two daughters, Sarah and Annie.
He died in his sleep in August 2020 of complications from Lewy body dementia and COVID-19.

c: His first big-league tryout, with Pittsburgh in 1897, ended at breakfast. He sat next to manager Patsy Donovan, who heard him talk and released him before the meal was over.

Connie Mack was the only manager who could handle him. To get him east from Los Angeles in 1902 he sent a pair of Pinkerton detectives along. Waddell joined the A's with 87 games left, went 24–7, and the A's won the pennant.
In 1904 he struck out 349, a record that lasted until Sandy Koufax struck out 382 in 1965.
On July 4, 1905, he beat Cy Young 4–2 in 20 innings and turned cartwheels off the mound. Legend says he traded the game ball for drinks, and soon dozens of bartenders owned the 'genuine' ball.
Late in 1905 he hurt his shoulder scuffling with a teammate over a straw hat on a train platform and missed the World Series. Not everyone believed it; rumors said gamblers paid him to sit out.
His first contract was $500 with Louisville in 1897. He reportedly blew his whole bonus on a binge, and The Sporting News called him a "sousepaw."
In Detroit's minor-league club he skipped out on his rent, was fined by the owner, and left in late May to pitch in Canada and then semipro ball.

When Louisville folded in 1900 he was one of 10 players moved to Pittsburgh. Fred Clarke suspended him that July, and he pitched for semipro teams until Connie Mack, then managing Milwaukee, picked him up.
Pittsburgh sold him to Chicago in May 1901. After winning 14 games there he jumped to semipro teams in Wisconsin, and in 1902 he signed with the Los Angeles Looloos.

Ban Johnson once suspended him for five days for climbing into the stands to beat up a gambler who had been heckling him. Mack, tired of his unexcused absences, later suspended him for the rest of a season.
After his 1905 shoulder injury, rumors spread that gamblers had paid him to sit out the World Series.
His drinking split him from his catcher and friend Schrecongost, who had sworn off the bottle. Mack sold him to the St. Louis Browns in February 1908, and Browns attendance jumped 48 percent.
He passed out in the middle of a 1909 game against New York.
p: At 3 he wandered off to the local fire station and stayed for several days.

He might miss a start to go fishing or to play marbles with street kids, and was once found wrestling an alligator in a lagoon in spring training. He did call his fielders off and strike out the side, but only in exhibitions.
When teammate Danny Hoffman was knocked out by a pitch, Waddell carried him across the field on his shoulder, flagged a carriage to the hospital, and sat up most of the night holding ice to his head.

He met his second wife three days before marrying her. In the 1903 offseason he toured in a melodrama, The Stain of Guilt; one critic said the repair bills for his two minutes per scene were pretty bulky.

In the winter of 1912 he stood in icy water for hours stacking sandbags against a Mississippi River flood in Hickman, Kentucky. He caught pneumonia, then tuberculosis, and died on April Fools' Day 1914, down to 130 pounds.
He wasn't a farm boy: his father was a Scottish immigrant who worked in the Pennsylvania oil fields for a Standard Oil company. Rube was the sixth child.
He built up his arm as a boy by throwing rocks at birds, and worked at mining and drilling sites.
He chased fires all his life, from a bucket brigade in Pewaukee, Wisconsin, to the big-city departments in Philadelphia, Cleveland, Detroit and Washington.
After the 1899 season he married Florence Dunning. She divorced him in 1901 for "gross neglect of duty."

He and his second wife, May Wynne Skinner, rarely lived together, and she often had him jailed for nonsupport. She sued for divorce in 1908, and soon after he was accused of assaulting both of her parents. A warrant kept him from pitching in Massachusetts for two seasons.
After the theater company dumped his bags in an alley over a fight about advances, he started tending bar in Camden.
According to Lee Allen, in 1903 alone he also toured in a melodrama, married and separated, saved a woman from drowning, accidentally shot a friend through the hand, and was bitten by a lion.
In a football practice Mack and John Shibe organized, he tackled a little would-be quarterback from Wanamaker's and broke the man's leg.
In 1910 he married 19-year-old Madge Maguire. May threatened to prosecute him for bigamy, but the divorce was legal. Ken Burns's Baseball claimed he had lost track of how many women he had married.

c: As a 2–13 minor leaguer at Taunton in 1899, his club folded and the players had to stage an exhibition to raise their fare home. The next summer at Norfolk he was 20–2 by mid-July and chose the Giants over the Phillies because New York needed pitching more.
To save $900, the Reds drafted him for $100 and immediately traded him back to the Giants for a washed-up Amos Rusie. The Reds owner was busy buying the Giants.

In the 1905 World Series he threw three shutouts in six days: 27 innings, 14 hits, one walk, no runs. A week later he went hunting in Michigan, was talked into pitching for a town team, and lost 5–0 to semipros.

In 1908 he won 37 and walked less than one batter per nine innings, then lost the one-game playoff to the Cubs after the Merkle game with "nothing on the ball." He felt responsible for the four people who died in falls at the Polo Grounds that day.

As Reds manager in 1918 he suspended Hal Chase for throwing games. He was in France when the case was heard, and without him Chase was cleared. Covering the 1919 World Series, he reportedly circled suspicious plays on his scorecard.

Phenomenal Smith, an old big-league pitcher, signed him for Norfolk right before a Bucknell–Penn football game. In that game Matty kicked two long field goals, worth five points each then, the same as a touchdown.
Smith let him choose whether to be sold to Philadelphia or New York.
In July 1900 the Giants paid Norfolk $1,500 for him.
He played pro football as a fullback for the Pittsburgh Stars. He left the team, either because the Giants ordered him to stop risking his arm or because the coach replaced him with a local player.
Diphtheria nearly killed him in 1906, and he fell to 22–12.
He confronted Hal Chase over suspicious misplays and a $50 payment to pitcher Jimmy Ring. When he got back from France he quit the Reds to become McGraw's assistant manager.
He reportedly suspected the 1919 Series was fixed before it began, agreed with Hugh Fullerton to circle suspicious plays on his scorecard, and sent what he found to the National Commission.

In February 1923, after McGraw urged Judge Emil Fuchs to buy the Boston Braves, Mathewson became the club's president, against his doctors' warnings. His cough came back in 1925, reportedly after he got soaked in a spring-training rain, and he went back to Saranac Lake.
p: At Bucknell he was the football team's fullback and kicker (Walter Camp called him the greatest drop-kicker in college football), class president, and a member of the band and glee club. He majored in forestry.
He turned down an offer to put his name on a pool hall and saloon when his mother asked, "Do you really want your name associated with a place like that?"
His youngest brother, Nicholas, shot himself in 1909, and another brother, Henry, who once walked 14 Cubs in a Giants start, died of tuberculosis in 1917.
Dying of tuberculosis at Saranac Lake in 1925, he told his wife: "Now Jane, I want you to go outside and have yourself a good cry. Don't make it a long one; this can't be helped."
He was the oldest of six children. His father, a Civil War veteran, was a postal worker and farmer.
He married Jane Stoughton in 1903. They shared a duplex at Columbus and 85th with John and Blanche McGraw, who treated him like the son they never had.
Their only child, Christy Jr., was born on October 6, 1906.
Christy Jr. served in World War II and was killed in an explosion at his Texas home in 1950.
Nicholas killed himself in a neighbor's barn. Henry died in 1917, at 30, leaving four young daughters, and Christy may have caught TB from him.
With ghostwriter John Wheeler he wrote a series of children's baseball novels, starting with Won in the Ninth in 1910.
He was buried in Lewisburg in view of the Bucknell campus. The Pirates and Senators wore black armbands in the World Series, which began the day he died.

c: He taught himself to hit by swatting bottle caps with broom handles, batting cross-handed. He hit that way until Jacksonville manager Ben Geraghty got him to switch, and that's when his power came.
In 1952 he had telegrams from both the Giants and the Braves, and he chose Boston because it offered $50 a month more.

In 1953 he and four other Black players integrated the South Atlantic League in the Deep South. He led the league in nearly everything. One writer said he "led the league in everything except hotel accommodations."

His 1957 Topps card was printed in reverse, so he appears to bat left-handed with his number backwards; Topps never fixed it. That September his 11th-inning homer off Billy Muffett, the only one Muffett allowed all year, clinched the pennant. His teammates carried him off the field.

Through 1973 thousands of letters a week poured in, many of them racist hate mail and death threats. On April 8, 1974, he hit 715 off Al Downing. Vin Scully: "A black man is getting a standing ovation in the Deep South for breaking a record of an all-time baseball idol."
When Barry Bonds passed him in 2007, Aaron congratulated him by video on the scoreboard: "I move over now and offer my best wishes to Barry and his family."
At 15 he tried out for the Dodgers, inspired by Jackie Robinson, and wasn't offered a contract, probably because of his cross-handed grip. He played for the semipro Mobile Black Bears for $3 a game.

The Indianapolis Clowns signed him in November 1951 for $200 a month. In Washington he heard a restaurant break all the plates the team had eaten off: "they had to destroy the plates that had touched the forks that had been in the mouths of Black men."
The Braves bought him from the Clowns for $10,000; GM John Quinn thought he was worth $100,000. He finished 1952 helping the Clowns win the Negro American League title.

He played winter ball in Puerto Rico and learned the outfield. His big-league chance came in spring 1954, when Bobby Thomson broke his ankle sliding. That September Aaron broke his own ankle sliding into third, the only serious injury of his career.
In the 1957 World Series he had 11 hits, three of them home runs, in 28 at-bats.
He and Tommie were the first brothers to play together in a League Championship Series.
He refused to be there when Barry Bonds broke his record, which was widely taken as a snub over steroids.
p: He grew up so poor in Mobile that he made his own bats and balls from what he found in the street. His boyhood idol was Jackie Robinson, whom he saw on exhibition swings through Alabama.
He preferred his given name, Henry. "Hank" was invented by a Milwaukee publicist to make the quiet young player seem more approachable.
He and his brother Tommie hold the record for career home runs by brothers, 768, with Henry supplying 755. Tommie died of leukemia in 1984: "It was the hardest night of my life."
As the Braves' director of player development after he retired, he became one of the first minority executives in baseball's upper management.
His father was a riveter at a Mobile shipyard, and he was one of eight children. He was a Boy Scout and later filmed a commercial for the Scouts.
As a boy he picked potatoes and worked on an ice-delivery truck.
He married Barbara Lucas in 1953, and they had five children: Gary, Lary, Dorinda, Gaile and Hank Jr. They divorced in 1971. In 1973 he married Billye Suber Williams and adopted her daughter, Ceci.
He was a vice president and board member at Turner Broadcasting. He owned BMW and Toyota dealerships around Atlanta, with an autographed ball in every car, and a chain of 30 restaurants.
He died in his sleep at home in Atlanta in January 2021, at 86.

c: In a 1920 high-school all-star game at Cubs Park he hit a ninth-inning grand slam over the right-field wall. The Chicago Tribune said it was hit "by a boy who hasn't yet started to shave."

At a 1921 Giants tryout he hit six straight batting-practice home runs and then let a grounder go through his legs. "Get this fellow out of here!" John McGraw said. Gehrig played that summer for Hartford as "Lou Lewis" and was suspended from Columbia sports for a year.

At Columbia he was also the ace. On the day Yankee Stadium opened in 1923 he struck out 17 Williams batters. The Yankees scout who came to see him called the general manager to say he'd found another Babe Ruth.

As a 1924 call-up he got into a cursing match with Ty Cobb and went after him in the tunnel after the game. He swung, missed, fell, and knocked himself out on the concrete. When he came to he asked, "Did I win?"

In spring 1939 Joe DiMaggio watched him swing and miss at 19 straight batting-practice fastballs. On May 2 he took himself out of the lineup, ending his streak at 2,130 games. "I haven't been a bit of good to the team since the season started."

The Giants' Arthur Irwin told him John McGraw had seen him play and wanted to sign him. McGraw had never seen him and promised nothing. Instead Irwin got him a spot with Hartford for the rest of 1921, where he played as "Lou Lewis."
Columbia's coach, Andy Coakley, found out and begged rival schools to treat it as an innocent mistake. They agreed to a one-year suspension rather than banning him.

Yankees business manager Barrow signed him in 1923 for a $1,500 bonus and $400 a month, a fortune to his family. After seven games Miller Huggins sent him back to Hartford, and he wasn't added to the World Series roster.
After another year at Hartford, where he hit .369 with 37 homers, Huggins reportedly told Wally Pipp, "Suppose you take the day off. I'll use that big kid, Gehrig, at first base today."
He won six World Series, two MVPs and a Triple Crown, and his 23 career grand slams stood as the record until Alex Rodriguez.
p: He was the only one of four children to survive childhood. His mother worked as a maid, and in high school Lou helped her serve dinner and wash dishes at a Columbia fraternity house.

He lived with his mother until he was 30. She broke up every romance until he met Eleanor Twitchell, who helped him leave home and hired Babe Ruth's agent. He became the first athlete on a Wheaties box.

Doctors at the Mayo Clinic diagnosed ALS on his 36th birthday. He then served as a New York City parole commissioner, turning down better-paid offers, with Eleanor guiding his hand when he signed documents.
He died on June 2, 1941, sixteen years to the day after he replaced Wally Pipp at first base. Babe Ruth and his wife went straight to the house to comfort Eleanor.
He weighed a reported 14 pounds at birth. One sister died at three months, another at under two of measles, diphtheria and bronchopneumonia, and a brother died just after birth.
His father, a sheet-metal worker, was often out of work because of his drinking and epilepsy. His mother was the family's breadwinner.
His mother called baseball a mere schoolyard game and wanted him to go into business. He worked part-time in butcher shops and grocery stores.
He studied engineering at Columbia for two years.
Eleanor was the daughter of Chicago's parks commissioner. She hired Babe Ruth's agent, Christy Walsh, who made Lou the first athlete on a Wheaties box.
To take the parole job he moved from New Rochelle to Riverdale. He went to his office until a month before he died, with Eleanor guiding his hand when he signed documents.
Eleanor never remarried: "I would not have traded two minutes of my life with that man for forty years with another." She died on her 80th birthday in 1984 and was buried with him.

c: Detroit scout Wish Egan signed him at 17 for a $500 bonus paid in $100 bills. Minutes later Cleveland's head scout pulled up in a shiny new car, offering $15,000 and the car. He was late because he had stopped to pick up the car. That night Egan said he'd just signed the greatest left-hander he ever saw.

After five seasons he was 34–52 and his father had found him a well-paid drafting job at Chrysler. He gave baseball one more shot. In 1944 Paul Richards told him, "I'm going to make you a pitcher," and taught him a slider. He won back-to-back MVPs in 1944 and 1945.

Pulled from a game, he could destroy a clubhouse; once he smashed an entire case of Coke bottles against the wall. "I didn't win because I controlled my temper. I controlled my temper because I began to win."
Released by Detroit, he joined Hank Greenberg's Indians as a reliever in 1954 and was part of the bullpen for their 111-win team.

As an Astros scout he begged the club to take a Kalamazoo high schooler named Derek Jeter with the first pick in 1992: "No one is worth a million dollars, but if one kid is worth that, it's this kid." Houston took Phil Nevin, and Newhouser quit.

At Wish Egan's suggestion he quit his trade school team for American Legion ball. As a rookie he went to school three hours each morning before reporting to Briggs Stadium, even during the 1940 World Series.

In 1943 he led the league with 111 walks, and was so frustrated being pulled in the middle innings that he demanded a trade. Without the wartime player shortage, he might have been sent down or released.
Mexican League boss Jorge Pasquel offered him $200,000 for three seasons plus a $300,000 bonus. The Tigers paid him $10,000 to stay, and fearing a ban if the Mexican League collapsed, he stayed.
Manager O'Neill once fined him $250 for being stubborn. It was the first fine of his career, despite all the clubhouses he had wrecked.
As an Orioles scout he found Milt Pappas and Dean Chance. Then he spent 20 years working at a bank before going back to scouting for Houston.
When the Astros told him they'd take Phil Nevin over Derek Jeter because Nevin would sign for less, he quit baseball for good.
p: A Depression kid, he sold papers, set pins and collected deposit bottles, and in winter picked up flakes of coal at the coalyard in a gunnysack to take home.

He tried to enlist in the Army Air Force and was supposed to be sworn in on the mound at Briggs Stadium, but doctors heard his mitral-valve prolapse and classified him 4-F. He tried several more times.
When he finally made the Hall of Fame in 1992, after decades of being dismissed as a 'wartime pitcher', he cried, he said, because his mother, 92, was alive to see it.

His father, a former gymnast from Czechoslovakia, was an auto-industry draftsman, and his mother was from Austria. His older brother Dick signed with the Tigers but quit after a beaning fractured his skull.
He studied machining at trade school but found it too dangerous after driving injured classmates to the hospital, so he switched to drafting.
As a boy he survived several serious injuries, including being hit in the head with a brick.
His father, who worked afternoons, never saw him pitch in Detroit. Hal later bought his parents a house in Asbury Park, New Jersey, where they opened a pattern-making business.
He married Beryl in 1941, two years after they met at a party, and they had two daughters, Charlene and Sherrill. They stayed married until he died in 1998.

c: In a 2006 high school playoff game he struck out all 15 batters he faced in a mercy-rule-shortened perfect game, and also homered.

On May 4, 2010, he retired only four of 13 batters and was booed off the mound at Dodger Stadium. "It stings, it hurts. I've got to figure things out." Next time out he threw an eight-inning two-hitter, and credited command of his slider.
His only big-league home run came on Opening Day 2013, when he also shut out the Giants. He was the first pitcher to do both on Opening Day since Bob Lemon in 1953.
His no-hitter on June 18, 2014, had 15 strikeouts and no walks. The only baserunner reached on a Hanley Ramírez error in the seventh.
His windup's little pause, with his right foot lowered straight down, was dubbed the "kickstand move." He modeled his mechanics on his boyhood favorite, Roger Clemens.
He turned down Texas A&M and signed with the Dodgers as the seventh pick in 2006 for about $2.3 million, the biggest bonus they had ever given a draftee.
In spring training 2008 his curveball to Sean Casey started behind Casey and dropped into the strike zone for a called strike three.
In 2010 he was suspended five games for hitting Aaron Rowand with a pitch.

Back pain put him on the disabled list in 2016, and he had to skip the All-Star Game. He came back for the playoffs, saving the clinching Game 5 of the Division Series, then lost the deciding NLCS game to the Cubs.
He posted a 4.62 ERA in the postseason, much worse than his regular-season numbers. He won rings in 2020 and 2025 and got one from the 2024 team, which won while he was hurt.
After 2021 he went year to year with the Dodgers. On July 15, 2022, he took a perfect game into the eighth before Luis Rengifo doubled.
In 2023 he dropped out of the World Baseball Classic, reportedly because he couldn't get insurance. He had the worst start of his career in the NLDS opener and had shoulder surgery that November.
In 2024 he made only seven starts, then needed surgery on a torn knee meniscus and his left big toe.
He joined NBC's Sunday Night Baseball as an analyst in 2026.
p: At Highland Park High in Dallas he was the center snapping the ball to quarterback Matthew Stafford. In 2017 they were the highest-paid players in their sports. He wore 22 for his childhood hero, Will Clark.
He is the great-nephew of Clyde Tombaugh, who discovered Pluto. His parents divorced when he was 10, and his mother raised him.

After a 2011 mission trip to Zambia he pledged $100 per strikeout to build an orphanage in Lusaka, Hope's Home, named for an HIV-positive 11-year-old he met there. He struck out a career-high 248 that year and gave his $260,000 Players Choice award to the project too.
His father remarried after the divorce and died in 2013.
He married Ellen Melson, his girlfriend of seven years, in December 2010. They wrote a book about their faith, Arise, to raise money for the Zambia orphanage.

c: He showed up for a tryout with Home Run Baker's Easton club in 1924 wearing overalls and offered to catch if Baker needed one. He was 16. By the end of July the Athletics had bought his contract, and he went back for his senior year of high school.

When his first son was born just before the 1929 World Series, he promised to homer for him, and did in Game 1. In the ninth inning of a scoreless Game 5 in 1930 he told teammates he would "bust up the game right now" and hit Burleigh Grimes's pitch into the bleachers.
He hit 58 home runs in 1932, a month ahead of Ruth's pace in July before a wrist injury. He said he lost six to new screens in St. Louis alone that hadn't been there in 1927.
After the 1934 season a minor-league pitcher beaned him in a Winnipeg exhibition. He was in the hospital four days, and sinus trouble followed him the rest of his life.
Lefty Gomez said he "had muscles in his hair" and "wasn't scouted, he was trapped." Foxx cut the sleeves off his uniforms to show his arms.
His parents were tenant farmers. His father had played for a town team and passed the game on to him, and farm work built the physique on his 5-foot-11 frame.
Baker's Easton club was short on catchers, so Foxx, who had hoped to pitch or play third, went behind the plate. In July 1924 Connie Mack bought him for $2,000.
With Mickey Cochrane catching, he sat as a backup at $3,000 in 1927 and began moving to first base.

In 1931 knee and foot injuries and the start of his sinus trouble kept him under .300 for the first time. The A's lost that World Series to the Cardinals, his last Series. He hit .344 with four homers in three postseasons.
In 1933 he won the Triple Crown and his second straight MVP while playing through leg injuries.

Mack sold him to Tom Yawkey's Red Sox after 1935 with Johnny Marcum for $150,000, and Foxx got a $7,000 raise. He never respected Joe Cronin the way he had Mack, but Cronin later offered him jobs and money.
With the flu in 1937 spring training, he was hospitalized with forehead pain and vision problems.
He coached the University of Miami for two seasons, 1956 and 1957, then was let go. After his 1958 dinner plea, the Red Sox made him hitting coach of the Minneapolis Millers.
p: At 10 he tried to run away and join the army after hearing about his grandfather's Civil War exploits.

He tipped everyone, picked up every tab and would give away the shirt off his back. He loved Virginia ham and homemade peach ice cream and collected autographed photos of movie stars, Katharine Hepburn above all.

In 1952 he managed the Fort Wayne Daisies of the women's league, with his daughter as batgirl. Tom Hanks's Jimmy Dugan in A League of Their Own is loosely based on him, though his players remembered him as a perfect gentleman.

By 1958 he was broke and told a Boston writers' dinner that he couldn't pay his own way there. He gave the cash donations that followed to the Jimmy Fund. He died in 1967 after choking at dinner with his brother, as his wife had the year before.
When his fortunes turned he bought his parents a farm and eloped with Helen Heite. They had two sons and a stormy 14-year marriage, and both spent heavily on clothes.
Teammate Elden Auker said Helen constantly harassed him on the phone over money while she was having an affair.
After the beaning his sinus pain eased with alcohol, and he began drinking heavily. He was never violent, but drinking probably shortened his career.
Bad investments left him broke. He worked for the Lakewood, Ohio, recreation department near his children, and his son Jimmie Jr. played football at Kent State.

His second wife, Dorothy, choked to death in 1966, and he became lonely and depressed. The next July, at dinner with his brother Sam in Miami, he collapsed and died at 59. An autopsy found he had also choked. Sam died a few weeks later.

c: At 15 he worked out on Sunday mornings in Las Vegas with retired scout Ralph Medar, who taught him that movement mattered more than velocity and to throw softer in a jam, not harder. "I believed it. I don't know why. I just did."

His big-league debut, in 1986, came as a pinch-runner in the 17th inning of a suspended game. He stayed in to pitch the 18th and took the loss. Late that season he beat the Phillies' starter, his brother Mike, 8–3.

After his 1992 Cy Young he turned down more money from the Yankees and signed with Atlanta, partly because he thought it a better place to raise a family. Pitching coach Leo Mazzone: "I knew I was going to get a lot smarter, real quick."

In 1994 his 1.56 ERA was 37 percent of the league average, better relative to the league than Bob Gibson's 1.12 in 1968. During one 1995 start at Wrigley a writer muttered that giving him a 5–0 lead was "like giving a 15-0 lead to a regular human being."

He liked to tell his coaches how he would get out of an inning, down to the hitter fouling out to third on the second pitch. In 2001 he went 72⅓ innings without a walk, and the streak ended on an intentional one.

He was ready to go to the University of Arizona, but the Cubs drafted him in the second round in 1984, and two weeks later he signed. When scouts came to see his brother Mike, their father told them, "You will be back later for the little one."
In his first big-league start, four days after his debut, he went the distance and won 11–3, ending a seven-game Cubs losing streak.
He started Game 1 of the 1989 NLCS against the Giants, and the Cubs lost the series in five.

His free-agent talks with the Cubs turned bitter, with GM Larry Himes and agent Scott Boras each accusing the other of bad faith. Maddux said he'd have "heavily" considered the Cubs' original offer if they had put it back on the table, but they spent the money on other free agents.
Ryne Sandberg's comments about his leaving hurt him. Leo Mazzone called his signing the greatest free-agent deal in history.
He lost the deciding Game 6 of the 1993 NLCS to the Phillies. In Game 1 of the 1995 World Series he pitched a two-hitter with no walks and no earned runs, and the Braves won the title.
He pitched in two more World Series, and lost the final game when the Yankees won in six.

After retiring he worked for the Cubs, then for the Rangers with his brother Mike, and was the US pitching coach at the 2013 World Baseball Classic. For four years he coached pitchers at UNLV, where his son Chase pitched.
p: His father was in the Air Force, and the family moved from Texas to North Dakota to California to Spain. When his father retired he became a poker dealer in Las Vegas casinos.
He banked his signing bonus in case baseball didn't work out and lived on his minor-league salary and what he'd saved from summer jobs at Sears and Wendy's.
The bluegrass band Punch Brothers wrote a song about him, "Movement and Location."

His mother, Linda, married his father, an Air Force man, after high school; their daughter was born at an Anchorage base and Mike in Dayton. The kids were most active in sports while the family lived in Spain.
Coaches discouraged him and Mike from basketball so they would concentrate on pitching. His tutor, Ralph Medar, died before Greg graduated from high school.
He married Kathy Ronnow, whom he had known since high school, in 1988. They have a daughter, Paige, and a son.

c: In his big-league debut in 1988, he was so nervous he forgot the signs and kept crossing up his catcher. Umpire Steve Palermo walked out to the mound with a new ball: "You're OK, kid. Just relax. You're going to make it in this game."
With the Phillies facing elimination in Game 5 of the 1993 World Series, he threw a five-hit shutout.
In 2001 he went 4–0 with a 1.12 ERA in the postseason and shared World Series MVP with Randy Johnson. In five starts when his team faced elimination, his teams won all five.

When Theo Epstein came to recruit him in November 2003, armed with data on how Fenway suited a right-handed power pitcher, the Schillings had him to Thanksgiving dinner. Schilling acted as his own agent. On signing he said, "I guess I hate the Yankees now."

The bloody sock: with an ankle tendon sutured in place, he beat the Yankees in Game 6 of the 2004 ALCS and did it again in the World Series five days later. The surgeon said it probably couldn't be done a third time.
He kept notebooks on hitters and studied them on the bench between innings. His 4.38 strikeouts per walk is the best of any pitcher since 1900 with 1,000 strikeouts.

In high school, talks with scouts stopped after a hit-by-pitch broke his left elbow. He pitched Yavapai College to the 1986 Junior College World Series and was a Red Sox second-round pick in the last January draft.

In July 1988 Boston traded him and Brady Anderson to Baltimore for Mike Boddicker. Houston got him in a 1991 trade for Glenn Davis, and in April 1992 the Astros sent him to Philadelphia for Jason Grimsley.
He was the 1993 NLCS MVP, striking out the first five Braves in Game 1, a record. He lost Game 1 of the World Series to Toronto.
Bone spurs in his elbow cost him two months in 1994, and he tore his labrum in 1995. In 2000, unhappy with the losing Phillies, he asked to be traded and went to Arizona for four players.
He gave up a go-ahead homer in the eighth inning of Game 7 of the 2001 World Series. Randy Johnson came on in relief and got the win when Arizona rallied in the ninth.
He won World Series games for three franchises and went 11–2 in the postseason. That .846 winning percentage is the best of any pitcher with 10 or more decisions.

He started at ESPN in 2010. In 2015 the network suspended him for the rest of the season after he tweeted a meme comparing Muslim extremists to Nazis. In April 2016 ESPN fired him for an anti-transgender Facebook post. "I wasn't fired for speaking my mind; I was fired for being a conservative."
p: His father, an Army master sergeant, put a baseball glove in his crib, and the first game he ever saw was Roberto Clemente's last. His father died of brain cancer eight months before Curt's debut: "When he died, I kind of lost my family."

He and his wife, Shonda, started Curt's Pitch for ALS in 1993, giving money for every strikeout, and named their first son Gehrig. After Shonda survived melanoma they founded a skin-cancer foundation for children.

His video-game company, 38 Studios, went bankrupt after a $75 million Rhode Island loan, costing him much of his savings and leading to a state lawsuit. He also had a heart attack while working on the game, which he kept quiet for two years.

Outspoken to the end ("a man without a mute button"), he reached 71 percent of the Hall of Fame vote in 2021. He asked to be taken off the 2022 ballot; he wasn't, and his support fell to 58.6 percent.
In 1992 he married Shonda Brewer, a Towson State graduate he met while she was moonlighting at a Foot Locker. They have four children.
After the bloody sock game he wrote "K ALS" on his cleat below the wound for his World Series start, knowing the cameras would be on it.
He became a born-again Christian in 1997. He collects World War II memorabilia, including Nazi and SS uniforms: "It's not a Nazi collection. It's a collection of World War II stuff."

He testified to Congress in 2005 as an opponent of steroids, and said Roger Clemens should lose his Cy Youngs unless he could refute the PED allegations. He campaigned for George W. Bush and John McCain, joined Breitbart News in 2016, and announced a 2018 run against Elizabeth Warren, then dropped out.

Rhode Island had guaranteed a $75 million loan to 38 Studios, which promised 450 jobs. In May 2012 the company defaulted, missed payroll and laid off its staff by mass email. Schilling and the other defendants later agreed to repay the state $61 million.

c: Martinsburg had started its season on the road because its park had no fence. Baltimore's Jack Dunn bought Grove for enough to build one: "I was the only player ever traded for a fence."

Five years in the minors, he won 108 games for the Orioles. In exhibitions he told Babe Ruth "I'm not afraid of you," then struck him out in nine of 11 at-bats. Connie Mack paid $100,600, the extra $600 meant to top what the Yankees paid for Ruth.
Called the "$100,600 Lemon" after a wild rookie year, he went home and threw at a chalk mark on the barn door every morning at six. He led the league in ERA the next year.

On August 23, 1931, at 25–2 and going for a record 17th straight win, he lost 1–0 when a substitute left fielder misplayed a liner. He blamed the regular, Al Simmons, who was off getting treatment, and tore the clubhouse apart. He finished 31–4.

On July 25, 1941, Joe Cronin told him, "Pop, this is a nine-inning game. I'm not coming out to get you." He survived a 12-hit slugfest for his 300th win, helped by a two-run triple from his best friend, Jimmie Foxx.

As a boy he played with cork stoppers stuffed into wool socks and wrapped in black tape, and with fence pickets for bats. He didn't play real baseball until 17, or organized ball until 19, when a Midland storekeeper put him in town games.
Martinsburg offered him $125 a month, $50 more than his father and brothers made. He took a 30-day leave from his job and signed on May 5.

From 1920 to 1924 he went 108–36 at Baltimore and set a minor-league record with 1,108 strikeouts, but he was often wild and went 3–8 in the postseason. The Cubs and Dodgers reportedly offered $100,000, but Jack Dunn sold him to his old friend Connie Mack for $100,600.

In 1929 Mack, worried about the Cubs' right-handed hitters, didn't start him in the World Series, but Grove helped in relief. Across three straight Series (1929–31) he went 4–2 with a 1.75 ERA and two saves.

After his 16-game winning streak ended in 1931, he tried to tear the clubhouse door off, shredded the wooden partitions between lockers, broke chairs and ripped off his shirt: "giving Al Simmons hell all the while."

Hurt by poor Depression crowds, Mack traded him to the Red Sox in December 1933, with Max Bishop and Rube Walberg, for two players and $125,000. A sore arm in his first Boston spring held him to 8–8 with a 6.50 ERA.

Adjusted for his parks and leagues, his ERA was 48 percent better than average, fifth-best ever among pitchers with 1,000 innings. He threw out the first pitch at Game 4 of the 1972 World Series in Oakland.
p: He quit the coal mines after two weeks: "Dad, I didn't put that coal in here, and I hope I don't have to take no more of her out." He played his first real baseball at 17.

Once, when Cronin ordered him to walk Hank Greenberg and the next three batters singled, he threw his glove into the stands and smashed Cronin's bat. When pinch-hitter Wes Ferrell's homer won it, Grove silently rolled him a bottle of wine.

He built a bowling alley back home in Lonaconing and quietly employed his out-of-work brother and his disabled brother-in-law. In retirement he outfitted sandlot teams and paid for two youngsters' college.
At Cooperstown reunions he greeted old friends like Joe Cronin with a punch. "If he really liked you, he'd hit you both ways."
He was one of eight children. He spent $5,700 to build Lefty's Place in Lonaconing, with three bowling lanes, a pool table and a counter of cigars, candy and soda.

He married his childhood sweetheart, Ethel Gardner, in 1921 and they had two children, Robert and Doris. They divorced after he had an affair. In the 1950s he served on the Lonaconing town council and as its police chief.

In retirement he got divorced, outlived his only son and needed financial help from baseball. He paid for two young people's college. After his ex-wife died in 1960 he moved in with his daughter-in-law in Norwalk, Ohio.
He died of a heart attack in 1975 while watching a ballgame on TV.

c: In 1976, after Billy Martin left him idle in the bullpen for 47 straight games and sent him down again, he packed the car and started home to Louisiana to quit. On the drive his wife, Bonnie, told him: "Let the Yankees tell you you're no good before you think of quitting." He turned around.

George Steinbrenner told him, "Guidry, you'll never be able to pitch in this league." The Yankees nearly traded him to the White Sox for Bucky Dent, but team president Gabe Paul refused to let him go.

Sparky Lyle taught him the slider that made him. On June 17, 1978, he struck out 18 Angels, still the Yankee record. A fan's sign that night read "Louisiana Lightning," and Phil Rizzuto made it stick.
He finished 1978 at 25–3 with a 1.74 ERA and nine shutouts, and won the one-game playoff at Fenway (the Bucky Dent game).
In 1979 he volunteered to go to the bullpen when Goose Gossage hurt his thumb: "The team comes first."
Tendinitis cost him most of his junior year of college, and the Yankees took him in the third round in 1971 on the advice of scout Atley Donald.
On the drive home in 1976, his wife, Bonnie, asked him, "Are you sure you want to give up on everything you've been working toward for the last 10 years?" He stuck with it.
In June 1976 the Yankees almost included him in a deadline deal with Baltimore. They held him back only because they didn't want to give up a fourth left-hander.

His break came on April 30, 1977, when Mike Torrez hadn't reached the team in time for his first start and Guidry made an emergency start, shutting out Seattle. He won the World Series that year and again in 1978, both against the Dodgers.
In Game 4 of the 1978 ALCS he struck out seven in eight innings and beat Kansas City 2–1 to send the Yankees to the World Series.
After the 1981 season he signed for four years and $3.95 million. His last postseason was the 1981 World Series against the Dodgers.
He went on the disabled list for the first time with a rib injury. A bone spur in his elbow limited him in 1988 and needed surgery.
He was Joe Torre's pitching coach in 2006 and 2007, replacing Mel Stottlemyre. When Torre left, Joe Girardi didn't keep him.
p: A Cajun from Lafayette, he grew up hunting and fishing the bayous. On the mound he'd mutter "Pas bon" after a bad pitch, and he kept Louisiana coffee stocked in New York. With Cajun teammate Ray Fontenot he talked in French.
As a boy he sneaked off to a ballfield on his way to his grandmother's and threw a stray ball back so hard that a coach came running. "I thought I had done something wrong."
After 1983 he found that his agent and close friend had squandered nearly all his money. He worked out deals with his creditors and avoided bankruptcy.
His brother Travis, born 17 years after him, has an intellectual disability, and Guidry gave years to the Special Olympics: "He's the one who has made the truly significant achievements."
He married Bonnie Rutledge on September 23, 1972. They had three children, Jamie, Danielle and Brandon.
His company, Ron Guidry Enterprises, had invested in a Long Island photo studio, a cleaning-equipment business, a tool company and real estate.
He and teammate Fontenot often talked in French until Fontenot was traded after 1984. Yogi Berra's locker was next to his.
The book Yogi: Yogi Berra, Ron Guidry, and Baseball's Greatest Gift tells the story of their friendship.

c: At UCLA he was the school's first four-letter man, averaging 11 yards a carry in football, leading the conference in basketball scoring, and winning the NCAA long jump. Baseball was probably his weakest sport.
As an Army lieutenant at Fort Hood in 1944 he refused a bus driver's order to move to the back. He was court-martialed and acquitted. The episode helped put him at the top of Branch Rickey's list.

When his signing was announced, The Sporting News called him a Class C player, and Bob Feller said he had "football shoulders and couldn't hit an inside pitch." Robinson and Feller went into the Hall of Fame together in 1962.
He stole home 19 times, including Game 1 of the 1955 World Series. Leo Durocher said he "didn't just come to play. He came to beat you."
On the last day of 1951 he saved the Dodgers' season with a diving catch and won it with a homer in the 14th, forcing the playoff that ended with Bobby Thomson's home run.

Traded to the Giants after 1956, he had already secretly agreed to announce his retirement in Look magazine, and he did. He struck out in his last at-bat, but Yogi Berra dropped strike three and had to throw him out.

After UCLA he coached for the National Youth Administration, played semipro football with the Los Angeles Bulldogs, and in the fall of 1941 played pro football for the Honolulu Bears. He left Hawaii just after Pearl Harbor and was drafted in 1942.

Boxer Joe Louis, stationed at the same base, intervened to get a decision against him reversed. Still, he wasn't allowed on the segregated base baseball team, and he was so angry that he refused to play football even when officers pressured him.
After the Army he coached a college basketball team in 1944–45. His teams were outmatched, but he was known as a disciplinarian, and future Globetrotter Marques Haynes admired him.

He had rickets as a child and walked pigeon-toed. A sore arm made him look bad in his first spring training, in 1946, but he led Montreal to the International League pennant by 19½ games and won the Little World Series.

Just before his rookie year, his champion Leo Durocher was suspended for the season for associating with gamblers. In Cincinnati he got death threats. The story that Pee Wee Reese put an arm around him there is often told but undocumented.
In 1954, at 35, he stole second, third and home in a single trip, the first National Leaguer to do it in 26 years.
He won his only title in 1955, though he sat out Game 7, and he ended his career by striking out to end Game 7 of the 1956 Series. He played in six World Series and six All-Star Games.
The trade to the Giants was for Dick Littlefield and $35,000. Unknown to the Dodgers, he had already agreed to become an executive at Chock full o'Nuts.
p: When his family moved into a white Pasadena neighborhood, neighbors petitioned to get rid of them. His brother Mack finished second to Jesse Owens in the 1936 Olympic 200, then lost his job as a city janitor when Pasadena fired Black employees rather than integrate its pool.
His middle name honored Theodore Roosevelt, who died 25 days before he was born.
In 1959 he refused to leave the whites-only waiting room at the Greenville, South Carolina, airport. A march followed on New Year's Day, and the airport was desegregated soon after.
His son Jackie Jr. was wounded in Vietnam, fought drug addiction, got clean and became a counselor, then died in a car crash in 1971 at 24.

He was the youngest of five children of sharecroppers. His mother worked as a domestic, and leftovers from the families she worked for were often what they ate. He got into scrapes with white boys and had some run-ins with the police.

His brother Mack, after Olympic stardom and college,, could only find work as a Pasadena janitor. When a judge opened the city pool to Black residents, the city fired its Black employees, Mack included.
He and Rachel were married in Los Angeles on February 10, 1946.

In 1964 he helped found Freedom National Bank, a Black-owned bank in Harlem. He worked for Nelson Rockefeller as special assistant for community affairs, but broke with the Republicans in 1968 to back Hubert Humphrey against Nixon.
After retiring he was diagnosed with diabetes, which his brothers also had.

c: Watching him in high school, Seattle's scouting director asked which tree his home run hit. "Roger, it went over the trees." He had failed the Mariners' psychological test, the worst score they'd ever seen, so the scout retook it with him at home. He signed cheaply to be the No. 1 pick: "I'll make up for that later. Let's be No. 1."

At the end of his first spring, manager Jim Lefebvre spent five minutes on how tough the roster decisions were before telling him, "You're my starting center fielder." Days later teammates told him the club had traded for Dale Murphy to play center. It was April Fools' Day.
A Seattle company sold nearly a million Ken Griffey Jr. candy bars in his rookie year. He was allergic to chocolate.

On September 14, 1990, his father, now a teammate, homered off Kirk McCaskill in the first inning, and Junior followed with a home run on a 3–0 pitch. "It's about time," his dad told him in the dugout.
In 2007 he asked the commissioner and Rachel Robinson for permission to wear 42 on Jackie Robinson Day. Bud Selig opened it to every player, and the tradition began.

In June 2010, after reports that he had been asleep in the clubhouse when needed to pinch-hit, he packed up in the middle of the night and drove across the country home to Florida. He never played again.

Mariners owner George Argyros had made his own chauffeur, Mooney, a scout, and Mooney was the one covering Griffey's area. Ownership was wary of drafting another high schooler after its 1986 first-rounder flopped. Bobby Cox called Griffey the best prospect he'd ever seen.
In the minors, the teenage sons of the team bus driver reportedly shouted racial slurs at him, and one allegedly threatened him with a gun.
On July 25, 1989, he broke his right hand. The team said he fell coming out of the shower; club officials later admitted he had punched a hotel-room wall during a fight with a girlfriend.
In late August 1990 the Reds released his father, and Seattle signed him partly so Junior would have him around. On August 31 they became the first father and son to play in a game for the same team.
