In the 1995 Division Series against the Yankees he slid home with the winning run and came up into a pile of teammates. He said he would never play for the Yankees, who he said had treated his father badly.
After the reports that he had been asleep, teammate Mike Sweeney offered to fight anyone who said so, and his manager denied it, but Griffey never did.
Bill Simmons wrote that he was the 1990s slugger everyone was sure had never used steroids, the one whose fall would devastate a generation.
p: He was born in Donora, Pennsylvania, on Stan Musial's birthday, 49 years later. When his father was a Yankee, Billy Martin had the Griffey kids thrown out of the clubhouse, and Junior vowed never to play for New York: "I don't forget things like that."
At 17, depressed and fighting with his father, he swallowed 277 aspirin and ended up in intensive care. He moved into his own place, and slowly father and son came to understand each other.
Back in Seattle in 2007 for the first time since his trade, he got a four-minute standing ovation. "I met my beautiful wife here. Two out of my three kids were born here. This place will be home."
In retirement he is a licensed pilot and a credentialed sports photographer who has shot MLB, NFL and IndyCar events and the Masters.
He was raised mostly by his mother and grandmother and was often homesick. As a boy he was in the clubhouse when his father won the 1975 and 1976 World Series with the Reds.
He and his wife, Melissa, have three children: Trey, who played football, Taryn and Tevin.
Deals with Nike and Nintendo made him one of the most marketable athletes alive, and some credit him with helping baseball recover after the 1994 strike.

c: Every team passed on him in the early rounds of 1999. Tampa Bay's scout swore he'd hit 40 homers in the majors and quit when the club passed. The Cardinals took him in the 13th round and offered $10,000; he waited and got $60,000.
In his first junior-college game he hit a grand slam off future big leaguer Mark Buehrle and turned an unassisted triple play at shortstop.

In 2001 spring training Mark McGwire told Tony La Russa that leaving Pujols off the team "might be one of the worst moves you make in your career." La Russa said management had decided to keep him even before Bobby Bonilla got hurt.
Facing elimination in Game 5 of the 2005 NLCS, he hit a ninth-inning three-run homer off Brad Lidge to win it.
In Game 3 of the 2011 World Series he had five hits, three home runs and six RBIs. He then left St. Louis for the Angels.

Back with the Cardinals at 42 in 2022, he had seven home runs by early August, then hit 17 in his last 136 at-bats to reach 703. His final homer came off Mitch Keller, a record 458th pitcher he'd taken deep.
Doubts about his age, his build and his position scared teams off. The Cardinals first offered a $10,000 bonus and raised it to $60,000 after he finished a summer league.

As a high schooler he hit .449 with 11 homers and won a state title his first season. The next year opposing coaches, who thought he was older than 18, walked him 55 times, and he hit eight homers in 33 at-bats.
In 2003, with a damaged ligament in his elbow, he won his only batting title with two hits on the last day, beating Todd Helton by .0002.
After the 2003 season he signed for seven years and $100 million. In 2004 he moved to first base for good, and St. Louis won 105 games and the pennant.
After the 2009 season he had five bone spurs removed from his right elbow. In June 2011 a collision broke his left wrist, but he was back in two weeks.
He turned down a nine-year, $198 million extension before 2011, then signed with the Angels for 10 years and $254 million, plus a personal-services deal.

In 2013 Jack Clark said on a radio show that Pujols had used performance-enhancing drugs in St. Louis. Pujols said he had never failed a test and sued Clark for defamation, and he dropped the suit when Clark retracted.
The Angels released him in May 2021, hitting .198. He signed with the Dodgers a week later.
In 2024 he managed Escogido in the Dominican winter league and won the 2025 Caribbean Series. In 2026 he became president of baseball operations for the Estrellas Orientales.
p: Raised mostly by his grandmother in Santo Domingo, he played with limes for balls and a milk carton for a glove. He often carried his father home drunk after softball games, and never drank or smoked himself.
Soon after moving to New York at 16, he saw a shooting at a bodega, and the family left for Independence, Missouri. He spoke no English when he started at Fort Osage High.

On their first date, Deidre told him she had an infant daughter with Down syndrome. He adopted Isabella after they married, and at the Cardinals' annual Buddy Walk game for children with Down syndrome he once homered in his first three at-bats.
He scored a perfect 100 on his U.S. citizenship test in 2007.
"I don't want to be remembered as the best baseball player ever. I want to be remembered as a great guy who loved the Lord, loved to serve the community and who gave back."
His parents divorced when he was 3, and his mother left; he has rarely spoken of her. His father painted and did odd jobs.

He met Deidre Corona at a Latin dance club in high school, and they married on January 1, 2000. The wedding cost $150, and they honeymooned in Peoria, where he started in the minors. They had four children together.
In 2022, just before opening day, he divorced Deidre days after she had brain surgery. In early 2023 he married Nicole Fernández, the daughter of former Dominican president Leonel Fernández.

In 2023 the Angels hired him under a 10-year personal-services contract, and he became an MLB Network analyst. He also became global ambassador, and reportedly a part owner, of Baseball United, a league in the Middle East and South Asia.

c: At Stetson he was a light-hitting shortstop (.263 career) with a strong arm. He didn't pitch until his junior year, and the Mets took him in the ninth round. He needed Tommy John surgery after six pro starts.
He was called up in 2014 to pitch in relief and only started because Dillon Gee got hurt. He was Rookie of the Year.
In the 2015 All-Star Game he struck out the three batters he faced on 10 pitches, the first to do it since pitch counts were kept.

His agent, Brodie Van Wagenen, pushed the Mets for an extension in 2018. Then the Mets hired Van Wagenen as general manager, and in 2019 he signed deGrom to a five-year, $137.5 million deal from the other side of the table.
On April 23, 2021, he struck out 15 Nationals in a two-hit shutout with no walks, went 2-for-4 at the plate, and set a record with 50 strikeouts in his first four starts.
Scouts first noticed him when he pitched against Chris Sale of Florida Gulf Coast. The Mets gave him a $95,000 bonus.

Six starts into his pro career he tore his elbow ligament, and after four months of trying rehab he had Tommy John surgery in October 2010. He missed 2011, and while he recovered Johan Santana taught him a changeup.
In 2015 he tied Tom Seaver's Mets postseason record with 13 strikeouts in Game 1 of the Division Series. He lost Game 2 of the World Series to Kansas City.
In 2016 he refused, at first, to sign for the $607,000 the Mets assigned him, but the rules gave him no choice. That September he had surgery on his ulnar nerve for numbness in his fingers.
In 2019 he got a $17 million salary in arbitration, the biggest raise ever for an arbitration-eligible player.
A stress reaction in his shoulder blade cost him the start of 2022. After the season he opted out and signed with Texas for five years and $185 million.
He tore his elbow ligament again in 2023 and needed a second Tommy John surgery. The Rangers won the World Series without him. He returned in September 2024, 504 days after his last start.
He won his 100th game in June 2026. At that year's deadline he reportedly used his no-trade clause to block a deal, rumored to be with the Braves.
p: His father, an AT&T lineman, built a batting cage in the backyard and taught him to stay humble. Jacob grew up a Braves fan in DeLeon Springs, Florida, and still lives there.

His long hair spawned the hashtag #hairwego and a Citi Field 'deGrom Hair Hat' giveaway. He vowed never to cut it after a hitter said it hid the ball, then cut it anyway, saying it might add speed to his fastball.
In high school he was a District 9 Class 1A basketball player of the year.
He met his wife, Stacey, soon after high school. They married in November 2014, live in DeLeon Springs, and have a son and a daughter.

c: Mindful of Sandy Koufax's arm trouble, his father wouldn't let him throw a curve until he was about 14, so Bert imagined Vin Scully describing Koufax's curve instead.

His father built him a mound in the backyard with a canvas backdrop over the horseshoe pits. "I would go back there and just throw and throw and throw until I developed it, and it became my curveball."
He debuted at 19 in 1970, the first Dutch-born major leaguer. The first batter he faced homered on a 3–2 pitch; he gave up nothing else for seven innings and won 2–1.
In 1973 he set Twins records with 9 shutouts, 25 complete games and 258 strikeouts and finished seventh in the Cy Young voting. Catfish Hunter said, "The best pitcher in the league is Bert Blyleven."

In 1986 he gave up a record 50 home runs, 31 of them in the Metrodome, where "the ball carries." The record-breaker came from Jay Bell, who had been traded for Blyleven and hit his first pitch in his major-league debut.
Accused of not winning big games, he beat the 98-win Tigers twice in the 1987 ALCS and won his fifth straight postseason decision in the World Series as the Twins took the title.
He got just 17.5 percent of the Hall of Fame vote in his first year and climbed to 79.7 percent in 2011 as new statistics revealed how good he had been.
The Twins took him in the third round in 1969, and scouts Jesse Flores Sr. and Dick Wiencek signed him at his family's house for about $15,000.
He was called up in 1970 when Luis Tiant, then 6–0, fractured his shoulder. In that year's ALCS against Baltimore, Bill Rigney started Tom Hall instead, and Blyleven only pitched in relief.

In 1972 he had lost 12 of 15 decisions by mid-August. Rigney had been fired, and the new staff found he was landing on his left heel and not following through. He finished with a 1.45 ERA over his last nine starts.

In 1976 he fought owner Calvin Griffith over his $65,200 salary and wouldn't sign. On June 1 the Twins traded him to Texas for four players, two days after the Rangers agreed to give him three years and $550,000.

In September 1977, two weeks after a groin injury, he no-hit the Angels in his last start for the Rangers. After he gave the finger to a camera during a rare national broadcast, Texas sent him to Pittsburgh in December in the first four-team trade in major-league history, with 11 players changing teams.
He won the 1979 World Series with the Pirates. In Cleveland he fought injuries, then finished third in the Cy Young voting in 1984 and 1985. Back with the Twins, he reached 3,000 strikeouts in 1986.
He was a Twins TV commentator from 1996 to 2020, and pitching coach for the Netherlands in several World Baseball Classics.
p: He didn't know his own name until he was about to marry: he had always thought it was "Rikaalbert." It turned out to be Rik Aalbert Blijleven.
He was called the "Frying Dutchman" for setting teammates' shoelaces on fire. The Angels' clubhouse extinguisher read: "In case of Blyleven: Pull."

His parents married in the Nazi-occupied Netherlands and emigrated to Canada and then California. He credited their "stubbornness and determination" in his Hall of Fame speech. His father learned baseball from Dodgers radio and argued every ball and strike at Bert's games.
He was the third of seven children. His father, a carpenter, learned baseball from Dodgers radio broadcasts, came to every game, and argued balls and strikes so much that umpires and fans got angry.
He married Patricia Ann Whitehead in July 1971. They had four children, Todd, Tim, Kimberly and Tom.
Todd pitched in the minors from 1993 to 1997 and later scouted for the Diamondbacks and Rockies.
He played himself in the 1990 James Belushi movie Taking Care of Business. On a 2006 broadcast he forgot the movie's name, and a technician in the booth had to remind him.

c: He quit school at 14 to work beside his father in a Clinton, Massachusetts, textile mill. At 5-foot-6 with thick, powerful legs, he saw speed as his ticket out.

In 1894 he scored 198 runs, a record never seriously challenged, and reached base in more than half his plate appearances. Officially he hit .399, one hit short of .400; later researchers found the missing hits and put him at .403.

His slides earned him the name 'Sliding Billy'. One Cleveland third baseman, Chippy McGarr, got so angry that he picked Hamilton up, carried him to the stands and threw him over the railing into the seats.
He scored 1,697 runs in 1,594 games, the highest rate ever, and no modern player has come close.
At 38, managing in the minors at Haverhill in 1904, he won the batting title by hitting .412 and led the league in steals and runs.
Worcester sold him to the Kansas City Cowboys in July 1888, and in January 1890 the Cowboys, who were folding, sold him to the Phillies for $5,000.
He chased fly balls well enough but dropped a lot of them, and threw poorly.
In November 1895 the Phillies traded him to Boston for Billy Nash in one of the worst deals in the club's history. Frank Selee put him at leadoff and let him run as he pleased.
In 1899 he wrenched his knee sliding, damaged a tendon and missed much of the season. His career was in danger, but at 34 he played all of 1900 and hit .333.
He scouted for Boston in 1911 and 1912, managed Fall River and Springfield, and sold his share of a club in 1917 and left the game for good.
p: Bill James wrote that he left behind "no legend, no stories, no anecdotes," and that he reached the Hall of Fame in 1961 purely on his numbers. Three of his children accepted for him, 21 years after his death.
He was fiercely proud of his steals. In 1937 he wrote to The Sporting News: "I was and will be the greatest base stealer of all time... if they ever re-count the record I will get my just reward."
After baseball he worked as a foreman at a Worcester leather plant into the early 1930s.
His parents were Scottish immigrants, and he was born in Newark. He was proud of his Scottish ancestry all his life.
He married Rebecca Carr in 1888 and they had four daughters, Ethel, Mildred, Ruth and Dorothy.
He had heart disease after retiring from the factory, spent most of his last year in bed, and died at home in Worcester in 1940. Rebecca lived until 1957.

c: He lied about his age to join the Army at 15 and starred as a pitcher for the 24th Infantry in the Philippines. Back home with the Indianapolis ABCs in 1915, he threw a three-hit shutout in his first game.

In an October 1915 exhibition against white major leaguers he ran in from center field and punched the white umpire during a scuffle, setting off chaos as fans and police poured onto the field. He was arrested and later apologized publicly.
He played so shallow in center, just behind second base, that he was almost an extra infielder. After one game-saving catch in 1920, fans ran onto the field and showered him with money.

In 1925 he hit .427 with 20 home runs for Harrisburg. That October, in an exhibition against a team that included young Lou Gehrig, he went 4-for-6 with a homer. In Cuba fans called him "El Terror de los Clubs."

As manager of the Pittsburgh Crawfords he brought in Satchel Paige and Josh Gibson. Once, furious at an umpire, he put himself in to pitch and walked six straight batters to show he considered the game a farce.
Branch Rickey hired him in 1945 to manage the Brooklyn Brown Dodgers and to scout Black players, including Roy Campanella.

After the 1915 brawl he and teammate DeMoss were arrested and jailed, then got out on bail and went straight to Cuba for winter ball. The ABCs sent him to the Lincoln Giants in New York until things cooled down.
In 1918 he left the ABCs for the Colored Officers' Training program during World War I. The war ended before he was commissioned, and he was discharged that December.

In 1921 he signed with the St. Louis Giants for $400 a month, the league's top salary. He clipped an article saying he was worth more than Rogers Hornsby or Babe Ruth, and led the league in home runs.

In December 1922 the ABCs traded him to Rube Foster's American Giants. Foster, worried about league balance, then paid the ABCs a subsidy to keep him one more year. When Indianapolis folded, he went to Harrisburg as player-manager instead of Chicago.
With Harrisburg in 1924 he reportedly had 36 home runs by August 24.
He credited the late ABCs owner Taylor with teaching him how to manage.
His younger brother Bennie played alongside him on the 1932 Pittsburgh Crawfords.
p: His middle name, McKinley, came from his Republican parents, who named him after the party's 1896 presidential nominee. As a boy he was a batboy for the ABCs.
Legends had him yanking the hood off a Klansman and throwing a pro wrestler off a train. He neither drank nor smoked, and he clipped every article that compared him to Ty Cobb for his scrapbook.
He fell down the stairs at home in 1954 and died days later at 57. He lies in Indianapolis under a plain military headstone that says nothing about his baseball career.
He was the seventh of 11 children. He clocked 23 seconds in the 220-yard dash in the Army, and offseasons he worked as a grocery clerk and a chauffeur.
In January 1917 he married Hazel Grubbs, the teenage daughter of a school principal. They separated within a year and divorced in 1921.

In November 1922 he married Jane Blalock Howard, a Harrisburg widow, and they honeymooned in Cuba while he played winter ball. She didn't like baseball, and newspapers reported him out with other women. After a car crash he walked away from, the Pittsburgh Courier wrote that he "wiggled out of some love tangles the same, same way."
He and Jane separated in 1940. He filed for divorce in 1941, but the case was dismissed; she didn't believe in divorce. He left no children.

c: His mother pitched to him and his father shagged flies. If he hit one up the middle near his mother, he got extra chores, so he learned to pull. He signed with the Braves a few minutes after midnight on his graduation night, taking less money because he and his father had studied rosters and figured Boston would need a third baseman soon.
Ty Cobb, watching him as an 18-year-old minor leaguer: "I've only known three or four perfect swings in my time. This lad has one of them."
A poor fielder at first, he took 50 to 100 grounders a day in spring training, knocking them down with his chest. He broke his nose three times.

Hitting .091 in the 1957 World Series, he won Game 4 with a 10th-inning home run when the Yankees pitched to him rather than face Hank Aaron on deck. He ended the Series by backhanding Moose Skowron's grounder with the bases loaded and stepping on third.
As Braves manager in 1974 he planned to sit Aaron in Cincinnati so the record could fall in Atlanta. Commissioner Bowie Kuhn threatened to suspend him if Aaron didn't play.

On his first day with the Tigers in 1967 he found "We'll win it despite Mayo" on the clubhouse chalkboard, erased it, and lectured the team about backing their manager. A year later he retired a World Series champion.

Rules said he couldn't sign until he graduated from high school, so he and Braves scout Johnny Moore waited until a few minutes after midnight on graduation night in 1949. Other teams offered more, but he and his father figured third baseman Bob Elliott would be gone in a few years, and in 1952 Mathews beat him out for the job.
The Navy drafted him during the Korean War, but after a few months he got a hardship discharge as the sole support of his family while his father was ill.

In 1962 he tore the ligaments in his right shoulder swinging at a high pitch from Dick Farrell. That year he hit 29 home runs, ending a nine-year streak of 30 or more, and he was never as dangerous again.
The Braves traded him to Houston after the 1966 season, and in August 1967 the Astros sent him to the Tigers for a player to be named later, after an injury to Detroit's Don Wert.

In 1968 he led the Tigers' charge in what umpire Ed Runge called "the best fight I have ever seen on a baseball field," punching Oakland's Jack Aker in the cheekbone. In July he had surgery for a ruptured disk and was expected to retire. Instead he came back, made the World Series roster, and started Game 4 at third base.
The Braves fired him as manager in July 1974, with the team 50–49. He later coached and scouted for the Rangers, Brewers and A's.
p: He was famous for his fists. He hit Frank Robinson with three punches "that not even Muhammad Ali could have stopped," Warren Spahn said, and told Lew Burdette, "Let the son of a gun charge you and get the hell out of the way."

Married four times and a hard drinker, he admitted in his autobiography that alcohol cost him several jobs, including managing the Braves. In 1996 he fell between a boat and a pier and never fully recovered.
At his Hall of Fame induction he said, "I'm just a beat-up old third baseman."
After his playing career the Tigers offered him a scouting job, but he went into business instead.
He married Virjean Lauby in 1954 and they divorced in 1970. After a second marriage ended, he married Elizabeth Busch Burke, Gussie Busch's daughter, in 1977.
In 1982, while working as a minor-league instructor for Oakland, he was found to have a spot on his lung. It wasn't cancer but tuberculosis, and after treatment he went back to work.
He died of complications from pneumonia in La Jolla in 2001 and was buried in Santa Barbara, where his high school field bears his name.

c: He went to work in a South Carolina textile mill at 6 or 7 and never went to school. A local fan made him a 48-ounce hickory bat darkened with tobacco juice. He called it "Black Betsy" and carried it to the majors.

The nickname came from a single 1908 minor-league game he played in his stocking feet because new spikes hadn't been broken in. "That was the only day I ever played in my stockinged feet, but it stuck with me."
He signed his first contract with an X. Homesick and teased by Athletics teammates for not being able to read, he twice jumped the team and went home to Greenville.

He hit .408 as a rookie in 1911 and .395 the next year and lost the batting title to Cobb both times. "What a hell of a league this is... I ain't won nothing yet!" Babe Ruth said he copied Jackson's swing: "His is the perfectest."

By his own later admission he took $5,000 to help fix the 1919 World Series. He hit .375 and tried to tell Charles Comiskey afterward, waiting outside his office for hours, but Comiskey wouldn't see him.
The famous "Say it ain't so, Joe" was, Jackson said, made up by a reporter: "It just didn't happen, that's all."
The Greenville Spinners signed him for $75 a month, much more than the $45 he was making at the mill and playing ball. "I'll play my head off for $75 a month."
He started as a pitcher, until he accidentally broke another player's arm with a fastball.
Connie Mack bought him in August 1908 for a reported $900 and traded him to Cleveland in July 1910 for Bris Lord and $6,000.
A broken leg cost him 35 games in 1914. Cleveland's owner, Charles Somers, fired manager Joe Birmingham after Birmingham blamed a sore arm Jackson got trying first base on the position switch.
In 1915, with the Federal League reportedly offering $10,000 a year, the near-bankrupt Somers extended his contract and traded him to the White Sox for $31,500 and three players.
In the 1917 World Series he hit .304, made a circus catch to save Game 1, and used his $3,669 winner's share to buy an Oldsmobile.
In 1918 his draft board revoked his deferment. Instead of reporting for induction, he took a job at a Delaware shipyard building battleships and playing ball in a factory league.
In the 1919 Series he set a record with 12 hits, made no errors and threw a runner out at the plate. He hit .286 in the games Chicago lost and .545 in the games it won.
p: He married 15-year-old Katie Wynn in 1908. For 43 years she wrote his letters, managed his money and read his contracts.
In the 1914–15 offseason he toured the South in a vaudeville show and enjoyed it so much he threatened to quit baseball for the stage. Katie filed for divorce, though they soon reconciled.

"All the big sportswriters seemed to enjoy writing about me as an ignorant cotton-mill boy... I was able to fool a lot of pitchers and managers and club owners I wouldn't have been able to fool if they'd thought I was smarter."

Banned for life, he played outlaw ball in the South until nearly 50, then ran a liquor store and restaurant near the Greenville mill. He died two weeks before he was to appear on Ed Sullivan's TV show.
He was the oldest of eight children. His father moved the family into a company house at Greenville's Brandon Mill, which paid $1.25 a day.

He couldn't read menus, so in restaurants he waited for teammates to order and asked for something he'd heard. His wife often signed for him, so autographs proven to be his own bring a premium; one sold for $23,500 in 1990.
In 1922 he and Katie moved to Savannah and opened a dry-cleaning business. For about 20 years he played for and managed semipro teams in Georgia and South Carolina under assumed names.
Ty Cobb and Grantland Rice once came into his liquor store, and he gave no sign that he knew Cobb. Cobb finally asked, "Don't you know me, Joe?"
He died of a heart attack in 1951, at 64, the first of the eight banned players to die.

c: He was so small as a freshman (5-foot-1, 105 pounds) that the JV coach wanted to cut him. As a teen he would rather bum around Redondo Beach than practice, and he said that without baseball he'd probably have been a bartender. He showed up to his first pro team in beach clothes and was told to wear shoes and a shirt next time.

Hitting barely .200 in 1974, he started working daily with hitting coach Charley Lau. When he skipped a session, Lau called him a "mullet head," and "Mullet" stuck. He never missed again. He switched to number 5 for Brooks Robinson.

He won the 1976 batting title on the last day when Steve Brye let his routine fly ball fall for an inside-the-park homer. Teammate Hal McRae, who lost the title, accused Brye of racism. Brett said he'd gladly have split the award.
In the 1977 ALCS, after he slid hard into third, Graig Nettles kicked him in the face, and Brett came up swinging. In 1978 he hit three home runs off Catfish Hunter in one playoff game.

The Pine Tar Game, July 24, 1983: his ninth-inning homer off Goose Gossage was disallowed because of too much pine tar on his bat, and he charged out of the dugout in a rage. The league reinstated the homer on appeal.

In 1990, at 37 and hitting .267 at the break, he hit .388 the rest of the way and won his third batting title in a third different decade. On his 3,000th-hit night he was picked off first by umpire Tim McClelland, the same umpire from the Pine Tar Game.

Many scouts passed on him because of his baby fat. The Royals took him in the second round in 1971, helped perhaps by the fact that his high school coach and the Royals' Lou Gorman had served in the Navy together.
He debuted on August 2, 1973, filling in for the injured Paul Schaal. The next April the Royals traded Schaal to the Angels and the job was his.
In the 1976 ALCS, his first postseason, he made two errors in the first inning of Game 1. He homered in Game 5, but Chris Chambliss's ninth-inning homer sent the Yankees to the Series.

After the 1978 ALCS, Whitey Herzog let Charley Lau go, and the Yankees hired him right away. Brett started 1979 with a right thumb he had broken in a charity basketball game, but still led the league with 212 hits and 20 triples.

In 1980 the Royals finally swept the Yankees, who had beaten them in three straight ALCS. He hit .375 in the World Series, missing part of it for minor surgery and homering in his first game back, but the Phillies won in six.
In 43 postseason games he hit .337 with 10 homers, and he won the 1985 World Series.
After retiring he became a Royals vice president, and in 2013 he was interim hitting coach for two months.
p: At 14 he watched from the stands as his brother Ken pitched in the 1967 World Series at 19. In Ken's last big-league game, in 1981, George was his teammate and homered. All four Brett boys played pro ball.
His father, a wounded World War II veteran and Mattel accountant, was hardest on George, the one who seemed lazy.
A lifelong bachelor as a player, he married Leslie Davenport in 1992. He turned down big money to play another year: "The game deserves better than that."
He raised money for ALS research in memory of his friend Keith Worthington, who died of the disease in 1984.
His father dropped out of high school to work in a factory, then earned a business degree at Pace and became Mattel's accountant. His mother was a bookkeeper for a furniture company.
As a boy his favorite players were Mickey Mantle, Carl Yastrzemski and Brooks Robinson. He broke his wrist and sat out his freshman season.

His brother Bobby signed with the Royals too, and he, Bobby and Ken ran a glove and equipment company, Brett Bros., until Ken died in 2003. He also lent his name to a restaurant on Kansas City's Country Club Plaza.
He and Leslie live in Mission Hills, Kansas, and have three sons, Jackson, Dylan and Robin.
On the TV show Brockmire he played himself, dating and then marrying Jules, Brockmire's love interest, before the two divorced.

c: His father played catch with him daily from age 4, built arc lights in the barn so they could throw on winter nights, and in 1931 built a ballpark on the Iowa farm, Oak View Park, that sometimes drew 1,000 fans. His Legion catcher was future Heisman winner Nile Kinnick.

Cleveland signed him at 16 for $1 and an autographed baseball. In his first exhibition, at 17, he struck out Leo Durocher on three fastballs. "I feel like a clay pigeon in a shooting gallery," Durocher told the umpire.

Giants shortstop Dick Bartell said in 1937 spring training that Feller wasn't so fast. Feller then struck him out 16 times in 19 tries as the teams barnstormed north. Time put the 18-year-old on its cover.
Game 1 of the 1948 World Series: he and Johnny Sain were scoreless in the eighth when Feller picked Phil Masi off second by a foot, but umpire Bill Stewart called him safe. Masi scored the only run.
Left off the 1951 All-Star team by Casey Stengel, he threw his third no-hitter the day after the team was announced.

He had secretly signed with Cleveland's Cy Slapnicka in July 1935, tipped off by a Des Moines semipro umpire. When at least eight scouts watched him at the national amateur tournament in Dayton that September, he had to turn down their bonus offers.

To keep him out of sight, the Indians shifted his contract to the New Orleans Pelicans and listed him as voluntarily retired while he finished the school term. Then Landis looked into alleged irregularities in the signing, called Feller and his father to Chicago, and threatened to make him a free agent.
A sore arm wrecked much of 1937, and the Associated Press named him "flop of the year." Cleveland still raised his salary to $17,500, in line with Joe DiMaggio's.
After the 1936 and 1937 seasons he barnstormed against Satchel Paige and other Negro league stars.
After his Navy service on the Alabama, he took over the Great Lakes Naval Training Station team from Mickey Cochrane in 1945 and threw a 10-strikeout no-hitter in front of 10,000 sailors.
In 1954 Al López never gave him a start as the Giants swept Cleveland in the World Series. His real last chance at a Series win, he said, had been 1948.
Hank Greenberg offered him his release or a front-office job. He retired that December to keep selling insurance.
p: He finished high school after his rookie year in the majors, and his flight home for graduation in 1937 made national news.
He lost almost four prime seasons to World War II, serving in the Navy as a chief petty officer aboard the battleship USS Alabama.
His wife, Virginia, became addicted to barbiturates and amphetamines after the war. For the last decade of his career he hid it, hiring a live-in maid for their three sons. They divorced in 1971.

He was the first president of the players' association, and criticized the reserve clause on national TV in 1957. He threw a ball every day into his 80s and pitched in an exhibition at Cooperstown at 90.
His mother, Lena, was a schoolteacher and registered nurse, and his father, William, was a farmer.

He started dating Virginia Winther, the daughter of a wealthy Chicago family who was at college near the Indians' spring camp in Fort Myers, in 1941. His father died in January 1943, and as his father had wanted, he married her anyway and went back to his ship.
He and Virginia had three sons and divorced in 1971; she kept the house they had built. He later lived with his second wife, Anne, in Gates Mills, outside Cleveland.
He was among the first stars to sign at memorabilia shows, and one ESPN writer guessed he had signed more autographs than anyone alive.
In a 2007 interview, published as he entered hospice in 2010, he said, "They overhyped Jackie Robinson." He died of complications from leukemia at 92.

c: On September 5, 1938, with the Mexican League pennant at stake, he dueled Satchel Paige for eight innings at 1–1. After Paige wilted in the heat, Dihigo homered over the center-field wall to win it. That season he went 18–2 with a 0.92 ERA, led the league in hitting at .387, and managed the team.
He started out as a skinny 17-year-old infielder who hit .179 and couldn't touch a curve. He practiced against curveballs in batting practice until he hit .386 and led the Negro league in home runs.
At the Havana ballpark he took on a jai alai player in a throwing contest. The jai alai player's sling reached the center-field fence on a bounce; Dihigo, throwing from home plate, hit it on the fly.

He once jogged a ball in from the outfield, politely asked the runner on second if he could straighten the base, and tagged him out when he stepped off. He threw no-hitters in Mexico, Venezuela and Puerto Rico.
Buck Leonard: "You take your Ruths, Cobbs, and DiMaggios. Give me Dihigo and I bet I'd beat you almost every time."
Buck Leonard said one of his home runs at Pittsburgh's Greenlee Field went over 500 feet and landed on the roof of a hospital next door.
In Cuba he hit .344 in 1926 and .413 in 1927, then .450 after he was traded from Habana to Marianao halfway through that season.
From 1931 to 1935 he played in Venezuela, mostly for Concordia, the club owned by a son of the dictator Juan Vicente Gómez. He was player-manager of the New York Cubans in 1935 and 1936.
As a player or manager he won league titles in Cuba in 1936 and 1937 and in Mexico in 1942. He managed Caracas in the 1953 Caribbean Series.
When he retired he became a radio announcer for the Cuban Winter League.
Al Campanis told Jaime Jarrín that Dihigo was the best player he had ever seen.
p: His grandparents are said to have been indentured at the sugar mill where his father later worked, and his childhood home stood less than 100 yards from the Palmar de Junco, supposed site of Cuba's first baseball game.
He left Cuba in protest when Batista took power in 1952, reportedly helped fund Castro's rebels from Mexico, and came home after the revolution to teach in the new amateur programs.
Minnie Miñoso got into the ballpark as a boy by carrying Dihigo's shoes and glove: "I'd have to say he was most responsible for me getting to the major leagues."
He is in the Halls of Fame of the United States, Cuba, Mexico and the Dominican Republic.
He was an only child. His father was a sergeant who fought against Spain in the 1890s war for independence.
In the late 1930s he married Africa Reina. Their son Martín Jr. was born in Torreón in 1943, and their son Gilberto was born in Cuba a decade later.

Martín Jr. signed with the Reds at 16 and played in their farm system alongside Pete Rose and Tony Pérez until Cuba's doors closed in 1962. He studied physical education in East Germany and became a professor at Cienfuegos University. Gilberto became a sportswriter in Havana.

He lived with his elder son near Cienfuegos, in his wife's home village of Cruces. After several hospital stays in early 1971, reportedly for a cerebral thrombosis, he died that May. Cruces now has a Martín Dihigo Museum, and the revolutionary government treated him as a fallen hero.

c: He signed with Seattle as the first pick in 1993 on the eve of his first class at the University of Miami. His sister, an attorney, helped negotiate. He debuted at 18 and was sent back down.

In spring 1996 he started writing "A-ROD" on his equipment bag, and the name stuck. He won the batting title at 21. Runner-up for MVP, he said, "How can I be considered the MVP of the league when I'm not even the MVP in this room?", meaning Ken Griffey Jr.

After 2000 he signed with Texas for $252 million over 10 years, the largest contract ever given an athlete. A trade to the Red Sox was vetoed by the players' union, and he went to the Yankees instead.

Given the longest suspension in the Biogenesis case, he fought it and then sat out all of 2014. "I accept the fact that many of you will not believe my apology... That's on me." In 2015 he got his 3,000th hit with a home run.

Saying goodbye in 2016: "I do want to be remembered as someone who was madly in love with the game of baseball. I also will hopefully be remembered as someone who tripped and fell a lot but kept getting up."
The Mariners gave him a $1 million bonus and a three-year, $1.3 million contract. Miami had also recruited him to play quarterback.
On June 11, 1997, he collided with Roger Clemens at home plate, hurt his ribs and spent two weeks on the disabled list. The injury bothered him the rest of the season.
In 2000, his first season after Ken Griffey Jr. was traded, Seattle swept the White Sox in the Division Series. He hit .409 with two homers in the ALCS, but the Yankees won in six.

The Rangers finished under .500 in all three of his seasons there. In February 2004 they traded him to the Yankees for Alfonso Soriano and paid $67 million of the $179 million left on his contract. New York needed a third baseman after Aaron Boone tore his ACL.
He and Derek Jeter became close friends after they met in 1993. The friendship broke in 2001, when he criticized Jeter in an interview with Esquire.
In Game 3 of the 2004 ALCS against Boston he scored five runs, tying the postseason record, in a 19–8 rout.

He opted out of his contract during the eighth inning of the clinching game of the 2007 World Series, and baseball's chief operating officer accused agent Scott Boras of selfishness. A few weeks later he signed again with the Yankees, for 10 years and $275 million, with bonuses for home run milestones.
In 2009 he finally won a World Series. He hit .365 with six home runs in the postseason and won the Babe Ruth Award as its MVP.

Major League Baseball suspended him for 211 games for his role in Biogenesis, saying it was conduct detrimental to baseball. A first offense usually brought 50 games. Twelve other players were also suspended.
p: His father left the family in Miami when Alex was 9. The next time Alex heard from him was the day of the 1993 draft.

His youth coach, Juan Diego Arteaga, took him to school with his son, enrolled him on travel teams and fed him when his mother was working two jobs. "Without J.D. Arteaga, there would have been no Alex Rodríguez."
He once offered his mother $10,000 for a vacation; she invested it instead.
He grew up a Mets fan whose favorite players were Keith Hernandez, Dale Murphy and Cal Ripken Jr.

His parents ran a shoe store in Washington Heights, and his mother also worked on a GM assembly line. The store failed. He grew up with a half-brother and half-sister from his mother's first marriage. His father had been married before and had another son.
His mother worked two jobs to raise the three children, and later owned an immigration office and a Latin American restaurant.
He married Cynthia Scurtis in 2002. They had two daughters, Natasha and Ella. In July 2008 she filed for divorce, and the very public case centered on his infidelity.

c: Across from his house in Chatham, Ontario, was a coal yard. He learned control throwing lumps of coal at an ice chute when its rubber flap opened, and timing rocks to pass between moving boxcars. The coal-yard owner complained to his father.

In his first All-Star Game, in 1967, he struck out Mickey Mantle, Harmon Killebrew, Rod Carew and three others in three innings, and counted it among his greatest games. That year began six straight 20-win seasons.
On September 9, 1969, at Shea Stadium, a black cat walked around Ron Santo in the on-deck circle and hissed at Leo Durocher. Jenkins lost to Tom Seaver that night and the Cubs kept sinking.

In 1971 he won the Cy Young with 263 strikeouts and 37 walks. He also drove in 20 runs and hit six homers. "If you just stand there, you're a weak sister. But if you swing the bat, you're a dangerous part of the lineup."
In 1968 alone he lost five starts 1–0.
He never played for a first-place team. He joined Boston a year after its pennant and retired the year before the Cubs won the division. In his career he lost 13 complete games 1–0.
Phillies scout Gene Dziadura, a former Cubs minor-league shortstop, worked with him until he graduated from high school, and the Phillies signed him in 1962.

In April 1966, after one appearance that season, the Phillies traded him to the Cubs with Adolfo Phillips and John Herrnstein for Bob Buhl and Larry Jackson. Joseph Reichler's Baseball Trade Register ranks it as the fourth-best trade in Cubs history.
In October 1973 the Cubs traded him to Texas for Bill Madlock and Vic Harris. Billy Martin called him a workhorse and a winner. After two seasons with the Rangers he was traded to Boston.
The Toronto customs search in 1980 turned up 3 grams of cocaine, 2.2 grams of hashish and 1.75 grams of marijuana. Bowie Kuhn suspended him indefinitely.

He admits he used drugs now and then in those years, which he regrets, but says the drugs in his luggage weren't his. Kuhn's ruling ended up as a 20-game suspension, a $10,000 fine and the league's drug-education program.
He, Greg Maddux, Curt Schilling and Pedro Martínez are the only pitchers with more than 3,000 strikeouts and fewer than 1,000 walks.
After his playing days he was pitching coach for the Rangers' Triple-A club. In 1995 he was the National League All-Stars' honorary pitching coach.
p: His mother's ancestors escaped slavery through the Underground Railroad. His father played semipro ball for the all-Black Chatham Coloured All-Stars.
He played basketball for the Harlem Globetrotters in the offseasons from 1967 to 1969.

In 1980 drugs were found in his luggage on a road trip to Toronto; he said they weren't his. The case was dismissed, but "It was about two years before (my father) believed me when I told him I didn't do it."

His second wife died after a car accident in 1991, and the next year his fiancée killed herself and his three-year-old daughter, Samantha. "At one point I told a reporter I should be in a rubber room." He started a charitable foundation instead.
He was an only child. His father was a chef and chauffeur, the son of immigrants from Barbados.
His mother was blind. They were very close, and she died of cancer in 1970.
He married Kathy Silas in 1965 and they had three daughters. They divorced in 1987.

In 1988 he married Mary-Anne Miller, a softball player, and moved to a ranch near Guthrie, Oklahoma. She broke her neck in a car accident near the ranch in December 1990 and died of pneumonia that January. She was 32.

In December 1992 his girlfriend, Cynthia Takieddine, died of carbon monoxide poisoning in her car near Perry, Oklahoma, along with Samantha. It was ruled a murder-suicide, and her note didn't make her motives clear. That fall he had planned to take a job coaching the Reds' farm club in Chattanooga.
He married Lydia Farrington in 1993; she died in 2018.

c: At Michigan the freshman talked his way into an upperclassmen-only tryout run by the new coach, Branch Rickey, and was the best player there. He called Rickey "Coach" for the rest of his life.

Pittsburgh claimed him from a contract he signed at 17 with a minor-league club he never reported to. Rickey noticed it was void without his father's signature and won him free agency. He signed with Rickey's Browns.
As a rookie pitcher in 1915 he beat Walter Johnson 2–1 with the help of a hidden-ball trick, and called it his greatest thrill in baseball.
In 1920 he hit .407 with 257 hits, a record that lasted 84 years. In 1922 he hit .420 and was the first American League MVP.
A sinus infection in 1923 damaged his optic nerve and gave him double vision. He missed the whole season and was never quite the same, though he still hit .340 for his career.
He signed with the St. Louis Browns for $300 a month plus a $5,000 bonus, less than Pittsburgh had offered. In June 1916 the National Commission finally turned down Barney Dreyfuss's claim to him.

He came back in 1924 and also became the Browns' manager, but he was never the same player. Before the 1928 season they shipped him to Washington, and the Senators traded him to the Boston Braves early that season.
As a scout he signed Johnny Podres in 1951. With Rickey he taught Duke Snider the strike zone, and he also helped Carl Furillo and Gil Hodges.
He was one of the scouts Rickey sent to evaluate Black players. They thought they were scouting for an all-Black team outside the majors.
When he was in his prime his fielding was compared to Hal Chase's. After his vision trouble he led the league in errors several times.
p: His parents met at Hiram College. His hometown had no high school, so at 14 he moved to Akron to live with his brother, who died of tuberculosis during George's senior year. Local papers called the handsome boy "Gorgeous George."
He didn't drink, smoke or swear. During his 1923 eye trouble he turned to Christian Science and brought a spiritual adviser to spring training for his comeback.

As a scout for Rickey's Dodgers he scouted Jackie Robinson and helped him learn first base. With the Pirates he taught Roberto Clemente to keep his head still when he swung. Two of his sons, Dick and Dave, played in the majors.

He met Kathleen Holznagle in 1913, and they married on October 21, 1916. They had three sons. Dick played eight years in the majors and later managed the Reds, and Dave pitched seven seasons in the big leagues.
Out of baseball, he co-owned a sporting goods store in St. Louis, which he sold at a profit in 1940. In 1936 and 1937 he did color commentary for Browns and Cardinals home games on KWK radio.
After serious abdominal surgery in 1957 he moved back to St. Louis but kept working as the Pirates' roving hitting coach, with players like Willie Stargell and Donn Clendenon.
In St. Louis for the 2009 All-Star Game, Ichiro Suzuki, who had broken his single-season hits record, visited Sisler's grave.

c: When he asked to try out for Olean in 1890, manager Bert Kenney doubted his curve would fool professionals. McGraw promised he could play any position and got the contract. He was in the majors with Baltimore at 18.
With Willie Keeler, Hughie Jennings and Wilbert Robinson, his 1890s Orioles perfected the hit-and-run and the 'Baltimore chop' and set out to win by intimidating opponents and umpires.
Taking over a last-place Giants team in 1902, he released four players by telegraph while the team was still on the road, and two more when it got home.
He made Sammy Strang one of the first regular pinch hitters.
In 1909 he hired baseball's first full-time coach, Arlie Latham.

He won 10 pennants and 2,763 games. By 1932 some players resented that he called every pitch and policed their private lives, and he stepped down. He managed the National League in the first All-Star Game in 1933 and said, "I'm through with it. I have quit."
After Olean he played for Wellsville, then signed with Cedar Rapids, the first club to wire him money.
In the 1892–93 offseason he coached baseball at Allegany College, later St. Bonaventure, in exchange for free tuition. He came back the next year with Wilbert Robinson as his assistant.
Baltimore almost traded him to the woeful Washington club for Duke Farrell, but the deal fell through.
He liked to hold baserunners by the belt. One runner who saw it coming loosened his belt, and when he broke for home McGraw was left holding it as he scored.
The Orioles lost the Temple Cup in 1894, amid fights over money, and again in 1895. With McGraw, Jennings, Keeler and Kelley all holding out to start 1895, they still won the pennant.
He became Baltimore's player-manager in 1899, at 26. He left the team in late August when his wife fell ill.
He fought with American League president Ban Johnson and jumped to the Giants in 1902, taking several Orioles players with him.
Already sick, he managed the National League in the first All-Star Game, in 1933, against Connie Mack. He went to all five games of that year's World Series, which the Giants won.
p: A diphtheria epidemic in the winter of 1885 killed his mother and four of his siblings. His grieving father beat him after he broke another window playing ball, and the boy ran to a neighbor, Mary Goddard, who ran the local hotel and took him in.
As a poor boy in Truxton, New York, he saved a dollar from odd jobs to mail-order a cheap Spalding ball to practice pitching.
His widow, Blanche, kept a lifetime box at the Polo Grounds, went to the Giants' last game there and their first in San Francisco, and returned in 1962 for the Mets' home opener.

His father, a railroad worker, had been widowed once before, and the family of eight children was poor. After his father beat him, he ran away to a neighbor, Mary Goddard, who ran the local hotel. She persuaded his father to let him stay with her, and he delivered newspapers.
In February 1897 he married Minnie Doyle, the daughter of a Baltimore city official.
He had prostate cancer that had spread. He went into a coma on February 24, 1934, received the last rites, and died the next morning at 60.
In 1958 St. Bonaventure named its athletic fields after him and Hughie Jennings.

c: As a young Cardinal he walked up to Tim McCarver, who was shaving, and told him to call more breaking balls when behind in the count. "Who are you to tell me…?" McCarver said. Years later McCarver was his personal catcher.

After Sadaharu Oh hit two home runs off him on a 1968 tour of Japan, he tried a new pitch: "I threw Oh the slider. When he backed away and the ball was a strike, I knew I had something." In 1969 he struck out 19 Mets in a game and lost.
A night watchman named Briggs wrote him four or five letters a week in 1970 with passages from Nietzsche and Schopenhauer about concentration. Carlton considered him a spiritual guide.
The Cardinals traded him to Philadelphia over a $5,000 salary dispute. He went 27–10 with a 1.97 ERA in 1972 for a team that won 59 games. He won 46 percent of its games.
He picked off 144 runners, by far the most on record. Asked why he was put on earth, he said: "To teach the world how to throw a slider."
He signed with the Cardinals for a $5,000 bonus in October 1963, while he was a student at Miami Dade College.

In the 1967 World Series he started Game 5 and allowed only an unearned run in six innings, but lost 3–1; the Cardinals beat Boston anyway. In the 1968 Series he gave up three runs in four innings of relief as the Tigers came back to win in seven.
After making $26,000 in 1969 he held out for $50,000. The Cardinals offered $31,000, and he skipped spring training in 1970.

Curt Flood had just refused a trade to Philadelphia and sued. Coming right after that, Carlton's holdout infuriated Gussie Busch, who ordered him traded. He went to the Phillies for Rick Wise, who had thrown a no-hitter in 1971 and hit two home runs in the same game. Carlton was furious about being sent to Philadelphia.

When he went 13–20 in 1973, reporters started questioning his unusual training methods, and he stopped talking to them. Braves announcer Ernie Johnson said, "The two best pitchers in the National League don't speak English: Fernando Valenzuela and Steve Carlton."
The Phillies lost the NLCS three straight years from 1976 to 1978. In the 1980 postseason he went 3–0 with a 2.30 ERA and won Game 6 of the World Series, 4–1, to clinch the franchise's first title.
He pitched for six teams before he was done in 1988, then went unsigned in 1989.
p: As a boy in Miami he killed a rabbit with a rock from 90 feet when his rifle jammed. As a teenager he took up Eastern philosophy and the meditation teachings of Paramahansa Yogananda.
He stopped talking to the press for years. When the 1987 Twins visited the White House, the official photo labeled him an unidentified Secret Service agent.

Before his Hall of Fame induction he told a writer that AIDS was created by the government and that the world was ruled by Jewish bankers. McCarver, his closest friend, defended him: "He is a very complicated person and has a hard time being human."
He retired to the mountains near Durango, Colorado, with an orchard of 150 fruit trees. "Before Al Gore was green, I was green." He went 15 years without a television.
His father, Joe, was an airline maintenance worker. Steve was the only son and grew up with two sisters on 144th Street in Miami.
A high school teammate, Richie Mehlich, beat Charlie Hough 1–0 in a playoff game and was later murdered.
He and his wife, Beverly, were married 33 years and divorced in 1998.
He played himself on Married... with Children, in an episode where former athletes humiliate Al Bundy while filming a shoe commercial.

c: In 1909, running to break up a double play at Galesburg, he was hit in the temple by the shortstop's throw. He was unconscious for a day and a half or more and saw double into the next spring. Indianapolis heard about it and passed him along to Syracuse sight unseen. He won 29 there.

The Phillies drafted him for $500 as insurance after paying $3,000 for another prospect. As a rookie in 1911 he won 28 games, still the 20th-century rookie record, including a 1–0 one-hitter over Cy Young.
In 1916 he threw 16 shutouts, still the major-league record, while pitching half his games in tiny Baker Bowl. He won 30 or more three years running.

Game 7 of the 1926 World Series: having won Games 2 and 6, he came out of the bullpen in the seventh with the bases loaded and struck out Tony Lazzeri to save the title. Whether he had been drinking the night before has never been settled; he and his wife always said he was sober.
He finished with 373 wins and believed he had passed Christy Mathewson for the National League record. In the 1940s researchers found an extra win for Mathewson, and the two are tied forever.
Before baseball he dug postholes for the Howard County Telephone Company. He signed his first pro contract at 20 for $50 a month.
Galesburg sold him to Indianapolis, which, having heard about his double vision, sold him to Syracuse without even looking at him. He finished his year there with 52 straight scoreless innings.
He won Game 1 of the 1915 World Series, the Phillies' last Series win for 65 years, but felt too worn out to pitch Game 5, and they lost.

Betting he'd be drafted, the Phillies traded him and Bill Killefer to the Cubs in December 1917 for two players and $55,000. Cubs owner Charles Weeghman gave him a $5,000 bonus, which he put into Liberty Bonds. He pitched three games before the Army called.

Joe McCarthy thought his drinking was hurting the Cubs, who waived him to St. Louis in June 1926. Teammate Bob O'Farrell said he got drunk the night after winning Game 6 and was still feeling it when he came in to pitch in Game 7.

Lazzeri, whom he struck out in Game 7, was also hiding epilepsy, and died in 1946 falling down a flight of stairs during a seizure. Alexander struck out 17 Yankees in that Series after just 48 all season.
The Cardinals traded him back to the Phillies in December 1929. In the late 1930s and early 1940s he toured as player-coach of a House of David team, facing Negro league stars like Satchel Paige.
p: He was a Nebraska farm boy named for the sitting president. His father credited corn-shucking for his powerful wrist. He learned control throwing stones at clothespins, or at chickens when his mother needed dinner, giving them a running start. Ronald Reagan later played him in The Winning Team.

Seven weeks under bombardment as an artillery sergeant in France left him deaf in one ear and shell-shocked. He came home an alcoholic and epileptic, and drank partly to hide the seizures, since being taken for a drunk was more acceptable.

Out of baseball, he retold his strikeout of Lazzeri at a Times Square flea circus. The league secretly arranged a $50-a-month 'pension' that the Cardinals actually paid. "I'm in the Hall of Fame, and I'm proud to be there, but I can't eat the Hall of Fame."

His wife, Amy, divorced and remarried him, and divorced him again, but stayed close to him all his life. He died in 1950 in a St. Paul hotel room after mailing her a letter saying he looked forward to seeing her.
His father hoped he'd study law like his namesake, Grover Cleveland.

Shrapnel in his right ear in France may have caused the cancer he got nearly 30 years later. He hid his epilepsy behind drinking, since being a drunk was more socially acceptable than having seizures.
He married Amy Arrants a month before shipping out in 1918, in a courthouse in Manhattan, Kansas. They divorced in 1929, remarried in 1931 and divorced again in 1941.
He saw the Phillies lose Game 3 of the 1950 World Series at Yankee Stadium and died less than a month later.

c: The eldest of five Delahanty brothers to reach the majors, he hit .228 as a rookie. He worked out every day one winter and came back in 1892 in the best shape of his life. He hit .400 three times.
On July 13, 1896, he hit four home runs in a game against Chicago, two of them inside the park. He is the only player to have both four homers and four doubles in a game.
Pitcher Crazy Schmit's advice on facing him: "you just want to shut your eyes, say a prayer and chuck the ball." One 1892 line drive broke a charging third baseman's ankle.

Paid $3,000 a year by the Phillies, he recruited teammates for the new American League in 1901 and took eight of them with him. He won the 1902 AL batting title, at least officially. Research later gave it to Nap Lajoie.
Mansfield paid him $50 a month in 1887, and the Phillies bought him from Wheeling for about $2,000. He jumped to Cleveland's Players' League team in 1890 and came back the next year.
He liked to swing at the first pitch, figuring a control pitcher would try to "do his business" with it. He stole 455 bases, leading the league with 58 in 1898.

Owner John Rogers kept the Phillies' salaries down, and after 1901 nine Phillies, Delahanty included, jumped to the AL. He signed with Washington for $4,000 with a $1,000 bonus. Lajoie looked to have won the 1902 batting title until official figures two months later gave it to Delahanty.

To pay his debts he signed a three-year deal with the Giants with a $4,000 advance. When the leagues made peace, it was voided. Washington paid back the advance, deducting $2,000 a year from his salary, and he reported out of shape and soon hurt his back and ankle.
p: By 1903 he was drinking and gambling heavily, buried in debt, and caught between the Senators and the Giants in a contract fight. He gave away keepsakes like his gold watch and took out a life insurance policy naming his daughter.

On July 2, 1903, he was put off a train at the Canadian border for drunkenly menacing passengers. He walked out onto the International Railway Bridge and fell or jumped into the Niagara River. His body was found a week later at the foot of Horseshoe Falls.
His father worked a series of blue-collar jobs in Cleveland, while his mother turned their home into a boardinghouse. Five of his brothers also played in the majors.

By late 1902 his wife, Norine, was ill and he was gambling away their money on horses and drinking. It was rumored that he once tried suicide by turning on the gas in his Washington room, and before his last road trip he took out life insurance naming his daughter, Florence, as beneficiary.
His body was found below Niagara Falls a week after he vanished. Mike Sowell's book weighs accident, suicide and a possible robbery-murder; a mysterious man was reportedly following him.

c: His Canton teammates nicknamed him "Cyclone" in 1890. In his last game there he threw a no-hitter with 18 strikeouts and no walks, and Cleveland bought him for $300. Before his first big-league start Cap Anson called him "just another big farmer." Young beat Anson's Colts on three hits.
He pitched without a glove until partway through 1896. He umpired a couple of games when the regular umpire quit or didn't show, and he was never once thrown out of a game.

St. Louis wouldn't match Boston's $3,500 offer in 1901, sure he was washed up at 34. He won the pitching Triple Crown that year for the new American League team and won 192 games for Boston, and he threw the first pitch in World Series history.
In 1908, at 41, he no-hit the Highlanders. He walked the leadoff man, who was thrown out stealing, then retired the next 26.
In May 1912, at 45, he tried to warm up for the Boston Braves and gave up: "It's no use. I'm not going on. These poor fellows have lost too many games already."
Canton paid him $60 a month in 1890; after his no-hitter, Cleveland bought him for $300. Cap Anson called him "just another big farmer" before his debut; Young three-hit Anson's Colts.
He lost two games in the 1892 postseason series to Boston, but later won in the Temple Cup, the only pitcher to win in both the Temple Cup and the World Series.
Usually quiet, he charged into the stands on August 20, 1899, to confront a heckler who'd accused him of quitting on the team.

He threw the first pitch of the first modern World Series in 1903 and lost Game 1, 7-3, after giving up four in the first, then won twice as Boston beat Pittsburgh. In spring 1902 he coached Harvard's pitchers.
He finished 1904 with three straight shutouts to help clinch Boston's pennant.
In 1913 he managed the Cleveland Green Sox of the outlaw Federal League, and never worked in baseball again.
p: He left school after sixth grade to work the family farm, and practiced pitching on his lunch breaks: "I usta kill squirrels with a stone when I was a kid." He signed with Canton hoping to earn enough to marry Robba Miller, the girl on the next farm.
His offseason training was splitting wood on his Ohio farm. "It isn't any secret, just outdoor life, moderation, and a naturally good arm." He also built trunks to sell to traveling ballplayers.

His and Robba's only child, a daughter, died hours after birth in 1907. When Robba died in 1933 he sold the farm: "Somehow, after she died I didn't want to live there anymore." He spent his last years boarding with a local couple and clerking in a store.
He married Robba Miller, the girl from the next farm, on November 8, 1892. He'd gone into pro ball partly to earn enough to marry her.
In 1910 he was reported to have become a vegetarian. After Robba's death he tried several jobs and moved in with friends John and Ruth Benedum, doing odd jobs on their farm, where he died in 1955.

c: Indianapolis manager C.I. Taylor: "If I should see Torriente walking up the other side of the street, I would say, 'There walks a ball club.'"

The legend on his Hall of Fame plaque: on November 5, 1920, he outslugged Babe Ruth with three home runs against the visiting Giants in Havana. Havana papers show all three were inside the park, hit off first baseman George Kelly, who was pitching on a lark, to probably hung-over outfielders.
Frankie Frisch claimed one Torriente grounder past him at third "dug a hole about a foot deep on its way to left field."

He led Rube Foster's Chicago American Giants to the first three Negro National League pennants, 1920–22, hitting a reported .411 in 1920. He left the Kansas City Monarchs years later after a dispute over some stolen jewelry.

In 1915 he was ejected for arguing, then kicked umpire Kelly after being called out stealing third. A fight with a player named Crawford spilled into the street, where they went at each other with paving stones until Rube Foster broke it up.
After an argument with his manager in 1916 he joined J.L. Wilkinson's All Nations. In 1923 he threw dirt on umpire Bert Gholston's "newly creased trousers."

He homered in Game 1 of the 1921 series against Hilldale. Traded to Kansas City in 1926, he hit .407 in the playoff against his old American Giants, then walked off the team after a dispute over a stolen diamond ring.
Researcher Roberto González Echevarría found that his famous three homers off the Giants in 1920 were all inside-the-park against a weak pitcher, not the Ruth-outslugging legend.
p: At 17 he joined the Cuban army and was put in the artillery because he was strong enough to lift the guns onto the mules.
His love of nightlife and drinking caused fights with team managements throughout his career. Fellow Cubans found him in poor circumstances in Chicago in the mid-1930s.

He died in New York in 1938, at 44, after a long fight with alcoholism and tuberculosis. A teammate said his coffin was draped in a Cuban flag and returned to Havana. After years of doubt, his grave there was identified in 2020.
After baseball he lived briefly in Ybor City, Florida, before fading into obscurity.

His death certificate, found in 2016, suggests his body was never returned to Havana but lies in a pauper's grave in Queens' Calvary Cemetery. He had spent his last years at Riverside Hospital on North Brother Island, and Martín Dihigo had moved him to New York.

c: The Red Sox took him in the fifth round in 2011 and signed him away from a Tennessee scholarship for $750,000. Between 2013 and 2014 he reached base in 71 straight minor-league games.
In the 2015 home opener he robbed Bryce Harper of a home run, stole two bases on one play, and homered into the Green Monster seats, all in the first three innings.
From September 2016 to April 2017 he went 129 straight plate appearances without striking out.
In 2018 he was the first player to win the MVP, a Silver Slugger, a Gold Glove, the batting title and the World Series in the same season.
Traded to the Dodgers in 2020, he signed a 12-year, $365 million extension and later moved to shortstop, a position he had barely played, when the team needed one.
He reached base in 66 straight minor-league games in 2013-14. With Dustin Pedroia locked in at second, Boston moved him to the outfield.

Unable to agree on a contract, the Red Sox renewed him for $950,000 in 2017. He won arbitration in 2018, $10.5 million to the team's $7.5 million, and reportedly turned down eight years and $200 million.
He hit just .210 in the 2018 postseason, but homered in the World Series clincher, and in Game 4 of the ALCS fan interference on his leaping try at a Jose Altuve drive turned it into an out.

Boston traded him, David Price and $48 million to the Dodgers for Alex Verdugo and two prospects in February 2020. His extension included a $65 million signing bonus. That fall he made three straight game-saving plays in NLCS elimination games and homered in the World Series clincher.
He cracked a rib in 2022, and hit 2-for-14 in the Dodgers' NLDS loss to San Diego. He won the World Series again in 2024 and 2025.
p: His parents gave him the initials M.L.B. on purpose, and named him Mookie after watching the NBA's Mookie Blaylock, whom he has never met. When Little League coaches turned him away for being too small, his mother started her own team.
He was Tennessee's boys' bowler of the year in high school and bowled a perfect game in the PBA's World Series of Bowling in 2017. He has competed as a professional bowler.
He and his wife began dating in middle school; she runs his 5050 Foundation. He kept wearing a necklace a 13-year-old fan gave him at spring training in 2018.
Shumpert, a big-leaguer finishing his career with Triple-A Nashville in 2004, worked extensively with young Mookie.
He and his wife had their first child in November 2018, married in December 2021, and had a second child in 2023. He bought Chip Kelly's former mansion in Encino for $7.6 million.

c: The Yankee scout who came to the family's dining table wrote $60,000; his father wrote $100,000. The scout flipped his pencil into the ceiling: "Are you crazy?" "Nobody throws a pencil in my house. Get the hell out and never come back." That was the end of the Yankees.

He signed with Boston for $108,000 plus the rest of his college costs. Joe Cronin met the 160-pound kid and blurted, "We're paying this kind of money for this guy?" His father raised his weekly allowance from $5 to $7.50.

His first time in the Fenway clubhouse, Ted Williams told him, "Don't let them screw around with your swing. Ever." Struggling as Williams's replacement in 1961, he got a visit from Ted, who told him he had a great swing and should just go out and use it.
In the last 12 games of 1967 he went 23-for-44, and 7-for-8 in the final two must-win games against the Twins. He won the Triple Crown and missed a unanimous MVP by one vote, cast for Cesar Tovar.
In 1965 Satchel Paige, 59, came back for one last three-inning start. The only hit off him was by Yastrzemski.

His father wouldn't let him play football as a high school senior, for fear of an injury hurting his baseball value. Signed, he started at Class B Raleigh in 1959 and finished with Minneapolis in the American Association playoffs.
He hit .400 with three homers in the 1967 World Series, which Boston lost in seven to St. Louis.

In February 1971 he signed a three-year deal reportedly worth $500,000, then the largest contract in baseball history. Hand injuries in the early 1970s and a permanent shoulder injury cut his power and made him change his stance.
In 1975, after hitting .269, he went 5-for-11 in the ALCS sweep of Oakland and hit .350 with 11 runs in ten postseason games as Boston lost the World Series in seven.
After retiring he did sportscasting, worked as marketing director for a meat manufacturer, and was a Red Sox hitting instructor until 2020.
p: He grew up on his family's Long Island potato farm. His father, who turned down chances to try pro ball during the Depression, ran a semipro team made up almost entirely of relatives. Carl joined it at 14, and his father kept playing only to play beside him.
When his father visited him in the minors and decided his roommates were a distraction, he moved Carl into an apartment by himself while the others were out golfing.
At his farewell in 1983 he broke down at the microphone, asked for a moment of silence for his mother and Tom Yawkey, and finished: "New England, I love you."
His son Mike played in the minors and died at 43 in 2004. His grandson, also Mike, made the majors.
His father formed and managed a semipro team, the Bridgehampton White Eagles, playing shortstop; Carl was its batboy at seven. Once Carl signed, his father never played again.
He married Carol Casper in January 1960; they had four children. Keeping a promise to his parents, he finished his business degree at Merrimack College in 1966.
His son Carl Jr., "Mike," a third-round Braves pick in 1984, died at 43 of a blood clot after hip surgery. Yaz himself had emergency triple-bypass surgery in 2008.

c: Joining Kansas City at 17 and weighing no more than 135 pounds, he looked more like a batboy than a pitcher, and the older players named him "Kid."

On May 12, 1890, he and Amos Rusie threw scoreless innings into the 13th at the Polo Grounds, while fans at the Players' League game next door tried to watch over the fence. Mike Tiernan's homer finally beat him. Writers called it one of the great duels of the early National League.
He won 30 games seven times, still a record. Bill James ranked him behind only Babe Ruth and Mickey Mantle for deciding pennant races: Boston's 1891, 1892, 1897 and 1898 flags.
In late September 1897, three days after allowing 12 runs in one inning to Brooklyn, he beat Baltimore twice in a three-game series that effectively decided the pennant.
He was the youngest pitcher to reach 300 wins. He was proud that no relief pitcher had ever replaced him in a game.
After going 39-8 for Omaha under Frank Selee, he held out against being sold to St. Joseph, insisting he was free to sign elsewhere. Boston signed him in September 1889.

In spring training he coached college pitchers at Amherst, Yale and Brown. After 1901 he bought into the Kansas City minor-league club. Despite his reputation, he had several contract fights with Boston's owners and held out a few times.
Made manager of the Cardinals in 1904, he was fired early in 1905 and released after going 1-5. Former teammate Hugh Duffy signed him for the Phillies, where he went 10-6.
He managed Oshkosh in the Wisconsin-Illinois League, scouted the Texas League for Detroit, and coached Missouri Valley College in 1915 and 1916.
p: A Madison butcher's son, he moved to Kansas City as a boy. His brothers worked in the family shop while he played ball.

After baseball he ran bowling alleys, won the Kansas City bowling championship at 63, and patented an electric scoreboard that used lights to show baserunners moving in out-of-town games. He opened a movie theater with Joe Tinker.
Young Casey Stengel lived across the street and always named Nichols as an early influence. Ty Cobb campaigned loudly for him to make the Hall of Fame, and he got in in 1949.
When doctors wanted to run tests at 83 in 1952, he refused until the World Series was over. He was dying of cancer.
He married Jennie Curtin on January 29, 1890, and they had one child, Alice, born that December.
He went into the movie-distribution business with Joe Tinker, supplying Midwest theaters.

c: His father, a friend of a friend, got Ted Williams to come to the house when Mike was 15. After watching him hit, Williams signed his copy of The Science of Hitting: "To Mike, follow this book. As good as you look now, I'll be asking you for tickets."

Scouts said he couldn't hit or run. The Dodgers took him in the 62nd round as a favor to Tommy Lasorda. When the scout balked at signing another first baseman, Lasorda said, "Well, then sign him. He's a catcher!"
To learn to catch he volunteered for the Dodgers' Dominican academy, the first U.S.-born player to go there. In 1993 he hit 35 home runs, the most ever by a rookie catcher.

On September 21, 2001, in the first game in New York after the attacks, he hit a two-run eighth-inning homer to beat the Braves. "The hardest thing I've ever had to do as an athlete was play that game."
In Game 2 of the 2000 World Series, months after Roger Clemens beaned him, his bat shattered and Clemens threw the barrel in his direction. Clemens said he thought it was the ball.

His father, Vince, made more than $100 million in used cars and real estate and tried to buy a big-league team. Tommy Lasorda, Vince's childhood friend and godfather to one of Mike's brothers, let Mike be a Dodgers batboy in Philadelphia.

After a .362, 40-homer 1997 he turned down six years and $80 million to test free agency. In May 1998 the Dodgers traded him to Florida in a deal involving $108 million in contracts, and a week later the Marlins sent him to the Mets for three prospects.

The Mets then signed him for seven years and $91 million, at the time the richest contract in baseball, and drew over 2 million fans every year he was there. He played in one World Series, losing to the Yankees in 2000.
He told the New York Times he'd used androstenedione, then legal, for a short time but stopped when he saw no big change. Around then he also said players could accept an openly gay teammate.
He finished with one-year deals with San Diego and Oakland, and later managed Team Italy at the 2023 World Baseball Classic.
p: Growing up near Philadelphia he studied Mike Schmidt from his family's season-ticket seats behind the Phillies dugout. His father built him a backyard batting cage where he hit 300 balls a day, even in winter.
A devout Catholic, he had an audience with Pope John Paul II on a 2002 tour of Europe for MLB. He played for Italy in the 2006 World Baseball Classic and later managed the Italian team.
A heavy metal fan and drummer, he appeared on a Black Label Society album, is godfather to Zakk Wylde's son, and co-hosts a rock radio show in New York.
He bought an Italian soccer club, Reggiana, in 2016. It collapsed financially and folded two years later.
In 2005 he married actress and Playboy Playmate Alicia Rickter in Miami; they have three children.
His father dropped out of school and worked as a car salesman, real-estate investor and entrepreneur. Mike had four brothers.

c: As a boy he carried Monte Irvin's bag into San Juan's ballpark to get in free and studied how Irvin threw. Clemente said his arm also came from his mother, who even at 74 could throw from second base to home "with something on it."

The Dodgers signed him in 1954 mainly to keep him from the Giants. Their GM later said Jackie Robinson advised against promoting another Black player at a white player's expense, so Clemente spent a year in Montreal. Pittsburgh drafted him away that winter.
In the 1971 World Series he hit .414, homered in Game 7 for the first run of a 2–1 win, and was named MVP.

He got his 2,999th hit in Philadelphia and was pulled so he could get number 3,000 at home. When a chopper the next night was scored an error, he was furious. The following afternoon he doubled off the wall for 3,000.
Early in his career he faced racial sniping from the press and some teammates as a Black, Spanish-speaking Puerto Rican. His answer: "I don't believe in color."

The Dodgers gave him a $10,000 bonus and $5,000 salary in 1954. Under the bonus rule they had to keep him in the majors or risk losing him, and biographers argue they hid him in Montreal by limiting his play; Pittsburgh drafted him anyway after the season.

A back injury early in his career hampered him the rest of the way. His Pirates manager, Bobby Bragan, fined him for missing a bunt sign, and was angry again when Clemente ran through his stop sign at third.
When Santurce's new owner sold him to Caguas mid-winter while he was leading the league, the deal was so unpopular the Santurce manager resigned.
Bragan: "I'd rather have a Clemente with some ailment than a Clemente who says he feels great." Clemente's tendency to play well while hurt fed charges that he wasn't really injured.
p: As a boy he earned money hauling milk for neighbors and loading his father's trucks, and spent it on rubber balls he squeezed to strengthen his hands. He threw the javelin well enough in high school that people thought he might make the Olympics.

His great dream was a 'Sports City' for Puerto Rico's young people. He told his manager the most important moment of his life would be building it, not his 3,000th hit. His widow, Vera, revived the stalled project in the late 1980s.
