After managing Puerto Rico's amateur team in Nicaragua in 1972, he organized relief when an earthquake struck Managua that December. He boarded a cargo plane of supplies on New Year's Eve. It crashed into the ocean just after takeoff. He was 38.
The Hall of Fame waived its waiting period and elected him in 1973, the first Latin American player inducted. Baseball's award for character and community service now bears his name.
His mother, Luisa, was a laundress and his father a foreman on sugarcane crops. His brother Luis died of a brain tumor on New Year's Eve 1954.
He married Vera Zabala in 1964 in Carolina, Puerto Rico; they had three sons. Vera later revived his Sports City project with corporate help.
Vera said he told her several times he thought he would die young.

c: His father, a truck driver who ran Johnny's first boys' team, told him catching was the quickest way to the big leagues. By second grade he was telling his teacher he'd be a major leaguer, and he was soon practicing his autograph.

As a 19-year-old call-up he told veteran shortstop Leo Cardenas where to play. As a rookie he walked out to lecture star pitcher Jim Maloney. Manager Dave Bristol told Maloney, "You know, he's right."
He could hold seven baseballs in one hand, caught one-handed with his throwing hand tucked behind his back, and used a hinged mitt. He won the Gold Glove in each of his first 10 seasons.
In the 1972 World Series the A's signaled an intentional walk on 3–2. Catcher Gene Tenace stood up, then crouched back down, and Rollie Fingers threw strike three past a stunned Bench.
Late in 1972 doctors found a mass on his lung. He kept it secret, played through the postseason, and had surgery in December. It was benign.
After the 1976 sweep Sparky Anderson said God had touched his mother's forehead and told her she'd have "one of the greatest baseball players ever seen."
Cincinnati scout Tony Robello signed him for $6,000 plus college tuition, and he gave up the idea of college ball.

Baltimore had scouted him first; had the Orioles listened to their scout, he and Jim Palmer would have been teammates. Instead he hit a grand slam off Palmer in Triple-A, the only one Palmer ever allowed as a pro.

In his first inning for Buffalo in 1966 a foul tip broke his right thumb, ending his season. Driving home in the Ford Fairlane he'd bought with his bonus, he was hit by a drunk driver and hospitalized.
His leadoff homer in the ninth inning of Game 5 of the 1972 NLCS tied the game, and the Reds won the pennant. The 99-win 1973 Reds lost the NLCS to an 82-win Mets team.

He played 1975 through a shoulder hurt in a collision at the plate and the flu in the postseason. In 1976, after perhaps his worst regular season, he hit .444 with three homers in the sweeps of the Phillies and Yankees.
As the Big Red Machine broke up, he alone stayed, signing for five years at $400,000 a year after 1977, less than he could have gotten elsewhere.
He broke six bones in each foot from foul tips and his thumb twice, and later needed both hips replaced, injuries he traced to his teenage bus and car crashes.
p: In high school, the valedictorian of a class of 21, he survived a bus crash that killed two of his teammates when the brakes failed and the bus rolled into a ravine. At 18, driving home from the minors, he was hit by a drunk driver and needed 27 stitches.
He saw a former Miss South Carolina in a toothpaste ad, called her for a date, proposed after four days and married her seven weeks later, in 1975. They separated that season.
He went to Vietnam with Bob Hope's USO tour, hosted his own TV show at 22, and later taught kids the game on The Baseball Bunch. After 50 he played on the Senior PGA Tour.

Bench reportedly suggested his first wife, Vicki Chesser, accept Hustler's $25,000 offer to pose nude. They split at the end of the 1975 season, divorcing after 13 months; he reportedly told her, "Now I'm done with two things I hate: baseball and you."

He has married five times. With Laura Cwikowski he had a son, Bobby Binger Bench, named for Bob Hope, Bobby Knight and his hometown. He divorced his third wife in 2000 citing infidelity, and his fourth after she wouldn't move to Florida; he has custody of their two sons.
In 1989 he became the first individual player on a Wheaties box.

c: Pitching pro ball at 16, he was nearly cut at his first Reds camp in 1899 before owner John Brush insisted on keeping him. He went 23–8 and led the league in strikeouts as a rookie, which he credited to swearing off drink, apart from one beer at a barbecue when there was no water.

Holding a 1–0 lead in Pittsburgh with a runner on third in the ninth, he stopped mid-delivery, set the ball on the ground, took a plug of tobacco from his shirt pocket, and then got the last outs. Pittsburgh's manager called it the greatest game he ever saw a young pitcher throw.
On July 12, 1900, he threw the season's only no-hitter, against a strong Phillies lineup.

In 1901 he won 22 games for a last-place team that won only 52, 42 percent of its victories, and he struck out 16 in a game, a mark not passed until Dizzy Dean in 1933. He won his 100th game at 24. Three years later his arm was dead.
Before he turned 15 he signed for $35 a month with a team in Clarksville, Tennessee, and waited outside saloons while his teammates drank.
Detroit won the bidding for him, and after two so-so seasons there Charles Comiskey recommended him to the Reds, who bought him. He credited his strong debut to swearing off drink.
Boston's owner offered him $4,000 to jump to the American League, and he stayed in Cincinnati for $4,200, up from $1,800 two years earlier, the highest salary on the team.
He hurt his arm in 1905. Though he was 5-3 in 1906, the Reds released him, the decision probably made easier by his "wartime" salary of over $4,000.
p: Nobody agrees on where 'Noodles' came from. One friend said he carried his father's noodle-soup lunch to a Nashville piano factory; other stories involve selling his mother's soup or carrying it to a poor neighbor.

At 23, foreseeing ballplayers' fade into the saloon business, he enrolled in veterinary college while still pitching. "'Hoss doctors': why, they're lined up along the boulevards waiting to give those boys money." He became a government veterinary inspector.

He pitched batting practice at Crosley Field into his late 60s. Reds players of the 1940s didn't know he had been a star until one found an old clipping, since he never told stories about the old days.
Shortly after marrying Salome Stevens in 1905, he was bitten by a dog that turned out to have rabies.
By 1910 he was giving private lessons to Reds prospect Rube Benton. In the early 1950s he and his wife moved to Candler, North Carolina, where he died at 80.

c: He was 32–1 in high school, then hurt his shoulder throwing sidearm on a cocky whim and almost took a basketball scholarship to Duke. The Angels drafted him in the first round anyway; he couldn't pitch his first pro summer. "I didn't have many friends on that team."
He and Nolan Ryan anchored the Angels staff: "Tanana and Ryan and two days of cryin'." He led the league in strikeouts in 1975 and in ERA in 1977.
Arm injuries in 1977 and 1979 ended his mid-90s fastball, so he reinvented himself with forkballs and screwballs and lasted until 1993, winning 240 games.
Traded to his hometown Tigers in 1985, he threw a shutout on the last day of 1987 to clinch the division. He's one of two pitchers to give up home runs to both Hank Aaron and Barry Bonds.
Tendinitis kept him from pitching at all in his first pro season: "Here were guys being cut off the team, and I, who couldn't throw, was staying because I had this bonus."
After a shoulder injury cost him two months in 1979, he came back to pitch the complete game that clinched the Angels' first-ever division title, then started Game 3 of the ALCS.
In January 1981 the Angels traded him to Boston with Joe Rudi for Fred Lynn. He went 4-10, signed with Texas for $375,000 a year, and was traded to Detroit in June 1985 for a minor-league pitcher.
He faced Frank Viola in Game 4 of the 1987 ALCS. After the Mets and a September 1993 trade to the Yankees, he was released by the Angels in spring 1994 after a 13.50 ERA, ending his career.
p: His father played pro ball in the 1950s before joining the Detroit police to support the family. Frank grew up rooting for Al Kaline and Mickey Lolich.

As a young star he said his idol was himself: "Nothing I do awes me." Shaken by his injuries and the 1978 murder of teammate Lyman Bostock, he became a born-again Christian in an Arizona hotel room on November 6, 1983, and later ministered to athletes.
He met his wife at a Newport Beach disco in 1977. Five hundred guests came to the wedding.
As a young pitcher he had a reputation as a partier and drinker.
He and Cathy, a Long Beach State dance major, have four daughters, including twins. He's an elder at his Baptist church, assists the Tigers' chaplain, and does marriage counseling.

c: At 7 he won his age group in the NFL's first national Punt, Pass & Kick contest. He was a high school All-America quarterback with nearly 100 scholarship offers until torn knee ligaments made him choose baseball. He had caught only six games when the Expos drafted him as a catcher.
Teammates called him "The Kid" in his first camp because he tried to win every sprint and hit every pitch out. Others, put off by his eagerness, called him "Camera Carter" for his love of interviews.
He wore number 8 because he was born on April 8, married on February 8 and moved into his first house on November 8.
In his last at-bat, at Olympic Stadium on September 27, 1992, manager Felipe Alou let him hit before pulling him. He doubled in the game's only run.
Larry Bowa said Carter was one of the few catchers unafraid of base stealers: he would still call breaking balls with a runner going.

He'd played only six games at catcher in high school, but Montreal saw his build and drafted him in the third round in 1972 as one. Torn knee ligaments had already cost him his senior football season.
In his first camp the Expos roomed him with veteran catcher John Boccabella, who led him back to his Christian faith. A pitcher hyped him as "The Kid" partly to needle incumbent catcher Barry Foote.
In 1981, Montreal's only postseason, he went 8-for-19 with two homers against Philadelphia and 7-for-16 in the NLCS loss to the Dodgers.

In February 1982 he signed a seven-year deal for about $14 million, then the richest in the sport, or close to it. The Expos never made the playoffs again, and owner Charles Bronfman was losing money.
His 12th-inning single won Game 5 of the 1986 NLCS, and his two-out single in the 10th inning of Game 6 of the World Series started the Mets' comeback.
p: His mother died of leukemia when he was 12, which led to his lifelong fundraising for leukemia research. He lost his faith then and found it again through veteran catcher John Boccabella, his roommate in his first camp.
He married his high school sweetheart in 1975 and honeymooned at the Expos' spring training camp.
When the IRS investigated the 1980s Mets for unreported card-show income, Carter spent $25,000 on accountants to prove he had reported everything. He was dropped from the probe.

He was coaching at Palm Beach Atlantic University, alongside his daughter Kimmy, the softball coach, when he was diagnosed with brain cancer in 2011. He died the next February at 57. Darryl Strawberry: "I wish I could have lived my life like Gary Carter."
His father inspected aviation parts for Hughes Aircraft and later worked in procurement for McDonnell Douglas.
He and Sandy had three children, Christy, Kimmy and D.J. Kimmy caught for Florida State softball.
After playing he broadcast for the Marlins and Expos, then coached and managed in the minors, independent ball and college, never getting the big-league job he hoped for.

c: Childhood friends called him Arky as soon as they found out he'd been born in Arkansas. He hit .318 as a 20-year-old rookie shortstop and also led the league with 46 errors.
The Pirates made Honus Wagner a coach in 1934 partly to fix Vaughan's fielding. Wagner roomed with him: "They said if I couldn't make a shortstop out of Arky Vaughan, nobody could."

In 1935 he was hitting .401 in mid-September before finishing at .385, still the Pirates' record. He was the first player to hit two home runs in an All-Star Game, in 1941, until Ted Williams's ninth-inning homer stole the day.

In July 1943, when Leo Durocher lied to the press about Bobo Newsom, the quiet Vaughan threw his uniform in Durocher's face: "If you would lie about Bobo, you would lie about me and everybody else." The team nearly went on strike, and after the season Vaughan quit for three years.
He came back in 1947 at 35 and hit .325 as a part-timer. Jackie Robinson remembered him as "one of the fellows who went out of his way to be nice to me."
A neighbor tipped off Pirates scout Art Griggs, who signed him in January 1931. He got his first start at short when Tommy Thevenow broke a finger.
One August he was beaned in an exhibition game in London, Ontario, and got a concussion.
In December 1941 the Pirates traded him to Brooklyn for four players, a deal believed to stem partly from bad feelings with manager Frankie Frisch. Fans were outraged.
He came back in 1947 only after Leo Durocher was suspended. He pinch-hit three times in the World Series loss to the Yankees, and was released after hitting .244 in 1948.
p: Richard Nixon, a substitute tackle on the Fullerton High team when Vaughan was its star halfback, wrote his daughter after his Hall of Fame election, remembering Arky as "fast, hard-nosed and even then a real professional."
In 1952, at 40, he drowned in Lost Lake near his Northern California ranch when his fishing boat capsized. A witness said he swam back to help his friend, who could not swim.
He married his high school sweetheart, Margaret, in 1931; they had four children.
His mysterious drowning helped give Pittsburgh the phrase "The Ghost of Arky" for hard times.

c: He turned pro at 15 with the Bacharach Giants when they offered more for a weekend of catching than his father made in a week. By 19 he was rivaling Josh Gibson, and he caught the whole 1941 East-West All-Star Game and was named MVP.

In 1945 he spent four hours listening to Branch Rickey ("the talkingest man I ever did see") and turned him down, thinking Rickey was recruiting for a new Negro League team. Days later Jackie Robinson told him in confidence that he had signed with Brooklyn. Campanella rushed a telegram to Rickey.

At Nashua in 1946, when Walter Alston got thrown out of a game, Campanella took over and became the first Black man to manage in organized baseball. He sent Don Newcombe up to pinch-hit, and Newcombe homered to win.
A Nashua poultry farmer gave 100 chicks for every home run. Campanella collected 1,400 and shipped them to his father, who started a farm outside Philadelphia.
He won three MVP awards in five years and threw out 57 percent of base stealers in his career, the best rate on record.

At 17 he took over as the Elite Giants' regular catcher when Biz Mackey was traded in 1939, and helped beat Newark and the Homestead Grays in the playoffs. In 1942 he jumped to Monterrey in the Mexican League over a contract dispute.
The Dodgers first assigned him and Don Newcombe to Danville in 1946, but Danville's general manager said his league wasn't ready for integration, so they went to Nashua instead.
In 1948 Leo Durocher wanted him to start for the injured Bruce Edwards, but Brooklyn sent him to St. Paul to integrate the American Association. He went 0-for-4 with an error in his first game there.
After the accident the Dodgers made him a scouting supervisor and spring-training coach for young catchers; in 1978 he joined the community-relations staff under his old teammate Don Newcombe.
p: The son of a Sicilian-American vegetable peddler and an African-American mother, he was taunted as a "half-breed" by kids of both races and became a Golden Gloves boxer. The Phillies withdrew a workout invitation when they found out he was Black.

In January 1958, driving a light rental car home after helping close his Harlem liquor store, he skidded on ice into a telephone pole. The crash broke his neck and left him paralyzed from the chest down.

In May 1959, 93,103 fans, then a baseball record, filled the Los Angeles Coliseum for an exhibition in his honor. Over years of therapy he learned to feed himself and sign autographs with a device strapped to his arm, and he lived to 71. "It's Good to Be Alive" was the title of his autobiography.
As a teenager he helped on his father's vegetable truck, sold papers, shined shoes and ran a milk route.
Married with dependents, he was classified 3-A in World War II and worked in war industry instead of serving.

He married three times. With Bernice Ray he had two daughters before divorcing. He married Ruthe Willis in 1945; they had three children, including TV director Roy Campanella II, and separated in 1960 after his accident. Ruthe died of a heart attack at 40 in 1963, and he married Roxie Doles in 1964.

c: A three-sport athlete from small-town Georgia, he pitched at Georgia Tech and went fourth overall in the 1986 draft. By 1989 he was second in the Rangers' rotation behind Nolan Ryan.
In 1996 he led the majors with a 1.89 ERA. In 1997 he threw a no-hitter against the Giants in which the only baserunner came on a hit batter, and won the World Series with Florida.
After the Marlins' fire sale he pitched one year in San Diego and beat Randy Johnson twice by 2–1 scores in the 1998 Division Series.
In December 1998 the Dodgers made him the first $100 million player: seven years, $105 million. Injuries made it look to many like one of the worst deals ever.

After the 1994 strike he signed with Baltimore for one season, then with Florida for three years and $12.9 million. Sick with the flu, he threw a complete game in Game 6 of the 1997 NLCS to put the Marlins in the World Series.

The Marlins traded him to San Diego for Derrek Lee. He struck out 16 Astros in Game 1 of the 1998 Division Series, threw a three-hit shutout of Atlanta in the NLCS, and lost Game 4 as the Yankees swept.

The Dodgers traded him to the Yankees in December 2003 for Jeff Weaver and others. In Game 7 of the 2004 ALCS, with the Yankees trying not to blow a 3-0 lead, he lasted under two innings and gave up a two-run homer to David Ortiz.

Kirk Radomski told the Mitchell Report he sold Brown human growth hormone and Deca-Durabolin for two or three years starting in 2000 or 2001. Dodgers executives' 2003 meeting notes read "Steroids speculated by GM."
p: Late in 2004, frustrated with the Yankees, he punched a concrete column and broke his hand. The Mitchell Report later named him as a buyer of human growth hormone.
Back home in Macon, Georgia, he coaches high school baseball. In 2018 he held two suspected mail thieves at gunpoint until police arrived.
He and his wife, Candace, have four sons, and he's an assistant coach at Tattnall Square Academy in Macon.

c: In his first professional game as a catcher he tried to throw out a runner at second and hit the batter in the back of the head, knocking him out. Louisville's smallest uniform was so big on him that a writer said his red head stuck up "like a red peony in a field of chrysanthemums."

With the 1890s Orioles he hit .401 in 1896 and was hit by 51 pitches, still the record. In 1897 Amos Rusie fractured his skull with a pitch. He kept crowding the plate and was hit 287 times in his career.
When his arm went in 1899, Ned Hanlon tried to trade him to Pittsburgh. Jennings wrote the Pirates to warn them he was damaged goods.

Managing Detroit, he waved rubber snakes and jack-in-the-boxes at Rube Waddell from the coaching box, and another time brought dogs, since Waddell loved animals. His "Ee-yah!" yell, leg raised and fists clenched, was later taken up as a Marine battle cry.

On a player: "If that guy's brains were made of nitroglycerin and they exploded, the bust wouldn't muss his hair." He won pennants in his first three years with Detroit and was one of the first managers to platoon.
Against his father's wishes he left the mines in 1889 for $5 a game with a semipro team in Lehighton. Louisville signed him as a fill-in for an injured first baseman and soon made him its shortstop.

He was never the same after hurting his arm in 1898. Four teams in two leagues claimed him in 1901 before the Phillies won out. In 1905 a pitch broke his arm, and he broke it again in a collision weeks after returning.

Detroit wouldn't meet Baltimore's price for him as manager after 1906, so it simply drafted him as a player for $1,000. He nearly traded Ty Cobb over Cobb's spring-training fights, then lost the World Series in 1907, 1908 and 1909.
He was suspended in 1907 for taunting opponents with a tin whistle. Bill James credits him with one of the first platoons, with his catchers in the 1907 World Series.
p: He left school at about 12 to work as a breaker boy in the coal mines for 90 cents a day. Even when he was well off, he would visit the mines in the offseason and give miners rides home or groceries for their families.

He studied law at Cornell in the offseasons, coaching the baseball team for his tuition. One night he dove into the darkened campus pool without knowing it had been drained. His players never let him forget it: "At least I never dived into an empty pool." He became a respected trial lawyer in Scranton.
His first wife died in childbirth after 13 months of marriage. In 1911 his car went off a bridge into the Lehigh River, and he survived two broken legs, a broken arm and another head injury.

Though two semesters short of a Cornell degree, he passed the bar in 1905 and became a respected trial lawyer, defending accused murderers. Investments and his off-season practice made him comfortable.
He married Nora O'Boyle after the 1911 season. Elizabeth Dixon, his first wife, had left him a young daughter.
He died in 1928 at 58 of spinal meningitis, with tuberculosis a contributing cause.

c: On May 1, 1955, right after Bob Feller threw a one-hitter in the first game of a doubleheader, the rookie struck out nine in the first three innings and 16 in the game. As a rookie he struck out 245, breaking a record that had stood since Grover Alexander in 1911.

Red Sox general manager Joe Cronin offered a million dollars for him before the 1957 season. Score's reaction: "I wonder what Nancy will think when she reads that I am supposed to be worth a million dollars."

On May 7, 1957, Gil McDougald's line drive hit him in the right eye. His delivery left him defenseless. McDougald ran to the mound instead of to first. Score told him it could happen to anyone, but McDougald was haunted by it and retired three years later.

He came back but never regained his fastball, and always insisted his arm, not the eye, was the reason. At 30 he tried one last year in the minors: "I didn't want to be sitting somewhere when I was 60 and wondering."
Cy Slapnicka, who had signed Bob Feller, scouted him on a local policeman's tip and signed him on his 19th birthday, June 7, 1952, with a $60,000 bonus.
His 245 strikeouts in 1955 were the rookie record until Dwight Gooden in 1984.

McDougald's liner broke his nose and cheekbone, cut his eyelid and damaged the eye; he spent three weeks in the hospital. Feeling better than ever in 1958, he tore an elbow tendon on a damp night in Washington, changed his motion to protect it, and lost velocity.
Frank Lane traded him to the White Sox for Barry Latman on April 18, 1960, a day after trading his roommate Rocky Colavito.
p: At 3 he was run over by a truck that crushed both legs, and he later spent 10 months in bed with rheumatic fever. His mother had named him after St. Jude, patron saint of hopeless causes, and both believed his recoveries were answered prayers.
For 34 years he broadcast Indians games, many of them bad. His last call was Game 7 of the 1997 World Series, a Cleveland loss: "I would like to thank all the fans for their kindness over the years."

"People will tell me I was unlucky. Me? Unlucky?... That's a guy who has been in the right place at the right time." He roomed with Rocky Colavito in the minors and majors, and they called each other "roomie" for life.

His father was a New York City traffic cop. His mother, separated from him for years, moved the family to Lake Worth, Florida, for a bank job. As a freshman Herb broke an ankle and, still in the cast, had an emergency appendectomy.
He met his fiancée, Nancy MacNamara, at Lake Worth High; she rushed to Cleveland after the injury, and his old coach Father Kelly married them.

Driving home the morning after his 1998 Broadcasters Hall of Fame induction, he was badly hurt in a car crash, fracturing an eye socket, three ribs and his sternum. He threw out the first pitch the next Opening Day. He had a stroke in 2002 and died in 2008.

c: Roommate Elmer Stricklett taught him the spitball at his first White Sox camp in 1904, but he didn't use it regularly until 1906. That October he beat the crosstown Cubs twice in the World Series, striking out a then-record 12 in his Game 3 shutout.
In 1908 he went 40–15 with 464 innings, the last pitcher to win 40. During one nine-day stretch he pitched five times. One of those was a four-hitter he lost to Addie Joss's perfect game.

He went to his mouth before every pitch so hitters couldn't tell when the spitter was coming. Sam Crawford: "I swear, when it went past the plate it was just the spit went by." In 1909 Cleveland noticed he touched the bill of his cap before throwing it, and he had to change his style.
He fielded bunts "like a territorial animal." He once told a new third baseman who'd charged a bunt, "If you do that again, I'll kill you."

He blamed himself for his decline: "My arm was played out after the 1912 season — it needed a rest." He pitched anyway, and finished with the lowest career ERA in history, 1.82, but short of 200 wins.
He umpired half a season in the American League in 1922 and hated it, mostly because he didn't like calling strikes. "I remember when I wanted every pitch to be a strike."
Meriden signed him for $150 a month in 1902, and the White Sox bought him for $750 after 1903.
In the 1906 World Series he beat the Cubs twice, striking out a record 12 in Game 3, at least one in every inning.
When his arm gave out he asked for a year off, and Charles Comiskey released him instead. He later pitched some in the Eastern League and coached the White Sox.
During World War I he worked in a munitions factory. Later he was the battery coach at Notre Dame, where his son pitched.
p: One of 13 children of an Irish shoemaker and a Welsh mother, he left parochial school at 12 to pick slate in the Pennsylvania mines for 75 cents a day. He lasted two days at Fordham before leaving, put off by his roommates.
In July 1916 he rescued two girls from drowning in Lake Michigan.

The Depression wiped out his investment in Meriden, Connecticut, and he spent six years running a baseball school for the WPA. His son Ed Jr., who pitched for the White Sox, stopped Joe DiMaggio's 61-game minor-league hitting streak and died of rheumatic fever in 1937.

He was the only one of the 15 inductees at the 1947 Hall of Fame ceremony to attend. Dying of cancer, his weight fell below 100 pounds, and the White Sox held an Ed Walsh Day in 1958 to help pay his bills.
His son Ed Jr. pitched for the White Sox from 1928 to 1932 and died of rheumatic fever in 1937; that year his son Bob quit baseball after a line drive nearly hit him.
Late in the 1930s he became a chemical engineer at Meriden's water filtration plant. He and his wife, Rosemary, struggled to make ends meet even after his Hall of Fame election.

c: Cool Papa Bell saw him play for a Texas barnstorming team as a teenager and steered him to the Kansas City Monarchs. "Playing for the Kansas City Monarchs was like my school, my learning, my world." Touring with Jackie Robinson's All-Stars in 1950, he got lessons from Robinson on turning the double play.

The Cubs bought him from the Monarchs in 1953, and he never played a day in the minors. A Cubs scout said one reason they signed him was so that Gene Baker, the club's other Black call-up, would have a roommate. Banks played his first 424 games in a row.

In 1955 he hit five grand slams, a record. He won back-to-back MVPs in 1958 and 1959 for losing teams. Ralph Kiner said that at the plate he "would lightly rap his fingers on the bat; he looked like he was playing the flute."
Leo Durocher took over in 1966. Ferguson Jenkins remembered that every spring Durocher gave Banks's job to someone else, and every spring Banks won it back.
"Let's play two" dates to July 1969, when he tried to fire up his teammates before a game in 100-degree heat. On May 12, 1970, before 5,264 fans on a gloomy day at Wrigley, he hit his 500th home run.

He was the Cubs' first Black player and was quiet about it. Jackie Robinson visited him at his first game and told him, "just listen and learn." When he later thought about speaking out, Billy Williams warned him that fish get caught once they open their mouths.
Drafted into the Army in 1951, he served in Germany. Discharged in 1953, he finished the season with the Monarchs, hitting .347.
The Cubs signed him for $800 a month. A knee he'd first hurt in the Army kept bothering him.

Under P.K. Wrigley's "College of Coaches" in 1961, he agreed to move to left field so a bonus baby could play short. Later, beaned and briefly hospitalized, he came back two days after release and hit three straight homers against Milwaukee.
Teammate Ken Hubbs died in a plane crash in February 1964, and that June the Cubs traded Lou Brock. In 1967 Banks was oddly named a "player-coach." He coached first base in 1973 and 1974.
In 1983, soon after the Tribune Company bought the team, the Cubs briefly cut ties with him; he'd been working as their corporate sales representative.
p: His father, who had caught for the Dallas Black Giants, had to pay Ernie nickels and dimes to play catch, since the boy wasn't interested. Once he did start hitting, "he smashed so many windows that I was almost broke trying to pay for them."

He served two years in the Army in Germany. During the 1960s owner P.K. Wrigley offered the players a trust fund. Banks was the only one to take it, putting in half his salary, and at 55 he cashed out more than $4 million.
In 1967 he became the second African American in the U.S. to own a Ford dealership. He later sat on Chicago's transit board and the Cubs' board of directors.
A lifelong Republican, he ran for Chicago alderman in 1963 and finished a distant third with 12 percent. "People knew me only as a baseball player."
He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013. Barack Obama called him the man "who came up through the Negro Leagues, making $7 a day."

He died in January 2015. The October before, shortly after a dementia diagnosis, he had changed his will to leave everything to his caregiver, and a fight over his estate followed. The Cubs paid for his funeral.
His father, who had worked construction and loaded trucks for a grocery chain, played semipro ball in Texas.

He married Mollye Ector in 1953 and divorced her in 1959, paying $65,000 instead of alimony; she later sued over life-insurance payments. He then eloped with Eloyce Johnson, had twin sons and a daughter, and divorced in 1981; she got his 500th-homer ball and sold it.

He married four times; Hank Aaron was best man at his 1997 wedding to Liz Ellzey, and they adopted a baby daughter in 2008. Off-season he worked at a bank, owned a gas station, and later worked in insurance and for a moving company.
After his 2015 death a legal battle broke out over his estate and even the disposition of his body.

c: The hometown Cardinals took him in the 43rd round out of high school. He went to Missouri instead, where early on he threw so hard his cap kept flying off. A coach got him to stop leaping at hitters.
Rather than sign with Arizona after the 2006 draft, he pitched for the independent Fort Worth Cats: "It was my decision. I've never second guessed it."
In his debut, in relief against Houston in 2008, he retired all 13 batters he faced, a record for a relief debut.
In 2013 he became the first Tiger ever to start a season 12–0 and won his first Cy Young. In 2015, the first year of a $210 million deal with Washington, he threw two no-hitters.
On May 11, 2016, he struck out 20 Tigers, his old team, to tie the nine-inning record. In 2019 he won Game 1 of the World Series and started Game 7 as the Nationals won their first title.

Drafted by Arizona in 2006, he and agent Scott Boras couldn't agree, and he signed a four-year, $4.3 million deal just before midnight on the club's deadline the next May. The scouts were already calling him "Mad Max."

In December 2009 Arizona sent him to Detroit in the three-team deal that moved Curtis Granderson to the Yankees. Pitching through a late-season injury, he reached his first World Series in 2012, which the Tigers lost to the Giants.
His seven-year, $210 million Nationals deal included a $50 million signing bonus paid out over 14 years, the largest deferral in MLB history.
Traded to the Dodgers in 2021, he signed with the Mets, then was traded to Texas midway through 2023 and started Game 3 of the World Series as the Rangers won their first title.
p: His right eye is blue and his left is brown. The Tigers made sure his 2011 bobblehead got it right.
He met his wife Erica, a softball pitcher, at Missouri. On the day their son was born in 2021, he pitched a complete game first and then left for the hospital.
His younger brother Alex, who loved sabermetrics, died by suicide in 2012. Since then Scherzer has dedicated every start to him.

In 2016 he and Erica matched donations to an anti-trafficking group for every strikeout he threw. As a Met he paid adoption fees for big dogs at a New Jersey shelter for a week, and more than 270 animals were adopted.
He and Erica dated more than eight years before marrying in November 2013. They have three daughters and a son, and bought a home in Jupiter, Florida, in 2023.
In 2015 Erica led Nationals spouses in promoting the team's Night Out event for LGBT fans.

c: He enlisted in 1911. On the Army's famous 25th Infantry team in Hawaii he went 36–3 in the box scores that survive, and hit .356. His Army nickname was "Cap": "in the army at that time a Captain was somebody and on the ball field Cap Rogan was somebody."

He picked up "Bullet," probably for his fastball, in the California Winter League in 1920–21. Kansas City papers started calling him "Bullet Joe" that summer, possibly after the A's pitcher Bullet Joe Bush.
In the first Negro League World Series, in 1924, he batted .325 and won two games. His 12th-inning infield hit won Game 7.
In 1925 he went 15–2 with a 1.74 ERA and also led the Monarchs with a .360 average. In the pennant series he won Games 1, 4 and 7, all complete games.
In 1932, at 39, he pitched for a semipro team in Jamestown, North Dakota. In the last game of their season he hit a grand slam and threw a six-hitter for his 20th win.
His son at his 1998 induction: "When Satch was on the mound, he needed a designated hitter. When my dad was on the mound, he was in the cleanup spot."

On an Army furlough he pitched for the Los Angeles White Sox and took a no-hitter into the ninth. J.L. Wilkinson signed him for the All Nations during that leave and offered him a Monarchs contract on discharge in 1920.
Before the 1925 World Series rematch with Hilldale he hurt his knee playing with his young son and needed surgery. Without him the Monarchs lost in six.
Made manager in 1926, he started both games of the deciding doubleheader against the Chicago American Giants and lost both to Bill Foster.
An undisclosed illness hospitalized him in August 1930 and kept him out most of the year. In 1938 Wilkinson turned down offers to trade him to Detroit.
p: Growing up in Kansas City after his mother died, he had a hard time with his stepmother and didn't look like an athlete. Nobody, his stepmother included, believed him when he said he'd be a pro ballplayer.

Unhappy at home and at his segregated high school, he dropped out and joined the Army at 18, lying about his age. That's why some records, his Hall of Fame plaque among them, say he was born in 1889 and not 1893.
He married Kathrine McWilliams, a Colorado farm girl, in 1922. Their son was born right after the 1924 World Series. Between seasons he was reported to sell life insurance.
After baseball he umpired Monarchs home games and worked for the Post Office until 1959. His grave marker reads simply: Arizona, SGT US Army, World War 1.
Between the 1923 and 1924 seasons he was reported to be selling life insurance.

c: Jack Dunn tried him out at Baltimore in 1907 and released him after two singles in 15 at-bats, deciding he "could not hit." Two years later Baker was the first to hit a ball over Shibe Park's right-field fence.
He swung a 52-ounce bat. Jake Daubert: "Frank Baker doesn't look so big, but he has big wrists." He was bowlegged and ran "like a soft-shell crab," but stole 20 or more bases five years in a row.

In 1909 Ty Cobb spiked him sliding into third, and Connie Mack called Cobb the dirtiest player ever. Then a Detroit News photo showed Baker reaching across the bag, and a Detroit paper called him a "soft-fleshed darling." He was branded as easy to intimidate.

The Giants tried to exploit that in the 1911 World Series, and Fred Snodgrass spiked him twice. Baker homered off Rube Marquard to win Game 2, and off Christy Mathewson in the ninth to tie Game 3. He was "Home Run" Baker from then on.
When Mack wouldn't give him a raise after 1914, he sat out 1915 at 29 and played for town teams. Many towns held Home Run Baker Days. Mack sold him to the Yankees.
Managing in the Eastern Shore League in 1924, he discovered Jimmie Foxx and sold him to Mack. He was fired the next year, partly because the price he'd gotten was considered "paltry."
Buck Herzog signed him to a Ridgely, Maryland, semipro team for $5 a week in 1905. He turned down the Texas League to play in Cambridge, Maryland, where he met his wife.
He hit .409 in the 1910 World Series, and .450 with a homer in 1913. Late in 1914 Mack sent him, Eddie Collins and Chief Bender to scout the Braves, who then swept the A's.

Locked into a three-year contract, he tried to renegotiate after 1914 and Mack refused. Under pressure from Ban Johnson, Mack sold him to the Yankees for 1916. He played in the 1921 and 1922 World Series, both losses, as a part-timer beside Babe Ruth.
p: His father could do every trick he saw at the circus. Frank remembered him cartwheeling the length of the street and landing on his feet.
A friend said the quickest way to get him talking was to go duck hunting with him: "Frank is the best shot in Talbot County, and he's wild about duck shooting."
A modest man, he never drank, smoked or swore. Twins born to him and his wife in January 1914 died before they were two weeks old.
After the 1919 season scarlet fever killed his wife. His two small daughters caught it too but recovered. Grieving and quarantined, he sat out 1920.
In 1924 he stepped in to stop the lynching of a Black man in Easton, Maryland, who had assaulted Baker's sister-in-law.
When he was finally elected to the Hall of Fame in 1955: "It's better to get a rosebud while you're alive than a whole bouquet after you're dead."
As a young man he clerked at a relatives' butcher shop and grocery.
He married Ottilie Tschantre, daughter of a Swiss jeweler, in 1909. After her death he married Margaret Mitchell of Baltimore, and had two children with each wife.
Back in Trappe he sat on the town board, collected taxes, directed the State Bank of Trappe, and was a volunteer firefighter.

c: Boston drafted him in 1989. In August 1990 it traded him to Houston for 37-year-old reliever Larry Andersen, one of the worst trades ever. "All my life everything had been Boston." When he called his grandmother in Newton with the news, she started crying.

He'd never played first base until two weeks before the 1991 opener, when Houston decided to keep him. He played first in minor-league games in the morning and for the Astros in the afternoon, then won Rookie of the Year.

His stance had his legs spread far apart in a deep crouch, "like he is sitting on the john." It left his hands in the strike zone, and pitches broke them three years in a row, until he started wearing a pad.
In the 1994 strike year he hit .368 and slugged .750 and was the unanimous MVP. "Every pitch that I was looking for, I got." The day before the strike, a pitch broke his hand again.

He was never linked to steroids by testing or any investigation, but suspicion delayed his Hall of Fame election until 2017. "I know what I did; I know how hard I worked... I can't go take a blood test now."

His crouched stance left his hands over the plate, and he broke his left hand three years running, the 1994 break coming from an Andy Benes pitch the day before the strike. After the third, in 1995, he wore a protective pad and never broke it again.
The Astros won just one of 13 postseason games in his first four trips to the playoffs, a 5-4 win over San Diego in 1998.

Shoulder surgery for bone spurs and a torn labrum, then arthritis in the other shoulder, wore him down. In 2005, unable to throw, he pinch-hit as the Astros won their first pennant; he and Craig Biggio, after 4,714 games together in Houston, finally reached a World Series, and were swept by the White Sox.

In 2006 the Astros filed a $15.6 million disability insurance claim on him, and his reporting to spring training anyway complicated it. Cigna rejected it, he was eventually paid in full, and the Astros settled with the insurer the day he retired.
p: His mother, later a police officer, said he "could throw a ball before he could walk." Soccer was his main sport in high school.
He grew up in a Red Sox house in Connecticut, "one of those places where you couldn't mention the word Yankees."
The Astros' weight room had a sign: "Bagwell's Gym. Work Hard. Play Hard. Or Leave." He later came to think the muscle he built up wore out his shoulder and ended his career at 37.

In 2010 he turned down a two-year deal to stay on as Astros batting coach, citing his family. Of the Hall of Fame wait: "Baseball does not define me as a person. It's what I do with my kids, and as a husband, that's going to define me."
His father pitched in college at Northwestern and then semipro, and Jeff went to the University of Hartford on a baseball scholarship.
His parents divorced when he was 11.
He's married to his third wife, Rachel, and they have five children in a blended family. He and Biggio were in the stands when the Astros won the 2017 World Series and got rings.

c: In high school, pitchers stopped throwing him strikes and he started chasing. His father gave him Ted Williams's The Science of Hitting. He went back to taking balls and finished the season at .485. The Major League Scouting Bureau still called him a nonprospect.

He played in the longest professional game ever, Pawtucket's 33-inning game against Rochester in 1981. "When I doubled in the tying run in the 21st inning, I didn't know if the guys wanted to hug me or slug me." He led the league in hitting that year and still wasn't called up.

He got his chance in June 1982, when Carney Lansford sprained his ankle, and hit .358 the rest of the way. Boston traded Lansford that winter. From 1985 to 1988 Boggs won four straight batting titles.
Tommy John said Boggs always seemed to know what pitch was coming: "He's a phenomenon, a pure hitting machine. I've never seen anything like him. He lit me up."

His Hall of Fame plaque ends "Legendary for his superstitions." He ate chicken before every game, fielded exactly 150 grounders in practice, and drew "chai," the Jewish word for life and good luck, in the dirt every time he batted. "Believe me, I have a few superstitions, and they work."
After winning the 1996 World Series with the Yankees, he rode around Yankee Stadium on the back of a police horse. His 3,000th hit, for his hometown Devil Rays in 1999, was a home run.
The Scouting Bureau called him a nonprospect. Scout George Digby talked Boston into drafting him in the seventh round in 1976, and he signed for $7,500, giving up a football scholarship.
He hit 24 homers in 1987, more than double any other season. The Red Sox reached the playoffs in 1988 and 1990 and were swept by Oakland both times.
Jean Yawkey promised him a five-year deal, but she died first and new management offered a year and an option. He felt betrayed, lost his focus in his last Boston season, and left as a free agent.

He signed a three-year, $11 million deal with the Yankees, who beat the Dodgers by adding the third year. After his last two years in Tampa Bay, reports said the Devil Rays paid him to choose their cap for his Hall of Fame plaque; he denied it.
He retired in 1999 after a knee injury, with a .328 average and 3,010 hits.
p: His father was a Marine and Air Force pilot, and his mother flew mail planes. Wade loved the regimented military routine, and it carried into his game-day rituals.

In June 1986 his mother was killed by a cement truck driver on work release who ran a red light. After Game 7 of the World Series he cried in the dugout. Baseball had kept his mind off her: "Now I've got to go home and when I walk in the house, she's not going to be there."

In 1988 Margo Adams, a woman he'd had a four-year affair with, sued him for palimony and told her story everywhere, Penthouse included. He told his wife Debbie everything, and she stayed. The same year, he said he "willed himself invisible" during a knife fight outside a Gainesville bar.
Teammates told stories of him downing dozens of beers on cross-country flights. He didn't deny them, and in retirement he did promotional tours for Miller.
He married Debbie in December 1976, soon after reaching the minors; they had Meagann and Brett, named for George Brett.
Adams's suit sought $12 million; an appeals court threw out $11.5 million of it, and the rest was settled out of court.
In 1988 he got a minor knife cut on the neck in an altercation outside a bar in Gainesville, Florida.
After his mother's death he and his father bought a fish camp near Hawthorne, Florida, called Yankee Landing-Finway Fish Camp, which his father ran.

c: At McClymonds High in Oakland, Bill Russell was his basketball teammate, and Vada Pinson and Curt Flood were his baseball teammates.
He crowded the plate and dared pitchers to hit him, and they hit him 118 times in 10 years with Cincinnati. His slides were "deliberately vicious." One in 1960 started a fistfight with Eddie Mathews.

Cincinnati owner Bill DeWitt called him "an old 30" and traded him to Baltimore. In 1966 he won the Triple Crown, the MVP and the World Series MVP. His homer off Luis Tiant that May was the only fair ball ever hit out of Memorial Stadium.
In Baltimore he ran a clubhouse kangaroo court as "da Judge," in a robe with a mop for a wig. Only he could tell Earl Weaver, "Stand up, Earl. Oh, you are standing."

In 1975 he became the first Black manager in the majors. In his first game, with Rachel Robinson there, he put himself in to bat and homered. Jackie Robinson had said he hoped to see a Black manager soon, nine days before he died in 1972.
Bobby Mattick signed him for $3,500 in 1953. At Ogden, Utah, no restaurant or movie house would serve Black customers; he found segregated Columbia, South Carolina, "much better."
On August 15, 1960, his hard slide into third set off a fistfight with Milwaukee's Eddie Mathews.

The 1961 diner incident started when a short-order cook taunted him; two policemen across the street saw him brandish the pistol and arrested him. Owner Bill DeWitt remembered it when he traded him. In the 1961 World Series he had three hits as the Reds lost to the Yankees.
The Pappas trade became shorthand for a bad deal; in Bull Durham, Susan Sarandon's character says, "Who can forget Frank Robinson for Milt Pappas?"
In 1967 he banged his head on an infielder's knee sliding into second and had a concussion and prolonged double vision. "I haven't been the same hitter since."

He homered in the 1969 Series loss to the Mets, won again in 1970, and lost to Pittsburgh in seven in 1971, finishing with eight World Series homers. Baltimore then traded him to the Dodgers to make room for Don Baylor.
p: He barely knew his father, who told Frank's brothers that Frank "will never make a big-league baseball player." Proving him wrong became a drive.
At a team party in 1966 his teammates threw him in a pool, not believing he couldn't swim. They thought he was joking as he sank, until Andy Etchebarren dove in and pulled him out.

House-hunting in Baltimore, a professor who was happy to rent to them changed his mind on meeting his wife. "He must have thought I was Mrs. Brooks Robinson." To a reporter who mixed the two Robinsons up: "Can't you see we wear different numbers?"
He had refused to join the NAACP unless he wouldn't have to make public appearances. Baltimore's segregated housing changed his mind, and he became an outspoken speaker on race.
In February 1961 he pulled a .25-caliber pistol during an argument in a Cincinnati restaurant. He pleaded guilty to carrying a concealed weapon and paid a $250 fine.
His parents divorced when he was an infant; he was the youngest of his mother's ten children and the only one from her marriage to his father.
He married Barbara Ann Cole in October 1961 after meeting her that year; they had a son, Kevin, and a daughter, Nichelle. Barbara sold real estate in Los Angeles.
His kangaroo court donated its 1969 fines to Reds catcher Pat Corrales, whose wife had died in childbirth that summer.
He died of bone cancer in 2019 at 83.

c: MLB was on strike and the Astros wouldn't fund scout Andres Reiner's 350-mile trip to see a teenage lefty in Tovar, high in the Andes. GM Bob Watson paid for it from his own expense account. Reiner won Santana over with a photo of the spring complex: "I had never seen four or five diamonds together."

The Twins got him in the 1999 Rule 5 draft and had to keep him in the majors all of 2000, though he'd never pitched above Class A. He posted a 6.49 ERA. In 2002 Baseball Prospectus pegged him as a future lefty specialist.

Sent to Triple-A in 2002 to work on his changeup, he threw it over and over until it looked just like his fastball out of his hand. Bret Boone said the gap between the two was sometimes 20 mph. He won unanimous Cy Youngs in 2004 and 2006.

On August 19, 2007, he struck out a Twins-record 17 Rangers in eight innings without shaking off his catcher once. Torii Hunter: "I didn't get a single ball in center field. I was bored. I could have brought a lawn chair."

On June 1, 2012, in the Mets' 8,020th game, he threw the first no-hitter in franchise history, coming back from shoulder surgery. He told manager Terry Collins he wasn't coming out and needed 134 pitches. "I don't even think I've thrown a no-hitter in video games." The shoulder tore again the next spring.
The Marlins took him from Houston in the Rule 5 draft, and the Twins, who really wanted him, traded draftee Jared Camp plus cash to Florida to get him.

When Eric Milton got hurt and the Twins still kept Santana in long relief, he was angry enough to consider asking for a trade, but he took the role and proved himself. He started Game 1 of the 2003 ALDS against the Yankees.
The Twins gave him a four-year, $40 million deal, the biggest in team history. Frustrated when they traded Luis Castillo in 2007 and stood pat, he let it be known he was open to leaving.

In February 2008 the Twins traded him to the Mets for Carlos Gómez and three others, and he signed for six years and $137.5 million, the largest pitcher contract ever. That September he went 4-0 with a 1.83 ERA on a torn meniscus that needed surgery afterward.
A tear in his shoulder's anterior capsule, first treated as a pectoral strain, cost him all of 2011.
Comeback tries with the Orioles in 2014, when he tore an Achilles tendon in extended spring training, and the Blue Jays in 2015 never got him back to the majors.
p: A ballpark in Tovar, his small Andes town, carries a sign: "Welcome to the territory of Johan Santana." His coach sent him home from his first youth practice for not being properly dressed. He came back the next day in the uniform of his father, a semipro infielder.
Told a lefty couldn't play shortstop, he taught himself to throw right-handed so he could.
Leaving home to sign: "I was crying. I said, 'I don't think I can do this.' But then I told myself that I was going to do it for my family." He has known his wife Yasmile since he was 9.
In 2006 he started a foundation to help hospitals, and he and the Twins bought a yellow fire truck for Tovar's fire department.
His father, Jesus, was an electrician and semipro infielder. Johan wanted to be an engineer, and wasn't even the best player in the family; that was his older brother Franklin.
He missed the Mets' first game at Citi Field in 2009 for the birth of his son. He and Yasmile have two daughters and a son.
In 2009 a woman accused him of sexual battery on a Florida golf course. He said the encounter was consensual; she filed a civil suit and he countersued for extortion.
A minor-league pitcher in the Angels system also named Johan Santana changed his name to Ervin Santana in 2003 because of him.

c: Signing out of an aircraft plant, he and his father cared more about a spring-training invitation than a bonus. The Cardinals and Dodgers said no. The Reds said yes, and Bill McKechnie told his GM, "Boss, you've got a natural."

Red Smith said he was "built like a slouchy flyrod, being composed largely of arms and neck and ears." His sidearm delivery terrified hitters. Ralph Kiner: "Your legs shook when you tried to dig in on him." An unnamed Dodger couldn't keep breakfast down on days Blackwell pitched.

In 1947 he won 16 straight, including a no-hitter against Boston. In his next start he was two outs from back-to-back no-hitters, matching teammate Johnny Vander Meer, when Eddie Stanky's grounder skipped between his legs. "I must have replayed that moment a thousand times."
He refused to wash his sweatshirt during the streak. His roommate: "Frankly, it stinks."

In 1952 the Dodgers scored 15 runs in the first inning. He had already showered and was watching it in the hotel bar when his reliever sat down beside him. "Don't you want to know what the score is?" "Frankly, no."
He signed for a $750 bonus plus $250 more if he lasted until midseason. In 1942 he threw three playoff shutouts in the International League, then got pneumonia and missed the Junior World Series.
When Eddie Stanky broke up his second straight no-hitter in 1947, he greeted the next batter, Jackie Robinson, "with an explosion of racist insults," according to Robinson's biographer.

Going 3-12 in August 1952, he was traded to the Yankees for Johnny Schmitz, three minor leaguers and $35,000, one of the late-season waiver deals that got the rule changed. He pitched in that World Series and retired the next July because his arm "hurt too much."
He kept trying comebacks, including in the Dominican Republic, and finished his career helping Seattle win a PCL pennant.
p: Drafted in 1943, he told the Army about his aircraft experience, and it made him a cook. "I'd never boiled an egg in my life." After Germany surrendered he served his unit a banquet with apple pies and ate one himself.

In 1945 he won a game before more than 50,000 soldiers at the Nuremberg stadium where Hitler had held his rallies. When a writer asked where he could see the Reds' phenom, McKechnie answered: "Germany."
In January 1949 surgeons removed his infected right kidney, cutting through the back muscles a pitcher needs, and one doctor said his career was over. He came back to win 17 games in 1950.

He fondly remembered one season-ending train ride when the Reds got so drunk some lost their shirts and undershorts. Then they saw their wives on the Cincinnati platform. "Very quietly we all shook hands... and then went home to face the music."
His father worked as a cleaner and dyer and later sold real estate.
His wartime marriage to Arlene Knowlton broke up. He settled in Tampa with his second wife, Dorothy Davenport, and their two daughters, ran a liquor store, and became a distillery salesman.

c: He was a basketball star at Michigan State and walked onto the baseball team unannounced. Asked what position he played, he said, "Well, I can pitch." Two years later he was in the majors.

Pitching in Vermont, he turned to watch a steal attempt and his catcher's throw knocked him out cold. He insisted on staying in and retired 12 in a row. That was the day that most impressed the Phillies scout who signed him.

At his first camp he overheard owner Bob Carpenter say, "Well, it looks like I blew another $25,000." Coach Cy Perkins told him, "Wait till they see you pitch." In 1950 Perkins put him alongside Walter Johnson and Lefty Grove. When the Phillies let Perkins go for being too old, Roberts offered to pay his salary.
From 1950 to 1955 he won 20 every year and averaged 323 innings. He completed 28 starts in a row. His control was so good that the joke was his catchers brought rocking chairs.

He wouldn't throw at hitters, though Dizzy Dean and his own pitching coach urged him to. He remembered doing it on purpose only twice. He gave up 505 home runs, a record until 2010, many of them solo shots in games already decided.
Masaichi Kaneda saw him pitch on a tour of Japan at 17 and copied his drop-and-drive delivery. He became Japan's greatest pitcher, with 400 wins.
The Phillies' bonus went from $10,000 to $15,000 to $25,000 over three days of workouts. He finally paid his father back with his 1950 World Series check.
He clinched the 1950 pennant by pitching ten innings on the last day of the season, then started Game 2 of the World Series against Allie Reynolds, his only postseason game, as the Yankees swept.
He was so upset when the Phillies let coach Cy Perkins go after 1954 for being too old that he offered to pay Perkins's salary himself. By 1955 he'd switched to sidearm to favor a sore arm.

The Phillies sold him to the Yankees after 1961 for a little over the waiver price, and the Yankees released him in May 1962 without using him. Baltimore signed him, and he later pitched for Houston and the Cubs, where he also helped coach.
After baseball he coached the University of South Florida for nine seasons, winning six conference titles.
p: His father, a Welsh coal miner, had fought at Gallipoli and brought the family to the Illinois coal fields, where at one point the mines ran one day a week. Robin broke one of his father's hoes on purpose to get out of farm chores.

In eighth grade a Hall of Famer, Grover Cleveland Alexander, spoke at his school's sports banquet. An alcoholic living in a Springfield hotel, he said only: "don't take to drink, because look what it has done to me." Then he sat down.

As a boy he promised his mother, "Then I'll build you a house." When the Phillies' bonus reached $25,000 he signed and bought his parents a $19,000 home. He didn't know about income tax, and his father loaned him what he owed.
He took losses hard. After one in Milwaukee he walked seven miles back to the team hotel. At home he'd lie in his backyard hammock with a six-pack and watch the sun come up.
His father's verdict, in 1956: "Ah, well, he could have done a lot worse."
His father left coal mining in 1929 to be a maintenance foreman at Sangamo Electric. When Robin broke a hoe on purpose to skip chores, his father paddled him with a fly swatter.
His sister set him up with Mary Ann Kalnes, a teacher who'd moved to Springfield because she admired Lincoln. They married in December 1949 and raised four boys.
He coached his son Dan in high school. Dan later coached Army and left after an alcohol-related arrest.

c: At 14, already six feet and 180 pounds, he left Waterbury for New York to try to catch on as a ballplayer, despite the strappings his father gave him for skipping work. He started out as a left-handed-throwing third baseman.

A Troy shirt factory had to tailor his uniform because none fit him. He fell for the seamstress, Angeline Mayer, but was too shy to follow up. When he finally waited for her outside the factory, she said, "Hello, Roger Connor." They were married for 47 years.
He hit baseball's first grand slam on September 10, 1881, for Troy: two outs in the bottom of the ninth, his team down three.

His size is the main reason the New York team came to be called the Giants. In 1885 he won the batting title and struck out eight times in 506 plate appearances. In 1886 he hit the first ball known to clear the original Polo Grounds.
He retired with 138 homers, the career record until Babe Ruth. Hank Aaron's 715th, in 1974, made people ask whose record Ruth had broken. Two years later Connor was in the Hall of Fame.
In 1880, his rookie year at Troy, he made 60 errors in 83 games at third and hurt his shoulder, which moved him to first base.
He hit .303 in the 1888 postseason series against St. Louis and .343 with 12 RBIs as the Giants beat Brooklyn in 1889.
Paid $3,500 in 1889 and not exactly oppressed, he still jumped to the Players' League out of loyalty to the Brotherhood, and John Day's pleas at his Waterbury home couldn't change his mind.
The Philadelphia Athletics signed him for 1892 but broke up, and his contract went to the Phillies. St. Louis released him in May 1897, hitting .227.
In 1898 he bought the Waterbury minor-league team; Angeline kept the books and their daughter took tickets. He worked as a Waterbury school inspector until 1920.
p: His infant daughter Lulu died before being baptized, and the devout Connor took it as God's punishment for marrying Angeline, who wasn't Catholic. She had secretly been taking Catholic instruction and planned to surprise him by being baptized on what would have been Lulu's first birthday.
He played almost 2,000 games without being ejected. His only ejection came in the minors in 1902, for pummeling Tommy Tucker after Tucker threw his brother Joe to the ground.
Angeline had a weather vane made from two of his bats. It became a Waterbury landmark.

The Florida real-estate crash and the 1926 Miami hurricane wrecked his savings, and he and Angeline moved in with their daughter Cecilia's family. Angeline died in 1928. The next year cancer took most of his voice box.
He was buried in an unmarked grave until Waterbury residents and fans raised money for a headstone, dedicated in 2001. Umpire Bill Klem had long campaigned to get him into the Hall of Fame.
His father, who'd strapped him for playing ball, died suddenly in 1874, two months before his youngest brother was born. Roger became a father figure to the younger children.

Lulu caught dysentery when she was brought on a road trip in 1887 and died just before her first birthday. Later he and Angeline adopted a blond girl from a Catholic orphanage who ran straight to him and threw her arms around his neck.

c: Ramfis Trujillo, son of the Dominican dictator, saw him win a 2–1 game and had him drafted into the Air Force at once. He never flew or fixed a plane. He pitched.
He threw sidearm until a minor-league manager talked him into going overhand, and the high-kicking delivery was born. In his 1960 debut he one-hit the Phillies and struck out 12.
On July 2, 1963, he beat 42-year-old Warren Spahn 1–0 in 16 innings, both men going the distance, until Willie Mays homered. Some call it the greatest game ever pitched.
He threw five pitches from three arm angles, and Pete Rose called him the best pitcher he ever faced. He never seemed to sweat and always seemed to be smiling. One nickname was "Laughing Boy."
He won 191 games in the 1960s, the most of anyone, but in each of his four best seasons Koufax or Gibson won the Cy Young unanimously.

Writers held his attack on John Roseboro against him, and he missed the Hall of Fame by seven votes in 1982. Roseboro made a personal appeal, and Marichal got in the next year. At Roseboro's funeral in 2002 he was a pallbearer: "I wish I could have had John Roseboro as my catcher."
The Giants signed him for a $500 bonus in 1958.

In Game 4 of the 1962 World Series, leading 2-0, he smashed the thumb of his pitching hand trying to bunt off Whitey Ford and was finished for the Series. The Giants didn't reach another World Series until 1989.

For hitting Roseboro he was suspended eight games, fined a then-NL record $1,750, and barred from the Giants' final two games at Dodger Stadium. He also paid Roseboro a financial settlement. The 14-minute brawl ended when Koufax, Mays and others broke it up.
Finally back in the postseason in 1971, he lost a 2-1 complete game to the eventual champion Pirates.
p: He grew up in a palm-bark shack with no electricity. His father died when he was 3. At 10 he lay in a coma for nine days. The boys made balls by paying a shoemaker a peso to sew cloth around found golf balls, and grew up with the Alou brothers.

When Trujillo's assassination threw the country into chaos in 1961, manager Alvin Dark let him leave spring camp to bring his fiancée Alma back from the Dominican Republic, and even gave him two plane tickets. They married in March 1962.
He served as the Dominican Republic's Minister of Sports from 1996 to 2000. On his farm: "I have 48 head of cattle and a lot of chickens."
From his autobiography: "I want to be remembered more for helping people than for what I did in baseball."
As a boy he tended the family's horses, donkeys and goats, and at 11 he briefly worked cutting sugarcane.
He and Alma had six children, 13 grandchildren and a great-grandchild, and celebrated their 50th anniversary in 2012.

c: His father hit him 100 ground balls at a time and counted the errors. His high school had no baseball team. At Illinois he was a basketball All-American, and the sport wrecked his ankles, which he taped before every game for the rest of his career.

At 24 he wrote the Indians asking to be manager. The board first voted 11–1 against him, then hired him. One writer: "The Indians get a Baby Snooks for a manager and ruin the best shortstop in baseball." Veteran pitchers told him, "Listen, college boy, you play shortstop and I'll do the pitching."

On July 14, 1946, after going 5-for-5 and watching Ted Williams hit three homers, he drew up the Williams shift between games of a doubleheader. When Williams came up, Boudreau yelled "Yo" and the fielders moved to the right side. Williams laughed, then grounded out to him.
After 1947 Bill Veeck tried to trade him. More than 4,000 letters protested, and a newspaper ballot ran 10 to 1 for Boudreau. Veeck backed down.

In the 1948 one-game playoff at Fenway he started knuckleballer Gene Bearden, which Bob Feller called "a stroke of genius," and went 4-for-4 with two homers himself. He hit .355, won the MVP, and won the World Series, the only manager ever to win both in the same season.
Before signing with Cleveland he had offers from the Cubs, a movie role, and $150 a game from a pro basketball team. He coached Illinois freshman basketball while starting his baseball career.
In his first spring as manager, Ben Chapman, Gee Walker and Hal Trosky each came into his office to say they'd asked for the job and could do it better.
Arthritis in his ankles from basketball made him 4-F in World War II, so he played and managed through the war.
In 1945 a broken ankle held him to 97 games.

He told Bill Veeck he'd refuse to play shortstop and demand a trade if he were replaced as manager. After the 1948 title, the only time a manager also won the MVP, Veeck tore up his contract and gave him a raise to $62,000.
Cleveland released him as player and manager after 1950. He managed the Red Sox (1952-54) and was the first manager of the Kansas City Athletics, fired 104 games into 1957.
p: His mother was Jewish, and as a boy he celebrated Passover seders with his Orthodox grandparents. His father raised him Catholic after his parents divorced.
He married Della DeRuiter, whom he'd met in high school, in 1938. Their son Louis was wounded in Vietnam with the Marines. Their daughter Sharyn married Denny McLain.

After managing, he spent 30 years in the Cubs broadcast booth, apart from 1960, when the Cubs swapped him with manager Charlie Grimm. He stumbled over names but could tell you what was about to happen.
Bob Feller: "Boudreau drew people to him. He had the looks of a matinee idol."
His parents divorced when he was seven. His mother remarried a man who didn't like sports and paid him little attention, and his father never saw him play in the majors.
He and Della had four children; son James pitched in the minors until he hurt his arm. Daughter Sharyn married Denny McLain, who later served two prison terms.
He retired after the station didn't renew him for 1988, at 71, after 50 years as player, manager and broadcaster.

c: The Rockies drafted him in the 21st round out of high school in Lakeland, Florida. He went to Florida Gulf Coast instead, where he picked up the "funky" sidearm motion. In 2010 he went 11–0 and was Collegiate Baseball's player of the year.
He was the first 2010 draftee in the majors, debuting less than two months after the White Sox picked him. His delivery got him the nickname "The Condor."

In 2016 he hated the White Sox's baggy throwback pullovers, which he said hurt his mechanics, so before his start he cut them up with scissors. The team sent him home and suspended him five days. He later said he regretted it.

In Game 4 of the 2018 World Series, down four runs, he screamed at his teammates in the dugout to start hitting. They came back to win. In Game 5 he pitched the last inning and struck out Manny Machado to end the Series.

Injuries kept him to a handful of games from 2020 to 2022: Tommy John surgery, a broken rib, a broken finger from a line drive, and a broken wrist from falling off his bike on the way to lunch. Boston's Chaim Bloom said someone must have a Chris Sale voodoo doll. Traded to Atlanta, he won the Triple Crown and the Cy Young in 2024.
The White Sox drafted him 13th overall in 2010. In 2013 he signed a five-year, $32 million deal with two team options.
In April 2015 he was ejected and suspended five games for his part in a bench-clearing brawl with Kansas City after Yordano Ventura's exchange with Adam Eaton.
The White Sox traded him to Boston in December 2016 for Yoán Moncada, Michael Kopech and two others. In his first postseason, 2017, he had an 8.38 ERA.
Shoulder inflammation sent him to the injured list twice in 2018, but he came back to close out the World Series, striking out Manny Machado for the final out.

Months after a five-year, $145 million extension in 2019, elbow trouble ended his season; Tommy John surgery followed in March 2020, performed in Los Angeles while Florida had suspended non-emergency surgeries for COVID.
Boston traded him to Atlanta for Vaughn Grissom after 2023. In 2024 he won the Cy Young and the pitching Triple Crown.
p: He switched to 41 in Boston because 49 is kept out of circulation for Tim Wakefield.
He and his wife have three sons and live in Naples, Florida.

During a 2022 rehab start in Triple-A he was videotaped smashing things in the dugout tunnel. Later that year he broke his wrist riding his bike to lunch, and Chaim Bloom said someone must have "a Chris Sale voodoo doll."

c: Catching for a poor Georgia team in 1905 with no mask, he took so many foul balls that both eyes swelled shut. He came back the next day with a wire wastebasket over his face. After that summer he moved to the infield, and Sol White taught him shortstop.
"Wherever the money was, that's where I was." He changed teams 17 times in 27 years, and played winter ball in Cuba, where he hit .500 against Ty Cobb's Tigers in 1910.
He was called the "Black Wagner." Honus Wagner's response: "It's an honor to be compared to him."
Ted Page said that he and Wagner both had hands "as big as a telephone book" and came up with dirt and everything on ground balls. Judy Johnson: "He looked like he was gliding over the ball."
Cum Posey called him "the Jekyll and Hyde of baseball," fierce against opponents and gentle with his own players. Judy Johnson said he "would soft sell you into doing what you had to do."
At 40, after moving to second base to make room for Dick Lundy, he hit .444 for the 1924 batting title, with 11 hits in a row at one point.
Asked on a radio show to name the greatest player of all time, anywhere, Babe Ruth reportedly answered John Henry Lloyd.
In 1913, as player-manager, his Lincoln Giants beat the Chicago American Giants in a playoff to become undisputed champions of Black baseball.
He left the Brooklyn Royal Giants early in 1918 to work at the Army Quartermaster Depot in Chicago, one of several non-baseball jobs he took when Black baseball's finances wobbled.
After leading Hilldale to the 1923 Eastern Colored League title and batting .349, he was suspended by owner Ed Bolden over whether to give Clint Thomas a raise, and fired at the end of the season.
Before the 1926 season the league declared him a free agent, ruling that Atlantic City's Bacharachs had broken his contract, and he went on to manage the Lincoln Giants through 1930.
He played and coached for the semipro Atlantic City Johnson Stars until 1942, when he was in his late 50s.
p: His father died when he was a baby, and his grandmother raised him in Jacksonville. He left elementary school to work, delivering for a grocery and then working as a railroad porter.

After baseball he turned down offers to manage and became a janitor in the Atlantic City schools. A local writer described kids clustering around him between classes until "Pop" had to carry them into their classrooms.

When Atlantic City named its ballpark Pop Lloyd Field in 1949, a reporter asked if he wished he'd been born later. "I do not consider that I was born at the wrong time. I felt it was the right time, for I had a chance to prove the ability of our race in this sport."
His third wife, Nan, campaigned to get him into the Hall of Fame. It happened in 1977, two years after she died.
He was a descendant of slaves. A great fire in Palatka, Florida, may have prompted his family's move back to Jacksonville.
He had no children of his own, but became a popular coach in Atlantic City's youth league.

c: In 1877, playing semipro ball, he collided at home plate with the catcher, John Quigley. His knee fractured Quigley's skull, and Quigley died. Brouthers thought about quitting the game.

They called him "Jumbo," after Barnum's elephant. His bats ran to 41½ inches. A reporter called him "the brawniest brandisher of the bludgeon that ever belted a ball." In 1889 he hit .373 and struck out six times in 565 plate appearances.
He was a master of the hidden-ball trick, and in 1884 he caught King Kelly with it.

He was vice president of John Ward's players' union, the Brotherhood, and jumped to its Players League in 1890. He won pennants with Boston in the Players League and then the American Association. He won five batting titles in all.
In Louisville in 1895 he taught young Fred Clarke to hit the low curve and suggested a struggling outfielder named Jimmy Collins try third base.
At 46, in 1904, he went 6-for-6 with two grand slams for Poughkeepsie. John McGraw put him in the Giants' lineup for two final games that October.
Troy released him twice as a young pitcher-first baseman; in one game he lost 16-0. Buffalo signed him in 1881 as an everyday player.
Buffalo, broke after 1885, sold its "Big Four" to Detroit for $7,000. He sprained an ankle stealing second in the 1887 season finale and missed all but one game of the World Series.

Traded to Baltimore with Willie Keeler after 1893, he won the 1894 pennant. After a falling-out with Ned Hanlon, the Orioles sold him to Louisville for $500 in 1895, and Louisville sold him to the Phillies for $500.
After the Phillies released him at 38, he kept playing in the minors through 1899, then came back in 1903 as player and part owner at Poughkeepsie, a venture that failed financially.
p: He was born Dennis Brooder, son of an Irish iron-furnace worker in New York's Hudson Valley. As a teenager he worked in a Wappingers Falls cloth-dyeing factory.
He left Louisville after 24 games to care for his sick wife.

After his career he kept a hotel and saloon in Wappingers Falls. He then scouted for McGraw, finding Fred Merkle and Larry Doyle, and later worked at the Polo Grounds as a ticket taker, press-box attendant and night watchman.
He married Mary Ellen Croak on New Year's Eve 1884, and they were married 48 years. They had five children, four of whom were living in 1900.
His first big-league homer, in 1879, should have been a double; the ball slipped into a hole in the fence and he circled the bases before anyone could dig it out.

c: A dental student, he signed with Chicago sight unseen as a backup catcher. Foul tips broke his fingers so often that in 1903 he was moved to first base. He threatened to retire until a raise calmed him down, then hit .327 and led the league in steals.

Made player-manager in 1905, he won 116 games in 1906. That year he stole second and then home on the next pitch to beat Cincinnati, and owner Charles Murphy gave him 10 percent of the club. He later sold the stake for about $150,000.

Jim Corbett and John L. Sullivan called him "the greatest amateur brawler of all time." He boxed in the offseason, threw beer bottles at Brooklyn fans, and fined players for shaking hands with opponents. "You do things my way or you meet me after the game."
He made Solly Hofman postpone his wedding until the offseason so marriage wouldn't hurt his play.

Repeated beanings left him deaf in one ear, with blood clots in his brain. The Cubs fired him in 1912 while he was in the hospital for brain surgery, after he argued with Murphy there over the owner's cost-cutting.
Angry at being moved to yet another position in 1903, he threatened to retire; a raise calmed him. He later sold his share of the Cubs for about $150,000.
He managed the Cubs in four World Series: lost to the White Sox in 1906, swept Detroit in 1907 (hitting .154), beat Detroit again in 1908 (hitting .421), and lost to the A's in 1910.

He was fired while in the hospital for brain surgery in 1912, after a heated argument at his bedside with owner Charles Murphy over Murphy selling off good players to save money. He then managed the Yankees in 1913 and 1914, resigning late in 1914.

Back in California he grew oranges, owned part of and managed the PCL's Los Angeles Angels, and as president of the California Winter League fined Ty Cobb for abusing an umpire. He managed a last-place Red Sox team in 1923.
p: His father was president of Fresno's first national bank.
He married Edythe Pancake in 1903. She urged women to come out to the ballpark.
In 1912 he put up the Frank Chance Building in Glendora, California. It housed the Cub Grocery for years and still stands.
He fell ill and died in 1924, before he could take over the White Sox. In 1946 he went into the Hall of Fame in the same class as Tinker and Evers.
He worked as a prizefighter in the off-seasons.
Hired to manage the White Sox for 1924, he came down with severe influenza and asthma and needed emergency surgery in April. He died that September at 47.
