c: In 1963 the Phillies, without telling anyone, made him the first Black player in Little Rock. On opening night Governor Orval Faubus was in the stands and fans waved signs reading "Let's not NEGRO-ize our baseball." He found threatening notes on his car. "Maybe if the Phillies had called me in, man to man, like the Dodgers had done with Jackie Robinson... Instead, I was on my own."

When he thought about quitting, his brother Coy came to Little Rock and told him that if he quit, he'd be working in a Wampum mill. He stayed, led the league in homers, and was voted team MVP by the fans.
The Phillies insisted on calling him "Richie." "It makes me sound like I'm ten years old. I'm 22." As a rookie in 1964 he hit .318 and hit .429 in the last two weeks as the Phillies collapsed.

In July 1965, teammate Frank Thomas called him "another Muhammad Clay" in batting practice. Allen punched him, and Thomas hit Allen's shoulder with a bat. The Phillies released Thomas, and many fans blamed Allen. Some booed him relentlessly from then on.
On May 29, 1965, he hit a homer an estimated 510 feet over the Connie Mack Stadium roof and into a tree a block away. "I don't measure them."

With Oakland in 1977 he wore number 60 and "WAMPUM" on his back, honoring his high school class. He finished with 351 home runs and was elected to the Hall of Fame in December 2024, four years after his death.
The Phillies signed him for about $70,000 in 1960, switched him from shortstop to the outfield, and told him he needed glasses.
On the last day of 1964, needing a win to keep their hopes alive after a ten-game collapse, the Phillies won 10-0 behind his 3-for-5 with two homers. They still missed the pennant.

After the Frank Thomas fight, Gene Mauch threatened to fine anyone who talked to the press, with Allen's fine set at $2,000. The Phillies waived Thomas, and fans blamed Allen for costing a popular white veteran his job.
In 1967, pushing his car up his driveway in the rain, his hand went through the headlight. After a five-hour operation doctors gave him a 50-50 chance to play again; the hand never fully healed.

In 1969 he missed a doubleheader and was suspended indefinitely and fined $1,000 a day. He stayed away for weeks until owner Bob Carpenter promised to trade him. He went to St. Louis in the deal Curt Flood refused to report for, setting off Flood's challenge to the reserve clause.

In February 1973 the White Sox made him the highest-paid player in baseball, $250,000 a year. That June he broke his fibula in a collision with Mike Epstein. After he led the league in homers in 1974, uncertain whether he'd keep playing, the White Sox sold him to Atlanta for $5,000.
p: As a boy he batted stones around Chewton, Pennsylvania, calling out the Dodgers' lineup. His mother kept paying for neighbors' windows. "There were no baseball fields in all of Chewton or Wampum that could hold a stone if Dickie hit it good."

He and his brothers Hank and Ron all made All-State in basketball and all played in the majors. They picked baseball because it paid better and they wanted to buy their mother a house. With his bonus, that's the first thing Dick did.
His daughter Terri was murdered by her boyfriend outside her Maryland apartment in 1991. He was married to his second wife, Willa, for 33 years.
Inducted into the Philadelphia Sports Hall of Fame in 2010: "I get stopped all the time by these fellows whose dads had taken them to the ballpark... they appreciate me because I didn't cheat them."
His father, Coy, was a truck driver; after his parents divorced, his mother raised the nine children working as a housekeeper.
With his first wife, classmate Barbara Moore, he had sons Richard Jr. and Eron and daughter Terri; the marriage ended in divorce. Terri's 1991 death was a murder-suicide.
In Little Rock, as the local team's first Black player, he got death threats from residents.

c: He started out with the barnstorming National Bloomer Girls. Their "all-girls" rosters routinely carried a few boys. Ted Williams told a radio audience in 1950 that Wood got his start "posing as a girl."
Walter Johnson: "Listen, mister, no man alive can throw harder than Smoky Joe Wood." A Boston writer watching him in 1912 said, "that boy throws smoke," and the nickname stuck.

On September 6, 1912, Clark Griffith had Johnson face him to defend Johnson's 16-game winning streak. So many people packed Fenway that fans stood along the foul lines and two fly balls fell into the crowd for doubles. Wood won 1–0. He went 34–5 and won three games in the World Series.
Injuries followed: a broken thumb from slipping on wet grass in 1913, appendicitis in 1914, then a dead arm. His doctor in 1917: "It is a wonder you have any arm left."
Done as a pitcher at 27, he remade himself into an outfielder with Cleveland, hit .366 in 1921 and played in the 1920 World Series.
Kansas City bought his contract for $3,500, and the Red Sox bought it after more wrangling. He debuted at 18 in August 1908.
In 1909 a Harry Hooper line drive in batting practice hit his ankle, and surgery to remove a blood clot cost him over a month.
He won three games against the Giants in the 1912 World Series, the last in relief in Game 8, and was the first pitcher with double-digit strikeouts in a Series game.
His broken thumb in 1913 ended his season, and he pitched through pain for three years. He sat out the 1915 Series, and in February 1917 Boston sold him to Cleveland for $15,000.
In 1926 he was accused, with Ty Cobb and Tris Speaker, of being one of three central figures in an alleged 1919 game-fixing scheme. Yale kept him as coach for 15 more years.
p: His father, a lawyer, couldn't sit still: he went to the Klondike for gold, took the family west by covered wagon, and ran a paper in Ouray, Colorado. Howard and his brother were nicknamed Joe and Pete after two circus clowns.
In 1909 he hurt his foot wrestling his best friend, Tris Speaker, in a hotel room.

He coached Yale baseball for nearly 20 years. Yale cut him in 1942, and he opened a golf range in California with his brother: "I made more money in that seven years than I did my entire time playing and coaching baseball." When Yale president Bart Giamatti gave him an honorary doctorate in 1985, he wept uncontrollably.
At 91, in 1981, he watched Yale's Ron Darling and St. John's Frank Viola match 11 scoreless innings and called it the best game he'd ever seen.

He married Laura O'Shea of Kansas City in the 1912-13 off-season. At Yale he coached his son Joe Jr., who pitched three games for the 1944 Red Sox; two other sons played at Colgate, and they had a daughter, Virginia.

c: Ted Williams called his overhand curve the "most feared curveball in the American League for 18 years."
He credited Adolfo Luque, Cuba's best big-league pitcher before him and his manager for a few months in the winter league, with developing his curveball.

At 19 his first Cuban winter club traded him away, in what one writer called a ridiculous swap of a prospect for a handful of bats. He became Cienfuegos's ace and won a league MVP, and still holds the record for wins in the Caribbean Series.
Stuck on the 1950s Senators, he went 24–59 from 1955 to 1958. In December 1959 Cincinnati reportedly offered Clark Griffith $1 million for him and Harmon Killebrew. Griffith said no.
Once the team moved to Minnesota he won 20 twice and led the league in strikeouts three years running. On Opening Day 1960 he struck out 15 Red Sox, still the Opening Day record.

After pitching he spent decades as a scout. He signed José Canseco for Oakland in 1982, then Alex Cora, Miguel Cairo and others for the Dodgers. His brother Carlos, also a scout, signed Dwight Gooden.
At 17 Joe Cambria signed him and sent him to Class D Chickasha, then to Geneva in the Border League, a team made up mostly of Cuban players Cambria had signed.

In 1965 he started 8-2, then injuries and shoulder surgery in August limited him. He came back for the stretch run and started Game 3 of the World Series, losing to Claude Osteen as the Dodgers won in seven.

The Twins traded him to the new Senators after 1966 for 35-year-old reliever Ron Kline. Washington sold him to Cincinnati in July 1969, and the Reds released him the next spring; the Dodgers picked him up.
He was the Twins' pitching coach under Gene Mauch from 1978 to 1980.
p: "Little Potato" is a mistranslation. His older brother Carlos was "Patato," Cuban slang for a runt, and Camilo was "Patato Pequeño."
In August 1964, with Senator Hubert Humphrey's help, his parents and sister got out of Castro's Cuba. They reached Minnesota just in time for the birth of his fourth child.
He never went back to Cuba. In 2014, at 80, he was in the first class of the revived Cuban Baseball Hall of Fame in Havana.
His brother Carlos also became a scout, for the Yankees, Orioles and Mets.

c: In high school in Leesburg, Georgia, he pitched and played shortstop. As a senior he went 12–0 with a 1.06 ERA, and his school lost the state title game to Jason Heyward's team. He didn't move to catcher until his sophomore year at Florida State.
He caught every inning of the 2010 postseason as a rookie and the Giants won the World Series.

On May 25, 2011, Scott Cousins ran him over at the plate in the 12th inning, breaking his leg and tearing ligaments in his ankle. The play led to the 2014 rule against blocking the plate, often called the Buster Posey Rule.

Back in 2012, he caught Matt Cain's perfect game ("as nervous as I've ever been on a baseball field") and won the batting title and the MVP. The Giants won another title that fall and again in 2014. Only he and Pete Rose have a Rookie of the Year, an MVP and three rings.
In 2014 he and pitcher Madison Bumgarner both hit grand slams in one game, the first time a catcher and pitcher had done it.
After sitting out 2020, he hit a home run on his first swing in 2021, helped the Giants win a franchise-record 107 games, then retired. In 2024 he became the team's president of baseball operations.

The Angels drafted him in the 50th round out of high school, but he went to Florida State, where an assistant coach moved him to catcher. The Giants drafted him fifth overall in 2008 and paid a franchise-record $6.2 million bonus.
He became the Giants' starter when they traded Bengie Molina to Texas in June 2010. In Game 4 of that NLCS he was the first rookie with four hits in an NLCS game.
Down 0-2 in the 2012 Division Series, the Giants won three straight in Cincinnati, with Posey's grand slam off Mat Latos deciding Game 5.
In 2013 he signed an eight-year, $167 million extension, the richest in Giants history.
A torn hip labrum in 2018 sapped his power and required season-ending surgery; he went over a year without a homer.
He's the second player, after Pete Rose, with Rookie of the Year, an MVP and three World Series titles. In 2024 he led the negotiations for Matt Chapman's $151 million deal with the Giants.
p: "Buster" was his father's childhood nickname. He graduated fourth in a class of 302.
He and his wife Kristen, married in 2009, had twins in 2011. He sat out the 2020 season mainly because they were adopting premature twin girls during the pandemic.
In 2016 they started the BP28 Foundation for children with cancer.
After retiring he and Kristen sold their East Bay home and moved back to Georgia, then returned to the Bay Area within two years.

c: At 15, a high school sophomore, he played for Piedmont College's varsity, since the school belonged to no conference and had no eligibility rules. Branch Rickey's brother signed him after seeing him play once.

In 1935, at 22, bone spurs from a groin injury made him think his career was over. Cincinnati sent him back to the Cardinals because he couldn't pass a physical. A daring operation that winter saved him, and as a rookie in 1936 he hit .329.

He started 1940 with 43 bats in the clubhouse and finished with 43 home runs. "To this day I wonder what would have happened if I had started the season with 61 bats." On the Giants, a roommate said, one bat trunk was for Mize and the other for the rest of the team.
In 1947 he hit 51 homers and struck out 42 times. He's still the only player with 50 homers and fewer than 50 strikeouts.

Sold to the Yankees in 1949 at 36, he won five straight World Series as a first baseman and pinch hitter and was MVP of the 1952 Series. In 1953 he grumbled that teammates should lay off Carl Erskine's curves in the dirt, then swung at one and became Erskine's record 14th strikeout. Billy Martin: "What happened, John, that low curve take a bad hop?"
Branch Rickey signed him at 17 after seeing him play once. Traded to Cincinnati in 1934, he was sent back when the Reds voided the deal over a groin injury.
He was something of a clubhouse lawyer and salary holdout in St. Louis, and Rickey traded him to the Giants after 1941.
In 1946 Joe Page broke his hand with a pitch in an exhibition, and he broke a toe on his return, finishing one homer short of Ralph Kiner for the title.
Unhappy with his playing time, he was sold to the Yankees in 1949. Nursing a bad shoulder, his bases-loaded pinch single in the ninth won Game 3 of that World Series.

In the 1953 Series he kept telling teammates not to chase Carl Erskine's curves in the dirt, then struck out on one, giving Erskine the World Series record. Billy Martin: "What happened, John, that low curve take a bad hop?"
p: As a boy he cared more about tennis and won a county championship. Ty Cobb was a distant cousin, and Babe Ruth's wife, born Clara Mae Merritt, was a cousin too.
In 1941 he sued a gum company for putting him on a baseball card without his consent. He lost, but the expense led the company to stop making the set.
His wife of 20 years, Jene, died in 1957 after falling asleep while smoking and setting their Florida house on fire. He gave his card-show fees to local Boy Scout troops.

At his 1981 Hall of Fame induction, after a 28-year wait: "Years ago the writers were telling me that I'd make the Hall of Fame, so I kind of prepared a speech. But somewhere along in the 28 years it got lost."
His parents separated, and his mother went to work in an Atlanta department store.
After baseball he ran Florida businesses including real estate, orange groves and a liquor store, and coached and scouted for the Giants and Kansas City A's.
Three months after his wife Jene's death in 1957 he married Marjorie Pope and adopted her two children.

c: The New Orleans Pelicans turned him down as too small. A lumber millionaire whose semipro team he played on mailed him instructions to report to John McGraw. Ott didn't take them seriously, so the man bought him a train ticket to New York.

Watching the 16-year-old at his tryout, McGraw said, "He's like a golfer; his body moves, but he keeps his head still." Rather than let a minor-league manager ruin him, McGraw kept him on the Giants bench for two years and had him tutored by himself and his veterans.
In 1929, at 20, he hit 42 homers and drove in 151, still the most by anyone that young. He hit more homers on the road than at the Polo Grounds, with its short right-field line.
In the 1933 World Series he hit .389 and won the clinching game with a 10th-inning home run.

Giants owner Horace Stoneham greeted him at the 1941 winter meetings: "Hiya, manager." It took several minutes to convince him he really had the job. Five days later came Pearl Harbor. When he was replaced in 1948, it was by Leo Durocher of the hated Dodgers.
McGraw gave him a $400 bonus and a contract in January 1926. When Ross Youngs died of kidney disease in October 1927, Ott took over right field at 19.
He played in three World Series, 1933, 1936 and 1937, hitting .295 with four homers in 16 games; the Giants lost the last two to the Yankees.

As player-manager in 1943 he hit .234 and missed games with a stomach ailment blamed on managing. Just before the 1946 opener one of his own pitchers beaned him in batting practice, and the next day he hurt his knee diving for a fly ball; he hit .074 the rest of the year.

He resigned as manager on July 16, 1948, replaced by Leo Durocher of the hated Dodgers. He then helped Carl Hubbell run the Giants' farm system, managed the Oakland Oaks in 1951, and broadcast Tigers games from 1956 to 1958.
p: At 14 he was already being paid to hit: his semipro team passed the hat whenever a home run helped win a game.
In 1944, war bond buyers voted him the most popular sports hero of all time, ahead of Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig and Joe Louis.
In November 1958, driving home through heavy fog from the cottage they were building in Bay St. Louis, he and his wife Mildred were hit head-on. He died a week later.
Arnold Hano called him "a little man with a bashful smile and a silken swing, baseball's legendary nice guy."
The National League's home run champion has received the Mel Ott Award since 1959. His name, with its short handy letters, turns up often in crossword puzzles.
Sport magazine named him Sports Father of the Year. He and Mildred had two daughters, Barbara and Lyn.
He died the way two other Giants Hall of Famers who were his teammates later did, Frankie Frisch in 1973 and Carl Hubbell in 1988: after a car accident.

c: In T-ball his father paid him 25 cents a hit and fined him 50 cents a strikeout. At dinner he drew diamonds on napkins and quizzed Nomar on game situations.

At the 1994 College World Series he was taken to the hospital for IV fluids after dehydrating in 100-degree heat. He got back after the second game had started, begged to play, pinch-hit, and homered on the first pitch.
After seeing him play, Ted Williams called the Red Sox GM, couldn't remember who Nomar reminded him of, then called back yelling, "DiMaggio!"

As a rookie in 1997 he hit in 30 straight games, an American League rookie record, and won Rookie of the Year unanimously. In 2000 he hit .372, the highest by a right-handed hitter since DiMaggio in 1939.

A pitch hit his wrist in September 1999 and split a tendon. He was never quite the same hitter. Bitter over contract talks and Boston's attempt to trade for Alex Rodriguez, which he learned about on his honeymoon, he was traded in July 2004, three months before the Red Sox finally won the World Series.
Milwaukee drafted him in the fifth round out of high school in 1991, but he went to Georgia Tech. His coach there, Danny Hall, said his defense was as good as Barry Larkin's.
Georgia Tech reached the 1994 College World Series final and lost to Oklahoma. The Red Sox took him in the first round that year.
Injuries kept him out until July in 1996, and he was called up August 31. In his first start he went 3-for-5 with a homer.
In spring 1998 he signed a five-year, $23.25 million deal, unheard of for a player just out of his rookie season. He hit .333 with three homers in the 1998 ALDS and .400 in the 1999 ALCS.
A shirtless magazine cover showing a much bigger Garciaparra than the skinny college kid fueled suspicion that he used steroids.

In 2003 he turned down a four-year, $60 million extension. That December, when Boston tried to trade for Alex Rodriguez, he asked, "How would you guys feel if your employer was trying to replace you?"
He retired in 2010 on a one-day contract with the Red Sox, then worked on ESPN's College World Series coverage and Dodgers broadcasts.
p: Nomar is his father Ramon's name spelled backwards. He went by it because it was unique.
He met Mia Hamm at a 1998 promotional event in Boston, where she beat him in a soccer shootout. They married in 2003.
In October 2005 he heard two women scream after they fell into Boston Harbor outside his condo. He jumped in and saved them both.
At Georgia Tech he made the Dean's List every quarter and was an academic All-American.
His father, Ramon, born in Mexico, was a graphic artist. He has two sisters, and his brother Michael played shortstop in the minors.
Mia Hamm was married when they met. They stayed friends, began dating after her 2001 divorce, and have three children.

c: Indiana's Mr. Baseball in 1993, he wanted to play basketball at Kentucky and even showed Rick Pitino his highlight tape on a baseball recruiting trip. Kentucky passed, and he chose the Phillies over a basketball scholarship at Georgia.

In 2001, Phillies manager Larry Bowa told a newspaper that his cleanup hitter was "killing us," and Dallas Green said on the radio that Rolen's personality kept him from greatness. Rolen turned down $90 million to stay and was traded to St. Louis, the team he'd grown up watching.
In 2004 he hit .314 with 34 homers as one of the Cardinals' "MV3." His two-run homer off Roger Clemens in Game 7 of the NLCS won the pennant.

Benched in the 2006 playoffs, he stopped talking to Tony La Russa but hit safely in his last 10 postseason games as St. Louis won the World Series. After a public feud, La Russa told him to quit if he didn't like it, and he was traded. GM John Mozeliak later said Rolen was the only player he regretted trading.
Teammate Jonny Gomes: "You know 'W.W.J.D., what would Jesus do'? Here, it's what would Scott do?" He won eight Gold Gloves and was elected to the Hall of Fame in 2023.
Kentucky didn't offer him a basketball scholarship, so he committed to Georgia. After the Phillies drafted him he hoped to do both, but he signed on July 22, 1993.

A fractured hamate needed surgery in the minors, and it seemed to help his hitting because inside pitches hurt less. In September 1996 a Steve Trachsel pitch broke his forearm one at-bat short of losing his rookie status.

He turned down a seven-year, $90 million Phillies offer that could have reached $140 million. In June 2002 anonymous Phillies called him a clubhouse cancer. On July 29 he was traded to St. Louis, where he had gone to games as a kid.
Before the Cardinals deal, a trade to Cincinnati for Brandon Larson fell through when the Reds' president balked at the money.
That September he signed an eight-year, $90 million extension with St. Louis, saying he didn't need to chase the last dollar. A season-ending injury in the Division Series kept him out of the NLCS.

He went hitless in the 2004 World Series sweep by Boston. In 2005 a collision with the Dodgers' Hee-Seop Choi tore his labrum, and he had season-ending surgery. He felt the Cardinals pushed him to put off surgery.
After 2007 he asked to be traded. In Toronto he broke a finger in spring training.
p: Both his parents were schoolteachers, as his brother and sister became. As a rookie he spent his free time reading books his parents assigned, including On the Road and Crime and Punishment.

With his brother, sister and wife he started the Enis Furley Foundation, named for his dog, and built a 40-acre retreat with horses, canoes and ballfields where families of sick children stay for free.
When he first went on the Hall of Fame ballot in 2018, his son predicted he'd get in someday. That year he became Indiana University's director of player development.
He married Niki Warner in 2002. In 2004 his father had a cancer scare and his five-year-old nephew had heart surgery.

c: The "Fordham Flash" captained Fordham's football, basketball and baseball teams and was an All-American halfback. He went straight to the Giants, talking John McGraw out of sending him to the minors by saying his father would make him join the family lace business.
As a rookie, a bad-hop smash bounced off his chest in a big game and he still threw the runner out. McGraw: "That was all I had to see."

As captain he took McGraw's clubhouse tirades for years. In August 1926, after one especially cruel one, he walked out and went home. That winter he was traded to St. Louis for Rogers Hornsby, and his 641 assists in 1927 are still the record for a second baseman.

He hit the National League's first All-Star Game home run in 1933. As player-manager in 1934 he led the Gas House Gang, so named after they took the field in filthy uniforms, to the World Series title.
In 1937 Terry Moore, who'd started the play on first, slid home right behind him. "Any time they can run down the Flash, it's time to quit."

Managing Pittsburgh, he got himself thrown out of a rainy game for walking to home plate under an umbrella. Coaching third once, he slid into the bag from the coach's box to get at Eddie Stanky and was ejected.
His father, a prosperous lace and linen manufacturer, expected him to join the family business.
McGraw worked with him every morning on fielding, sliding and holding the bat. The Giants won the World Series in 1921 and 1922.
He was traded to the Cardinals with Jimmy Ring for Rogers Hornsby, because Sam Breadon couldn't get along with Hornsby.
He was MVP in 1931 when St. Louis beat the A's in the Series. He played in eight World Series and holds the record for Series hits, 58, by anyone who never played for the Yankees.

He left the field in 1939 to broadcast Boston Bees games, then managed the Pirates for seven years. After broadcasting the Giants he coached for Durocher in 1949 and left in June to manage the Cubs, against his wife's advice.
On the air his catchphrase was "Oh, those bases on balls!" A heart attack in 1956 forced him to cut back, and Phil Rizzuto filled in.
p: He loved fine restaurants, classical music, good books and his rose garden. He called spring training "a country club without dues."
When Casey Stengel was hit by a car in 1943, Frisch wired that he understood why he'd attempted suicide and was sorry it hadn't worked.

On the Hall of Fame Veterans Committee he got six of his old Giants and Cardinals teammates elected, some of them called among the least deserving ever. He died in 1973 after a car accident coming home from a committee meeting.
He kept his home in Westchester County long after leaving the Giants, and was jokingly accused of getting thrown out of games to get home sooner.
After his wife, Ada, died in 1971, he married Augusta Kass. In 1973, returning from a Veterans Committee meeting in Florida, he was in a car accident and died in Wilmington, Delaware.
He always gave his birth year as 1898, but census, draft and passport records say 1897.

c: He was born Aloysius Szymanski. As a minor leaguer he wrote to a Giants farm manager offering himself for $150 in expenses and never heard back. "I'm not sure I would have enjoyed playing for McGraw. We were both hotheads."
His front foot pointed toward third base, so they called him "Bucketfoot Al," and he hated it. He made up for the stance with an unusually long bat.
Bill Dickey said the 1928 Yankees decided to rough Simmons up in a big September series. "So we roughed him up. In a four-game series, he had 11 hits, ten of them for extra bases."

In the 1929 World Series he homered to start the A's 10-run comeback inning against the Cubs and singled later in the same inning. On Memorial Day 1930 he tied one game with a ninth-inning homer and won the second with a pinch-hit grand slam on a swollen knee.
He finished 73 hits short of 3,000 and regretted the games he'd skipped with hangovers. He told a young Stan Musial: "Never relax on any at-bat; never miss a game you can play."
The hometown Milwaukee Brewers signed him in 1922 and sent him to Aberdeen, South Dakota, where he hit .365. Connie Mack bought him after the 1923 season.
In 1931 he held out until Opening Day, signed for $100,000 over three years, and got three hits with no spring training.
He hit .329 in four World Series. The A's won in 1929 and 1930 and lost to the Cardinals in seven in 1931.
In September 1932 Mack sold him, Jimmy Dykes and Mule Haas to the White Sox for a reported $100,000. After he slumped to .267 in 1935 Chicago sold him to Detroit for $75,000.

He didn't get along with Washington owner Clark Griffith, and the Senators sold him to the Boston Bees in December 1938. The Reds bought him in August 1939, and he got one hit in his last World Series.
By World War II he was a relic, hitting .203 in 40 games for the Red Sox. He coached for Mack through 1949, and was drinking more by his last coaching job, with Cleveland in 1950.
In April 1951 he announced an undisclosed illness and stepped down as an Indians coach.
p: The son of Polish immigrants in Milwaukee, he told a teammate one night over Scotch, "I have a reputation for being coarse and a little ornery, but believe me, enough things have happened to me in my lifetime to account for that."

After his marriage ended, his religious convictions kept him from remarrying. Connie Mack "seemed to look on me as his son," and the only player's picture Mack kept in his office was Simmons's. "If I could only have nine players named Al Simmons."
He died in Milwaukee in 1956, four days after his 54th birthday.
In August 1934 he married Doris Lynn Reader of Chicago. They had a son, John, before they divorced, and Mack tried in vain to get them back together.
He drank Scotch until 2:30 a.m. one night in a Boston bar with teammate Case, who drank ginger ale.

c: He's naturally right-handed. His father, a catcher in a local men's league, had him throw left-handed for the edge.

He debuted in May 2018 at 19, the youngest player in the majors and the first one born in 1998. In 2019 he was only the fourth player with 100 extra-base hits before turning 21, and the Nationals won the World Series.
As a rookie he started doing the "Soto Shuffle" after taking a ball: swiveling his hips, sweeping the dirt with his leg, hopping. He ranks among the best ever in walk rate.
He reportedly turned down a 15-year, $440 million extension from Washington in 2022 and was traded to San Diego. Ten days later he came back to Washington and got a 45-second standing ovation.
After a season with the Yankees that ended in the 2024 World Series, he signed with the Mets for 15 years and $765 million, the largest contract in pro sports.
The Nationals signed him for $1.5 million in July 2015. An ankle injury sliding home and then a hamstring cost him most of 2017. He was called up in May 2018 when Howie Kendrick got hurt.

In the 2019 Wild Card game his bases-clearing single off Josh Hader won it. He homered off Clayton Kershaw to tie the deciding NLDS game, and off Gerrit Cole in Game 1 of the World Series. Game 3 fell on his 21st birthday, as his father had predicted a decade earlier, and Washington won its first title.
In 2020 he missed the first week after a positive COVID test, then became the youngest NL batting champion at .351.
Before the 2021–22 lockout he turned down 13 years and $350 million, saying he and Scott Boras would wait for free agency.

Washington traded him and Josh Bell to San Diego for six players, a deal compared to the NFL's Herschel Walker trade. The Padres lost the 2022 NLCS to Philadelphia, and after 2023 sent him to the Yankees for five players.
His 10th-inning homer in Game 5 of the 2024 ALCS sent the Yankees to their first World Series since 2009.
His Mets deal included a $75 million signing bonus. On his first trip back to Yankee Stadium he was booed and heckled throughout and got one hit in three games.
p: New in the U.S., he threw himself into learning English and was praised for how quickly he learned.
Twice he's paid teammates for number 22: a "really nice watch" for Nick Martinez in San Diego, and a Chevy Tahoe for Brett Baty with "thanks for #22" written on the back window.
In 2021 he gave $200,000 to Dominican athletes at the Olympics. His younger brother Elian signed with the Nationals in 2023.
His father was a salesman. He has an older sister as well as his brother Elian.

c: At 15 his father got him a cheese-factory job. He worked a week, left early Saturday to make $3 in a ballgame, and never held a non-baseball job again. "I think I'm the luckiest guy in the world. I get paid for doing what I'd rather do than anything else."

At 5-foot-4½ he swung a 30-inch bat, the shortest in big-league history, and choked so far up that Sam Crawford said, "He only used half his bat." His whole theory of hitting: "Keep your eye clear and hit 'em where they ain't; that's all."
With John McGraw on the 1890s Orioles he perfected the Baltimore Chop and turned the hit-and-run into an art. McGraw: "It was impossible to play for him."

In 1897 he hit in 44 straight games to open the season, 45 counting the last game of 1896. It was the record until Joe DiMaggio in 1941. He hit .424 that year, still the highest ever for a left-handed hitter.
In 1897 he and McGraw fought naked in the Orioles' shower room while teammate Jack Doyle guarded the door. As Doyle predicted, McGraw gave up first.
McGraw called his barehanded diving catch in 1898, his throwing arm stuck in a barbed-wire fence, the greatest he ever saw.
He quit school at 15 to play for a factory team. Binghamton signed him in June 1892 for $90 a month, and that September the Giants bought him for $800.

He broke his leg sliding into second the day after the Times praised him, missed eight weeks, and was shipped to Brooklyn. On January 1, 1894, Ned Hanlon got him and Dan Brouthers from Brooklyn in one of baseball's most lopsided trades.
He didn't drink or swear, and was the polite one among the rough Orioles, though he would still use deception to get an edge.
When the Orioles' owners also took over Brooklyn, Keeler, Joe Kelley and Hughie Jennings were moved there to join Hanlon. In 1901 he had his eighth straight 200-hit season.
His eight straight 200-hit seasons stood as the record until Ichiro broke it in 2009. His 206 singles in 1898 also lasted more than 100 years.
He stayed in Brooklyn when the American League started raiding, then signed with the New York Highlanders in 1903. He coached Manhattan College's team while still playing.
After retiring he scouted and coached for Brooklyn, the Boston Braves and the Federal League's Brooklyn Tip-Tops.
p: Born William O'Kelleher in Brooklyn, son of a County Cork immigrant trolley switchman. As a teenager he sold programs at the Players League park in his hometown.
The "Brooklyn Millionaire" lost his money when his real estate collapsed after World War I, and he and his brothers had to sell their childhood home. The major leagues raised $5,500 to pay his debts.

Dying of heart disease, he vowed to see 1923. When the bells rang at midnight he sat up and told his brother, "You see, the new year is here and so am I—still." He had a drink and a smoke, said he was ready for a long sleep, and died a short time later.
A lifelong bachelor, he left his estate to Clara Moss, the woman whose house he boarded in. He was buried in his mother's grave at his request.
His father had left a farm in County Cork 12 years before and married Mary Kiley, another Irish immigrant, in Brooklyn. Willie had two older brothers, Tom and Joe.
He invested in mining companies as well as real estate. On his last night he had a drink and a smoke and said he was ready for a long sleep. He died at 50.

c: A Yankees scout took the teenager to see Lou Gehrig and whispered, "He's all washed up. In a few years, you'll be the Yankee first baseman." Greenberg signed with Detroit instead.

In 1934, with the Tigers in a pennant race, he consulted a rabbi and played on Rosh Hashanah, homering twice in a 2–1 win. Ten days later he sat out Yom Kippur. Edgar Guest wrote a poem: "But he's true to his religion — and I honor him for that!"

"How the hell could you get up to home plate every day and have some son of a bitch call you a Jew bastard... without feeling the pressure." In time he came to feel that "if I, as a Jew, hit a home run, I was hitting one against Hitler."

In 1938 he needed two homers in the last five games to tie Ruth's 60 and didn't hit another. When umpire George Moriarty called the final game for darkness: "I'm sorry, Hank, this is as far as I can go." Greenberg: "That's all right, George, this is as far as I can go too."

Discharged on December 5, 1941, he re-enlisted after Pearl Harbor two days later and missed four seasons. Back in 1945, he won the pennant on the last day with a ninth-inning grand slam in the rain: "I wasn't sure whether I was awake or dreaming."

In Pittsburgh in 1947, his last season, he took young Ralph Kiner under his wing. When Jackie Robinson came to town that May, Greenberg encouraged him: "Just stay in there and fight back. Always remember to keep your head up."
Tigers scout Jean Dubuc signed him in September 1929.
He had one year of college, and the Tigers paid $9,000.

He sprained his wrist sliding home in Game 2 of the 1935 World Series and missed the rest of it as the Tigers won their first title. In April 1936 he broke the wrist again in a collision with Jake Powell and missed the season.
After 1939 the Tigers asked him to take a $5,000 cut and move to left field. He demanded a $10,000 bonus if he learned the position, since he was the one taking the risk, and got it.
His flat feet left his draft status uncertain for months.
Rumors that he had bribed the draft board, and fear of being compared to Jack Dempsey, led him to ask to be examined again.
In 1947 he signed for a record $85,000 and was then sold to Pittsburgh for $75,000.
As Cleveland's general manager he built the team that won 111 games in 1954. He followed Bill Veeck to the White Sox as part owner and vice president, then sold his stake at a profit.
p: His parents meant to name him Hyman, but the man filling out the birth certificate had never heard of the name. Growing up across from Crotona Park in the Bronx, he got neighborhood kids to shag his hits for hours.
Basketball was his best sport in high school. Early in his baseball career he played pro basketball for teams in Brooklyn and Trenton.
He married department-store heiress Caral Gimbel in 1946. The marriage was unhappy and ended in divorce. He made millions in the stock market in the 1960s and moved to Beverly Hills.
In 1956 he became the first Jewish player elected to the Hall of Fame.
Shirley Povich: "He was the perfect standard-bearer for Jews. Hank was smart, he was proud, and he was big."
He was the third of four children. He grew up in an Orthodox household but wasn't observant, and raised his own children secular.

Caral cared about art, music and show horses; he was all baseball business. The marriage helped both of them financially, but there wasn't much else, and they divorced. They had three children: Glenn, Steve and Alva.
He moved to Beverly Hills, and in 1966 married actress Mary Jo Tarola, known on screen as Linda Douglas. He died of kidney cancer in 1986.

c: Once in high school, his baseball game stopped so he could climb the center-field fence and run the 100 at the track meet next door. He ran it in 9.8 seconds in his baseball cleats, climbed back, played a few innings, and went back to long-jump 24 feet, 11 inches, still in cleats.
In his first major-league game, in 1968, he hit a grand slam, something no one had done since 1898.

He had five 30–30 seasons and missed the first 40–40 by one homer in 1973. Sparky Anderson that summer: "As of today, Bobby Bonds is the best ballplayer in America." He also set strikeout records, 189 in 1970.
After a shouting match over his contract, Giants owner Horace Stoneham said, "He'll never play another game for me," and traded him. He played for seven teams in seven years after that.
He swore he'd retire before playing for Gabe Paul in Cleveland. Then he played there: "I'm just sick and tired of being traded."
His brother Robert played college football at San Jose State and was drafted, but broke his collarbone in a car accident.
He signed with the Giants in 1964. In the minors he heard racist taunts for the first time.
He set a strikeout record, then broke it the next year with 189; that lasted until 2004. A bruised rib cage limited him in the 1971 NLCS, his only postseason.

He blamed his 1972 slump partly on Willie Mays being traded away; Mays was Barry's unofficial godfather. Reporter Glenn Dickey said the Giants also traded Bonds because they were sure drinking would end his career early.

The Giants traded him to the Yankees on October 22, 1974. He tore knee cartilage making a diving catch in 1975 and still had 32 homers and 30 steals. That December the Yankees traded him to the Angels for Ed Figueroa and Mickey Rivers.
When the Cubs bought him in 1981 he had played for eight teams in eight years. In his first Cubs game he tripped on the turf and broke a bone in his wrist.
He held the records for leadoff home runs, 35 in a career and 11 in a season. He coached hitting for Cleveland and rejoined the Giants as a coach when Barry signed there in 1993.
p: His brother Robert set a California high hurdles record, and his sister Rosie ran the hurdles in the 1964 Olympics. He grew up next to Dusty Baker's family.

He started drinking before high school and once drank a beer under the bleachers before a long jump. Married at 17 to his neighbor Patricia Howard, he was the father of Barry Bonds. Willie Mays was Barry's unofficial godfather.

He was arrested for drunk driving in 1973 and again in 1978. After he was fired as an Indians coach in 1987, he joined Alcoholics Anonymous. Sober, he went back to the Giants to coach under Dusty Baker alongside his son.
A lifelong smoker, he died of lung cancer and a brain tumor in 2003 at 57.
As a boy he caddied, worked at his father's construction site and collected bottles for the deposits.
They married in 1963 and had three sons: Barry, Rick and Bobby Jr., who played 11 years in the minors. His wife later filed for divorce.

Once his brother Robert got into an argument with a police officer after being pulled over for speeding, and both brothers were arrested, Bobby for interfering. In February 1978 he was arrested for drunk driving after causing a two-car accident.

c: As a boy in Little Rock he delivered papers to Bill Dickey. In eighth grade he wrote an essay called "Why I Want to Play Professional Baseball," specifically third base for the Cardinals.

The P.A. announcer at York announced him as "Bob Robinson." Gene Woodling, after a workout: "He couldn't hit, he couldn't run, and his arm wasn't that strong." He hit .232 in his first 216 big-league games.
In Vancouver in 1959 he slipped chasing a foul and a dugout hook tore a 24-inch gash in his arm. His manager: "If he had fallen, he would have been done."

In the 1970 World Series he hit .429 and kept diving to rob the Reds. He was nicknamed "Hoover" after the vacuum cleaner. Pete Rose, when Robinson got a car as Series MVP: "If we knew he wanted a car so badly, we'd have bought one for him ourselves."
Before Game 5 of that Series it was pouring. Andy Etchebarren joked, "Brooksie, make it stop raining." Robinson looked up and said, "Stop raining." It did.

He won 16 straight Gold Gloves. At Thanks Brooks Day in 1977, a writer, still sore over Reggie Jackson's exit, wrote: "Brooks never asked anyone to name a candy bar after him. In Baltimore, they name their children after him."
Scout Lindsay Deal, an old minor-league teammate of Paul Richards, tipped off the Orioles.
The Giants, Reds and Orioles each offered $4,000. He chose Baltimore, and Art Ehlers signed him.
A Hank Aguirre fastball broke his thumb, the first games he had missed in four years.

He hit .583 in the 1970 ALCS sweep of the Twins. Sparky Anderson during the Series: "If I dropped this paper plate, he'd pick it up on one hop and throw me out at first." He won a Dodge Charger as Series MVP.

Late in his career he asked for a trade to get more playing time, but vetoed a deal to the White Sox because they wouldn't sign him through 1978. He retired on August 21, 1977, to open a roster spot when Rick Dempsey came off the disabled list.
A Norman Rockwell painting of him appeared as an ad in the 1971 World Series program.
p: On a 1959 team flight he kept ordering iced tea from a flight attendant, Connie Butcher. In the galley he told her he was the only single guy on the team, though nearly half of the Orioles were single. They married in 1960.
Broadcaster Chuck Thompson said he signed autographs while asking how many kids you had and whether you had a dog. He once signed a pet rock.
His sporting goods business went under in the 1970s, and he paid nearly $180,000 from his savings to keep his house.

He and his mentor George Kell, who grew up 90 miles away in Arkansas, went into the Hall of Fame on the same day in 1983. His son later gave him the original Norman Rockwell painting "Gee Thanks, Brooks."

His father worked for a bakery and later became a Little Rock fire captain. His mother worked for Sears and the state controller. He also ran the scoreboard and sold soft drinks at Lamar Porter Field.
He married Connie Butcher on October 8, 1959, at her family's summer home in Windsor, Ontario. They raised four children in Baltimore.

In 1961 he became part owner of the Gorsuch House restaurant near Memorial Stadium. His sporting goods company, started in 1963, borrowed to expand to York, Pennsylvania, in 1974 and went under. Afterward he and Ron Shapiro founded a firm that managed money for athletes.

c: He was too small to start in high school. Climbing telephone poles as a cable splicer built him up: "I was really tiny in high school." The Red Sox reportedly bought the whole Louisville club to get him, then sold him because Joe Cronin wouldn't give up shortstop. Hearing he'd been sold to Brooklyn: "Oh, not Brooklyn!"
Leo Durocher, the player-manager, hit him grounders his first spring until he was exhausted: "He'll do. I'll be the bench manager."

Coming home from Guam with the Navy, he heard the Dodgers had signed a Black shortstop. In 1947 he refused to sign the petition against Jackie Robinson. "If he's man enough to take my job, I'm not gonna like it, but, dammit, black or white, he deserves it."

Accounts disagree on where and when he put his arm around Robinson on the field with the crowd jeering, but the essence of the story holds, and they became close friends. When Robinson got a death threat before a game in Atlanta, Reese joked, "Don't come near me. I don't want to get shot."
Named captain in 1949, he waved the starters onto the field from the dugout steps before every game. He told Duke Snider, "if you're hurryin' out of the clubhouse, you're hurryin' out of baseball."
After the 1953 season the Dodgers offered him the manager's job. He turned it down, and they hired Walter Alston.
He got into only five games as a high school senior. Louisville signed him for a $200 bonus and $150 a month.

Red Sox farm director Billy Evans liked him so much that he recommended Boston buy the Louisville club. When Tom Yawkey sent Joe Cronin, Boston's shortstop, to scout him, Cronin realized he was looking at his own replacement, downplayed Reese and suggested trading him.
Midway through 1939 the Red Sox sold him to Brooklyn for $35,000 and four players.
As a rookie in 1940 he spent two and a half weeks in a Chicago hospital, then broke a heel bone sliding into second in August. Durocher once fined him $50 for being out of position on a relay.
He hit .200 and made three errors in the 1941 Series. He joined the Navy in 1943 and played for the Aiea Naval Hospital team in Hawaii.
Pittsburgh tried to trade for him to captain the Pirates. He hit .272 in 44 World Series games.
He finally won the World Series in 1955, scoring an insurance run in Game 7, and got a second ring as a Dodgers coach in 1959.
After coaching, he was a TV color man for CBS from 1960 to 1965, partnered with Dizzy Dean on the Game of the Week and a chat show.
p: His nickname came from marbles, not his size: as a boy he finished second in a Louisville pee-wee marbles tournament.
His father reportedly once showed him a tree in Brandenburg, Kentucky, that had been used to lynch Black men, and implied it was wrong.
He and his hometown sweetheart Dottie married in Daytona Beach in 1942, the same day as teammate Pete Reiser. They were married 57 years.
At his funeral, Joe Black said: "When you touched Jackie, you touched all of us."
As a boy he delivered newspapers and sold box lunches to help his family. After high school he worked as a cable splicer for the Louisville phone company.
Dottie and Pee Wee had two children, Barbara and Mark, a documentary filmmaker. Dottie died in 2012, 22 days short of their 70th anniversary.
He appeared as himself in A Question of Romance on CBS's General Electric Theater in 1958.
Later he worked for Hillerich & Bradsby, the maker of Louisville Slugger bats. He had prostate and lung cancer and died at home in Louisville in 1999.

c: He hit .650 as a senior at George Washington High in Washington Heights. His family didn't know he was New York's high school player of the year until someone called and told them to turn on the news because he'd been drafted. One Cleveland scout warned that no Latin American immigrant kid had ever gone in the first round. The Indians took him 13th.
Called up from Triple-A in 1993, he asked his manager, Charlie Manuel, "Can you come with me?" In his second game, at Yankee Stadium with family in the stands, he hit two home runs.
Back at his old high school, asked to say something to the team about hitting: "See the ball. Hit the ball."

Behind the goofiness he was one of the hardest workers on the team and studied video of other sluggers against new pitchers. Allard Baird believed he'd swing and miss at a pitch in April so he'd see it again in September.

"Manny being Manny": he once stepped inside Fenway's Green Monster during a mound visit and didn't come out until after the next pitch. He won the 2004 World Series MVP and has the most postseason home runs ever, 29. After failing a drug test for the second time, he retired in 2011 rather than serve a 100-game suspension.

Indians scout Joe DeLucca watched him from a distance so rivals wouldn't notice. Told no Latin American immigrant kid had ever gone in the first round, he stuck to his guns, and Cleveland took him 13th in 1991 with a $250,000 bonus.
A broken hamate bone in his left hand ended his 1992 season at Kinston.
His first big-league hit, at Yankee Stadium, bounced into the left-field seats for a ground-rule double.
He went 4-for-26 in the 1997 World Series. In the 1998 ALCS he misjudged a catchable Derek Jeter triple that drove in two big runs in Game 6.
Before he signed with Boston for eight years and $160 million, he insisted they also hire Cleveland clubhouse man Frank Mancini.
In 2003 Boston put him on irrevocable waivers to clear money for Alex Rodriguez, and all 29 teams passed.

In June 2008 he swung at Kevin Youkilis in the Fenway dugout. Weeks later, arguing over a request for 16 tickets in Houston, he shoved the 64-year-old traveling secretary Jack McCormick to the ground. He apologized publicly but not to McCormick in person until 2014. Boston traded him to the Dodgers that summer.

In 2009 he was suspended 50 games for hCG, a fertility drug often taken after steroid cycles. After joining Tampa Bay in 2011 he failed again and retired rather than serve 100 games, without telling the Rays himself.
He played in Taiwan in 2013 and for an independent team in Japan in 2017, and signed in Australia but was released in 2021 without playing.
As a hitting consultant in the Cubs system he earned a 2016 World Series ring.
p: As a teenager he got up at 5 a.m. to run the city's hills, dragging a 20-pound tire tied to his waist.
Though he lived near Yankee Stadium, he rooted for the Toronto Blue Jays, who had his Dominican heroes George Bell and Tony Fernández.
He left a paycheck in a boot under his locker in Texas, and it had to be mailed to him. A friend said he loved going to shopping malls, sometimes two or three times a day.
He missed a game in May 2004 to become a U.S. citizen. The next day he ran onto the field carrying a small American flag to a standing ovation.

In 2014, after nearly four years in church with his wife Juliana: "Now, I realize that I behaved bad in Boston." As a Cubs hitting consultant he mentored Javier Báez and earned a 2016 World Series ring.

His mother had a desk job in the Dominican Republic but became a seamstress in New York. His father had driven an ambulance and tank trucks. Manny had three older sisters, and the family's Washington Heights block was full of drug dealing.
He has three sons, one from an earlier relationship. Lucas, the youngest, was drafted by the Angels in 2024.
In September 2011 he was charged with misdemeanor battery for allegedly slapping his wife. The charge was dropped when she wouldn't cooperate.
He once got Red Sox teammates, including Ellis Burks, to drink alcohol he had spiked with Viagra.

c: The Cardinals signed him in 1949 as a pitcher. In 1950 his Class D manager put him at third in what was meant to be a temporary move, and he hit .342.
Playing winter ball in Havana after 1954, he was hit by a fastball behind the ear and was unconscious for three days. The Cardinals still traded their third baseman to make room for him.
In 1957 he moved to center field to make room for rookie Eddie Kasko and led National League outfielders in fielding. He went back to third the next year and won five Gold Gloves.

In 1964 he drove in a league-leading 119 runs and won the MVP. In Game 4 of the World Series his grand slam beat the Yankees 4–3, and in Game 7 both he and his brother Clete homered, the only time brothers have done it in the same World Series game.
Fans said he didn't hustle because he made it look easy. "That's the way I am." Stan Musial: "The ballplayers know he's a good one, but nobody else does."
Cardinals scout Runt Marr recommended him. St. Louis signed him for $6,000, just $1,000 under the bonus-baby limit, as a pitcher who might play some third.
At Rochester he played alongside his brother Cloyd.
Out of the Army in 1954, he helped Houston win the Texas League playoffs.
In September 1962 he broke Rogers Hornsby's Cardinals record for home runs by a right-handed hitter.

His Game 4 grand slam in the 1964 Series came off Al Downing after Bobby Richardson botched a double-play ball. Clete, playing in his fifth straight Series for the Yankees, was privately thrilled for him.

After the 1965 season the Cardinals traded him to the Mets for Al Jackson and Charley Smith, then the biggest trade in Mets history. In July 1967 the Mets sent him to the White Sox, who released him in 1968, and he finished as a Dodgers pinch hitter.
He managed in the minors and won a title at Tulsa in 1974, developing Keith Hernandez and Garry Templeton. In 1978 he took over the Cardinals after Vern Rapp was fired and went 62–81.
p: He was one of 14 children in Alba, Missouri. All seven boys played pro ball, and Cloyd and Clete also made the majors.
He served two years in the Army during the Korean War and played ball in Germany and Africa.
He died of cancer in 1982 at 51, after trying laetrile treatments in Mexico.
The Cardinals retired his number 14 in 1984. He was, at the time, the only player with a retired Cardinals number who wasn't in the Hall of Fame.
He was the third-oldest son of 14 children. His father ran a general store and service station in Alba.
He married Kathleen Oliver in April 1952; they had four children and later divorced. Son David played in the Cardinals' farm system.
He was slated to manage Louisville when he was diagnosed with lung cancer, and died in September 1982.

c: As kids in Nizao they played "La Placa," with a license plate for home and the batter's bat touching it until the pitch. That's where his talent for hitting low balls emerged.

At the Dodgers' academy at 16 he was judged slow and fat with a long swing. He went to the Expos' tryout on the back of a friend's motorcycle, in mismatched spikes with a sock stuffed in the one that was too big, and pulled a muscle running to first. Montreal signed him anyway, for $2,000.
After he threw out Todd Hundley at the plate on one bounce from the warning track, Bobby Valentine said: "That guy doesn't need a cutoff or relay. He needs a bigger ballpark."
He swung at everything and hit it anyway: .363 on the first pitch, .417 on 3–1. He and Garry Templeton are the only major leaguers with a third of their walks intentional.
The game's premier bad-ball hitter, in August 2009 he got a hit on a pitch that had bounced in front of the plate.

The Mets couldn't get insurance on his bad back, so Arte Moreno signed him for the Angels in 2004. He carried them to the division title in September and won the MVP. He went into the Hall of Fame in an Angels cap, the first player to do so.
He dropped out after fifth grade because he missed so many classes working in the fields.
As a teenager he worked out at the Dodgers' Dominican academy and was sent home after eight months without a contract.
At his Expos tryout he pulled a muscle running to first in his only at-bat, but scout Fred Ferreira signed him anyway, two weeks after his 17th birthday, for $2,000.

In his first spring with the Expos he broke a bone in his left foot fouling a ball off it. Felipe Alou and Pedro Martínez mentored him, and before the end of 1998 Montreal signed him through 2003 for $28 million.
In 2003 he herniated a disk and could barely get out of bed in his Miami hotel; Montreal went 18–29 while he was out.
Playing hurt, he still hit for the cycle on September 14, 2003.
He turned down five years and $75 million from Montreal. The Orioles, Mets and Dodgers chased him, but the Angels signed him for five years and $70 million with a $5 million bonus.
In the last seven games of 2004 he hit six homers to pull the Angels from three games back to the division title. In 2008 the managers voted him one of the most feared hitters in baseball.
He retired on a one-day contract with the Angels in 2014.
p: His father left before he was born. The family shared two beds in one room after a hurricane took the roof, and his mother slipped into Venezuela and Colombia to work as a cook and maid and sent her pay home. He drank from puddles and left school after fifth grade.
Pulling stubborn bulls in from the fields with his grandfather gave him his grip: "That's what made me strong up here."
As a rookie in Montreal, he brought his mother to the city to cook for him, and he brought the leftovers to teammates. Pedro Martinez gave him his apartment address in case he got lost.
Back home he built a concrete-block factory, a propane company, a supermarket and a farm, creating jobs in his hometown. His son Vladimir Jr. was born in Montreal in 1999.
He was one of nine children. His brother Wilton played with him in Montreal, and brothers Eleazar and Julio Cesar played in the minors.

He has eight children with five women. Vladimir Jr. became a Blue Jays star, and sons Pablo and Vladimir Miguel signed with the Rangers and Mets. In 2021 he and Vlad Jr. became the second father and son with 40-homer seasons, after Cecil and Prince Fielder.

c: He sat out his senior season of high school after a fight with his coach over playing time, and the Cardinals drafted him in the 42nd round.
In 1979 he won the batting title at .344 and shared the MVP with Willie Stargell. He won 11 straight Gold Gloves.

He later said he started using cocaine heavily in 1980 after he and his wife separated. Whitey Herzog traded him to the lowly Mets in June 1983. "Whitey thought he was going to bury my ass in New York... Didn't happen. It revitalized my career."

Caught up in the 1986 drug investigation, he agreed to give 10 percent of his salary to antidrug programs and be tested for the rest of his career so he could play that season. The Mets won 108 games and the World Series.
Teammates called him "Mex" because people assumed his surname meant he was Mexican. His father's family was Castilian Spanish.
He played a season at the College of San Mateo before the Cardinals drafted him. He was the last player taken in the 1971 draft to make the majors.
In 1982 he drove in eight runs as St. Louis beat Milwaukee in seven games in the World Series.
On June 15, 1983, the Cardinals traded him to the Mets for Neil Allen and Rick Ownbey. At first he was upset, but he later said the young, hungry Mets "reenergized" him.
He had seven hits in the 1986 NLCS.
He won two World Series, one with each team, and was a co-captain of the Mets.
In 1989 a collision with the Dodgers' Dave Anderson broke his kneecap and cost him eight weeks. He signed with Cleveland, played 43 games in 1990, and had back surgery in 1991.
He has written five books, including If at First, his diary of the 1985 season, and I'm Keith Hernandez in 2018.
p: His father, once a Brooklyn Dodgers prospect, drilled him and his brother Gary for hours as boys.
His guest role on Seinfeld made him a pop-culture figure: "Saying 'I'm Keith Hernandez' is still worth a lot of money." He was still getting royalty checks decades later.
His mother developed dementia at 50 and died in 1989. In 2012 he shaved off his famous mustache to raise $10,000 for the Brooklyn adult day care center named for her.
As a Mets broadcaster: "I am paid handsomely, with six months off, and it's baseball. Not bad, right?"
His Bengal cat Hadji, internet-famous in his own right, died in 2024 at 22.
His father played minor-league first base, and his mother was the daughter of a Texas oil wildcatter. His oldest brother was born prematurely and died soon after.
He married Sue Broecker in 1979 and adopted her daughter, Jessie. They had two daughters, Melissa and Mary, and divorced in 1983. He was married to Kai Thompson from 2005 to 2011.
He has broadcast Mets games since 1998, working with Ron Darling and Gary Cohen on SNY since 2006.

c: At 11 he went second in his Little League draft, behind a girl, Jane Sepko, who led the league in homers. His father said years later he kept bringing it up. Over the next two seasons he won all 18 games he pitched.
A Reds pitching coach told him his high leg kick, copied from Dennis Eckersley, would keep him out of the majors. "All that did was harden me and make me more determined to prove him wrong."

With Norm Charlton and Randy Myers he was one of the "Nasty Boys" who carried Cincinnati to the 1990 title. That year he was the first setup man named to an All-Star team ("It made me speechless for the first time in my life") and co-MVP of the NLCS.
In 1991, unhappy after closing out a win, he threw the game ball over the center-field fence and hit a first-grade teacher on the elbow. He was suspended three times that season.

In September 1992, after Dibble accused Lou Piniella of misleading reporters about his shoulder, the two wrestled in the clubhouse on camera. "The next day, we were best of friends. I loved Lou... We hate losing more than we like winning."
He was the fifth of six children, and his father coached him until he was 15. He made the Little League all-star team anyway and helped Southington reach one win from the Little League World Series.

The Cardinals drafted him in the 11th round in 1982, but he went to college. He didn't like it, worked in a department store, and got the commissioner to let him into the 1983 secondary draft. Cincinnati took him in the first round.
In 1986 he survived a car crash when a guardrail kept the car from going down a 50-foot ravine.

In 1989 he was fined for throwing behind Willie Randolph, suspended for throwing Terry Pendleton's bat into the backstop, and suspended again after hitting Tim Teufel and starting a second brawl by charging out of the dugout.
He was co-MVP of the 1990 NLCS with Randy Myers. In 1991 he brawled with Houston's Eric Yelding.
He broke his forearm in April 1993 and had rotator cuff surgery in 1994. The White Sox suspended him in 1995 for saying strike replacement players would be "labeled like child molesters."

He co-hosted The Best Damn Sports Show Period and worked on Fox's Saturday baseball. During a 2010 Nationals broadcast he drew criticism for ridiculing a group of women in the stands. He coached Calabasas High and was fired 10 games into the 2013 season.
p: His mother: "We never said, 'better luck next time.' We said, 'Rob, how come you were so bad.'" His parents once got a joke trophy as the worst Little League parents in history.
When he was 11, parents circulated a petition with 2,500 names to keep him off the Little League all-star team. His parents kept it from him. "Going back to 11 years old, people hated me."
His father was a Connecticut radio newsman. When his pitching career ended he studied for the state police exam, but his father steered him into broadcasting.
His time as a Nationals TV analyst ended in 2010 after he criticized Stephen Strasburg on his radio show for complaining of an arm injury in the middle of a game.
He married his high school sweetheart, Joanne Abate, in 1987. They had two children, Ashley and Ryan, and divorced in 2000.

c: Told to become a reliever in Seattle in 1961: "A reliefer? What the hell do I want to be a reliefer for?" Johnny Pesky: "Because the Red Sox need one." "That's different."
Told he'd get the $7,500 minimum as a rookie: "I don't care if you give me five bucks, as long as you take me back to Boston." He threw 34 straight scoreless innings that first season.

The 6-foot-6 "Monster" won 15 games in relief in 1963 and 16 in 1964, and his 181 strikeouts in 1964 are still the record for a reliever. He often went three or four innings. He insisted to the end that there was no such thing as overwork.

Bill Monbouquette was going for his 20th win and a $5,000 bonus in 1963 when Radatz relieved him: "Bill, I'm not only going to win you this game because it's No. 20, but also as a wedding present. So go sit down and stop worrying." He did.

A story often printed says Mickey Mantle struck out 47 times in 63 at-bats against him. Retrosheet found 16 at-bats and 12 strikeouts. In Radatz's first three seasons Mantle got one hit off him, a home run.
In the 1964 All-Star Game, Johnny Callison's ninth-inning homer beat him. "On one pitch I go from MVP to donkey."
Michigan State coach Johnny Kobs steered him away from basketball. He went 10–1 with a 1.12 ERA as a senior but drew little interest from scouts.
He started out as a starter. Johnny Pesky converted him to relief at Seattle in 1961, against his will, because of a sore arm, and he saved 24.
Pesky worked him hard: in one season 132⅓ innings in 66 games, with four or more innings six times. Ralph Houk called him "the best relief pitcher I have ever seen."
New manager Billy Herman announced he would only use Radatz with Boston ahead. His top salary was a reported $42,500 in 1966. That June Boston traded him to Cleveland for Don McMahon and Lee Stange.
In a 1968 Cubs spring game he threw 24 balls in a row and was released nine days later. The Tigers signed him, sold him to Montreal in June 1969, and the Expos released him that August.
His 104 saves were a Red Sox record until Bob Stanley broke it. He finished as pitching coach of the independent North Shore Spirit.
p: His father had helped raise Hal Newhouser in their Detroit neighborhood, and Dick grew up idolizing him.

He told one story of watching a game on TV at home in Milton, the kids running around the house, getting restless, driving to Fenway, and winning it in extra innings. The real version seems to be a spring game when he was watching from the stands with his family.
Having lost his control, before the 1969 season he went through hypnosis with a Detroit psychiatrist to try to get it back.
He died in 2005 at 67 after falling down the basement stairs at his home in Easton, Massachusetts.
His father, Norman, was an auto body design draftsman in Detroit.
He married Sharon Lee Cooper in September 1958, at the start of his senior year. They had three children: Leigh, Dick Jr. and Kristine.
Out of baseball he sold insurance, worked for a copier company and sold industrial lumber.
In the 1970s he suffered from severe cluster headaches after his mother and a close friend died. He had his own weekly radio show, and his son Dick Jr. became a Red Sox minor-league executive.
In 1984 Jerry Moses, a former teammate, got him a job with a packaging company near Boston: "I felt I had formed a love affair with this town."

c: He got "Goose" from a friend who didn't like "Goss" and thought he looked like a goose when he stretched his neck out to read the catcher's signs.
He threw basically one pitch, a rising fastball near 100 mph. For all his high-and-tight reputation, he said he threw at only three hitters on purpose: Ron Gant, Andrés Galarraga and Al Bumbry.
In the 1978 one-game playoff at Fenway he got Carl Yastrzemski to pop up to Graig Nettles with two on in the ninth. Ten days later he got the last out of the World Series too.
In April 1979, when Reggie Jackson passed along Gossage's teasing, Cliff Johnson came out of the shower and fought him. Gossage tore ligaments in his thumb and missed three months.

In Game 5 of the 1984 World Series he waved off the order to walk Kirk Gibson with first base open. On the second pitch Gibson homered to clinch it for Detroit. At their 2008 Hall of Fame induction, he and his old manager Dick Williams were still ribbing each other about it.
He often worked two and three innings, with 53 saves of seven or more outs to Mariano Rivera's one. "Don't tell me [Rivera's] the best relief pitcher of all-time until he can do the same job I did."
After 1976 the White Sox traded him and Terry Forster to Pittsburgh for Richie Zisk and Silvio Martinez. A year later he signed with the Yankees for six years and $3.6 million.
He got the last out of the 1978 ALCS clincher against Kansas City, five days after the playoff at Fenway.

George Steinbrenner fined both him and Cliff Johnson for the 1979 fight, and Johnson was traded two months later. In the 1980 ALCS George Brett hit a three-run homer off him into the upper deck to finish a Royals sweep.
He saved all three Yankee wins in the 1981 Division Series. After 1983 he refused to re-sign, joined San Diego, and saved the 1984 NLCS clincher against the Cubs.
The Cubs released him in March 1989. He pitched for the Giants, the Yankees again, Texas, Oakland and Seattle.
He got the final out to clinch a division, pennant or World Series seven times.
p: He grew up in Colorado Springs and married Corna, a fellow Wasson High graduate. The city named a five-field youth sports complex for him in 1995.
He struck out Pete Rose in Rose's last major-league at-bat, in 1986.
In retirement his attacks on Yankees players and executives, Rivera among them, got him disinvited from Yankees spring training and Old-Timers' Day.
He owned Burgers N Sports restaurants in Greeley and Parker, Colorado, and wrote an autobiography, The Goose Is Loose. His son Todd played independent-league ball.
At his 2008 Hall of Fame induction he and Kirk Gibson ribbed each other on ESPN about the 1984 home run.

c: A natural right-hander, he broke his right arm twice as a small boy, the first time when a neighborhood kid fell on it during a football game, and taught himself to throw left-handed.
At 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds out of high school he drew no scouts. At Division III Ferrum College he set an NCAA record with 19.1 strikeouts per nine innings, and Houston took him 12th overall.
The day after he learned he was being called up in September 1995, his wife's parents were murdered. He wore number 13 for his whole career.
On a move from starting to closing: "if you go through what I went through as a kid, not knowing if I was going to eat or who I was going to live with, this is nothing."
In 1998 a line drive hit him in the head. He came back calmer, with better control. Houston traded him in 2003 after he criticized management: "They had become tired of my bluntness."

Meeting his boyhood hero Dale Murphy at Braves camp in 2010: "I was so nervous, I couldn't even talk, and you know me, I can talk." He struck out the last four batters of his career and was elected to the Hall of Fame in 2025, his last year on the ballot.

Held back a year by his chaotic home life, he was promoted to high school anyway because officials feared he threw hard enough to hurt middle schoolers. As a senior he was only 5-foot-5 and 135 pounds.
Houston drafted him 12th overall in 1993, after his junior year. He then went back to Ferrum to propose to his girlfriend, Sarah Quesenberry.
He set a record with 14.4 strikeouts per nine innings, beating Rob Dibble's 14.1.
The 1998 liner gave him a concussion, and he was carried off on a stretcher. A torn flexor tendon in 2000 ended his season and needed surgery.

Houston traded him to the Phillies for three pitchers in November 2003. In September 2005 his Phillies teammates confronted him after he said publicly they had "no chance" to make the playoffs, and Pat Burrell reportedly called him a "rat."
The Mets signed him for four years at $10.5 million a year, the most for any reliever then. He had Tommy John surgery in September 2008. The Mets traded him to Boston in 2009, still chasing a ring.
p: His parents married when his mother was 16. Some days there was little to eat. After they divorced he was passed among parents and grandparents until his cousin's family took him in at 14.
Breakfast as a boy, he said, was often a "few crackers with peanut butter and a glass of water."
He and his family raised alpacas on their Virginia farm. He coached at the Miller School, where his son Will played second base.
In 2005 he started the Second Chance Learning Center to help at-risk kids like he had been.
His parents married the day his father graduated from high school. After his sister Chastity was born they divorced, and he was shuttled among his parents and relatives, mostly his grandparents.
He and Sarah have four children: Jeremy, William, Kason and Olivia. He coached at the Miller School near Charlottesville.
At Miller he coached against his own high school and old coach, and coached his sons Will and Kason. Will reached the majors with Toronto in 2024.

c: UCLA's Tommy Prothro recruited him for football and, by one account, practically promised him a shot at the Heisman. He signed with the Orioles instead: "I figured I was too small to make a career out of pro football."
As a rookie he told Frank Robinson, who'd asked what a rookie knew about hitting: "Tell you something, pal. I'll be hitting for ten years around here after you're gone."
Reporting to Earl Weaver as a nervous 21-year-old, he knocked on his door to say he'd arrived. "What do you want?... Is that all?" "That was my greeting to the big leagues."

He won four straight Gold Gloves alongside shortstop Mark Belanger, who won four of his own. A writer, recalling how Leo Durocher prized Eddie Stanky, imagined what Durocher would have given for Grich.

He hurt his back lifting an air conditioner before his first Angels season. Back in form in 1979, he hit 30 homers batting eighth. In 1981 he tied for the home run lead, the first American League second baseman to win a share of the title since Nap Lajoie.

His Game 5 homer in the 1986 ALCS bounced off Dave Henderson's glove and over the fence. The Angels were one strike from the World Series when Henderson homered off them. After losing Game 7, Grich announced his retirement.
He signed a letter of intent with UCLA, but the Orioles took him in the first round in 1967. He hit .254 and then .228 in his first two minor-league seasons.
He was on the 1970 World Series roster but didn't play. Baltimore traded second baseman Davey Johnson after 1972 to make room for him.
He hit 2-for-20 in the 1973 ALCS loss to Oakland. His teams lost five ALCS, and he hit .154, .200 and .182 in the Angels' three.

The Yankees chased him hard as a free agent, but he signed with the Angels for $1.35 million: "you can't put dollar signs on what Southern California has to offer." He had surgery for a herniated disk in July 1977 and played just 52 games.
When the Angels clinched their first division title in 1979, he dumped a can of beer over Richard Nixon's head in the clubhouse celebration.
After the 1986 ALCS loss to Boston, he announced his retirement in the Angels' locker room.
p: His father, a Long Beach shipping clerk, had been an amateur boxer with a 40–2–2 record and didn't want his skinny son playing baseball. His mother talked him into it.
In 1974 he said he wanted a $2 million estate so he could quit working, fly solo around the world and explore remote places. He later visited all 50 states.
A 2.5-handicap golfer, he played 89 of Golf Digest's top 100 U.S. courses. In 1988 he became the first player in the Angels Hall of Fame.
His mother waited tables at a fine-dining restaurant in Long Beach for a few years.
When he joined the Angels at 29 he was single, and a writer said he had "the rugged good looks of the Marlboro man."

c: As a boy he threw every night to his father, who caught sitting on a five-gallon bucket. After a junior-college career, friends promised to buy him beer if he went to a tryout. He went and was noticed.

Texas protected 24 players when Toronto got to pick one as compensation for losing Cliff Johnson. On their scout's insistence, the Jays took the 25th, Henke. His Triple-A manager: "Gosh, Texas let this guy go!"

When he first pitched at Exhibition Stadium, the ovation lasted, by his estimate, at least 10 minutes. Teammate John Cerutti named him "the Terminator" after they watched the movie, and fans wrote him a song.
His record in 1987 was 0–6 with a league-leading 34 saves. "A lot of times, wins come from blown saves. I prefer saves." He set records for strikeouts per nine innings two years running.
In Game 3 of the 1989 ALCS he closed out Toronto's only win. His wife, unbeknownst to him, was in labor during the game.

At 37 he signed with the Cardinals, his boyhood team ("if it hadn't been with St. Louis, I probably would have retired"), saved 36, made the All-Star team and quit. "People don't understand that this game takes a lot away from your life."
He was one of 11 children. His father had been a catcher who interested the Cardinals before serving in the Navy in Korea, then worked as a supervisor and at the Jefferson City prison.
At East Central College he studied building construction. Teammates called him "The Hose." He turned down the Mariners in 1979 and the Cubs as a first-rounder in January 1980, then signed with Texas.
Rangers manager Doug Rader doubted his makeup and once berated him on the mound for throwing to the wrong base. In winter ball for Santurce he learned to throw his split-finger fastball for strikes.
After his strong 1986 he held out into spring training, and in 1988 an arbitrator sided with Toronto and set his salary at $725,000, leaving him bitter.
He saved five games in the 1992 postseason as Toronto won its first World Series. He left for Texas in 1993 and was hurt much of 1994.
He retired after his 1995 season with the Cardinals: "I'd like to see my kids grow up."
p: He met his wife Kathy, a 6-foot-1 volleyball player, when she sold him a Big Mac in college. "I was finished." It took him two months to ask her out.
From a Missouri town of under 900, he hated New York and never rode the subway. In Toronto he rented a downtown apartment and found it wasn't for him.

His daughter Amanda was born with Down syndrome. "She's taught me so much about patience, about how it's not that bad to have a bad game." His charity golf tournament has raised more than $1.4 million.
He gave his $25,000 Rolaids Relief prize to the Taos parks board and St. Francis Xavier School. He went home to farm.
He lives on a 1,000-acre farm in Taos, Missouri, with Kathy and their children Linsay, Ryan, Kim and Amanda.
Since 1995 his charity golf tournament in Jefferson City has raised money for a school for disabled children. He also volunteers with the Special Olympics and the Cancer Society.
