c: His father was a Twins draft pick whose minor-league career ended with injuries. Angels scout Greg Morhardt, who'd played with his father in the minors, called Mike the fastest and strongest 17-year-old he had ever seen.

As a senior at Millville High in New Jersey he moved from shortstop and pitcher to the outfield and hit a state-record 18 home runs. The Angels drafted him 25th in 2009, with a pick they got from the Yankees for signing Mark Teixeira.
He wore 2 as a boy for his hero Derek Jeter, and grew up a Phillies fan who went to their 2008 World Series parade.
He led the American League in WAR in each of his first five full seasons. Through age 24 he had more WAR than anyone since 1913, ahead of Mickey Mantle.
In the 2023 World Baseball Classic final, as Team USA's captain, he struck out against his Angels teammate Shohei Ohtani for the last out.
He gave up a commitment to East Carolina to sign with the Angels on July 2, 2009, for a $1.215 million bonus.
The Angels called him up on July 8, 2011, to replace the injured Peter Bourjos in center field.
Before 2014 he signed a one-year, $1 million deal, the most ever for a player not yet eligible for arbitration. Weeks later the Angels gave him six years and $144.5 million.
He homered off James Shields in Game 3 of the 2014 Division Series against Kansas City. As of 2025 that was his only postseason.
In 2017 he tore a ligament in his thumb, his first trip to the disabled list, and missed 39 games after surgery.
In March 2019 he signed for 12 years and $426 million, at the time the richest contract in North American sports. That September he had surgery to remove a neuroma.
Injuries took over from there: a torn calf in 2021, back spasms in 2022, a broken hamate bone in 2023, a torn meniscus twice in 2024, and a knee bone bruise in 2025.
p: He picked up the nickname "Millville Meteor" after a vandal added it to his Wikipedia article and it caught on. He loves fishing, hunting and the weather.
He holds Philadelphia Eagles season tickets. In 2014 President Obama compared the Farm Bill to him: "somebody who's got a lot of tools."
In 2020 one of his trading cards sold for $3.93 million, then a record for a sports card.
In 2026 he opened Trout National, a private golf club near Millville co-designed with Tiger Woods, limited to 227 members.
His father, Jeff, played four years in the minors before a torn plantar fascia and knee injuries ended his career.
He married his longtime girlfriend, Jessica Cox, in December 2017. They have two sons, born in 2020 and 2024.
He has invested in BodyArmor sports drink since 2012 and endorsed SuperPretzel. In 2021 Topps signed him to the biggest and longest deal it had ever given an individual athlete.
Trout National cost $100 million to build, in Vineland, New Jersey.

c: He grew up in Vega Baja playing with a stick and a ball of tape. His coach moved him to catcher at about 7 because he threw too hard and scared the other kids. "I threw seven no-hitters, two in one day."

At a Rangers tryout at 16 he was clocked throwing 93 mph from home to second, and the scouting director made sure he signed that day. A minor-league coach called him "Pudgy" for being small and cocky.

He was supposed to marry his childhood sweetheart Maribel between games of a doubleheader in Tulsa. The Rangers called him up the day before, so they married that morning and flew to Chicago (he later said the real wedding came the next spring). That night he threw out two runners and drove in two with his first hit.
On deadline day in 1997, with a trade to the Yankees all but done, he walked into the Rangers president's office himself and negotiated a five-year deal. His mother had told him to go talk to them.

In 1999 he hit 35 homers, stole 25 bases and won the MVP. He retired with records for games caught and catcher Gold Gloves (13), and joined his boyhood hero Johnny Bench as the only catchers elected to the Hall of Fame on the first ballot.
His father, an amateur catcher who worked as an electrician, taught him the position. He played Little League with Ricky Otero and against future Rangers teammate Juan Gonzalez.
Coach Chino Cadahia called him "Pudgy" because he was small and cocky. Over the winters he studied under Benito Santiago in Puerto Rico.
In his debut, on the day he was supposed to marry, he threw out two runners and drove in two with his first hit.
A stress fracture in his lower back, from overuse, bothered him for the rest of his career. Hubie Brooks's backswing broke his cheekbone, and he was back four days after surgery.
The 1997 Yankees deal would have sent him to New York for Eric Milton, Tony Armas Jr. and Jorge Posada.
A broken right thumb ended his 2000 season, and a herniated disk sidelined him in 2001.
He signed with Florida for one year and $10 million in 2003, won the NLCS MVP and the World Series, then signed with Detroit for four years and $40 million.

In his 2005 book Juiced, Jose Canseco claimed he had personally injected Rodríguez with steroids in Texas. Rodríguez said he was "in shock" and denied it, but the suspicion was seen as a possible obstacle to the Hall of Fame.
p: He crossed himself and prayed before every at-bat and wore a medallion of Jesus under his shirt. "I never say, 'I want you to give this to me today.'"

He liked to bring a friend or relative on road trips to keep from getting bored. His wife: "He watches ESPN when he comes home from the ballpark at night. Then he gets up in the morning... and watches ESPN again."
His son Dereck was drafted as an outfielder, switched to pitching and reached the majors with the Giants in 2018. He didn't want to be a catcher: he wanted to make his own way.
At his 2012 retirement ceremony in Arlington he threw the ceremonial first pitch from behind the plate, down to second base.
His mother taught elementary school, and his first job was handing out flyers in shopping malls.
He and Maribel had three children, Dereck, Amanda and Ivanna, and started a foundation in 1993. They divorced in 2006, and in 2007 he married Patricia Gómez, from Colombia.

c: At Seminole High he stole home 10 times, rushed for 1,000 yards in eight football games and reportedly had more than 100 football scholarship offers. He picked baseball because a running back's career is short: "in baseball I ended up playing 23 years."
He stole 27 straight bases over parts of three seasons before Mike Scioscia threw him out in May 1981. He was called "Rock" because he had 7.8 percent body fat.
He began using cocaine early in his career to fit in and got hooked. He went to rehab after 1982 and leaned on Andre Dawson. He named his second son Andre, nicknamed "Little Hawk."

After winning the 1986 batting title he got no real offers in free agency during the owners' collusion and had to wait until May 1 to re-sign with Montreal. In his first game back, with no spring training, he tripled on the first pitch and hit a 10th-inning grand slam.

In 2001, after beating lupus, he and his son Tim Jr. played together for the Orioles, only the second father and son to do it after the Griffeys. "I'm not a guy who sheds many tears... I couldn't help but get emotional."
He retired with the best stolen-base percentage of anyone with 400 steals, and was elected to the Hall of Fame in 2017.
Montreal took him early in the fifth round in 1977. As the first non-pitcher the Expos drafted that year, he joked that he was a "number 1 pick."

In 1982, when he spent about $40,000 on cocaine, he kept it in his hip pocket so it wouldn't be in his locker, and slid headfirst. He used it before games, after games and sometimes between innings. He testified at the Pittsburgh drug trials in 1985.
Once allowed to negotiate with Montreal again, on May 1, 1987, he signed for three years and $5 million plus a $900,000 bonus.
That July he was All-Star Game MVP, breaking up a scoreless tie with a two-run triple in the 13th.

Montreal traded him to the White Sox in December 1990; he later said he wanted to win and didn't think the Expos "had what it took." He tore a thumb ligament stealing a base in 1993, but hit .444 in that year's ALCS.
The White Sox traded him to the Yankees for a minor-leaguer after 1995. Injuries held him to about 81 games a year, but he won rings in 1996 and 1998.
Before he joined his son in Baltimore, he and Tim Jr. played against each other in a 2001 Triple-A game, the first father and son to do so in an official pro game.
p: "We'd race against Pop as kids until somebody beat him. I was the first to do it. I was 15." In one childhood all-star game he and three brothers made up the entire infield. A local headline: "When It Raines, It Pours."
He married his high school sweetheart, Virginia Hilton, in 1979, the year Tim Jr. was born.

In July 1999 he felt suddenly exhausted after a routine jog to the outfield. Doctors found lupus attacking his kidneys, and his weight dropped to 170 pounds. "My jeans would hang off my body, like the kids today wear them. But it wasn't on purpose."
Sanford, Florida, gave him a key to the city in 2019, and his high school field is now Tim Raines Athletic Park.
His father, Ned, played semipro ball. He was one of seven children; a sister was killed by a car when she was 4.
In 1982 he blamed his slump on his wife's miscarriage and an uncle's death.
He and Virginia divorced in 2005. In 2007 he moved outside Phoenix and married Shannon Watson.

c: A skinny shortstop who hit .230 as a high school senior, he got to Stony Brook only because his assistant coach had roomed with the Stony Brook coach in college. He shot up to 6-foot-4 and hit .394.

Drafted as a shortstop, he quit at 21 when the Giants asked him to pitch, went back to finish his degree, and worked as a barback and on a golf course. A week of Wall Street cold calls convinced him to try. He had to write the Giants a letter to convince them he was ready.

In his big-league debut in 1999 he threw seven shutout innings. His knees were shaking in the first. After shoulder surgery he was throwing 83 mph and gave up four straight homers in Triple-A. "There was never in my mind a thought I was going to quit."

Traded to Minnesota while on a cruise, he became the closer and saved 246 games from 2004 to 2009, the most in the majors. When the Twins left the Metrodome he scooped up a container of dirt from its mound, and he spread it on the Target Field mound before his first save there.
He never got past the first round in six postseasons. He finally got a ring from the 2016 Cubs, for whom he'd pitched three games.
He never threw a pitch in high school.
Before the Giants drafted him in the sixth round in 1995, scouts from nearly every team came to see him pitch, and the game was rained out.
After graduating he went back to the Giants. He was called up in April 1999 when Barry Bonds had elbow surgery. Ron Perranoski called his debut the best since Fernando Valenzuela's.

His shoulder tendinitis and inflammation led to arthroscopic surgery on his rotator cuff and labrum. In 2003, in his postseason debut, he blew a save and took the loss in Game 2 of the NLDS against Florida.
The Giants traded him, Boof Bonser and Francisco Liriano to the Twins for a catcher. Twins pitching coach Rick Anderson had pushed for him, and he won the closer's job in 2004.
His 2004 ALDS save against the Yankees was his only postseason save. In March 2008 the Twins signed him for four years and $47 million.
He had Tommy John surgery in 2010 and missed the season. He then pitched for Texas and Detroit, and retired on a one-day contract with the Twins in 2017.
p: His grandfather Bob Brock played center field for Texas's national champions in 1949 and 1950.

In 2008 he gave Stony Brook $500,000 for a new ballpark, now Joe Nathan Field. He remembered they couldn't host a regional as the top seed because their field was so bad. Stony Brook had already retired his number 22, the first number it ever retired.
In 2014, booed at Comerica with Detroit in first place, he flicked off the fans, then apologized. "Should I have done it? No."

After his parents divorced he and his mother moved to Circleville, New York, where she married Walter Feuerstack and worked at his trucking company. He had an older sister, a half-brother and four step-siblings.
He met Lisa Lemoncelli in Arizona in 1997 and married her in November 2002. They had a son, Cole, and a daughter, Riley Grace.

c: As a boy at his father's minor-league park in Asheville, he was playing catch with Doug DeCinces when a man started firing a rifle at the field. DeCinces carried him into the dugout.

The Orioles' scouting director saw a pitcher. A scout and his father thought he'd be an everyday player, and Cal Sr. told him he could always go back to pitching. In 1981 he played all 33 innings of the longest game in pro history, at Pawtucket.

When Earl Weaver moved the 6-foot-4 rookie to shortstop in July 1982, some in the front office objected. Weaver: "Fire my butt out of here, I told 'em, but as long as I'm here, the kid's at short every day."

In 1987 his father, then his manager, took him out late in a blowout in Toronto, ending a streak of 8,264 consecutive innings dating to 1982. "I wanted to take the monkey off of his back. It was my decision, not his."

He'd write out pitch sequences for his pitchers and later flashed pitch signals to catcher Chris Hoiles from shortstop. In 1990 he made three errors all season, the best fielding percentage ever at the position, and didn't win the Gold Glove.

On September 6, 1995, when the warehouse banner turned to 2,131, Rafael Palmeiro and Bobby Bonilla pushed him onto the field, and he jogged a lap around Camden Yards slapping hands. The ovation lasted more than 22 minutes. He ended the streak himself at 2,632 in 1998.
He started high school at second base because his coach wasn't sure about his arm. He pitched in the state championship game.
He signed in 1978 for a $20,000 bonus. In 1982 Doug DeCinces was traded to California to open third base for him.
His first major-league steal was a steal of home on a double steal against Texas. The Orioles later beat the White Sox and then the Phillies to win the World Series.
In a brawl with Seattle at Camden Yards, after Mike Mussina hit Bill Haselman, he ended up at the bottom of the pile and was hurt.
In 1999 he passed Hank Aaron for grounding into the most double plays.
He was a top advertising figure, for Nike, Chevrolet, True Value, Wheaties and small Maryland businesses.
p: His father was in Topeka with one of his teams when Cal was born. Cal Sr. said the boy's questions were better than the reporters'.
An honor student, he heard from West Point about playing soccer there.
In his last All-Star Game, in 2001, Alex Rodriguez switched positions with him so he could start at shortstop. He homered and was named MVP.

With his brother Bill he started the Cal Ripken Sr. Foundation for underprivileged kids, and in 2007 he went to China as a State Department sports envoy. In 2024 he joined the group that bought the Orioles.
His father was a catcher whose career ended with a shoulder injury.
He married Kelly Geer in November 1987. They had Rachel and Ryan, who played in the minors, and divorced in 2016. In 2018 he married Laura Kiessling, a Maryland appeals judge.
In July 2012 his mother was kidnapped at gunpoint and returned safely. In 2020 he announced he had been treated for prostate cancer.
His autobiography, The Only Way I Know, was a best seller.

c: His father died when he was 6. He and his brothers shined shoes in San Pedro de Macorís. One customer, an American opening a shoe factory, became a surrogate father and bought him his first glove. He wanted to box until his mother made him quit.
His contract with the Phillies at 15 was voided because he was underage. Texas finally signed him for $3,500. His first homer, in 1989, went over the Green Monster off Roger Clemens.
Leaving the White Sox for the Cubs in 1992: "Okay boys. I'm out of here. You guys will see me again. I'm going to be the best player in this game."

In 1998 he hit 20 home runs in June, a record for a month. During the chase with Mark McGwire he hopped after homers, tapped his heart and blew kisses to his mother. When McGwire hit 62 against the Cubs, Sosa ran in from right field to hug him. He finished with 66 and the MVP.

He's the only player with three 60-homer seasons, and he didn't lead the league in any of them. In 2003 his bat shattered and umpires found cork inside. He said it was a batting practice bat he'd grabbed by mistake.

On the last day of 2004 he asked out of the lineup and left early; security cameras caught him driving away. His furious teammates smashed his boombox. He wasn't welcome back at Wrigley until he sent the Cubs a letter of apology in 2025.
Omar Minaya and Amado Dinzey signed him for Texas. Minaya protected him from coaches who weren't used to Latin players.
In July 1989 Texas traded him, Wilson Álvarez and Scott Fletcher to the White Sox for Harold Baines and Fred Manrique.
With the White Sox he clashed with hitting coach Walt Hriniak's rigid ideas. GM Larry Himes, who had traded for him, was fired and became GM of the Cubs.
Before the 1992 season the White Sox traded him and Ken Patterson to the Cubs for George Bell. Cubs announcer Chip Caray nicknamed him "Slammin' Sammy."

In his first Cubs season a Dennis Martínez fastball broke his wrist, and later a foul ball broke his ankle. After a broken bone in his hand needed surgery, he signed a four-year, $42 million deal on June 27, the third-highest pay in baseball.
Cubs announcer Chip Caray nicknamed him "Slammin' Sammy." In 1996 a pitch broke a bone in his hand, and in June 1997 he signed for four years and $42 million.

In 2003 he went on the disabled list for the first time since 1996 after an injured toenail was removed. His cork suspension was cut from eight games to seven. In 2004 he went on the disabled list with back spasms after an odd injury while chatting with reporters at his locker.

In 2003 he went on the disabled list for the first time in years after an infected toenail was removed. His cork suspension was cut from eight games to seven. In 2004 he went on the disabled list with back spasms from a sneeze in the clubhouse.
The New York Times reported in 2009 that he had tested positive in 2003. In 2024 he said he had "made mistakes" recovering from injuries.
p: His family calls him "Mikey," a name his grandmother took from a soap opera she liked.

After his first big-league season he bought his mother a house. When a hurricane hit the Dominican Republic after 1998, he gave money and handed out food, water and medicine himself. President Clinton introduced him at the State of the Union.
In 2009 he showed up looking much lighter-skinned and explained on Spanish-language TV that he'd been using a bleaching cream at night.
He was one of seven children. His father died of a cerebral hemorrhage, and his mother, a maid and cook, went back to her maiden name and later married Carlos Peralta.

In 1990 he married an American, Karen Lee Bright. It lasted eight months, and the legal mess followed him into 1991, when his stepfather also died. He married Sonia Rodríguez, a former Dominican TV dancer, in 1991, and they had six children.

c: The Cardinals gave his friend across the street, Joe Garagiola, a $500 bonus. Berra refused to sign for less, turning down Branch Rickey's $250. The Yankees gave him his $500.

At 19 he was a Navy machine gunner on a rocket boat off Normandy on D-Day and spent 10 days on the 36-foot boat. Back home, Mel Ott offered the Yankees $50,000 for him. Larry MacPhail later admitted he'd never heard of Berra but figured that if Ott thought he was worth that much, they'd better keep him.

Allie Reynolds warned the young catcher he'd cross him up if he looked to Casey Stengel in the dugout for pitch calls. Berra ignored his manager at the risk of a fine, and that won over the staff. Bill Dickey spent hours tutoring him, and he went on to win three MVPs.

He swore to the end that Jackie Robinson was out on his steal of home in the 1955 World Series, and signed photos of the play "He was out." Don Larsen said he didn't shake Berra off once during his 1956 perfect game.

Managing the Yankees in 1964, he slapped Phil Linz's harmonica away on the team bus. The team then got hot and won the pennant, and he was fired anyway. In 1985 George Steinbrenner fired him 16 games into a season he'd promised him, and Berra stayed away from Yankee Stadium until 1999.
His father, from a town near Milan, came over to work and later brought his mother. An older brother was stuck in Italy until 1919 because of World War I.

Both his jobs, one at $25 a week and one on a Pepsi truck, ended because he left early to play ball. He also turned down the Browns. A friend named Browne wrote to George Weiss, and Berra signed with the Yankees in 1942 for $500 and $90 a month.
At the Groton submarine base after the war he bribed guards to sneak out and play for the Cranston Chiefs under another name for $50 a game.
At Newark in 1946 his team lost the playoffs to a Montreal club with Jackie Robinson. Bill Dickey was assigned to tutor him in catching.
In 1953 he hit .429 in the World Series. Later he set records for most consecutive chances and games without an error by a catcher.
He played or coached in 21 World Series and won 13; he holds Series records for games, at-bats, hits and doubles.
He coached the Mets from 1965, came back to the Yankees in 1976, coached eight seasons and managed two, then coached Houston. He managed his son Dale with the Yankees in 1984 and 1985.
p: "Yogi" came from a movie: a Hindu yogi waddled across the screen and a friend said he walked like Lawdie Berra. Even his parents started calling him Yogi.
He quit school after eighth grade over the objections of his father, the principal and the parish priest, then lost two jobs by leaving early to play ball.
At his 1947 night in St. Louis he thanked everyone "for making this night necessary." He met his wife Carmen, a waitress at a restaurant Stan Musial co-owned.

He and Carmen were married 65 years. After she died in 2014, their Montclair house was listed for $888,000, a nod to his number 8. He died in 2015, and his boyhood friend Joe Garagiola died six months later.
His friend Joe Garagiola grew up directly across the street, and Jack Buck also lived on the block, later renamed Hall of Fame Place.
His three sons all played pro sports: Dale in the majors, Tim for the Baltimore Colts and Larry in the minors.

c: He arrived at Notre Dame with a sore shoulder and was last on the pitching depth chart. By his junior year he threw 97 and went 17th overall in the 1998 draft.

His curveball kept hurting his elbow, so a minor-league coordinator told him to throw it away and throw a slider "as hard as you can." He'd never seen anyone pick it up so fast. It came without the red dot hitters look for on a slider.

Catcher Brad Ausmus told him after a September 2002 start: "Your changeup is kind of garbage. I think you should be in the bullpen." In 2004 his 157 strikeouts were more than any reliever has had since.

In Game 5 of the 2005 NLCS he was one strike from the pennant when David Eckstein singled. After a walk, Albert Pujols hit a hanging slider through the left-field support towers and rounded the bases in near-silence.

In 2008 with Philadelphia he went 41-for-41 in saves. One out from the World Series title, Carlos Ruiz came out to ask if he wanted to throw a fastball. Lidge said slider. "OK, give me the good one." He struck out Eric Hinske with it and fell to his knees.
The Giants drafted him in the 42nd round in 1995, but he went to Notre Dame. As a junior he was Big East player of the year.
Houston drafted him with a compensation pick it got when Colorado signed Darryl Kile. He missed parts of his first four pro seasons with injuries, including a torn rotator cuff and a broken forearm.
Larry Walker called his slider "wicked and nasty." The 2003 Astros bullpen was later rated one of the 10 best ever.

In Game 2 of the 2005 World Series he gave up a walk-off homer to Scott Podsednik, and in Game 4 Jermaine Dye's chopper scored the only run. In 2006 he went 1–5 with a 5.28 ERA and lost the closer job.

Philadelphia got him for Michael Bourn and two others in November 2007, a deal a writer called "bold and risky." Despite knee surgery that spring, he earned a three-year, $37.5 million extension in 2008. His 18 postseason saves rank second to Mariano Rivera.
Injuries limited his last four seasons. He finished with the Nationals in 2012 and retired on a one-day Phillies contract in 2013.
p: A former altar boy, he finished his religious studies degree in 2008. After retiring he spent summers in Italy doing archaeology fieldwork and earned a master's in Roman archaeology. His thesis: "Nails: An Underutilized Tool in Ancient Roman Archaeology."
He met his wife Lindsay through friends back home in Colorado after his sophomore year. On why he stays home now: "You miss a lot when you are playing."
In 2009 he called himself a nondenominational Christian leaning toward Catholicism and said he thought Jesus was ideologically more compatible with Democrats than Republicans.
His parents met at the University of Arizona. His father was a real estate broker who helped coach his teams. He has an older sister, Catherine.
He and Lindsay married in 2001 and have a daughter, Avery, and a son, Rowan.

c: At USC he played for Rod Dedeaux with Randy Johnson. He played on the 1984 Olympic team and went 10th overall in the draft that year.
In 1987 he hit 49 home runs, a rookie record that lasted until Aaron Judge. He had two games left to get to 50 and skipped them to be at the birth of his first child.
In 1991 he hit .201, and Tony La Russa sat him out of the last game so he wouldn't drop below .200. He called it the worst year of his life. He hadn't lifted a weight all season.

On September 8, 1998, he hit his 62nd homer against the Cubs, so Sammy Sosa could congratulate him in person, with Roger Maris's family in the stands. The stadium worker who found the ball gave it back to him. He finished with 70.

Before Congress in 2005 he declined to say whether he'd used steroids: "a man, any man, should be regarded as innocent unless proven guilty." In 2010, about to coach for the Cardinals, he admitted using them on and off for a decade, including in 1998. "I wish I had never touched steroids."
He retired in 2001 with years left on his contract: "I am unable to perform at a level equal to the salary the organization would be paying me."
Montreal drafted him in the eighth round out of high school in 1981, but he went to USC, where his teammates included Randy Johnson, Jack Del Rio and Rodney Peete.
His walk-off homer off Jay Howell won Game 3 of the 1988 World Series, Oakland's only win. The A's won it all in 1989.
In 1991, the "worst year" of his life, his marriage was falling apart and he "didn't lift a weight" all season. Foot injuries held him to 74 games in 1993 and 1994.
Oakland traded him to St. Louis on July 31, 1997, with 34 homers. Everyone assumed he'd leave for Southern California as a free agent, but he signed to stay.
Knee tendinitis cost him two months in 2000, and he was reduced to pinch-hitting in the postseason. He went 1-for-11 in the 2001 NLDS and was pinch-hit for in the ninth of Game 5.

He was Cardinals hitting coach from 2010 to 2012, then Dodgers hitting coach to be closer to his family, and Padres bench coach from 2016. In 2013 he was ejected and suspended two games for a brawl with Arizona.
p: His father was a dentist. His brother Dan was an NFL quarterback, and another brother, Jay, a bodybuilder, wrote a book about their shared steroid use.
Missouri named a stretch of I-70 near Busch Stadium the Mark McGwire Highway. In May 2010 the state renamed it for Mark Twain.
He and his wife Stephanie started a foundation for children who have been physically and sexually abused. Their triplet daughters were born in 2010.

He was married to Kathlene Hughes from 1984 to 1990, and they had a son, Matthew. He married Stephanie Slemera, a former pharmaceutical sales rep, and they have five children; sons Mason and Max both signed pro contracts.
Before he admitted to steroids he avoided the media and spent much of his time playing golf.

c: The summer before his senior year he lived with his older brother Larry, a Triple-A pitcher, in Oklahoma City, taking grounders and hanging around the clubhouse. The scout who signed him called him "the best athlete I've ever been associated with."

He was the majors' starting shortstop at 18, with 64 games of A-ball behind him. His first homer came minutes after his error had let Baltimore tie the game. "If I didn't play well, they would send me back to the minor leagues which was probably where I belonged anyway."
In 1978, unsigned and hurting, he left the team and considered becoming a pro golfer. Bud Selig waited him out: "Give the young man all the time he needs."

On the 1982 World Series and his record hitting: "If there is a drawback, I suppose it would be all the exposure." After shoulder surgeries he moved to center field and won a second MVP in 1989, one of three players to win it at two positions.
Coach Larry Haney said he'd seen only a couple of players in 19 years who never dogged it, and Yount was one of them. He got his 3,000th hit in 1992.
He was co-MVP of his league and Los Angeles City player of the year, hitting .455. Milwaukee drafted him on scout Gordon Goldsberry's recommendation days after he graduated.
In 1975 he broke Mel Ott's record for most games played before turning 20.
In his first big-league spring he was briefly reunited with his brother Larry, whom the Brewers acquired that March.
After Peter Seitz's free-agency ruling he threatened to play a season without a contract to test his value, then signed in late April.

In 1978 he was also struggling with foot tendinitis and a sore elbow. That May he signed for five years and more than $2.3 million, up from $80,000, in a deal negotiated by his brother Larry, by then a real estate developer.
He had two four-hit games in the 1982 World Series, the only player to do that, but Milwaukee lost to St. Louis.

After 1989 the Angels were ready to make a serious offer, but he re-signed with Milwaukee for three years and $9.6 million. A kidney stone in 1991 sent him to the disabled list for only the second time.
He coached for Arizona from 2002 to 2004 and quit when Bob Brenly was fired. He later was Milwaukee's bench coach under Ned Yost and then Dale Sveum.
p: His father was an aerospace engineer at Rocketdyne. Robin took up golf at 9 and motorcycle racing at 11, and kept at both all his life.
He met his wife at Taft High School. His brother Larry was officially sent in to pitch for Houston in 1971 but hurt his elbow warming up and never threw a pitch in the majors.
In 2008 he launched an all-natural lemonade called Robinade. Hunting in Arizona in 2012, he accidentally hit his friend and former teammate Dale Sveum with shotgun pellets.
He married Michele Edelstein in 1979. They had four children, Melissa, Amy, Dustin and Jenna; Dustin played in the minors.
He threw out the first pitch at Game 1 of the 2026 World Series between Milwaukee and Tampa Bay.

c: In a fog-shortened Cape Cod League game in 2004 he struck out 12 in four innings. His slider hit several batters on the back foot as they swung through strike three, and nobody was sure whether they were out or hit by pitches. The game never counted.
A potential first overall pick, he went sixth to Detroit in 2006, then was part of the trade for Miguel Cabrera. In 66 starts with Detroit and Florida he had a 5.70 ERA.

After Boston non-tendered him, Terry Francona said he "must have made 15 calls that winter" to get him back, convinced his mechanics were fixable. Moved to the bullpen for good in 2012, he held left-handed hitters to .149 that year.
Playing catch in the Boston bullpen, Edward Mujica suggested he keep his back foot on the rubber as long as possible, and it helped his delivery.

Reunited with Francona in Cleveland in 2016, he pitched anywhere from the fifth inning on. That year he became the first pitcher with 120 strikeouts and fewer than 10 walks in a season. He struck out 10 of 12 Blue Jays in his first two ALCS outings and was the series MVP.
At North Carolina he pitched in the 2006 College World Series, where the Tar Heels finished second to Oregon State. Detroit gave him a $3.55 million bonus.

In December 2007 Detroit traded him, Cameron Maybin and four others to Florida for Miguel Cabrera and Dontrelle Willis. With the Marlins he had knee tendinitis and an oblique injury. In 2010 they traded him to Boston for Dustin Richardson.
In July 2013 he tore ligaments in his foot covering home plate and missed Boston's World Series run, but got a ring.

Boston traded him to Baltimore in July 2014 for Eduardo Rodríguez. That winter he signed with the Yankees for four years and $36 million. Late in spring training a liner broke his pisiform bone, and he pitched with it: "according to Wikipedia, it's not really an important bone."

The Yankees traded him to Cleveland in July 2016 for Clint Frazier, Justus Sheffield and two others. He was ALCS MVP with 14 strikeouts in 7⅔ scoreless innings, and set postseason records for relievers with 30 strikeouts and 17 straight scoreless innings before Dexter Fowler homered in the World Series.
He helped Team USA win its first World Baseball Classic in 2017 and pitched in seven straight postseasons.
p: His father was an accountant and real estate developer, his mother a pediatric nurse practitioner. His uncle Dan was an NFL and USFL kicker.
He married Katie Roark, a fellow Gainesville native who played soccer at Duke. North Carolina retired his number 33 in 2016.
After retiring in 2022 he went to work for the players' union.
He and Katie have a son, born in 2012.

c: A minor-league manager told him: "Go get a lunch pail, son. You're never going to make it in this game." In 1950, replacing the beloved Ken Keltner, he hit 37 homers, a rookie record then, to lead the league.
An expert boxer, he once walked over to the White Sox dugout after someone called him a Jew bastard and asked whoever said it to step forward. No one did.
When Ed Sullivan wrote that Rosen was Catholic because he drew a cross on home plate, Rosen said it was an X and wished his name were "more Jewish."

On his last at-bat of 1953, needing a hit for the Triple Crown, he was called out on a close play at first. The umpire said he'd missed the bag, and Rosen agreed. He still won the MVP unanimously, the first since Hank Greenberg in 1935.

He retired at 32 after Greenberg, his boyhood idol and now his general manager, wanted to cut his salary again. Years later, as Yankees president in 1978, he replaced Billy Martin with Bob Lemon, and the Yankees won the World Series.
He started at Thomasville, North Carolina, the lowest level in the minors, for $90 a month. His high school football coach once asked why he was trying out when he was Jewish.
The Indians had him added to the 1948 World Series roster after he played just five games that season.
He went 0-for-1 as a pinch hitter in 1948 and 3-for-14 across his two World Series.

In 1950 he hit 37 home runs, the most ever by an American League rookie, and four grand slams, a team record until Travis Hafner in 2006. He hit two straight homers in an All-Star Game while playing with a broken finger and was the game's MVP.

Cleveland cut his salary from $42,500 to $37,500 for 1955, though he'd had five straight 100-RBI seasons. He broke a finger when they switched him to first base, and a rear-end car crash hurt his back.
He spent 17 years as a stockbroker in Cleveland, managing Bache and Company's office, then went to work for Caesars Palace in 1973.

As Yankees president he and Billy Martin made a pact to stand together against Steinbrenner, but after Martin's "one's a born liar" remark, Martin was out. Rosen quit in July 1979 when Steinbrenner took baseball decisions away from him.
At Bally's in Atlantic City he authorized a $2.5 million loan to four casinos that had been defrauded in a scam. Five people were arrested; he wasn't, but admitted bad judgment.

He replaced Tal Smith as Astros president in 1980, though Smith had just been named Executive of the Year, and then needed open-heart surgery. In 1985 he took over the last-place Giants and built them into a pennant winner that Oakland swept in the World Series.
p: He was a sickly asthmatic as a boy. His family moved to Miami, where they were the only Jewish family in a rough neighborhood and he fought a lot. His high school football coach asked him why a Jew was going out for football.
He piloted an assault boat in the first landing on Okinawa.
In 1971 his wife Terry fell to her death from a Philadelphia hotel under mysterious circumstances.
Born on February 29, at 80: "By all rights, I'm only going to be 20. Heck, I'm not even legal yet."
His father deserted the family. His mother sold dresses, and his grandmother looked after him and his brother Jerry.
He and Terry had three sons. He later married Rita Kallman and gained a stepson and stepdaughter. He died in Rancho Mirage in 2015.
In 1979 he did a Miller Lite commercial in which two baseball executives at a stuffy club turn out to be trading baseball cards.

c: He broke his leg playing basketball as a high school senior and missed baseball season, so he worked out, put on weight and got stronger. The Giants, his hero Willie Mays's team, drafted him. Traded to Cincinnati in 1971, he was crushed: the Giants were in first, the Reds near the bottom.

Sent back to Triple-A in 1973, he roomed with Ken Griffey, who helped him relax. That year he found his faith, gave up alcohol and tobacco, and came back a new hitter. Sparky Anderson: "When George gets into a pitch, no one hits a ball harder than he does."
He swung a big black 35-ounce bat and joked that he'd integrated the bat rack.

In Game 6 of the 1975 World Series he threw out the potential winning run at the plate in the ninth. In the 12th he caught Carlton Fisk's home run ball after it bounced off the foul pole and kept it. It sold at auction in 1999 for more than $100,000.

After losing the 1976 MVP to teammate Joe Morgan he said he should have won it, then regretted saying so. In 1977 he hit 52 homers and won it, the most homers since Mays in 1965 and the last 50-homer season until 1990.

In 1986 he was quoted suggesting the Mets would rather promote white stars than Black ones like Darryl Strawberry and Dwight Gooden. He said he'd been taken out of context. The Mets released him the day the story ran.
Giants scout Jack French saw him in a fall league. After a year at El Camino College he was a third-round pick in 1968. In San Francisco he roomed with Bobby Bonds, who mentored him.
On May 29, 1971, the Giants traded him to the Reds for Frank Duffy and Vern Geishert, a vastly one-sided deal. He started in center because Bobby Tolan had torn his Achilles.
As a pinch runner in Game 5 of the 1972 NLCS, he scored the pennant-winning run on a Bob Moose wild pitch. He didn't bat in that World Series.
Ted Kluszewski worked with him on inside pitches. He hit .364 in the 1975 NLCS. Sparky Anderson: "Having George in left field made the difference."

In February 1982 the Reds traded him to the Mets, who gave him five years and $10 million, the biggest contract in the NL. He hit 13 homers that year. The Mets released him in 1986, and he finished with the White Sox, homering in his first game.
p: As a small boy in Alabama he picked cotton. A columnist: "It is against George Foster's convictions to smoke, drink, chew, curse or leave men on base."
He honeymooned on a 1977 exhibition tour of Japan, where he was voted tour MVP.
A Dayton writer called him "the greatest person in baseball." Asked to lend his name to a group for underprivileged kids, Foster said: "No, you'll have more than my name. I'll be there too."
He married Sheila Roberts on November 3, after his MVP season, and they had two daughters.
He runs a nonprofit for children of military families and inner-city kids, and sponsors Foster's Force, a Cincinnati select team.

c: He grew up in Mascouche, near Montreal, playing baseball and hockey. At junior college in Oklahoma he learned English mostly by watching the sitcom Kenan & Kel.
After struggling as a starter, he moved to closer in 2002. When he came in at Dodger Stadium, "Game Over" flashed on the scoreboard while "Welcome to the Jungle" played.
In 2003 he went 55-for-55 in saves and won the Cy Young, the only pitcher to win it with a losing record (2–3). He converted 84 straight save chances, a major-league record.
His changeup had the same arm speed and release as his fastball. Writer Dan Habib called it "a bowling ball rolled off a picnic table."

The 2007 Mitchell Report named him as an HGH buyer. In 2009: "I have to live with this for the rest of my life. I'm going to have to explain this to my kids." A year later he admitted using it to recover from a knee injury.
He went to the same Montreal high school as Russell Martin. The White Sox drafted him in the 30th round in 1994, but he signed with the Dodgers in 1995 and had Tommy John surgery in 1997.
In arbitration he asked for $8 million, up from $550,000, and settled for $5 million.
In 2005 surgeons opening his elbow for Tommy John found a trapped nerve instead. More nerve surgery followed in 2006, and then back surgery for two herniated disks.

He signed with Texas in 2007, was traded to Boston that July, and pitched a perfect ninth in Game 1 of the World Series. Days after signing with Milwaukee for $10 million he was named in the Mitchell Report.
In 2010 he admitted using HGH, saying it was to recover from a knee injury.
He coached and pitched for the Québec Capitales and helped win the 2009 title. He later coached in the Rangers' system.
p: His father coached his Little League teams. He grew up an Expos and Canadiens fan. His father's cousin Paul Gagné played in the NHL.
He later coached France's national team, and pitched for and co-owned teams in Quebec's independent leagues.
He was married to Valerie Hervieux, and they have four children.
In July 2020 he was involved in several hit-and-run crashes in Terrebonne, Quebec, and police reportedly caught him after he fled.

c: At his first camp in 1944 the homesick 17-year-old, who had forgotten to bring a coat, sulked instead of running laps. Then he apologized and hit a long three-run homer against West Point. Branch Rickey raved about the "steel springs in his legs."
He refused to sign the 1947 petition against Jackie Robinson, and he ate with Robinson and kidded with him around the batting cage to ease the strain.
Rickey and George Sisler spent the spring of 1948 teaching him the strike zone. "Without (Rickey), I would never have made it."

His teammates thought he was a crybaby, and even Pee Wee Reese told him to grow up. In 1955 he called Brooklyn's fans the worst in the league and insisted he be quoted. They booed him harder than ever the next day, and he answered with three hits.

He hit four homers in both the 1952 and 1955 World Series, the first to do it twice, and was the last player to homer at Ebbets Field. The song "Talkin' Baseball" made him one-third of "Willie, Mickey, and the Duke."
The Dodgers signed him for a $750 bonus and $250 a month. Pittsburgh later offered $15,000, but he honored his contract.
In Montreal in 1948 manager Hopper fined him for missing a sign and scolded him for insolence. In 1949 Shotton made him the everyday center fielder.
When Bobby Thomson's homer won the 1951 pennant, Snider dropped to one knee and slammed his glove on the ground. After the season he asked to be traded.
After hitting .277 in 1951 he was roundly criticized, and told Walter O'Malley he couldn't take the pressure.

More than 50 newspaper articles once called him a brat for complaining about travel, time away from his family and abuse from fans, and for wanting to quit to grow avocados with his partner, ex-catcher Cliff Dapper.

He twisted his knee on a wooden sprinkler cover at Yankee Stadium during a World Series and played Game 7 anyway, and later had knee surgery. In 1958 a spring car accident, a back injury and an arm strain held him to 106 games.

In 1962 he and Leo Durocher reportedly begged Walter Alston to bring in Don Drysdale in the ninth of the deciding playoff game against the Giants. He was sold to the Mets, and Drysdale, his roommate, reportedly cried. He finished with the Giants in 1964.
He broadcast for the Padres and then the Expos from 1973 to 1986. In 2017 President Obama pardoned him and McCovey.
p: His father nicknamed him Duke for his self-assured swagger. At Compton High he threw a 63-yard touchdown pass and was the top scorer on a basketball team with future NFL commissioner Pete Rozelle.
He married his high school sweetheart, Beverly Null, in 1947. They raised four children and had an avocado ranch in Fallbrook, California.
In 1995 he and Willie McCovey pleaded guilty to tax charges for not reporting card-show income. He got two years' probation and said he'd made the wrong choice.
He played himself on Father Knows Best and turned up on The Rifleman.
Their four children were Pam, Kurt, Kevin and Dawna. In Los Angeles he had a daily radio show and the team's top salary, $46,000.
He died in 2011 at 84, the last living Brooklyn Dodger who was on the field for the final out of the 1955 World Series.

c: His high school coach made him run a sprint for every bad pitch he swung at. "Some days it was like puking out there." Before he was "the Big Hurt" he was "the big boomer."
He went to Auburn on a football scholarship to play tight end. Pat Dye let him skip spring practice for baseball, then kept him on the scholarship just to play baseball.
In the on-deck circle he swung a three-foot piece of rebar weighing about four pounds. Teammate Steve Lyons: "Frank is too big to be a man and too small to be a horse."
From 1991 to 1997 he hit .300 with 100 walks, 100 runs, 100 RBIs and 20 homers every year, something no one else has done for seven straight seasons. He won MVPs in 1993 and 1994.
He was the only active player who agreed to meet with George Mitchell for his steroid report: "I had nothing to hide."

After a bitter exit from Chicago, he came back with Oakland in 2006, got a three-minute standing ovation, and homered twice. He hit his 500th in 2007 and in 2014 went into the Hall of Fame on the first ballot.
Nobody drafted him out of high school in 1986. He played in the Pan Am Games, came back to Auburn for football and was hurt twice, and Auburn kept funding him as a baseball player.
The White Sox drafted him seventh overall in 1989.
White Sox hitting coach Walt Hriniak became his hitting guru, and broadcaster Hawk Harrelson named him "the Big Hurt."
His first three-year, $4.3 million contract was a bargain that caused bad feelings. Later he signed for $43 million through 2000, second only to Barry Bonds.
The rebar he swung on deck reportedly came from a renovation at old Comiskey Park.
He tore a triceps in 2001, the same week his father died. He broke a bone in his foot in 2005 and missed the White Sox' World Series title. He retired on a one-day White Sox contract in 2010.
p: His 2-year-old sister Pamela died of leukemia on Thanksgiving Day 1977, when he was 9. "From that point forward, she has stuck with me every day of my life." He charged a dollar for autographs and gave the money to leukemia research.
His father, a church deacon, preached: put God, family and education first; see the ball and swing at strikes; clean your plate. Frank wore size 14 shoes at 14.
In 1999 his divorce, the deaths of his friend Derrick Thomas and his agent, and his father's kidney failure left him "at rock bottom." His father died in 2001 the same week Frank tore his triceps.
His mother filled orders at Fieldcrest Mills. His father was a bail bondsman, an animal catcher and a liquor-truck driver. His siblings chipped in to buy shoes for his growing feet.
He charged $1 for autographs and matched it for the Leukemia Society, and gave $45,000 to the society and the fund for Rod Carew's daughter Michelle.
When a strike gave him unexpected time off, he stayed home with his wife, Elise, and their children, Sloan and Sterling.

c: At 6-foot-1 and 170 pounds he got no college scholarship offers; even USC backed out. After a year at Rio Hondo Community College, Long Beach State took him. Troy Tulowitzki already had shortstop, so he moved to third.
On the last night of 2011, with Tampa Bay nine games back earlier that month, his 12th-inning homer beat the Yankees and put the Rays in the playoffs as Boston collapsed.
He reached the World Series as a rookie in 2008 and again with Arizona in 2023, 15 years apart, the longest gap for a position player.
In a commercial for MLB 2K10 he broke up a perfect game with a homer. That August he broke up Brandon Morrow's no-hitter with two outs in the ninth.
Tampa Bay gave him a $3 million bonus. He was the 2007 MVP at Double-A Montgomery.
Days after his April 2008 call-up the Rays signed him for six years and $17.5 million plus options, considered one of the most team-friendly deals in baseball. He broke his wrist that August.
He homered in his first two postseason at-bats, the first rookie to do it, and set a rookie record with four homers in a series.
A partially torn hamstring in 2012 put him on the 60-day list. That November he got a six-year, $100 million extension.
The Rays traded him to the Giants in December 2017. He broke a bone in his left hand in 2018. He finished with Arizona in 2023 on a $4 million deal.
p: He was teased endlessly about actress Eva Longoria, no relation. When he made the 2008 All-Star team she sent him champagne for "doing the Longoria name proud," and he sent her three signed jerseys.
A self-taught drummer, he kept a drum kit at Tropicana Field and owns a drumhead signed by Rush.
In a 2011 viral video he barehanded a foul ball flying at a reporter's head. Ten years later he admitted it was staged.
In 2011 burglars took an estimated $56,000 from the Port Charlotte rental house he shared with David Price and Reid Brignac.
He married Edmondson on December 31, 2015, and owns Ducky's, a South Tampa restaurant.

c: He turned down $850,000 from the Dodgers out of high school to go to UCLA, which moved him from shortstop to second because of his arm.
His first big-league hit, in his first start in 2003, was a grand slam.
He tied the record with five home runs in the 2009 World Series. His seven career World Series homers are the most by a second baseman.

He was famous for his preparation in the video room and cage, and criticized for hard slides. In the 2015 playoffs his slide broke Mets shortstop Rubén Tejada's leg. When Noah Syndergaard threw at him the next May, he hit a homer and a grand slam that night.
He was hit by 200 pitches in his career, one of eight players to reach that.
The Phillies took him 15th in 2000 and signed him for $1.78 million. Their scouting director called him a mix of Jeff Kent and Adam Kennedy.
On January 21, 2007, the day after his wedding, he signed a seven-year, $85 million extension. That July a John Lannan pitch broke a bone in his right hand.

At the 2008 championship parade he cursed into the microphone after calling the Phillies "world champions," and it went out live on Philadelphia TV with no tape delay. He had hip surgery that November.
In Game 1 of the 2009 World Series he hit two homers off CC Sabathia, the second left-handed hitter after Babe Ruth with two homers off a lefty in a Series game.

The Phillies traded him to the Dodgers in August 2015. MLB suspended him two games for the slide that broke Rubén Tejada's leg, then dropped the suspension. In 2016 Noah Syndergaard threw behind him, and Utley answered with a solo homer and a grand slam in the same game.
p: He and his wife Jennifer, whom he met at UCLA, raised money for the Pennsylvania SPCA and championed rescue pit bulls.
Dave Roberts said his pressed white shirts and European-cut pants reminded him of James Bond. He has played himself on It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia.
In 2022 the family moved to London when he became MLB's ambassador to Europe.
He and Jennifer married in January 2007 and have two children. They raised more than $45,000 for the Pennsylvania SPCA.

c: As a boy he paid his younger brothers in cookies to toss him rocks to hit with a broomstick. An uncle nicknamed him "the Hawk" for the way he attacked ground balls.
Knee injuries in high school kept scouts and college recruiters away, so he took out student loans and walked on at Florida A&M.

Montreal's artificial turf wore down his knees and pushed him from center to right. In 1987, with the owners colluding against free agents, he and his agent handed the Cubs a blank contract and told them to fill in the salary. "I had taken back control of my own life."
That July Eric Show hit him in the face with a pitch after he'd homered. Dawson needed 21 stitches. He finished with 49 homers and was the first MVP from a last-place team.
He went into the Hall of Fame in 2010 in an Expos cap, against his wishes. He asked the Hall to change it, and in 2026 it agreed to recast his plaque with a blank cap.
He tore cartilage and ligaments in his knee playing high school football in 1971, the first of many knee surgeries. Montreal drafted him in the 11th round in 1975.
In 1981 he hit .300 in the Division Series win over the Phillies, but .150 as the Dodgers won the NLCS. The Expos never made the playoffs again.
The Cubs paid him $500,000 for his blank contract, second-lowest among their regulars, plus bonuses but no clause for an NL MVP award.
By then he'd had eight knee surgeries and wanted natural grass. If the Cubs had said no, he might have gone to Japan, which Vanessa was wary of.
He dedicated 1987 to his grandmother, Eunice Taylor, who had died early that year. After Eric Show hit him, Rick Sutcliffe charged out of the dugout after Show.
He went 2-for-19 in the 1989 NLCS loss to the Giants, his last postseason. At the 1991 All-Star Game he homered off Roger Clemens into the SkyDome restaurant windows, more than 450 feet away.
A knee injury on a passed ball in 1993 made him a DH in Boston, and another knee surgery came in 1994. He won a ring in 2003 in the Marlins' front office.
p: His father was often away, so as the oldest of eight he looked after his siblings while his mother worked.
He owns a funeral home in Richmond Heights, Florida, where his wife Vanessa runs the office. During the pandemic: "people mourn and grieve differently, and they're not getting through that process."
His father was in the Army and often away.
He married Vanessa Turner in 1978. Their son Darius was born in 1989 and daughter Amber in 1990.

He invested in his younger brother's funeral home in 2003 and took over Paradise Memorial in 2008. He also owned a Miami Gardens soul-food restaurant, The Mahogany Grille, and wrote a 2012 autobiography.

c: He was a catcher in high school and idolized Manny Sanguillen and Gale Sayers. His football coach arranged for Sayers to visit him in the hospital after an injury. He signed with Kansas City for $90,000, and part of the bonus paid his mother's bills.
Dwight Evans: "I always hope he hits the ball to left so I can watch him run." He hit 13 inside-the-park home runs, and in 1980 he was the first player with 700 at-bats.
He struck out 12 times in the 1980 World Series, including on the final pitch. "It went from the highest high beating the Yankees in New York to the lowest low."

To protect his lead in the 1982 batting race, he sat out the last day, and the Royals and Billy Martin's A's stalled on the field until word came that Robin Yount had been hit by a pitch. Wilson won by .0009.
After the 1983 season he pleaded guilty to attempting to buy cocaine and was sentenced to jail. He came back to lead the Royals with 11 hits in their 1985 World Series win.
He signed a letter of intent to play football at Maryland, but the Royals drafted him in the first round in 1974. He signed for $90,000, some of which paid his unemployed mother's bills.
In Dominican winter ball he improved his hitting working with Licey teammate Manny Mota. An injury to Al Cowens in May 1979 made him a regular.
His 12 strikeouts in the 1980 World Series broke the record, and stood until Ryan Howard struck out 13 in 2009.
In July 1983 police questioned him after his voice turned up on a wiretap of a call to his cocaine supplier.

After the 1983 season he, Willie Aikens, Vida Blue and Jerry Martin pleaded guilty to attempting to buy cocaine, and became the first active major leaguers to serve jail time. Bowie Kuhn suspended him for 1984, but on appeal he returned May 15.
The Royals traded or released the other three. Owner Ewing Kauffman stood by Wilson.

He hit .310 in the 1985 ALCS and .367 in the World Series against St. Louis. He later coached in the Blue Jays' system and managed the London Monarchs of the Canadian Baseball League, which folded in 2003.
p: He was raised by his grandmother in Montgomery through first grade, then took a long bus ride to New Jersey and met his mother for the first time.
Bankrupt by 2001 after bad investments, he had to auction off his memorabilia, including his World Series ring. In 2014 about 100 friends paid to recast the ring and surprised him with it.
His mother remarried, and the family settled in Summit, New Jersey; she and his stepfather later divorced. Willie spent summers working on the family farm in Alabama.
He and his wife, Kathy, had a daughter, Shanice, in 1979 and a son, Donnel, in 1983. They separated in 1984 and divorced in 1987.

c: He didn't join a baseball team until 15, as a first baseman, until a coach noticed his arm. After a failed attempt to defect in 2008 he had to meet Raúl Castro, who suspended him and kept him off the Olympic team. In 2009 he walked away from Cuba's team in Rotterdam.
In his big-league debut in 2010 his first pitch was a 98-mph strike. A month later he threw 105.8 mph, later certified as the fastest pitch in MLB history.

In spring training in 2014 a Salvador Pérez line drive fractured his skull above the left eye, and doctors put a metal plate in his head. That July he set a record for consecutive relief appearances with a strikeout; the streak reached 49.
In 2015 he was accused of choking his girlfriend and firing eight gunshots. No charges were filed, but he became the first player suspended under MLB's new domestic violence policy, for 30 games.
He won Game 7 of the 2016 World Series for the Cubs, and another ring with Texas in 2023. In 2026 he passed Hoyt Wilhelm for the most strikeouts by a reliever.

After his failed 2008 defection Raúl Castro kept him out of the Olympics but let him back for the 2009 World Baseball Classic. After defecting he established residency in Andorra to become a free agent, and in 2010 signed with Cincinnati for six years and $30.25 million.
In 2012 he was sued by a man who claimed Chapman had been a government informant after his failed defection and had helped turn him in, to get back on Cuba's national team.

The domestic-violence report killed a pending trade to the Dodgers; three weeks later Cincinnati sent him to the Yankees instead. In July 2016 the Yankees traded him to the Cubs for Gleyber Torres and three others.
After the 2016 title he re-signed with the Yankees for five years and $86 million, then the biggest deal for a reliever. José Altuve's walk-off homer off him ended New York's 2019 season.

In 2022 he lost the closer job, went on the injured list with an infection from a tattoo, and was left off the playoff roster after skipping a workout. He then pitched for Kansas City, Texas, Pittsburgh and Boston.
p: His father was a boxing trainer. His grandparents came to Cuba from Jamaica, which made him eligible for Great Britain's team.
When he defected he left behind his parents, two sisters, his girlfriend and a newborn child, and later helped them all come to the United States. He became a citizen in 2016.
His father was a boxing trainer who later worked for the city. His son was born in Cincinnati in 2014.

c: At 18 months old he was on local TV showing off a "picture perfect" golf swing. In high school in Alabama he was the state's Gatorade Player of the Year and set a football record with 11 interceptions.
He came up as a catcher and hit a home run on the first pitch for his first big-league hit, in 2010. Oakland moved him to third base.
Traded to Toronto, he lost his salary arbitration case, then drew the most fan votes for the 2015 All-Star Game and won the MVP.
He got the nickname "The Bringer of Rain" from an episode of Spartacus, and played a character on Vikings.
In 2022 he was suspended a game for calling Tim Anderson "Jackie."
At Faith Academy he hit .515 and set a school record with 11 interceptions in football. At Auburn he played third and learned to catch.
The Cubs drafted him 48th as a catcher in 2007, then traded him to Oakland in July 2008 for Rich Harden in a six-player deal.
Oakland traded him to Toronto in November 2014 for Brett Lawrie and three prospects. Fans gave him a record 14 million All-Star votes in 2015, in a campaign backed by Don Cherry.
He was traded to Cleveland in 2018, signed with Atlanta for 2019 and Minnesota in 2020, went to the Yankees in 2022, was released in 2023, and finished with Milwaukee.
p: His father was in prison for most of his childhood. He saw his son play in person for the first time in 2013, and Donaldson homered and doubled that day.
A lifelong golfer, he once hit a 309-yard drive in a simulator on Golf Channel.
His father, a construction worker, was sentenced in 1992 for sexual battery, false imprisonment and aggravated battery, and was released in 2007. His mother raised him.
He and his fiancée, Briana Miller, had a daughter in 2020 and married in January 2024.

c: His father, a high school coach, would poke his head into the room after dinner, and Albert and his twin brother would jog to the junior high field with Dad driving behind them, to hit hundreds of balls into the night.

At LSU in 1987 he went after a fan shouting racial slurs and was suspended for the College World Series. In 1991 he fired a ball from 15 feet into the chest of a fan who'd shouted "Hey Joey, keg party at my house."
After his 1990 stay in alcohol rehab he stopped going by "Joey" and went back to his given name, Albert.

When umpires impounded his bat for cork in Chicago in 1994, pitcher Jason Grimsley crawled through the ceiling ducts into the umpires' room and swapped it, but he had to use Paul Sorrento's bat because, teammates said, all of Belle's were corked.
In 1995 he became the only player with 50 homers and 50 doubles in a season, in just 144 games. He lost the MVP to Mo Vaughn by one first-place vote and suggested writers shouldn't vote at all.
That Halloween he chased down neighborhood kids who had egged his house in his truck and was convicted of reckless driving. An arthritic hip ended his career in 2001.
At LSU two teammates had to tackle him in the stands, and coach Skip Bertman suspended him for the College World Series.
The Indians sent him to the Cleveland Clinic for two months of alcohol rehab in 1990.
Indians people said Grimsley had to swap in a Paul Sorrento bat because all of Belle's were corked. His suspension was cut from 10 games to seven.

During the 1995 World Series he cursed out reporters in the dugout. He smashed postgame buffets and once took a bat to Kenny Lofton's boombox. In 1996 he was fined for leveling Fernando Viña on the basepaths.
The White Sox gave him five years and $55 million with a clause keeping him among the three highest-paid players. He invoked it after 1998 and signed with Baltimore for five years and $65 million.
The Tribune's White Sox writer said he once cursed out a broadcaster for coming into the trainer's room to get an aspirin.
After his hip gave out, Baltimore kept him on its 40-man roster for three more years as a condition of the insurance policy that reimbursed most of his contract.
p: His mother: "He could spell backwards when he was five. Did you know my Joey was an Eagle Scout?" He finished sixth in his high school class and took French.
His twin brother Terry, who had an MBA, tried to advise him on public relations. Terry died after a car accident in 2011.
Mellowed in retirement, he lives near Phoenix with his wife and three daughters. He skipped his 2016 Indians Hall of Fame induction, citing family commitments.
His mother was a math teacher. In high school he was in the National Honor Society and vice president of the local Future Business Leaders of America.

The guardian of the teenager his truck chased sued him for $850,000, claiming the truck bumped the boy; it settled in 1997. In 2006 he got 90 days in jail and five years' probation for stalking his former girlfriend. In 2018 he was arrested in Scottsdale for indecent exposure and drunk driving.
In 2005 he married Melissa Galus, a former TV reporter.

c: A shoulder injury his senior year dropped him to the seventh round of the 1988 draft, where the Angels took him. His father lived a few miles from Anaheim Stadium.
On June 10, 1997, in Kansas City, he ran straight back and dove headfirst for a ball over his head, making the catch on the warning track. It's considered one of the greatest catches ever.
In 1998 some Angels teammates criticized his nonchalance about losing the division. He said he wasn't "going to come in the next day and want to kill himself."

Traded to St. Louis in 2000, five days after being told he wouldn't be. In Game 6 of the 2004 NLCS he won it with a 12th-inning homer, then made a spectacular catch in Game 7. With Pujols and Rolen he was one of the "MV3."
In 2006 he crashed into a wall in Chicago and was later diagnosed with post-concussion syndrome, then helped the Cardinals win the World Series that fall. He won eight Gold Gloves in all.
He got regular time in left after Bo Jackson was benched. Groin and stomach injuries once sidelined him for a month.
In 1999 spring training he tore the labrum in his right shoulder lifting weights and missed half the season. Newcomer Mo Vaughn accused him of not taking responsibility.

He was ejected in Game 4 of the 2004 NLCS for arguing balls and strikes. Two months after his 2006 crash he was diagnosed with post-concussion syndrome, but he played all 16 postseason games for the champions.

The Cardinals traded him to San Diego for David Freese in December 2007. The Padres released him in May 2008, hitting .178, and the Cubs signed him. After sitting out 2009 he played for Milwaukee and Cincinnati.
He opened Jim Edmonds 15 Steakhouse in 2007 with partner Mark Winfield, and later other restaurants that closed. He left the Cardinals' broadcasts before 2025.
p: Cardinals fans call him "Jimmy Baseball." He became a Cardinals TV analyst in 2013.
His first wife died of cancer in 2015. His third wife was on The Real Housewives of Orange County, and he appeared on the show.
His parents divorced when he was a boy and shared custody.

He had two daughters with Lee Ann Horton and a son and daughter in his second marriage, from 2008 to 2014. He married Meghan King in October 2014; they had a daughter and twin boys, and he filed for divorce the day after their fifth anniversary.

c: His spring break-in in 1972 came by accident: sent to a B game to fill out the outfield, he went 3-for-4, was rushed to Yuma to replace an injured outfielder and went 4-for-5, then won the next game too. He opened the season in right field.

Voted second among third basemen in 1975 and picked as a reserve, he turned down the All-Star Game: "I know I don't deserve it as much as some of the other guys." Manager Alvin Dark said he admired him more for it.
Graig Nettles, whose job he had taken in Cleveland, became the man he went to for advice on playing third. He won six straight Gold Gloves with Texas.

Traded home to Cincinnati in 1985, he wore number 25, his father's old Reds number. He retired in 1989 without fanfare: "My career was pretty much a secret to begin with, I might as well keep it that way." No one had played more games without reaching the postseason except Ernie Banks, Luke Appling and Mickey Vernon.
He and his sons went to Moeller High in Cincinnati, as did Ken Griffey Jr. and Barry Larkin. He credited his coach there, Tim Rose, more than his father for his fundamentals.
After 1978 Cleveland traded him to Texas for Toby Harrah. In 1985 the Reds got him to replace a Nick Esasky–Wayne Krenchicki platoon.

The Reds traded him to Houston in June 1988, and Houston released him that December. He finished with Texas and retired in June 1989. Only three players had played more games without reaching the postseason.

He coached for Cleveland in 1994 and 1995, while his son David played there. He managed Detroit, finishing second for Manager of the Year in 1997, then Colorado, which fired him after a 6–16 start in 2002, and Kansas City.
He managed the American team at the 1999 Pan American Games.
p: His father Gus, who got the first hit in Mets history, gave him the nickname to tell him apart from another David in the family. Gus said Buddy's high school coach taught him more than he did.
His sons David and Mike both reached the majors, making the Bells a three-generation family. When David became Reds manager in 2018, they became the fourth father-son pair of big-league managers.
His nephew, Marine Lance Cpl. Timothy Bell, was killed in Iraq in 2005. The next year Buddy was treated for throat cancer and came back to manage the Royals.
He was one of seven children. He and his wife had five: David, Michael, Ricky, Kristi and Traci.

c: He went to Michigan on a football scholarship. When he told Bo Schembechler he was quitting football, the coach pounded his desk, sent papers flying and shouted, "No one comes to the University of Michigan and plays stinkin' baseball!"
Sitting on the bench at the 1984 Olympics fueled him: "I remember that being the point in my life where I said, 'I just have to be better than everybody else.'"

He arrived for his 1986 debut 35 minutes before the game with no equipment. Pete Rose lent him his bat and spikes, then asked for them back after the game. Soon after, Larkin told Rose, "I'm the shortstop here for the next 15 years." It turned out to be 19.

He tore an elbow ligament in the relay-throw competition at the 1989 All-Star workout, and that helped end skills competitions at the game. He was also the first shortstop to hit 30 homers and steal 30 bases in a season.

He was 1995 MVP over Dante Bichette, which surprised him: "I thought the MVP would go to a guy like Dante Bichette because of the home runs... But I was wrong." He then re-signed with the Reds for less than he could have gotten.

Michigan, with future Reds Chris Sabo and Hal Morris, went to the College World Series in 1983 and 1984. Scout Gene Bennett recommended him, and the Reds took him fourth overall in 1985 to replace Dave Concepción.

He hit .353 as the Reds swept Oakland in the 1990 World Series, his only Series. After 1991 he questioned the team's commitment, but in January 1992 he signed for five years and $25.6 million, the most for any shortstop.
After his MVP he signed a three-year, $16.5 million extension, and was criticized for costing other players by taking less than the market.

Injuries limited him from 1997 to 2003. A 2003 contract dispute with the Reds kept him from working for them after he retired, so he joined the Nationals' front office. He managed Brazil in World Baseball Classic qualifying and joined Reds broadcasts in 2021.
p: When owner Marge Schott was suspended in 1993 for racial slurs, civic leaders asked him to lead protests. He wanted only to play, and got hate mail and death threats. That year he won the Roberto Clemente Award.
In 2020 he publicly asked why the MVP award still carried the name of Kenesaw Mountain Landis. The writers removed it that October.
His daughter Brielle D'Shea is named for Shea Stadium. His son Shane played in the NBA. In the offseason minor leaguers train with him in Orlando at what they call "B-Lark University."
He grew up in Silverton, Ohio, Roger Staubach's hometown, with siblings Robin, Michael, Byron and Stephen.
His brother Byron was an All-American basketball player at Xavier and became its radio commentator.
He won the 1993 Roberto Clemente Award for the Caring Program for Children, which paid needy kids' medical bills.

c: He didn't play high school baseball in New York, to concentrate on his studies and his English. A Twins scout, also a transit police officer, chased him around New York's sandlots: "a pair of wrists that exploded with the pitch."
Billy Martin taught him to run. In 1969 he stole home seven times, five of them in the first inning, one short of Ty Cobb's record. "Pitchers don't expect you to take a risk so early."
He won seven batting titles; only Cobb, Honus Wagner and Tony Gwynn won more. In 1977 he hit .388 and was over .400 into July, on the covers of Sports Illustrated and Time the same week.
When rosters were cut to 24 in 1986, no team offered him a job, even for less money, so he retired with 3,053 hits. In 2016 the American League named its batting title for him.

Bird-dog scout Monroe Katz, whose son played with Carew on the Bronx Cavaliers, tipped off Herb Stein. At his April 1964 tryout Sam Mele cut it short so the Yankees wouldn't see him. He signed at a Bronx restaurant that June for $400 a month.
Billy Martin, his 1969 manager, gave him what he called "meaningful, fatherly advice." The Twins were swept by Baltimore in the ALCS in 1969 and 1970.
On May 20, 1970, he hit for the Twins' first cycle. In June, hitting .374, he badly broke his left leg and needed surgery on cartilage and torn ligaments.
With free agency approaching and a veto over any trade, he was dealt to the Angels. California made the playoffs in 1979 and 1982 and lost the ALCS both times.
He was hitting coach for the Angels from 1992 and later for the Brewers, and has worked as an international youth instructor for MLB.
p: He was born on a segregated train in the Panama Canal Zone, in the rear car for non-white passengers. The doctor who delivered him was Rodney Cline, and that became his name.
His father was a violent alcoholic who beat him. Carew later said, "Baseball was the one thing that kept me from killing my father."

He married Marilynn Levy, who was Jewish and white, in 1970 and shrugged off the death threats. Their daughter Michelle died of leukemia after no bone marrow match was found, but his appeals added 500,000 people to the donor registry.
In 2016 he had a heart transplant. The heart came from former NFL player Konrad Reuland, who had died at 29.
His father, a sign painter along the Canal, beat his sons, and his mother wanted to get the children away from him. She went to New York and sent for them; Rod worked there as a grocery stock clerk.
In his memoir he said his father was a violent alcoholic who also beat his mother, and that Carew came close to killing him with a machete.
He and Marilynn had three daughters, Charryse, Stephanie and Michelle. Michelle was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia in 1995 and died the next April at 18.
Rod and Marilynn divorced after 26 years of marriage.
He chewed tobacco from 1964 until 1992, when a cancerous growth was removed from his mouth. In 2015 he had a heart attack and got a heart pump before his transplant. He married Rhonda Jones in 2001.
Konrad Reuland had met Carew at school when he was 11. Both wore 29.

c: He was on his way to buy a saxophone when he saw a baseball glove in a store window and bought that instead. At Orange High in New Jersey he won 16 varsity letters and set a state javelin record.

He played for the Newark Eagles under the name Jimmy Nelson to keep his amateur status. In Mexico in 1942 an owner ordered him to hit a home run; he did, and split the $500 reward with the opposing catcher, Roy Campanella. "For the first time in my life I felt really free."

Cool Papa Bell: "Most of the black ballplayers thought Monte Irvin should have been the first black in the major leagues." Three years in the Army took his prime: "I had been a .400 hitter before the war. I became a .300 hitter after the war."

He finally reached the Giants in 1949 at 30. In 1951 he led the league in RBIs, hit .458 in the World Series and stole home in Game 1. Campanella: "As great as he was in 1951, he was twice that good 10 years earlier."
In college he clashed with his coach and couldn't keep his athletic scholarship while studying pre-dentistry.
After hitting .401 in 1941, Effa Manley refused him a raise, so he took Jorge Pasquel's much bigger offer to play in Mexico, where he could go anywhere and eat in any restaurant.

He was drafted after the 1942 season despite his bad knee, a wife and a daughter. His all-Black engineers unit built roads and guarded German prisoners in England and France. He was demoted from sergeant to private on his last day for coming back an hour late.

Branch Rickey wanted him after the war, but Effa Manley demanded compensation and threatened to sue, so Rickey backed off. In 1946 he hit .462 with three homers as Newark beat Kansas City in the Negro World Series. The Giants bought him for $5,000 in 1949.
He broke his ankle sliding in spring training in 1952. He went 2-for-9 as the Giants swept Cleveland in 1954.
After retiring he worked for Rheingold beer and scouted for the Mets, then worked in the commissioner's office until Bowie Kuhn left in 1984.
p: On his senior prom night in 1937, a local restaurant refused to serve him and his friends because they were Black.
He couldn't afford to move to Ann Arbor to take a football scholarship at Michigan.

When Willie Mays came up in 1951, the Giants asked Irvin to mentor him. In 1968 he became baseball's first Black executive, in the commissioner's office. He was sent in Bowie Kuhn's place to see Hank Aaron's 715th home run.
His parents were Alabama sharecroppers who moved to New Jersey for their children's sake. He was the eighth of 13 children; his brother Cal also played in the Negro leagues.
He and his wife, Dee, had two daughters, Pamela and Patricia. He died in Houston in 2016 at 96, the oldest living former Negro leaguer.

c: A Parade All-America quarterback, he signed to play football at Washington State. The Phillies drafted him in the 20th round anyway. His brother Del, who had played in the College World Series, told him to sign if he really preferred baseball.

The Phillies saw him as a utility man and traded him to the Cubs with Larry Bowa in 1982. "At one point, I was just hoping to be a utility infielder." He started his rookie year with one hit in his first 36 plate appearances, at third base, before Chicago moved him to second.
Not knowing it was Ernie Banks's number, he asked for 14 his first spring. He was handed 23 instead.

On June 23, 1984, he homered off Bruce Sutter to tie the Cardinals in the ninth and again with two outs in the 10th. "The Sandberg Game" made him a national star. "It was the turning point of my career... it completely changed my life."

Manager Jim Frey asked him: "How come you're not more of a power hitter and not an MVP?" He won the MVP that season, and in 1990 led the league with 40 homers. He went 123 straight games without an error, a record, and won nine Gold Gloves.
