In June 1994 he retired suddenly, giving up about $15 million: "I lost the edge that it takes to play." He came back in 1996. At his 2005 Hall of Fame induction he took aim at the steroid era: "Respect for the game of baseball. It's something I hope we see again."
His high school passing record stood until future Super Bowl MVP Mark Rypien broke it, and one of his basketball rivals was John Stockton.

Phillies scouts Bill Harper and Moose Johnson talked Dallas Green into drafting him despite his football commitment. Harper offered $20,000, second- or third-round money, and Sandberg took it after a walk with his brother Del.
When Larry Bowa's contract talks broke down, the Cubs' Dallas Green insisted on Sandberg in the deal for Iván DeJesús. Phillies scouts had said he'd be no more than a utility man.
The Phillies had dangled him in trade talks for pitching since 1980, including a reported 3-for-1 offer to Milwaukee for Mike Caldwell.
In 1984 the Cubs won the East, their first playoff trip since 1945, and lost the NLCS to San Diego.
He coached in the minors for the Cubs and Phillies and managed the Phillies from mid-2013 until he resigned in 2015.
p: His father was a mortician and his mother a nurse. They named him after Yankees pitcher Ryne Duren. His father's advice: "Keep your mouth shut and eyes and ears open. Then you might learn something."
He married his high school sweetheart Cindy as a 19-year-old minor leaguer. They divorced in 1995, and he married Margaret Koehnemann.
After treatment for metastatic prostate cancer, he died in July 2025. Days later every Cubs player and manager Craig Counsell wore number 23.
His father, born in Fargo to a Swedish immigrant, worked long hours at a funeral home. His mother was born in the Belgian Congo, the daughter of a missionary. His brother Del was named for Del Ennis.
He and Cindy had two children, Lindsay and Justin.
He began treatment for metastatic prostate cancer in January 2024 and was declared cancer-free that August, but in December it came back and spread. He died at home in Lake Bluff, Illinois, at 65.

c: He grew up in South Central Los Angeles, where his father went to the playground with him to protect him; once they had to dive for cover from gunfire. He and Darryl Strawberry were friends and rivals at crosstown high schools.
Basketball was his first love. He didn't take baseball seriously until his senior year, when he hit .531 and stole 50 bases and the scouts started coming.
In 1986 he had 27 homers and 80 steals, and he and Rickey Henderson are the only members of the 20–80 club. In 1987 he became the first player to hit three grand slams in one month.

Diving for a ball in the final game of the 1990 World Series, he lacerated his kidney. Left in an Oakland hospital, he asked the Reds for a plane home. He was told, "He's making $3 million, let him get his own plane." He did, and sent them the bill.

After retiring with a neck injury, he came back in 1996 and was Comeback Player of the Year. In 1997 he had colon cancer surgery, then rejoined the Orioles in September while still getting chemotherapy.
Darryl Strawberry at Crenshaw drew more scouts than Davis at Fremont. The Reds took him in the eighth round in 1980. He was 6-foot-2 and only 165 pounds.

A Duane Walker hamstring injury got him his first call-up, and a knee injury sliding that July put him on the disabled list. Hitting coach Billy DeMars got him to shorten his swing and go with the pitch.
In 1987 he crashed into the Wrigley wall robbing Ryne Sandberg, hurt his ribs, missed 17 of the last 27 games and fell short of 40–40.

In 1988 a Cincinnati Enquirer story quoted an unnamed NL executive on rumors he used drugs. The Reds' GM flatly denied it. Having been accused of not playing hurt, he was now criticized for coming back too soon.

He homered off Dave Stewart in his first World Series at-bat in 1990. Hurt that winter and in 1991, he was traded to the Dodgers for Tim Belcher and John Wetteland, then to Detroit. He hit .183 in 1994 and retired.
He blamed 1996 Reds manager Ray Knight, with whom he'd brawled in 1986, for not backing his comeback. Back from colon cancer, he hit a game-winning homer in the 1997 ALCS.
p: Paul O'Neill called him "the best hitter, best runner, best outfielder, best everything" he ever saw.
He made a documentary, Harvard Park, about the crime-ridden neighborhood park where he and Strawberry grew up and the athletes it produced.
His father worked for the Boys Market grocery chain. He has an older brother and a younger sister.
He supported Boog Powell after Powell was diagnosed with colon cancer soon after him. He has worked as a roving instructor for the Reds.

c: At Denver in 1967 Billy Martin screamed at him in the dugout: "What the hell is wrong with your brain? Are you a dummy?" "The first month or so, I didn't like Billy. To be more precise; I hated him." He came to see Martin as an extraordinary leader, and they were together for 20 years.
Rumored to be unable to play third, he wrote "E-5" on the new glove he was breaking in. In 1971 he set records for assists and double plays by a third baseman.
In 1974 his bat broke on a single and the end flew off, revealing cork. "That was the first time I used it."

In Game 3 of the 1978 World Series he dove to rob the Dodgers again and again, with five assists, to keep Ron Guidry in the game. Reggie Smith: "It's Dodgers 2, Nettles 1." Nettles: "I'm not an overnight success."

He caught the final out of the 1978 playoff game at Fenway: "The toughest part of the play was not fainting." In 1984 the Yankees traded him to San Diego after his book Balls ripped George Steinbrenner.
Bird-dog scout Pete Coscarart recommended him, and the Twins took him in the fourth round in 1965.
In December 1969 the Twins traded him to Cleveland with Dean Chance for Luis Tiant. After a feud with manager Ken Aspromonte, Cleveland traded him to the Yankees for four young players.

In a 1976 brawl with Boston he tackled Bill Lee from behind and, after Lee said something about his sister, broke Lee's collarbone. He wasn't suspended. "It would have been worse if I had broken his jaw."
In 1977 he set career highs with 37 homers and 107 RBIs. In his last World Series with the Yankees he broke his thumb diving for a ball in Game 2.

His 1984 book with Peter Golenbock, Balls, blasted George Steinbrenner, and he was traded to his hometown Padres that March for Dennis Rasmussen. In San Diego he charged the mound after Donnie Moore beaned him on purpose.
He later played for Atlanta and Montreal, retired at 43, coached for the Yankees and Padres, and managed Bakersfield to a 39–101 record in 1996.
p: His mother didn't like Craig or Greg, so she combined them. His father was away at the war and had no say.
He went to San Diego State on a basketball scholarship and found his baseball power playing summer ball in Fairbanks, Alaska.
On Thurman Munson's death in 1979: "I broke down and cried like a baby. I thought we would be friends forever." In 1982 he succeeded Munson as Yankees captain.
Tommy John called him the team's pressure valve, "the guy with the acerbic wit who can take your mind off a bad situation."
His father, a San Diego police officer who became a high school teacher, was away at the war. He was the middle of three sons; his brother Jim also played in the majors.
He married Virginia Mechling, whom he met through a college teammate, on November 25, 1965. They had four children: Mike, Tim, Jeff and Barrie.
His son Michael has since died.
In 2008 he announced he had prostate cancer, which his brother had been diagnosed with the year before.

c: His father was in his third big-league season, with the Cardinals, when he was born, and he grew up in clubhouses. He practiced with Robinson Canó, also from San Pedro de Macorís.
The White Sox traded him to San Diego at 17 for James Shields before he'd played a pro game.
In 2020 he hit a grand slam on a 3–0 pitch with the Padres up seven runs, and set off a debate about baseball's unwritten rules.

In 2021 he signed for 14 years and $340 million, then led the league with 42 homers. He missed all of 2022 with a fractured scaphoid bone, possibly from a motorcycle accident (asked when it happened, he said, "Which one?"), and a drug suspension.
Moved to right field in 2023, he won a Gold Glove and led NL defenders in runs saved.
The White Sox signed him out of the Dominican Prospect League in 2015. He broke his left thumb in a headfirst slide in 2018, and a back injury ended his 2019 season.

His 2021 deal was the richest ever for a player not yet eligible for arbitration. On April 23, 2021, 22 years to the day after his father hit two grand slams in one inning, he hit two homers off Clayton Kershaw.
In August 2022 he was suspended 80 games after testing positive for clostebol. He said it came from ringworm medicine he didn't check, an explanation many doubted.
He hit two homers in Game 2 of the 2024 NLDS against the Dodgers as the Padres set a franchise postseason record with six.
p: At 22 he was the youngest cover athlete for MLB The Show. His younger brother Elijah also signed a pro contract.

c: His father, a bank executive and devoted Mickey Mantle fan, built a backyard batting cage, turned the right-handed Jason into a left-handed hitter, and taught him patience with Ted Williams's strike-zone chart. Jason wore 16 and 25 because the digits add up to Mantle's 7.
Mark McGwire was his mentor in Oakland: "He's the one who got me lifting." He won the 2000 MVP and had an even better 2001, leading the league in on-base percentage and OPS.

Signing with the Yankees, his father's team, in 2001, he said with tears in his eyes: "Look, Pop, it's not number 7, but it's pinstripes." He cut his hair and gave up his motorcycles to fit the Yankee code.

His 2003 grand jury testimony that he had used steroids became public. The Yankees tried to get rid of him and Yogi Berra didn't want him back. He apologized without using the word "steroids," won Comeback Player of the Year in 2005 ("That award meant as much to me as my MVP"), and in 2007 admitted it plainly.
In Colorado and Cleveland he became a mentor. Terry Francona: "I've never been around anybody who has his presence." At 42 he passed Hank Aaron as the oldest player to hit a walk-off homer.

At Long Beach State he went to the 1991 College World Series. He was one of Team USA's last cuts for the 1992 Olympics, but after signing with Oakland in the second round he was invited back to replace a slumping Ryan McGuire.
He couldn't handle left field and threatened to ask for a trade if made a full-time DH; José Canseco's problems in the field put him back out there.
He turned down Oakland's six-year, $91 million offer in 2001 because it had no no-trade guarantee, and lost the MVP to Ichiro despite leading the league in WAR.
The Yankees' rules made him cut his hair and give up hobbies like riding his custom motorcycle. In 2003 teams shifted on him, and the Yankees lost the World Series to Florida.

In 2004 a benign tumor put him on the disabled list, and he played so poorly he was left off the postseason roster. His leaked grand jury testimony said he had used steroids in the 2001–03 offseasons and injected himself with HGH in 2003. The lawyer who leaked it went to prison.
That summer he was sick and fatigued with a mysterious illness, and his weight loss raised suspicion; he blamed giving up fast food.
In 2007 he apologized specifically for using steroids, and the Mitchell Report named him and his brother Jeremy.
After the Yankees declined his option in 2008 he went back to Oakland, was released, and joined Colorado for the stretch drive.
p: As a young player he wore a T-shirt that read "Party Like a Rock Star, Hammer Like a Porn Star, Rake Like an All-Star." He said he'd once driven his Ferrari 170 mph: "If it sounds fun, I want to try it."
His high school team also produced his brother Jeremy, Cory Lidle, Aaron Small and Shawn Wooten. His nickname was "Gumby," which he put on his license plate.
"Some of us have to walk through the darkness to see the light. I did that."
He married Kristian in February 2002; she designs and owns a lingerie company. His brother Jeremy, his Oakland teammate, died in 2022.
He had a tattoo on his left arm of a skull melting in a blazing sun, which meant "Live life, taste death."

c: At 11 he traveled from Curaçao to Japan with a youth select team. He signed with Atlanta at 16, and in his first at-bat at Class-A Macon he homered.
In Game 1 of the 1996 World Series, at 19, he homered in his first two at-bats, breaking Mickey Mantle's record as the youngest to homer in the Series, on what would have been Mantle's 65th birthday.
His relaxed style once angered Bobby Cox enough to pull him mid-inning in 1998 for letting a single drop. He won ten straight Gold Gloves.
On Willie Mays's advice he widened his stance in 2005, and he led the league with 51 homers. He was elected to the Hall of Fame in 2026, the first from Curaçao.
His speed won him the last spot on Atlanta's 1996 playoff roster. He had been named minor league player of the year by USA Today and Baseball America.
He hit .222 in the 1996 NLCS and .273 with a homer in the 1998 NLCS against San Diego.
The Dodgers signed him for two years and $36.2 million after 2007. He was dropped to eighth in the order, had knee surgery, and was released with money deferred.
He played for Texas, the White Sox and the Yankees on cheap deals, then went to Japan with Rakuten in 2013 and helped win the Japan Series.
He managed the Netherlands at the 2026 World Baseball Classic.
p: He showed up to the Dodgers out of shape in 2008, then reported to the White Sox in 2010 thirty pounds lighter and hit his 400th homer.

He was arrested for battery on Christmas 2012; a police report alleged he put his hands around his wife's neck and threatened to kill her. He pleaded guilty and was placed on probation. The couple tried to reconcile, and supported a nonprofit for domestic violence survivors.
His son Druw was the second overall pick in the 2022 draft.
In 2001 he testified at the federal trial of an Atlanta club owner charged with facilitating prostitution.
Nicole filed for divorce in January 2013 but withdrew it, and they tried to reconcile. They later supported Jaden's Ladder, a nonprofit for domestic violence survivors.

c: A teacher noticed he could run faster backward than most kids ran forward. He found "my refuge in baseball," the only place he felt "worthy of measuring up." The White Sox signed him for $7,000 plus $3,000 under the table.
Called "the next Mickey Mantle" at 19, he hit .173 for the 1959 White Sox and was traded to the Phillies, where Gene Mauch made him his special project.
From 1962 through 1965 he had 90 assists from right field, more than any right fielder in the majors; Roberto Clemente had 59. In 1962 Mauch benched him on the last day to keep him at .300.

His three-run homer off Dick Radatz won the 1964 All-Star Game. He was asked about it so often he felt like Bill Murray in Groundhog Day. He hit well through the Phillies' collapse that fall and defended Mauch: "It wasn't all Gene's fault. We played!"
At 27 his power vanished, and nobody could say why: injuries, his eyes, glasses, his confidence. He had called himself "the biggest worrier around."
The White Sox signed him in 1957 for a $7,000 bonus plus $3,000 under the table and started him with his hometown Bakersfield team. He led the American Association with 29 homers in 1958.
He wasn't on the 1959 World Series roster, and that December the White Sox traded him to the Phillies for Gene Freese.
He got two first-place MVP votes in 1964; Ken Boyer won.
After 1969 the Phillies traded him to the Cubs, and after 1971 the Cubs sent him to the Yankees, where he finished in 1973 hitting .176.
In 1978 he was a player-coach for a pro slow-pitch softball team that played at Veterans Stadium.
p: His family were poor Oklahomans who moved to Bakersfield, California, during the war while his father was in the Army.
After baseball he sold cars and tended bar and never found a way back into the game. He was a regular at the Phillies' fantasy camps.
He married his high school sweetheart, Dianne Hammitt, while still in school. They raised three daughters, Lori, Cindy and Sherri, in Glenside, outside Philadelphia.
After baseball he had bad ulcers and a heart attack, and he died of cancer in 2006 at 67.

c: His mother was 14 when he was born, weighing about 3 pounds, and his blind grandmother Rosie raised him in East Chicago, Indiana. She taught him to throw. At his high school games, people sitting next to her told her what he was doing.

He played basketball at Arizona, filled in for an injured Steve Kerr, and was sixth man on the 1988 Final Four team. He only joined the baseball team as a junior, and turned down instructional league to finish his degree as he had promised his grandmother.
He could get from home to first in 3.1 seconds. As a rookie in 1992 he stole 66 bases, an AL rookie record, and led the league in steals the next four years.
In the final game of the 1995 ALCS in Seattle he scored from second base on a passed ball.
He played for 11 teams and in the postseason for six, and retired with a record 34 postseason steals.

His East Chicago high school also produced Tim Stoddard; they are the only two men to play in both a Final Four and a World Series. He played just five baseball games at Arizona, but Astros scout Clark Crist saw his speed.
Houston drafted him in the 17th round in 1988. With Steve Finley in center, the Astros traded him to Cleveland for Eddie Taubensee and Willie Blair, a deal one report called "the steal of the year."

First-base coach Dave Nelson taught him baserunning and bunting. In the 1995 World Series loss to Atlanta he hit .200, and years later he blamed the umpires for giving Tom Glavine and Greg Maddux generous strike zones.
He hit .458 in the 1995 ALCS against Seattle.
He hit .458 in the 1995 ALCS. In the World Series loss to Atlanta he hit .200, and years later he blamed umpires for giving Tom Glavine and Greg Maddux generous strike zones.

In March 1997 Cleveland traded him and Alan Embree to Atlanta for David Justice and Marquis Grissom. He hurt his groin twice and led the league in times caught stealing, then went back to Cleveland as a free agent.
The Giants got him from the White Sox in 2002 and he reached his second World Series. He and David Wells share the record for postseason appearances with six teams.
He fell off the Hall of Fame ballot after one year, often cited as one of the worst snubs. Pedro Martínez named him one of the toughest hitters he faced.
p: When he made the majors he built his grandmother a new house in East Chicago.
He gave $125,000 to build the Kenny Lofton Little League Complex in East Chicago: "I started here just like you, and look where I am now."
He earned a degree in studio production and later founded a TV production company.

His home had concrete floors and broken windows. His grandmother, whose glaucoma kept her from working, refused welfare and lived on Social Security; he was one of eight grandchildren she helped raise. Head Start helped him overcome a speech impediment.
He worked as a Dodgers TV analyst and in 2011 coached baserunning for Cleveland in spring training.

c: As kids in Compton they played "sock ball," a sock stuffed with rags and wrapped in tape, light enough that you could throw a curve or a screwball from 25 feet. At Centennial High he and Reggie Smith were the double-play combination.
Hitting about .210 in Class A in 1962, he wondered what he'd do if he couldn't play baseball. He finished at .284.
In 1968 Ralph Houk moved him to cleanup behind Mickey Mantle, because teams kept walking Mantle. Mantle later called him as good as any of the old Yankee stars.
He was the only player from the Yankees' losing late-1960s teams to take part in their 1977 and 1978 championships, both won against his hometown Los Angeles Dodgers.
He batted .313 in the 1978 ALCS, homering in the clincher, and .333 with a homer in the World Series.

In 1980 he went to Japan's Yomiuri Giants and batted cleanup behind Sadaharu Oh in Oh's final season. He homered twice in his first game and won a Japan Series. "I was probably more popular in Japan than I was in America."
Yankees scout Tuffy Hashem signed him on July 1 for $6,000, with a $4,000 bonus if he made the big club.
He once fell into a slump trying to hit home runs. One season his power dropped to seven homers and he demanded a trade.
In the 1976 ALCS against Kansas City he set a record with five walks and reached base .455 of the time. After that season he got the first multi-year contract of his career.
In 1979 he hit .215 in part-time play, and the Yankees didn't try to re-sign him.
He coached for the Yankees in the mid-1980s and again from 2004, and was a minor-league hitting coach for Oakland.
p: His parents separated when he was five, and his mother raised him and his younger brother in Compton.
Playing in Georgia for the Columbus Confederate Yankees in the 1960s, he had to deal with overt racism.
He started a foundation that gives college scholarships to young people who can't afford school.
His father, Marcus White, was white, and his mother was Black. His Double-A Columbus team in Georgia wore a Confederate flag patch on its uniforms.
He started the Roy White Foundation in 2002.

c: He grew up in San Diego sneaking into Padres games by showing up early and hanging around. Scouts doubted he'd hit; he worked his scouting grades up from the low 40s to nearly 59.

He met Lou Whitaker as his roommate in the 1976 instructional league: "The very first day, we clicked." They debuted the same day in 1977, and in 1995 they passed George Brett and Frank White for the most games played together in AL history.
He hurt his knee in tall Frankenstein boots at a Halloween party in 1983. The next fall he hit .450 in the World Series against his boyhood Padres and was the MVP.
Moved to cleanup in 1987, he hit .343 with 28 homers and lost the MVP to George Bell. Whitaker took second base after the season finale and wrote on it, "To Alan Trammell, 1987 AL MVP."
He turned down Cleveland to stay a Tiger his whole career: "It means something to me to be with one club." He got a single up the middle in his first big-league at-bat and in his last.

As a teenager he sold concessions at Chargers games. Detroit drafted him in the second round in 1976, and he passed up UCLA and Arizona State to sign for $35,000. Scout Dick Wiencek also signed Jack Morris and Dan Petry that year.
In 1977 at Montgomery he set a Southern League record with 19 triples, with only nine doubles, and was the league MVP. After his rookie season he signed for seven years and $2.8 million.
After the 1984 World Series he had surgery on the knee from Halloween and on his shoulder. Hitting coach Gates Brown had given him a more closed stance.
In 1987 he carried Detroit in September, hitting .416 with six homers, while George Bell slumped. The Twins beat Detroit in the ALCS.
Knee and ankle injuries limited him to 101 games in 1991. He coached for San Diego, managed the Tigers from 2003 to 2005, and was bench coach for the Cubs and Arizona.
p: He married Barbara Leverett on his 20th birthday. They named a son Lance, after teammate Lance Parrish.
He and Whitaker made a cameo on Magnum, P.I.
As Tigers manager in 2003 he lost 119 games, and his mother died that September. He was elected to the Hall of Fame in 2018 by the Modern Era Committee.
He and Barbara had three children: Lance, Kyle and Jade Lynn.
Jim Leyland, who replaced him as manager and took Detroit to the 2006 World Series, credited some of that success to Trammell's work.

c: At 12 he practiced catching fly balls at night by throwing the ball higher than the street light. His mother secretly bought him a glove and shoes. His father wanted him working in the family grocery.

He had played fewer than 100 games when Houston signed him at 16 in 1967. Pat Gillick doubled his offer to $3,000 when he heard a Cardinals scout was 15 minutes away, then held up the signed contract when the scout arrived: "You're a few minutes too late."

He learned English watching cowboy movies and The Flintstones. At 22 he had two straight seasons of .320, 20 homers and 50 steals, and Leo Durocher said he was as good as Willie Mays at that age. "I don't want to be the second Clemente. I would rather be the first Cedeño."

Traded to St. Louis late in 1985, he hit .434 with six homers in 28 games and carried the Cardinals to the division title. Whitey Herzog: "If we hadn't got Cedeño, we would have been at least three games out of first."

His father bought a grocery store and wanted him running errands, not playing ball. Pat Gillick and Tony Pacheco took him 60 miles away for a private workout so other scouts wouldn't see, and when the Cardinals' Diomedes Olivo arrived, Gillick held up the contract: "You're a few minutes too late."
Rico Carty helped him with his hitting in winter ball. Harry Walker said he and Roberto Clemente were the two most exciting players in baseball, and both were accused of hot-dogging.
In 1970 he hit an inside-the-park grand slam on a bloop when the Dodgers' right fielder and second baseman collided.

Houston GM Spec Richardson questioned his toughness: "Cedeño got hurt and stayed hurt." He hurt his right knee in winter ball in 1972 and never fully recovered, and his ankles took 20 to 30 minutes to loosen up each day.
After a confrontation with a fan he was suspended and fined $5,000; he apologized to the fan by phone and in writing. In December 1981 Houston traded him to Cincinnati for Ray Knight.
In 1977 spring training he tore finger ligaments ducking a pitch from a pitching machine.
In St. Louis in 1985 he filled in at first for the injured Jack Clark and in the outfield in the playoffs for the injured Vince Coleman.
p: In December 1973 a 19-year-old woman was killed by his gun in a Santo Domingo motel room. He was jailed for 20 days, convicted of involuntary manslaughter, and fined $100. Fans never forgave him, and the next season a caller threatened to shoot him.
His temper brought fines and suspensions throughout his career. He was later arrested twice for assaulting a girlfriend, in 1988 and 1992.

He said he carried the gun for protection after being robbed of $5,000. Police paraffin tests found only the woman had recently fired a gun. Her parents sued him for $100,000 on behalf of her 3-year-old daughter.
His American wife, Cora, brought him food in jail every day. Bowie Kuhn never suspended him or commented. Before a game in Pittsburgh, a caller threatened to shoot him "just like he shot that girl."
The 1988 charges were assault causing bodily injury and resisting arrest; in 1992 his girlfriend, Pamela Lamon, was pregnant. He later coached hitting in the Nationals' and Astros' farm systems.

c: A straight-A student whose worst grade was a B in AP Chemistry, he went to Miami on an academic scholarship: "I think the girls were the deal closer on the recruiting trip."

He was Rookie of the Year at third base in 2007 but made 34 errors in the minors the year before, mostly on throws. When Milwaukee told him he was moving to left field, he picked up his outfield glove and started taking fly balls.

He won the 2011 MVP. A leaked test showed elevated testosterone; the result was thrown out because of how the sample was handled, and he publicly accused the collector. In 2013, tied to the Biogenesis clinic, he was suspended for the rest of the season and admitted using PEDs in 2011, apologizing to the collector too.
In August 2015 he hit his 252nd home run, the most in Brewers history.
He hit .451 with a .675 on-base percentage as a high school senior and went undrafted because he said he was going to college. Milwaukee took him fifth overall in 2005 and gave him $2.45 million.

In May 2008 he signed an eight-year, $45 million extension, the biggest ever for a player with under three years in the majors. That September his 10th-inning grand slam, and three days later a go-ahead homer against the Cubs, sent the Brewers to their first postseason since 1982.
Biogenesis records listed his name three times. He said his lawyers had hired clinic owner Anthony Bosch as a consultant for his appeal.

His 2013 suspension was 65 games plus the postseason, 15 more than standard, because MLB considered his attacks on the sample collector, whom he suggested was a Cubs fan or anti-Semitic, conduct detrimental to baseball. He later admitted using PEDs in his 2011 MVP season.
He had surgery in 2014 to deaden pain receptors near the base of his right thumb. In 2018 he became the Brewers' career leader in postseason hits.
p: His father was born in Israel; most of his father's family was killed in the Holocaust. His mother is Catholic. He said he was "extremely proud to be a role model for young Jewish kids."
His PONY League teammates included Jack and Matt Cassel, Jason and Jarron Collins, and Jon Garland.

c: A natural right-handed hitter, he learned to switch-hit in the Royals' system. He spoke no English when he arrived in 1995: "Imagine – how can you communicate with a coach?"
After he was traded to Houston in 2004, he hit .435 with eight home runs and 21 runs in 12 postseason games. Craig Biggio: "Every ball he hit was hard."

With the bases loaded and two outs in the ninth of Game 7 of the 2006 NLCS, he took a two-strike curveball from Adam Wainwright for strike three. It's how many Mets fans remember him, though he hit three homers in that series.

In 2017, in his last season, he was a "driving force" behind the Astros' sign-stealing scheme and the only player named in MLB's report. The Mets fired him as manager before he managed a game. He was elected to the Hall of Fame in 2026.

He's the all-time leader in stolen-base percentage among players with 200 attempts, 86.4 percent, and one of four players with 1,500 runs, 1,500 RBIs, 400 homers and 300 steals, along with Bonds, Rodriguez and Mays.
His father worked at a pharmaceutical company. A collision with a teammate in the minors hurt his right knee, which bothered him his whole career.
He taught himself to switch-hit with advice from Bernie Williams and coach Kevin Long.
When he hurt his knee he refused to rehab at the Royals' facility, and they tried to suspend him without pay until the union filed a grievance.
Injuries limited him to 98 games in 2000, and he lost center field to Johnny Damon until Damon was traded.

The Astros offered five years and up to $84 million but no no-trade clause, and the Yankees wouldn't match the Mets' seven years and $119 million. Mike Lupica called him "a thinner Mo Vaughn" after a slow first season.

He was questioned by FBI agents about Dr. Galea, who pleaded guilty to bringing HGH into the US; Beltrán said Galea never gave him HGH. In January 2010 he had knee surgery that strained his relationship with the Mets, and he missed their first 88 games.
After the surgery he wore a knee brace and stole only 26 bases in his last eight seasons. In 2012 he joined the 300–300 club, and a cross necklace popped out as he slid into second.
p: His father made him give up volleyball at 17 to concentrate on baseball. His younger twin sisters became volleyball stars.
He put more than $4 million into a baseball academy in Florida, Puerto Rico, that helps high school players with baseball and schoolwork. It opened in 2011.
He won the 2013 Roberto Clemente Award, in part for a scholarship fund he and his wife started for Hispanic students in St. Louis.
He married Jessica Lugo, a high school classmate, in 1999. They have two daughters and a son, and his nephew Matthew Lugo was drafted by Boston.
In 2004 he signed a letter endorsing George W. Bush. He joined the Mets' front office in 2023.

c: At a Mets tryout he was asked if he was the batboy: "I'm Lenny Dykstra and I'm the best player you're going to see today." The Mets took him in the 13th round, one round after Roger Clemens, who didn't sign.

His ninth-inning homer off Dave Smith won Game 3 of the 1986 NLCS. In 1993, now 200 pounds of muscle, his 10th-inning homer won Game 5 of the NLCS, and he yelled "DIDN'T I???" at his third-base coach.
In 1991, driving drunk after John Kruk's bachelor party, he wrecked his car and broke his ribs, collarbone and cheekbone. Darren Daulton, his passenger, was badly hurt too.

In the 1993 World Series he hit four homers and scored nine runs. "I basically went from star to superstar." He hit a homer every 11 at-bats in the postseason, against one every 56 in the regular season.
He put on 30 pounds of muscle before 1990 and credited "special vitamins." The Mitchell Report said he had admitted steroid use to the commissioner's office.
The Mets took Roger Clemens in the 12th round and Dykstra in the 13th, figuring nobody else wanted him. He'd committed to Arizona State and wasn't happy to go so low.

He was a platoon center fielder with Mookie Wilson on the 1986 Mets, a team known for drinking, drugs and chasing women, and loved gambling until sunrise. He led the Mets in average, on-base and slugging in the NLCS.
Unhappy as a part-timer, he was traded to the Phillies with Roger McDowell for Juan Samuel in June 1989.
His blood alcohol after the 1991 crash was 0.179, and he also had burns on his arm and back.
That August he broke his collarbone again crashing into the wall in Cincinnati, and a broken finger ended another season early.
A 2005 lawsuit by a former business partner alleged he used steroids and had the partner bet on Phillies games in 1993. He denied it.
p: As a kid he sprayed people outside Disneyland with a stolen fire extinguisher, and got caught sneaking into Angel Stadium on Christmas Day. Three of his uncles played in the NHL.
After baseball he ran car washes and wrote stock picks for Jim Cramer. He bought Wayne Gretzky's old estate, went bankrupt in 2009 and went to prison in 2012.
His mother married Dennis Dykstra, a phone company worker with three daughters, who adopted her three sons. Lenny met his wife, Terri, playing in Jackson.
In 1999 he was arrested for sexually harassing a 17-year-old girl who worked at his car wash; charges were dropped.

His magazine, The Players Club, was accused by a former editor of credit card fraud and bounced checks. Reports in 2009 said he used slurs about Black people, women and gay people. His World Series ring was auctioned for $56,762.
Worth an estimated $58 million in 2008, he filed for bankruptcy in 2009 and lost the Gretzky house. He wrote a memoir, House of Nails.
He was later sentenced to three years in a California state prison for grand theft auto and providing a false financial statement.

c: Houston Chronicle writer John Wilson first called him the "Toy Cannon" in 1967. At 5-foot-9 he took it as a dig at his size at first, but he later used it as the title of his memoir.
The Colt .45s drafted him away from the Reds after his first pro season, in 1962, under a rule that let teams take first-year players left off a club's 40-man roster.
In 1967 he hit 37 homers, second to Hank Aaron, and led the NL with 22 on the road. On June 15 he became the first player to hit three homers in a game at the Astrodome.
Manager Harry Walker wanted him to choke up and hit to the opposite field. "I didn't get all those home runs being a Punch-and-Judy hitter." In 1969 he drew a league-leading 148 walks.
Traded to the Dodgers, he set a Los Angeles Dodger record with 32 homers in 1974, and fans named part of the bleachers "Cannon Country." He homered off Rollie Fingers in Game 1 of the World Series.
The Astros retired his number 24 in 2005. Jason Lane, who had been wearing it, switched to 16.
In the Florida minors he faced vicious racism, though he credited managers Johnny Vander Meer and Hershell Freeman with treating Black players humanely.
Grady Hatton fined or benched him for playing nonchalantly. Harry Walker, who replaced Hatton in 1968, once fined him for ignoring a take sign; Joe Morgan called Walker a racist.
After 1971 Houston kept both Walker and Wynn and traded Morgan, whom Walker saw as a bad influence. In December 1973 the Astros traded Wynn to the Dodgers for Claude Osteen.

He walked nine times in the 1974 NLCS and homered off Rollie Fingers in Game 1 of the World Series. A shoulder injury in 1975 moved him to left, and he was traded to Atlanta in the deal that brought Dusty Baker to LA.
The Yankees bought him in 1977 and released him; he finished with Milwaukee.
TV footage of him rounding third appears in the movie Apollo 13.
p: He grew up a few blocks from Crosley Field, the oldest of seven. His father, a garbage man who had played semipro ball, threw him pitch after pitch and took him to pitching machines near the airport.

On their sixth anniversary in 1970, a fight with his wife Ruth ended with her stabbing him in the stomach. They divorced, and it was years before he repaired his relationships with their two children.
He and Marie married on a trip to Hawaii in 2000, in shorts and Hawaiian shirts, with Gaylord Perry, Steve Carlton and Ferguson Jenkins among the best men.
He worked in community relations for the Astros from 1988, and in 2011 the team opened the Jimmy Wynn Training Center for urban youth.
His mother, Maude, raised seven children in a strict religious home.

He married Ruth Mixon in 1964 and they had two children, Kimberly and Jimmy Jr. He admitted he was not a good husband. In the 1970 fight he grabbed an unloaded shotgun, and he needed abdominal surgery.
He married Joanne in 1972; they divorced as his Dodgers years ended. Ruth's early death from cancer ended any chance of a reconciliation.
After baseball he did appearances for a beverage company in Los Angeles, moved back to Houston in 1985, and was hitting coach for New Orleans in 1997.
He died in Houston in 2020, two weeks after turning 78.

c: Cleveland outbid 14 other teams with a $75,000 bonus. Before reporting he went on To Tell the Truth, and only Tom Poston guessed he was a ballplayer.

Wild for years, he turned it around at Portland in 1964, going 8-0 with a 1.18 ERA after he decided to stop listening to everyone's theories. Manager Johnny Lipon "was the first person in baseball to handle me that way."
In 1965 he struck out 325 and led the league with a 2.18 ERA. Luis Aparicio: "I never saw anybody so fast." In 1966 Sports Illustrated put him on its cover: "Faster Than Koufax?"
In 1968 he had a 1.81 ERA but went 15-14; in his losses Cleveland was shut out five times. He struck out 16 A's and then 14 Yankees, breaking Bob Feller's AL record for two straight games.
Twice in 1970 Alvin Dark moved him to the infield so Dean Chance could face Frank Howard, then put him back on the mound. The first time, he struck out the side in the ninth for 15 strikeouts.
He led the AL in strikeouts five times. Only Nolan Ryan and Randy Johnson led their league more often.
At the 1960 Colt World Series he threw two no-hitters and a one-hitter, and every big-league team offered him a bonus. In his debut he broke two ribs throwing a pitch.
His parents insisted he start in the low minors and work his way up.
In 1970 he went 20–12 with 304 strikeouts. In 1971 Bowie Kuhn voided his incentive-laden contract; he left the team, argued he should be a free agent, and was suspended twice.
Cleveland traded him to the Giants for Gaylord Perry, a deal that turned out a disaster for San Francisco. On June 7 the Giants sold him to the Yankees.
With the Giants a circulation problem numbed his fingers, and the team was unhappy with his drinking.
A slipped disk sidelined him in 1974. He finished with his hometown Pirates in 1975.
p: His father was a heat inspector at U.S. Steel. His high school was two blocks from Forbes Field, and he threw batting practice to the Pirates.
He said he never drank until the majors. After a celebration dinner with Gary Bell and Barry Latman, "I didn't want to stop." His Giants manager said of the fines: "We call it the Sam McDowell Fund."
Blacklisted by every club, divorced and living with his parents, one morning in 1980 he sat on the couch and said "You beat me." He got sober, and Pennsylvania certified him as a counselor in 1982.

He counseled players for the Blue Jays and Rangers and earned a World Series ring with the 1993 Blue Jays. In 1998 he started City of Legends, a retirement community for former players in Clermont, Florida.
He married his high school sweetheart, Carol Beisgen, in 1962; they had two children, Debbie and Tim.
A failed business left him $190,000 in debt. Sober, he paid it off and earned degrees at Pitt in sports psychology and addiction, then worked for the Baseball Assistance Team.
In 2001 he married Eva, a Slovak tourist he met when he asked her for directions in Florida. The creator of Cheers said in 2026 that Sam Malone wasn't based on him. He died that October at 84.

c: His high school had no baseball team, so the principal formed one around him. He once threw a seven-inning no-hitter with 21 strikeouts and lost, because he walked ten.
At Triple-A Iowa in 1970, veteran Juan Pizarro helped him rework his delivery: "He helped me more than any single person in my career." That September he no-hit the Twins.

On July 9, 1971, he pitched 11 shutout innings against the Angels with 17 strikeouts and no walks, and got no decision; the A's won 1-0 in 20 innings. Days later he was the youngest winning pitcher in All-Star history.
Charlie Finley offered him $2,000 to change his middle name to "True" and put "True Blue" on the scoreboard anyway. Blue liked his name and refused.
After his Cy Young and MVP year, Finley offered $50,000. Blue held out, announced he was taking a job with Dura Steel Products, and missed the start of 1972 before signing for $63,000.

In 1976 Finley sold him to the Yankees for $1.5 million, and Commissioner Bowie Kuhn voided the deal as not in the best interests of baseball. With the Giants he became the first pitcher to start the All-Star Game for both leagues.
Notre Dame, Purdue and Houston recruited him for football, but he signed with the A's for $12,500 a year to support his family after his father's death.
Joe DiMaggio, then an A's coach, said it was a shame to rush him up before he'd pitched two pro seasons.
In 1971 he started the season opener, the All-Star Game and the playoff opener, the only pitcher ever to do all three in one season.
During his holdout he asked for $92,500 and later $85,000. Finley insisted the deal was $50,000 plus a $5,000 bonus and $8,000 for his college fund, and Blue signed on May 2.
He saved Game 5 of the 1972 ALCS with four scoreless innings and threw a 1–0 shutout against Baltimore in the 1974 ALCS.
Overall he went 1–5 with a 4.31 ERA in the postseason.
Kuhn also vetoed Finley's 1978 deal to send him to Cincinnati for Dave Revering and $1.75 million. In March 1978 the A's traded him to the Giants for seven players and $300,000.
p: He was the oldest of six in segregated Mansfield, Louisiana. Houston recruited him to play quarterback, but his father died during his senior year and he signed with the A's to support the family.
In his senior year of high school he threw for 3,400 yards and 35 touchdowns and ran for 1,600 more.
He pleaded guilty to cocaine possession in 1983 and served 81 days in prison. He retired abruptly in 1987: "I reached the point where I had to choose between baseball and life."
He married Peggy Shannon on the pitcher's mound at Candlestick Park in 1989, with Willie McCovey as best man.
His father worked in a Mansfield iron foundry.
He and Peggy had twin girls and divorced in 1996. He also had a son, Derrick, and two other daughters. He worked as a Giants TV analyst and died of cancer complications in May 2023, at 73.

c: In his second big-league start, in 1998, he took a no-hitter into the ninth before Bobby Higginson homered with two outs.

After an ERA of 10.64 in 2000, the Blue Jays sent him all the way down to Class A. Mel Queen rebuilt his delivery: "You're wasting talent, Doc." Harvey Dorfman's books on the mental game, which his wife Brandy bought, became his bibles.
In 2003 he won 15 straight after an 0-2 April and took his first Cy Young.

In 2010, with the Phillies, he threw a perfect game against the Marlins, then a no-hitter against the Reds in his first postseason start, the second no-hitter in postseason history. He won his second Cy Young unanimously.
His nickname "Doc," after the gunslinger Doc Holliday, came from Blue Jays announcer Tom Cheek. He led his league in complete games seven times, the most of any pitcher who started after 1945.
He retired on a one-day contract with Toronto. Bryce Harper wouldn't wear his number 34 in Philadelphia: "Roy Halladay should be the last one to wear it."
He trained from age 13 with Bus Campbell, who had worked with nearly every top pitcher from the Denver area, including Goose Gossage and Brad Lidge.
Campbell, then scouting for Toronto, made the phone call when the Blue Jays drafted him. He passed up Arizona and signed for a club-record $895,000.
At 13 he bought Nolan Ryan's Pitcher's Bible and followed Ryan's conditioning program. In high school he threw a no-hitter in his first start.
He had shoulder problems in 2004, and a broken leg later ended another season. He took out a full-page newspaper ad thanking Toronto fans when he left.
He retired after 2013 citing a persistent back injury and wanting more family time. In 2017 the Phillies made him a "mental skills coach," and he coached his son's high school team.
p: His family moved to Arvada, Colorado, for a basement long enough for a 60-foot-6 pitching distance. Mentor Bus Campbell never took money for lessons; Halladay used part of his bonus to give him a grandfather clock.
His father, a pilot, began teaching him to fly when he was a small child, and he built model airplanes.
In Toronto he and Brandy brought kids from the Hospital for Sick Children to "Doc's Box" at games, and he gave $100,000 a year to the Jays Care Foundation.
He died in 2017 when his amphibious plane crashed into the Gulf of Mexico. The autopsy found morphine, amphetamines and other drugs in his blood. He was elected to the Hall of Fame in 2019.
He was one of three children and the only boy. His mother, Linda, was a homemaker, and his father flew for a food-processing company.
He and Brandy had two sons, Braden and Ryan, both born while he was a Blue Jay. One offseason they moved to Florida to escape the attention in Colorado.
Braden committed to Penn State shortly after his father died.
A pathologist said the drugs in his system were "similar to a speedball." The NTSB found he was doing aerobatics, coming within five feet of the water, before the plane lost speed and nosedived.

c: The Tigers let him finish each spring semester at Xavier, so he missed spring training for three years. He spent almost six seasons in the minors, and after a bad 1952 went back to the three-quarter, sidearm delivery the Tigers had tried to coach out of him.

When a Charleston loss left him singing in the shower, manager Charlie Metro told him, "Losers don't sing." The two bonded, and in 1957 he won 20 and started the All-Star Game, retiring all nine batters he faced.

On Father's Day 1964 at Shea Stadium he threw the first NL perfect game since 1880. Teammates kept quiet to avoid a jinx, but Bunning talked about it, and with one out in the ninth asked Gus Triandos to tell him a joke.
That September the Phillies led by 6½ games with 12 to play and lost ten straight; three of the losses were his. He blamed the team as a whole, himself included, not Gene Mauch.
As the Phillies' player representative he won free parking at the ballpark and permission for wives on some road trips, and helped lead the search for a union chief.
When he retired he had the second-most strikeouts in major-league history. He's the only big-leaguer elected to both the Senate and the Hall of Fame.
Scout Bruce Connatser approached his father in Bunning's freshman year at Xavier. Signing cost him his basketball scholarship, and his parents paid for the rest of his education.
When demoted to Charleston in 1956 he told GM Muddy Ruel he'd rather be traded. Pitching in relief there, he learned a slider he could throw for strikes.
He was a tough negotiator but never held out. His work as union rep and as an offseason stockbroker irritated the Tigers, and in December 1963 they traded him to the Phillies.

After the 1964 collapse he was sick and despondent for weeks. The Phillies traded him to Pittsburgh for four players. He managed in the Phillies' system from 1972 to 1976, and felt farm director Dallas Green had given him false hope.
He was one of seven pitchers with both a perfect game and another no-hitter. In 1965, when the minimum salary was $6,000, he helped build the players' union.
p: As a boy he was too shy to ask his hero Bucky Walters for an autograph at a restaurant, so his older brother did. Walters moved his beer bottle off the table before the photo.
He used his $4,000 signing bonus to buy an engagement ring for his childhood sweetheart, Mary Theis. They were married more than 60 years and had nine children.
He said he'd had "better professors of economics at Xavier University than Alan Greenspan had at New York University." He was elected to the House in 1986 and the Senate in 1998.
His son David became a federal judge and presided over the Kim Davis case.

He married Mary Theis in January 1952. They had five daughters and four sons, and by 2013 had 35 grandchildren, including Kentucky quarterback Patrick Towles. At the time of the perfect game he had seven children.

In a Senate race he said his opponent, Daniel Mongiardo, "looked like one of Saddam Hussein's sons," and accused Mongiardo's staff of assaulting his wife. He later apologized for predicting that Ruth Bader Ginsburg would die within a year of pancreatic cancer.

c: He turned down the Marlins out of high school and the Orioles out of junior college, and signed with the Expos in 2000. Two years later they traded him to Cleveland with Grady Sizemore and Brandon Phillips for Bartolo Colón.
In 2007 he went 5-8 with a 6.38 ERA and was sent back to the minors. In 2008 he won the Cy Young, leading the majors with 22 wins and the AL with a 2.54 ERA.
Stuck in traffic before Game 1 of the 2009 World Series, he rode the subway to Yankee Stadium, then beat the Yankees with a 10-strikeout complete game.
After 2010 he turned down seven years and $150 million from the Yankees to return to the Phillies for five years and $120 million, joining Roy Halladay, Cole Hamels and Roy Oswalt as the "Four Aces."
In 2012 he pitched 10 innings against the Giants in a game the Phillies lost 1-0. As of 2025 no big-league pitcher had gone more than nine innings in a game since.

In high school he threw 91 mph but had trouble with control, and a shoulder injury moved him to the outfield. He played at Meridian Community College and then Arkansas before Montreal took him in the fourth round in 2000.
At Class A Jupiter he fought with pitching coach Ace Adams, who rested him when his arm was tired; Lee wanted to finish every start. Under Adams he learned the cutter.

After one season he had surgery for a sports hernia in Philadelphia and met future teammate Roy Oswalt in the hospital. Pitching through a flu bug in 2005, he threw seven scoreless innings while trying not to vomit on the mound.
In July 2009 Cleveland traded him to Philadelphia, and he reached the World Series. He was traded again and reached the 2010 World Series with Texas.

In 2014 he tore a flexor tendon in his pitching elbow, the first arm injury of his life. He tried rehab instead of surgery, never pitched again, and the Phillies bought out his last year for $12.5 million.
p: His father was a firefighter. His mother, born without one hand, pitched for a local softball team.
His son Jaxon was diagnosed with leukemia at four months old. In 2010 the Lees gave $1 million to Arkansas Children's Hospital, where he was treated.
A shy man, he was uncomfortable speaking to large groups. Away from baseball he hunts, fishes and plays chess online.
His father was also a one-time city council member in Benton.
He met Kristen in middle school; they married in 2000 and have a son, Jaxon, and a daughter, Maci. He filed for divorce in February 2026.

c: As a high school sophomore he started working with former big-league pitcher Tom House, who tutored young pitchers.
The Cubs took him second overall in 2001, behind Joe Mauer, and gave him $10.5 million, the biggest bonus for a draft pick until Stephen Strasburg's in 2009.

In Game 6 of the 2003 NLCS he was pitching a shutout in the eighth when Steve Bartman kept Moisés Alou from catching a foul ball. The Marlins scored eight runs that inning and won the series in seven games.

His "Inverted W" arm action, once praised as perfect mechanics, and Dusty Baker's heavy use of him in 2003 have both been blamed for his injuries; Prior doesn't blame Baker. Tears in his labrum, anterior capsule and rotator cuff kept him out all of 2007, and he never pitched in the majors again.
He spent six years trying to come back in the minors. In 2013 he called Baker, by then managing the Reds, to ask if Cincinnati was interested.
He became the Dodgers' pitching coach in 2020 and has won the World Series with them in 2020, 2024 and 2025.

The Yankees drafted him in the first round out of high school in 1998 and offered about $1.5 million, but they couldn't agree, so he went to college. He transferred to USC, where he went 15–1 with 202 strikeouts and 18 walks in 2001.
Dusty Baker had him averaging 126 pitches a start in September 2003 and 123 in the playoffs. He beat Greg Maddux in the Division Series.

An Achilles injury and elbow soreness cost him two months of 2004. In 2005 a 117-mph line drive from Brad Hawpe, who had homered off him in the 2000 College World Series, fractured his pitching elbow.

In 2006 a shoulder strain, an oblique strain and tendinitis limited him to nine games. James Andrews found vast structural damage in his shoulder, with tears in the labrum, anterior capsule and rotator cuff, and the Cubs let him go.
The Padres gave him a $1 million incentive deal, but he tore his shoulder capsule again in 2008. He later worked in San Diego's front office and joined the Dodgers as bullpen coach in 2018.
p: His father played college football at Vanderbilt. "Being the youngest of three kids, there's no room for me to step out of line."
He married Heather Gora in November 2003, and finished a business degree at USC, part time, in 2004.
He and Heather have three children: Amanda, Caitlin and Matthew.

c: His father, a $27-a-week wallpaper salesman, built a mound in the backyard and wouldn't let him play catch unless he threw correctly. "Without control you're nothing!" The smooth motion he taught was the secret of Spahn's longevity.

In 1942 Casey Stengel ordered him to brush back Pee Wee Reese. When he didn't, Stengel sent him to Hartford. Years later, released by Stengel's Mets: "I'm the only guy to play for Casey Stengel before and after he was a genius."
He didn't win his first big-league game until he was 25, then won 363, the most by a lefty. He won 23 at 42, and 75 after turning 40.

An old football shoulder separation kept him from raising his right hand above his shoulder, and the glove coming down through hitters' line of sight bothered them. "Whatever bothered hitters, I was for."
He hit 35 home runs, the most by an NL pitcher. Stan Musial: "I don't think Spahn will ever get into the Hall of Fame. He'll never stop pitching."
Released after 1965: "I didn't retire from baseball. Baseball retired me." He went on to manage Tulsa to a Pacific Coast League title and coach pitchers in Japan.

He was the fifth of six children. His family ate meat about once a week and stuffed newspaper in their shoes. Scouts thought he was too skinny, but Billy Meyers, a part-time Boston scout who sold tickets for the New York Central, signed him for $80 a month.
In his first pro season he tore tendons in his shoulder trying a new overhand curve. His father took it so hard that he went into a deep depression and was hospitalized.
In 1942 he got a complete game in a forfeit when scrap-drive kids swarmed the Polo Grounds with the Giants up 5–2. He enlisted that October.

Chuck Dressen said he was tipping pitches in 1946, and Johnny Cooney fixed it. In 1948, with LoRene pregnant, he went just 15–12, but he and Johnny Sain carried the Braves to the pennant: "Spahn and Sain and pray for rain."

Sold to the Mets after 1964 as pitcher and pitching coach, he went 4–12 and was released, then finished with the Giants at 44. He coached in Mexico City, for Cleveland and for six years with Japan's Hiroshima Carp.
p: A combat engineer, he fought in the Battle of the Bulge and was working on the Remagen bridge when it collapsed into the Rhine; he took shrapnel in his foot. He earned a Bronze Star, a Purple Heart and a battlefield promotion, the only ballplayer to get one.

He didn't count the wins the war cost him: "If I had not had that maturity, I wouldn't have pitched until I was 45." And he didn't want to be called a hero: "The guys who died over there were heroes."

A teammate's wild throw broke his nose in 1941. The Braves paid a specialist to fix John Berardino's nose, broken the same day, since Berardino was an actor, and told Spahn he wasn't a very good-looking guy anyway.

His wife LoRene, who was half Cherokee, got him to settle in Oklahoma, where he ran a 2,000-acre cattle ranch. At his statue's unveiling in 2003: "I took great pride in mooning people. That's the reason I developed that leg kick."

At Camp Gruber in Oklahoma a friend introduced him to LoRene Southard, an oil company executive secretary whose business sense later helped make him rich. Billy Southworth offered to be best man and pay for the wedding if they waited until after the season; Spahn got a day off and married her on August 10.
Their only child, Gregory, was born October 1, 1948. They owned the Diamond Star Ranch south of Hartshorne, Oklahoma, and retired near a golf course in Broken Arrow, where he died.

c: His grandfather, a Tigers usher and groundskeeper for three decades, talked the club into scouting him. Detroit took him in the 22nd round in 1985; at his election he was the lowest draft pick in the Hall of Fame.

In 1987 the Tigers traded him to Atlanta for Doyle Alexander. He felt rejected: "As far as I was concerned, the Braves were the worst team in all of baseball." He began a 19-year partnership with pitching coach Leo Mazzone.
He was 2-11 at the 1991 All-Star break. A psychologist gave him a highlight video to watch before every start; he went 12-2 the rest of the way and shut out Pittsburgh in Game 7 of the NLCS.

Pushed to the bullpen after Tommy John surgery, he turned down a reported $52 million from the Yankees to close for Atlanta, and set an NL record with 55 saves in 2002. He paid to air-condition Turner Field's bullpen and brought his recliner from home.

In 2004 he talked John Schuerholz into letting him start again: "Take my baseball card and turn it over." He's the only pitcher with more than 200 wins and 150 saves, and the only player on all 14 straight Braves division champions.
Scout Ken Madeja grumbled about chasing another tip on somebody's grandson, then reported, "This time we got a good tip." He signed the night before classes started.
He had committed to Michigan State, and was also an all-conference basketball guard in high school.

He said Detroit's roving coaches gave him little and contradictory instruction; Atlanta had real minor-league pitching coaches. Tom Glavine was called up after the trade, and Smoltz never let him forget how he got there.
He shut out Pittsburgh in Game 7 of the 1991 NLCS and held the Twins scoreless into the eighth of Game 7 of the World Series. He set postseason records with 15 wins and 199 strikeouts.
He was the 1992 NLCS MVP and went 15–4 with a 2.67 ERA in the postseason.

An orthopedic surgeon told him he had extraordinarily loose joints. He had bone spurs and chips removed in 1994 and later a second arthroscopic surgery, and dropped to a nearly sidearm delivery to ease the pain.
He had Tommy John surgery before the 2000 season. Moved to closer, he saved 45 with a 1.12 ERA in 2003 and passed Gene Garber's franchise saves record.
He was the first pitcher with Tommy John surgery elected to the Hall of Fame.
p: Both his parents moonlighted as accordion teachers, and he played polka parties from age 4. At 7 he said he'd be a ballplayer; his backup plan was gas-station attendant.
He was the best golfer of the Big Three and arranged their tee times. Tiger Woods called him the best golfer outside the PGA Tour he'd seen, and in 2018 he qualified for the U.S. Senior Open.
As Fox's lead analyst he won a Sports Emmy in 2021. He had to stop working in MLB Network's studio after he refused the COVID-19 vaccine.

His father, a salesman, embarrassed the kids by decorating his car to look like the calculators he sold. As a boy he pitched imaginary World Series games against the house, calling them in Ernie Harwell's voice.
He met Dyan Struble at the Omni Hotel in Atlanta; they had four children and divorced in 2007 after 16 years. In 2009 he married Kathryn Darden at home with 70 guests.

c: Every big-league team scouted him as a shortstop, but scout Bobby Mattick, who had signed Frank Robinson and Vada Pinson, saw a pitcher. At Fresno City College he threw 19 straight no-hit innings, and the Reds gave him a reported $100,000.
In 1963 he went 23-7 with a club-record 265 strikeouts and struck out eight Braves in a row. Hank Aaron: "He was faster than anyone I've seen this season."

On the last day of 1964, with a pennant in reach, manager Dick Sisler skipped Maloney, the Reds' hottest pitcher, for John Tsitouris. The Reds lost 10-0 and the Cardinals won the pennant; fans have argued about it ever since.
In 1965 he no-hit the Mets for ten innings with 18 strikeouts and lost in the 11th. Two months later he no-hit the Cubs for ten despite walking ten, on 187 pitches.
He left two other no-hitters in the seventh with injuries. In 1969 he pulled a groin running the bases during a no-hitter against Houston, refused to come out, and struck out Doug Rader to end it.
He held Willie Mays to .172. In 1970 he ruptured his Achilles running out a ground ball, and he pitched his last big-league game the next year, for the Angels.
His high school team included Dick Ellsworth and Pat Corrales. He signed with the Reds on April 1, 1959, for a reported $100,000.
He briefly attended UC Berkeley, then pitched at Fresno City College at Bobby Mattick's urging.
At Topeka he was homesick and lost weight. Pitching coach Jim Turner helped him relax, develop a curve and find his control.
He had one relief appearance in the 1961 World Series, in the final game.
Arm and shoulder problems that started in spring training followed him the rest of his career.

He fought the Reds over salary almost every year, signing late in spring training. In 1966, the year of Koufax and Drysdale's holdout, he stayed home in Fresno until the Reds gave him a reported $48,000.
Some teammates questioned his injuries and resented the extra rest he needed. The Reds traded him to the Angels for Greg Garrett in December 1970.
p: His father, nicknamed "Hands," played semipro ball and opened one of Fresno's biggest used-car dealerships; Maloney sold cars there after he retired.
"When I got out of baseball, I became an alcoholic. By 1985, I was out of my house and my wife was filing for divorce." He got sober and became director of Fresno's Alcoholism and Drug Abuse Council.
He and his first wife, Carolyn, had three children. He and his wife Lyn live in Fresno, where he directed the city's alcoholism and drug abuse council.

c: The Yankees signed him at 15 for $3,500, and he debuted at 18. George Steinbrenner hoped he'd rival the Mets' Dwight Gooden; he went 2-8 and was traded to Oakland in the Rickey Henderson deal.
With Oakland in 1986 he struck out 16 Mariners, a club record, then lost feeling in his left leg and couldn't throw his fastball. In three years with the A's he won 17 games.

Traded to Cincinnati for Dave Parker, he credited Pete Rose for letting him call his own pitches. Rose made him a starter over his objections: "He's a real horse, and he's going to win a lot of games — as a starter."
He had an ERA under 3.00 every year as a Reds starter from 1988 to 1993, and was World Series MVP in 1990 as Cincinnati swept the A's, his old team. In 1993 he led the NL in strikeouts.

After five years out of baseball and six elbow surgeries, he made it back to the Reds in 2001, the first pitcher to return to the majors after five seasons out of organized ball. "I feel like I'm a walking miracle right now."
Scout Willie Calvino signed him on August 1, 1980: "I signed because I hated school, and my family needed the money." He started at $600 a month.
In December 1984 the Yankees traded him to Oakland with four others for Rickey Henderson. In Tacoma he learned a changeup.
Cincinnati traded him and Tim Birtsas for Dave Parker in December 1987. He went on the disabled list 10 times as a Red, including for a stress fracture in his lower back in 1989.
Pitching coach Stan Williams challenged him in August 1990, telling him he wasn't one of the team's top starters.
He went 3–0 in the 1990 postseason, his only one, and his two-hitter in Game 4 clinched the sweep of Oakland.
Elbow injuries kept him out from 1995 through 2000. He was on the 2003 roster but hurt his elbow again and retired.
p: His father, a taxi driver, left when he was 4. "We were so poor, I had to play ball in a friend's shoes, which were too small."
In Fort Lauderdale at 18, speaking no English, he moved in with a local family, learned three English words a day, and refused to move to the team hotel the next spring.
He married Rosie Marichal, daughter of Juan Marichal, who was furious when he heard their plans; they later divorced.

The Nationals fired him in 2009 after Esmailyn Gonzalez, a prospect from his academy, turned out to have lied about his name and age. In 2011 he was questioned about ties to a drug trafficker; no concrete evidence was found.
His mother was a nurse. His father was a taxi driver with 13 children. José grew up in a crowded, aluminum-roofed house with grandparents, aunts and uncles.
In Fort Lauderdale he lived on a street full of drug users and spent most of his money calling home, then moved in with John Cummings, a computer programmer, and his Mexican-born wife.

He had a first wife, Alma, about whom little is known. He married Rosie Marichal, a San Francisco State student, in 1986: "I had the reputation of going out a lot." Their son, José Jr., was born in 1989, and she objected to his going out drinking. He later sued her for divorce.

Esmailyn Gonzalez was really Carlos Lugo and four years older than claimed; he testified he kicked back $300,000 of his bonus to Rijo, which Rijo denied. In 2012 Rijo was charged with money laundering; prosecutors said about 80 percent of a fugitive drug suspect's assets, including two hotels, were in his name.

c: He became a pitcher at 14 when his team's pitcher left for a club with better-looking uniforms. At 17, as "Mr. Zero," he was MVP of an all-star boys' game at the Polo Grounds, managed by Connie Mack.
Paul Richards met him as the teenage clerk at his father's drugstore without noticing. As White Sox manager, Richards taught him a slider and Pierce cut his walks by a third.
On June 27, 1958, he retired the first 26 Senators. Pinch-hitter Ed Fitz Gerald doubled on a curveball. "In later years, I wished probably that it had happened."
Despite 33 starts in 1959 he didn't start a game of the World Series. Teammate Al Smith: "We all knew why Lopez didn't pitch him, but we never told anyone and I won't say now."
Traded to the Giants, he went 12-0 at Candlestick in 1962, shut out the Dodgers in the first playoff game, and saved the pennant-clincher two days later. "It was the biggest thrill of my life."
He retired one strikeout short of 2,000, to be with his growing children.
He thought about studying medicine at Michigan but signed with his hometown Tigers for $15,000.
He was on Detroit's roster at 18 in 1945, pitched 10 innings all year, and got a World Series ring.

He hurt his back at Buffalo in 1946 and spent time in Ford Hospital. In November 1948 he learned from a disc jockey that the Tigers had traded him to the White Sox for catcher Aaron Robinson and $10,000.
He blamed a hip injury for his slump in 1959. Charles Comiskey appealed to Al López to start him in the World Series, without success.

Word around the league was that his hip and shoulder were shot, and in November 1961 the White Sox traded him and Don Larsen to the Giants for three players. In the 1962 postseason he won two, saved one and had a 1.44 ERA.
In 1961 he broke Ed Walsh's White Sox strikeout record. In 1963 sportswriters named him the Giants' top managerial prospect, but he never coached.
p: At 10 he refused to have his tonsils out until his parents offered him a major-league baseball and a good glove.
He didn't drink: "I could go along and have a Coke." Giants coach Larry Jansen: "the nicest man you'd ever want to meet."
He spent his off-seasons helping run his father's pharmacy in Detroit, and as a White Sox scout he discovered Ron Kittle.
The Nellie Fox Society renamed itself the Billy Pierce Society after Fox got into the Hall of Fame, and in 2007 the White Sox unveiled his statue.
His father, Walter, was a pharmacist.
He married Gloria McCreadie, whom he had dated since high school, in October 1949; they had three children. Once he had to tell Marty Marion to change the bunt sign because Gloria had figured it out.

After baseball he was a White Sox TV analyst, a car dealership partner and a stockbroker, then worked for Continental Envelope from 1974 to 1997. He ran Chicago Baseball Cancer Charities after Nellie Fox's death, and died of gallbladder cancer in 2015 at 88.

c: He left Fresno State after three appearances and went to Antelope Valley College, where coach Ted Henkel helped push his fastball into the 90s. The Royals took him in the first round in 1987.
In 1993 he led the AL with a 2.56 ERA and finished third for the Cy Young. When injuries took away his fastball, his slider and forkball kept him a top starter.
As of 2018 he was the Royals' career strikeout leader, with 1,458.

He helped the 2000 "Moneyball" A's to a division title, then signed with the Mets for four years and $42 million. A year later they traded him to Anaheim for Mo Vaughn, and he won a ring with the 2002 Angels.
Kansas City took him in the first round in 1987 after he went 11–6 at Antelope Valley College.
In 1996 he won an arbitration raise to just over $5 million.
In 1997 he signed a long-term extension, then a torn labrum cost him nearly all of 1998. In 1999, losing faith in the Royals, he asked for a trade.
He lost his only start in the 2000 Division Series. After one season with the Mets they traded him to Anaheim for Mo Vaughn.

He went 14–12 for the 2002 champions but struggled in the postseason, allowing 15 earned runs in 21⅔ innings. A torn flexor tendon in his elbow got him released in July 2003, and he finished with the Royals.
In October 2005 he applied for reinstatement and signed a minor-league deal with Seattle.
p: He was raised by his mother, an accountant, in Lancaster, California.
After baseball he moved full time to his soybean farm in Paola, Kansas. His son Garrett won three Division II national titles in the shot put.
He married Deann in 1987; they divorced in 1994. Since 1996 he has been married to Laurie, and they have three children: Garrett, Britney and Evelyn.

c: The Cubs' scout called him unsignable out of high school: his father, a lawyer, wanted $250,000. He went to Stanford, won a national title as a freshman, and wrote his senior thesis on the economics of signing out of high school versus college.
At the 1993 All-Star Game in Baltimore he warmed up in the ninth on his own and never got in, and the AL team left the field to boos from his home fans.

He took a no-hitter into the eighth or later four times without ever finishing one. Twice he was within an out or two of a perfect game: Sandy Alomar Jr. singled with one out in the ninth in 1997, and Carl Everett with two outs in 2001.
In Game 7 of the 2003 ALCS he made the first relief appearance of his career, came in with runners on the corners and no outs, and got a strikeout and a double play.
He won 20 for the first time in his last start, in 2008, at 39, and retired, one of only three pitchers to retire after a 20-win season. He was elected to the Hall of Fame in 2019.
He got the nickname "Moose" in Little League from the first syllable of his last name. At 10 he pitched for the Johnny Z's Restaurant team.

The Dodgers offered to fly him to meet Peter O'Malley. Baltimore took him in the 11th round in 1987 without making an offer, then in the first round in 1990, signing him for $225,000. His Stanford senior thesis was on the economics of signing out of high school versus college.
After the 1993 All-Star snub, Cito Gaston got death threats from Baltimore fans for years. Mussina missed time that summer with a sore shoulder.

After a 20-minute brawl, though not visibly hurt, he gave up 16 runs over three starts and missed six weeks with shoulder and back pain. In 1995 he won the game in which Cal Ripken broke Lou Gehrig's record.
In early 1997 he took a below-market three-year, $21 million deal. That postseason he struck out a record 15 in an ALCS game.
In the 1997 Division Series he twice outdueled Seattle's Randy Johnson.
In 1998 a Sandy Alomar Jr. liner broke his nose. After 2000 he signed with the Yankees for six years and $88.5 million. In the 2001 World Series he went 0–1 against Arizona.
p: As a boy he taped a strike zone on the basement wall; wild pitches hit the radiator and woke the family. He reportedly finished fourth in his class on purpose, since the top three had to speak at graduation.
Joe Paterno offered him a chance to play football at Penn State as a placekicker.
After a 1996 plane crash killed 16 students and 5 chaperones from Montoursville, he pitched the rest of the season with the 21 names written on the bill of his cap.
He appeared in the crossword documentary Wordplay. Back home he coaches the Montoursville High boys' basketball team: "I'm just Mike."
His father was a lawyer and his mother, Ellie, a nurse. His brother Mark became a sports radio host.
Mark later took over the Montoursville basketball job, and Mike came back to it in 2025.
He married Jana McKissick, a Montoursville woman two years ahead of him in school, on November 1, 1997, and adopted her daughter, Kyra. They had two sons, Brycen and Peyton.

c: Overuse in high school gave him a stress fracture in his elbow that took surgery and two screws, and he went undrafted in 2004. He went to Stetson, which noticed him at a wood-bat tournament in Jupiter, Florida.
The Padres traded him to Cleveland in a three-team deal for Jake Westbrook in 2010. He had an 18-24 minor-league record and wasn't one of San Diego's top 30 prospects.
He learned his two-seam sinker during a rain-induced bullpen session at Triple-A Columbus in 2012, on pitching coach Ruben Niebla's advice.
On May 13, 2015, he struck out 18 Cardinals in eight innings, tying Bob Feller's 77-year-old club record.
He won a second Cy Young in 2017, then 20 games in 2018. After two injury-wrecked years he threw a no-hitter for the Yankees in 2021 against the Rangers, his team the year before.
He threw a two-seam sinker and a breaking ball somewhere between a slider and a curve, and was known for his stoicism on the mound.
His high school coach, Don English, overused him. San Diego drafted him in the fourth round in 2007 with a $200,000 bonus.
He won the 2014 Cy Young over Félix Hernández, the lowest-drafted AL winner since Bret Saberhagen. In April 2015 he signed a team-friendly five-year, $38.5 million extension.
In the 2016 postseason he had a 1.83 ERA in six starts, striking out nine in six shutout innings of World Series Game 1, but the Cubs won Game 7.
A lower-back strain put him on the disabled list in May 2017. He started twice in that year's Division Series against the Yankees amid speculation he had hurt his back again, which he denied.
A line drive broke his right arm in May 2019. Cleveland traded him to Texas for Emmanuel Clase, and a torn teres major muscle ended his 2020 season.
He pitched for Tampa Bay in 2022 and Boston in 2023, where shoulder inflammation sidelined him. He retired in February 2024.
p: He and his wife Amanda have four children and live in Winchester, Massachusetts.
In 2025 Cleveland hired him back as a special assistant for pitching.

c: In his first Negro League game against Roy Campanella, his manager ordered a knockdown. The pitch wasn't inside enough and Campanella hit it out. They became lifelong friends.

Signed by Branch Rickey, he and Campanella couldn't play in the Three-I League, whose president reportedly said he'd rather close the league than integrate it. Buzzie Bavasi took them at Nashua: "we don't care what color they are."
At the 1947 camp in Havana the Dodgers put the four Black players in a third-rate hotel; Newcombe found a cockroach in his soup and lost 35 pounds. Two years later he was Rookie of the Year.
Carl Erskine: Jackie Robinson rattled him to make him pitch better, and Campanella soothed him. In turn, word got around that Newcombe would retaliate if pitchers threw at them.

In 1956 he went 27-7 and won the first Cy Young and the MVP. In the World Series he was knocked out twice by Yogi Berra homers, left the ballpark both times, and the first time assaulted a parking-lot attendant.
He hit .271 with 15 home runs in his career and was used as a pinch-hitter, a rarity for a pitcher.
His junior high coach didn't want to let him pitch. At 17, in a barbershop over checkers, he met a friend of Newark Eagles owner Abe Manley, and he quit high school to pitch for $170 a month.
Effa Manley never got compensation from Rickey and resented it. At Nashua he and his wife and the Campanellas were reportedly the only Black people in town; Walter Alston was his manager.
Upset at being sent back to Montreal in 1949, he went home and had to be talked into returning by his wife. Burt Shotton called him a fire-eater who "couldn't keep his mouth shut."
In 1949 he became the first Black pitcher to start a World Series game.
He used his 1949 Series share as a down payment on a house in Colonia, New Jersey, and worked offseasons at a men's clothing store in New York.

He was relieved by Ralph Branca in the ninth of the 1951 playoff game. After two years in the Army he went 20–5 in 1955. In 1958 the Dodgers traded him to Cincinnati, and he finished with Cleveland and in Japan with Chunichi.
p: At 15 he lied about his age to enlist in the Army; when it was discovered, his father had to come get him. His father had hoped he'd become a boxer.

He called himself "a stupefied, wife-abusing, child-frightening, falling-down drunk." He went bankrupt and pawned his World Series ring; Peter O'Malley bought it back for him. He quit drinking in 1966 when his wife threatened to leave with their son.
He helped others with substance abuse, including military personnel and teammate Maury Wills. At a fundraiser he attended, Barack Obama called him "someone who helped... America become what it is."
