"I think it shortened my major-league career by about six or seven years. I would like to have made the Hall of Fame, where I think I belong."
His father was a chauffeur for a wealthy family for 28 years. A sister, Dolly, died at 8.
He married Freddie Green in 1945; they had three children and divorced in 1960. A week later he married Billie Roberts, until 1994, and his third wife, Karen Kroner, survived him.
In 1965 he pawned his World Series ring for drinking money. He quit in 1966 when his wife threatened to leave. He later served as the Dodgers' director of community affairs.

c: His fastball topped out at 86 mph as a high school senior and 87 his first year at Old Dominion, where he broke the conference strikeout record. The Tigers took him second overall in 2004.
On July 4, 2006, he, Joel Zumaya and Fernando Rodney all threw multiple pitches over 100 mph in the same game, a first in MLB history.
In 2011 he threw his second no-hitter and won the pitching Triple Crown, a unanimous Cy Young and the MVP.
He could add velocity late in games: from 2008 on he threw pitches over 100 mph in the eighth inning or later 44 times.
The Tigers traded him to Houston seconds before the waiver deadline in 2017. He was ALCS MVP and won the World Series, then married Kate Upton in Tuscany two days later.
After missing almost two full seasons to injury, he came back in 2022, won 18 games with an ERA under 2.00, and took his third Cy Young and second ring.
At Old Dominion he set the school and conference career strikeout records, and he helped the US win silver at the 2003 Pan American Games. He signed with Detroit in October 2004.
In Game 1 of the 2006 World Series he and the Cardinals' Anthony Reyes were the first two rookies to face each other in a Series opener.
Before 2013 he signed for seven years and $180 million, the most ever for a pitcher. He threw 30 straight scoreless postseason innings against Oakland, a record against one team.
He had core muscle surgery in January 2014 and said he never fully recovered that season. A triceps strain ended his streak of seven Opening Day starts in 2015.
Pablo Sandoval homered twice off him in Game 1 of the 2012 World Series, and the Giants swept.
He signed with the Mets in December 2022, was traded back to Houston in 2023, and pitched for the Giants in 2025. In 2026 he returned to Detroit and announced he would retire after the season.
p: His parents wrote a 2012 book about raising him, Rocks Across the Pond. His younger brother Ben played in the Tigers' system.
In 2013 he started the Wins for Warriors Foundation for military veterans and gave it more than $1 million.
He and Kate Upton have a daughter and a son, born in 2025.

c: His father, a coal miner, learned the knuckleball after arm trouble and taught it to Phil at 8. His only high school loss came on a home run by Bill Mazeroski.
Released at Class D Wellsville in 1959, he refused to go: "I'm not going! Harry, I need to play." He had pictured ending up in a coal mine like his dad. The manager gave him another chance.

In 1979 he went 21-20, the first NL pitcher since 1905 to win and lose 20 in a season, and tied his brother Joe for the league lead in wins. Their father: "I'm proud of them and glad that they don't have to work for a living."
The Braves pushed him to retire after 1983. "I was born a Brave, and I wanted to die a Brave." He won 16 for the Yankees at 45.

Going for his 300th win in 1985 he threw no knuckleballs until the last pitch, a strikeout of Jeff Burroughs, as a tribute to his father, who was in the hospital. He was the oldest pitcher ever to throw a shutout.
He holds the record for wins after turning 40, with 121.

Braves scout Bill Maughn offered $275 a month, and his father negotiated a $500 bonus. He called signing in the family kitchen, with his parents, Joe and Phyllis there, his greatest thrill in baseball.
When Warren Spahn was sold before 1965, Niekro hoped for a rotation spot, but the Braves started him in the bullpen.
He lost his only start in the 1969 NLCS to Tom Seaver as the Mets swept.

He asked to manage the Braves before they hired Bobby Cox, and was passed over. After 1983, with Joe Torre and pitching coach Bob Gibson deciding he should retire, he asked for his release rather than take a job.

In September 1984 the Yankees traded for his brother Joe. During Phil's 300th win, George Steinbrenner had the radio broadcast piped by phone to their mother at the hospital where their father lay ill.
Released by the Yankees in March 1986, he pitched for Cleveland and Toronto, then signed back with Atlanta in September 1987. He played 24 seasons without reaching a World Series, a record.
p: His backyard catchers were his sister Phyllis and his boyhood friend John Havlicek.

He met his wife Nancy, a stewardess, on a charter flight in 1965 and told a teammate, "I'm going to marry that girl." They married twice in one weekend because the minister had left something out of the first ceremony.
He managed the Colorado Silver Bullets, an all-women's pro team, and became the "Godfather of the Knuckleball," mentoring Tim Wakefield and R.A. Dickey.
His parents' tombstone has a baseball on top inscribed 539, the brothers' combined wins.
His father's parents were Polish immigrants, and both died before his father was 5. His father had pitched semipro ball and learned the knuckler from another coal miner.
He and Nancy had three sons, Philip, John and Michael. A restaurant at Coolray Field is named for him. He had prostate cancer and died in his sleep in December 2020 at 81.

c: He was Rookie of the Year in the Mexican League with Ciudad Juárez in 1981. The Brewers bought his contract in 1983, and in 1985 he beat out Japanese pitcher Yutaka Enatsu for a rotation spot.

In 1986 he went 20-11, the first 20-win season by a Mexican-born pitcher in the AL. At the All-Star Game, Fernando Valenzuela struck him out for his fifth straight strikeout, tying Carl Hubbell's record.
In 1987 he set Brewers records with 240 strikeouts and 32 straight scoreless innings. Over his first four seasons he went 69-38.
Milwaukee signed him for four years and $13.1 million in 1990; the next year he tore his rotator cuff, and after several surgeries he missed all of 1992.
Injuries began early. Back surgery and sprained ankles limited him to 22 starts in 1989.
After the Brewers didn't offer him a contract in 1995, he tried a comeback with San Diego.
p: He was pitching coach for Mexico in three World Baseball Classics and entered the Mexican Professional Baseball Hall of Fame in 2011.

c: His high school had no baseball team. As a junior he gathered more than 700 signatures and found a field and coaches, and was still turned down, so he played summer ball against college-age men. His hometown Royals drafted him and paid him $17,500.

The Royals traded him to the Mets in 1987 for catcher Ed Hearn, who played 13 more big-league games. Keith Hernandez "made me feel more welcome in one day than the Royals had in six years." In 1988 he went 20-3.
In the last game of the 1991 season he struck out 19, tied for the second-most ever in a game.
Back from an aneurysm in Game 3 of the 1996 World Series, he loaded the bases. Joe Torre asked if he was okay, and he said yes. "I lied. But I had to make him believe my lie." Fred McGriff popped up.

He threw a perfect game on Yogi Berra Day in 1999, with Don Larsen watching. His ten years between 20-win seasons is a record. In 2000 he went 4-14, a season chronicled in Roger Angell's book A Pitcher's Story.
When his fastball slowed in his 30s he called himself "a finesse pitcher without the finesse," inventing arm angles and pitches on the spot.

At 16 he was invited to a Royals tryout and also tried out for the Cardinals. His father and Royals scout Carl Blando had known each other since childhood, and Kansas City drafted him in the third round in 1981.
He was called up on June 8, 1986, five years to the day after the draft, to replace a concussed Mark Gubicza. That winter he helped Ponce win the Puerto Rican pennant.
A day after making the 1987 team he was traded to the Mets, crushing for a hometown kid, and maybe the worst trade in Royals history. His first bullpen session made Mel Stottlemyre's jaw drop.
As a Daily News guest columnist in the 1988 NLCS he wrote that Orel Hershiser "was lucky for eight innings" and mocked Jay Howell. The Dodgers hit him for five runs in two innings in Game 2.
In Game 5 of the 1995 Division Series his 147th pitch walked in the tying run, and Seattle won in the 11th.
He won five World Series and had a 2.12 ERA in Series play. His memoir, Full Count, was a best seller.
p: His father, a mechanic, put floodlights in the backyard for Wiffle Ball games, at "Conedlestick Park." As a teenager he wanted to be a sportswriter, like his hero Oscar Madison of The Odd Couple.
He tore his ACL in 1983 and spent four months cutting rubber strips at a conveyor-belt company, worried he'd end up doing manual labor like his father.
The "Coneheads" wore pointy rubber heads in the left-field upper deck at Shea and hung an orange traffic cone for every strikeout.
As a broadcaster for YES and ESPN he's known for sabermetric analysis, and for the occasional recitation of "Rapper's Delight."

His mother was a secretary and travel agent. When a neighbor made armed death threats after a fight with David's brother, his father shot the man with a .22, a superficial wound. David, 14, learned not to "be bullied by anybody."
In basketball he once hit an opponent with the metal guard on his injured finger after fouling out.

In 1991 he was falsely accused of rape, and police cleared him within 72 hours. Three women sued, saying he threatened them at the ballpark and later that he lured them to the Shea bullpen in 1989 and masturbated in front of them. The sexual claims were dismissed; one woman settled over his calling her a "groupie."
He married Lynn DiGioia, an interior designer, in 1994. They had a son, Brian, in 2006 and divorced in 2011. He has another son, Sammy, born in December 2011.

c: An all-conference tight end, he had football offers, including one from UCLA, and signed to play both sports at Hawaii. Instead Cleveland took him 20th overall in 1998.
He was named to the 2000 U.S. Olympic team but was called up by Cleveland before the Games. In 2001 he was the youngest player in the majors.
Traded to Milwaukee in mid-2008, he helped the Brewers to their first playoffs in 26 years. The Indians got to pick the player to be named later, and took Michael Brantley.
His seven-year, $161 million deal with the Yankees was then the biggest ever for a pitcher. He won the 2009 World Series and was ALCS MVP.

Losing velocity and struggling with his knees and alcoholism, he reinvented himself as a control pitcher in his late 30s. He retired with 251 wins and over 3,000 strikeouts, and was elected to the Hall of Fame in 2025.
He signed with Cleveland for a $1.3 million bonus. In 2001, at 21, he became the second-youngest pitcher to win a Division Series game, after Fernando Valenzuela.
He struggled against Boston in the 2007 ALCS. With him headed for free agency, Cleveland traded him to Milwaukee in July 2008, and he and his wife took out a thank-you ad to Cleveland fans.

His complete game on the last day of 2008 clinched Milwaukee's wild card. He started Game 2 of the NLDS on three days' rest for the fourth straight time, and Mike Cameron said he "had nothing left." ESPN later ranked him the best deadline acquisition ever.
He wrote in his memoir that one unexpected plus of the trade was joining a roster with several other Black players.
In the 2010 ALCS he had a 5.63 ERA as Texas beat the Yankees. That winter he had surgery for a torn meniscus in his right knee.
p: On the eve of the 2015 playoffs he checked into an alcohol treatment center: "I want to take control of my disease, and I want to be a better man, father and player."
His PitCCh In Foundation helped renovate the field at Vallejo High, which now bears his name. Cleveland named a field for him in 2021.
A blocked coronary artery was found in 2018, and he had a stent put in. He then lost 60 pounds.
His son Carsten III was drafted by the Brewers in 2026 and signed on his father's birthday.
He and Amber have four children. The family lived in Fairfield, near his hometown of Vallejo, until he signed with the Yankees.
Before checking into rehab he had been binge drinking in the team hotel in Baltimore and drinking in the clubhouse after a rainout. In 2016 he wrote about his alcoholism for The Players' Tribune.

c: His father, a Negro Leagues star, didn't want him to play, thinking a Black man had little chance; his mother won out. He married in Mexico City in 1961, and when Cuba banned travel, his father advised him not to come home.
Called up in 1964, he was told he'd pitch the next day against Whitey Ford, and threw a four-hit shutout with 11 strikeouts.
In 1968 he had a 1.60 ERA and struck out 19 Twins in 10 innings. Denny McLain said they'd both be chasing 30 wins if Tiant had Detroit's hitting.

The Twins released him in 1971, believing he was finished at 30. In Boston a columnist compared signing him to throwing money off Pier 4. A year later he won the ERA title, and Fenway chanted "Loo-Eee" through every pitch.
In Game 4 of the 1975 World Series he threw 163 pitches for a complete-game win. Roger Angell named his windups, including "Call the Osteopath" and "The Runaway Taxi."
When Boston let him go to the Yankees after 1978, Carl Yastrzemski said he cried: "They tore out our heart and soul."
His 49 shutouts are the most by any pitcher not in the Hall of Fame.

Bobby Ávila scouted him in Cuba. He signed in 1959 for $150 a month with the Mexico City Tigers, and Cleveland bought him for $35,000 in 1961. At Charleston, he said, "I couldn't speak very good English but I understand racism."
In December 1969 he was traded to the Twins in the deal that sent Graig Nettles and Dean Chance to Cleveland. In 1970 he won his first six decisions, then fractured his scapula.

Released by Minnesota, he got only a 30-day trial with Atlanta's Triple-A club, then signed with Boston's Louisville affiliate. The Red Sox trade of Sparky Lyle in 1972 probably saved his roster spot.
He threw a five-hit shutout in Game 1 of the 1975 World Series. He held out in spring 1977 after watching teammates cash in on free agency.
He was a minor-league pitching coach for the Dodgers and White Sox, coached Nicaragua at the 1996 Olympics, and went 55–97 as coach at Savannah College of Art and Design.
p: After 14 years apart, his parents were allowed out of Cuba in 1975 after Sen. George McGovern carried a letter to Fidel Castro. His father threw out a first pitch at Fenway, a knuckleball for a strike. Both parents died in December 1976, two days apart.
He'd step out of the shower with a cigar, look in the mirror and declare himself a "good-lookeen sonofabeech." He called Yastrzemski "Polacko" and Fisk "Frankenstein."
Tommy John said Tiant could keep a cigar lit all night on the bus, even in the shower. He later launched his own cigar brand, El Tiante.
He returned to Cuba in 2007, a trip told in the documentary The Lost Son of Havana.
He was an only child. He and Maria married in August 1961 after a short courtship.
They had three children: Luis Jr., Isabel and Daniel.

His mother had visited him in Mexico City in 1968; his father was reportedly jailed until she returned. His father died in December 1976 after a long illness, and two days later his mother died in her chair, though she hadn't been sick.
He wrote two autobiographies and died at his home in Wells, Maine, in October 2024 at 83.

c: He started out in the outfield, became a pitcher after a growth spurt, and was the Mets' first-round pick, fourth overall, in 1967.

He gave up Roberto Clemente's 3,000th and last hit in 1972: "I had no idea he was sitting on 2,999. I was just an oblivious rookie." He was Rookie of the Year that season, with his locker between Tom Seaver's and Jerry Koosman's.
In May 1973 a line drive fractured his skull, and he was carried off on a stretcher. He pitched again 11 days later, then held the Big Red Machine to two hits in Game 2 of the NLCS.
In the 1973 World Series he allowed four earned runs in 16⅔ innings; the only two homers Oakland hit all Series came off him in Game 7.
He shared the 1975 All-Star MVP with Bill Madlock, the only time it's been split. In 1976 he threw nine shutout innings against J.R. Richard and got no decision.
He was on the players' negotiating committee during the 1981 strike, and later wondered if his reduced role in Texas was payback. He spent 15 years as the Tigers' minor-league pitching coordinator.
He married his high school sweetheart, Diana, the year he started at Williamsport. Later he went 14–7 as Tidewater won the International League title.
A Jerry Koosman injury opened a rotation spot for him in 1971.
In the 1973 NLCS he two-hit the Big Red Machine. In Game 1 of the World Series he allowed three hits in six innings but lost 2–1 on an error.
After going 7–15 in 1977, he was traded to Texas in an 11-player, four-team deal in March 1978. He went 15–13 with a 2.27 ERA, then had elbow surgery in 1979.
He was Detroit's pitching coach in 1996, when the Tigers lost 109 games, and was fired but stayed on as their minor-league pitching coordinator through 2011.
p: The oldest of eight, his middle name, Trumpbour, is his mother's maiden name, an old Dutch name from Saugerties, New York. He married his high school sweetheart, Diana.
His father died just before the 1969 season. "I had gone through revering my dad as a youngster to the teen years where I knew it all, and I hadn't really gotten beyond that when he died."
After baseball he tried commercial real estate and raising show horses in Texas before going back to coaching.
He and Diana had three children: Kristin, Jennifer and Dan, who played briefly for the Padres before injuries ended his career.

c: A Giants scout who was a delegate at the 1928 Democratic convention in Houston took a night off to see a Texas League game. Hubbell lost it in 11 innings, and the scout called John McGraw that night.
On May 8, 1929, he no-hit the Pirates. With two on and nobody out in the ninth after two errors, he struck out Lloyd Waner and started a double play on Paul Waner.
On July 2, 1933, he beat the Cardinals 1-0 in 18 innings, perfect in 12 of them, with no walks. That year he went 23-12 with a 1.66 ERA and won the MVP.
In the 1934 All-Star Game at the Polo Grounds he struck out Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig, Jimmie Foxx, Al Simmons and Joe Cronin in a row.
He won his last 16 decisions of 1936 and his first eight of 1937. Babe Ruth presented his 1936 MVP award between games of a doubleheader.
His 24 straight wins across 1936 and 1937 are the major-league record.
Years of screwballs left his left hand twisted, the palm facing out. "It isn't the break that fools the hitter, it's the change of speed."
He grew up on a pecan farm near Meeker, Oklahoma, and worked for an oil company after high school before starting at Cushing in 1923.

Detroit bought him after 1925, but at his first camp Ty Cobb and pitching coach George McBride told him to drop the screwball for fear of injuries. Fed up at Beaumont, he said he would quit for the oil business unless he was sold.
McGraw paid Beaumont $30,000 for him. In the 1933 World Series he won Game 4, 2–1 in 11 innings, as the Giants beat Washington.
He said the screwball began hurting his elbow in 1934, and by 1938 the pain was unbearable.
The Giants released him after the 1943 season.
Time's 1936 World Series cover story called it "a personal struggle between Hubbell and Gehrig," and said he had practiced as a boy by throwing stones at knotholes on a barn door.
p: Heywood Broun on his control: "There must be a skeleton in Hubbell's closet somewhere, perhaps a righthanded grandmother."
Bob Broeg called him "almost Lincolnesque in appearance," with "the longest shinbones in captivity." He was quiet, with a wry sense of humor.
He ran the Giants' farm system from 1944 until a stroke in 1977, then scouted part time. He died after a car crash in 1988, 30 years to the day after his friend Mel Ott died the same way.
He was one of seven children. Lucille died in 1967.
He married his high school sweetheart, Lucille, when he was 27; they had two sons, one a career Marine and the other a businessman. He later married Julia Stanfield of Casa Grande, Arizona.
He was the last player from McGraw's era still working in baseball. He died of blunt force injuries two days after the crash in Scottsdale.

c: At 5-foot-6½ he was passed over by nearly every scout. Phillies scout Jocko Collins later apologized: "I sure made a mistake with you, Shantzy." Shantz said he'd had doubts himself.
In his second big-league game, in 1949, he came in with the bases loaded and nobody out in the fourth, held Detroit hitless for nine innings though he walked seven, and won in the 13th.
Connie Mack forbade his knuckleball. In 1952 new manager Jimmie Dykes told him, "Throw the knuckleball. I am not Mr. Mack." He went 24-7 and won the MVP.
In the 1952 All-Star Game he struck out Whitey Lockman, Jackie Robinson and Stan Musial, and hoped to match Carl Hubbell's five in a row, but rain ended the game.
He won the first Gold Glove for pitchers in 1957 and won it every year after that he played, eight straight. Jim Kaat, who won 16, considered Shantz the better fielder.
In Game 7 of the 1960 World Series he held the Pirates to one hit for five innings. Then a sure double-play ball took a bad hop and struck Tony Kubek in the throat, and the Pirates came back.
His father, a Bethlehem Steel worker, had turned down a White Sox minor-league contract to play for love of the game. At 6 Bobby nearly died of a high fever, which may have stunted his growth.
He was a busboy at an aircraft plant and shined saws for $75 a week. In the Army he pitched against the Manila Dodgers, who gave him a tryout and turned him down.
Tony Parisse, a former A's catcher, told him not to sign a Class D contract, and A's scout Harry O'Donnell signed him to an A-ball deal in November 1947.

Catcher Joe Astroth, not Chief Bender, taught him the knuckleball. Late in 1952 Walt Masterson broke his left wrist with a pitch. Connie Mack had warned him that batting right-handed exposed his pitching hand.
In 1957 the A's traded him to the Yankees in a 13-player deal that included Clete Boyer. Later he went to Pittsburgh and Houston, and in 1964 the Cardinals included him in the Lou Brock trade.
p: Rejected by the draft board for being under 5 feet, he grew an inch and was sworn in; at Fort Knox his feet barely reached a tank's pedals, so he was moved to a mortar unit.
Before a charity game against bonus baby Curt Simmons, his manager smacked his swollen wrist with a book. "But, it worked!" Shantz won 4-1, and he and Simmons became golf buddies.
In 1964 his father ran out to the parking lot to turn off his car's headlights during a basketball game Bobby was playing in, came back, and died of a heart attack in his arms.
As of 2026 he's the last living Philadelphia Athletic and the oldest living MVP. He and Shirley were married 76 years.
He married Shirley Vogel and they had four children: Bobby, Kathy, Teddy and Danny. She died in May 2026. His brother Billy caught in the majors and coached for the Yankees.
He and Joe Astroth ran a bowling alley and dairy bar in Chalfont, Pennsylvania.

c: A basketball injury, crashing into the brick wall behind the basket, took away his fastball. After three days in a coal mine he hitchhiked to Chicago and dug ditches for the electric company.

Brooklyn's catchers wouldn't call his knuckleball. Casey Stengel to Babe Phelps: "Don't you think it might be a little hard to hit, too?" At Atlanta, catcher Paul Richards told him, "You keep throwing it, and it's my job to catch it."
"I just throw it straight forward like you'd flip a cigarette butt." The 1944 Senators had four knuckleballers, and catcher Rick Ferrell compared it to catching a butterfly.
Before the last game of 1944, a caller offered him close to $20,000 to let down against Detroit, which was fighting for the pennant. He told the caller where to go, reported it, and beat the Tigers.
At 37, sold to the Phillies, he went on a strict diet and lost 35 pounds. He pitched until he was 44, and Hoyt Wilhelm learned the knuckleball from a photo of his grip.
His Decatur team folded midseason in 1932, and he went home to drive a truck. Coach Otto Miller saw him throw a knuckler on the sidelines and told him to use it.

At Atlanta he went 13–3 with a league-best 2.29 ERA, with Paul Richards willing to call the knuckler. Brooklyn traded him to St. Louis, which sold him back to Atlanta two weeks later, and Washington drafted him for $7,500.
Writer Robert Ruark called him "a fat bald man." In 1942 he broke his ankle sliding into first in his second start.

He got a draft deferment because he had two children and supported his mother and sister. In 1945 his shoulder gave out in September, and he said Clark Griffith blamed him for losing the pennant and cut his pay.
He was the Cubs' pitching coach until the whole staff was fired after 1956.
p: His parents were Belgian, not Dutch. Elmore Leonard said he got his own nickname from him.
His rookie roommate, a fading Hack Wilson, ordered him to have a beer, then slapped it out of his hand, sobbing, and told him to stay away from booze.
After baseball he ran clinics for the Illinois Youth Commission, sometimes four a day, until he retired at 65: "If I can help just one kid go straight my job is worthwhile."
He was the oldest of five. His father was a coal miner who pushed him to find a better living.
He married Rose Dolene, 21, whose family lived a block away in Auburn. They had three children and were married nearly 49 years. He died of congestive heart failure in 1983 at 74.

c: As a 13-year-old in the right-field upper deck at Comiskey Park, he told his Boys Club friends he'd play out there one day, and they laughed. He made his big-league debut there in 1981, and called them.
He won a statewide drafting contest and a scholarship to study architectural drawing, but signed when the Blue Jays tripled their offer. He bought his mother a Ford Thunderbird.

In 1978 he hit .206 with two homers at Dunedin: "I believe my fielding is what kept me in the game until I learned how to hit." Cito Gaston later turned him from a pull hitter into one who drove the ball to all fields.
With George Bell and Lloyd Moseby he formed the AL's best outfield. Bobby Cox: "You can never play any better right field. It's impossible." In 1986 he led the majors with 40 homers.
He ranked second only to Chuck Klein in outfield assists per 1,000 innings and led AL outfielders in assists five times.
After hitting his 199th homer, he was robbed by Ken Griffey Jr. His next time up, he hit No. 200 off Randy Johnson and told the catcher, "If [Griffey] catches that one, I'm checking his urine."
As a high school junior he doubled off future No. 2 pick Bill Gullickson with Bobby Mattick watching; Mattick soon joined the new Blue Jays.
He hit the first home run in the history of the Knoxville Blue Jays in 1980, then broke his thumb.

He was the Blue Jays' first 20–20 player in 1985 and hit .280 with a homer in the ALCS loss to Kansas City, his only postseason. His $1.525 million salary in 1987 was the most ever for a Blue Jays position player.

The wrist he'd broken playing high school basketball grew worse, and he had surgery after Toronto's 1987 collapse. He and his wife had Dave Winfield to dinner to lobby him to veto a trade for Barfield. Toronto eventually traded him to the Yankees for Al Leiter.
Injuries forced him to retire at 32 in 1992. He tried a comeback with Houston in 1994, then coached for the Astros, Rangers and Mariners.
p: In 1986 a woman called to say she was his grandmother and that a man he'd known in the neighborhood was his biological father. "A father-son relationship is something I was deprived of."
He became a committed Christian at a Bible study at pitcher Roy Lee Jackson's home, and later led the Blue Jays' chapel services.
After baseball he designed custom furniture, like desks with ballparks carved into them and lamps made from bats, and holds 21 design patents. His son Josh played second base in the majors.
His mother, a seamstress, raised him and three half-siblings. Early in his career he said his priorities were "myself, money, and women," and he was quick to fight.
He married Marla Travis, of Houston, and their son Josh was born in Venezuela that December, while Jesse played winter ball.
Josh later played for the Padres and Cleveland.
In 2006 he was hospitalized with a head injury after his son Jeremy allegedly shoved him down a flight of stairs during a family argument. Jeremy was arrested for family assault.

c: He made Cal Poly as a walk-on, learned to switch-hit there, and became the starter when the regular shortstop broke his leg.
As a rookie he dove for a ball up the middle; it took a bad hop behind him, and he caught it barehanded in midair, bounced up and threw out Jeff Burroughs.
He started 1979 0-for-32 and didn't reach .200 until August. "I may not drive in 100 runs each year, but I can prevent 100 runs from scoring against us."
He used his no-trade clause to balk at the 1981 trade to St. Louis until Whitey Herzog talked him into it. "Some people would call it hot-dogging, but I call it flair."
His walk-off homer off Tom Niedenfuer won Game 5 of the 1985 NLCS, his first homer ever from the left side, and Jack Buck told Cardinals fans to "Go Crazy."
His 8,375 assists are the most by any player at any position. Bud Harrelson: "If any other shortstop misses a ball, your first thought is, 'Would Ozzie have had it?'"
Detroit drafted him, but he wanted a $10,000 bonus and the Tigers offered $8,500, so he went back for his senior year. San Diego took him in the fourth round in 1977 for $5,000.
His wife was a producer for a San Diego radio talk show, which may have figured in his reluctance to leave.
He waived the no-trade clause and was traded to the Cardinals for Garry Templeton.
He hit .208 in the 1982 World Series, .087 in the 1985 Series loss to Kansas City and .214 against the Twins in 1987. His walk-off in 1985 was his only postseason homer.
He hurt his rotator cuff in 1985. In 1987 he hit .303, his only .300 season, and finished second to Andre Dawson for MVP. Shoulder surgery cost him three months in 1995.
He clashed with Tony La Russa in 1996 and retired after the season. He came back to the organization after La Russa left, as a spring instructor in 2012.
p: As a boy in Watts he bounced a rubber ball off concrete steps to sharpen his reflexes, and practiced flips into sawdust piles at a lumberyard. During the Watts riots the family slept on the floor.
He voiced himself on The Simpsons, falling into the Springfield Mystery Spot, and called it one of the highlights of his career.
In 2012 he sold all 13 of his Gold Gloves at auction for more than $500,000.
He played the Wizard in the St. Louis Muny's 2001 production of The Wizard of Oz.

He was the second of six children. His father was a sandblaster at an Air Force base, then a Safeway delivery driver, and his mother a nursing-home aide. His parents divorced when he was in junior high.
He married Denise Jackson in November 1980; they had three children, Nikko, Dustin and Taryn, and divorced in 1996.
He opened a restaurant in 1988, a youth sports academy in 1990, and a salad dressing brand in 2008, and wrote a children's book.

c: He and his cousin Carmelo pitched rocks and bottle caps to each other; the caps curved like breaking balls. He came to a Mariners tryout at 20 straight from a night shift at a factory and signed for $4,000.
He didn't stick in the majors until he was 27. Sent back and forth to Calgary, "I never got frustrated. I was doing what I really liked."
Every new shipment of bats got weighed on a little kitchen scale, with the weight written on the knob. In 1992 he led the majors at .343.

He tore a muscle stealing a base in a 1993 exhibition at BC Place, where the infield dirt was loose sand after a Guns N' Roses concert. He became a full-time DH, and in 1995 led the majors in OBP and OPS.
His double in the 11th inning of Game 5 of the 1995 ALDS, "The Double," beat the Yankees and helped win public support for a new Seattle ballpark.
Mariano Rivera said Martinez was the only hitter he didn't want to face: "He had my breakfast, lunch and dinner." He hit .579 against him.
He studied business administration and worked as a furniture store supervisor by day and in a General Electric factory at night. Scouts watched his cousin Carmelo, not him.
Mariners scout Marty Martínez, no relation, finally signed him at a tryout camp in Dorado when he was 20.
At Bellingham he knew only enough English to order in a restaurant. A bad hop broke his nose in Tempe, and in 1988 he won the PCL batting title at .363.

He played 1990 on a torn knee ligament and had surgery after the season. In 1992 he got a three-year, $10 million deal, the biggest in team history then, but bone spurs in his shoulder ended his year in September.
In 1993 he missed 42 games. In his first at-bat of 1994, Dennis Martínez hit him in the right wrist.
In 1995, after Griffey went down on May 26, he hit 25 of his 29 homers and drove in 97 of his 113 runs.
A ruptured hamstring tendon needed surgery in 2002, and a foul ball broke his toe in 2003.
Pedro Martínez named him one of the toughest hitters he faced because he "would foul off pitches that would wipe out anybody else."
p: When his parents reconciled and called the kids back to New York, he locked himself in his room and stayed with his grandparents in Puerto Rico: "I felt my grandparents needed me."
Strabismus made his right eye wander. He did 30 minutes of eye exercises before every game, and the team optometrist had him batting tennis balls while doing math problems.
He starred in Mariners commercials, including one where he made a lamp out of a bat. "I never got the bat lamp." Seattle named the street by the ballpark Edgar Martinez Drive on his last day.
He and his wife Holli founded a foundation that gives scholarships to students of color training to be teachers.
He married Holli Beeler, a Seattle Pacific student, in October 1992. Soon afterward his grandfather died.
They met on a blind date in 1991 and live in Kirkland, Washington, with their three children.
He co-founded Plaza Bank, Washington's first Hispanic bank, in 2005, and a merchandise company he sold in 2010.

c: A catcher who "couldn't hit a lick," he was moved to the mound at 17. The Reds scout who signed him for $1,000: "Frankly, I wasn't impressed."
Scott Breeden taught him a changeup in the minors; Bill James called it one of the best ever. "I throw the changeup with the same motion that I throw the fastball."
For the 101-loss Reds in 1982 he struck out 274, breaking Luis Tiant's record for a Latino pitcher. Whitey Herzog: "If I had to build a pitching staff from scratch, I'd start with Soto."

In 1984 at Wrigley he charged an umpire over a disputed homer and was tackled by his own catcher, and then went after a fan with a bat. Three starts later he threw a ball into a brawl, hitting an umpire and a coach.
He taught Johnny Cueto and Edinson Vólquez their changeups.

He broke his elbow at the Reds' minor-league camp in 1974 and missed the season. After dropping the curveball that hurt his elbow, he led the Florida State League in ERA, innings and strikeouts in 1976.

In his first shutout, in 1977, he knocked down Bill Robinson on back-to-back brushbacks. Back pain landed him in the hospital in spring 1979, and he threw two scoreless innings in that NLCS, his only postseason.
Catcher Alex Trevino said he tended to get mad and lose focus in close games. When Ron Reed threw at him, he looked ready to sling his bat, and the benches emptied.

At Wrigley in 1984 he tackled Cubs coach Don Zimmer while going after the umpire, setting off a 10-minute brawl, and was suspended five games. In another fight, with Atlanta's Washington, he threw the ball and hit coach Joe Pignatano in the shin and drew a five-game suspension and $5,000 fine.
By 1986 a shoulder injury had wrecked his effectiveness.
p: His mother raised three children as a laundress: "We used to go down to the river at 6 in the morning, baskets of laundry on our heads." He quit school at 14 to work construction.
After shoulder trouble ended his career, he started a baseball school near his hometown of Baní in 1991 and became the Reds' director of Dominican operations.
As a boy he idolized Juan Marichal.

c: Scout Tom Couston, there to see another player, liked how hard the junior college shortstop hit the ball. He talked to Thome back to back so the other scouts wouldn't notice: "Don't look at me, keep looking into the distance." Cleveland took him in the 13th round.
Minor-league manager Charlie Manuel, watching The Natural, had him point the bat at the pitcher before every swing like Robert Redford, to relax him. The Indians' statue of Thome shows that pose.
On July 3, 1999, he hit a ball an estimated 511 feet off a pillar and onto Eagle Avenue, the longest home run in Indians history.
His 500th homer, in 2007, was a walk-off, the first time anyone reached 500 that way. Three days later he and his father drove 14 hours to deliver the ball to Cooperstown.
He hit Nos. 599 and 600 in the same game in 2011, the first to do that. Only Babe Ruth got to 600 in fewer at-bats.

He learned the game from his father on a tennis court and played basketball in a part of Peoria where he was the only white kid. At 175 pounds he drew little interest, and went undrafted out of high school.
Cleveland took him in the 13th round in 1989, as an afterthought.
Scout Tom Couston said the coach first sent over the wrong kid. In rookie ball Thome struggled with little power, and the next spring he was left in extended spring training.
He caught the final out of the 1995 clincher, Cleveland's first postseason since 1954, and hit four homers that postseason. In 2002 he broke Albert Belle's team record with 52.

The Phillies signed him for six years and $85 million after 2002. His mother died of lung cancer in January 2005, and elbow and back injuries held him to 59 games that year. With Ryan Howard emerging, he was traded to the White Sox.
He was traded back to Cleveland in August 2011, played for the Phillies and Orioles in 2012, and retired on a one-day Cleveland contract in 2014.
He is one of the few sluggers of the steroid era who was never suspected of using, and he denies ever using them.
p: As a boy at Wrigley he snuck into the Cubs' clubhouse looking for Dave Kingman's autograph. He came away with other players' signatures, which made him generous with fans later.
He wore his socks high in honor of his grandfather, a minor-leaguer who his dad said once homered off Bob Feller. His aunt is in the softball Hall of Fame.
Larry Bowa gave him the option to skip road trips. "He says: 'I like to ride the bus. I get to bond with my players.' I've never heard that in my life."
Joe Nathan called him "the world's nicest man." He set up funds to put his 10 nieces and nephews through college.
His father was a foreman at Caterpillar.
He and Andrea have two children, Lila and Landon; Landon was drafted 34th overall by the White Sox in 2026. In 2013 they pledged $100,000 for tornado relief near his hometown.
He raised more than $200,000 for the Children's Hospital in Peoria and another $200,000 for the United Way.

c: As a teenager he shined Vada Pinson's shoes in the Seattle Rainiers' clubhouse, and three years later he was playing against him. He took less money from the Cubs because he thought it was the fastest path to the majors.

At the end of a rookie camp, Rogers Hornsby told prospect after prospect they wouldn't make it. To Santo and Billy Williams: "You can hit in the big leagues right now." They were the only two who did.
In his debut in 1960, Smokey Burgess told him after a called strike, "That was a major-league curveball, kid." Santo singled on the next pitch.
In 1969 he started clicking his heels after every Cubs win. Gil Hodges told him he reminded him of a young Tug McGraw; the Mets passed the Cubs and Tom Seaver clicked his heels too.
His 164 games at third base in 1965 remain the major-league record.
His father drove a truck for an ice cream company and tended bar.
He grew up near Sicks Stadium in Seattle and worked there as a batboy, groundskeeper and clubhouse attendant. At 14 he made the Seattle team that went to the Babe Ruth World Series.

Cubs lead scout Johnson offered $20,000, less than other teams, and said he'd sign him as a catcher: "I don't think you can play third base in the big leagues." In the minors Grady Hatton fixed his throwing.
In the Cubs' College of Coaches, Don Zimmer said, one coach waved Santo deeper while another waved him in.
A Jack Fisher pitch broke his cheekbone and ended his playing streak. He came back wearing an improvised ear flap and set a club record with a 28-game hitting streak; ear flaps later became standard.
After the 1969 heel-clicking, Mets coach Joe Pignatano called him "bush," and Tom Seaver clicked his heels too.
In December 1973 he became the first player to veto a trade under the new ten-and-five rule, blocking a deal to the Angels.
He did Cubs radio on WGN from 1990 until his death, and raised more than $65 million for diabetes research.
p: He was diagnosed with diabetes just after high school and kept it secret until 1971, afraid it would look like an excuse. He later lost both legs below the knee to the disease and raised more than $60 million for research.
In 1970 he got a death threat warning he'd be killed if he played in New York, and sat out the series. His mother and stepfather were killed in a car crash in 1973 on their way to visit him.
Five old teammates, Banks, Jenkins, Hundley, Beckert and Williams, carried his casket, and his ashes were scattered on the field at Wrigley.
His parents divorced when he was young, and he grew close to his stepfather, John Constantino, whom he called Dad.
He married his high school sweetheart, Judy Scott, in January 1960. They had three children and divorced in 1982. He married Vicki the next year and lived in Bannockburn, Illinois.
He started a specialty insurance company and Santo's Pizzeria in Park Ridge.
He died of complications from bladder cancer and diabetes in 2010 at 70.

c: He lost his railroad job in the Depression and turned to baseball full time at 25, joining Ben Taylor's Baltimore Stars for a share of the gate. Teammates warned he'd starve.
Batting cleanup behind Josh Gibson, he was half of "The Thunder Twins." The Grays won nine straight Negro National League titles from 1937 to 1945, and another in 1948 when he was 40.

In 1943 Senators owner Clark Griffith asked him and Gibson if they could play in the majors. They said yes, and never heard from him again. "I think they believed we could play major league baseball but everyone hated to be the first."
Pitcher Dave Barnhill: "You could put a fastball in a shotgun and you couldn't shoot it by him." Monte Irvin: "they might have called Lou Gehrig the white Buck Leonard."
When the color line fell he was 40 and turned down Bill Veeck. "I'm not bitter. But it was too late for me." He went into the Hall of Fame in 1972.

At 17 he managed the Rocky Mount Black Swans. After losing his railroad job in 1932, he played for the Portsmouth Black Revels for $15 a week before Ben Taylor recruited him; he and his brother Charlie signed with Baltimore anyway.
When Baltimore went bankrupt in 1933, Dick Redding signed him for the Brooklyn Royal Giants. In 1934 Smoky Joe Williams, then tending bar in New York, recommended him to Grays owner Cum Posey.
He played the first Negro World Series against Kansas City with a taped broken hand, and hit .500 in the 1944 Series win over Birmingham.

In Mexico, where he was managed mostly by Martín Dihigo, teams played three games a week, which suited an aging player, though the water made him sick every year. In 1952, at 45, he turned down a big-league contract, fearing he'd embarrass himself and hurt the cause of integration.
He retired at 48 with arthritis in his back, after hurting his knee in his last season in Xalapa.
p: Rocky Mount had no high school for Black students, so he left school after eighth grade and worked in a hosiery mill, shined shoes and put brake cylinders on boxcars. Late in life he earned his high school diploma.
At about 7 he and his friends were arrested for peeking through the fence at the local white team's ballpark.

The Grays had no trainer. "I needed three stitches in my leg and they wouldn't put the three stitches in because I was going to lose some games." On the road they slept on newspapers to keep the bedbugs off.
His father, a railroad fireman, died in the 1918–19 flu epidemic, and his mother told him he'd have to work after school. He was one of six children.
On New Year's Eve 1937 he married Sandra Wroten, a widow whose first husband had been a funeral director. Her teaching income helped keep them afloat.
Back in Rocky Mount he washed cars at a garage, then worked 10 years as a truant officer and earned a real estate license by correspondence.
He later became vice president of a local minor-league team. He died in 1997 of complications from a stroke.

c: Osteomyelitis cost him part of a bone in his left foot as a boy, and he taught himself to run on the side of the foot. At a picnic he threw a ball 173½ feet; the judges made him throw again, and he threw 175.

After signing, he asked if he could still play in an amateur game he'd promised to play in. The scout let him, figuring a kid who wouldn't break a promise was special. His bonus paid off his parents' mortgage and his mother's eye surgery.
He went straight from high school to the Tigers. Ted Williams told him to swing a heavy bat and squeeze a baseball in the off-season, and he did it in the back room of a sporting goods store.
In 1955, at 20, he hit .340, one day younger than Ty Cobb had been, the youngest batting champion ever.
Back from a broken arm in 1968, he told Mayo Smith he didn't deserve to play in the World Series. Smith moved center fielder Mickey Stanley to shortstop to get him in, and Kaline hit .379.
Ernie Harwell and Yogi Berra both said he had the best outfield arm ever. He got his 3,000th hit in his hometown, Baltimore.
His father, a broom maker, had played semipro ball. In high school he broke his cheekbone playing football and quit, and coach Bill Anderson moved him from pitcher to center field.

Scout Ed Katalinas: "To me he was the prospect that a scout creates in his mind and then prays that someone will come along to fit the pattern." He signed for a $15,000 bonus, which paid off his parents' mortgage and his mother's eye surgery.
Under the bonus rule he had to stay on the big-league roster for two years, so he went straight from high school to the Tigers.
The Tigers briefly worked him at second base and shortstop before keeping him in the outfield.

He twisted his knee crashing into the seats and was hospitalized for five days; owner Spike Briggs had the seats removed. Later Briggs took offense when Kaline sent back a contract unsigned without a note.
In 1962 he broke his collarbone making a game-ending catch off Elston Howard and missed 57 games. His osteomyelitis foot hurt all through 1964, and he got corrective shoes.
He was a Tigers TV broadcaster from 1975 to 2002, mostly with George Kell, then special assistant to Dave Dombrowski until his death in 2020.
p: Out with a cheek injury in 1959, he demanded to play: "I don't bat or throw with my cheek." Once ejected for arguing a strike call, he went to the umpire after the game and apologized.
He and Gordie Howe went into business together selling auto parts design contracts.
He spent 67 years with the Tigers as a player, broadcaster and adviser, one of the longest tenures with one team in baseball history.
He married his high school sweetheart, Louise Hamilton, after the 1954 season. They had two sons, Mark and Michael.
His business partner Frank Carlin talked him and Gordie Howe into buying racehorses as a tax write-off; Kaline soon sold out to distance himself from betting.

c: In Plainview, Texas, in 1959, a man put a gun to his head and said he'd kill him if he played that night. He played, and later called it the moment he became a man.

Pirates management fined him for reporting at 235 pounds and put him on a crash diet; the next year he came in fit and his new manager called him too muscle-bound. Pie Traynor said if they'd quit worrying about his weight he'd be the team's greatest home run hitter.
Roberto Clemente talked him into a 38-ounce bat, and the move out of Forbes Field helped too. He led the majors with 48 homers in 1971.

Only 18 home runs ever cleared Forbes Field's right-field roof, and seven were his. Montreal painted the seat gold where his 535-foot homer landed. Don Sutton: "He didn't just hit pitchers. He took away their dignity."
As "Pops" he handed out gold stars for teammates' caps. In 1979, at 39, he shared the MVP, and his two-run homer in the sixth decided Game 7 of the World Series.
When Steve Blass lost his control, Stargell insisted on hitting first against him, without a helmet. "No one ever stood taller for me than Willie Stargell."
He is the only player to win the regular-season MVP, the NLCS MVP and the World Series MVP in the same year.
He had a serious football knee injury. Pirates scout Bob Zuk signed him for $1,500 in August 1958.
He nearly quit over the racism he faced in the minors, but letters from Zuk kept him going.
In 1971 he played with a knee injury that needed surgery after the season, and hit .132 in the postseason as the Pirates won the Series.
He led the majors in RBIs in 1973 and in OPS in 1973 and 1974. A broken rib in 1975 limited him to 124 games.
He wrecked his elbow in a 1977 brawl with the Phillies. In 1979 he hit .455 in the NLCS and .400 with three homers in the World Series.

He coached first base for Atlanta and was Chipper Jones's first minor-league hitting coach. At the 1985 Pittsburgh drug trials Dale Berra and John Milner said he handed out amphetamines; he strongly denied it.
p: His father left before he was born. Sent to an aunt in Orlando for six years, he was kept malnourished and spanked almost daily. He met his father at 19: "I accepted my father as he was."
In 1971 he pointed out that Black stars got few endorsements: "Clemente has been shaving for years. I eat cereal every morning."
He started the Black Athletes Foundation to raise awareness of sickle cell anemia. Joe Morgan: "There were 600 baseball players, and 599 of them loved Willie Stargell."
He died the morning of the first game at PNC Park in 2001, days after his statue was unveiled outside it.
His biracial grandfather, Will, whose own father had been enslaved, took him and his mother in until she remarried. His aunt Lucy intercepted the letters and money his mother sent him.
In 1976 his wife, Delores, had a brain aneurysm and spent six weeks in a coma. He missed significant time to care for her.
He opened a fried-chicken restaurant in Pittsburgh's Hill District, handed out T-shirts on Halloween and delivered turkeys to poor families at Christmas.
After years of kidney trouble he died of stroke complications in Wilmington, North Carolina.

c: Too poor to buy a ticket, he watched the Atlanta Crackers from trees outside the fence. They signed him as a pitcher at 15.
Working for Standard Oil in Memphis, he told John McGraw the Giants didn't mean anything to him: "I didn't come up here looking for a job." McGraw called back a month later and paid his $800 a month.
In the 1924 World Series he led all regulars with a .429 average; Walter Johnson said Terry was the hitter he least wanted to face.

When McGraw berated him after an error, Terry shot back, "You've been blaming other people for the mistakes you have made for 30 years." They didn't speak for two years, until McGraw asked him to take over as manager.
In 1930 he batted .401, and he's still the last National Leaguer to hit .400.

He loaded heavy flour sacks in the Atlanta railyards. The Crackers signed him in 1914 for his live fastball despite poor control, farmed him to Dothan and released him, and he bounced to Newnan and Shreveport.
Optioned to Toledo in 1922, he became the Mud Hens' player-manager that August.
The Giants bought him and Freddie Lindstrom from Toledo on the same day.
He was a hard bargainer, the last Giant to sign in 1925, and held out again in 1926. He couldn't stand McGraw's dictatorial ways.

He learned he'd replaced McGraw as manager in 1932 from a vendor who told writer Tom Meany; he had expected to hear he'd been traded. He traded Freddie Lindstrom, an old friend upset at being passed over.
In 1933, his first full year, he won the World Series over Washington. In 1934 his team blew a seven-game lead in September.
After 1933 the Giants gave him a five-year contract at $40,000 a year, matching McGraw's best salary.
He resigned as manager after 1941 and named Mel Ott his successor. In Jacksonville he bought the Double-A Braves in 1958.
p: He married Elvena Sneed at 18. He quit baseball in 1918 with a baby on the way and worked for a battery company.
He wouldn't give reporters his home phone number to protect his family, and they portrayed him as cold. Tom Meany joked that he raised white-faced cattle "so he can count their faces at night."
He turned down the Dodgers' managing job in 1953 because it would have cut his income. He had grown rich running a Buick dealership in Jacksonville.
His parents had an unhappy marriage and separated when he was in his mid-teens. He fell for Elvena Sneed as a teenager, and lived with her family until they married in November 1916.
He later moved from the battery company to a clerk's job with Standard Oil in Memphis and was promoted to sales.

c: His father made him a catcher as the fastest route to the majors and a left-handed hitter for the head start to first. In the minors he once beat the batter to first base and took the throw for the putout, and Eddie Sawyer moved him to center.
Commissioner Landis voided two earlier contracts, with Cleveland and the Cubs, which soured him on the game's integrity. One rookie writer: "He's no .300 hitter, he hits .100 and runs .200."

On the last day of 1950, with the score tied in the ninth, he threw out Cal Abrams at the plate to keep the Dodgers from forcing a playoff. Years later Abrams thanked him, since the play made him more famous than his career did.

George Sisler on one 1951 catch: "that's the greatest piece of center fielding I ever saw anywhere by any fielder. I still don't believe it." He's the only outfielder with four seasons of 500 putouts.
In 1958 he beat Willie Mays for the batting title on the last day, starting with a ball that bounced 50 feet in the air off home plate.
Elected in 1995 after a long fan campaign: "They didn't exactly carry me in here in a sedan chair with blazing and blaring trumpets."
His father ruled out football for fear of injury. Thirteen of the 16 big-league teams were interested in him before he went to Norfolk Junior College.

When he finally signed with the Phillies, scout Ed Krajnick said it was "about the most important deal I ever made." In the minors Eddie Sawyer moved him to center field, and his father eventually agreed.
One season ended in August when he broke a finger. A collision with Del Ennis in spring 1955 ended his streak of 731 straight games.
On August 17, 1957, a foul ball he hit broke the nose of Alice Roth, wife of the Bulletin's sports editor, in the stands. They became friends, and her son later served as a Phillies batboy.
The Phillies traded him to the Cubs in December 1959, a deal that looked bad as he played two good years in Chicago and one with the Mets.
p: Drafted in 1945, he was sent to Alaska: "like sending a dog sledder to the Sahara Desert."
He missed the births of all six of his children because they came during the season: "I was a miserable 0-for-6."
For 35 years he was the Phillies' broadcaster, puffing his pipe on the air, with lines like "Hard to believe, Harry." He died in his hotel room hours after calling a game in New York in 1997.
He met Herberta Cox at Norfolk Junior College, and returned to the Phillies a married man.
He was the American Cancer Society's Nebraska chairman during the offseason. His mother said he had planned to retire from broadcasting after 1997.

c: His first glove was a first baseman's mitt made from a horse collar, and he riveted cleats onto his dress shoes for his first spikes.
A Winston-Salem manager, seeing the 5-foot-6 rookie, asked if they expected him to win a pennant with that. Haddix went 19-5 and was the league MVP.
In 1954 a line drive by Joe Adcock hit him below the knee: "I was never the same after that."

Pitching with the flu on May 26, 1959, he retired the first 36 Braves, then lost in the 13th after an error, an intentional walk and a hit by Joe Adcock. "All I know is we lost. What is so historic about that?"
He won Game 7 of the 1960 World Series in relief: "That was the only time in my life I was really nervous."

As the Mets' pitching coach he was the first big-league coach for Tom Seaver, Nolan Ryan and Jerry Koosman. Ryan: "Harvey could not have been, from my perspective, more of the right person at the right time for me."
His parents farmed near Westville, Ohio, and his father was a well-known amateur pitcher. His brother Ben played for Walter Alston's Springfield Cardinals.
A farm deferment kept him out of World War II. He was later drafted into the Army and served as athletic director at Fort Dix in 1951 and 1952.
In May 1956 the Cardinals traded him to the Phillies, who traded him to Cincinnati for Wally Post. Then the Reds sent him, Smokey Burgess and Don Hoak to Pittsburgh.
He hurt his arm in 1965 spring training. Sold to the Braves on August 30, he refused to report, believing he couldn't help.
He was a pitching coach for 14 years, with the Mets, Reds, Red Sox, Indians and Pirates, and won a second ring with Pittsburgh in 1979.
p: The NL president gave him a silver tea service with 13 cups. Few days passed in the rest of his life without someone asking him about the game.
Sold to the contending Braves in 1965 with a bad arm, he refused to report and retired, believing he couldn't help them.
A heavy smoker, he died of emphysema in 1994: "I loved cigarettes, but they finally got to me."
He married Marcia Williamson before 1956. With money saved in two rent-free years in Philadelphia he bought his first farm.
He died of emphysema in Springfield, Ohio, at 68.

c: He'd rather beat the Yankees once than anyone else twice: "It was as if you ought not to beat them. You ought to just go out there and rather politely lose." He was 5-1 against them in 1942, when he led the league with 22 wins.

When he left for the Army in August 1944, the Red Sox were 6½ games out. Without him they lost 29 of their last 50. He said he "fought World War II with a bat and a glove," building a ballpark on Saipan with seats made of bomb crates.
He clinched the 1946 pennant with a 1-0 three-hitter, won on Ted Williams's only inside-the-park home run.
Circulation in his pitching arm failed in 1947. Years later, the first time he heard the term "rotator cuff," he thought it was a type of French shirt.

In his last big-league game, the 1949 finale at Yankee Stadium with the pennant on the line, Jerry Coleman's bloop off him cleared the bases. Ted Williams: "Tex makes a good pitch. A damn good pitch."
"The only man in baseball I completely disliked was Joe McCarthy." Sold to the Giants, he refused to report and retired.
He pitched at Texas and signed with the Red Sox in June 1937. He went 5–0 in the 1940 playoffs at Louisville; the Reds reportedly offered $50,000 for him after a three-hit shutout.
In 1942 he went 5–1 against the pennant-bound Yankees. A Jimmy Bloodworth liner once broke his pitching thumb.
In the Army Air Forces he pitched for the 73rd Wing Bombers, who won the Marianas League title. He was discharged in January 1946, the same week Ted Williams and Dom DiMaggio got out.

He started Game 1 of the 1946 World Series in St. Louis. In 1947 he, Boo Ferriss and Mickey Harris all came up with sore arms, and Hughson had surgery for an overdeveloped muscle cutting off circulation in his arm.
He was given a World Series ring at a 1986 reunion of the 1946 team and proudly wore the Red Sox jacket he got all over town. He went into the Red Sox Hall of Fame in 2002.
p: Back in San Marcos he started the town's Little League in 1952, and as school board vice president in 1954 he moved to integrate the high school after Brown v. Board of Education.
He was one of the first to bring French Charolais cattle to the U.S. He named a street in his housing development Fenway Loop, and his front license plate read "Boston is baseball."
His father ran the Hughson Meat Company, which was still in business decades later. His graduating class at Kyle High had a dozen or so students.
He and his first wife, Roena Moore, had Dixie, Stanley and Jane. Roena died young in 1968, and he later married Gladys Watson. He became a real estate developer and died of kidney failure at 77.
In the 1960s he developed part of his ranch into the Hughson Heights subdivision.

c: The Seals kept telling the 6-foot-2, 125-pound teenager to come back when he'd gained weight. When he finally made the Yankees, Jacob Ruppert sent him to a health farm three winters in a row.
Blaming abscessed teeth for his thinness, the Yankees had all his upper teeth pulled at 21.
He coined "gopher ball" for the pitches his outfielders had to "go fer." He credited his success to "clean living and a fast outfield" and won six World Series games without a loss.
Batting against a wild Bob Feller in the late-afternoon shadows, he lit a cigarette lighter at the plate: "I just want to make sure that wild man out there can see me."
He once held up a World Series game to watch a plane fly over. On his Hall of Fame election: "It's only fair. After all, I helped a lot of hitters get in."

He scraped sludge from refinery stills for Union Oil, whose company team wouldn't let lowly workers play. After he lost a 2–1 game to Novato in 1927, the Seals finally signed him and farmed him to Salt Lake City.
The Yankees bought him for about $39,000. They had him drink three quarts of milk a day and gave him unlimited meal money on the road.
Weakened by the dental surgery and false teeth, he was sent back down in July 1930. In 1931 he ended the A's 17-game winning streak and won 21.

He hurt his arm in 1940. After 1942 he worked as a $40-a-week dispatcher at a General Electric defense plant, and was sold to the Braves, who released him before he pitched; he finished with Washington.
He drew two walks in one inning of the 1937 World Series, a record.
p: He paid a chicken butcher's wages for saxophone lessons, five miles' walk away. On a job application he gave his reason for leaving baseball as "Couldn't get anybody out."
As a minor-league manager he paid a Ferris wheel operator to keep Whitey Ford on the ride past curfew so he could fine him. Ford later got his money back: "Thanks you SOB. You only fined me five."
When astronauts saw an unidentified white object on the moon: "It was a home run ball hit off me in 1937 by Jimmie Foxx." After triple-bypass surgery: "that's the first triple I ever got in my life."
His son Duane died in a motorcycle race in 1973. Lefty carried the $10 bill he had given Duane before the race, found in his pocket, for the rest of his life.
He was the youngest of eight. His father, known as "Coyote," was a cowboy who managed a 1,000-acre ranch where Lefty rode horses and worked as a hired hand.

He married Broadway actress June O'Dea in February 1933. By 1937 she learned from the tabloids that he was filing for divorce in Mexico. A devout Catholic, she refused but agreed to a separation, and he moved to Reno for a six-week divorce. They had two daughters and two sons.
After baseball he became a popular public speaker.

c: At 12 he was working in the coal mines, 72 hours a week for $3.75. He built his arm throwing rocks at tin cans, and said he could hit them blindfolded.
Connie Mack sent him to Spokane, thinking he'd keep his rights. When he asked about him later, Spokane sent Mack a box of big red apples and told him his rights had expired.
He learned the spitball at Portland, first with tobacco juice, then alum. It broke three ways depending on his wrist. He went to his mouth before every pitch whether he threw it or not.
His brother Harry, a Tigers star, refused to pitch against him. When the spitball was banned in 1920 he was one of 17 pitchers allowed to keep throwing it.
In the 1920 World Series he threw three complete-game wins with a 0.67 ERA, including the shutout that clinched it. That May his wife had died.
He was the youngest of five ball-playing brothers; his oldest brother, Jacob, died in the Spanish–American War.
He signed with Lancaster in 1909. Connie Mack brought him up in September 1912, and around then he married Mary Stivetts. Portland traded five players to Spokane to get him after 1914.
Joe McGinnity and Harry Krause suggested switching to alum. Cleveland bought him before 1916, and he started early when Ed Klepfer got hurt.
Cleveland traded him to Washington after a subpar 1924. He went 20–5 and won the ERA title in 1925, but lost both of his World Series starts to Pittsburgh. He finished with the Yankees in 1928.
He set Cleveland records for wins, innings and starts.
p: Shy and unworldly, he wouldn't sign with Lancaster until they signed his brother John too.
Asked if rookie Joe Sewell could swim, he pushed him out of a rowboat into a lake and rowed away. A rescue party saved Sewell; Coveleski thought it was very funny.
He married his late wife's sister Frances, who had been helping care for his two sons.
"I never did like Cleveland. Don't know why. Didn't like the town."
In South Bend he ran a gas station and gave local kids free pitching lessons in a field behind his garage.
His parents immigrated from Russian Poland in the early 1870s, and his father was a coal miner. He was rarely able to play as a child because of his work hours.
His wife Mary died suddenly on May 28, 1920, after seven years of marriage, and he returned to the team a week later. His son Jack died in 1937.
He was the oldest living Hall of Famer when he died in a nursing home in 1984 at 94. He had dropped the last "e" from his name after retiring.

c: Naturally right-handed, he hurt his left arm as a toddler when a motorcycle tipped onto him; the exercises to rebuild it made him a lefty.

He took the civil service exam so he could be a mail carrier if his arm failed. Ordered back to Class A in 1962, he went home to Portland instead, and pitching coach Gerry Staley taught him to stop throwing hard and throw strikes.
In the 1968 World Series he homered, his only big-league homer, in Game 2, won Game 5, and beat Bob Gibson in Game 7 on two days' rest, picking off Lou Brock and Curt Flood in the same inning.
In 1971 he won 25 games with 308 strikeouts in 376 innings. He never iced his arm, instead holding it under scalding water for 30 minutes after games.
In 1975 he got 14 runs of support in 14 starts and went 1-13. He retired with more strikeouts than any left-hander in AL history.

His Portland teams made the Babe Ruth World Series in 1955 and the American Legion World Series in 1957, and he battled future Yankee Al Downing in tournaments. He went 19–5 in high school and signed with Detroit scout Bernie deViveiros for $30,000 in June 1958.
He had a reputation as a wild flamethrower and went 0–4 with a 16.50 ERA at Denver in 1962, but found his control back home in Portland.
Pitching coach Gerry Staley helped him in Portland, and in 1964 Charlie Dressen, who had spotted him tipping pitches while scouting for the Dodgers, helped him win 18.
Johnny Sain, who became his friend, made him a complete pitcher. He was the last pitcher to win three complete games in one World Series, and got a sports car as MVP.
He had a 1.42 ERA in the 1972 ALCS against Oakland but lost one game and got a no-decision. The Tigers later traded him to the Mets for Rusty Staub, an unpopular deal.
With the Mets he fought with the trainer and pitching coach, who wanted him to run and ice his arm. He retired to get out of his contract, sat out a year, then pitched two seasons for San Diego.
He held the major-league record for strikeouts by a lefty from 1975 to 1980 and the AL record until CC Sabathia passed him in 2017.
p: "The beer-drinker's idol" said of his belly, "When I'm going good, nobody says anything about it." Mayo Smith called him "my sway-backed left-hander."
He rode his motorcycle 33 miles to Tiger Stadium on days he pitched. After the World Series, Hubert Humphrey invited him to watch Apollo 8 launch.
He served in the Air National Guard during the 1967 Detroit riots. After baseball he ran a doughnut shop in suburban Detroit.
His father was a parks director, so Mickey grew up outdoors.
In November 1964 he married Joyce Fleenor, a former airline stewardess; he said she had settled him down.
After the 1967 riots he got death threats, allegedly from the Black Panthers, for his role with the Guard.
A space buff, he organized annual spring tours of Cape Kennedy for Tigers players and their wives.

He met his doughnut-shop partner when he stopped there for breakfast, and for a while also sold spark plugs for an auto company. He had a small part in the 1977 horror movie The Incredible Melting Man. He died in February 2026 at 85.

c: At his first Cardinals camp he saw 11 players milling around third base, so he trotted out to shortstop, where there was less competition.

Sick with a 104-degree fever and living on orange juice, he played every inning of the 1944 all-St. Louis World Series and was called its best player. Connie Mack: "that fellow is the best I've ever seen."
He won the 1944 MVP by one point, 190 to 189, over Bill Nicholson, with the lowest batting and slugging averages of any MVP ever.

Offered $13,000 so the Cooper brothers would stay the highest-paid Cardinals: "I don't care what the Coopers are making. I won't play for $13,000." He got $15,000, and so did the Coopers. Mort bought him a hat to say thanks.
With trainer Doc Weaver, who roomed with him to treat his back, he drew up the players' first pension plan and pitched it to the owners in 1946. The plan they adopted was very close to his proposal.
Earl Weaver moved the 6-foot-4 Cal Ripken to shortstop because "he reminded me of Marty Marion."

He was one of four ballplaying sons; his brother Red played briefly for Washington. His family was said to descend from Revolutionary War hero Francis Marion. He was a year older than his baseball age.

Chattanooga gave him a tryout and a token contract. When the team went on the road he went home to see his girlfriend, and Calvin Griffith complained he should have stayed to work out. Branch Rickey's brother Frank signed him for St. Louis.
He was never drafted because of his childhood leg injury and a knee injury from his rookie year.
He hit .357 in the 1943 World Series loss to the Yankees.

Sam Breadon called him the toughest businessman among his players. His pension plan paid $50 a month at 50 to a five-year man and $100 to a 10-year man, funded partly by All-Star and World Series broadcast fees.
A 1947 report said some Cardinals planned to strike rather than face Jackie Robinson until Ford Frick threatened suspensions.

Knee and back injuries ended his playing career in 1951. He managed the Cardinals, then the Browns and White Sox. He bought the Houston Buffaloes in 1958 and tried to buy the NBA's Minneapolis Lakers in 1957.
p: At 10 he fell down an embankment and broke his leg; he couldn't walk for more than a year. The injury kept him out of the World War II draft.
Jackie Robinson later wrote that Marion "was always nice to me," and once helped him up after a hard slide and asked if he was okay.
The Cardinals' GM said he'd met scores of St. Louisans named Marty, after Marion. He was married to Mary for 73 years.
His father had hoped to play pro ball until a broken leg stopped him, and moved the family to Atlanta to work for Georgia Power.
He married Mary Dallas on December 27, 1937.
He died of an apparent heart attack in 2011 at 93.

c: As a boy in Richmond he played with a tree-branch bat and a golf ball wrapped in string and tape. His bowed legs earned him the nicknames "Hooks" and "Squat."
With Newark he played in the "Million Dollar Infield" with Willie Wells, Mule Suttles and Dick Seay.

Bill Veeck asked him to join Cleveland in 1947, a chance to be among the first Black major leaguers. He turned it down because he didn't want to move his family from Mexico, where Jorge Pasquel paid him $10,000 a year plus expenses.
He hit .362 in the Triple-A American Association in 1949 and tutored a young Willie Mays, but never got called up. Monte Irvin called him the greatest fielding third baseman he ever saw.
When Jorge Pasquel died in a plane crash, he came back from Mexico as player-manager of the New York Cubans.
p: His father made him quit football after a leg injury.
After baseball he scouted for the Giants and ran a recreation center in Newark. He was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1987.
As a boy he also boxed.

c: His father, whose foot was crushed in a mine, threw tennis balls off a brick wall for him to field, good practice for Forbes Field's rock-hard infield.
Every team but the Pirates wanted to start him in Class D, so he signed with Pittsburgh. Branch Rickey watched him make the pivot a couple of times and told him he was now a second baseman.
He forgot he was leading off the ninth of Game 7 in 1960 until a coach reminded him to get a bat. He hit Ralph Terry's pitch over the wall, the only Game 7 walk-off homer in World Series history.

Jim Murray: Tinker, Evers and Chance got a poem for nine double plays a season, while "Maz makes 161 and they abbreviate his name in the box score." Bill James called his defensive numbers the most impressive of any player at any position.
Nicknamed "Tree Stump" because sliding runners couldn't take him out. One Phillie who tried slowly melted into a clump and came away with three broken ribs.
At his Hall of Fame induction he choked up: "I think defense belongs in the Hall of Fame... I want to thank everyone who made the trip up here to listen to all this crap."
His father, who drank, didn't want him in the mines; family legend says he bought Bill's glove with pay from digging out an outhouse. Bill grew up a Cleveland Indians fan.
He signed with Pittsburgh for a $4,000 bonus and a promise to start him in Class A.
His high school coach, Al Burazio, took him to a Pirates tryout at 16. He won the second-base job in 1957, hitting .442 in exhibitions, and George Sisler taught him to go with the pitch.
Bobby Bragan dropped him to ninth for 10 games as a rookie, which he said hurt his confidence.

One year he broke his foot rounding third at the end of spring training, and still had a record-setting season. Roberto Clemente urged him to spend a winter in Puerto Rico getting in shape, but he said he was done fighting his weight.
He made the final putout in the last game at Forbes Field in 1970. He set NL records for games, assists, putouts and double plays at second, most later broken by Joe Morgan.
He coached third for the Pirates in 1973 and for Seattle in 1979 and 1980, but coaching didn't suit him.
p: His family lived in a one-room house with no electricity or plumbing, and his nickname was "Catfish" because he fished every day to feed the family. He bought his first glove with money from digging his uncle's outhouse.
Danny Murtaugh "ordered" the shy second baseman to ask out Milene Nicholson, a secretary in the scouting department. They married after the 1958 season.
In 1987 he ran for county commissioner in Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, and lost.
His father died in February 1959, at 59, having seen him play in the majors.
He and Milene lived in Panama City, Florida. Their sons are Darren, a junior college coach, and Dave, an atmospheric scientist. Bill died in February 2026 at 89.

c: He hoped for a $6,000 bonus; the Dodgers scouts offered a new suit, then $500, take it or leave it. His father took it. He spent eight years in the minors.
Manager Bobby Bragan in Spokane talked the natural right-handed hitter into switch-hitting: "I had just about given up on myself."
Struggling in 1960, he spent two weeks hitting to the opposite field in 100-degree heat at the Coliseum with coach Pete Reiser. He finished with 50 steals, the most in the NL since 1923.

In 1962 he stole 104 bases and was caught only 13 times, played a record 165 games, and won the MVP. Commissioner Frick said he had to pass Cobb within 154 games; he got his 97th in game 156, as many as Cobb had played.
Some groundskeepers packed sand around first base to slow him. Jim Murray: "His body is so bruised he constantly looks as if he had just crawled out of a plane wreck."
As Mariners manager in 1980-81 he called for a reliever when no one was warming up, named a center fielder the team had traded a month earlier, and was fired after a 6-18 start.
His father was a Navy Yard machinist and part-time Baptist minister, and his mother an elevator operator.
Detroit bought his contract for $35,000 before 1959 but sent him back after spring training. He got his chance when Don Zimmer broke a toe that June, and hit .250 in the 1959 World Series win.
He played a record 165 games in 1962, counting the three-game playoff with the Giants.
Montreal traded him back to LA with Manny Mota for Ron Fairly and Paul Popovich. He learned he had been released when a TV reporter walked up and told him.

After playing he broadcast for NBC's Game of the Week and won a Mexican winter-league title managing Hermosillo. As Seattle's manager he was suspended two games and fined $500. He later coached Dave Roberts, who credited Wills for his famous 2004 steal.
p: The seventh of 13 children, he made all-city in baseball, basketball and football in each of his last three years of high school.
He played banjo in the clubhouse and in nightclubs; the Country Music Hall of Fame put one of his banjos on display.

He said he spent more than $1 million on cocaine. With help from Don Newcombe, Tommy Davis and the Dodgers he got sober, and later coached baserunning for the team for about 15 years. Dave Roberts called him a mentor.
He married his high school sweetheart, Gertrude Elliot, as a senior. They had six children, including Bump, who played six seasons in the majors, and later divorced.
In his 1992 autobiography he wrote that he had an affair with Doris Day in 1962, when both were married.

In December 1983 he was arrested for cocaine possession after his former girlfriend reported her car stolen. He walked out of a Dodgers-paid treatment program and kept using until a new partner, Angela George, got him into vitamin therapy. He died in Sedona in 2022, two weeks short of 90.

c: In high school he stole home in his team's first-ever win at Koshien. Two teams took him in the first round of the 2010 draft, and Yakult won the lottery.
Before he'd played a regular-season game, injuries pushed him into a 2011 Climax Series start at shortstop, the first high school rookie ever to start in the Climax Series.
