In 2014 he homered to lead off a game in six straight months, April through September, an NPB first.

In 2015 he became the first NPB player to lead his league in both home runs and stolen bases. He's the only player with three "triple threes" (.300, 30 homers, 30 steals), earning the nickname "Mr. Triple Three."

In the 2017 World Baseball Classic a junior high student in the stands caught his drive and replay turned it from a homer into a double; the boy was harassed online afterward. At the 2020 Tokyo Olympics Yamada won gold and the MVP.
Scouts liked his hitting and running, but his defense was so poor some thought he was a second- or third-round talent. He signed with Yakult for 7.2 million yen.
Hitting coach Shigeru Sugimura worked with him one on one in 2014, and that October his grand slam broke Fumio Fujimura's 1950 record for hits by a Japanese right-handed hitter.
In 2020 he got free agency rights but stayed with Yakult on a seven-year deal at about 500 million yen a year. Later, after he caught COVID-19 in July, his slump got worse.
p: His father was a police officer. As a boy he did karate and gymnastics and played soccer before starting baseball in second grade.
His father had competed in Shorinji Kempo in high school.

c: He turned down the Braves as a 33rd-round pick in 2007 to go back to junior college and raise his stock. They took him again in the third round a year later.
As a rookie in 2011 he set the record for saves by a rookie with 46, and led the NL in saves four years running.
In 2012 he struck out 116 in 62⅔ innings, 16.7 per nine.
In 2017 he threw an immaculate inning, three strikeouts on nine pitches, and two weeks later struck out four in one inning.
He got his 300th save at 29, younger and in fewer games than anyone before him, and became the eighth pitcher with 400 in 2023.
He was called up in May 2010 to replace the injured Jair Jurrjens, and took the loss in Game 3 of that year's Division Series against the Giants.
After his record rookie season, his 4.76 ERA in September 2011 as Atlanta blew an 8½-game wild-card lead led to charges that Fredi González had overworked him.
Atlanta traded him to San Diego in April 2015, and that November the Padres sent him to Boston for four prospects. He hurt his knee warming up in 2016 and needed surgery.
He saved six games in Boston's 2018 title run. He turned down a qualifying offer and went unsigned until June 2019, when the Cubs gave him three years and $43 million.

He lost Games 3 and 4 of the 2023 NLCS for the Phillies, the first Phillie to lose back-to-back playoff games since Mitch Williams in 1993. After that he bounced among the Orioles, Braves, Rangers, Astros, Mets, Rays and Royals.
p: He was a high school quarterback in Huntsville, Alabama.

He married a former Wallace State cheerleader. Their first daughter was born in 2017 with heart defects and has had two surgeries. His brother Matt, a former Braves minor leaguer, died in a motorcycle crash in 2026.
He married in 2012. His brother Matt died in a motorcycle crash in Huntsville in September 2026.

c: He copied his boyhood idol Juan Marichal's high leg kick. Frank Robinson had to argue to keep the 20-year-old in Cleveland in 1975, and he threw a three-hit shutout in his first start.

Before the last out of his 1977 no-hitter, Gil Flores was stalling. "I pointed at him, 'Get in there. They're not here to take your picture.' I was pretty cocky back then." He ran his hitless streak to 22⅓ innings.
Teammate Dickie Noles on his slang: "'Throw some gas.' 'That man ain't taking me bye-bye.'" He went 20-8 for Boston in 1978.

Traded to Oakland in 1987, he was made the closer when Jay Howell got hurt. Tony La Russa kept him to one inning, inventing the modern closer. "I couldn't have been an every-day pitcher when I was drinking."
Kirk Gibson's homer off his backdoor slider won Game 1 of the 1988 World Series. "We were all so stunned, no one said a thing." In 1990 his ERA was 0.61, and from 1989 to 1991 he walked 16 batters.
In 1992 he saved 51 and won both the Cy Young and the MVP.
He was the first pitcher with both a 20-win season and a 50-save season.
He quit high school football as a senior to protect his arm. Cleveland took him in the third round in 1972; he was disappointed the Giants didn't.
Cleveland traded him and Fred Kendall to Boston in March 1978 for four players.
In Boston he developed a sore arm that never fully went away, and later back and shoulder injuries.
In May 1984 Boston traded him to the Cubs for Bill Buckner, and the Cubs made the postseason.
Shoulder tendinitis in 1986 made for a miserable year. Tony La Russa credited pitching coach Dave Duncan with the idea of making him a reliever.
He saved all four games of Oakland's 1988 ALCS sweep of Boston, and he is said to have coined the term "walk-off home run."

He walked three batters in 57⅔ innings in 1989. That year he saved the clincher of the World Series sweep of San Francisco. Roberto Alomar's two-run homer off him in Game 4 of the 1992 ALCS turned the series.
Oakland traded him to St. Louis in February 1996, and he saved all three games of that year's Division Series.
p: His first wife left him for Cleveland teammate Rick Manning, which led to his trade to Boston.
Over the holidays in 1986 he watched a videotape of himself drunk in front of his daughter. He checked into rehab and stayed sober from then on.
As a broadcaster he was known as "Honest Eck."
His father was a warehouse supervisor and his mother a keypunch operator. He married his high school sweetheart, Denise Jacinto, before the 1973 season.
He and Denise had a daughter, Mandee.
He married model Nancy O'Neil, and they adopted two children, Jake and Alexandra. They divorced shortly after he retired, and he married Jennifer, a former lobbyist.
Nancy went to Al-Anon meetings because of his drinking.

In December 2022 his daughter Alexandra was arrested on suspicion of abandoning her newborn in the woods in 18-degree weather. She got an 18-month suspended sentence contingent on mental health treatment.

c: After a pinched nerve, he paid for his own elbow surgery so the Cubs wouldn't cut him, and came back without a fastball. Minor-league instructor Fred Martin taught him the split-fingered fastball.
His minor-league manager reported, "When Bruce Sutter is ready for the big leagues, that's the day the Communists take over."
In 1979 he tied the saves record with 37 and won the Cy Young.
He saved Game 7 of the 1982 World Series for the Cardinals, striking out Gorman Thomas. Whitey Herzog: "But we've got Sutter."
When his splitter flattened in 1983, he found it was too fast: "The ideal speed is 78 or 79 miles an hour. I was throwing it over 80."
The Braves signed him in 1984 to a deal paying an estimated $44 million over 36 years, mostly deferred. He was the first Hall of Fame pitcher never to start a big-league game.
He's the only pitcher to lead the NL in saves five times.
The Washington Senators drafted him at 17. Cubs scout Ralph DiLullo saw him in semipro ball and signed him in September 1971 for $500 a month and a $500 bonus.
He briefly attended Old Dominion before dropping out.
While recovering from elbow surgery he worked at a plant that printed cigar boxes.
In 1980 he won a then-record $700,000 in arbitration and threatened not to report to spring training without a long-term deal. Instructor Fred Martin, his guru, had left for the White Sox.
When the splitter lost its bite in 1983 he sought out his old Cubs coach Mike Roarke, and the Cardinals hired Roarke as pitching coach.
In 1984 he tied the major-league record with 45 saves.
In Atlanta he had surgery for a pinched nerve in his shoulder that December, and went on the disabled list for the rest of 1986 and all of 1987.
By 1989 he had a badly torn rotator cuff, after three shoulder surgeries in all, and Atlanta released him.
p: The Cubs scout who signed him, Ralph DiLullo, had dreamed of signing a Hall of Famer; he died in 1999, before Sutter's election.
When he was inducted into the St. Louis Sports Hall of Fame, Whitey Herzog accepted in his place because Sutter's wife was in the hospital with cancer.
He was the fifth of six children. His father managed a Farm Bureau warehouse in Mount Joy.
He and his wife, Jayme Leigh, raised three sons in Atlanta.
His son Chad caught at Tulane, was drafted by the Yankees and later coached at Tulane. Sutter died of cancer in hospice in 2022 at 69.

c: His father built a hitting machine that dropped Wiffle balls through a coffee can and PVC pipes, which the boys hit with a skinny steel pipe. It was later sold as Mauer's Quickswing.
He was the top football recruit in the country and signed with Florida State to play quarterback. In three varsity baseball seasons he struck out once.

Picked first overall by his hometown Twins in 2001, he was the Opening Day catcher at 20. Torii Hunter: "He got me a drink of water the other day. I'm like 'What? A first-round pick getting me water?'"
On the last day of 2006 he passed Derek Jeter to become the first AL catcher to win a batting title. In 2009 he hit .365 and won the MVP.
A foul tip gave him a concussion in 2013, and he moved to first base for good. Elected to the Hall of Fame in 2024, he was the first player drafted in the 21st century to get in.
He signed with the Twins for a $5.15 million bonus. The Twins also drafted his older brother Jake, and signed his brother Bill as a free agent.
A torn knee meniscus in April 2004 required surgery, and he had surgery for a kidney obstruction in December 2007.
After the knee surgery he came back in June 2004, but after 33 more games the pain was too much.
The Twins were 0–10 in the postseason during his career; the Yankees swept them in the 2009 and 2010 Division Series even though he hit 5-for-12 in 2009.
In March 2010 he signed an eight-year, $184 million extension, the richest ever for a catcher. Knee surgery, a slow recovery and a late bout of pneumonia made 2011 the worst season of his career.
In his last game, in 2018, he caught one pitch, his first time behind the plate since the 2013 concussion.
p: Teammate Tony Leseman: "Once he figures out the concept of a game, he's good at it. It's amazing and annoying at the same time." Learning to bowl, he rolled a 265.
The Twins held "Joe Mauer Sideburns Night" in 2006 and handed out stick-on sideburns. That year he lived with teammate Justin Morneau.
He married his Cretin-Derham Hall classmate Maddie Bisanz, a nurse. After retiring he coached his kids' softball and baseball teams and ran a Chevy dealership with his brothers.
His father, "Big Jake," worked for a company that made plaques, trophies and ribbons, and his mother managed a religious goods store.
He and Maddie married in December 2012 before 600 guests. They had twin daughters in 2013 and a son in 2018.

c: Before college, lightning struck a summer-league field and knocked him to the ground; the shortstop next to him, the only player in metal cleats, was killed.
His Seton Hall coach called him "the worst defensive catcher I had ever seen." With Mo Vaughn and Marteese Robinson he was one of "The Hit Men."
Moving from catcher to second base, he fielded a thousand grounders a day with a padded paddle taped to his wrist instead of a glove, and gave one of his Gold Gloves to the coach who taught him.
In 1997 he grounded into zero double plays in 619 at-bats. In 1998 he joined Tris Speaker as the only players with 50 doubles and 50 steals in a season.
He reached 3,000 hits in 2007, then was thrown out trying for a double, the first to get there on a play where he was out. He pulled the retired Jeff Bagwell onto the field to share it.
He was hit by 285 pitches, the modern record. He took a hometown discount to stay an Astro his whole career.

His father, an air traffic controller, taught him to catch as the fastest way to the majors, and had him playing against 15-to-18-year-olds at 14. He turned down a football scholarship to Boston University and told the Tigers not to draft him.
Houston took him 22nd overall in 1987. He was called up in June 1988 when Alan Ashby got hurt, after spending spring with coach Yogi Berra.
He played 1,800 games without going on the disabled list until August 2000, when Preston Wilson's slide tore the ACL and MCL in his knee.
He moved to center field in 2003 for Jeff Kent and to left in 2004 for Carlos Beltrán. His first postseason homer came in Game 4 of the 2004 NLDS as Houston won its first postseason series.
p: As a teenager he befriended a neighbor boy with leukemia and became a big brother to his little brother after the boy died. He became a longtime spokesman for The Sunshine Kids, a charity for kids with cancer.
Though he batted and threw right-handed, he's naturally left-handed.
He coached his sons' high school team to two state titles. His son Cavan played in the majors.

In June 1989 he was arrested for drunk driving with teammate Ken Caminiti in the car. The officer testified that Biggio handed him $200 in what he thought was a bribe. Biggio was convicted, got two years' probation and 50 hours of community service, and was fined $350.
He married Patty Egan, a nurse he met at Seton Hall, in February 1990. They have three children: Conor, Cavan and Quinn.

c: A Senators scout who bought him in 1928 telegrammed Clark Griffith's niece and secretary, Mildred Robertson, that he'd signed her future husband. They married in 1934.
Named player-manager at 26, he won the 1933 pennant, still the youngest manager to reach a World Series.
Days after the wedding, Griffith called: the Red Sox had offered $250,000 for him. Cronin told his father-in-law to take it. The price followed him for the rest of his life.
In Boston his veterans openly defied him. Wes Ferrell refused to pitch until a reliever sat down and threatened "to punch Cronin in the jaw"; Lefty Grove criticized him in the press.
Connie Mack: "With a man on third and one out, I'd rather have Cronin hitting for me than anybody I've ever seen, and that includes Cobb, Simmons and the rest of them."

As GM he never fielded a Black player, despite the Red Sox having first crack at Jackie Robinson and Willie Mays. As AL president he hired Emmett Ashford, the first Black major-league umpire: "Jackie Robinson had his Branch Rickey; I had my Joe Cronin."
He turned down his dream team, the Seals, to take a better offer from Pittsburgh's Joe Devine in 1924. He sat on the bench for the 1925 World Series.
Washington needed a shortstop because Goose Goslin's arm injury kept him from throwing. A pitch chipped a bone in Cronin's thumb one season, but he still hit .318.

In 1934 he broke his left forearm colliding with pitcher Wes Ferrell. Tom Yawkey paid $250,000 plus Lyn Lary and gave him five years at $30,000 a year, and Cronin took it knowing Griffith needed the money.
A broken thumb once held him to 81 games, and some thought he was through at 30. He also had a famous fight with Jake Powell at Yankee Stadium.
Sent to scout Pee Wee Reese, his likely replacement, he downplayed Reese and suggested trading him.
He broke his leg in April 1945, ending his playing days. As GM he traded $375,000 and players to the Browns for Vern Stephens and Ellis Kinder.
p: Born six months after the 1906 earthquake, which destroyed his family's home, he grew up a block from a city playground and won the boys' city tennis title.
His grades improved only when the San Francisco Seals started giving tickets to students with good attendance and conduct.
Dying of cancer in 1984, he waved to the crowd from a suite as the Red Sox retired his number. Ted Williams: "In my book, you are a great man."
He and Mildred married after the 1934 season and had four children: Thomas Griffith, named after Yawkey and Clark Griffith, Michael, Maureen and Kevin.
Cancer spread to his prostate and bones, causing great pain. He died at home in Osterville, Massachusetts, in 1984, at 77.

c: The Giants sent him a bus ticket to a tryout camp at 17; "I couldn't have impressed anybody." The scout signed him anyway and sent $500 to his mother: "I didn't realize she was that good of an agent."
In his debut in 1959 he went 4-for-4 with two triples off Robin Roberts, and hit .354 the rest of the way.
With Orlando Cepeda also at first, the Giants put him in left field. One observer: "Don't give him a glove. Give him a cigarette and a blindfold."
His line drive to Bobby Richardson ended the 1962 World Series. Charles Schulz drew Charlie Brown wailing, "Why couldn't McCovey have hit the ball just three feet higher?"
In 1969 he was walked intentionally 45 times, a record for 33 years. Sparky Anderson: "I walked Willie McCovey so many times, he could have walked to the moon on all those walks."
Jim Bouton watching him take batting practice: "Every time a ball bounced into the seats we'd make little whimpering animal sounds." The Giants named McCovey Cove for him.
Ed Scott, the Mobile scout who signed Henry Aaron for the Indianapolis Clowns, saw him regularly and passed on him.
Playing for the Giants' Dallas farm club in the Texas League, he sat out the games in Shreveport because the city was segregated.
To get him into the lineup in 1959, manager Bill Rigney moved Cepeda to third base. The experiment lasted four games: two assists, three errors.
Injuries held him to 105 games in 1971, but the Giants won the NL West, his first postseason in nine years. Early in 1972 he broke his arm in a collision at first base.
In October 1973 the Giants traded him and Bernie Williams to San Diego for Mike Caldwell. In 1976 he lost the Padres' first base job to Mike Ivie.
Near the end of the 1976 season the Oakland A's bought his contract from the Padres.
p: Back with the Giants at 39 in 1977, the ovation on Opening Day brought him to tears: "I knew then that there is still some loyalty around."
He pleaded guilty to tax fraud on memorabilia income in 1996; Barack Obama pardoned him in 2017.
Long in a wheelchair after many knee surgeries, he married his longtime girlfriend Estela Bejar at the Giants' ballpark in 2018.

His father Frank was a railroad laborer, and Willie was the seventh of ten children. He delivered newspapers at 12 and dropped out of high school a year early, in 1954, to work in a bakery and help the family.
His first marriage, to Karen McCovey, produced a daughter.
In 2003 he and a business partner opened McCovey's Restaurant, a baseball-themed sports bar in Walnut Creek, California. It closed in 2015.
He died at 80 at Stanford University Medical Center in October 2018, after being hospitalized for an infection.

c: He was an amateur shortstop who had barely pitched when his manager called him in from right field in a 1989 playoff game. He threw scoreless ball, and the Yankees signed him for $2,000 at 20.

In his first pro start, at the end of 1990, he threw a seven-inning no-hitter and won the Gulf Coast League ERA title at 0.17, and still wasn't considered a top prospect. Both expansion teams passed on him after 1992.
His cutter appeared in 1997 playing catch in Detroit; Ramiro Mendoza stopped because he couldn't predict where the ball would go. "It is as if it dropped straight from the heavens."
He finished with 652 saves and an 0.70 postseason ERA, and is the only player to be MVP of a World Series, an LCS and an All-Star Game. He was the first unanimous Hall of Famer.
He tore his ACL shagging fly balls in Kansas City in 2012. In his last appearance at Yankee Stadium in 2013, Andy Pettitte and Derek Jeter came to the mound to take him out.
He was the last player to wear Jackie Robinson's No. 42, retired throughout baseball.

Scout Herb Raybourn had watched him play shortstop and decided he couldn't hit big-league pitching. At his tryout as a pitcher, Raybourn stopped him after nine or ten throws; Rivera thought he was finished, but Raybourn saw a major-league pitcher.
Hoyt Wilhelm, the first reliever elected to the Hall of Fame, was his first pitching coach.
Elbow pain put him on the disabled list in the minors. Dr. Frank Jobe decided he didn't need Tommy John surgery and removed bone fragments from the joint instead.

Called up when injuries hit the Yankee rotation in 1995, he was hit hard early; the Times called one start "another shabby outing by another young pitcher." Five days later in Oakland he got his first win.
He saved 42 postseason games, more than twice anyone else, and 14 of them took two innings. More people have walked on the Moon (12) than scored an earned run off him in the postseason (11).
Describing his job: "I get the ball, I throw the ball, and then I take a shower."
p: In Puerto Caimito, Panama, his family's two-room house had no water or electricity. He played ball with gloves made from milk cartons and balls of fishing net and tape.

His grandfather taught him to swing a machete in the cane fields, the flick of the wrist that became his delivery. Working on his father's fishing boat at 18, he survived an accident that killed his uncle.
He and Clara were classmates as children. In 2009 they founded a church in New Rochelle, where she's the pastor.
He loved soccer and played it competitively until he seriously hurt an eye in a match. His father bought him his first real glove, secondhand, when he was 16.
He dropped out of school in ninth grade and spent three years catching sardines six days a week on his father's boat. He wanted to be a mechanic, and was saving to open an auto repair shop.
He and Clara were married by a judge in November 1991 and in a formal ceremony three days later. They have three sons.

c: A knee injury in his first high school football game ended his college football hopes, and the Pirates took him in the 14th round. The Reds scouts laughed at them.
In 1977 he threw out 26 runners, the most by any outfielder since Roberto Clemente in 1961. He won the batting title in 1977 and 1978 and the 1978 MVP.
Running over Mets catcher John Stearns in 1978, he broke his cheekbone, then came back in a hockey goalie mask. "I'm the toughest man in the world. I can see, so I can play."

His 1979 deal was called baseball's first million-dollar-a-year contract, though he never got $1 million in any year he played. "These people work hard for their money and it's hard for them to imagine making this type of money playing games."

He testified in the 1985 Pittsburgh drug trials that he'd used cocaine, and the Pirates sued to get out of his deferred payments. He won the first Home Run Derby that year and later won a ring with the 1989 A's.
He was elected to the Hall of Fame in 2025 and died a month before the ceremony.
He was called up in July 1973 when Gene Clines tore ankle ligaments; Parker was leading the International League at .317. A hamstring injury cost him most of June and July 1974.
He won three straight Gold Gloves (1977-79). In the on-deck circle he warmed up swinging a sledgehammer.
By the early 1980s many Pittsburgh fans saw him as an overweight, injury-prone drug user whose production fell off after he signed the most lucrative contract in baseball history.

He left the Pirates as a free agent for the Reds in December 1983. Named a "regular user" in the drug trials, he was suspended for the next season, but the penalty was commuted for 10 percent of his salary, drug testing and 100 hours of community service.

The Reds traded him to Oakland for José Rijo and Tim Birtsas after 1987. He then signed with Milwaukee, was traded to the Angels for Dante Bichette, released, and picked up by Toronto for the 1991 stretch at $650 a game, too late to play in the ALCS.
He never got 25 percent of the Hall of Fame writers' vote in 15 years, perhaps because of the cocaine years.
p: Growing up a short walk from Crosley Field, he waited outside for Frank Robinson and Vada Pinson, who gave him gloves and balls. He later sold concessions at the ballpark.
"There's only one thing bigger than me, and that's my ego." Jerry Reuss: "Dave was an equal-opportunity offender."
Diagnosed with Parkinson's in 2012, he and his wife sold their Popeyes restaurants and started a foundation to fight it.
He weighed 11 pounds 14 ounces at birth in Grenada, Mississippi, one of six children. In 1956 the family moved to Cincinnati, where his father worked at a valve company and his mother as a maid.
At Western Hills High School he hit a home run onto the roof of a Frisch's restaurant.

After playing he coached first base for the Angels in 1997. He lived in Loveland, Ohio, with his wife Kellye, and died of complications of Parkinson's in June 2025 at 74. His son Dave Parker II accepted his Hall of Fame plaque.

c: In his first tee-ball game, at 4, he turned an unassisted triple play. As a boy he was a batboy for the University of New Mexico and got to see his favorite player, Dustin Pedroia.
As a high school sophomore he was the first high schooler named USA Baseball Player of the Year. At LSU he wore No. 30, for the 30 teams that passed on him in the first round of the 2012 draft.
He was the youngest player on the U.S. team that won the 2017 World Baseball Classic, and later said he probably should have played for Israel, since he got just four at-bats.
After the Astros' sign-stealing scandal broke, he answered reporters again and again with variations of one line: "The commissioner made his report, made his decision."
Signing with Boston in 2025, he offered to move to second base for Rafael Devers, who refused to move. Devers became the DH instead.

Projected as a first-round pick out of high school, he shattered a knuckle on his throwing hand bare-handing a bad hop and missed most of his senior season. He said he'd sign only as a first-rounder; Boston took him in the 29th round, and he went to LSU.

LSU coach Paul Mainieri: "If you don't think Alex Bregman can play shortstop at the Major League level, you don't know the first thing about baseball." The Astros signed him in June 2015 for $5.9 million.

In the 2017 postseason his eighth-inning homer off Chris Sale tied Game 4 of the ALDS. In the World Series he threw Austin Barnes out at the plate and drove in a run in each of his first five Series games, joining Amos Otis. The Astros won in seven.

After surgery for bone chips in his elbow in January 2019, he signed a six-year, $100 million extension. That October he broke out of a 4-for-31 slump with a grand slam in Game 4 of the World Series, the first ever by an Astro in the Series.
p: At his bar mitzvah he said he wanted to be a professional athlete who'd be "a good role model for all of the kids who look up to baseball players." His grandfather was the Washington Senators' general counsel and helped bring Ted Williams to the team.
He named childhood dogs Jeter and Koufax, and he owns racehorses. He worked on his Spanish with Astros teammates Jose Altuve, Yordan Alvarez and Yuli Gurriel.

His grandfather Stan Bregman, the son of Russian-Jewish immigrants, was general counsel for the Washington Senators. He negotiated the team's 1971 sale and move to Texas and helped it sign Ted Williams.
He married Reagan Howard in December 2020. They have two sons, born in 2022 and 2025.

c: From age 7 he practiced with his father every day, then took 250 to 300 more swings at a batting cage after dinner. "It bordered on hazing and I suffered a lot." His father had him bat left-handed because lefties get to first faster.
In high school he hit .502 and never struck out swinging, but at 5-foot-9 and 120 pounds he went in the fourth and final round of Japan's draft.

Orix put "Ichiro" on his jersey in 1994 because Suzuki is a common name. That year he had 210 hits, the first 200-hit season in the 130-game league. Letters addressed simply "Ichiro, Japan" reached him.
Nintendo president Hiroshi Yamauchi added some of his own money to Seattle's bid. In 2001 he won Rookie of the Year and MVP, then had ten straight 200-hit seasons, including a record 262 in 2004.
His 10th-inning single won the 2009 World Baseball Classic final against South Korea.
Counting Japan, he had 4,367 top-level hits, more than Pete Rose's 4,256. He was elected to the Hall of Fame in 2025 with 99.7 percent of the vote.

Orix manager Shōzō Doi wouldn't accept his unorthodox swing, so he spent most of his first two seasons on the farm team, hitting .368. In 1993 he homered off Hideo Nomo and was sent back down the same day.
After one throw from right field to third, Mariners announcer Dave Niehaus exclaimed, "I'm here to tell you that Ichiro threw something out of Star Wars down there at third base!"
He hit .600 against Cleveland in the 2001 ALDS, his only postseason with Seattle.

He asked the Mariners for a trade in 2012. The Yankees' conditions were that he'd play mostly left field, bat low in the order, and sit against some lefties; his first game for them was that night, at Safeco against Seattle. He hit his first postseason home run in the ALCS, which the Yankees lost to Detroit.
He signed with the Marlins as a fourth outfielder for 2015 and made his only big-league pitching appearance that year. At 42, at Coors Field, he got his 3,000th hit with a stand-up triple.
When a statue of him in his batting stance was unveiled in Seattle in April 2026, the upright bat was accidentally broken.
p: Shy with the media and always using an interpreter, he was very funny in private. Every All-Star Game from 2002 on, he got the last pregame word, a profane call to beat the NL.
Asked what he'd do after baseball, he said, "I think I'll just die."
He gave ¥100 million to the Japanese Red Cross after the 2011 tsunami. A wasp species found in Florida is named after him.
He married TBS announcer Yumiko Fukushima in 1999 at a small church in Santa Monica. Their Shiba Inu, Ikkyu, is named from the first characters of their two names.

His father Nobuyuki ran his finances until 2002, when he was found to have underreported income and was hit with a big tax bill. The scandal, and his father's relentless training, ended their relationship; his wife has handled his money since.

He used an interpreter in interviews to avoid being misunderstood, but spoke English with teammates and learned Spanish to banter with Latin players. He loved visiting Buck O'Neil in Kansas City, and made the largest gift by an active player to the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum.

c: He grew up near the Mets' Triple-A park in Norfolk, rooting for the Mets. His Tidewater youth teams also produced Ryan Zimmerman, Mark Reynolds and the Upton brothers.
Cliff Floyd, on the injured list, arrived at Shea midgame to an unusually loud roar: "I'd walked into a David Wright home run... that's what happens when you're the face of the franchise."
In 2007 he hit .325 with 30 homers and 34 steals, worth 8.3 WAR. The Mets blew a seven-game lead with 17 to play, though Wright hit .397 down the stretch.

Beaned by Matt Cain in 2009, he came back wearing an oversized "Great Gazoo" helmet, and had a coach fire tennis balls at him to stop bailing out. Not until he was hit again the next April did "something snap back into place."
Named "Captain America" at the 2013 World Baseball Classic, he accepted the Mets' captaincy only after his teammates approved.
Spinal stenosis eventually took three hours of preparation before he could take batting practice. He homered in Game 3 of the 2015 World Series.
He'd decided to turn pro if taken in the third round or earlier. The Mets took him 38th overall in 2001 and signed him for $960,000.
The pick was compensation for losing Mike Hampton to the Rockies. Coach Tom Robson had been sent to Virginia "to scout someone else."
Equipment manager Charlie Samuels gave him No. 5, the number of Brooks Robinson and George Brett.
He signed a six-year, $55 million extension in August 2006. In his first postseason that fall he went 4-for-25 in the NLCS loss to the Cardinals.
A diving tag on Houston's Carlos Lee in 2011 left him with a stress fracture in his lower back and more than two months on the disabled list.
He signed for eight years and $138 million, with a no-trade clause, so he could play his whole career with the Mets. In 2014 a shoulder injury and bruised rotator cuff cost him 24 games.
p: His father, a police officer who rose to assistant chief, cared more about conduct than results. When young David threw his helmet, his coach asked, "Are you going to tell your dad, or am I?"
His Vitamin Water endorsement included a 0.5 percent stake; when Coca-Cola bought the company in 2007 he netted about $20 million.
He helped raise nearly $2 million for the children's hospital in Norfolk.
He met model Molly Beers, then a senior at Arizona State, while preparing for an All-Star tour of Japan in 2006. They have two daughters, Olivia Shea and Madison, and a son, Brooks.
They were married in La Jolla, California, the day after Christmas 2013.

c: His father pitched tennis balls at a strike zone painted on the garage. Playing pretend Dodgers games, Chipper batted righty for Steve Garvey and lefty for Reggie Smith. His father later added the toe tap that became his trademark.

Top prospect Todd Van Poppel refused to sign with the lowly Braves, so Atlanta took Jones first overall in 1990. "If Todd Van Poppel didn't want to be an Atlanta Brave, I was more than happy to take his place."
He tore his ACL in spring 1994, then on Opening Day 1995 ran over Greg Maddux on a popup and got an earful for innings.
In 2008, at 36, he was hitting .418 in early June and finished at .364 for his only batting title.
He hit .309 with 49 homers against the Mets. On his farewell tour they gave him a piece of art; Houston gave him a cowboy hat and San Diego a surfboard.
He's the only switch-hitter to bat over .300 from both sides, and was elected to the Hall of Fame in 2018 with 97.2 percent.

He signed for $275,000, nearly a million dollars less than Van Poppel got from Oakland as the No. 14 pick. In the minors a hand he hurt fighting a high school teammate hampered his swing, and in one season he made 71 errors in 135 games.
In the Braves' minor-league system he was in a bench-clearing brawl with Manny Ramirez and Jim Thome.
He learned he was going to the big leagues while in the playoffs with Triple-A Richmond in 1993. Bobby Cox left him off the postseason roster but brought him along to Philadelphia for the NLCS.

Ron Gant broke his leg in an offseason dirt-bike accident, opening left field for him in 1994, but he spent the whole strike-shortened season on the disabled list. In 1995 the Braves beat Cleveland in six to win the World Series.
ESPN hired him as a Wednesday Night Baseball analyst in 2020. For his role with the Braves he got a second ring in 2021.
p: His mother, a competitive equestrienne, taught him what she called "necessary arrogance."
He skipped a minor-league playoff game in 1992 to get married, a decision he later regretted.
That marriage ended in 2000 after an affair produced a son.
He co-owned the Outdoor Channel hunting show Buck Commander.

Born Larry Wayne Jones Jr., he looked so much like his father that a relative called him a "chip off the old block." He grew up on a 10-acre fern farm in Pierson, Florida, the "Fern Capital of the World."

His father quit as baseball coach at Taylor High to head off complaints of favoritism. Chipper went off to Bolles, where he was named starting quarterback as a sophomore but grew overwhelmed and homesick; he said those memories kept him from ever testing free agency.
He met his first wife, Karin Fulford, while playing in Macon. His affair with a Hooters waitress lasted 18 months and produced a son in 1998.
He married Sharon Logonov in Pierson in March 2000; they divorced in 2012. He then dated former Playboy model Taylor Higgins, married her in 2015, and had sons in 2017 and 2018.
In 2008 he released a charity wine, "Chipper Chardonnay."

c: He played varsity baseball as an eighth grader, hit .709 as a senior, ran on a state-champion relay team and was reportedly offered a football scholarship to Miami.
Bobby Cox in 2010: "He catches the ball like Andruw Jones did when he was 19. You can't hit a ball [past him] out there."
He won the 2013 NL MVP. That year fans voted him onto the cover of MLB 13: The Show.
Traded to the Giants in 2018, he went 6-for-7 in one game, ending it with a walk-off homer in the 14th. When he got to the Yankees he had to shave his beard and give up No. 22.
Returning to Pittsburgh in 2023, he got a standing ovation of more than a minute on Opening Day and later got his 2,000th hit there.
Committed to the University of Florida, he went 11th overall in 2005 and signed with Pittsburgh for $1.9 million.
He was called up in June 2009, when the Pirates traded center fielder Nate McLouth to Atlanta.
In 2013 he led the Pirates to their first postseason since Barry Bonds's 1992 team; they lost the NLDS to the Cardinals in Game 5.
Dreading a trade, he admitted to googling his own name.
In January 2018 the Pirates sent him to the Giants for Kyle Crick and Bryan Reynolds.
He signed with the Phillies for three years and $50 million. In June 2019, while leading the NL in walks, he tore his ACL running the bases and missed the rest of the season.
Back with Pittsburgh, a partial Achilles tear ended his 2023 season.
In March 2026 the Rangers added him to their roster and released him the next day.
Atlanta signed him to a minor-league deal in July 2026 and released him in August.
p: His father gave up college football to come home and raise him; his mother wouldn't marry him unless he became a minister, which he did.
He cut off his famous dreadlocks in 2015 and auctioned them for Pirates Charities. He proposed to his wife on The Ellen DeGeneres Show.
After a TV anchor confused him with Rams running back Lawrence McCutcheon, he created the alter ego "Uncle Larry," complete with wig, sunglasses and merchandise.
He and his wife Maria have two sons and two daughters, born between 2017 and 2024.

c: His father, a Boeing engineer, built his delivery and made the University of Washington promise not to change it. As a high school freshman he was 4-foot-11 and 85 pounds.
Nine teams passed on the Golden Spikes winner because of his size and violent motion. Arriving for his big-league debut, security thought he was the batboy.
He never iced his arm and ate burgers, fries and a chocolate-strawberry shake before starts. He won the Cy Young in 2008 and 2009, and named his French bulldog Cy.
In 2010 he struck out 14 in a playoff shutout of Atlanta and won the clinching Game 5 of the World Series. In 2012, demoted to the bullpen, he allowed one run in 13 postseason innings.
He threw 148 pitches in a 2013 no-hitter. Bruce Bochy: "He wouldn't have talked to me the rest of the year if I'd have taken him out." He no-hit the Padres again the next year.
In his sophomore year at Washington, Cleveland drafted him in the 42nd round. He turned it down, holding out for more than a $700,000 bonus.
He held out for a bigger bonus so that his father could retire.
His hometown Mariners took Brandon Morrow fifth overall instead. The Giants' $2.025 million bonus was the most they'd ever paid an amateur.
In the first inning of his first big-league start he struck out Chase Utley, Pat Burrell and Aaron Rowand, all swinging.

His nicknames included "The Freak," "Big Time Timmy Jim" and "The Baby-Faced Assassin." He missed his first All-Star Game, taken to a New York hospital that day with flu-like symptoms and dehydration.
He asked for a record $23 million in arbitration and brought his two Cy Young Awards to the hearing. He signed for two years and $23 million, breaking Roger Clemens's arbitration record.
After the 2010 division series win he dropped an F-bomb in a live TV interview, sealing his cult status. He won the Babe Ruth Award as the best performer of that postseason.
By the 2012 All-Star break his fastball had fallen to the high 80s and he was 3-10 with a 6.42 ERA. His father said fans and media were "crucifying" him.
After an injury-plagued 2015 he made nine starts for the Angels in 2016. He tried again with Texas in 2018 but was released from Triple-A because of injuries.
p: After a 2009 marijuana citation, San Francisco answered with "Let Timmy Smoke", and the days he pitched became "Happy Timmy Day." Larry Baer: "It was like a lot of the fans felt their son was pitching."
He wore No. 44 in Texas in honor of his brother Sean, who died in 2018. His wife Cristin died of cancer in 2022.
"I think the hardest part was coming to grips with who I was after baseball, and I haven't even done it fully yet."
His mother is the daughter of Filipino immigrants. His father is distantly related by marriage to Natalie Wood.
The Giants haven't reissued his No. 55.

c: The Yankees took him in the first round in 2008 and were ready to offer about $4 million, but he never negotiated and went to UCLA, where he majored in political science, minored in theater and considered acting.
The Pirates took him first overall in 2011 and signed him for a record $8 million bonus 15 minutes before the deadline.
In his debut in 2013 he struck out the first batter on three pitches, the last at 99 mph, and drove in two with a bases-loaded single in his first plate appearance.
He struck out 326 for Houston in 2019, then signed with the Yankees for nine years and $324 million, the biggest contract ever for a pitcher. In 2023 he won the Cy Young unanimously.
In 2021 he struck out 61 batters in a row without a walk, a major-league record.
UCLA coach John Savage made him the Friday night starter as a freshman. The Bruins reached the 2010 College World Series and lost the championship series to South Carolina.
He won Game 2 of the 2013 NLDS against the Cardinals, and lost the 2015 Wild Card Game to the Cubs.

In January 2018 the Pirates traded him to Houston for Joe Musgrove, Michael Feliz, Colin Moran and Jason Martin. His leap there was credited to the Astros' intervention. In the 2018 ALDS he struck out 12 without a walk, something only Tom Seaver had done in the postseason.
His Yankees deal let him opt out after five years, unless the club added a year at $36 million. In his Yankees playoff debut he struck out 13 Indians without a walk.
After pitching in the 2024 World Series against the Dodgers, he opted out. Two days later he was back with the Yankees for four years and $144 million.
He had Tommy John surgery in 2025. Back in May 2026, he threw six scoreless innings against Tampa Bay, and in September his 161st win tied Mike Moore for the most by a No. 1 overall pick.
p: At age 11 he held up a sign at the 2001 World Series: "YANKEE FAN TODAY TOMORROW FOREVER." He brought it to his introductory press conference 18 years later.
He married UCLA softball player Amy Crawford, Brandon Crawford's sister. He plays piano and guitar and reads music, and they kept a recipe blog.
His father, raised in Syracuse, passed down his love of the Yankees. Gerrit and Amy's sons, Caden and Everett, were born in 2020 and 2023.

c: He was mainly a high school shortstop who hit 31 career homers, then became a starter as a senior and posted a 0.55 ERA. The Royals took him sixth overall in 2002.
He debuted at 20 as the youngest player in the majors. Depression and anxiety nearly derailed his career, and he missed most of 2006.
He came back as a reliever in 2007 and in 2009 led the majors in ERA and won the AL Cy Young.
Wanting to win, he asked the rebuilding Royals to trade him in 2010. He later won six straight Gold Gloves, from 2014 to 2019.
He's one of three pitchers to win a Cy Young, a Silver Slugger and a Gold Glove, and hoped to finish with ten homers and ten steals; he got to nine of each.
He turned down a Clemson scholarship to sign with the Royals for $2.5 million.
The Royals put him on the 60-day disabled list for psychological issues, and he left baseball entirely for a while. He named FIP as his favorite statistic.

Traded to Milwaukee for Alcides Escobar, Lorenzo Cain, Jeremy Jeffress and Jake Odorizzi, he admitted he'd been "pretty rude" on the way out. Before his first Brewers spring training he broke a rib playing basketball.
When extension talks broke down, Milwaukee traded him to the Angels in July 2012 for Jean Segura and two pitchers.

His six-year, $147 million Dodgers deal was the largest ever for a right-hander. In April 2013 Carlos Quentin charged the mound after a pitch hit him, and the brawl broke Greinke's collarbone. After 2015 he opted out of the last three years.
He signed with Arizona for six years and $206.5 million.

Arizona traded him to Houston in July 2019 and paid $24 million of his salary. He started Games 3 and 7 of that World Series. In the 2021 Series he got the Astros' first World Series hit by a pitcher, then a pinch-hit single, the first by a pitcher in the Series since 1923.
As of 2025 he was the last pitcher to get a hit in a postseason game.
p: As a teenager he helped his team win the 1999 Senior League World Series, hitting close to .700 as a shortstop. He also excelled at tennis and golf.
He married Emily Kuchar, whom he met at Apopka High; she later cheered for the Dallas Cowboys.
He was born in Orlando, the son of teachers Donald and Marsha Greinke.
He and Emily have three sons, born in 2015, 2017 and 2021.

c: The Yankees and Braves reportedly offered more, but he signed with Seattle at 16, partly because his idol, Freddy García, pitched there. A Mariners blog nicknamed him "King Felix" in his first U.S. season.
At 19 he was the youngest pitcher to reach the majors since José Rijo, and won his second start 1-0 with eight shutout innings.
In 2008 he threw an immaculate inning and, in his only at-bat of the year, hit a grand slam off Johan Santana.
In 2011 the Mariners created the "King's Court" cheering section, the first stadium promotion built around a single player.
He won the 2010 Cy Young and threw the first perfect game in Mariners history in 2012. He started 30 or more games ten years in a row.
Part-time scout Luis Fuenmayor spotted him at 14 in a tournament near Maracaibo. He signed on July 4, 2002, for $710,000; his father, who owned a trucking business, handled the talks.
In 2006 he switched to No. 34, which Freddy García had worn in Seattle.
His 2007 duel with Daisuke Matsuzaka, in the Japanese rookie's Fenway debut, made him a national name. Soon after, a strained forearm put him on the disabled list.
In January 2010 he signed a five-year extension worth about $78 million. That September Nelson Cruz broke up his no-hitter with an eighth-inning homer.
His seven-year, $175 million extension in 2013 made him the highest-paid pitcher ever, until Justin Verlander's deal weeks later.
In 2016 he strained his calf jumping up to celebrate a home run.
Starting at 30 came injuries, lost velocity and rising ERAs. He signed with Atlanta and then Baltimore, but never pitched in the majors again.
p: His family calls him by his middle name, Abraham. He became a U.S. citizen in 2018.
He's a spokesman for the Seattle humane society; his dogs are King and Oreo.
In the 2006 offseason he lived at his parents' home in a modest Valencia neighborhood while a house was built for him, his girlfriend and their daughter.

c: His father, a factory worker and Puerto Rico's all-time amateur hits leader, came home every evening and took his three sons across the street to the park. All three became big-league catchers, and each won a World Series.
At about 15 his father got him onto an adult amateur team, against players 10 years older, and he became the starting catcher after one workout.
The first scouting report: "defensive catcher, great arm, weak bat." He finished with more than 2,100 hits and nine Gold Gloves.
He and Adam Wainwright won 203 games as a battery, a record. He also pitched twice in his final season.
Jorge Posada and Brian McCann both called him the best defensive catcher in baseball.

Before the draft he worked out for the Reds at Riverfront Stadium, and his arm and bat caught the eye of Johnny Bench and Bob Boone. The Cardinals took him in the fourth round in 2000 and signed him for $325,000.

He got his first big-league chance in 2004 when Mike Matheny went on the disabled list with a strained rib. Tony La Russa started him over Matheny in Game 4 of that World Series, and when Matheny left for the Giants, the job was Molina's.
A pitch broke a bone in his hand in July 2005 and cost him 33 games.

In Game 7 of the 2006 NLCS against the Mets, his two-run ninth-inning homer cleared the wall too high for Chávez to catch. In the bottom of the inning, with the bases loaded, he had rookie Adam Wainwright start Carlos Beltrán with a changeup, against Dave Duncan's teaching; Beltrán struck out looking at a curve. The Cardinals beat Detroit for Molina's first ring, and his mask went to the Hall of Fame.
After his playing days he became manager of Navegantes del Magallanes in Venezuela and a special assistant with the Cardinals.
p: His father died of a heart attack in 2008 while tending a field he'd built for kids in Bayamón.
After Hurricane Maria in 2017 he and his wife raised money for Puerto Rico, and he won the 2018 Roberto Clemente Award. He's a big St. Louis Blues fan.
He married Wanda Torres in 2007; they have two sons and a daughter, born in 2008, 2010 and 2016.
In 2009 Steiner Sports Marketing sued him for $175,000 after he missed autograph shows it had paid him to attend.
He and his brothers Bengie and José are the only trio of brothers who all won World Series rings. The only other trio who all played in a Series were the Alous.

c: At 16 he got his first pro hit in the Venezuelan winter league. He debuted with the Marlins at 20 with a walk-off homer, one of three players since 1900 to win a game with a homer in his first game, and helped them win the 2003 World Series.
In 2006 he reached out and singled on an intentional-walk pitch that came too close, driving in the winning run.
A spring-training grounder broke a bone below his eye in 2012, but he was ready for Opening Day and went on to win the first Triple Crown in 45 years: .330, 44 homers, 139 RBIs.
Barry Bonds in 2013: "He's the best. By far. Without a doubt. The absolute best." He won a second straight MVP that year.
He's one of three players, with Hank Aaron and Willie Mays, with a .300 average, 500 homers and 3,000 hits, and the career leader in hits and homers among Venezuelans.
Marlins coach Ozzie Guillén had him move from shortstop to third base in the minors.

In 2003 he homered in Games 1 and 7 of the NLCS against the Cubs. In Game 4 of the World Series, Roger Clemens threw a 92-mph fastball near his chin; Cabrera stared at him, then hit a two-run homer later in the at-bat. The Marlins won the Series, and he landed on the cover of ESPN The Magazine.

In 2006 teammate Scott Olsen shouted at him after a ball glanced off his glove. In the dugout Cabrera poked a finger at Olsen, then charged him and tried to kick him before teammates pulled them apart.

In December 2007 the Marlins traded him and Dontrelle Willis to Detroit for six players, including Andrew Miller and Cameron Maybin. He then signed an eight-year, $152.3 million extension, the largest in Tigers history.
He hit .400 in the 2011 ALCS, which the Tigers lost to Texas in six.
After his Triple Crown season, he was the last out of the 2012 World Series, called out on strikes as the Giants finished a sweep.
In 2014 he signed an eight-year, $248 million extension, a ten-year commitment of $292 million.
He was Venezuela's hitting coach at the 2026 World Baseball Classic.
p: As a boy in Maracay he also played volleyball, and at 14 he went to a baseball school in Cagua so he could keep studying.
He's a Catholic and a practitioner of Santería, and became a babalawo in 2006. During the pandemic he appeared on a rap single, "Miggy al Bate."

Police took him in for questioning in October 2009 after he came home at 6 a.m. from a night of drinking and argued with his wife; his blood alcohol was reported at .26. He spent three months in alcohol treatment. In February 2011 he was arrested for drunk driving in Florida and pleaded no contest.

His former mistress, Belkis Mariella Rodriguez, sued for $100,000 a month in child support for their two children. He had paid $20,000 a month without a court order, then cut it by $5,000; in 2018 a court ordered him to pay $20,000 plus expenses and her legal fees.
His wife Rosangel filed for divorce in 2017 and changed her mind. She filed again, and the divorce was final in 2025. They have two daughters and a son.

c: His father, a former Twins minor-league catcher, taught him to hit in the garage off a tee made from a washing-machine hose when he was 5.
He went to Tennessee on a football scholarship, backing up Heath Shuler. When he hurt his knee as the starter, Peyton Manning replaced him. His baseball coach: "He's the best pitcher I ever coached."
In 2000 he hit .372 with 59 doubles and 103 extra-base hits. In 2003 he lost the batting title to Albert Pujols by .00022 after being walked intentionally in his last at-bat.
His two-out, two-strike walk-off homer off Takashi Saito on September 18, 2007, started a run in which the Rockies won 13 of their last 14 and reached their first World Series.
He took No. 17 as a tribute to his hero Mark Grace.
He wore 17 for 17 seasons, and it was the first number the Rockies retired.

He played high school quarterback for his uncle, Joel Helton. San Diego drafted him in the second round in 1992, but he went to Tennessee, where baseball coach Rod Delmonico called him "the best pitcher I ever coached."
The Rockies took him in the first round in 1995 and signed him for $892,000. He was hitting .352 at Colorado Springs when he was called up in 1997.
In April 2001 he signed a nine-year, $141.5 million contract.

Cardinals broadcaster Wayne Hagin claimed Don Baylor had said Helton "tried the juice" in the 1990s. Helton denied it and considered legal action; Hagin apologized, saying he meant creatine, not steroids.
After the steroid claim, teammates covered his locker with police tape and a sign: "This area closed pending a search for evidence."
In 2005 he went on the disabled list for the first time, with a strained calf. In 2006 he was hospitalized with acute terminal ileitis, a painful intestinal inflammation.
The Rockies won a tiebreaker against the Padres in extra innings in 2007, putting him in the playoffs for the first time.
p: As a teenager his India-ink drawing "Shadows" won best print at the Tennessee Valley Fair. He honeymooned at the Rockies' fantasy camp.
The Rockies gave him a horse on his last day, and his ranch is called the 17 Ranch. His daughter asked the crowd at his number retirement, "Do you want him back?"
He was arrested for drunk driving in 2013 and again in 2019, and entered treatment after the second.
He met his wife Christy Bollman in his freshman year at Tennessee. They have two daughters, Tierney Faith and Gentry Grace. His father Jerry died in 2015 at 65.
For the 2013 DUI he was fined $400, given a year's probation and 24 hours of community service. For the second, he was sentenced to two days in jail in 2020. He lives in Knoxville.

c: He went to San Diego State on a basketball scholarship and still holds the school's assist records. The Padres and the NBA's San Diego Clippers both drafted him on the same day in 1981.
He was one of the first players to study video, carrying multiple VCRs on the road to tape his at-bats and watch them in his hotel room. "I am a natural hitter, but I have to work hard to keep it."
He hit the ball between short and third so often because "my hands come through the zone first, and the barrel trails and it kind of hides the ball from the fielder."
He was hitting .394 when the 1994 strike ended the season. "I'd be lying if I didn't say I wanted to make a crack at .400."

His 3,000th hit came in Montreal in 1999, with his college teammate umpiring at first base. He hit over .300 in 19 straight seasons and won eight batting titles; the NL batting title is now named for him.
Gwynn turned down several invitations to appear on Jay Leno's show and didn't much care to go to a White House dinner. "I was not a game-changer. I was not a dominant player."
The Padres took him in the third round in 1981, the same year the Clippers drafted him in the 10th.
In 1984 he led the Padres to their first postseason; they beat the Cubs in the NLCS and lost the World Series to Detroit.
In the 1998 World Series the Yankees swept the Padres, but Gwynn hit the only postseason home run of his career.

He earned $47 million as a player but never more than $6.3 million a season, staying with a small-market team that had seven winning seasons in his 20 years. Jack McKeon called him "the father of the video in baseball."
Injuries held him to 36 games in 2000 and 71 in 2001, his last season.

He lobbied for the San Diego State job in his last season as a player, and started as an unpaid volunteer before a $100,000 salary. Crowds came mainly to see him; one writer said he had "rock star status."
p: As kids he and his brothers used figs off a tree and homemade sock balls so they wouldn't break windows, and pretended to be the Cardinals and Pirates "because they had all the left-handed hitters."
He coached San Diego State for 12 seasons and went 363-363, coaching Stephen Strasburg.
He died of salivary gland cancer at 54, which he blamed on chewing tobacco. Chris Sale quit chewing the day Gwynn died: "I owe him a huge thank you."
He met his wife Alicia in elementary school, and they married right after the 1981 draft. Their son Tony Jr. played at San Diego State and reached the majors; daughter Anisha is a recording artist.
After his father died in 1993, Gwynn took his advice and became more outspoken and more of a team leader.
He weighed more than 300 pounds at one point. He had two benign tumors removed before a third turned out to be cancer.
Cancer surgery kept him away at the start of 2012, and a clinical trial in 2013. Days before he died, San Diego State gave him a one-year extension.

c: He tried three times to defect from Cuba and was jailed after each attempt. On the fourth, at 15, his mother fell overboard and he dove in to save her.
The Reds were ready to sign him for $1.3 million when Florida ruled him ineligible for his senior season; he won his appeal, threw two no-hitters and went to the Marlins 14th overall.
He made the Marlins' Opening Day roster in 2013, partly because of injuries, and won Rookie of the Year.
In 2014 he was the youngest Opening Day starter since Dwight Gooden. That May he tore his elbow ligament and had Tommy John surgery.
The day after his death, Dee Gordon wore his helmet, stood briefly in the right-handed batter's box, then switched sides and hit his only home run of the year.
He signed with the Marlins for a $2 million bonus.

Owner Jeffrey Loria hoped promoting him in 2013 would win back fans after the previous winter's fire sale. At that year's All-Star Game he struck out Dustin Pedroia and Chris Davis in a perfect inning.
Coming back from Tommy John surgery, he began 2015 on the disabled list and went back in August with a biceps strain.
His fastball averaged 94 to 97 mph and topped out at 100.2.
p: He called his grandmother Olga the "love of his life"; they were reunited in Miami after six years apart in 2013.
He died in 2016 when the boat he was piloting at 65 mph hit a jetty off Miami Beach, killing two friends too. Investigators found he was drunk and had cocaine in his system.
He married his high school sweetheart, Alejandra Baleato Marichal, in Tampa in December 2012.
Five days before he died, he announced that his girlfriend Maria Arias was pregnant. Their daughter was born in February 2017.

His blood alcohol was 0.147 percent, and he had cocaine in his system. Investigators found he could have been charged with involuntary manslaughter and vessel homicide. The families of the two friends who died sued his estate for $2 million each and settled. A family lawyer claimed he wasn't piloting the boat and that his drink was spiked with cocaine.

c: A U.S. senator from Idaho tipped off the Senators. Their scout waited out a rainstorm and watched the 17-year-old hit one 435 feet into a beet field. Killebrew had wanted to sign with Boston.
As a bonus baby he joined the team in Comiskey Park having never seen a big-league stadium. He bounced between Washington and the minors for five years before breaking out with 42 homers in 1959.

Paul Richards: "The homers he hit against us would be homers in any park — including Yellowstone." Dean Chance threw him a 2-0 fastball once: "The home run he hit on that pitch was hit so hard that no one in the stands even yelled."
In 1969 he played every game, led the league with 49 homers, 140 RBIs and 145 walks, and won the MVP. He hit 40 homers eight times, a total topped only by Babe Ruth.
Stuck at 498 homers in 1971, he said he didn't feel the pressure "until they passed out those mugs" the Twins had made for No. 500.
He was a fullback at West Virginia Wesleyan. The Red Sox's Northwest scout had talked to him for years, but he signed with Washington for $6,000 a year for three years plus a $4,000 bonus.
When Eddie Yost was traded after 1958, Cookie Lavagetto gave him the third-base job and helped him with his throwing.
In the 1968 All-Star Game he tore his hamstring, and a bone tore away from his pelvis.
The Twins were swept by Baltimore in the ALCS. In 1973 a knee injury cost him almost three months, and he played in only 35 games.

Offered a job as player-coach or Triple-A manager for 1975, he signed instead with Kansas City as its DH. Jim Kaat had told him that when he stopped hitting home runs, the front office would forget how to spell his name.
After retiring he broadcast games for the Twins, the A's and the Angels.
He's the model for the logo of the Players Alumni Association, which he helped found, and he'd compliment umpires on good calls even when they went against him.
p: As a boy he lifted ten-gallon milk cans as a farmhand. Despite the nickname "Killer," he was a quiet man who never smoked or drank; asked his hobbies, he said, "Just washing the dishes, I guess."
In 1964 an 8-year-old fan was in the hospital with severe burns. Killebrew visited, said "Maybe I'll hit you a couple," and homered twice that night.
After baseball his car businesses failed and he went bankrupt: "It's been a living hell."
He co-founded a golf tournament in Sun Valley, named partly for teammate Danny Thompson, that has given more than $23 million to leukemia and cancer research.
His father, a sheriff who later ran a house-painting business, died of a heart attack at home when Harmon was 16.
He married his high school sweetheart, Elaine Roberts, and they had five children. They divorced after more than 30 years.

His house went into foreclosure in 1988, and the next year he was reported $700,000 in debt. In 1990 a collapsed lung and damaged esophagus, then an abscess and staph infection, led to three surgeries; he nearly died and used a wheelchair for a time. That December he married Nita Patten.
He died of esophageal cancer at home in Scottsdale in 2011, days after stopping treatment and entering hospice.

c: In his pro debut in Maracaibo in 1953, his father, a famous shortstop, led off, took the first pitch, then handed the bat to his son. The crowd stood for 15 minutes.
Hank Greenberg passed on him as too small. The White Sox signed him for $10,000 on Chico Carrasquel's tip, then traded Carrasquel. Frank Lane: "that's precisely what we have — a machine."
He was the first Latin American Rookie of the Year, in 1956. Early on his throws so often went into the stands that fans were afraid to sit behind first.
In 1959 he stole 56 bases as Comiskey Park yelled "Go! Go! Go!" when he reached first, and the "Go-Go" White Sox won their first pennant in 40 years.
Released by Boston at 40, he got a blank contract from George Steinbrenner. He sent it back: "I just get released once in my lifetime."

At 19 he played for Venezuela at the 1953 Amateur World Series in Caracas, mostly at third and in left. His selection was criticized, especially because his father was on the coaching staff. Venezuela took silver.

He showed up overweight in 1962 and had an off year. When the White Sox offered a pay cut, he said he'd quit first and demanded a trade. In January 1963 they sent him and Al Smith to Baltimore for Hoyt Wilhelm, Ron Hansen, Dave Nicholson and Pete Ward.
He helped the Orioles sweep the Dodgers in the 1966 World Series. In that year's MVP vote he finished ninth, behind three teammates.
With Mark Belanger coming up, the Orioles traded him back to Chicago in November 1967. There he broke Luke Appling's team record for games at shortstop.
In 1970, at 36, he hit a career-high .313.
Traded to Boston for Luis Alvarado and Mike Andrews after 1970, he broke Appling's major-league records for hits and total bases by a shortstop.
p: His father told him: "You will never be a number two of anybody, always be the number one." On making the majors he wrote his mother, "please tell Dad that my debt with him is finally paid."
In Memphis in 1955 he met a young singer in a small bar named Elvis Presley.
In 2017 he declined an MLB honor: "I cannot celebrate while the young people of my country are dying while fighting for freedom." Every team in Venezuela retired his No. 11.

His father became the first player "exported" from Venezuela when he signed with the Dominican team Licey in 1934, the year Luis was born. Luis's first baseball job was as batboy for his father's team.

He came home after his first season with his wife, Sonia. His father died on New Year's Day 1971; his biggest regret was that his father didn't live to see him in the Hall of Fame. Back in Venezuela he managed in the winter league.
Since Johnny Romano died in 2019 he's been the last surviving player from the 1959 White Sox World Series team.
Since Willie Mays died in 2024 he's been the oldest living Hall of Fame player.

c: At North Carolina he was a football star; Fordham's coach said he "got the creeps every time we had to punt to him." The NFL's Chicago Cardinals drafted him, but he signed with his hometown Yankees.
He got his nickname at Newark when he stuffed his mouth with chewing tobacco and lit a cigar, and a teammate cracked, "What, no snuff?"
An ulcer kept him out of the wartime Army, and in 1944 he led the AL in runs, hits, triples and steals.
He won the 1945 batting title .308544 to .308457 on the last day, after a scorer changed an error to a hit, without ever having led the race during the season.
In 1948 he set records for fielding average and fewest errors by a second baseman, records that lasted until 1964 and 1988.
He hit .390 as a senior at North Carolina, and top Yankees scout Paul Krichell was determined to sign him. He signed with his hometown team the day he graduated.
In the 1943 World Series his only plate appearance came pinch-hitting for Hank Borowy in Game 3. An error on his sacrifice bunt set off a five-run rally, and the Yankees won 6–2.

Unhappy with a $15,000 contract, he once held out and sent it back unsigned. Arthur Daley warned that Larry MacPhail would probably sell him to the Cubs "for $100,000 and a couple of used bottle tops." He signed by March.

At the June trading deadline the Yankees shipped him to the St. Louis Browns, who traded him to Cleveland in April 1951. Released after one game in 1952, he later managed the Phillies' Schenectady farm team and became a roving batting instructor.

In the offseasons he played and coached for the Norfolk Shamrocks pro football team, was athletic director at William and Mary, coached at Canterbury Prep and at North Carolina, and ran a baseball school in Bartow, Florida.
p: When Phil Rizzuto was released in 1956 and fuming, Stirnweiss told him to cool off; Rizzuto did, and was offered a broadcasting job. As a broadcaster Rizzuto sometimes said "George Stirnweiss" when he meant George Steinbrenner.
He died at 39 in 1958 when his commuter train ran off an open drawbridge into Newark Bay. He left six children.

He started dating Jayne Powers, an ardent baseball fan, while playing for the Newark Bears, and married her. At his death their six children, two boys and four girls, ranged from 17 months to 15 years old.
After baseball he worked for a bank until he collapsed at its Columbus Circle office in June 1957, possibly from a heart attack. When he died he was a foreign freight agent in Manhattan.

c: The Giants signed him as a pitcher in 1959 and made him a hitter. It took three years, and coach Hiroshi Arakawa's "flamingo" one-legged stance, for him to blossom.
He hit 868 home runs, a homer every 10.7 at-bats, and won 13 straight Central League home run titles. With Shigeo Nagashima he formed the "ON Cannon."
He wrote that he "craved hitting a baseball in the way a samurai craved following the Way of the Sword." His autobiography, A Zen Way of Baseball, is about his work with Arakawa.
As a manager his teams walked Randy Bass, Tuffy Rhodes and Alex Cabrera as each closed in on his 1964 single-season home run record. Oh denied ordering it.
He managed Japan to the first World Baseball Classic title in 2006.
Arakawa first saw him in November 1954, when the big-leaguer stopped by chance to watch a sandlot game featuring the 14-year-old.
As Waseda's No. 2 pitcher he threw a no-hitter in a qualifier for the Koshien tournament.
He hit .161 as a rookie and .270 in 1960. He broke out in 1962 with 38 homers.

Giants pitcher Keith Comstock later said a coach threatened a $1,000 fine for every strike thrown to Randy Bass. Of Tuffy Rhodes, a Hawks pitching coach said, "I just didn't want a foreign player to break Oh's record." Alex Cabrera called it racist. Wladimir Balentien finally broke the record in 2013.
He was assistant manager of the Giants from 1981 to 1983 under Motoshi Fujita.
p: His father was a Chinese immigrant who ran a noodle shop in Tokyo and was jailed during the war. Oh kept his Republic of China passport all his life.
Born left-handed, he was trained to write and use chopsticks right-handed. His twin sister died at 15 months, and he wrote that he always felt he carried two lives.
He met his wife Kyoko when she asked for an autograph in his rookie year; they wrote letters for years before marrying. After she died in 2001, her ashes were stolen from the family grave.

His father wanted one son to be a doctor and the other an engineer. When his older brother broke an ankle playing ball as a medical student, their father banned baseball for both. His brother obeyed; Oh nodded and kept playing out of sight. When he failed the exam for a pre-college school, his path changed.
He and Kyoko had three daughters; Rie became a radio sportscaster. Kyoko died of stomach cancer in 2001 at 57, and he had the same disease in 2006.

c: He'd said he would join only the Yomiuri Giants, but Hanshin drafted him first in 1968. He hit 22 homers and threw out the most base stealers in the league to win Rookie of the Year.
In 1970 a pitch hit him on the left ear; he was unconscious for two days and hospitalized for three months. The beaning led Japan to adopt ear-flap helmets.
In 1975 he hit 43 homers to lead the Central League, ending Sadaharu Oh's 13-year run of home run titles.
Known for towering, high-arcing homers, he hit one every 12.41 at-bats, second only to Oh among players with 300 homers. With pitcher Yutaka Enatsu he formed the "Golden Battery."
Traded to Seibu after 1978, he won the Japan Series in 1982 and 1983.
The year after the beaning he was hospitalized for over a month with nephritis just before the season, and didn't join the team until June.
After retiring in 1984 he managed the Daiei Hawks and coached the Tigers. He became head batting coach of Japan's national team.
p: At Hosei University he was one of the "Hosei Trio" with Koji Yamamoto and Masaru Tomita. He later managed the Daiei Hawks and has long been a TV commentator.
He has been a TBS commentator in three stints, from 1985 to 1989, 1993 to 2001, and from 2004 on.

c: Still in high school, he played second base for the Newark Eagles under the name Larry Walker. In 1946 he caught the final out of the Negro League World Series against Satchel Paige's Monarchs.

On his first day with Cleveland in 1947, teammates looked away and wouldn't speak to him, and none would lend him a first baseman's glove. "I had to take it, but I fought back by hitting the ball as far as I could."
In Game 4 of the 1948 World Series he became the first Black player to homer in a Series. His embrace with pitcher Steve Gromek afterward became one of baseball's most famous photos.
He led the AL in homers in 1952 and 1954, and in 1954 drove in 126 with only two errors in center field.
In 1978 he became the second Black manager in the majors. "Why did it take this long? You tell me."
Drafted into the Navy, he was sent to Camp Robert Smalls, the Black division of the Great Lakes training station. The segregation left a deep impression on him.
He managed only two singles in the 1954 World Series as the Giants swept Cleveland.
After a 1955 season fighting a wrist injury, Cleveland traded him to the White Sox for Jim Busby and Chico Carrasquel. In Chicago he got into an on-field fight with Billy Martin.

The Comiskey Park fans booed him, and Al Lopez said, "We wouldn't start another season with Doby because the fans are down on him." Traded to Baltimore, he was dealt again before playing a game, then went to Detroit, and the White Sox bought him back in May 1959.

Playing for the minor-league San Diego Padres, he broke an ankle sliding into third in Sacramento. He tried out with Toronto of the International League in 1960, but was released when X-rays showed his ankle bone deteriorating.
p: His father, a horse groomer and semipro ballplayer, drowned on a fishing trip when Larry was eight. As a boy in Camden, he and his friends used worn-down broom handles for bats.
He married his high school sweetheart Helyn in 1946 and drove to a game in Trenton that night; it was rained out. They were married 55 years.
When Cleveland retired his number in 1997, Hank Aaron told him, "if it had not been for you, I wouldn't have been able to have the career that I had."
In Montclair, New Jersey, Yogi Berra was a neighbor, and the two families' kids played ball together.
His parents met when his father was playing ball in the street in front of her home. With his father traveling and his mother attached to her own mother, he was often raised by his grandmother.
He attended Jackson School in Camden, segregated under South Carolina law. Richard Dubose, who had managed his father, gave him his first baseball lessons.
He wanted to become a physical education teacher and coach. He went to Long Island University partly to play basketball for Clair Bee and partly to be near Helyn, then transferred to Virginia Union.
He and Helyn had five children. He had a kidney removed for cancer in 1997; Helyn died of cancer in 2001, and he died of cancer at home in Montclair in 2003, at 79.

c: He signed with the Giants in 1958 for 18 million yen, then the most ever for a Japanese player, and struck out four times in his debut against Masaichi Kaneda, as Oh would a year later.
As a rookie he missed a .300/30-homer/30-steal season because one homer was taken away when he forgot to touch first base.
On June 25, 1959, in the first game Emperor Hirohito ever attended, he won it with a walk-off homer off Minoru Murayama. Rookie Sadaharu Oh also homered.
Batting cleanup behind Oh in the "ON Cannon," he won five MVPs and made the Best Nine every season of his career as the Giants won nine straight championships.

As Giants manager he brought in Davey Johnson, the team's first non-Japanese player, and finished last in 1975, then won pennants in 1976 and 1977. Fans were so angry when he was fired in 1980 that the owner's newspaper lost readers.
Every pro team wanted him by his senior year, with the Nankai Hawks and Hiroshima Carp the most active.
The Giants wanted him to succeed Tetsuharu Kawakami as manager, so in his last seasons he was a player-coach.
He was named Giants manager in November 1974, a month after retiring.
In his second stint as manager, 1993 to 2001, the Giants won pennants in 1994, 1996 and 2000 and the Japan Series in 1994 and 2000.
p: Known as "Mr. Pro Baseball" and "Mr. Giants," he was considered a national figure of postwar Japan alongside singer Hibari Misora and actor Yujiro Ishihara.
He met his wife Akiko while covering the 1964 Tokyo Olympics as a newspaper reporter with Oh. Their son Kazushige played for the Giants while his father managed them.
In 2013 he received the People's Honour Award alongside Hideki Matsui, whom he had drafted, and in 2021 he carried the Olympic torch in Tokyo.
His father, a town tax collector and deputy mayor, died of a heart attack in 1954, when Shigeo was 18.
He married Akiko Nishimura in January 1965. They had two sons and two daughters; Kazushige became a sportscaster and Masaoki a race-car driver. Akiko died of heart failure in 2007 at 64.
He had a brain hemorrhage in 2022 and died of pneumonia in Tokyo in June 2025, at 89.

c: Warming up under the stands on a rainy day in Atlanta, he threw a ball into a wooden post. The next pitch with the roughened ball sailed with a dip, and he had discovered the emery ball.
He first scuffed balls with a broken pop bottle, then hid a piece of emery on a string under his undershirt and dropped it into a hole in his glove.
Ty Cobb: "He kept his secret a long time by pretending he was pitching a spitter." Ford told the press he had 14 versions of his "spitball."
In 1910 he won 26 games with a 1.65 ERA, still the AL rookie record for wins.
When the Yankees offered a pay cut, he jumped to the Federal League and went 21-6. The emery ball was banned in 1915, and his big-league career ended that year.
On his older brother's recommendation he signed with the Minneapolis Millers in 1904. He was sold to Springfield, drafted by Atlanta, and bought by the New York Highlanders.
The unimpressed Highlanders farmed him out to Jersey City at 26. Hiding his new pitch all season, he struck out 189 Eastern League batters.
In 1911 the Highlanders paid him $5,500, second on the team only to manager Hal Chase.
In 1911 he went 22-11 for a sixth-place team. That July he pitched four innings, after Joe Wood and Walter Johnson, for the all-stars in the benefit game held after Addie Joss's death.

Without the emery ball, Buffalo released him in July and re-signed him later that month. When the Federal League folded his rights went back to the Yankees, who released him. He pitched in the minors for Denver and Toledo, and in 1922 coached the University of Minnesota baseball team.
p: Born in Manitoba, his mother was a second cousin of Grover Cleveland. His older brother Gene also pitched in the majors.
After baseball he graduated from college, worked as a bank cashier in North Carolina and later as a draftsman in New York.
His family moved to the U.S. when he was three and settled in Minneapolis, where his father worked as a clerk.
He married Mary Hunter Bethell in 1912; they had two daughters, Mary and Jean. He died of a heart attack in Rockingham, North Carolina, near her hometown, in 1960 at 76.

c: Working at a hotel in Sanford, North Carolina, he met Yankees scout Paul Krichell, told him he was a pitcher, and got a tryout. He went 17-4 as a rookie in 1932.
Bill Dickey called his sidearm fastball "the meanest delivery in the league for a right-handed hitter." He boasted that if he wasn't better than teammate Johnny Broaca, "I'll eat his shirt."
In 1937 he started 15-0. In the last game he lost 1-0 on an error by third baseman Odell Hale, and his manager had to restrain him twice from going after Hale.
