In 1938 he refused to cut off the tattered sleeves of the sweatshirt he wore to distract hitters and walked off the mound. The sweatshirt ended up in the Hall of Fame.
With Brooklyn in 1943 he charged umpire George Barr over a balk call; writers said they'd never seen such an attack on an umpire. He later became a minor-league umpire himself.
Allen said the bellhop story was wrong: scout Johnny Nee approached him after a game in Asheville in 1929. The Yankees signed him for $7,500, beating out Cleveland.
Starting Game 4 of the 1932 World Series, he was knocked out in the first inning after giving up three runs on five hits.

Tired of his holdouts and sour attitude, the Yankees traded him to Cleveland in December 1935 for Monte Pearson and Steve Sundra. Razzed by the Tigers one day, he charged their coach Del Baker and had to be held back by umpires.
During the 1938 All-Star break something snapped in his shoulder; some said it happened in the game, others that he slipped on a bar of soap in the shower.

The Browns bought him for $20,000 before 1941 and waived him in July. After his attack on umpire Barr he was suspended 30 days, and the Dodgers sent him and Dolph Camilli to the Giants, who released him in April 1945.
p: His father, the police chief of Lenoir, North Carolina, died of appendicitis, and his mother sent him to a Baptist orphanage, where he learned baseball. There he lost two toes when his shotgun went off.
After a loss to Boston he overturned stools in the hotel bar and sprayed a fire extinguisher down the corridor; his 1959 obituary mentioned it.

He married Leta Shields of Greensboro in 1931; they had a son and a daughter. After baseball he worked as an automobile tag inspector and in real estate. He was buried in Greensboro, but his son later had his body exhumed and reburied beside Leta.
He died of a heart ailment in 1959 at 54.

c: His high school had no baseball team, so he went to the Manhattan School of Aviation Trades, an hour's bus ride away, which did. He played first base until a Yankees scout at a tryout said he was too small and taught him a curve.
In a 1946 sandlot championship at the Polo Grounds he threw a two-hitter with 18 strikeouts and broke up the other team's no-hitter with a 10th-inning double.
Pitching winter ball in Mexico, he got amoebic dysentery and nearly died; the team owner kept stopping him at the airport when he tried to fly home.
He won 10 World Series games and pitched 33⅔ straight scoreless Series innings, breaking Babe Ruth's record. His .690 winning percentage is the best for any 200-game winner since 1900.
Late in his career he doctored baseballs: catcher Elston Howard coated them in mud from a wet spot by the plate, and Ford scuffed them with his wedding ring.
Once he called Johnny Blanchard to the mound; asked what was wrong, he said, "Nothing. I just figured you could use a breather."
Yankees scout Paul Krichell noticed his arm in fielding practice. His size worked against a big bonus, and he'd have signed for almost nothing, but competition pushed the offer to $7,000 on the spot.

As a rookie he brushed off Eddie Lopat's tips: "I did it this way in Binghamton and it worked for me there." When Boston hit him hard, he learned Red Sox coach Earle Combs had been picking up his pitches.
In 1961 he went 25-4, his first 20-win season, and won the Cy Young, but the season was overshadowed by Roger Maris and Mickey Mantle's home run chase.
In August 1966 he had surgery for a circulatory problem in his throwing shoulder.
He was the Yankees' pitching coach in 1964 while still pitching, first base coach in 1968, and pitching coach again in 1974 and 1975. In 1977 he was on the broadcast of the Blue Jays' first game.
p: Lefty Gomez named him "Whitey" in the minors because he couldn't remember the rookies' names. Elston Howard dubbed him "the Chairman of the Board."

Retiring in 1967: "I came in wearing a $50 suit, and I'm going out wearing a $200 suit." When his first grandchild was born, he called Mickey Mantle: "Last night for the first time in my life I slept with a grandmother."
He died at 91 while watching a Yankees playoff game at home.

He was the only child of Jim and Edna Ford; his father worked for Con Edison and his mother was a bookkeeper at an A&P. His father later ran a bar in Astoria, the Ivy Room. As a boy Whitey checked the box score every morning to see how many hits DiMaggio had.
He married Joan Foran in 1951, and they had two sons and a daughter. They lived in Glen Cove on Long Island for a time.
In 2002 he opened Whitey Ford's Cafe in Garden City, with a replica of the Yankee Stadium facade. He had dementia for several years before he died.
In 1998 the musician Everlast released an album called Whitey Ford Sings the Blues and took "Whitey Ford" as a nickname.

c: "Chino" Morán played third base and the outfield from 1902 to 1914 for Fe, Habana, Carmelita and the Cuban Stars, and was elected to the Cuban Baseball Hall of Fame in 1945.
p: A native of Matanzas, he was the older brother of ballplayer Francisco Morán.

c: The Hawks signed him after a 1954 tryout as a bullpen catcher. He went hitless as a rookie, and kept his job reportedly by offering to play for free and threatening to throw himself in front of a train.
In 1965 he became the first NPB batter to win the Triple Crown. He led the Pacific League in homers nine times and won five MVPs.
His 657 homers, 1,988 RBIs and 2,901 hits are all second in NPB history. His Hall of Fame plaque shows him with his cap on backwards and no logo.
As Yakult's manager in the 1990s his data-driven "ID baseball" won four pennants and three Japan Series.

He began managing as the Hawks' player-manager in 1970, the start of a 24-year managing career. At Yakult he mentored catcher Atsuya Furuta and pitcher Tetsuya Iida, the "poster child for ID baseball."

He managed Hanshin from 1999 until December 2001, when his wife Sachiyo was arrested for tax evasion, accused of hiding ¥45 million of his income. He resigned the next day; he wasn't accused himself. After managing the corporate team Shidax, he spent four seasons turning Rakuten around.
p: His father died serving in China when he was three, and he grew up poor in a fishing village; his older brother helped him get through high school.
Playing in the rarely televised Pacific League, he openly resented the attention that went to Oh and Nagashima.

Married since 1960, he began dating TV personality Sachiyo in 1971 and moved in with her in 1972. He divorced his first wife in 1978 and married Sachiyo; they stayed married until her death in 2017. Her sons, agents Don and Kenny Nomura, are his stepsons.
He died of heart failure in February 2020, at 84.

c: He hit .497 over two varsity seasons at Maryland. Herb Pennock said he hit the ball harder to left than any left-handed hitter he'd seen except Babe Ruth.

The Yankees wanted another Ruth who'd pull balls into the short right-field porch. "They can save Babe Ruth's crown for someone else." He hit .353 at Newark anyway and was Minor League Player of the Year.
Benched when Joe DiMaggio came back in 1939, he cried. He took over in right in August and hit .438 with three homers as the Yankees swept the World Series.
With DiMaggio and Tommy Henrich he formed perhaps the best outfield of its time. From 1940 to 1943 he averaged 28 homers, 102 RBIs and 107 walks.
His career OPS+ of 152 ranks ahead of more than a dozen Hall of Famers.

A slipped disk in 1947 ended his prime. Asked to carry the lineup card in the World Series, he said, "The next time I go on to that playing field, I'm going out to play, not to try to get some sympathy."

At Maryland, coach Burton Shipley, who'd managed Hack Wilson in 1922, said Keller looked as good. An ankle injury made him drop football so he wouldn't risk his baseball future. He signed with Yankees scout Gene McCann.
He signed for $22,000 in 1947. In July doctors removed a slipped disk from his spine. The surgery forced him to change his batting style, and the Yankees released him in December 1949.

Detroit signed him for $20,000 as "the highest-paid pinch-hitter in the game" and released him in 1951. Back with the Yankees for two weeks in 1952, he struck out in his one at-bat, and the team still voted him a $1,000 World Series share.
In four World Series he hit .306 with five homers. He coached for the Yankees from mid-1957 through 1959.
p: As a boy he played ball after school, then ran two and a half miles home and changed in the barn so his father wouldn't know.

He hated the nickname "King Kong." When broadcaster Curt Gowdy asked if Joe McCarthy drank, Keller followed him to his train cabin and grabbed him: "I never want you to make another remark about Joe McCarthy like that."

He used the money from his Yankees day to start a scholarship at Maryland, and played ball to buy a farm. His Yankeeland Farms bred champion harness horses for 35 years; his son said he liked listening to the horses eat.
He was born on a 140-acre farm near Middletown, Maryland. The family lost it in the Depression when he was 17. At Maryland he dug ditches for $15 a month.

He and Martha were married 52 years and had three children. His son Donald, who worked beside him on the farm for 30 years, said his father "liked feeding horses and liked just listening to them eat." He died of colon cancer in 1990 at 73.

c: His father, a tailor who flew P-51s in the war, raised him; Reggie said he could still cuff a pair of slacks. At Arizona State on a football scholarship, he tried out for baseball and replaced Rick Monday in center.
Playing summer ball in Baltimore, the white team's manager didn't know he was Black until the tryout: "The more I saw you that day, the whiter you got."
He had 34 homers by July 5, 1969, and finished with 47. "Microphones were shoved in my face for the first time."
Stealing home in the 1972 ALCS, he tore his hamstring 20 feet from the plate, slid in anyway with the tying run, and was carried off. He missed the World Series.
Pulled mid-inning at Fenway in 1977, he nearly came to blows with Billy Martin on national TV. That October he hit three homers in Game 6 of the World Series and became "Mr. October."
He has the most strikeouts in history, 2,597, and is the only 500-homer hitter who never had back-to-back 30-homer seasons.
Playing high school football, he fractured five cervical vertebrae and spent six weeks in the hospital and another month in a neck cast.

He took over center field at Arizona State from Rick Monday, who "was a big league ballplayer when he was 19." The A's drafted Jackson second overall in 1966, and he and his father, now out of jail, went to Charlie Finley's Indiana farm and agreed to an $85,000 bonus.

Playing in Birmingham he felt "the uncomfortableness, the awkwardness, the fear … in the heart of Dixie." After his divorce, winter ball at Santurce under Frank Robinson helped put his life back on track.
Finley issued each player two caps and 24 bats a season, and the trainer saved the leftover tape from every roll. Jackson: "he was cheap."

He had a serious fight with teammate Bill North, who alleged Jackson spent too much time with whites, especially white women. Another time he angrily threw a bat into the stands, and it narrowly missed manager Alvin Dark's wife and two young sons.
He hit his first World Series home run in Game 7 in 1973.
Over 21 seasons he reached the postseason 11 times, winning six pennants and five World Series.
As an adviser to the Astros he got a ring in 2022, and stepped down in November 2024 to spend more time with his family.
p: His father was jailed for making moonshine in the basement near the end of Reggie's senior year of high school.
An assistant football coach at Arizona State tried to break up his relationship with Jennie Campos because he was Black and she was considered white. They married anyway, and divorced in 1973.
He played a crazed assassin sent to kill the Queen in The Naked Gun.
His father, who was half Puerto Rican, had played second base for the Newark Eagles. His parents divorced when Reggie was six, and his mother left with three of the children.
He married Jennie, whom he met at Arizona State, in 1968; they later divorced.
His only child, Kimberly, was born in the early 1990s.
While still playing, he worked offseasons as a reporter and color man for ABC Sports.
A 1976 fire at his Oakland home destroyed his 1973 MVP award, World Series trophies and All-Star rings. In 2005 his car was hit from behind in Tampa and flipped several times.

c: He spent World War II as a Navy pilot flying antisubmarine patrols, and "barely touched a bat." He came back 20 pounds heavier and led the NL in homers as a rookie.

Hank Greenberg, "the single biggest influence of my adult life," made him a pull hitter and fixed his wardrobe after spotting brown shoes with a tuxedo. The bullpen built for Greenberg, "Greenberg Gardens," became "Kiner's Korner."
He led the NL in home runs seven straight years, a record. Teammate Fritz Ostermueller: "Home run hitters drive Cadillacs. Singles hitters drive Fords."
He put his name on a 1949 magazine article saying he wouldn't want to break Babe Ruth's record. Fifty years later: "That was a big fat lie."
Branch Rickey cut his pay after he led the league again in 1952: "Son, we can finish last without you." Rickey traded him, and the Pirates did finish last.

He joined the expansion Mets' broadcast booth in 1962 "because I had a lot of experience with losing," and stayed more than 50 years. On Garry Maddox: "Two-thirds of the Earth is covered by water. The other third is covered by Garry Maddox."
He played shortstop for a Yankee-sponsored youth team, but Pirates scout Hollis Thurston convinced him he'd have a better chance in Pittsburgh. He signed as soon as he graduated from high school.
He admitted his 1946 home run title was a fluke: Johnny Mize, one behind, missed weeks with a broken wrist.
The Pirates tripled his salary to $30,000 for 1948 and paid him $90,000 by 1952. A booking agent said a show-business star of his size would make $30,000 a week.

In a confidential letter, Branch Rickey complained that Kiner got special privileges, demanded expensive clubhouse air-conditioning, and wanted a contract clause guaranteeing the short fences. Bill James: "it's nuts, but that's what he was doing."
In June 1953 the Pirates traded him, Joe Garagiola, George Metkovich and Howie Pollet to the Cubs for six players and $150,000.

Facing 50-50 odds that back surgery would work, he retired at 32 to become general manager of the minor-league San Diego Padres. He started doing play-by-play there because he couldn't afford an announcer.
He, Lindsey Nelson and Bob Murphy broadcast Mets games for the team's first 17 seasons.
p: Bing Crosby, a Pirates part-owner, drew him into Hollywood. He escorted a 17-year-old Elizabeth Taylor to a premiere and dated Janet Leigh.
He married tennis star Nancy Chaffee with Greenberg as best man, and after two years of lessons beat her at tennis, two weeks before she gave birth.
Asked on his postgame show what his wife was like, Mets catcher Choo Choo Coleman said, "Mrs. Coleman, and she likes me, Bub."
His father died when he was four, and his mother took a job in Alhambra, California. Even as a star, he still lived with her there.

He and Nancy Chaffee divorced in 1968; their son Michael played briefly in the Mets' farm system. He married Barbara George in 1969, and when they divorced, he said, much of his baseball memorabilia disappeared with her.
His third wife, DiAnn Shugart, a Palm Springs businesswoman, died of cancer in 2004. In his 80s he married and divorced Ann Benisch.
He attended every Hall of Fame ceremony from his induction until his death. The Mets named their broadcast booth for him.

c: Ty Cobb was so impressed at his tryout that he went up in uniform and pulled the owner out of his office to watch. "I would've signed for nothing."

He got his chance in 1926 when the starting second baseman got the measles: "I owe everything to O'Rourke's measles." Later Cobb stopped speaking to him, wouldn't even give him the signs, and never said why.
Lefty Gomez named him "the Mechanical Man": "you wind Gehringer up in the spring and turn him off in the fall and in between he hits .340." He won the 1937 batting title and MVP at .371.
By 1938 he was the only player to have started every All-Star Game, and he hit .500 in them. Satchel Paige called him "the toughest of all those stickers."
Hank Greenberg: "I would dive for one and it would bounce off my glove. Charlie would be standing there, right behind me, and he'd say, 'I could've gotten that one.'"
He went to the University of Michigan to study physical education, earned a freshman letter in baseball, and worked part-time in an ice-cream plant.
He hit .379 in the 1934 World Series, which the Tigers lost to the Cardinals, and .375 in 1935 as Detroit beat the Cubs for its first championship.
Once, after neither he nor Rogell covered second on a steal attempt, player-manager Mickey Cochrane charged out from behind the plate shouting at both of them.
By one account he hurt his back shoveling snow. By the 1940 World Series he "covered little ground," and in 1941 his average fell from .313 to .220.
He enlisted in the Navy in September 1942, coached baseball at the preflight school at St. Mary's College in California, and was discharged in 1945 as a lieutenant commander.
As Tigers general manager he inherited a team paid well for nearly winning the 1950 pennant, and had to trade players to cut the payroll.
p: He skipped his own Hall of Fame induction in 1949 because he was getting married; the couple sneaked into a church in San Jose through the back door to avoid crowds.
His company made the upholstery buttons Ford, Chrysler and GM bought: "We sold a jillion." He'd tell skeptical buyers he hadn't known much about baseball when he started either.
Given a set of right-handed golf clubs, the lefty learned to golf right-handed. Asked by strangers if he was the ballplayer, he'd say, "My name is Schultz."
His parents were German immigrants, and he had nine half-siblings. He grew up on a 220-acre dairy and grain farm near Fowlerville, Michigan.
His father died during Charlie's first year in pro ball, never having seen him play except in high school or at the fairgrounds.

He stayed single for years because his diabetic mother lived with him and needed care. He met Josephine Stillen on sales calls to Nash-Kelvinator, where she worked in purchasing; she remembered him from the 1934 and 1935 World Series.

In earlier winters he'd worked as a department store sporting-goods clerk and sold coal wholesale. He chaired the Wayne County March of Dimes for 20 years: "I think I've been in every church basement in the city."
He had a stroke in December 1992 and died the next month, at 89, in a nursing home in Bloomfield Hills.

c: A college pitcher, he filled in at catcher for a friend in a semipro game and was signed by Little Rock's manager on the back of an Elks membership card. A Yankees scout wired that he'd "quit scouting if this boy does not make good."
Miller Huggins told the rookie to stop trying to hit like Ruth: "We pay one player here for hitting home runs and that's Babe Ruth." He caught 100 games 13 straight seasons and hit over .300 in 11.
In 1932 he punched Washington's Carl Reynolds after a collision at the plate and broke his jaw in two places, drawing a 30-day suspension. "I never was so sorry about a thing in my life."
He played the 1936 World Series with a broken bone in his hand and kept it quiet so the Giants wouldn't know; Lou Gehrig told reporters afterward.

As a coach he made Yogi Berra a catcher: "Bill was learning me all his experience." Elston Howard: "Without Bill, I'm nobody." Bob Feller: "I believe I could have won 35 games if Bill Dickey was my catcher."
When Jackson waived him, Yankees scout Johnny Nee wired Ed Barrow, "I will quit scouting if this boy does not make good." The Yankees paid the $12,000 waiver price.
One August he broke the second finger of his right hand in a game against Cleveland, cutting his season short.
He held out in 1936 for $25,000, up from $14,500, and settled for $17,500. In 1943 he hit .351 and homered to clinch the World Series.
In the Navy he served as an athletic officer in the Pacific and managed the team that won the 1944 Service World Series in Hawaii.
He became player-manager when Joe McCarthy resigned in 1946, but owner Larry MacPhail wouldn't give him a new contract until after the season.
p: Lou Gehrig was his roommate and best friend. At Gehrig's memorial at Yankee Stadium, Dickey broke down partway through his speech.
He married a New York showgirl, Violet Arnold, three days after the 1932 World Series.
In retirement he was an excellent quail hunter and lived by a lake in southwest Arkansas.
He was born in Bastrop, Louisiana, one of seven children. The family moved to Kensett, Arkansas, where his father was a brakeman for the Missouri Pacific Railroad.
He became Lou Gehrig's road roommate after Joe Sewell was released after the 1933 season. He and Violet had one child, Lorraine, born in 1935.
He died in Little Rock in 1993. The city's ballpark is named partly for him and his brother George.

c: He taught himself the knuckleball in high school from a photo of Dutch Leonard's grip. A Charlotte paper wrote, "Wilhelm is never going any place. He throws like a washer-woman."
He won a Purple Heart at the Battle of the Bulge and didn't reach the majors until he was 29. In his first big-league at-bat he homered, the only home run of his career.
As a rookie reliever in 1952 he won the ERA title, the only full-time reliever ever to do it. In his first start for the Orioles in 1958 he no-hit the Yankees.

Catchers dreaded him. Wes Westrum woke up shaking the night after catching him, and Paul Richards designed an oversized mitt. Ted Williams: "Don't let anybody tell you they saw a better knuckleball than Wilhelm's."
He broke Cy Young's record of 906 games pitched in 1968: "The next 900 won't be so tough." He was the first to pitch in 1,000 games and the first reliever in the Hall of Fame.
He passed up Davidson to sign with Mooresville, 12 miles from home, in the Class D North Carolina State League. He went 10-3 in 1942 before being drafted into the Army.
He was once dropped from a Class D team by a manager who told him to forget the knuckleball. He kept throwing it.

In his second season he was cited for doing 60 in a 25-mph zone in Tarrytown, plus disorderly conduct for cursing the desk sergeant. Another run-in ended in a crash that left him with a bruised arm and a hurt back; Peggy and a police officer were slightly hurt too.
In the 1954 World Series he pitched 2⅓ scoreless innings over two games as the Giants swept Cleveland.
In February 1957 the Giants traded him to the Cardinals to get Whitey Lockman back.
Cleveland GM Frank Lane, alarmed at the number of passed balls, let Baltimore claim him off waivers in August 1958.

Ray Katt once had four passed balls in an inning catching him. The 1959 Orioles had 49, 30 more than any other team. When baseball limited mitts to 38 inches in 1965, the White Sox built him one with a hinged thumb.
The only significant injury of his career came in spring 1966, when a pitching machine broke the middle finger of his pitching hand during bunting practice.

Traded to Atlanta in September 1969 for Mickey Rivers, he arrived too late for the playoffs. In 1970 the Braves sold him to the Cubs with ten days left, then got him back after the season; Bowie Kuhn investigated but let it stand.
He was a Yankees minor-league pitching coach for 22 years. He didn't teach the knuckleball, believing you had to be born with the knack, but worked with Joe Niekro on his.
p: He spotted his wife Peggy in the stands in Columbus, Georgia, and sent a vendor to get her phone number. They wrote for three years before marrying.
His death certificate revealed he was born in 1922, a year earlier than anyone thought. He pitched until five days before his 50th birthday.
He was one of 11 children of tenant farmers in Huntersville, North Carolina.
He and Peggy lived in Sarasota and raised three children, Patti, Pam and Jim. He died of heart failure in a Sarasota nursing home in 2002.

c: He became a catcher in high school after a collision chasing a foul pop with his brother Calvin knocked out Calvin's teeth, and the mask no longer fit over Calvin's swollen jaw.
In 1972 he became the first unanimous Rookie of the Year. Eddie Kasko: "If you play against him you hate him, but if you play with him and want to win, you love him."
His 12th-inning homer in Game 6 of the 1975 World Series, as he waved his arms trying to keep it fair, is his best-known moment.
In 1985 he tagged out two Yankees, Bobby Meacham and Dale Berra, on the same play at the plate.
At 42 he told a rookie Deion Sanders, who hadn't run out a popup, "Next time run it out." He caught 2,226 games, then a record.
Fenway vendors complained that games went 20 minutes faster after he left, costing them sales.

One scout told his Legion coach that Fisk's bat wasn't quick enough. He took a basketball scholarship to the University of New Hampshire, and the Red Sox drafted him in the first round in January 1967.
He won the job in 1972 when starter Duane Josephson was hurt in the third game. His salary went from $18,000 to $30,000, reportedly as big a raise as anyone in the game got.
Collisions and run-ins with Thurman Munson, Frank Robinson, Graig Nettles and others made him unpopular around the league.

In June 1974 Cleveland's Leron Lee crashed into him at the plate and tore several knee ligaments. He was told he'd never play again, and was back twelve months later after reinjuring himself in spring 1975.
He hit .417 as Boston swept Oakland in the 1975 ALCS. Of a disputed play in Game 3 of the World Series he said after retiring, "To this day, I still think it was interference."
p: Born across the river in a Vermont hospital, he grew up in Charlestown, New Hampshire, and made the Red Sox recast his team Hall of Fame plaque, at a cost of $3,000, to remove the Vermont reference.
After he scored 42 points and grabbed 38 rebounds in a high school playoff game, his father's only comment was that he'd missed four free throws. Celtics owner Walter Brown asked, "who is that kid?"
When the White Sox released him in 1993, he and his wife hired a plane to tow a banner over Fenway: "IT ALL STARTED HERE. THANKS BOSTON FANS."
He grows and collects orchids, and appears briefly on a TV screen in Field of Dreams.
His father, Cecil, was a tool-and-die engineer in Springfield, Vermont, and also worked the family farm; he'd hop off the tractor, go win a tennis match, and come back to his chores.

Brother Calvin was drafted by both the Orioles and the military, and the military won. Younger brother Conrad, thought the best pitcher in the family, signed with the Expos, but an arm injury ended his career.
He met his wife, Linda Foust, at UNH; they have three children. His sister Janet married his teammate Rick Miller in 1973.
In 2012 he was charged with drunk driving in New Lenox, Illinois, after being found unconscious behind the wheel beside a cornfield.

c: He was Cascade High's all-time leading rusher and signed to play football and baseball at Washington, but took a $2 million bonus from the Expos instead.
Montreal traded him to Cleveland with Cliff Lee and Brandon Phillips for Bartolo Colón in 2002.
He played 382 straight games and was the only AL hitter with 20 homers and 20 steals each year from 2005 to 2008. In 2009 he hit the first grand slam at the new Yankee Stadium.
Elbow surgery and microfracture knee surgery derailed him, and he missed two full seasons before coming back with Boston in 2014, where he homered on Opening Day.
Trying to get back into baseball, he took a $15-an-hour internship with the Diamondbacks. As White Sox interim manager in 2024 he oversaw the end of the most-losing modern season, 41-121.

An injury to Juan González before Opening Day won him a spot on Cleveland's roster. Before 2006 he signed for six years and $23.45 million. In his first postseason, in 2007, he homered twice in 11 games.
A groin injury in 2009 forced him out of the World Baseball Classic. That September he had elbow surgery, and a week later surgery for a related hernia.

Microfracture surgery on his left knee ended his 2010 season after 33 games. In 2011 he hurt his right knee twice and had a second hernia surgery. He missed all of 2012 after back surgery, then had microfracture surgery on his right knee.
Boston signed him in January 2014 for a $750,000 base salary, with incentives up to $6 million, and released him that June.
In November 2025 the Twins hired him as first base coach and outfield and baserunning instructor.
p: His father is Black and his mother is white. He graduated from high school with a 3.85 GPA.
He and his wife Brittany have three children. He once stepped away from a coaching job to spend more time with them.

c: He threw from his ear with no windup, a motion he picked up playing second base. Larry Doby: "I didn't see anyone in the major leagues who was better than Leon Day."
He beat Satchel Paige in three of their four matchups, once winning 1-0 with his own ninth-inning homer. Monte Irvin: "Leon was as good as Satchel Paige... but he never made any noise."
In 1937 he went 13-0 and hit .320 for Newark. In 1942 he struck out 18 Baltimore Elite Giants, a Negro League record.
He helped land supplies at Utah Beach six days after D-Day, then pitched his Army team to a championship before crowds of 50,000 in Nuremberg.
Back from the war, he threw a no-hitter on Opening Day 1946 and led Newark to the pennant. He got word of his Hall of Fame election in a hospital bed in 1995 and died days later.
Rap Dixon of the Baltimore Black Sox signed him in 1934. In 1935 he, Dixon and Yokely jumped to the Brooklyn Eagles, where he went 9-2 and made the first of seven All-Star Games.

He hurt his arm in Cuba when he slipped in the shower and caught himself with his right arm. In 1940 he chased a bigger salary to Venezuela and then Vera Cruz, Mexico, and helped both teams win titles.
Though Newark didn't win the 1942 pennant, he still played in the Negro World Series, thanks to an odd transaction.

Buck O'Neil's scouting report: "Front line starter, short arm type, everything quick, strike out pitcher, very durable, worked with three days rest, played 2B or LF between starts, top athlete, very desirable."
Despite a sore arm in 1946, he led the league in wins, strikeouts and complete games, and pitched in two games as the Eagles beat the Monarchs in a seven-game World Series.
He finished in the St. Louis Browns' farm system and with the Edmonton Eskimos, retiring in 1955 at 39.
In 1993 he fell one vote short with the Veterans Committee, when Roy Campanella was out sick.
p: He grew up in a Baltimore house with no electricity or running water and got into Black Sox games "over the fence, under the fence." He left high school because it had no baseball team.
"When they told me they was gonna pay me to play baseball, I said they must be crazy. I said I'd play for nothing."
After baseball he tended bar in Newark and worked as a security guard in Baltimore.
He was born in Alexandria, Virginia, the son of a glass factory worker. His high school had no baseball team, so at 17 he dropped out to play for the semipro Silver Moons.
He died five days after hearing he'd been elected. "I think that's what he was waiting for," said his sister. His wife Geraldine spoke for him at Cooperstown.
Historians contrast him with Satchel Paige: Paige was tall, boisterous and self-promoting; Day was short, slender and shy of attention. Geraldine founded the Leon Day Foundation in 2001.

c: A screwball from Cy Blanton and patient catching from Dick Luckey turned the wild lefty into a 21-game winner in Class B. He then spent years stuck in the Cardinals' crowded farm system.
"The Cat" got his nickname for quick reflexes; he made eight errors in more than 1,900 innings. Red Smith called him "a scrawny little scrap of meat, just a fragment of whale bone and rawhide."
In the 1946 World Series he shut out Boston in Game 2, won Game 6, and won Game 7 in relief with a cold. He was the first left-hander to win three games in one Series.
In 1948, with an elbow that swelled like a balloon after every start, he opened with three straight shutouts and led the league in ERA, shutouts and strikeouts.
As Baltimore's pitching coach for 14 years he developed Jim Palmer and Dave McNally, and turned 36-year-old Hoyt Wilhelm into an ERA-champion starter.

The Cardinals drafted him on Eddie Dyer's advice, though he'd called their organization a "chain gang" for its low pay and huge farm system. At Houston in 1936 he went 18-7, with four straight shutouts and 38 scoreless innings in a row.
A boyhood broken ankle and a spinal malformation made him 4-F during the war.
In Game 4 of the 1944 World Series he threw a complete-game 5-1 win despite nine hits and four walks.
A sore elbow in 1945 bothered him for the rest of his career. With the war over, he was rumored to be traded before 1946, until Dyer took over as manager.
In the 1946 pennant playoff against the Dodgers he struck out the last two batters to send the Cardinals to the World Series.
His career World Series ERA of 0.83 was the record from 1946 until Jack Billingham broke it in 1976.
His playing career ended after he strained his pitching arm lifting a heavy suitcase.
p: A natural lefty, he fought his teachers' attempts to make him write right-handed. As a boy he always had a bat, a glove, a fishing rod or a gun in his hand.
He married his high school sweetheart, Vera, in 1933; they were together 63 years.
The oldest of three children of Texas parents, he tried out with Tulsa at 18 and was overmatched. He went home to Ada, married Vera, and found construction work in the Depression.
He died at 89 in a nursing home in Bethany, Oklahoma.

c: In a showcase game for scouts after high school he struck out 17 straight batters. He gave half his $60,000 bonus to his father, getting his parents out of debt for the first time.
A struggling reliever in 1964, he learned the spitball from teammate Bob Shaw. He first used it in a big spot in the 13th inning of a 23-inning game at Shea and threw 10 shutout innings.

Asked on TV in 1971 whether her daddy threw a grease ball, his five-year-old daughter answered, "It's a hard slider." He confessed in a 1974 book, then claimed the book itself might have been part of the act.
In 1978, at 40, he became the first pitcher to win the Cy Young in both leagues. He and his brother Jim are the only brothers who both won the award.
He wasn't ejected for doctoring the ball until 1982, his 21st season, at almost 44. That May he won his 300th game.
During George Brett's pine-tar incident in 1983, he grabbed the bat and ran off with it before security caught him.

He hoped to sign with Cleveland, where Jim was pitching, but the Indians dropped out of the bidding early. He split his bonus with his father, and in 1961 the IRS came after him for the full tax plus penalties, on a minor-league salary.

He was summoned in the ninth inning of the second game of the 1962 pennant playoff against the Dodgers, but wasn't eligible for the World Series. His half share of the Series money went toward a farm near his family's.
Pitching coach Larry Jansen taught him a hard slider and had him throw over the top. He played pepper before his starts, believing he pitched better after working up a sweat.
In his only postseason, in 1971, he won Game 1 of the NLCS and lost the deciding Game 4 to Pittsburgh. That November the Giants traded him and Frank Duffy to Cleveland for Sam McDowell.

Vaseline allegedly turned down his endorsement offer with a postcard: "We soothe babies' backsides, not baseballs." Gene Mauch said he should be in the Hall "with a tube of K-Y Jelly attached to his plaque." Catcher Gene Tenace said the ball was sometimes too greasy to throw back.
p: He was named for a friend of his father's who had died while having his teeth pulled.
He and his brother Jim plowed with a mule at seven, and in high school both Perrys were 6-foot-3; he averaged nearly 30 points and 20 rebounds.

His farm failed in 1986, and he started Limestone College's baseball program. His wife Blanche was killed in a car accident in 1987; his son Jack, who threw two no-hitters for him at Limestone, died of leukemia in 2005.
His father was a good enough athlete to be offered a minor-league contract, but the family couldn't spare him from the farm.
He retired to a 500-acre tobacco and peanut farm, went bankrupt in 1986, and briefly worked as a sales manager for Fiesta Foods.

Blanche was killed when a car ran a stop sign and hit hers. They'd had three daughters and a son, Jack, who pitched for his father at Limestone and threw the school's only no-hitters, two in two weeks in 1990. Jack died of leukemia in 2005.
He got COVID in 2021, never fully recovered, and died at home in 2022 at 84.

c: The Royals took him in the 19th round in 1982. Days later he threw a no-hitter in the Los Angeles city championship at Dodger Stadium, retiring the last 20 batters.
In 1985, at 21, he won the Cy Young and was World Series MVP, throwing an 11-0 shutout in Game 7. His son was born eight hours before Game 6.
He was great in odd years and struggled in even ones: 20-6 in 1985, 7-12 in 1986, 23-6 with a 2.16 ERA in 1989, 5-9 in 1990.
In 1994, for the Mets, he walked 13 batters in 177⅓ innings and won his last seven decisions with an 11-to-1 strikeout-to-walk ratio over the final nine starts.
After a titanium anchor was drilled into his shoulder in 1996, he came back to win 15 for Boston in 1998 and received the Tony Conigliaro Award.
In his first postseason start, in the 1984 ALCS against Detroit, he gave up two runs in eight innings.
After his down 1986 season his salary was cut to $740,000. One May he tripped in his New York hotel room and needed 16 stitches in his forehead and five more under an eye.
Once, with his record at 5-7, he had surgery in late July to remove two loose bone chips from his elbow.
In December 1991 the Royals traded him and Bill Pecota to the Mets for Kevin McReynolds, Gregg Jefferies and Keith Miller. In New York his odd-year pattern vanished.
He tore a knee ligament stepping on a ball while jogging in the outfield.
With Colorado in 1995 he lost his only start of the playoffs, Game 4 of the NLDS against Atlanta.
After his last game in 2001: "When your son says to you, 'Dad, I want to be there at the last game you pitch,' you tell him, 'Kid, you might have been there already.'"
p: A clubhouse prankster, in 1993 he set off a firecracker near reporters and sprayed bleach; the Mets suspended him and fined him a day's pay, $15,384.
He played himself in the movie The Scout, throwing pitches to Brendan Fraser.
He said that if he were elected to the Hall of Fame he wouldn't attend the ceremony, because Pete Rose should be in.
He and his wife Kandace, a three-time breast cancer survivor, started SabesWings to help cancer patients pay medical bills.
He married his high school sweetheart, Janeane Inglett, in 1984. They had three children and separated in 1992. He met his second wife, Lynn Critelli, in New York and married her in 1996.
His son Drew played college ball at Western Carolina and Pepperdine, and son Dalton pitched for Tennessee. His daughter Brittany married Jacob Zachar, a star of Greek.
He coached Calabasas High from 2006, quit in 2007 after battles with the school district, and came back in 2008.

c: At 6-foot-8 he never lost a high school game he started. In one he hit four straight home runs while pitching a 48-0 win. He turned down more than 200 basketball scholarships.
In his first big-league start, in 1971, he struck out 15, tying the record for a debut.
In 1979 he struck out 313, an Astros record until Gerrit Cole in 2019. In one game he threw six wild pitches, a modern record, and still struck out 13 and won.
Johnny Bench and Dale Murphy both named him the toughest pitcher they ever faced.
On July 30, 1980, he collapsed from a stroke while warming up. A blood clot in his neck ended his career at 30.
He struck out Willie Mays three times in his debut.
He bounced between Houston and the minors for four years because of his wildness, but he often told reporters racism had kept him from becoming a regular sooner.

Before 1975 the Astros traded Claude Osteen and lost their ace, Don Wilson, who died of carbon monoxide poisoning at 29. Richard still walked eight batters in each of his third and fourth starts that year.
In 1978 he broke Tom Seaver's NL record for strikeouts by a right-hander.
In 1979 he threw nine straight complete games and 86 straight innings without a reliever, then signed a four-year contract.

In 1980, as his arm troubles went unexplained, some said he was egotistical, couldn't handle the pressure, or was jealous of Nolan Ryan's $4.5 million contract. Doctors studied his neck arteries on July 25 and found nothing wrong. After the stroke, his wife Carolyn said, "It took death, or nearly death, to get an apology."
During his comeback the graft from his 1980 surgery closed off, and he needed a bypass in his leg. The Astros released him in 1984.
p: "There were other guys in my high school with as much ability as I had, but instead of working at a job, they wanted to drink wine on Saturday nights."
After baseball he lost money in an oil scam and two divorces and was homeless in Houston by 1994. He found help at a church and became a minister.

Back in Louisiana he lost over $300,000 in an oil business scam and paid $669,000 to Carolyn in their divorce. A second marriage and divorce cost him his suburban Houston home. In 1989 he was cut by the Orlando Juice of the senior league.
Later he helped set up baseball programs for children in Houston. He died there in 2021, at 71.

c: He played second base until his senior year of high school, where his classmate was Robert Redford.
Branch Rickey, scouting him at 17: "A lot of artistry about this boy. Way above average fast ball."

Mickey Mantle: "He'll even come to the batting cage and say, 'Where do you want it today, big boy?'" He led the league in hit batsmen three straight years, and the Braves called him "the Shooting Gallery Kid."
Fined $100 for hitting Frank Robinson in 1961, he paid NL president Warren Giles in pennies. Giles made him roll them up.
He won 25 games and the Cy Young in 1962, and with Sandy Koufax won 49 games in 1965. That year he also hit .300 with seven homers.

In 1968 he threw 58⅔ straight scoreless innings, breaking Walter Johnson's record. When Orel Hershiser wanted out of the game rather than break Drysdale's mark in 1988, Drysdale said he'd have kicked him in the rear.
Brooklyn signed him for a $4,000 bonus. One minor-league season he started 10-2, then broke a bone in his hand, pitched through it, and finished 11-11.
The Braves called him "the Shooting Gallery Kid." Once Logan charged the mound and set off one of the biggest brawls in years.
In Game 3 of the 1963 World Series, the first Series game at Dodger Stadium, he beat the Yankees 1–0.
When Sandy Koufax sat out the 1965 Series opener for Yom Kippur, Drysdale started and was knocked out in the third. As Walter Alston came to get him: "Hey, skip, bet you wish I was Jewish today too."
In 1966 he and Koufax held out together, each asking for $500,000 over three years.
A torn rotator cuff ended his career. He went straight to the broadcast booth, working for NBC and ABC as well as the Dodgers.
p: As a broadcaster he made cameos on The Brady Bunch and The Beverly Hillbillies.
He married basketball star Ann Meyers: "I won't play against her, she's too tough one-on-one."
When Meyers made the Basketball Hall of Fame in 1993, they became the first married couple in their sports' Halls of Fame.
He died of a heart attack in a Montreal hotel while broadcasting a Dodgers series in 1993. Vin Scully had to break the news on the air.
In 1958 he married Ginger Dubberly, a model and former Rose Parade queen. They had a daughter, Kelly, and divorced in 1982.
Ann Meyers was the only woman to sign an NBA contract, with the Indiana Pacers in 1979. They had three children; Don Jr. was born on his father's 51st birthday.

When he didn't show up for the broadcast in Montreal, hotel staff found him face down in his room; he had been dead at least 18 hours. Vin Scully: "Never have I been asked to make an announcement that hurts me as much as this one."

c: From 8 to 18 he got up between 1 and 4 a.m. to help his father deliver the Houston Post. By junior high he could throw a softball more than 100 yards.

In high school one batter refused to step in after Ryan cracked the leadoff man's helmet and broke the next one's arm. His catcher's mitt wore through, and fans thought his pitches had razor blades in them for all the bats they broke.

The Mets traded him to the Angels for Jim Fregosi in 1971. There he cut calluses off his fingers with a scalpel before every start, tried rattlesnake oil on his elbow, and became the first big-league pitcher to lift weights seriously.
In 1973 he struck out 383, breaking Sandy Koufax's record. He finished with 5,714 strikeouts and seven no-hitters, both records.
He struck out seven pairs of fathers and sons, among them Bobby and Barry Bonds.

At 46, when Robin Ventura charged the mound in 1993, Ryan put him in a headlock and punched him, stayed in the game and won. In his last start he tore his elbow ligament: "I heard the ligament pop like a rubber band."
Mets scout Red Murff called his arm "the BEST arm I ever saw ANYWHERE in my life!" The Mets took him in the 12th round of the first draft in 1965, the 295th pick.
An elbow injury came soon after he started pro ball. The team doctor recommended surgery; Ryan refused and rehabbed it on his own.

He missed much of 1967 with illness, an arm injury and Army Reserve duty. In 1969 he won Game 3 of the NLCS in relief, his first playoff win (the next took 12 years), and saved Game 3 of the World Series in his only Series appearance.
Fregosi, who had never played third base in the majors, was gone from New York by July 1973.

From 1994 to 1997 he was a volunteer pitching coach at TCU, where his sons Reid and Reese played. He threw out the first pitch at the first World Series game in Texas in 2005, and owned the Express Bank of Alvin and a restaurant in Three Rivers.
p: As a teenager he was so mesmerized watching Sandy Koufax pitch in Houston that he wouldn't talk to his girlfriend Ruth, who later became his wife.
Ruth, a state tennis champion in high school, put on catcher's gear and caught him in the off-seasons.
He celebrated no-hitters with orange juice instead of champagne.
Opening a minor-league park on an old cornfield in Round Rock, he announced, "If we build it, they will come." They did; he later ran the Texas Rangers.
He was the youngest of six children. His mother was a descendant of John Hancock.
He married Ruth on June 26, 1967, as scout Red Murff looked on.
They have three children, Reid, Reese and Wendy, and Ruth coached the boys' Little League teams for a few summers.
A documentary, Facing Nolan, came out in 2022.

c: An Orioles scout said he looked "like he's playing on roller skates to the accompaniment of music." Another: "Belanger could be a major-league shortstop if he never got another hit in his life."
He broke in two tiny black gloves a season with spit and coffee and never dove for a ball, believing a sprint was faster. He won eight Gold Gloves and never wore a protective cup.
He was pinch-hit for 333 times, the AL record. Earl Weaver told him, "You're my shortstop if you hit .0001."
When Peter Gammons called him a "140 lb. weakling," Belanger found him at Fenway: "I'm 170 pounds, and I'm not a weakling."
After retiring he worked for the players' union as Donald Fehr's right hand, once interrupting Fehr's legalese in a meeting: "Don. You lost them."
His 14th-inning double in August 1960 sent Pittsfield's American Legion team to the national championship in Hastings, Nebraska. On scout Joe Cusick's reports, the Orioles signed him for $35,000.

Ron Hansen, just traded away by the Orioles, told the rookie, "Learn to rock forward as the pitcher delivers the ball instead of starting from zero." He still made 20 errors in 44 games at Bluefield in 1962.
Called "the greatest shortstop prospect in baseball history," he drew many trade offers. GM Harry Dalton: "I will never trade Belanger."
On April 30, 1967, playing second, he dropped Aparicio's feed and let in an unearned run, and Steve Barber lost a game in which Baltimore allowed no hits.
On the fourth night of his honeymoon in the Poconos in 1967, he heard the Orioles had traded Aparicio, opening the shortstop job.
He'd tell newcomers, "We don't do it that way," and said it even to Jim Palmer in 1978. Fined a dollar by the clubhouse Kangaroo Court, he'd shout, "I appeal!"

He homered in the first ALCS game ever played, in 1969, and hit .333 in the 1970 ALCS. Granted free agency in 1981, perhaps for publicly criticizing Earl Weaver, he played one season for the Dodgers and retired.
p: He scored 1,455 points in high school basketball, a Pittsfield record until 2003.
He and his wife Dee suggested the Orioles play John Denver's "Thank God I'm a Country Boy" during the seventh-inning stretch, a tradition that spread.
A longtime smoker, he quit in 1991 but was diagnosed with lung cancer in 1997 and died at 54.
His father, of French-Canadian descent, was a maintenance man in Cheshire, Massachusetts. Mark, third of four children, learned to field playing with his siblings in a cow pasture.
In the offseason he sold sporting goods at the Besse-Clarke department store in Pittsfield.
He and Dee had homes in Timonium, Maryland, and Key Biscayne, Florida, hosted Orioles players there, and had two sons, Richard and Robert. In early 1997 he married his second wife, Virginia French.

c: At Southern University he lost his academic scholarship and tried out for the baseball team, shagging flies for four weeks. One day he chased every fly ball until he passed out; when he came to, the coaches let him hit five balls, and he hit all five over the right-field fence.

On June 17, 1962, he hit a ball out of the Polo Grounds to center field, only the third player to do it in a major-league game. He sprinted all the way around, thinking the umpire was waving him to an inside-the-park homer.
On June 15, 1964, the Cubs traded him to St. Louis in a deal built around Ernie Broglio. Broglio went 7-19 as a Cub; Brock hit .348 for the Cardinals and they won the World Series.

When Maury Wills wouldn't share his notebook on pitchers, Brock bought an 8-mm camera and filmed pickoff moves. Don Drysdale told him he didn't want to be in his movies and threw at him his next time up.
In three World Series he hit .391 with 14 stolen bases. After the 1967 Series, when Bob Gibson won the MVP, radio station KMOX gave Brock a Cadillac.
His 118 steals in 1974 broke Wills's record. He finished second in the MVP vote to Steve Garvey: "I'm not bitter. I just think I deserved it."
His 3,000th hit, on August 13, 1979, was a line drive off the hand of the Cubs' Dennis Lamp, knocking him out of the game.
He was named NL Comeback Player of the Year in 1979, his last season, the first player so honored in his final season.
He tried out for the Cardinals, but the scout who'd recommended him was in Seattle signing Ray Washburn. The Cubs signed him in 1960.

Cubs teammate Larry Jackson: "He'd break out in a big sweat just putting on his uniform." Under the Cubs' rotating coaches, one told him to hit to the opposite field, another to bunt more, and another to pull the ball.
When he arrived the Cardinals were 28–31, in eighth place, behind the Cubs. Four months to the day after the trade they won the World Series.
In his first World Series at-bat he fouled off five pitches, then singled off Whitey Ford.
In May 1965, hitting .315, he bunted on Sandy Koufax and stole two bases. Next time up Koufax hit him in the back and broke his shoulder blade, and he fell to .261.
He hit .414 with a record seven steals in the 1967 World Series against Boston.
He slumped and lost his job early in 1978, then hit .345 in spring training in 1979 to win it back.
p: His father left shortly after he was born. He grew up in Collinston, Louisiana, where his school had one teacher and no running water.

Sent to the library in fourth grade for throwing a spitball, he had to research DiMaggio, Musial, Newcombe and Jackie Robinson. Their salaries were so large he had to ask the teacher what the numbers meant, and he decided to become a ballplayer.
He held the patent on the Brockabrella hat. He and his wife, Jacqueline, were ordained ministers at Abundant Life Fellowship Church.
His son Lou Brock Jr. played in the NFL, and he was the granduncle of broadcaster Taylor Rooks.
He was born in El Dorado, Arkansas, one of nine children his mother bore over three marriages. As a boy he lay awake at night wondering how he'd escape the poverty around him.
He didn't play organized baseball until 11th grade, but learned how big-league hitters stood from Harry Caray's Cardinals broadcasts.
He was diagnosed with multiple myeloma in 2017 and declared cancer-free later that year. He died in 2020 at 81.

c: He started as a knuckleball pitcher. After he struck out eight against the St. Louis Stars in a 1922 semipro game, the Stars signed him at 19 for $90 a month.

Manager Bill Gatewood is most often credited with the nickname, after Bell struck out Oscar Charleston in a tight spot; "Papa" was added later. Gatewood moved him to the outfield and had him bat left-handed, and he switch-hit the rest of his career.
Rube Foster matched him in a race against Jimmy Lyon, the league's fastest player. Bell won easily, and Foster sent him to buy the best spikes in the store on his account. Bell paid back the $21.
In the 1934 East-West Game he walked in the eighth, stole second, and scored from second on a bloop single for the only run of the game.
Leading the batting race late in 1946, he sat himself down so Monte Irvin could win the title: "Monte was young and had a chance for a future."
Managing the Monarch Travelers after his playing days, he is credited with spotting Ernie Banks and recommending him to Buck O'Neil.
He played 1,202 games in the Negro major leagues, the most of any player.
In the 1928 championship series against the Chicago American Giants he hit .407, and the Stars won Games 8 and 9 facing elimination.
He was often called "the black Ty Cobb."

In 1937 Paige lured him, Josh Gibson and others to the Dominican Republic to play for dictator Rafael Trujillo's team, to help Trujillo's re-election. The players soon realized the predicament they were in.
His own version of the light-switch story: the switch had a delay of about three seconds, so he turned off the light, jumped in bed and pulled the covers up to his chin before it went out.
In an exhibition against white all-stars, he reportedly broke from first on a bunt with Paige at bat, saw the third baseman charge, and kept running.
After the Grays lost the 1945 World Series he became a player-manager for Negro league farm teams until 1950, and later a part-time scout.
p: He was born James Thomas Nichols. When he moved to St. Louis he took his stepfather's name: "They said you got to have your father's name. Just changed my name to Bell."
His roommate Willie Wells was courting Clara first, but Wells's mother disapproved. Bell and Clara married in 1928 and honeymooned in Cuba; he and Wells stayed close friends for life.
Back in St. Louis he worked 22 years for the city, as a City Hall custodian and then a night watchman, for a $130-a-month pension.
Clara, his wife of 62 years, died in January 1991, and he died that March. Lou Brock was a pallbearer.
The St. Louis street he lived on, Dickson Street, was renamed James "Cool Papa" Bell Avenue.
His mother was widowed a month after her wedding, before he was born. He claimed his grandfather was three-quarters Indian.
As a teenager he worked at the creamery at Mississippi A&M, now Mississippi State. In St. Louis he worked at a packing company and played on Sundays.
Lou Gossett Jr. played him in the 2009 film The Perfect Game. He died of a heart attack weeks after Clara.

c: In his debut, on September 9, 1880, for Troy, he caught fellow rookie Tim Keefe in a 1-0 loss to John Montgomery Ward, who became his career-long rival, even in the years they were teammates.
In 1883 he led the NL with 10 home runs, then a league record. He was the first to win a home run title batting mostly leadoff.

He blocked the plate with his foot, dropped his mask near the plate to slow down runners, and sometimes muffed a pitch on purpose to lure a runner into stealing. He complained about umpires loudly enough for the stands to hear, but never to the umpire himself.
Mickey Welch, his batterymate for almost his whole career, said Ewing started the pregame clubhouse meeting and let him call every pitch. Connie Mack called Ewing the greatest catcher of all time.
On February 28, 1893, the Giants traded him to Cleveland for George Davis, a deal now seen as one of the most one-sided in history.
In 1939 he became the first catcher elected to the Hall of Fame. In the 1947 film Life with Father, a character reads that Buck Ewing homered for the Giants the day before.
Horace Phillips offered him $85 a month plus board to turn pro with Rochester in 1880.
Cincinnati official Opie Caylor swore to his dying day that late in 1882 Ewing had signed with his club for 1883 and promised to bring along Mickey Welch and Pat Gillespie.

In spring 1891 his arm "dropped perfectly lifeless to his side" after a snap throw to second, and he played only 14 games. Shortstop Jack Glasscock sneered that he'd simply lost his nerve now that the Giants had fireballer Amos Rusie.

In the Giants' last series of 1891, at Boston, Ewing was accused of persuading manager Jim Mutrie to bench regulars, including Rusie, Roger Connor and his own brother John, to help Boston beat Cap Anson's Chicago team for the pennant. Arthur Irwin claimed Ewing even gave Boston captain Mike Kelly the Giants' signals.
Cleveland dropped him in July 1894, and that December his hometown Cincinnati signed him as player-manager.
He managed seven seasons in all: the 1890 Players' League Giants, the Reds from 1895 to 1899, and half of 1900 with the Giants.
p: As a boy in Pendleton, Ohio, he played marbles with a bigger boy named Buck, and the bettors called them "Big Buck" and "Little Buck." Writer Ren Mulford later admitted inventing the middle name "Buckingham," which reference books used for decades.
In the late 1870s he drove a mule team for a Cincinnati distiller and played ball on Sundays, his one day off.
His brother John pitched to him in 1890 and 1891 before lung ailments ended his career and his life. Buck was buried beside him.
He came home to Cincinnati wealthy from real estate, mostly row houses, opened a baseball school, and coached amateur teams. He died in 1906 of Bright's disease and diabetes.

"Buck" was only a boyhood nickname; his family called him Billy, and he preferred Will. Reference books listed him as "William Buckingham Ewing" until late in the 20th century. His nephew Bob Ewing also pitched in the majors.

c: When the Yankees brought him up, Tony Lazzeri, whose job he was meant to take, taught him the tricks of playing second base and gave him batting tips.
As a rookie in 1938 he hit 25 homers, a new record for a second baseman.

He was named the outstanding player of the 1941 World Series after hitting .500. In 1942 he beat Triple Crown winner Ted Williams for the MVP. Williams: "I was glad Gordon got it. I really think he kept the Yankees up there."
On Larry Doby's first day with Cleveland in 1947, no one would warm up with him until Gordon yelled, "Hey kid, come on. Throw with me." Doby: "Joe Gordon was a class guy."

Managing Cleveland in 1959, he said he wouldn't come back under Frank Lane, and Lane fired him. Fans sent Lane more than 700 telegrams, and after firing him a second time Lane rehired him: "The best man to replace Joe Gordon was Joe Gordon."
On August 3, 1960, Cleveland traded him to Detroit for the Tigers' manager, Jimmy Dykes. Dykes: "I'm bringing no magic to Cleveland. If I had any, I would have used it on the Tigers."
He hit .418 as an Oregon sophomore. Scout Bill Essick: "at his best when it meant the most and the going was toughest."
He got his chance at Oakland in 1936 when shortstop Bernie DeViveiros broke a finger. In 1937 at Newark he played for a team that won 109 games and came back from 0–3 to win the Little World Series.

He hit .400 in the 1938 World Series sweep of the Cubs. In 1941 his two-run double came four batters after Mickey Owen's dropped third strike. Joe McCarthy: "The greatest all-around ballplayer I ever saw, and I don't bar any of them, is Joe Gordon."
Unhappy with Babe Dahlgren at first base, the Yankees traded him and moved Gordon there. In the 1942 World Series, a five-game loss to the Cardinals, Gordon hit .095.

In 1946 GM Larry MacPhail accused him of being out of shape and tanking. Bill Dickey refused MacPhail's order to bench him. With Lou Boudreau pushing for it, the Yankees traded him to Cleveland for Allie Reynolds.

In Kansas City, owner Charlie Finley fired him on June 19 and replaced him with Hank Bauer. He scouted for the Angels from 1961 to 1968, managed the expansion Royals for one season in 1969, then went into real estate.
p: His father, a gold miner, died when he was four, and his mother took the boys to Portland, Oregon. At 14 he played violin in the Portland symphony.
He was nicknamed "Flash" after his favorite comic book character. At Oregon he was on the gymnastics team, which is where his acrobatic play at second came from.

A licensed pilot who owned his own plane, he joined the Army Air Force in 1944. On Guam he pinch-hit for the war correspondents' softball team under the alias Joe Hollister, until his towering foul ball gave him away.
He insisted on no funeral. Inducting him in 2009, his daughter Judy said the family considered the Hall of Fame his final resting place.
He met his wife, Dorothy Crum, in Portland. They had a daughter, Judith, and later a son, Joe Jr. Missing Oregon, he once talked of quitting, but the New York press didn't take it seriously.
They married in Elkton, Maryland, in June 1938. He had a heart seizure in 1974, and another killed him in 1978, at 63.

c: When Pittsburgh traded him to Baltimore for George Van Haltren in 1892, he went home to Cambridge instead, worried the Orioles were broke. Ned Hanlon reassured him, then made him a personal project, hitting him fungos and grounders in private sessions.
On September 3, 1894, he got nine straight hits in a doubleheader against Cleveland, ending with four straight doubles off Cy Young. That year he hit .393 and scored 165 runs, both career highs.
Before the 1894 Temple Cup, many Orioles made side deals with Giants players to split the shares whatever happened. Amos Rusie paid Kelley $200; the other Giants said they'd never agreed to anything.
He was said to hide extra baseballs in the outfield grass in case the one in play got past him. In 1896 he led the league with 87 steals.

In 1902 he sold his Orioles stock to his father-in-law, Sonny Mahon, who sold control to John T. Brush and Andrew Freedman. They moved Baltimore's best players to their own clubs, and Kelley became the Reds' player-manager.
In 1907 Toronto paid him $5,000 to be its player-manager, then the most ever paid to a minor-league player. He led the club to first place.
He hit .244 in 12 games for Boston in 1891 and was released. He then turned down $1,200 from Oakland to play for Omaha.
The Orioles lost the first Temple Cup to the Giants, 4–0, and the next to Cleveland, playing carelessly. They took it seriously in 1896 and swept Cleveland, and beat Boston in the last one.
In 1897 he coached Georgetown's baseball team and held out with Willie Keeler and Hughie Jennings; Hanlon had to pay them. He hit .362 that year with 44 steals.
When Brooklyn took over the Orioles' stars in 1899, he asked to go to Washington instead, so he could manage and stay near Baltimore. Washington didn't have enough to offer.

In July 1902 Ban Johnson suspended him indefinitely for fighting with umpires. The day Andrew Freedman and John Brush took over the Orioles, they released the best players: Kelley and Cy Seymour went to the Reds, Joe McGinnity and Roger Bresnahan to the Giants.
He quit as Reds manager in November 1905: "I am tired of being roasted."
After Toronto released him in 1914 he scouted for the Yankees, and in 1926 old teammate Wilbert Robinson made him a Brooklyn coach.
p: His parents came from Ireland to escape the famine; his father was a marble cutter in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
Baltimore's female fans called him "Handsome Joe" and filled the left-field bleachers, which became known as Kelleyville. He kept a small mirror and comb in his back pocket during games.

He married Margaret Mahon, daughter of Baltimore Democratic boss Sonny Mahon, with Willie Keeler as best man. Later he clerked at the Baltimore courthouse and sat on the Maryland State Racing Commission.
He was buried in Baltimore's New Cathedral Cemetery, where John McGraw, Wilbert Robinson and Ned Hanlon also lie.
He went to a parochial school run by a priest who was a Civil War veteran, and worked for a piano manufacturer.
After their October 1897 wedding, he and Margaret joined the Orioles in Cincinnati for a cross-country barnstorming tour. Baltimore's single women let out a collective sigh.

c: As teenagers he and Al Spalding played together in Rockford, Illinois. Their Forest Citys upset the touring National Club of Washington in 1867, and in 1870 they beat the Cincinnati Red Stockings 12-5.
Harry Wright signed both of them for Boston in 1871. Boston ran away with the National Association title the next four years.
He set National Association records for steals in a season (43 in 1873) and a career (103). Tim Murnane said he was the first player to throw himself wide of the base and hold onto the bag.
On May 2, 1876, at Cincinnati, he hit the first home run in National League history.
In May 1877 he was struck by a mysterious illness, possibly the ague: "I don't feel badly, but I grow weaker every day." He was never the same player again.
In 1878 he became the first pro ballplayer to sue his club over a contract, for three months' pay he'd missed while sick. He lost.
He umpired in the Players' League in 1890 and found it a bitter experience. With nine pro seasons, he's one short of the ten the Hall of Fame requires.

Signed by Boston as a second baseman, he moved to shortstop when George Wright, widely thought the best player in the country, was hurt. Teammate Fred Cone said his "fielding was the cleverest ever seen."

In mid-July 1875 the Chicago Tribune announced that William Hulbert had signed Barnes, Deacon White, Cal McVey and Al Spalding for Chicago. It was a death blow to Boston, and part of Hulbert's plan for a new league.

The fair-foul hit was banned before 1877, and his average fell from .399 over six seasons to .272. Many later researchers dismissed him as a fluky fair-foul hitter. While he was sick, the Chicago Times claimed he was faking it; the Tribune called that "scandalous and utterly unfounded."
Nate Silver argues the illness, not the rule change, was the main thing that hurt his career.
In 1878 he signed as player-manager of the London Tecumsehs of the International Association.
p: For decades he was misidentified as Roscoe Conkling Barnes, after the New York congressman and senator of that name.
His brothers became industrialists and bankers in Rockford. In the 1880s newspapers put his own net worth at $100,000 and said he was a member of the Chicago Board of Trade.
He later worked as an accountant for the Peoples Gas Light and Coke Company in Chicago, and was buried in his parents' plot in Rockford.
His parents, Joseph, a farmer, and Mary, were New Jersey natives who had at least eight children.
A bachelor most of his life, he married Ellen Welsh in 1900. He died of heart disease in 1915.

c: Scrappy Brown of the Baltimore Black Sox found him on the Foggy Bottom sandlots in 1922. Wilson quit the team twice and went home before he stuck on his third try. Teammates named him "Boojum" for the sound his line drives made hitting the outfield walls.
In his first Cuban winter, 1925-26, he led the league at .430 and hit a ball over the right-field wall at Almendares Park, more than 400 feet, which earned him the nickname El Jorocón.
He got the first hit in the history of the East-West All-Star Game in 1933. In 1934 his single scored Cool Papa Bell from second for the only run of the game.

In the 1934 Negro National League championship series he apparently struck an umpire and stayed in the game. When the commissioner considered banning him, owner Ed Bolden threatened to boycott the rest of the series, and Wilson played on.

Josh Gibson called him the greatest hitter he'd ever seen, and Satchel Paige named him and Chino Smith as the two toughest hitters he faced. Wilson on Paige: "I timed his blinding stuff and just raked him for base hits."
When Chino Smith slid hard into third, Wilson picked him up and threw him. Clint Thomas: "All ball players were scared of him."
His two-out, two-run single won the 1940 pennant for the Homestead Grays, and he was part of six straight Negro National League titles from 1940 to 1945.
He's credited with hitting .467 for the 1922 Baltimore Black Sox, who went 49-12.
In 1929 Baltimore was rumored to be trading him to the Homestead Grays for both Martín Dihigo and John Beckwith, perhaps the only man with a meaner reputation than Wilson.
He began 1932 as the Grays' player-manager, then defected to the crosstown Crawfords. In 1933 he jumped again, to Ed Bolden's new Philadelphia Stars.

He crowded the plate and was hit often, including a pitch that broke his elbow in 1926, and he knocked down grounders with his body. When the Stars' bus overturned outside Pittsburgh in 1937 and broke his rib, it was one of the few times he didn't try to play through an injury.
Once, wrongly accused of hitting an umpire, he exploded when thrown out; it took three policemen with nightsticks to subdue him and haul him to jail.
Late in his career he developed epilepsy. During one Negro World Series game he began drawing circles in the dirt, apparently unaware of his surroundings.
p: His birthdate has been given as 1893, 1894, 1896 and 1899. As he put it, "These fellows in our league lie too much about their ages." He served in World War I as an Army corporal.

After the 1933 All-Star Game his roommate and best friend, Jake Stephens, came in drunk and woke him. Wilson held him by the leg out a window 16 stories up. Stephens: "He loved me. I could do anything with him."
He married Betty in 1923, often crossing a stream on a log to visit her in rural Virginia. After baseball he worked on the road crew that built the Whitehurst Freeway, and later as a janitor.
He is buried in Arlington National Cemetery. Hall of Fame officials thought he had no living relatives, but a great-niece heard about his 2006 induction and accepted on his behalf.
His seizures may have been brought on by an auto accident, all the pitches to the head, or the beatings he took in fights. His last job was as a janitor, and he died of a heart attack in 1963.

c: He worked at New York's Penn Station and played second base for its team, the Pennsylvania Red Caps, beside shortstop Dick Seay, before joining the Brooklyn Royal Giants in 1925.
Satchel Paige called him one of the two most dangerous hitters in Negro league history; the other was Jud Wilson.
In the Pittsburgh Courier's 1952 poll of players on the best Negro leaguers ever, he got the second-most votes in right field, on what would have been his 51st birthday.
p: He was born in Greenwood, South Carolina. He fell ill with yellow fever while playing in Cuba and died at 30.

c: Playing for Cincinnati in 1879, he was called safe at second and the Chicago players swarmed the umpire. No one had called time, so Kelly got up and ran home. It caught Cap Anson's attention, and Kelly joined Chicago the next year.

He's credited with inventing the hook slide, then called the Chicago slide, and was an expert at the hit-and-run. As a backup catcher he started wearing a glove, mask and chest protector to stay in games.
When the umpire wasn't looking he would cut 15 or 20 feet inside third base. After Chicago swept Providence in 1882, Harry Wright blamed the losses on "Kelly's infernal tricks."

On third against Detroit, he faked an injury to bring Ned Williamson over from second, then broke for home with Williamson right behind him. As Charlie Bennett went to tag Kelly, Williamson slid through Kelly's legs to score too.
Boston bought him from Chicago for $10,000 and then John Clarkson for another $10,000, billing the pair as the "$20,000 battery."
In 1890 Al Spalding put a $10,000 check on the table to lure him out of the Players' League. Kelly took a walk and came back: "I can't go back on the boys." Then he borrowed $500 from Spalding.
When Cincinnati's owner released all his players in September 1879, saying he couldn't pay them, Kelly was free to sign elsewhere. He held out until Cap Anson met his price.

In 1886 Al Spalding hired detectives to follow his players and fined some $25 for excessive drinking. Nothing curbed Kelly's fondness for alcohol, though teammate Billy Sunday quit drinking that summer.
Boston paid him $5,000: the $2,000 league maximum plus $3,000 for the use of his picture in advertising. He spent it at the faro table, the track and the saloons, where he preferred whisky to beer.
He backed out of a world tour at the last minute, citing "business interests" in New York. In 1889 he missed at least one crucial game down the stretch because he was too hung over to play.
He was captain and manager of the Players' League Boston Reds in 1890, but struggled with the business side of running a club.
In 1892 he hit a career-worst .189 for Boston, and his contract went to the Giants for 1893.
p: Orphaned young in Paterson, New Jersey, he carried buckets of coal from a basement to a roof; once the day's load was done he could go play ball. His best friend, Jim McCormick, went on to win 265 big-league games.

He was the first ballplayer to "author" an autobiography and the first to have a hit song written about him, "Slide, Kelly, Slide." In the off-seasons he played vaudeville, sometimes reciting "Casey at the Bat."
Anson called him "a whole-souled, genial fellow, with a host of friends, and but one enemy, that one being himself." He earned the game's top salary and spent every cent.

He caught pneumonia on a boat to Boston for a theater engagement in 1894. When his stretcher slipped to the floor at the hospital, he reportedly said, "This is my last slide." He died at 36, and some 7,000 people came to his funeral.
He was born in Troy, New York, to Irish immigrants, and was orphaned by 18.

He married Agnes Hedifen in Paterson in October 1881, and they often spent offseasons at her brother's farmhouse in Hyde Park, New York. He made his stage debut in a Boston play called A Rag Baby, and his book Play Ball sold for 25 cents.

His wife and brother didn't arrive in time to see him before he died. Aggie never remarried, made a living sewing until her eyesight failed, and called him "just an overgrown kid." Their only child had died in 1894 after living just an hour.

c: He came up with the 25th Infantry's all-Black baseball team in Hawaii, the "Wreckers," alongside future Monarchs Bullet Rogan, Heavy Johnson and Lemuel Hawkins.

In 1919 Casey Stengel brought a team of big-leaguers to Nogales, Arizona; Moore homered in one game and hit a grand slam in another. Stengel may have recommended him to the Monarchs, and called him "one of the best shortstops who will ever live."
He was a great bad-ball hitter. Newt Allen: "I'd let them go, but he'd knock them two blocks. There were no bad pitches for him."
In the first Colored World Series, in 1924, the Monarchs were down three games to one when Moore went 3-for-4 in a 6-5 Game 6 win. They won the series five games to four.
That winter in California he hit .487 and won a new suit for hitting the Diamond Tailoring Company's sign on the outfield wall. He's the California Winter League's all-time batting leader at .385.
In May 1926, hitting .400, he was shot in the leg by a woman named Elsie Brown; the leg was broken in six places and his career was over at 29. Accounts of what happened that night differ.
The Seamheads statistics credit him with 8.8 wins above replacement per 162 games, the best ever for a shortstop.
Monarchs manager José Méndez worked tirelessly with him on his defense, and he became perhaps the best all-round shortstop in the game, Black or white.
The Monarchs lost a postseason series to the minor-league Kansas City Blues while Moore was hurt. The next year, with him healthy, they won five of six.
In the 1925 World Series rematch with Hilldale he led the Monarchs with a .364 average.

Elsie Brown said she shut the door on him, he threw something at her window, and she came back with a pistol and fired once. Reports said she was his girlfriend; he was married. Some accounts say it was his jump from a second-story terrace, escaping a second shot, that shattered his leg. Brown soon left for Anthony, Kansas, fearing for her safety.
Cumberland Posey: "Moore is the peer of all shortstops, colored or white."
p: He had a third-grade education and joined the Army in 1915. "Dobie" was likely a variation of "doughboy," slang for an infantryman.
In the Army he ran track and reportedly played receiver on the regiment's football team. In 1918 his unit guarded the new border wall at Nogales.
After his injury he moved to Detroit to live near family. A 1943 Chicago Defender photo showed him with crutches, pointing to where he'd been shot. He died of a heart attack in 1947 at 51.
He married Frances Davis. When he moved to Detroit after the shooting, she apparently didn't go with him. He lived there with his sisters, and died of a heart attack at home in 1947, at 51.

c: At 15 he was at the Bedford train station to see off the town team when the manager, one player short, pulled him from the crowd. He played both games of a doubleheader barefoot, with no uniform, and hit well.

Before his first pro season he got ready by throwing a ball off the side of a building and catching it, and by turning his own bat on his father's lathe. In Dayton, kids chanted, "Elmer Flick, you are slick / Hit a homer pretty quick."
In 1900 he fought teammate Nap Lajoie over who owned a bat. Flick, at least four inches shorter and 30 pounds lighter, held his own; Lajoie missed a punch and broke his thumb.

On July 6, 1902, he hit three triples in a game for Cleveland, an AL record that has since been tied. His .308 to win the 1905 batting title was the lowest winning average until Carl Yastrzemski's .301 in 1968.
In spring 1907 the Tigers offered Ty Cobb for him straight up. Cleveland said no.
A stomach illness his doctors could never pin down cost him most of 1908 and ended his big-league career. "My last three years were awful. I shouldn't have played at all."
