The Phillies signed him as a reserve, but Sam Thompson hurt his back six games into 1898 and retired in May, and Flick took over right field. Later he hurt his knee badly in August, and hurt it again by coming back too soon.
When Lajoie and Ed Delahanty held out before 1900, the papers reported Flick might be needed in his father's chair business. He signed an extension instead.
After 11 games with the Athletics in 1902, the Phillies' injunction barred him from playing in Pennsylvania, so he and Lajoie signed with Cleveland, where it couldn't be enforced.

He developed a distaste for southern cooking at spring training. When the stomach illness came, many doctors called it acute gastritis, and he took pills for the rest of his life. Released to Kansas City in July 1910, he refused to report.
Toledo bought him from Cleveland and released him after 1912. He never played in a World Series.
He was largely forgotten until Ty Cobb died in 1961 and articles about the aborted trade revived interest. The Veterans Committee elected him in 1963.
p: His father, a Civil War veteran and chair maker, was known around Bedford for trying to fly without an airplane.
Back in Bedford he farmed, hunted, raised trotting horses, built houses and office buildings, and "dickered in real estate." He and his wife, Rose, had five daughters.
When Branch Rickey called in 1963 to say he'd been elected to the Hall of Fame, Flick didn't believe him until his family convinced him. At 87, he was the oldest living inductee in Hall history.
Proud of living so long, he often signed autographs with the date and his age.
He also scouted for Cleveland. He died of congestive heart failure in 1971, two days before his 95th birthday; a lymphoma, mycosis fungoides, contributed.

c: At 16, clerking in Coleridge, Nebraska, he got five hits with three homers in a local game, and started taking baseball seriously.
Boston let him go after two pinch-hit strikeouts in 1903. At Milwaukee in 1904 he hit .406, an American Association record until the league folded in 1997.
Jimmy Collins didn't like his batting style: crouched over the plate with the bat against his shoulder, taking two steps into the pitch. Stone said the crouch put his eyes in line with the pitch.
In 1906 he hit .358 and beat Nap Lajoie for the batting title. From 1901 to 1928, he was the only AL batting champion who isn't in the Hall of Fame.

He held out for $5,000 in 1907 and got it, but fans expected more of a player paid that much and booed him when he slumped. An ankle injury in 1909 took his speed, and he was out of the majors after 1910.
Boston bought him back from Milwaukee late in 1904, but he refused to report, and that December the Americans traded him to St. Louis.

By one account he caught malaria in 1908. He went back to Milwaukee in 1911 and hit .282, then retired 12 games into 1912, writing Hugh Duffy that he was done for good and would attend to his business in Nebraska.
p: He was called "Silent George." A 1906 article said he'd rather be a great violinist with a modest income than a great ballplayer with a handsome salary.
Even at his peak he said he planned to go into business for himself in Nebraska. He became a banker in Coleridge and owned the Western League team in Lincoln in 1916.
In 1940 he and his wife Pearl moved to Clinton, Iowa, near where he was born. He died of a heart attack there in 1945, survived by Pearl and their son, a doctor.

c: He started with the Austin Black Senators in 1923 and briefly attended Samuel Huston College before St. Louis called him up.
With the St. Louis Stars he hit 27 home runs in 1926, a Negro leagues single-season record. In 1930 he won the Triple Crown, hitting .411, the fourth player to do it.
He produced the three best single seasons in Negro major league history by wins above replacement: 1927, 1929 and 1930.

At Newark he was part of the "Million Dollar Infield" with Ray Dandridge, Dick Seay and Mule Suttles. After a beaning there gave him a concussion, he became the first player to wear a batting helmet, starting with a construction helmet.
Mexican fans called him El Diablo for his intensity, and "The Devil" followed him home. He said that in Mexico he experienced democracy, acceptance and freedom.
He taught Jackie Robinson how to turn the double play.
He managed the Birmingham Black Barons after returning from Mexico.
p: In 1948, with the Memphis Red Sox, he played alongside his son, Willie Wells Jr.
After baseball he worked at a deli in New York, then went home to Austin to look after his mother. He was later reinterred in the Texas State Cemetery.
His daughter, Stella, started a scholarship fund in his name at Huston–Tillotson University. In 2022 the ballfield at his old school, Anderson High in Austin, was named for him.
He died of congestive heart failure in Austin in 1989.

c: He was an infielder until he saw a rival catcher stand right behind the batter instead of taking the pitch on a bounce. His own catcher wouldn't try it ("I think too much of my hands"), so Bennett did, and stayed there.
On June 12, 1880, he caught the first perfect game in the majors, Lee Richmond's. Richmond later called him "the best backstop that ever lived."
After a home run on Opening Day 1881, Detroit fans wouldn't stop cheering until he bowed, which Peter Morris calls the first recorded curtain call.
He signed a preliminary deal with Pittsburgh in 1882, changed his mind, and won when the club sued, called "baseball's first real case of contract litigation."

He caught more games than anyone before him and set the career marks for fielding percentage, putouts and double plays by a catcher. King Kelly: "If I had hands such as Charlie Bennett, I wouldn't catch a game of ball for a whole church full of millionaires."
Detroit named its new ballpark Bennett Park in 1896. He caught the ceremonial first pitch at every Tigers home opener through 1926.
As a hard hitter for the Neshannocks, he "nearly broke the directors of the club because of the number of balls knocked into the Shenango river."
Early on, in one 1-0, 10-inning loss to Chicago, he made seven errors and was released after the game.
One account: "A score of times when his hands were badly injured he would continue to catch, and the only way we would find out that he was hurt was to discover blood on the ball."

When the Wolverines folded in October 1888, they sold him, Brouthers, Richardson, White and Charlie Ganzel to Boston for $26,000. He reportedly made $3,500 in 1889, and caught John Clarkson, Old Hoss Radbourn and Kid Nichols there. He used a Players' League offer to get a three-year deal from Boston.
Kid Nichols always insisted on having Bennett catch him. Bill James noted he caught 50 percent more innings than Buck Ewing with fewer errors and passed balls per inning.
p: His wife, Alice, worried about him catching without protection, so they made a chest protector from strips of cork sewn into bedticking. He wore it under his jersey so fans wouldn't taunt him.
In January 1894, on the way to a hunting trip with John Clarkson, he slipped under a moving train near Ottawa, Kansas, and lost both legs.
At a benefit in Boston that August, 9,000 fans raised $6,000 for him. When Charlie Ganzel proposed a race, Bennett said he'd do it with a 98⅓-yard head start.

When he announced plans for a cigar store in Detroit, a woman wrote, "If Charlie Bennett opens a cigar store in Detroit, all the ladies will commence smoking." Later he took up china painting with his broken fingers, and sold his work.
He was the eighth of 11 children. His father ran a hardware store in New Castle, and Charlie helped in the shop.

He and Alice had no children. In later years he took up china painting, "the last thing one would expect" from a man whose every finger had been broken. He died in 1927, at 72, after an abscess on his face spread poison through his system.

c: Back home in Findlay, Ohio, in 1894, some players objected to having two Black teammates, him and Bud Fowler; management signed him anyway. He reportedly hit 60 home runs, and fans named him "Home Run" Johnson.

With the Page Fence Giants from 1895, the team lived in its own train car with a porter and cook, which got around Jim Crow restrictions, and rode bicycles to the ballpark in bright red outfits. When Fowler left midseason, Johnson took over at 22.
A Findlay writer in 1899: "He's the Hughie Jennings of colored players." In 1903 his plays at short helped preserve Dan McClellan's perfect game, the first in Black baseball history.
In a 1907 essay on hitting, he advised studying the first pitch, then meeting the ball "with only ordinary force" rather than swinging for home runs, and practicing bunts before every game.
In 1910 he moved to second base to make room for John Henry Lloyd on the Leland Giants, who went 123-6. At 37 his teammates called him "Dad."
In his last Cuban winter, 1911-12, he hit .410 and led Habana to the pennant. A Cuban paper: "Like wine, he appears to improve with age."
Against the visiting Cincinnati Reds on October 7, he hit two of Tony Mullane's pitches over the left-field fence as Findlay won 5-4. That December he signed with New York's Cuban Giants.
In a rare pitching appearance he won the clinching game of the 1896 Black Baseball World Championship against the Cuban X Giants, in Caro, Michigan.

When Page Fence stopped sponsoring the team after 1898, he and Bud Fowler bought grounds in Findlay, but he signed instead with Chicago's Columbia Giants. He opened a cigar store in Chicago, and the team was renamed the Royal Tiger Giants after a cigar brand.

In 1909 his Brooklyn Royal Giants beat the American League's New York Highlanders 9-6. In February 1910 his owner tried to trade him to the Phillies for John Henry Lloyd; instead both jumped to Rube Foster's Leland Giants.
In May 1913 Jess McMahon of the Lincoln Giants lured him away from the new Mohawk Colored Giants in Schenectady.
That year the Lincoln Giants won the eastern title and beat the Chicago American Giants in the championship playoff.
p: He was named for Ulysses S. Grant; his father had served in the Union Army's 13th Colored Infantry. As a young man he played organ at his A.M.E. church and later sang bass in its choir.
A small spotted terrier named Money traveled with him from his Page Fence days. He hid her from train conductors in his overcoat, and later in a basket.
He settled in Buffalo and worked as a railroad porter. He later lost his sight and lived at the Erie Home of the Blind. In 2014 SABR's Negro Leagues Grave Marker Project put a plaque near his grave.
As a young man he delivered newspapers, ran a fish and poultry stand, and debated in his church's literary society.

He married Moena Scott in Florida in April 1909 and helped raise her daughter Grace. A son of his, apparently from an earlier union, played for the Lima Giants in 1916, and records suggest he may have married again in 1954.
In Buffalo he worked for the New York Central Railroad. He died there at 90.

c: As a boy he was a batboy when the Monarchs trained in Shreveport. He turned pro with the Monroe Monarchs for $8 a week plus room and board: "I thought that was big money."
Josh Gibson called him "Home Run" Brown. Teammates called him "Sonny" because he played his best on sunny Sundays in front of full stands, and he sometimes read Reader's Digest in the outfield.
He led the Negro American League in hits eight times, tied with Ty Cobb for the most times leading a league.

On August 13, 1947, for the St. Louis Browns, he hit an inside-the-park homer off Hal Newhouser, the first homer by a Black player in the AL. Jeff Heath, whose bat he'd used, smashed it; Heath was known to be superstitious about his bats.
The Browns released him after 21 games. "The Browns couldn't beat the Monarchs no kind of way, only if we was all asleep."

In Puerto Rico in 1947-48 he won the Triple Crown, hitting .432 with 27 homers, still the league's single-season record, and was nicknamed Ese Hombre, "That Man." His .350 career average there is the best in league history.
In 1950 a Yankees scout came to Kansas City to look at Brown. Buck O'Neil told him, "Elston Howard is the player you're looking for."
Kansas City's Wilkinson spotted him and Buck O'Neil while barnstorming against the Shreveport Acme Giants. He gave Brown a $250 bonus, $125 a month and a dollar a day for meals.

In the Army he served in the Quartermaster Corps. In the 1946 Negro World Series he hit three homers in six games, but Newark won after Satchel Paige and Ted Strong jumped the team with two games left.

The Browns bought him and Hank Thompson from the Monarchs for a reported $5,000 apiece. The AP called him "the prize package of the lot" among Black players signed that year, "with only his age against him." Teammate Paul Lehner was the unfriendliest, and A's coach Al Simmons reportedly rode him hard.

When the Browns released him and Thompson in August, they went back to the Monarchs, where the money was actually better. Buck O'Neil alleged the Browns cut them to avoid owing the Monarchs more if they lasted the season.
He won a second Puerto Rican Triple Crown in 1949-50, worth a $200 bonus. Back in Kansas City he won the 1951 Negro American League batting title at .417.
p: When he reached the majors he was billed as born in 1921. Later, saying he'd been too old when he got his chance, he gave 1911 and 1913. Records confirm 1915.

In World War II he crossed the English Channel in the Normandy invasion, hauling ammunition and guarding prisoners. In 1945 he and Leon Day played for the OISE All-Stars, who won the ETO World Series.

Back in Puerto Rico for an Old-Timers' Day in 1979, he said the island "was where I was treated best." Santurce owner Pedrín Zorrilla: "He didn't have to be Puerto Rican... he became a brother to us."
He and his wife Dorothy, who was some years older, had one child, Willard Jr. The marriage broke up when the boy was about nine. He later reportedly worked in the steel industry.
He died in 1996 at 81, after several years with Alzheimer's.

c: At 18, in 1877, he got $40 a month to play third base for the Wheeling Standards, West Virginia's first pro team. In 1879 he became the first West Virginian in the majors.
At Cleveland he, Fred Dunlap and Bill Phillips formed the "Stonewall infield," which Al Spink called perhaps the greatest infield ever.

Jumping to the Union Association in 1884, he said, "I have played long enough for glory, now it is a matter of dollars and cents." In Cincinnati a writer nicknamed him "Pebbly Jack" for picking stones out of the infield.

In 1889 he led the majors with 205 hits and hit .352, then the highest ever by a shortstop. He took over as Indianapolis manager midseason and turned a 25-43 team into a winning one, but disliked managing and never did it again.
He stayed with the National League in the 1890 players' revolt and was expelled by the Brotherhood. That season he won the batting title with the Giants and went 6-for-6 in one game.
He was the hardest batter of his day to strike out. In 1890 he struck out once every 64 at-bats, a rate no one beat until Joe Sewell 35 years later.
He was nicknamed "Pebbly Jack" for scanning the infield for small stones and pocketing them, which spared him bad hops.
In 1889 he hit for the cycle and managed Indianapolis for the second half of the season.
He didn't enjoy managing. Back home in Wheeling he was once jailed for being drunk and disorderly.
An 1891 hand injury cut into his hitting. Traded to Pittsburgh in June 1893, he hit .341 the rest of the way and drove in 100 runs for the first time.
Washington released him midway through his 17th season, in 1895. In 1896 he led the Western Association at .431.
p: He liked to say he'd lived his whole life at 9 Maryland Avenue in Wheeling. He was named for John Wesley, the founder of Methodism, though he went to an Episcopal church.
He left school after fourth grade to become a carpenter like his father, and went back to carpentry after baseball.
After the majors he played for Ed Barrow's Wheeling team, hit over .400, and won the first pennant of either man's career.
He and his wife, Rhoda Rose Dubla, who died in 1925, raised two sons and a daughter. He died of a stroke in 1947 and was buried in Wheeling's Greenwood Cemetery.

c: Walter McCreedie remembered seeing him fill in for Oakland in 1912: "a big, gawky, overgrown kid" in homemade spiked shoes who lined four straight balls on the nose.
In 1922 he led the AL with 39 homers and 155 RBIs. He was the first player to hit 30 homers and steal 30 bases in a season, and the first to hit more homers than he struck out.
On April 22, 1922, he became the first American Leaguer to hit three homers in a game. A Post-Dispatch poem asked, "Who makes the fan forget Babe Ruth? Ken Williams."
He wouldn't join the comparisons with Ruth: "No player in the game could hope to match Ruth over a full season's course." He swung a 48-ounce bat.
Beaned behind the ear in 1925, he was about to shower when Chick Fewster, who had nearly died after a similar beaning, warned him not to. X-rays showed a concussion.
On August 8, 1929, he and Wally Gerber collided chasing a fly ball and both fractured their skulls, which ended both men's big-league careers.

Semipro ball around Oregon got him a contract with Regina of the Western Canada League. Portland bought him later, and Browns business manager Bob Quinn signed him for 1918, but he was called up for World War I and missed much of the season.
In November 1924 the Yankees were rumored to be trying to trade for him to team him with Ruth. In December 1927 the Browns sold him to the Red Sox for $10,000.

Cleveland's By Speece hit him on August 14, 1925, ending his season. He spent ten days in the hospital. Later that year he read about a minor leaguer who took a cold shower after a similar beaning and died.
p: He left school after eighth grade and worked in a box factory in Grants Pass, Oregon. Though a natural right-hander, he batted left.
Even at his peak he was little known; one photographer sent to shoot him swinging photographed teammate Baby Doll Jacobson instead.
Back in Grants Pass after baseball, he was a policeman and owned the Owl Billiard Parlor.
He married Edith Wilerons in 1919, and they had two sons, Kenneth Jr. and Jack. He died in 1959 of a heart condition he'd had for years.
His Owl Club in Grants Pass, on G Street, was a restaurant as well as a billiard parlor.

c: In 1923, while still at Boston University, he played for Dover in the Eastern Shore League under the name Frank King, as a catcher, because that was the spot Dover needed filled. "I didn't want to be a catcher. It was thrust upon me. Oh boy, I was terrible back there."
He caught both Lefty Grove in 1931 and Schoolboy Rowe in 1934 during their 16-game winning streaks, which are still the AL record.

Sold to Detroit as player-manager, he led the Tigers to pennants in 1934 and 1935 and the franchise's first World Series title. Time put him on its cover. "If one of them eats something that makes them sick, I get sick too."
In his first season managing, his Tigers won 101 games, the most by a rookie manager for 27 years.
He had a breakdown in 1936. On May 25, 1937, soon after he came back, a Bump Hadley pitch hit him in the head and nearly killed him, ending his playing career.
In 1947 he became the first catcher elected to the Hall of Fame by the baseball writers.

In Bridgewater and at Boston University he was called "Kid," and was better at football and basketball than baseball. Catchers Tom Daly at Portland and Cy Perkins at Philadelphia helped teach him the trade; he took Perkins's job before the end of 1925.
Detroit owner Navin first hoped to make Babe Ruth his player-manager, and turned to Cochrane when those talks fizzled. The Tigers hadn't finished higher than third since 1923.
Having lost money in a bank failure, he was embarrassed when Pepper Martin ran wild in the 1931 World Series. The blame dogged him for the rest of his life.
He was hospitalized after Game 6 of the 1934 World Series. He came back for Game 7, an 11-0 loss best remembered for Detroit fans pelting the Cardinals with garbage.

He took his pitchers' troubles personally: "If one of them eats something that makes them sick, I get sick too." His breakdown in 1936 followed his promotion to general manager on top of playing and managing.
The 1937 beaning put him in the hospital for seven days. He managed through 1937 and was replaced midway through 1938 by Del Baker.

In July 1942 he managed an All-Service team that lost 5–0 to the AL All-Stars in Cleveland. Later in the war he had a similar job in the Pacific. He was general manager of the A's in 1950, Connie Mack's last year, and later ran an auto business.
p: Of Scottish descent, he got the name "Mickey" when a scout assumed he was Irish. Family and friends called him Mike.
Many parents in the Depression named children after him, including an Oklahoma family named Mantle.
He loved music and dancing and played the saxophone. In the late 1940s he ran a dude ranch in Montana with his family. His only son, Gordon Jr., was killed in Europe in World War II.
In World War II he was a Navy officer at Great Lakes, overseeing recruits' physical training and coaching the baseball team.
He was the fifth of seven children of Scottish immigrants in Bridgewater, Massachusetts.

At the 4K Ranch in Montana he lived with his wife Mary and daughters Joan and Sara, with his father and brothers there full-time. He died of lymphatic cancer in 1962 at 59. Mary outlived him by 37 years.
Ty Cobb, late in life, remembered lending Cochrane money; Cochrane's wife and daughter denied any debt, and a biographer thinks Cobb forgot it was repaid when the ranch was sold.

c: He umpired a major-league game before he played in one. As a rookie with Cleveland in 1880 he led the NL in doubles. His nickname, "Sure Shot," came from his hard, accurate throws to first.
Union Association president Henry Lucas asked how much he made a year. "Seventeen hundred and fifty." Lucas pulled out a wad of bills: "Here's your $1,750 and as much more as you want."
For the St. Louis Maroons in 1884 he hit .412, then the highest single-season mark ever recorded in a major league, and scored 160 runs. How good the Union Association actually was is still debated.
He was the highest-paid player in the majors from 1884 to 1889.
John Montgomery Ward: "Fred Dunlap was the king. He was something of a grandstand player, because of his tendency to make one-handed catches and stops, but he got there just the same."
He broke his leg sliding in April 1891. Washington stopped paying him, and he argued that a player hurt serving his club deserved at least part of his salary. He never played again.
His November 1883 contract with the St. Louis Maroons paid $3,400, including $1,000 in advance, the highest salary in baseball.

Detroit bought him in August 1886 for $4,700, then the highest price ever paid for a player, and gave him $4,500 a season. He helped the Wolverines win the 1887 pennant and played 11 games of the World Series. When Detroit moved to sell him to Pittsburgh, he said, "I am sick and tired of being sold without gaining anything by it," and demanded half the sale price, his freedom, or the contract he'd been promised.
His 1887 season ended in September with a leg injury.
He played for Pittsburgh from 1888 to 1890 and managed the Alleghenys for part of 1889.
p: Both his parents died when he was about 10, and he got little schooling.
He remained illiterate his whole life.
He retired with a reported $100,000 and went into the building business in Philadelphia, then lost it on horse racing and speculation. By 1902 a paper called him "clean broke."
He died later that year at 43 in a Philadelphia boarding house. A policeman at the morgue thought the body was his, and former player Lave Cross was called in to confirm it.
Sporting Life said he "dropped out of the game in 1892 to follow the racing game, at which he lost the respectable fortune he accumulated in base ball."

There's no record that he ever married. He spent his last years in poverty and gloom, and was buried in Philadelphia's Odd Fellows Cemetery; reportedly there weren't enough friends at the funeral to serve as pallbearers.

c: John McGraw reportedly sent Jesse Burkett to scout him, and Burkett said his hands were too small for a big-league catcher.

At his first Cubs camp, manager Bill Killefer had him catch Grover Cleveland Alexander for a whole game. Alexander said he was "all right," and he made the team. He was so shy that teammates called him "Gabby" as a joke, and he later grew into the name as a chatterbox behind the plate.
In 1925 he hit 24 homers, a new single-season record for a catcher. In 1935 he hit .344 and was the NL's MVP.

He was catching when Babe Ruth supposedly called his shot in 1932: "He didn't call the shot. He held up the index finger of his left hand and said, 'It only takes one to hit.'" He also caught Carl Hubbell's five straight strikeouts in the 1934 All-Star Game and Dizzy Dean in the 1937 game where Dean's toe was broken.

Made Cubs player-manager in July 1938, he homered off Mace Brown on September 28 in near-darkness to win a key game against Pittsburgh, the "Homer in the Gloamin'." "I don't think I saw third base, and I don't think I walked a step to the plate. I was carried in."
On August 28, 1939, he caught his 1,728th game, breaking Ray Schalk's record for games caught.

His arm was so good that in 1920 American Steel and Wire in Worcester gave him a shipping-department job just to play on its company team. After a season with the Worcester Boosters, Cubs scout Jack Doyle signed him for $2,500.
When O'Farrell fractured his skull in a game in July 1924, Hartnett took over as the Cubs' starting catcher.
At the December 1925 winter meetings he was rumored to be going to the Giants for Frank Snyder and Irish Meusel, but Cubs president Bill Veeck Sr. said he wouldn't be traded for anybody.

In 1929 he hurt his arm making a hard throw without warming up, caught only one game, and struck out in all three World Series at-bats. On April 1, 1930, he caught a baseball dropped from the Goodyear Blimp, from either 550 or 800 feet.
He was behind the plate when Carl Hubbell struck out five straight future Hall of Famers in the 1934 All-Star Game, and when Earl Averill's liner broke Dizzy Dean's toe in 1937.
After playing he managed five seasons in the minors, and in the mid-1960s coached and scouted for the Kansas City A's.
p: The oldest of 14 children, he left school after eighth grade to work at the rubber shop in Millville, Massachusetts, where his father worked. His father, a semipro catcher, was known for a tremendous throwing arm.
He was also called "Old Tomato Face." One writer: "a red face, a big cigar, and a laugh in which he simply wound up and let go. His frame shook like a dilapidated jalopy."
He and his bride, Martha, made 1929 spring training on Catalina Island their honeymoon.
After baseball he ran Gabby Hartnett's Recreation Center outside Chicago, which grew to 20 bowling lanes, a barbershop, a soda fountain, a cocktail lounge and a sporting-goods store.
He also did color commentary on CBS's baseball telecasts.
He and Martha married on January 28, 1929. They had a son, Charles Leo Jr., known as Bud, born in 1931, and a daughter, Sheila.
He died of cirrhosis on his 72nd birthday, in 1972.

c: He played every position in the majors: 585 games at second base, 544 in the outfield and 178 at third.
With Dan Brouthers, Jack Rowe and Deacon White he formed Buffalo's "Big Four." The Sporting News: "Even in hostile cities the fans praised them in the next breath after they had jeered them."
In 1885 Detroit bought all four from Buffalo. When the league threatened to void the sale, Richardson said the Big Four would "retire to Canada." Together they won Detroit the 1887 pennant.
In 1886 he led the NL in home runs. His Boston manager, Jim Hart, said he and Ed Williamson would "pretty nearly make a tie as to being the best ball player since professional base ball has existed."
In 1898, at 43, he made a brief comeback with the Utica Pent-Ups.
Detroit paid $7,000 for the Big Four in September 1885. When the Wolverines folded in 1888, they sold him, Bennett, Brouthers, Ganzel and White to Boston for about $30,000.
He helped Boston win the only Players' League pennant in 1890. A broken bone in his foot held him to 74 games in 1891.
Washington released him in April 1892 after he hit .108 in 10 games. He finished that season with the Giants and played his last big-league game at 37.
p: At 15 he was working on a farm in South Jersey. He started out as a third baseman and catcher for Gloucester City.
After baseball he worked as an art glass stainer in Utica and later for the Remington Typewriter Company. In 1910 and 1911 he wrote his baseball memories for the Hearst papers.
On Boardwalk Empire, Nucky Thompson recalls a catcher's mitt signed by Hardy Richardson that older boys stole from him as a child.
He married Lillie in Utica in January 1886, and their daughter Dorothy was born in 1895. By 1930 the couple were boarders in a cement salesman's home. He died in Utica in 1931 at 75.
In Boardwalk Empire, Nucky's father made him fight four older boys to get the mitt back; he was beaten unconscious and spent 11 days in the hospital.

c: During the Civil War he moved up from the Gothams' juniors to the senior team at 15, and at 17 was its regular catcher. In 1868 he won the Clipper Medal as the best shortstop in baseball.

He was the highest-paid player on the 1869 Cincinnati Red Stockings, the first fully professional team, at $1,400 for nine months. As they toured the country undefeated, he hit .633 with 49 home runs in 57 games.
On April 22, 1876, he was the first batter in National League history. He grounded out to shortstop Davy Force.
Hired to lead Providence in 1879, he won the pennant ahead of his brother Harry's Boston club. He's the only man to win a pennant in his only season as a manager.
He sat on the 1906-07 Mills Commission, which named Cooperstown as baseball's birthplace without any historical evidence.
A broken leg cost him half of the National Association's first season; one more win would have given Boston the pennant.
When Harry moved to Providence in 1882 he inherited the right to sign George again.
Spalding bought Wright & Ditson in 1892, but kept the name for years. Future U.S. Open champion Francis Ouimet worked at the store as an amateur.
p: He grew up as a cricket "club pro," helping his father, Samuel, at the St George's Cricket Club, which played at Elysian Fields in Hoboken, where many early baseball clubs played.

He took up cricket seriously again in Boston and in 1891 captained Longwood against Lord Hawke's touring English side. In 1892 he donated gear to cricketers from British Guiana, starting a tradition of West Indian cricket in New England.
In December 1890 he and three friends got a permit and chopped nine holes into the frozen ground of Franklin Park. Boston later named its George Wright Golf Course for him.
His son Beals became a tennis great.
He died of a stroke in Boston in August 1937, at 90, soon after his election to the Hall of Fame.

c: When Rockford came to Marshalltown, Iowa, in 1870, Anson, his father and his brother all played so well that Rockford offered contracts to all three. Only Adrian accepted.
On the 1874 baseball tour of England he led both teams in batting, and began a 30-year friendship with Al Spalding.

His bat control was such that he struck out once in all of 1878. Named Chicago's captain and manager in 1879, he became "Cap" Anson, and his 1880 team won at a .798 clip, still the National League record. His tirades at umpires earned him the title "King of Kickers."

In 1883 he refused to take the field at Toledo against its Black catcher, Moses Fleetwood Walker, and gave in only to save the gate. In 1887 he refused to play Newark unless Walker and pitcher George Stovey sat out. Other teams followed his lead, and by the early 1890s no Black players were left in the professional ranks.
On August 5 and 6, 1884, he hit five home runs in two games, helped by a left-field fence 180 feet away. The record has been tied but never broken.
He was the last first baseman to play barehanded, finally putting on a glove in 1892. At 42 he hit .388, and he retired after 1897 as the all-time leader in games, hits, runs, doubles and RBIs.
Spalding offered a testimonial benefit to raise $50,000 for him. Anson refused, saying it would "stultify my manhood" and smacked of charity.

His father sent him to a preparatory course at Notre Dame in 1865, but he cared more for baseball and skating than his studies. When Rockford disbanded, the Philadelphia Athletics signed him, and he managed them for the last weeks of 1875.
As manager he marched his players onto the field in military formation and banned drinking during the season.

After the 1888-89 world tour Spalding signed him to an unprecedented 10-year contract. When most stars jumped to the Players' League in 1890, Anson stayed, called the jumpers "traitors," and took a team of youngsters, "Anson's Colts," to second place.
When Spalding stepped down as president in 1891, Anson clashed often with Jim Hart. After 1897 Spalding and Hart declined to renew his contract, and after 27 seasons his career was over.
In 1900 he was named president of a new American Association.
p: He was born in a log cabin in Marshalltown, Iowa, the first pioneer child born in the town his father founded. His mother died when he was seven.
He didn't want to leave Philadelphia and his girlfriend, Virginia, so he offered Chicago $1,000 to let him out of his contract. When the club refused, he asked her father for her hand instead.
A teetotaler, he later ran a bowling and billiards hall and captained a team that won the American Bowling Congress five-man title in 1904. He was elected Chicago city clerk in 1905.
He went bankrupt in 1910 and refused the National League's offer of a pension. He toured vaudeville with his daughters in a skit Ring Lardner wrote, and when he died the league paid for his funeral.
In The Simpsons' "Homer at the Bat," Mr. Burns wants him as a ringer, until he's told Anson is long dead.
He met Virginia Fiegel in Philadelphia when he was 20 and she was 13. They married in November 1876 and stayed married until her death in 1916. Of their seven children, three sons died in infancy.

His failed businesses included a handball arena and a bottled ginger beer that exploded on store shelves. Elected Chicago city clerk in 1905, he campaigned on the nativist claim that Catholic immigration from Ireland and Italy was causing "race suicide."

On the vaudeville stage with his daughters Adele and Dorothy, he batted papier-mâché baseballs into the audience. In April 1922 he became general manager of a new golf club, and he died that month of a glandular ailment, three days short of 70.

c: Umpire Bill McGowan saw him pitch for a DuPont factory team and wired a minor-league manager about a "can't-miss" prospect. Goslin later returned the favor by recommending McGowan to the majors.

Clark Griffith tricked a golfing buddy into revealing the prospect's name, rushed to South Carolina and signed him, then watched from the stands as a fly ball hit Goslin on the head. A writer named him "Goose" for the way he flapped his arms chasing fly balls.

Needing a hit in his last at-bat in 1928 to win the batting title, he took two strikes and tried to get himself ejected. Umpire Bill Guthrie wouldn't throw him out or walk him. Goslin got a hit and won, .379 to Heinie Manush's .378.
In 1932 he came to bat with a zebra-striped bat designed to bother pitchers. The umpire ruled it illegal, and Goslin went 3-for-4 with a regular one.

During the 1934 World Series he called Bill Klem "Catfish," a name the umpire hated. Landis found that Klem had used "over-ripe language" in reply and fined him $50, the first fine Landis ever gave an umpire.

In the ninth inning of Game 6 in 1935 he told Elden Auker he had a hunch he'd bat with the winning run on base. He singled home Mickey Cochrane for Detroit's first World Series title. Gabby Hartnett: "He just hit a $50,000 pitch."
Signed by Columbia as a pitcher, he went 6-5, but his bat moved him to the outfield, and he led the Sally League at .390 in 1921. Griffith signed him for $6,000.

In 1924 he drove in 129 runs, 50 more than any teammate, and hit .344 in the World Series with a record six straight hits. In 1925 he homered three times in the Series, which Washington lost after leading 3–1.

After a salary dispute, Washington traded him to St. Louis in June 1930. Reading the telegram, he said, "They weren't kidding, were they?" His father-and-son relationship with Clark Griffith was over.

Back in Washington in 1933, he expected to be named manager, but Joe Cronin got the job. They never got along, and he was traded to Detroit for John Stone. There he urged Mickey Cochrane to trade for General Crowder.
He played every game of all three World Series the Senators ever played in.

Columnist Leonard Lyons reported he won more rolling dice in a week at a Miami Beach club than his $12,000 Tigers salary. At his peak he earned $16,000 a year and reportedly more than $35,000 in World Series money, and he stayed thrifty.
p: When his father got sick, he milked 25 cows every morning and evening on the family's 500-acre dairy farm in South Jersey.
His hand-eye coordination was so good that he once beat New Jersey's skeet-shooting champion by hitting 50 of 50 clay pigeons.
Later in life he ran a fishing spot on Stow Creek, renting boats, tackle and cabins and selling fish, crabs and lunches.
At his 1968 Hall of Fame induction he broke down crying until Commissioner William Eckert put a hand on his shoulder: "I will never forget this. I will take this to my grave."
He married Marion Wallace in 1940; she died in 1959 after a long illness. At his Stow Creek property he shipped 100 or more bushels a day.
In January 1969 he was hospitalized with burns after falling asleep smoking on his couch, which caught fire. He died in 1971 at 70.

c: He weighed 100 pounds when he signed with Troy, and fans in Albany thought he was a comedy act. When Troy asked the Cubs for $1,500 for a pitcher, Frank Selee said, "If you throw in that kid who played short today, I'll give you the $1,500."
He and Joe Tinker didn't speak off the field for years. Evers traced it to a hard throw in 1907 that bent back his finger: "Tinker and myself hated each other, but we loved the Cubs."
He sought walks: "I have frequently faced the pitcher when I had no desire whatever to hit." In 1910 he drew 108.

On September 23, 1908, Fred Merkle left the field without touching second, and Evers got a ball and stepped on the bag. Buck Herzog: "He looked like the Statue of Liberty." Umpire Hank O'Day called Merkle out, and the Cubs won the pennant in the replay.

In 1914, the highest-paid player in baseball, he captained the "Miracle Braves" from last place to a World Series sweep, hit .438 in the Series, and won the Chalmers Award as MVP. Rabbit Maranville: "He'd make you want to punch him, but you knew Johnny was thinking only of the team."
He was the first man to manage both Chicago major-league clubs, and the only one until Rick Renteria almost a century later.
Bobby Lowe's knee injury opened second base for him, and Troy was willing to sell him partly because of his temper.
He hit his first big-league home run on his 24th birthday, July 21, 1905.
He hit .150 in the 1906 World Series loss to the White Sox and .350 in the 1907 and 1908 wins over Detroit. A broken leg kept him out of the 1910 Series.

Named player-manager on a five-year contract, he was fired after 1913 anyway; owner Charles Murphy claimed he'd resigned and tried to trade him. The NL owners voided the trade and let Evers sell himself to the Braves for $25,000 plus bonuses.
Rabbit Maranville: "He'd make you want to punch him, but you knew Johnny was thinking only of the team."
Injuries and suspensions cost him half of 1915. Waived by Boston in 1917, he finished with the Phillies, then made the 1918 Red Sox and was cut before playing a game.
He was nicknamed "The Human Crab" for his combative play. The Merkle ball sold at auction in the 1990s for $27,500.
p: He said Ev-ers was the correct pronunciation, but everyone in his hometown of Troy said E-vers.
To keep weight on his 125-pound frame he ate candy bars on off days. In 1911 he missed most of the season with a nervous breakdown he blamed on losing all his savings in a failed business.
In 1914 his three-year-old daughter, Helen, caught scarlet fever while visiting her sick brother, and died. His marriage fell apart soon after.
His father was a saloon keeper.

He married Helen Fitzgibbons in January 1909; he lived in Chicago and she in Troy. When their son John Jr. was 11, Evers bought part of the Albany Senators and gave him the stock. John Jr. served as a lieutenant in the Pacific in World War II. When Helen died in 1974 she was buried with Evers.
He opened a sporting goods store in Albany in 1923, went bankrupt in 1936, and was superintendent of Bleecker Stadium. He died of a cerebral hemorrhage in 1947.

c: In 1870, his hands black and blue from catching barehanded, he wore buckskin gloves in a game. He wasn't the first catcher to wear gloves, but it was a notable early case. The Clipper: "A cat after a mouse is not quicker than James is after a foul ball."

Leading off the first National Association game, on May 4, 1871, he doubled, the first hit and first double in pro league history. He then became part of the first double play when he got caught off second on a fly ball.

Before 1873 he had a religious conversion and didn't report to Boston on time. Harry Wright: "He has been converted, and thinks at present that he would not be doing right if he should play baseball." He came a week later. The Clipper said it had never known him to growl at an umpire.
When Detroit tried to sell him and Jack Rowe in 1889, he objected: "I don't want a man to sell my carcass without I get half." They ended up getting part of the sale money from Pittsburgh.
He retired second all-time in RBIs. Left out of the first Hall of Fame classes, he died weeks after the 1939 Cooperstown ceremonies, reportedly deeply disappointed. He was finally elected in 2012.

He could pitch too. The Cleveland Plain Dealer called him "probably the swiftest pitcher in the world": a batter once tipped one of his pitches straight up into the forehead of Sutton, standing close behind the bat.
In 1874 Boston paid him $1,800, the same as Barnes, Spalding and both Wrights.

As Cincinnati captain he resigned after a 9-9 start. One summer his wife fell ill and his father died, manager John Clapp fined him $10 for not going to third, and he filed a $55 claim for his wife's travel expenses. Cincinnati was then expelled from the league for playing Sunday games and selling alcohol.

When Buffalo tried to sell its stars, managers came bidding "in about the same manner that slaves were sold during the rebellion"; the players kicked and "smashed the whole scheme." When Detroit bought the franchise for $7,000 to get the Big Four, the leagues ruled they could sign anywhere for no more than $2,000, and Detroit's manager rushed to Corning to sign White.
The Detroit win over St. Louis in the 15-game 1887 World Series was his sixth championship.
He led his league in RBIs three times; no other catcher did it until Roy Campanella in 1953. In 1891 he managed the minor-league Elmira Gladiators.

He was elected to the Hall of Fame in December 2012 with 14 of 16 votes; his great-grandson gave the speech. With more than 166 years between his birth and induction, he's the "oldest" person ever inducted.
p: At 91 he said he learned baseball in 1865 from a Union soldier, possibly his older brother LeRoy.
His cousin and teammate Elmer White died in 1872, the first pro league player ever to die.
After baseball he owned a broom factory, a livery business and an optical company in Buffalo, and helped incorporate the city's Advent Christian Church in 1896.
At Mendota College in Illinois, where his daughter studied, he and his wife lived as head residents of the young ladies' dormitory.
In 1936 NL president Ford Frick invited him to the All-Star Game as one of three living players from the league's first season. His daughter replied that he was nearly 89 and too frail to go.

He married Marium Van Arsdale of Caton in April 1871. When her father died he inherited another farm, and said he knew he should quit baseball for his farms, horses and cattle. Around then his peers started calling him "The Deacon."

They lived on his farm in Corning for much of his career and moved to Buffalo in 1881; their only child, Grace, was born there in 1882. Marium died in 1914, and he married again, to Alice. He died at 91 in a 1939 heat wave.

c: In 1904 a Phillies scout getting off a train in Carlisle overheard fans raving about a local kid. Magee didn't believe the offer until he saw the contract and a roll of bills. Two days later, at 19, he started in left field, listed as "McGee" in the box score.
In 1910 he ended Honus Wagner's hold on the batting title, hitting .331, and led the NL in runs, RBIs, on-base percentage and slugging.

On July 10, 1911, ejected by rookie umpire Bill Finneran, he knocked him down with a punch. He was suspended for the rest of the season, the harshest punishment since 1877, though he was reinstated after about a month.
Named Phillies captain in 1914, he volunteered to play shortstop ("I can't do any worse than some of the men that have been in there") and led the NL in hits, doubles, RBIs and slugging.

Fifteen minutes into his first Braves workout in 1915, he stepped in a hole and broke his collarbone, and was never the same player. He is the only non-Hall of Famer to lead the NL in RBIs four times.
The old umpire-baiter became an NL umpire in 1928, and surprised the old-timers with his cool decisions.
An injury to John Titus in 1904 opened left field for him, and he played so well the Phillies traded Shad Barry. His 55 steals in 1905 were a modern Phillies record until Juan Samuel in 1984.
In 1909 he slumped and played with "marked indifference," and was rumored to be going to the Giants for Mike Donlin.

After the punch, Finneran came to, ripped off his chest protector and went after the Phillies bench, then went to the hospital with what was thought to be a broken nose. Manager Red Dooin said the rookie umpire had bragged all season about his fighting. Magee was fined $200.
He was allegedly drunk when he hit Finneran. On appeal his suspension was cut to 36 games.
In the 1912 city series with the Athletics, a batting-practice pitch broke his right wrist and forearm, and he missed the first month.
In 1919 he was seriously ill for two months. He finished his career pinch-hitting twice in the World Series, with one hit, and got a ring.
p: He was also a crackerjack bowler and a football and basketball standout. As a young Phillie he felt the old leather belt captain Kid Gleason kept for misbehaving players.
Out of work in 1925 he wrote to the Reds' owner asking for a job: "You know I never drank Whiskey and don't to-day and have a lot more sense than I had there before."
He died of pneumonia in March 1929, at 44, after his first season as an NL umpire.
He was the son of an oilfield worker in Clarendon, Pennsylvania. One writer said "the Irish traits of quick wittedness, a hot temper and an aggressive love of fighting are his by birthright."

c: Harry Wright signed him for the 1869 Cincinnati Red Stockings at 18, so young that his father had to sign the contract. He was the youngest player on the first openly professional team and the first pro born west of the Mississippi.
On their undefeated 1869 tour the Red Stockings were invited to the White House to meet President Grant, and became the first ballclub to ride the new transcontinental railroad.
In the first National Association season, 1871, he hit .431 and finished second for the batting title. He went on to play all nine positions, including pitcher.
In 1873, at 22, he became the youngest manager in the league, with Baltimore. In 1876 he helped Chicago win the first National League pennant.
A scout's report on him: "a good fielder, but his strength is with the ash in his hands... and he doesn't drink."
In 1870 the Red Stockings split into factions over drinking and discipline. Champion resigned as president, and the club went back to amateur status.
With him in Cincinnati, the Reds finished a close second his first year and fifth in 1879. In San Francisco in the 1880s he played for, managed and organized several teams.
p: As a boy he was known for cartwheels and handsprings and fought bare-knuckle. He reportedly turned flips on the field after Red Stockings wins.
Charmed by San Francisco on the 1869 tour, he moved to California to play out his career. His voter registrations listed an identifying mark: "baseball marks on fingers."
The 1906 earthquake destroyed his home, and later a 30-foot fall in a Nevada mine crippled him. Old teammate Doug Allison asked the National League for help, and it gave a little.
In 1919 Cincinnati invited him back as an honored guest for the 50th anniversary of the Red Stockings, and he rode in the parade before the World Series.
His father farmed without much success, then became a tax collector and piano tuner. His parents later followed him to California.

He married Abbey, from Indiana, in 1874, though a later census found her not living with him. In 1901 he was a special policeman and watchman in San Francisco, and after the earthquake injured him and his wife, he worked ten years as a night watchman for a lumber company. He died in 1926 at 76.

c: Fielder Jones recommended him to Detroit, which reportedly paid $1,500. Playing alongside Ty Cobb, Heilmann said, taught him the secret of elite hitting.
In 1921 he beat his manager, Cobb, for the batting title, .394 to .389. His daughter-in-law said that afterward Cobb "didn't really talk with him again."
He hit .403 in 1923. Only Ted Williams has hit .400 in the AL since. That winter, in his off-season job, he sold Babe Ruth a $50,000 life insurance policy.
Teammates told him to sit out the second game of the 1925 finale once he'd passed Tris Speaker. "I'll win it fairly, or not at all." He went 3-for-3 and won by four points.
On the last day of 1927, trailing Al Simmons by a point, he went 7-for-9 in a doubleheader to win his fourth batting title, all of them in odd-numbered years.
In 1933 he became the first former player to be a play-by-play broadcaster, calling Tigers games for 17 years. He took public-speaking classes and recreated road games from ticker-tape reports.

Former Tigers pitcher Dutch Leonard wrote Heilmann that he'd given AL president Ban Johnson letters from Joe Wood and Ty Cobb implicating them in betting on a September 1919 Tigers-Cleveland game. Cobb and Wood admitted the letters but said the bet was on horses, and claimed Leonard was angry at Cobb for sending him to the Pacific Coast League.
After his 1929 season the Tigers put him on waivers, and Cincinnati claimed him. He briefly retired in 1931 and finished in 1932 as a Reds player-coach, hitting .258 in 15 games.
His 164 home runs for Detroit were a club record until Hank Greenberg broke it in 1938.

Before broadcasting, he ran unsuccessfully for Detroit city treasurer and operated a semipro team. From 1934 to 1942 he called Tigers games on WXYZ and a statewide network while rival Ty Tyson called them for WWJ in Detroit.
p: His older brother Walter, a promising pitcher, drowned at 16 trying to swim ashore after his boat capsized.
When he first brought home baseball pay, his parents feared he was doing something dishonest.
On July 25, 1916, he dove into the Detroit River to save a woman from drowning, and got a thunderous ovation at the ballpark the next day. In 1918 he served on a Navy submarine.
Dying of lung cancer in 1951, he was visited by Cobb, who told him he'd been elected to the Hall of Fame. It wasn't true yet; he was elected the following year.
His Irish mother and German father were much concerned about his early ballplaying. His daughter-in-law said, "He invented the word class."
He sold insurance in Cincinnati while playing for the Reds and kept at it in Detroit after retiring.

He fell ill at spring training in Lakeland in 1951, and his lung cancer wasn't disclosed until after he died. He got a warm ovation at Briggs Stadium on June 1 and called a few more games. He died July 9, and the All-Star Game in Detroit the next day began with a moment of silence for him.
Ty Cobb led a campaign for a special election so he could be inducted before he died. He was elected in January 1952 with 86.75 percent of the vote, and his widow represented him at Cooperstown.

c: In 1892 Hastings, Nebraska, sent a railroad ticket to a Des Moines semipro named Byron McKibbon. McKibbon backed out and gave the ticket to Clarke.
At Hastings he caught barely half the fly balls hit to him, so on an old-timer's advice he practiced from 8 a.m. until game time every day.
In his big-league debut, in 1894, he went 5-for-5 against the Phillies' Gus Weyhing, four singles and a triple.

Barney Dreyfuss warned the young, carousing Clarke that he'd "go back to the minors and be swallowed up" if he kept it up. Clarke cleaned up, and in 1897, at 24, Dreyfuss made him Louisville's manager, which is how he got the nickname "Cap."
He hit the first official cycle in the majors, on July 23, 1901, against Cincinnati.
As Pittsburgh's player-manager he won four pennants, the 1909 World Series, and 14 straight first-division finishes. At the plate he'd try to hit the catcher with his backswing.
Back as Dreyfuss's assistant, he helped fire up the Pirates to the 1925 title. In 1926 three veterans moved to get him off the bench, and the ensuing "ABC Affair" ended with him leaving the club.
His first three teams were all put out of business: Hastings and St. Joseph when their leagues collapsed, Montgomery by a yellow fever outbreak.
For many years his 1897 average was listed at .406; it's now .390, second only to Willie Keeler's best season.
He hit .265 in the first World Series, a loss to Boston. In 1909 he hit only .211 but both of Pittsburgh's home runs, and drew a record four walks in Game 7.

As manager he gambled and won: moving Claude Ritchey to second, putting Honus Wagner at short, and starting Babe Adams in Game 1 of the 1909 World Series. On the bases he fought Cupid Childs, Fred Tenney and others.
He wanted to retire after the 1909 title to be with his family, but Barney Dreyfuss talked him out of it.
After the 1925 World Series, the players, seeing him as front office and knowing he was already a millionaire, voted him just $1,000, the same as the scouts, while full shares were $5,332.71.
p: As a boy in Des Moines he delivered newspapers for Ed Barrow, the future Yankees executive.
After the 1893 season he tried to stake a claim in Oklahoma's Cherokee Strip and leave baseball. He failed, and went back to playing.
He held patents on flip-down sunglasses, a sliding pad and a mechanical tarp handler. After oil was found on his Little Pirate Ranch in Kansas in 1916, his wealth was put at $1 million.
Late in life he survived three hours in a lake after his boat capsized, a hunting companion's stray shot deflected by the bill of his cap, and an exploding furnace.
He was the ninth of 12 children; his father, a blacksmith and farmer, moved the family by covered wagon to a farm near Winfield, Kansas. His younger brother Pepper also played in the majors.

He married Annette Gray of Chicago in July 1898. They had two daughters, Helen and Muriel, and lived together for over 62 years, mostly on the Little Pirate Ranch, which grew to 1,320 acres. Pitcher Chick Fraser married one of her sisters.
He bought the ranch with a down payment in his first big-league year. He died at Winfield at 87.

c: Cleveland signed him at 19 in 1890 to replace players who had jumped to the Players' League. He played center field and led the NL's outfielders with 35 assists.

Traded to the Giants for Buck Ewing in 1893, he hit .355 with a then-record 33-game hitting streak. He grew a handlebar mustache like his mentor John Montgomery Ward's, so people had trouble telling them apart.
In 1895, at 24, he became the youngest manager in baseball history to that point.

Ward, now a lawyer, helped him jump to the White Sox in 1902 and then return to the Giants. Charles Comiskey got court injunctions, and Davis played four games for New York before ending up back in Chicago.
He was the best hitter on the 1906 "Hitless Wonders" White Sox, and drove in six runs in the last two games of their World Series win over the Cubs.
He was the first switch-hitter to reach 2,000 hits.
On April 26, 1900, on the way to the Polo Grounds, he, Kid Gleason and Mike Grady came on a tenement fire and rescued two women and a three-year-old. Face blistered, he played that evening.
In 1899 manager Buck Ewing accused him of faking a knee injury to stay in New York and plot for his job. When Ewing resigned, Davis took over.
A $4,000 salary induced him to jump to the White Sox in 1902.
Ill, he missed the first three games of the 1906 World Series.
He stole home in Game 5 of that Series.
Managing Des Moines in the Western League, he finished last at 49-113. While coaching Amherst he also scouted for the Yankees and the Browns.
p: Local papers show him playing on tavern-sponsored teams in Cohoes, New York, by 16, already a switch-hitter.
After baseball he ran a Manhattan bowling alley and was pictured as a star bowler at 43. He coached Amherst College from 1913 to 1918.

He then vanished from public view. In 1968 historian Lee Allen found that he had died in a Philadelphia hospital in 1940 and was buried in an unmarked grave. His family didn't learn of his death for years. A SABR chapter later gave him a headstone.
He was the fifth of seven children of an Irish immigrant father and a Welsh mother.
Admitted to Philadelphia General Hospital in 1934, he was moved three weeks later to a mental hospital. He died in 1940, and his family didn't learn of it until years later.
He died suffering the effects of syphilis.
After Amherst he sold cars. His wife Jane, said to have been angry at him, spent $41 to have him buried within a day at Fernwood Cemetery.
No relatives could be found for his Hall of Fame induction, but about 50 people from Cohoes came.

c: Detroit catcher Bruce Petway scouted him in Memphis and begged him to come north in 1922. Stearnes stayed to finish high school first: "I at least wanted to finish high school, because I knew I couldn't go to college."
He leaned way forward with his back foot pointing up and flapped his elbows when he ran, which one historian gives as the source of "Turkey." Stearnes said it came from a potbelly he had as a kid.

As a rookie in 1923 he hit for the cycle, hit .366 with 18 homers in league play, and learned to clear Mack Park's tall screened fence: "You got to hit a tall fly ball." That October he homered and tripled as the Stars took two of three from the St. Louis Browns.
He led the Negro National League in home runs six times. His .616 career slugging percentage ranks fifth in major-league history.
Homers didn't impress him: "If they didn't win a ball game, they didn't amount to anything." Satchel Paige: "Turkey Stearnes was one of the greatest hitters we ever had. He was as good as Josh."
At 44 he was field captain of the Toledo Cubs in Branch Rickey's United States League in 1945.
Stearnes himself said the nickname came from the potbelly he had as a kid.

One day the stands at Mack Park caught fire; the Free Press headline read "Fear-Stricken Spectators Leap Upon Those Beneath." Over 100 were injured, the owner refused refunds, and the Stars moved to Dequindre Park. Its cavernous center field helped push Stearnes to jump to the New York Lincoln Giants for 1930.
His only postseason with Detroit came in 1930, when the Stars won the second half and lost the playoff to St. Louis.
In the California Winter League he once led with 7 homers and a .377 average. In 1934 he and Mule Suttles each hit 16 to lead the league for the Nashville Elite Giants.
When the Detroit Stars folded after 1931 he joined Cole's American Giants of Chicago and helped them win the 1932 pennant.
p: His father died when he was 15 or 16, and he left high school to help support the family, tending hogs and cows, driving a grocery wagon and working as a janitor at the Baptist Publishing Board.
On first coming north he painted car bodies at Briggs Manufacturing, owned by the man who owned the Tigers. After baseball he worked in Detroit's rolling mills from 1938 to 1964.
In retirement he took the bus to Tiger Stadium and sat in the bleachers, his daughter said, "because he thought those were the normal everyday people."
His wife, Nettie, was a niece of Double Duty Radcliffe. After his death she campaigned for 20 years to get him into the Hall of Fame, and he was inducted in 2000.
He married Nettie, a schoolteacher, in 1946; they lived in a modest house on Detroit's east side and had two daughters, Joyce and Rosilyn. She said, "Norman was very shy."

He worked 30 years in the foundry at Ford's River Rouge plant. In 1979 he fell into a coma after surgery for a large stomach ulcer, and died at 78. In 2023 his granddaughter made a podcast about the Negro leagues, Reclaimed: The Forgotten League.

c: Filling in for an injured player on his hometown Columbia team in 1894, he tripled against the Cuban Giants.
In September 1901 he hit grand slams in consecutive games, the first 20th-century player with two in a season.
Before the 1906 World Series he bragged he'd hit .400 off the White Sox. He went 0-for-21 and never hit the ball out of the infield.
On June 2, 1908, teammate Heinie Zimmerman threw a bottle of ammonia that broke between his eyes, nearly costing him the sight of his left eye. The Cubs tried to cover it up.
Fed up with Pirates hits falling around him, he spun several times, threw his glove in the air, and stood where it landed near the foul line. Fred Clarke lined the next pitch right to him.
His 147 walks in 1911 were the NL record until Eddie Stanky broke it in 1945. In 1912 he nearly forgot to finish a walk-off home run trot after detouring to pick up his glove in left field.

When Jones jumped to the American League in 1901, Sheckard took his place and led the NL in slugging and triples while hitting .354. He jumped to the AL's Baltimore Orioles for four games in 1902, then changed his mind and went back to Brooklyn.
In December 1905 Brooklyn traded him to the Cubs for four players and $2,000, one of the deals that shifted NL power from New York to Chicago.
He led off the final game of the 1908 World Series, the last the Cubs would win for 108 years.
Johnny Evers: "he was a bigger cog in the old invincible Cub machine than he ever received credit for being."
The Cubs sold him to the Cardinals in April 1913. He hit .199, was waived to Cincinnati, and hit .190 there. He later coached at Franklin & Marshall and managed the Lancaster Red Roses in 1932.
p: He was named Samuel James Tilden Sheckard after New York's anticorruption governor, and was one of the few big-leaguers of Pennsylvania Dutch heritage.
With Artie Hofman and Lew Richie he formed three-quarters of a Cubs barbershop quartet. He sang baritone.
Managing semipro ball in Columbia, he wore white socks and chewed tobacco. Les Bell: "By the end of a game those white socks were always a very distinctly brownish color."

He lost his savings in the 1929 crash and later drove a truck collecting milk cans from farms. In January 1947, on his way to a gas station job, he was struck by a car and killed. Bill Klem presided over a ceremony in his honor in Lancaster.
He limped from arthritis in his left foot that doctors blamed on an old baseball injury. The car hit him from behind, and he died of head injuries three days later.

c: In 1878, Providence's first season, he led the NL in home runs, RBIs and batting average, the first Triple Crown in major-league history, though nobody knew it at the time.

On May 8, 1878, he caught a fly behind short and kept running to third, which both runners had passed. Some accounts call it the first unassisted triple play; others say he threw to second for the last out.
Before a game in 1881 he took a blank scorecard from a reporter, wrote "one home-run," and marked the fifth inning. In the fifth he hit one over the left-field fence.
In the 1884 series against the New York Metropolitans, now considered the first World Series, he got the first hit and scored the first run.
When a wild teenage Amos Rusie was about to be pulled in 1889, Hines talked captain Jack Glasscock out of it and walked Rusie back to the box with an arm around him. Rusie won.
He was the only player on Providence's roster all eight of its National League seasons.
When Boston owner Arthur Soden bought the Providence franchise for $6,600 in November 1885, he kept Radbourn and catcher Con Daily and released the rest.
After agreeing to terms for 1887 he reneged and held out until April; even his wife and father gave him grief. Washington then traded him to Indianapolis for Gid Gardner and a reported $5,000.

In 1890 he played for the Pittsburgh Alleghenys, one of the worst teams ever, hit .182 and was released in June. With Washington in 1891, the Boston Globe blamed "his stupid baserunning" for a 13-inning tie.
p: He was almost completely deaf for most of his career. Later stories that a beaning caused it, or that umpires made hand signals for him, are apocryphal.
When the Washington Monument was finished in 1884, friends urged him to catch a ball dropped from the top, 555 feet up. After the Clipper did the physics, he declined.
In 1897, working as a government clerk, he helped break down an office door in his building, clubbed an armed attacker and knocked away his gun: "I simply did what any man of sense would have done."
President William McKinley helped him get his government job.
His parents were Irish immigrants; his father was a laborer and later a building contractor.

He married Katie May Duffy in February 1886, and they were married nearly 50 years; she died in March 1935, months before him. After baseball he worked in the Department of Agriculture, rising to postmaster.

In 1922, at 67, he was arrested for picking a pocket in a police setup: he lifted a detective's pocketbook from a policewoman's overcoat. One official was inclined to regard it as "kleptomania attendant upon advancing years."
He died at 80 in Hyattsville, Maryland, deaf and blind.

c: Released by Worcester with a sore shoulder in 1882, he went to Saginaw, where manager Arthur Whitney spent hours behind the team hotel converting him to an overhand delivery. In 1884 he went 34-9 there with 388 strikeouts and a 0.64 ERA by mid-August.

In 1885 he went 53-16 for Chicago over 623 innings and threw a no-hitter against Providence. Cap Anson: "Scold him, find fault with him, and he could not pitch at all. Praise him and he was unbeatable."
He wore a shiny belt buckle to flash in batters' eyes until umpires made him take it off. Sam Thompson: "Never in all that time did I get a pitch that came where I expected it."
Boston paid $10,000 for him, and he and King Kelly became the "$20,000 Battery."

He threw the first known immaculate inning, nine pitches and three strikeouts, on June 4, 1889. In a game running into dusk, he once threw a lemon to the plate to get the umpire to call the game for darkness.
His 24 home runs were by far the most of any 19th-century pitcher, a record that lasted decades.
Teammate Fred Pfeffer on his control: "I stood behind him day in and day out... as confident of success, especially in tight places, as I would have been with the United States army behind me."

In the deciding game of the 1886 World Series against St. Louis, Arlie Latham and the baserunner Welch heckled him and faked toward home. When Welch finally broke, King Kelly had called a pitchout, but Clarkson threw a wild pitch and Welch scored the winning run.
During that series the Chicago players drank heavily. Clarkson may not have been drinking by day, but he was tearing it up at night.

Wanting a house of his own in Boston, he asked Spalding for a trade, threatened to sit out and join the family jewelry business, and said, "I will not play in Chicago under any circumstances." Spalding threatened to blacklist him. Rumor also had it he'd fallen out with Ned Williamson.
Boston's new manager, Frank Selee, released him in June 1892, and he signed with Cleveland.
p: Unlike most players of his day he came from money: his father had a jewelry and watchmaking business in Boston, where Harry Wright worked as a watchmaker, and John trained in the trade.
Every winter he coached college pitchers, at Dartmouth, Harvard, Yale and Michigan. On trains and in hotels he and King Kelly sang for their teammates.
Sporting Life called him the "bright particular dude" of the team. He wore a silk handkerchief on the outside of his uniform.

He ran cigar stores in Bay City, Michigan, after retiring. In 1905 he had a breakdown and spent most of his last years in hospitals, and died of pneumonia in 1909 at 47. Bay City named a ballfield for him.
He stayed in Chicago one offseason to be near his girlfriend, Ella Moorhead McKenna, and they married in March 1886; it was the only year he skipped coaching college pitchers.
Some have even claimed that, deranged, he mutilated his wife.
After he died, Cap Anson said, "not many know what amount of encouragement it took to keep him going."

c: Pitching for the Sturm Avenue Never Sweats in 1888, he shut out two touring National League teams, Boston and Washington, and Indianapolis signed him. He debuted at 17.
On May 12, 1890, he and Kid Nichols traded zeroes for 12 innings before Rusie won 1-0 in the 13th. That year he walked 289, a record no one has approached since.

Restaurants named drinks after him and vaudeville acts did skits about him. Connie Mack: "Rusie was the fastest without a doubt. All I saw of them was what I heard when they went into the catcher's mitt." His catcher lined his glove with a sheet of lead.

Batters' fear of his fastball helped push the league to move the pitcher back to 60 feet, 6 inches in 1893. In 1894 he won the pitching Triple Crown, then won twice in the Temple Cup sweep of Baltimore.

When owner Andrew Freedman fined him $200 in 1895, he sat out all of 1896 and sued. The other owners, fearing for the reserve clause, paid him $5,000 to drop it: "almost $2,000 more than I would have been paid for playing."
A snap pickoff throw in 1898 hurt his shoulder, and he never won another big-league game. In 1900 the Giants traded him to Cincinnati for Christy Mathewson, who went on to win 372 games.

After 1892 Andrew Freedman released him to make him sign for less. Despite a gentleman's agreement, Chicago grabbed him for $8,250 including a $2,000 bonus. The Giants bought him back and tried to count the bonus as salary.
Fans called him the "Hoosier Thunderbolt." A quarter bought the paperback Secrets of Amos Rusie, The World's Greatest Pitcher, and Lillian Russell sent him a message.
In the 1894 Temple Cup he won two complete games with a 0.50 ERA and batted .429.
During Game 3 of that series a horse bolted, smashed its buggy, and charged through the crowd ringing the Polo Grounds outfield onto the field.
Freedman fined him $100 for being out after curfew and $100 for "not trying hard enough," a big bite of his salary.
When Freedman accused him of slacking off, Rusie publicly thumbed his nose at him, the 19th-century version of the middle finger.
He rested his arm for two years after the injury. Forty years later he still said, "Even today I'm often bothered by twinges of pain here."
With the Reds he pitched poorly in three games and retired.
p: His father lost a leg in the Civil War, joining up at 16, and still worked for years as a brick mason.

His wife, May, divorced him in 1900 over his New York lifestyle. He promised to stay sober and leave New York, and they remarried less than three months later. The marriage lasted until her death in 1942.
After baseball he worked in a paper mill, hunted pearls in the Wabash River, and was a steamfitter in Seattle. In 1921 John McGraw brought him back to work at the Polo Grounds.
When the Rusies lost their farm to foreclosure in 1935, the Seattle Post-Intelligencer and The Sporting News raised enough money to support them for the rest of their lives.
He quit school at 16 and worked in a factory and as a varnisher in an Indianapolis furniture store. His father died in a home for disabled veterans in 1925.
He married May Smith in Muncie in 1890, and their daughter Jeannette was born in 1897. Their second marriage lasted until May died in 1942.
He was a ticket taker at a Seattle ballpark, worked in a bottle factory, umpired two weeks in the Northwestern League, then spent ten years in Seattle as a gas fitter and a shipyard steamfitter.

c: As an 18-year-old rookie with the Brooklyn Atlantics in 1874, he pitched every game but one. On October 20 he lost a no-hitter with two outs in the ninth; it would have been the first in major-league history.
In 1876 he accused his Hartford manager, Bob Ferguson, of throwing a game. Club director Morgan Bulkeley offered $1,300 for proof; Bond couldn't provide it and was suspended.
He moved to Boston and won the pitching Triple Crown in 1877. From 1877 to 1879 he threw 1,609 innings.
He said he kept a wet sponge to moisten his fingers, and his catcher Charley Snyder confirmed it gave the ball "a peculiar shoot."

When the pitching distance went from 45 to 50 feet in 1881, his tired arm couldn't handle it. A Cincinnati paper said "the fifty-foot rule has shelved Tommy Bond." As an umpire in 1885, he called more runners out for missing a base than anyone else.
Suspended by Hartford after his accusation, he retracted it, but the suspension stood, and Boston signed him for 1877.
After his arm gave out he worked out with Harvard in 1882, tutored its pitchers, and came back with Worcester.
He also managed Worcester for six games.
He became a National League umpire late in one season when an umpire resigned. Later he pitched for Indianapolis of the American Association, won his first three games, and was released soon after.
p: Born in Granard, Ireland, he was the first Irish-born major-leaguer. The Irish Baseball League's best-pitcher award is named for him.
He married Louise Siebert, joined her family's leather business, and later worked 35 years in the Boston Assessor's Office.
At 80, at a 1936 Old-Timers gathering, he still played catch with old teammates.
He was the last survivor of the National League's first season, 1876.
He worked in a Boston grocery store in the offseason. He and Louise had three children, Helen, Edward and Fred; he later moved into his daughter's home.
He died in Boston in 1941 at 84, the last living player from the 1878 season.

c: In 1877 a homeowner refused to pay him $22 for 11 days of carpentry, and Keefe had to sue. He decided he'd do just as well as a professional ballplayer.

Reserved by Troy, he had to take $1,500 a year. "I was considered a robber because I held out for $2,100." It started a decade-long fight for fairer contracts, and he became secretary-treasurer of the players' Brotherhood.

To move him from his Metropolitans to his Giants in 1885, owner John Day had manager Jim Mutrie take Keefe and Dude Esterbrook on a boat to Bermuda, out of other teams' reach while their ten-day releases ran out.
His change of pace carried him to 19 straight wins in 1888, still the major-league record, tied by Rube Marquard in 1912. When he retired he was the career strikeout leader.
As an NL umpire in the 1890s he was once mobbed at the Polo Grounds and broke down in tears. He quit in 1896: "Base ball has reached a stage where it is absolutely disgraceful."
Some versions of "Casey at the Bat" name him as the pitcher, "Sir Timothy." In 1938 the real-life Dan Casey said Rogers Hornsby "didn't have as much on the ball as Tim Keefe did."
He won Utica's pitching job by beating Harvard in an exhibition. When Utica folded in July he joined Jim Mutrie's New Bedford team, then Troy.

When Troy's franchise ended he played bidders against each other, drew a $2,800 offer from Detroit, and signed with John Day of New York for $3,100. Day owned teams in both leagues, and assigned Keefe to his American Association Metropolitans, who won the 1884 pennant.
He designed the Giants' famous all-black "funeral" uniforms.

Before the Players' League fight he transferred his real estate to his mother to keep it safe from lawsuits, and started a sporting goods business. In 1891 he refused New York's $3,000 offer, down from $4,500: "I do not think I am wanted in the New York team, and this cutting method is being pursued to keep me out." He signed for $3,500 and was released during the season.
He umpired 243 major-league games, 129 of them in 1895.
p: His father, a carpenter, wanted him to study math and science and become an engineer, and disliked his baseball.
In New York he started wearing tailored suits and taught himself accounting and shorthand to make up for having no college education.
He coached Harvard's pitchers for six winters, and was hurt when Harvard dropped him in 1898. He mostly kept out of public view after that.
He built two apartment houses in Cambridge and lived the last two decades of his life at 1653 Cambridge Street, where the corner is now Tim Keefe Square.
He was one of seven children of Irish immigrants, and was actually born in Somerville, probably at a relative's home.
His father served in the Union Army and was a prisoner of war for several years. Father and son fought often over Tim's baseball.

c: In Omaha he often pitched to his brother Charlie, or caught him, and he soon took Charlie's place as the team's main pitcher.
As a Boston rookie in 1881 he was started in 14 straight games and then 11 more, and led the NL in ten categories, including wins, losses, innings and wild pitches.
In a September 1883 series against first-place Chicago he won three of the four games, and Boston took the pennant. He went 37-21 that year and led the league with 345 strikeouts against 35 walks.
"Grasshopper Jim" was probably named for a hopping windup one writer compared to "a running high jump and a back handspring." A rule change in 1887 made him keep his back foot planted.
Though he was aloof and not popular with teammates, he was trusted enough that three times the opposing captains chose him to umpire when the assigned umpire didn't show up.
Jim O'Rourke: "It was a wonder that anyone was able to hit him at all. He was the swiftest pitcher I ever saw."
At 6-foot-2 he towered over batters and pitched inside, when there was no penalty for hitting them.

Hampered by arm trouble and illness in 1884, he gave up the ace role to Charlie Buffinton. In March 1886 Boston sold him and catcher Mert Hackett to the new Kansas City Cowboys. The highlight of that year was a postseason exhibition against his brother Charlie, playing second for Rochester.
Sold to Washington in 1887, he went 24-21 for a seventh-place team that went 22-55 in its other games.
