Early in 1888 a line drive by Pittsburgh's Bill Kuehne hit him hard in the right chest. His family later traced his fatal illness to it, though reports of consumption had circulated before.

Put in salary Class B, he resented Washington citing his illness to pay him less: "Last year I was unfortunately ill, and they want to bring this up against me." He held out, was traded to Indianapolis for Egyptian Healy, released in June 1889, and finished in the minors. With the 1890 Athletics he gave up 23 hits to St. Louis, and was released days later.
p: His marriage to Lillian Haddock brought him into her brothers' Boston grain business, Whitney & Haddock, so he didn't depend on baseball for a living.
Released in 1890, he was so low that friends feared for him: "It breaks him up that he cannot pitch as he could in days gone by."
He went home to Binghamton and died there of tuberculosis in May 1891, at 33.
The youngest of three children of a farmer, he grew up in Binghamton. He and Lillian had a daughter, Mollie.
He died at his father's home.

c: When Chicago first saw him warming up in Bloomington, the White Stockings laughed at the way he turned to face second base before pitching. Al Spalding said the smiles faded as he sent one batter after another back to the bench.

He hurt his shoulder with Buffalo in 1880 and went back to the slaughterhouse, sure his career was over. His friend Bill Hunter answered a Providence telegram pretending to be Radbourn, borrowed money from his father, and sent him to Hot Springs to get in shape.
In an 18-inning game in 1882 the score was 0-0 after 17½ innings. Radbourn, playing right field that day, hit the first walk-off home run in a 1-0 game in major-league history.
In 1884 he won 60 games (59 by some counts), long considered the greatest of all pitching feats.
He won the pitching Triple Crown that year, then pitched every inning of the World Series as Providence swept the Metropolitans.

Ted Sullivan said he "was continually inventing a new delivery." He called his own pitches, trained with an iron ball, and taught fellow Bloomington native Clark Griffith to cut a ball for a better grip on his sinker.
In 1891 Cincinnati signed him for $5,000 and a promise that he wouldn't have to pitch on Sundays.

A game-fixing scandal hit the Bloomington Reds in 1876. Radbourn admitted drinking heavily the night before and talking with two gamblers. Butchers said he told them the gamblers offered him $25 to throw the game; he didn't deny saying he'd take it, but said he was drunk. His brother Henry backed his story.
He jumped to St. Louis of the American Association, then re-signed with Providence when the National League threatened to blacklist jumpers, for about $2,000, half what he'd been promised.

In 1884 he grew jealous of fellow pitcher Sweeney's success, and their tension broke into violence in the clubhouse. Blamed for starting it, he was suspended without pay after a July 16 game in which he was accused of losing on purpose by lobbing pitches. Six days later a drunk Sweeney walked out mid-game, leaving Providence with eight players.
The Providence Journal called him "careless and indifferent" that July, and he seemed to be drinking more heavily than usual.
The 1884 record books all agree on his 678⅔ innings; only the count of wins is disputed, because early scorers had more latitude.
He jumped to the Players' League's Boston club in 1890 and got his 300th win with Cincinnati in 1891.
p: As a teenager he strengthened his arm throwing a ball against the barn, worked as a butcher alongside his father, and worked as a railroad brakeman.
A crack rifle shot, he once issued an open $1,000 challenge to all comers, and kept a kennel of thoroughbred pointers for hunting.

He lived for years with Carrie Stanhope, whom he met in Providence, and her son. They married quietly in 1895. After his death his family contested her claim to his estate, unaware that they had married.
In April 1894 a friend accidentally shot him in the face while hunting. He lost his left eye, lived mostly as a recluse afterward, and died in 1897 at 42.
He may be the namesake of the "charley horse," though the term may simply come from "Charley" being a common name for horses.
His parents came from Bristol, England; his father was a butcher. One of eight children, he was called Charles Jr. as a boy.
After baseball he opened a successful billiard parlor and saloon in Bloomington.

c: He started as a maskless catcher until a foul tip over the eye sent him looking for another position. New Bedford pounded him in his first try at pitching, but he beat them the next two times.
Tim Murnane said his drop "fell into the hands of his catcher like a snowflake." In 1884 he went 48-16 with 407 strikeouts, overshadowed by Old Hoss Radbourn's 60 wins.
He sat on the executive council of the players' Brotherhood. Before the 1887 season Boston sold him to the Phillies for $500.
When the Players' League began in 1890 he took over as manager of its Philadelphia club and spread the pitching among three men instead of carrying it himself.
Pitching for the American Association's Boston Reds in 1891, he led the league with a 29-9 record.
Baltimore cut his pay by 37.5 percent in 1892. He refused, was released, and never pitched in the majors again, at 31.
He turned pro with Al Reach's independent Philadelphia club in 1881, played four games in the outfield, and was released. Boston signed him and used him mostly on its reserve team.
Arm trouble dropped him to 7-10 in 1886.
He was reportedly a modest investor in the Players' League Philadelphia club. Phillies co-owner John Rogers argued that an automatic rollover clause still bound him, but the argument failed.
When the American Association folded, its rosters were parceled out, and he was assigned to a weak, shakily financed Baltimore club.
p: As a teenager he clerked in a Fall River grocery store. He married Alice Thornley, an English-born mill worker.
After baseball he worked for a family-connected coal company in Fall River, and was rumored to pitch for local amateur teams under the name Brown.
He died suddenly in 1907, at 46, the day before a planned gallstone operation. The county medical examiner was his old catcher Tom Gunning: "He had the greatest drop ball I ever saw."
He was the older of two sons of a teamster turned businessman, both parents from Rhode Island. He and Alice had three children, Phebe, Charles and Alton.
He invested in coal and cotton after baseball.
He died of heart disease at 46.

c: Pitching for his Army post in San Antonio, he caught a Cardinals scout's eye. His sergeant told the scout he was "the dizziest kid I ever had in my outfit," and the name stuck. His father helped him raise the $100 to buy his way out of the Army.
He won his debut on the last weekend of 1930, a complete game in spikes borrowed from Burleigh Grimes, who said Dean was "as unconcerned as if he was tossing rocks at a mud turtle."
He was the last National League pitcher to win 30 games in a season, in 1934.

Before Game 7 of the 1934 World Series he told Hank Greenberg, "Old Diz is goin' to pitch, and he's goin' to pin your ears back." He shut out the Tigers 11-0; he and his brother Paul each won two games in the Series.
In the 1937 All-Star Game an Earl Averill liner broke his toe. He came back too soon, couldn't pivot, threw with his arm alone, and hurt it. He was never the same.

As a broadcaster he mangled English, but Mel Allen said it was deliberate: once Dean said "slid" correctly by mistake and corrected it to "slud." In 1947, after saying on the air he could outpitch the Browns' staff, he pitched four shutout innings for them at 37.

His father vouched that he was 18 so he could join the Army, where he started with menial jobs in a Quartermaster wagon company. His father helped raise the money to get him out, and he took a job reading gas meters for San Antonio Public Service, really to pitch on its team, where a Cardinals scout signed him.
By another story the nickname came from a White Sox manager yelling, "Knock that dizzy kid out the box!"
As a young Cardinal he ran up bills and charged them to the club, broke team rules, and once left the team claiming his contract was invalid because he'd been underage when he signed it.

Sent in as a pinch runner in Game 4 of the 1934 World Series, he was hit in the head by a throw and knocked unconscious; X-rays "revealed no lasting injury." Told in 1937 that his toe was fractured: "Fractured, hell, the damn thing's broken!"
Chicago got him in April 1938 for three players and $185,000. He pitched gamely in Game 2 of that World Series before losing to the Yankees, "Ol' Diz's Last Stand."

Broadcasting for the Browns, he said on the air, "I can pitch better than nine out of the ten guys on this staff!" The pitchers' wives complained, and the club let him pitch the last game. At 37 he threw four scoreless innings and singled.
p: His mother died of tuberculosis when he was seven, and the family sharecropped across the South. He took the name Jerome Herman, likely after a childhood friend who died, to comfort the boy's mother.
Served calves' brains by mistake in a Houston diner, he protested, "I didn't order no brains." His manager: "Be quiet, she knows what you need."
His wife, Pat, took over his wild spending, serving as his business manager, banker and bookkeeper. They were married 43 years.
At his 1953 Hall of Fame induction he said, "The Good Lord was good to me. He gave me a strong body, a good right arm and a weak mind."
His two oldest siblings died in infancy. After his mother died his father married a widow, Cora Parham, whose three children doubled the household.
He married Patricia Nash of Bond, Mississippi, in June 1931. They had no children.

In retirement in Bond he was investigated in an interstate gambling ring; 1970 indictments named him and his nephew Paul as co-conspirators but not defendants. He died of a heart attack in Reno in 1974, at 64. Pat willed their home, Deanash, to the Mississippi Baptist Convention for foster homes.

c: As a boy he lost most of his right index finger in farm machinery, then broke his other fingers falling while chasing a rabbit. The mangled hand gave his pitches a bewildering movement.

He was called "Miner" for his teenage years in the coal mines. Playing third base for Coxville in 1898, he filled in as pitcher and dominated. In 1901, 600 Terre Haute fans threatened a boycott unless he made the team.
His 1.04 ERA in 1906 is the third-best single season in baseball history.

After death threats, he came in from the bullpen in the first inning of the October 8, 1908, playoff at the Polo Grounds and beat the Giants for the pennant: "I was about as good that day as I ever was in my life." Afterward the Cubs left the park under police escort.

After losing Christy Mathewson's 1905 no-hitter, he beat Mathewson nine straight times. Their last meeting, on September 4, 1916, was both men's final big-league game; Brown finished 12-11 against him.
At 51, in a 1928 exhibition against the House of David, he pitched three innings and struck out all nine batters.
He learned to pitch by throwing rocks at knot-holes in the barn wall. His grip gave the ball unusual spin.
His great-nephew: "It didn't only curve, it curved and dropped at the same time."
After the 1903 season he and catcher Jack O'Neill were traded to the Cubs.

In the 1906 World Series he lost Game 6 to the White Sox, 8-3. After the 1908 playoff, a spectator hit Frank Chance in the throat so hard he couldn't speak for days, and the Cubs needed a police paddy wagon to escape.
He went 5-4 in World Series games and beat Ty Cobb's Tigers every time he faced them. The last game of the 1908 Series still has the lowest attendance of any World Series game.
After a knee injury in 1912 a doctor told him another one could cost him the use of his leg. He played on with Cincinnati, then jumped to the Federal League the same day as Joe Tinker.
Later he pitched for Tinker's Columbus Senators and filled in as manager when Tinker was out scouting.
p: Born in 1876, he got "Centennial" as a third given name. Mordecai came from an uncle and Peter from his father.
From 1920 to 1945 he ran a filling station in Terre Haute that doubled as a town gathering place and an unofficial museum.
He signed off his instruction book How to Pitch Curves: "Mordecai Brown's hand is reaching out to you in the distance and he is wishing you—good luck."
F. Scott Fitzgerald mentions "Three-finger Brown" in This Side of Paradise.
He married Sarah in Rosedale, Indiana, in December 1903, and they were married 45 years.
He died of diabetic complications in 1948, and was elected to the Hall of Fame the next year.
In 1994 his relatives, led by great-nephews Joe and Fred Massey, put up a granite marker at his Nyesville birthplace.

c: At Augusta in 1905 he fought his young teammate Ty Cobb, who had taken popcorn out to center field as a joke and made an error that cost Cicotte a shutout.

He estimated that 75 percent of his pitches were knuckleballs. He also threw a "sailor," a spitter, an emery ball, and a shine ball, rubbed on talcum powder hidden in his trouser pocket. "Perhaps no pitcher in the world has such a varied assortment of wares," The Sporting News wrote.
Boston owner John I. Taylor suspended him so often that "it was like having no job." After he was sold to the White Sox in 1912, his control came around.
In 1917 he led the AL in wins, ERA and innings, threw a no-hitter, and helped Chicago win the World Series. Grantland Rice called him "the most feared pitcher of the series."

He agreed to throw the 1919 World Series for $10,000, and found the money under his pillow before the team left for Cincinnati. His first pitch of the Series hit Morrie Rath in the back, the signal to the gamblers that the fix was on.
In September 1920 he confessed to a grand jury: "I didn't care whether I got shot out there the next minute." He was acquitted in court but banned from baseball for life.
Boston bought him for $2,500 after 1907. In 1911 owner John I. Taylor tried to waive him, then pulled back when another team put in a claim.
After his 1917 season Comiskey gave him $5,000 plus a $2,000 bonus, one of the best pitcher contracts in the game. In 1918 he wrenched his ankle in May and limped to 19 losses.
His 1919 salary was $6,000, with a $10,000 bonus for winning 30 games. Legend has it Comiskey had Kid Gleason bench him for five games late in the season to deny him the chance.
Eight Men Out portrays him resisting Chick Gandil's repeated approaches until days before the Series, when it was clear Comiskey would never pay him even part of the bonus.

In Game 4 he made two errors, including an inexplicable cutoff of an outfield throw; Gleason said there "wasn't any occasion for Cicotte to intercept that throw." Many conspirators hadn't been paid, so they decided to win Game 7, and Cicotte did.

He went 21-10 in 1920. That September gambler Billy Maharg named him as the man who started the plot. The next day Cicotte confessed to White Sox counsel Alfred Austrian, implicating seven teammates, then told the grand jury.
p: His father died when he was a teenager, and he left school to work as a boxmaker while his mother supported the family as a dressmaker.

By 1920 he headed a household of 12: his wife, Rose, their three children, her parents, his brother and sister-in-law, and another brother-in-law's family. He'd taken a $4,000 mortgage on a Michigan farm to house them.
After baseball he was a game warden and worked at Ford until 1944, then raised strawberries near Farmington, Michigan. "I admit I did wrong, but I've paid for it the past 45 years."
To house his family of 12 he took out a $4,000 mortgage on a Michigan farm.
His wife was Rose Ellen Freer; they had two daughters, Rose and Virginia, and a son, Edward Jr.
His brother Alva's grandson, Al Cicotte, pitched in the majors from 1957 to 1962.
After the ban he managed a service station in Livonia. He died at Henry Ford Hospital in 1969. David Strathairn played him in the 1988 film Eight Men Out.

c: Carlos Royer was scouting another pitcher at a 1907 provincial tournament when he spotted "a scrawny black kid playing shortstop" for Remedios who threw a mean fastball. Almendares signed him, and he went 9-0 in his first winter.

On November 13, 1908, he carried a no-hitter into the ninth against the touring Cincinnati Reds, broken up by Miller Huggins's slow roller. He threw 25 straight scoreless innings against the Reds that fall, and his streak reached 45 innings.
The wins over big-leaguers during the American occupation made him a national hero, and a crude early nickname was replaced by El Diamante Negro, "The Black Diamond."
Box scores compiled by researcher Gary Ashwill show him 9-11 against big-league teams in Havana from 1908 to 1913, facing pitchers like Christy Mathewson, Chief Bender and Eddie Plank.
He was in the first class of the Cuban Baseball Hall of Fame in 1939 and was elected to Cooperstown in 2006.

Barnstorming the States with the Cuban Stars in summer 1908, he threw at least five shutouts. His streak of scoreless innings against the touring big-leaguers reached 45 before the Habana Reds broke it. With the Cuban Stars in 1909 he's estimated to have gone 44-2.
One of his losses came in Chicago, 1–0 to Rube Foster's Leland Giants, on an unearned run after a dropped fly.
After a 10-0 winter for Almendares, his arm gave out late in 1914 and he gradually stopped pitching.
A probably apocryphal story says he killed a teammate with a fastball to the chest in batting practice.
He pitched for the 1923-24 Santa Clara Leopards, considered the most dominant team in Cuban baseball history, alongside Oscar Charleston, Alejandro Oms and Dobie Moore.
In the first Negro World Series, in 1924, he recovered some of his old magic, throwing a shutout and winning another game in relief.
He was elected to Cooperstown in 2006 by a one-time special committee on African-American baseball.
p: Born in Cárdenas, he apprenticed as a carpenter and played guitar and clarinet. "De la Caridad" in his name entrusted him to the Virgen de la Caridad del Cobre, Cuba's patron saint.

He died in 1928, in obscurity and apparent poverty, probably of tuberculosis. He had been too ill to attend a ceremony the Cuban League planned to honor him. He has no individual tombstone; his name is inscribed on a ballplayers' monument in Havana's Colón Cemetery.

c: As a semipro with the San Antonio Bronchos he went 28-4 in his first season, 1905. He introduced himself to Rube Foster in 1910 as "Cyclone." After he joined the Homestead Grays, owner Cum Posey and the Pittsburgh Courier renamed him "Smokey Joe," after the Smoky City.

Against white major-league teams he was 19-8 by one count, with 28 complete games in 28 starts. After Williams beat his Phillies in 1913, Grover Cleveland Alexander told him, "Joe, you are the equal of any great pitcher I have faced and superior to most."
In his first game for the Lincoln Giants, on May 12, 1912, he threw a no-hitter with 16 strikeouts.
Teams carried only 10 to 12 men, so he played the outfield when he wasn't pitching: "I was awful as a hitter when I started, but I finished with a lifetime batting average of .345."

Under the Kansas City Monarchs' portable lights on August 2, 1930, he struck out 27 in a 13-inning one-hit 1-0 win over Chet Brewer. The Courier said both pitchers were throwing emery balls; Williams used "everything but a blacksmith's file."

Tending bar in Harlem in 1934, he recommended a young Buck Leonard to Cum Posey, who sent Leonard a bus ticket and $5. In 1952 the Pittsburgh Courier's poll named Williams the greatest pitcher in Negro league history, one vote ahead of Satchel Paige.
He tried Birmingham in 1909 but got homesick and went back to the Bronchos. In California the Los Angeles Times reported he struck out 19 Doyles at Vernon, breaking "all Coast records."
In 1914 he went 41-3 for the Lincoln Giants, and that October he dueled Rube Marquard and the New York Giants to a 1-1 tie, striking out 12.
After the Lincolns finished fifth in the Eastern Colored League's first season, they released him in spring 1924. He pitched a season for the Brooklyn Royal Giants, then joined the Homestead Grays.
In the 1930 game against Chet Brewer, the Courier said both gave "a remarkable exhibition of emery ball pitching" and that Williams used "everything but a blacksmith's file."

In 1932 the Grays traded him to the Detroit Wolves, where Cum Posey had a conflict of interest. That fall he pitched for the Pittsburgh Crawfords as they beat Casey Stengel's Major League All-Stars five games to two.
p: His grandfather Calvin Williams was born into slavery, served in the Union Army, and traded his horse for the land in Seguin, Texas, where Joe grew up.
As a boy, "someone gave me a baseball. I carried it in my pocket and slept with it under my pillow. I always wanted to pitch."
In Florida's winter Hotel League, players also worked as busboys, porters and waiters at the white-only resorts. Williams played and managed there from 1914 to 1931.

After integration he said, "There were many Negro players just as good as them, they just never had the chance. The important thing is that the long fight is over. I praise the Lord I've lived to see the day."
His mother, Lettie, was a laundress who built the family home. His grandfather Calvin married a former slave, Fanny Elam, after reaching Seguin.
In 1922 he married Beatrice, a showgirl, and they stayed together until his death. "He was very quiet, didn't say much, unless you got him on baseball."
He tended bar until he died of a heart ailment, and was buried in a grave shared with his wife's mother and stepfather.

c: He came up as an infielder with his hometown Philadelphia White Stockings in 1873 and turned to pitching with Louisville in 1876.
His best pitch was a "drop," now called a sinker, which he may have been the first to throw. In 1877 he threw every pitch of Louisville's 61 games, the only pitcher ever to do so.

Louisville led the 1877 pennant race by four games in mid-August, then collapsed on a road trip full of bonehead plays, while some Grays turned up around town in new jewelry. Devlin and George Hall confessed to throwing games.

The National League banned him, Hall, Al Nichols and Bill Craver for life. Legend says Devlin begged William Hulbert on his knees; Hulbert gave him $50 and said, "Damn you, you have thrown a game, you are dishonest, and this National League will not stand for it!"

Courier-Journal writer John Haldeman, son of the Grays' president, was first to accuse the team publicly. Vice president Charles Chase, who had ignored telegrams warning that gamblers were betting against the Grays, investigated; the telegrams showed Nichols coordinating with New York gamblers.
Shortstop Bill Craver, the only player to refuse to hand over his telegrams, was presumed guilty and banned too, though no proof of gambling against him was ever found.
p: He appealed for reinstatement every year for the rest of his life, and even wrote to Harry Wright for help, but never got an answer.
He became a police officer in Philadelphia and died poor of tuberculosis in 1883, survived by his wife and son.

c: At Carlisle Indian School his first real coach was Pop Warner. A Connie Mack scout found him pitching for a Harrisburg semipro team, and at 19 he won his debut in relief against Cy Young.
On a single day near the end of the 1905 pennant race he won both games of a doubleheader against Washington, pitching 15 innings and going 5-for-6 with seven RBIs.
His sharp curve was a forerunner of the slider, and he may have invented it. On May 12, 1910, he no-hit Cleveland, facing the minimum 27 batters.

In the 1911 World Series he threw three complete games, tying a record, and beat the Giants twice. Ty Cobb called one of his plays in that Series "the greatest bit of brainwork I ever saw in a ballgame."
Connie Mack: "If I had all the men I've ever handled, and there was one game I wanted to win above all others, Albert would be my man."

He was rarely written about without demeaning references to his race. "I do not want my name to be presented to the public as an Indian, but as a pitcher," he said in 1905, and he signed his autographs "Charles."
When bench jockeys made war whoops after he'd pitched a good inning, he might yell back, "Foreigners! Foreigners!"

The family was so poor on the White Earth reservation that as a young boy he reportedly worked as a farmhand for a dollar a week. Carlisle, run by Richard Henry Pratt, strictly drove its pupils to assimilate.
He battled health problems for years, later drank heavily, and never pitched more than 270 innings in a season.
In 1912 he went nearly 40 games without a start and was suspended in September for alcohol abuse. His next contract required him to stay sober to earn his full salary.

His 1914 World Series start was the only Series game he failed to finish, after nine straight complete games. When the Federal League's Baltimore Terrapins offered him a big raise, Mack knew he couldn't match it and released him.
He went 4-16 for the last-place Terrapins and was released. With the Phillies in 1917 he went 8-2 with a 1.67 ERA and was released anyway. Managing Richmond in 1919, he went 29-2 on the mound.
p: His mother was Ojibwe and his father a German-American homesteader. At seven he was sent to a boarding school for Indian children near Philadelphia. Back home at 12, he and his brother ran away to work on another farm, where a Carlisle teacher recruited them.
He was a top trap shooter, an excellent golfer, a billiards player, and a painter of oil landscapes. Grantland Rice quoted him: "Tension is the greatest curse in sport. I've never had any tension."
Late in life he tended a garden in Haddon Heights, New Jersey, nearly every day, though he lived 12 miles away. As the A's pitching coach he helped Bobby Shantz win the 1952 MVP.
He was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1953, the first Minnesota-born player inducted, and died a few weeks before the ceremony.
As a child he was named Mandowescence, perhaps "Little Spirit Animal."
His mother had at least 11 children; he was the fourth.

He worked in sporting goods at Wanamaker's and opened Bender Sporting Goods in 1914. In February 1917 he was charged with manslaughter when a car he owned hit and killed a boy in Philadelphia and the driver sped off.
His brother John was suspended from the minors for three years after stabbing his manager, Win Clark, several times in a 1908 fight. John died at a restaurant in 1911.

He hid a cancer while coaching. Hospitalized in 1954, he sent his wife Marie to Shibe Park for every home game to report on the pitching. Coach Bing Miller brought him ice cream nearly every day. He died of prostate cancer that May.

c: At 14, throwing clamshells on a Brooklyn beach with friends, he watched them curve and thought "it would be a good joke on the boys if I could make a baseball curve the same way." It took him four years.
In 1867, against Harvard, he finally saw the ball curve: "A surge of joy flooded over me that I shall never forget. I wanted to tell everybody." For years he was the only pitcher who could throw it.
He was so dominant as a teenager that people called him "Candy," Civil War slang for the best of anything. He never weighed more than 120 pounds and had small hands.
Henry Chadwick named him the outstanding player in the country in 1871. On June 15, 1874, he struck out six Chicago batters in a row.

At Hartford in 1875 he taught the curve to young Tommy Bond, who soon replaced him as the team's top pitcher. On September 9, 1876, he won both games of the first scheduled doubleheader in National League history.
In 1877 he was elected the first president of the International Association while still pitching.

Before 1872 he signed with three National Association clubs; the Association awarded him to the New York Mutuals, making him a pro for the first time. In 1873 he shared Baltimore's pitching with Asa Brainard.
In late June 1877 he left the Live Oaks of Lynn for the National League's Cincinnati Red Stockings, while staying on as International Association president.
He also invented a railway coupling device, patented in 1877.
p: His family was well off, and he went to boarding school in Fulton, New York.
After baseball he ran a paint and wallpaper business in Athol, Massachusetts, for more than 30 years.
For decades he defended his claim to the curveball in letters and articles against rivals like Fred Goldsmith. His 1908 Baseball Magazine piece, "How I Pitched the First Curve," helped settle it.
He was the second of 12 children of a dry goods merchant, and grew up in Brooklyn.
He married Mary Augusta Roberts in 1870, and they raised five children. Widowed, at 72 he moved to Toledo to live with his son Arthur, and died there in 1924.

c: In 1867, pitching for Rockford's Forest Citys, he beat the touring Washington Nationals 29-23, after they had routed the Chicago Excelsiors 49-4. In 1870 he beat the famous Cincinnati Red Stockings.

He led the National Association in wins all five years of its existence, and his win total went up every year, topped by 54-5 with 23 straight wins in 1875. He won 91 percent of Boston's games in that league.
In 1874 Harry Wright sent him to England to organize the first overseas baseball tour. The Americans also played seven cricket matches against top British sides and lost none.

He disapproved of drinking and gambling, and William Hulbert lured him to Chicago, where he won 47 games and the pennant as captain-manager in the National League's first season. He was done as a player at 27.
He set a trend by wearing a glove. He holds the career records for the highest winning percentage (.794) and the fewest home runs allowed per nine innings.

As White Stockings president he started spring training in Hot Springs in 1886, and in 1888-89 led a world tour that played by the pyramids and before the king of Italy. Later he promoted the myth that Abner Doubleday invented baseball.
He threw 617 innings in 1874. He was also a good opposite-field hitter and a savvy fielder who helped perfect the dropped-popup double play.

Hulbert signed him in complete secrecy during the 1875 season, playing on his wish to return to the Midwest and challenging his integrity. Players were free agents every year, and neither wanted Boston or its fans to know.

He became White Stockings secretary after he stopped playing, and president when Hulbert died in 1882. Railing against drinking, he sold Mike Kelly to Boston for $10,000 and got rid of Jim McCormick and George Gore.
His books under the Spalding Athletic Library name ran from 1892 to 1941. The store chain had 14 locations by 1901.

"Our good old American game of baseball must have an American Dad," he wrote just before the Cooperstown commission issued its findings. In 1912 he wrote that baseball was "too strenuous for womankind," who could cheer from the grandstand.
p: His father died when he was eight. Sent ahead to live with an aunt in Rockford, he reportedly took up baseball to fight loneliness.
In February 1876 he and his brother Walter opened a sporting-goods store on Randolph Street in Chicago. It grew into stores across the country, and he supplied the league's balls, bats and uniforms.
Married to Josie Keith, he had a son with the widow Elizabeth Churchill and married her after Josie's death. She was a theosophist, and they moved to the Point Loma community near San Diego.
He ran for the U.S. Senate from California in 1910 and was the popular choice, but the legislature picked John D. Works. His nephew, also Albert Spalding, became a world-class violinist.

He and Elizabeth Churchill had been secret lovers for some time, and their son was born Spalding Brown Spalding, later renamed Albert Goodwill Jr. After they married Spalding acknowledged him and adopted her other son, Durand Churchill. He left an estate of $600,000 to his wife and three sons.

In San Diego he joined other businessmen to buy the original Presidio site, developed it as a historic park and gave it to the city, and was second vice president of the 1915 Panama–California Exposition.
He died of a stroke in San Diego in September 1915, a week after turning 65.

c: His unorthodox delivery left him off balance with his back to the plate, which made it hard for him to field bunts.
As a Philadelphia rookie in 1888 he led the NL in shutouts. On September 18 he lost a perfect game with one out in the ninth when the opposing pitcher, Gus Krock, singled. He still won 6-0.
He jumped to the Players' League in 1890 and went 19-18.
On August 22, 1892, for Louisville, he no-hit Baltimore 6-2, the first NL no-hitter in which the losing team still scored.
p: He was born in Catharpin, Virginia, and was buried there in the Sudley United Methodist Church cemetery.

c: Pitching for the Austin Black Senators, he beat the touring Monroe Monarchs, who blamed Austin's big park. The next Sunday he beat them 4-2 in their small park, and Monroe signed him. He said he went 31-0 for them in 1932.

In 1935 he stayed on with Bismarck, North Dakota, for $150, in a rotation behind Satchel Paige, as the integrated team won the first national semipro tournament. Smith mostly played right field and batted cleanup.
Monarchs owner J.L. Wilkinson saw him pitch for Bismarck and signed him in 1936. "I didn't really learn how to pitch until I came to the Monarchs," he said, crediting Bullet Rogan and Andy Cooper.
His first game in Kansas City was a 4-0 perfect game against the Chicago American Giants. Mexican fans named his curveball El Diablo.
He played in seven straight East-West All-Star Games, and started the 1942 game when Paige showed up late. Teammate Lefty Bryant: "Hilton was the best pitcher we had, including Satchel."

He said he urged Wilkinson to sign Jackie Robinson after facing him in 1942. In 1946 Roy Campanella asked him about joining the Dodgers, but at 39 he worried about the minors and a pay cut: "Had I been three or four years younger, I probably would have been the first Negro signed."

Bismarck's owner, Churchill, was a local auto dealer who worked with booking agent Abe Saperstein to bring in Negro league talent. In the 1936 tournament, with Paige gone, Smith won four games, but Bismarck lost the semifinal 6-2 to the Cementers.
Bullet Rogan and Andy Cooper helped polish him in Kansas City. He opened 1937 with a no-hitter and went 11-4.
In 1946 exhibitions he threw two complete games against Bob Feller, winning 3-2 and losing 6-3: "I broke even with them."
An arm injury in the 1940s sent him to first base and the outfield for two years. In October 1944 he and several teammates formed the Kansas City Royals in the California Winter League.
On living in Paige's shadow: "I just took my baseball serious; I just went out there to do a job." His son said he "did not complain one way or another."
p: He put his age back five years to help his career, his son said, because as the oldest of six he'd stayed home to help raise his siblings. He made the dean's list at Prairie View.
After baseball he was a supervisor at Armco Steel in Kansas City. He coached young players, including future Royals star Frank White: "He not only taught me the game, he got you to love the game."
He was scouting for the Cubs alongside Buck O'Neil when he died in 1983. His hometown of Giddings, Texas, named a ballfield for him.
In Monroe he met and married Louise Smith in 1934. They had two sons, Hillton, born in 1935, and DeMorris, in 1938.
After baseball he worked as a schoolteacher before becoming a steel-plant foreman.

c: As a rookie with the 1887 Browns he won 32 games. In 1888 he led both major leagues with 45 wins, 64 complete games and 584⅔ innings, with a 1.63 ERA.

He was credited as one of the first pitchers with a crossfire delivery, starting at one corner of the pitcher's box and stepping across. "My pitching stock consisted mainly of speed. You simply had to be a Colossus or you couldn't stand the gaff."
In 1889 owner Chris von der Ahe accused him and Arlie Latham of conspiring with gamblers to throw games to Brooklyn. King said he felt like punching his owner.
With the 1892 Giants he left the club without warning for three weeks in a salary dispute. He, Amos Rusie and Ed Crane still started all but one of the Giants' games.
Rather than take a 70 percent pay cut in 1894, he walked away from the game. He came back with Washington in 1896 and won his first four starts until a line drive broke his pitching arm.

He debuted late in 1886 with the Kansas City Cowboys, going 1-3. When the Cowboys folded, Browns official George Munson asked The Sporting News for the best unsigned pitcher, and passed King's name to Chris von der Ahe.
He was a career .198 hitter. One of his one-hitters was spoiled in the ninth when outfielders Tip O'Neill and Harry Lyons "stood and looked at each other while the ball dropped."

In 1889 he held out until a week before the season. His arm went lame, he reportedly had malaria, and he once gave up 11 earned runs in an inning of relief. The Browns blew a first-place lead late in the year, and after one riot Browns players were roughed up leaving the park.
He was one of the first sidearm pitchers. In the 1890 Players' League he won 30 games and another ERA title for Chicago.

In March 1891 his old teammate Mark Baldwin was arrested in St. Louis for tampering with King's contract on Pittsburgh's behalf. King finally signed with Pittsburgh for $5,000, the largest contract of his career.
p: Born Charles Koenig, he took the English version of his German surname. With his silvery hair and red complexion, one writer said that in the sun he looked like a silverside fish.
His father was a bricklayer who became a contractor. King learned the trade, and a steady income as a St. Louis contractor let him walk away from bad contracts.
After retiring he said he never attended another major-league game.
His parents were German immigrants, and he was the third of eight children. He married Della Loring around 1890, and they raised four children, Charles Jr., Helen, Oliver and Ethel.

c: At 22, in 1910, he became the youngest pitcher ever to start the Yankees' opener. He and Joe Wood pitched shutout ball until darkness ended it, a 4-4 tie after 14 innings.

On May 2, 1917, he and Cincinnati's Fred Toney both threw nine no-hit innings. In the 10th Vaughn gave up two hits, and Jim Thorpe's slow roller drove in the only run. Christy Mathewson called it the greatest pitching performance he'd ever seen.

In 1918 he won the pitching Triple Crown. On June 29 he shut out Cincinnati, the same day his only child was born. In the World Series he had a 1.00 ERA in three complete games and went 1-2, losing 1-0 to Babe Ruth and 2-1 to Carl Mays.
Grover Cleveland Alexander said Vaughn liked to throw a batter the pitch he hit best "just to show him that he couldn't hit it."

After Pancho Snyder hit a grand slam off him on July 9, 1921, he left the team. When he signed with a semipro team in Beloit, Commissioner Landis suspended him, and he never pitched in the majors again.
With 178 big-league wins and 223 more in the minors and semipro ball, which he pitched until 1937, at 49, he is one of the few pitchers credited with 400 wins.

In 1911 he started the Highlanders' opener again, at Shibe Park against the champion Athletics and Chief Bender. On June 26, 1912, he was sold to Washington, and later to Kansas City of the American Association.
In 1917 he went 23-13 with a 2.01 ERA and a career-high 195 strikeouts. The 1918 season was cut to 140 games and ended September 2 under the government's "Fight or Work" order.

Under manager Johnny Evers in 1921 the Cubs went 41-55. Vaughn, a quiet professional, seems to have found Evers particularly annoying, and left the team in late June, officially with a sore arm. Evers suspended him for failing to keep in shape.

Landis ruled that by signing with the Beloit Fairies, an "outlaw team which harbors ineligible players," Vaughn had ignored his Cubs contract. The Tribune: "The affair has been bungled." He later considered a comeback with the Cubs, but it never happened.
p: His father was a stonemason in Weatherford, Texas, and Jim was one of eight children.
At 6-foot-4 and well over 200 pounds, with a lumbering, side-to-side walk, he was given the nickname "Hippo." What he thought of it isn't known.
After baseball he worked as an assembler for a refrigeration products company in Chicago.
He married Edna Coburn DeBold in February 1916.

In October 1921 his wife called the Chicago police from Kenosha to say he'd been missing for days and that their three-year-old, "Little Hippo," was sick and crying for him. She sued for divorce, and while they were at odds her father stabbed Vaughn in a quarrel in a Kenosha saloon.
He died in Chicago in 1966 at 78.

c: The winter before the first season, catcher Nat Hicks went to Baltimore to work with him, probably when he got control of his curveball. Candy Cummings said Mathews never claimed to have invented the curve, and always said he learned it from Cummings.
On June 18, 1874, in a gale, he two-hit Chicago as the Mutuals won 38-1; Chicago made 21 errors.

He threw his first pitch over the batter's head on purpose and sometimes hid the ball under his arm and turned his back to the batter. James Hart: "He had the most remarkable memory for a batter's weaknesses of any pitcher who ever lived."
In July 1876 he handed the league a telegram from a gambler. The league ran a sting and published the telegrams to discourage future fixes.
He won 297 games, the most of any pitcher not in the Hall of Fame, and is the only pitcher to win 50 games in each of three major leagues.
Offered an American Association umpiring job for $1,200, less than any other umpire made, he turned it down, saying it would drag down every umpire's pay.
He was known for "careless habits," usually taken to mean drinking and poor conditioning. With Baltimore, his regular catcher, Bill Lennon, was released for excessive drinking.

The Chicago Tribune once called a Mutuals loss "palpable and unblushing fraud," saying the odds had shifted to Chicago before the game. Mathews, leading 4-2, left after the fifth with a lingering groin injury, and the Tribune believed he did it to appease gamblers. Researcher Daniel Ginsburg found the accusations against him contradictory.
He said he learned the curve by watching Candy Cummings. After the spitball became popular, Hank O'Day and others said Mathews had thrown it long before.
Worcester expelled him for drunkenness one July; he soon returned, and the team signed a temperance pledge.
He was on the umpiring staff of the Players' League in 1890 and returned to the American Association in 1891.
p: He learned to play on the Belair Market lots in Baltimore, and was called the best Baltimore-born player before Babe Ruth.
As his arm failed he coached pitchers privately and at the University of Pennsylvania, and may have been the first professional pitching coach.
Broke and sick by the late 1890s, he no longer recognized old friends. Baseball people across the country took up a collection for his care, and he died at home in Baltimore in 1898.
He was the only son of Irish immigrants John and Mary Mathews.
He died in Baltimore in 1898, at 46, of paresis caused by syphilis.

c: At Cal he was a football star, playing guard, fullback and punter and serving as captain, and pitched for the baseball team. He turned down the PCL to stay in school before signing with Tacoma in 1904, to his father's great disappointment.

Frank Chance, who had played with him in California, thought Cincinnati's Ned Hanlon was overworking him. After the Cubs traded for him in 1906 he went 12-3 the rest of the year. The deal was long considered the Reds' worst until they traded Frank Robinson.
He predicted that a 1908 rule banning pitchers from soiling the ball would send hitting averages soaring. They fell to the lowest level in league history; his ERA was about the only one that rose.
He held Ty Cobb to .125 in the 1907 and 1908 World Series, and won both his starts in 1908, including the 2-0 clincher. He finished 3-1 with a 1.58 ERA in four World Series.
Johnny Evers said his curve, thrown with a wide overhand swing and a sharp jerk at the finish, "actually darts downward." His 2.23 career ERA ranks eighth in major-league history.

He had sore-arm trouble even in college. To his father's great disappointment he left Cal in 1904 to sign with Tacoma for $300 a month, and went 32-25 as Tacoma won the PCL pennant. Cincinnati outbid the Cubs for him.
The Reds traded him to the Cubs in June 1906 for Bob Wicker. Many considered it the worst deal in Reds history until they traded Frank Robinson in 1966.
In one 1908 Series game he struck out 10, still a Cubs World Series record, including four in the first inning, the only time a World Series pitcher has done it.

By 1910 his arm was sore, but Chance still started him in Game 1 of the World Series. After seeing Bonesetter Reese he said his arm was better, but a contract dispute with owner Charles Murphy kept him from testing it in the majors.
p: He was nicknamed the "Big Groundhog" because he was born on February 2. His father owned Visalia's Palace Hotel and a citrus farm.
During a contract dispute in 1911 he worked a California gold mine that he owned with teammate Mordecai Brown.
After baseball he ran the family citrus farm, ran unsuccessfully for Congress in 1918, and rose to vice-president of the Security-First National Bank of Los Angeles.

After a job with the Maier Brewery Company he took over the family citrus farm when his father fell ill. When his father died in 1921 he sold the estate's holdings and became wealthy. He died of a heart attack in Fresno in 1947, at 66.

c: Though not a student, he played for the University of Virginia's team in 1882, where a Richmond leather merchant who owned a team spotted him.
In his Phillies debut on May 1, 1884, he pitched a complete game and had three hits. On August 29, 1885, he threw the franchise's first no-hitter, 1-0 over Providence.
In 1886 he went 30-9, won his last 11 starts, and won both games of a doubleheader on the final day to end Detroit's pennant hopes.

Harry Wright increasingly used him in the outfield and at second base on days he didn't pitch. In 1887 he hit .337 and led the team in RBIs; during a closing 16-0-1 run he hit .361 and went 7-0. Another club reportedly offered $10,000 for him.
Wilbert Robinson in 1931 named him among the five greatest players ever: "Cobb, Keeler, Ruth, Wagner, and Ferguson."
He signed with the Quakers in spring 1884 for $1,500.
In 1885 he improved to 26-20 with a 2.22 ERA, and the Phillies finished third.
p: He grew up in Charlottesville's Random Row neighborhood, near the University of Virginia, where his father was a baker. He coached Princeton's baseball team in the off-seasons.
Sick in Chicago in August 1886, he begged Harry Wright to let him go home and finally took a train south on his own; a doctor's note said he spent ten days in bed.

In spring 1888 he caught typhoid fever and died at 25, in a room he and his wife rented from teammate Arthur Irwin. Four teams wore black crepe on their sleeves that season. His infant daughter had died the year before.
Random Row was a rough neighborhood where drunken brawls were common. His father built small wooden additions on the family home and rented them to grocers.
He married between the 1885 and 1886 seasons. Their infant daughter died in June 1887, and they had no other children.
He died on April 29, 1888, less than two weeks after his 25th birthday. The whole Quakers organization and the Princeton players he'd coached attended his funeral in Charlottesville.

c: At 18 he chose baseball over hanging wallpaper. When he had days off he climbed the fence at Kansas City's ballpark and carried bats so he could watch games. In Kansas City he played alongside future Cubs teammate Johnny Kling.
He refused to sign with Cincinnati because the Reds were trying to take him from Portland for nothing. The Cubs offered Portland $600 if he "made good," and he did.
The first time a scorer wrote "Tinker to Evers to Chance" in the scorebook was September 15, 1902, a few months into his first season.
In 1914 he jumped to the Federal League to manage Chicago, where the team outdrew both the Cubs and the White Sox. In 1915 his Whales won the pennant by .001.
Running the Columbus club in 1918, he made the entire ballpark staff women, from ticket takers to the ground crew, so the men could do war work.
Asked to go on the radio together during the 1938 World Series, he and Johnny Evers, who hadn't spoken in years, had nothing to say; they just embraced.
Coffeyville teammate Billy Hulen recommended him to Denver, which sold him to Great Falls. Broke, Great Falls sold him to Helena for $200.
He made 74 errors at shortstop as a rookie, but he and Evers built a chemistry where each knew the other would be at second without looking.

Traded to Cincinnati as player-manager in December 1912, he was seen as a poor manager as the Reds fell to seventh. Garry Herrmann sold him to Brooklyn for $15,000, and Charles Ebbets offered him $10,000 to sign, but he jumped to the Federal League instead.

At Columbus he named Bill Clymer manager for 1920 over Grover Hartley, who asked to be traded. In 1929 he scouted the Athletics for the Cubs before the World Series and toured with Evers in a ten-week theatrical baseball skit. He later managed Jersey City, and quit when the team couldn't pay him.
During World War II he was a boiler inspector at the Orlando air base.
p: His mother was an unwed teenager scorned in their Kansas farm town, and they kept moving until she met William Tinker, whose name Joe took. His twin sister died young.
He met Ruby Rose Menown at a church youth event when she was 16, and waited four years, until he was a big-leaguer, to propose. He opened a saloon on Chicago's South Side.

Moving to Orlando for his wife's health, he won a state title with the Orlando Tigers, and the city named its ballpark Tinker Field. He made a fortune in the 1920s real-estate boom and lost it when the boom collapsed.
There's no record that his mother married William Tinker; Joe simply took the name.
On Christmas morning 1923 his wife, Ruby Rose, shot herself during an apparent nervous breakdown. He married Mary Eddington of Orlando in 1926 and Susanna Margaret Chabot in 1942.
His real-estate firm made him up to $250,000, and he bought the Longwood Hotel in 1926. In the Depression he had to sell off most of his holdings.
In 1927 a partner sued him, claiming he spent company money without the board's permission and shorted him on profits. He was also arrested for running a gambling house.

Diabetes and Bright's disease nearly killed him in 1936 and again in 1944. An infection cost him a toe in 1947 and then his left leg above the knee. He died on his 68th birthday in 1948, survived by four children.

c: In the deciding game of the 1919 Texas Colored League championship, he relieved Steel Arm Davis and held Dallas down while Davis's double won it for San Antonio.
The nickname "Biz" came from "giving them the business," talking to batters to break their concentration. He hit .411 for Indianapolis in 1922.

On a 1927 tour of Japan, the first by a Black team, he hit a huge home run at Tokyo's new Meiji Shrine Stadium and bowed back to a pitcher who bowed to apologize for hitting him. Japanese historian Kazuo Sayama credits the tours with speeding baseball's growth in Japan.

Washington signed a teenage Roy Campanella for $60 a month, and Mackey taught him to catch. Campanella: "Biz Mackey was the master of defense of all catchers." In 1952 a Pittsburgh Courier poll named Mackey the Negro leagues' greatest catcher, ahead of Josh Gibson.

He managed Newark to the 1946 Negro League World Series title, and the next year advised moving Larry Doby from second base to the outfield. Monte Irvin: "As a player, as a manager, and as a personality, he was in a class by himself."
At Campanella's 1959 tribute in the Los Angeles Coliseum, Campanella called Mackey onto the field in front of 93,000 fans to make sure everyone knew what Mackey had done for him.

In the first Negro World Series, in 1924, he played third base as Hilldale lost to the Monarchs 5 games to 4. Sharing the catching with Louis Santop and the shortstop job with Pop Lloyd, he took over as full-time catcher in 1925 and hit .360 as Hilldale beat the Monarchs for the title.
In the 1934 playoff he hit .368 for the Philadelphia Stars and drove in the first run of their 2–0 Game 7 win over the Chicago American Giants.
In 1942 he fell out with Newark owners Abe and Effa Manley over salary and was replaced as manager by Willie Wells.
During World War II he worked at North American Aviation.
Through the 1990s, reference books listed his death as 1959, apparently from Campanella's memory.
p: The son of Texas sharecroppers, he went to school through 10th grade and passed the "Common Exam" for his diploma. His grandson Riley Odoms played tight end for the Denver Broncos.

On his first trip to Japan he met a young woman named Lucille. They lost touch during the war, and reunited in San Francisco after her family came to the U.S., and spent the rest of their lives together.
Talkative behind the plate, he was private at home. He drove a forklift for Stauffer Chemical in Los Angeles, and his 1965 death got no coverage in The Sporting News.
He was one of six children. His father had left the household by 1900, and in 1903 his mother married a farmer, Montgomery Meriwether, who brought three daughters of his own.

He married Ora Lee Dorn in Luling in October 1917; they separated in 1919 and divorced later. He had a daughter, Narcissus, born in 1914. Late in life he reconnected with Ora Lee, who handled his funeral arrangements.
Lucille, called "Aunt Lucy" in the family, died a few months before he did.

c: When the Giants played Dallas in spring 1908, the rookie sassed them back, slid in spikes high and crowded the plate when they threw at him. John McGraw bought an option on him: "That's my kind of ball player." Fletcher later admitted, "I was a pretty fresh busher."
Self-conscious about his jutting chin, he had a collar sewn onto his uniform and wore it turned up.

He was hit by more pitches than anyone in the NL nearly every year from 1913 to 1918, and he fought opposing players, umpires and fans. At the Polo Grounds a woman in a big hat yelled "Come on, Artie!" before every game, and he waved his glove back.

As Phillies manager he had the next day's baseballs kept in a freezer overnight to cut down scoring in the tiny Baker Bowl. In 1924 he exposed a Giants player's $500 offer to his shortstop "not to bear down," and two Giants were banned.
He coached third base for the Yankees from 1927 to 1945 and turned down several managing offers to stay. He was said to have cashed more World Series checks than anyone in baseball history.
His father pushed him to keep his Ingersoll-Rand job, but with business slow his boss let him have the summer off to try out. McGraw bought an option on him for $1,500.
In 25 World Series games he hit .191 and made a dozen errors. His error in the 11th inning of Game 3 in 1911 helped hand Christy Mathewson his first World Series loss.

He quit as Phillies manager, tired of losing and afraid his fighting ways would ruin his health. Miller Huggins brought him to the Yankees, and he managed them for 11 games in 1929 while Huggins was hospitalized. Joe McCarthy kept him despite their 1926 feud.
Jacob Ruppert offered him the Yankees' managing job three times; he said he'd rather coach without the extra responsibility, and Bob Shawkey got it.
On September 10, 1945, he had a heart attack in the third-base coach's box during a game against Cleveland, then caught pneumonia in the hospital. Bill Dickey replaced him.
p: His parents opposed a baseball career, so he graduated from business college in stenography and worked for Ingersoll-Rand, which made the drills digging the Panama Canal. His boss let him take the 1908 summer off to try out in Dallas.
After his father and brother died in spring 1921, he went home to Collinsville and sat out the whole season. He and his wife, Irene, went back there after every season.
His World Series and first-division checks, more than $75,000, let him and Irene live in extreme comfort in Collinsville.
He died of another heart attack in February 1950, sitting in a car in Los Angeles with Irene while on vacation.

c: He played his whole Cuban National Series career for Industriales. His fielding earned him the nickname "El Imán," "The Magnet," and comparisons to Ozzie Smith and Omar Vizquel.
He led the league in stolen bases three times, and won Olympic gold with Cuba in 1992 and silver in 2000.

Dropped before the 1996 Olympics, he was banned that October along with Orlando and Alberto Hernández, accused of taking money from an American agent. The other two defected; Mesa stayed, and was reinstated in 1998.
As a manager he won a 2010 title with Industriales and three in Nicaragua, and was named manager of Cuba's team for the 2026 World Baseball Classic.
Eduardo Paret replaced him at shortstop for the 1996 Olympics.

He managed Industriales from 2008 to 2011. In Nicaragua he won titles with Chinandega in 2013 and Rivas in 2016 and 2024. He managed El Salvador at the 2017 Central American and Bolivarian Games and was bench coach for Cuba's fourth-place team at the 2023 World Baseball Classic.

The day before his 20th birthday in 1912 he saw his first major-league game, as the starting catcher. He arrived by streetcar minutes before the first pitch and manager Jimmy Callahan told him, "Young man, here's your pitcher, Doc White. You're the catcher." "That first game was my greatest day."
Coach Kid Gleason had him out practicing at 9:30 every morning for 3 p.m. games. At 148 pounds he was thought too small to catch Ed Walsh's spitball, but soon handled it better than anyone.

He played catcher like a fifth infielder, backing up throws at first and third, and claimed he was the only catcher to make a putout at every base. His 30 steals in 1916 were a record for catchers until 1982.

One of the honest men of the 1919 World Series, he hit .304 and knew something was wrong when Eddie Cicotte and Lefty Williams kept crossing him up. Of the day the eight were told they were through: "Those tears got me."
In 1923 he discovered Ted Lyons at Baylor, and they were inducted into the Hall of Fame on the same day in 1955. His .253 average is the lowest of any position player in the Hall.
The White Sox bought him from Milwaukee for $10,000 and two players. Of his debut he said, "You think of no-hit games and playing in the World Series, but that first game was my greatest day."
On a rainy day in Washington in 1915 he walked into a tavern where Cicotte, Ed Walsh and Shano Collins were drinking, and the bartender growled, "We don't allow no school kids in this joint."

His 30 steals in 1916 were the record for a catcher until John Wathan stole 36 in 1982. In the 1917 World Series the base-stealing Giants tried only six steals against him, and he threw out two. In 1920 he caught 151 of 154 games.
After he gave up managing the White Sox, Comiskey cut his salary from $25,000 to $6,000 to stay on as a catcher. He considered suing, then joined John McGraw's Giants as a coach in 1929.
He caught four no-hitters, a record until a 1991 scoring change removed one that was broken up in extra innings.
He scouted for the Cubs from 1944. At Purdue he coached under Ward Lambert and Hank Stram. He caught Red Faber's ceremonial first pitch at the 1959 World Series, the White Sox' first in 40 years.
p: He left high school to learn the printer's trade and went to Brooklyn to learn to run a Linotype machine before baseball offered him a better future.

He caught a ball dropped 463 feet from the top of the Tribune Tower for a movie stunt. When Charles Comiskey scolded him about what might have happened had he misjudged it, Schalk said, "But I didn't misjudge it."
He co-founded Baseball Anonymous to help needy former players, coached at Purdue for 18 years, and called to congratulate the catcher of every no-hitter.
In 1948 robbers held him, his wife and 34 others in the basement of his bowling alley for two hours until pinboys broke down a door.
He was the fifth of six children of German immigrants; his father was a day laborer in Litchfield, Illinois. As a boy he delivered the Chicago Tribune and captained the high school basketball team.

At his induction he thanked his strongest supporter, his wife, the former Lavinia Graham, for whatever he'd accomplished. They had two children. When he died of cancer in 1970, the White Sox and Angels held a moment of silence.

c: A left-handed catcher at Brown, he was called to fill in for Boston on the night of his senior dinner in 1894. He broke a finger in that game, and the owners offered him $300 a month. Thinking it was a joke, he asked for $150 in advance to call their bluff, and got it, half in cash and half by check.

Moved to first base in 1897, he turned the first 3-6-3 double play in major-league history that June. He's credited with starting the practice of playing deep and off the line, as first basemen do today.
He sat out just one game for the Giants in 1908, with lumbago, on September 23. Rookie Fred Merkle took his place at first and failed to touch second in the famous Merkle game.
In 1916 he bought the Newark Indians, and the mayor declared Opening Day a half-holiday for the city.
After his debut Boston owner James Billings offered him $300 a month. Tenney asked for an advance, and another director counted out $75 in cash and wrote a $75 check on the spot.

He was suspended ten games in May 1902 for fighting Pirates manager Fred Clarke. Named Boston manager in 1905 with no raise, he was offered a bonus if the team didn't lose money. That year he tried to sign William Clarence Matthews, a Black infielder from Harvard.

After a 158–295 record as manager, he was traded to the Giants in December 1907 in an eight-man deal called "one of the biggest deals in the history of National League baseball." He also coached Tufts in 1902 and 1903.
The Giants released him after he hit .235 in 1909. Back in Boston he managed the 1911 club to a 44–107 record and was paid not to manage the second year of his contract.
p: He was nicknamed the "Soiled Collegian" because college men turning pro were frowned on. Early in his career he refused to play on Sundays for religious reasons.
He led his class in drawing as a boy, and kept painting and sketching in the winters. He also wrote for the Boston Post, Baseball Magazine and The New York Times.
After baseball he sold life insurance and went into the shoe business in Lynn, Massachusetts. In 2023 he was inducted into the Braves Hall of Fame.
He was the third of five children; his father nearly died from "intense suffering" serving in the Civil War.

He married Bessie Farnham Berry of Georgetown in 1895; their daughters were Barbara, born on July 4, 1899, and Ruth. He worked for the Equitable Life Insurance Society, and died at Massachusetts General Hospital in 1952 after a long illness.

c: He batted with a golf grip, his left index finger clamped over his right pinky, though he never played golf. A photo shows him holding seven baseballs in one hand.

In Johnny Vander Meer's first straight no-hitter, in 1938, Lombardi turned a double play, picked a runner off first, and hit a two-run homer. Umpire Bill Stewart said his pitch-calling was "just as perfect and just as important" as Vander Meer's pitching.

He won the 1938 NL batting title and MVP, while grounding into a record 30 double plays. He was so slow that it was said he could double to left and beat out a single, and infielders played back on the outfield grass.
When Vander Meer threw a pitch way outside, Lombardi caught it barehanded. Vander Meer: "The least you could do is shake your hand a little like I had something on the pitch."

In Game 4 of the 1939 World Series, Charlie Keller crashed into him and he lay dazed while Joe DiMaggio scored, a play mocked as "Lombardi's Snooze." DiMaggio: "Ernie was wronged. Keller put Ernie out of commission."
He hit .330 for the 1942 Braves to win a second batting title.

After running his father's grocery for a while, he changed his mind and called the Oaks. He threw out runners for 95 assists in 1929 and 102 in 1930. In Brooklyn, Wilbert Robinson preferred veterans and kept him on the bench behind Al Lopez.
The Brooklyn Robins bought his contract for $50,000.
Brooklyn traded him to Cincinnati shortly before spring training in 1932.
His 30 double plays in 1938 stood as the record for 70 years, until Miguel Tejada broke it in 2008.

In 1940 his backup, Willard Hershberger, who felt he was struggling while filling in for the injured Lombardi, told Bill McKechnie, "my father killed himself, and I'm going to do it, too!" He became the only major leaguer to commit suicide during a season.
Lombardi's season was over, and he caught only one game of the 1940 World Series.
His 1942 title was the last for a catcher until Joe Mauer in 2006.
Despite his fine year in Boston, he asked the Braves to trade him and held out until they did.
p: His father, an Italian immigrant, ran a grocery store in Oakland, and Ernie worked behind the counter. He turned down the Oaks at first because he didn't want to leave home, until a stint running the store convinced him he'd rather play ball.
He was called "Schnozz" for his nose, mostly by fans, and took the kidding well. He refused to sign autographs until a boy asked if he couldn't write.
Later in life he worked as a press-box attendant at Candlestick Park. He was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1986, nine years after his death, and has a statue outside Great American Ball Park.
He married Bernice Ayers of Oakland in 1944.

In April 1953, visiting relatives in Castro Valley, he cut his throat with a razor. He was saved and entered a private sanitarium. Bernice died in 1973 and he died in 1977 after a long illness. The "Snooze" and the suicide attempt were major obstacles to his Hall of Fame election.
He also worked as a gas station attendant in Oakland.

c: He began as a pitcher, going 30-9 with 240 strikeouts for Worcester in 1889, but went 3-10 with the 1890 Giants and was moved to the outfield.
He hit .409 in 1895 and .410 in 1896, mostly singles. Scout Frank Shaughnessy thought he was the greatest bunter who ever lived. His 240 hits in 1896 were the major-league record until Ty Cobb.
After fouling off a tough pitch, he did "a snappy little jig." He holds the career record for inside-the-park home runs with 55.
Teammates on the rowdy Cleveland Spiders called him "The Crab." On August 4, 1897, he was ejected from both games of a doubleheader, and police had to remove him the second time.

Pinch-hitting in the New England League, he told the umpire who asked who he was batting for, "None of your blankety blank business." The umpire announced, "Burkett batting for exercise." He struck out.
Coaching Holy Cross from 1917 to 1920, he went 88-12-1.
He signed with Scranton in 1888 for $85 a month. Jack Glasscock, a fellow Wheeling native rumored to be a distant cousin, recommended him to Worcester.
Cleveland bought him in February 1891. After he led the league with 46 errors in 1893, outfielder Jimmy McAleer coached him on his fielding.

In October 1901, nearly 33, he jumped to the AL's St. Louis Browns for more money, but never hit .300 again in the majors. After 1904 the Browns traded him to Boston for George Stone, bringing him closer to his home in Worcester.
As a Giants coach he was assigned to chaperone alcoholic pitcher Phil Douglas. He failed: in 1922 Douglas got away from him on a drinking binge that ended in a sanitarium.
He managed Worcester in the Eastern League in 1923 and 1924 and Lewiston in 1928 and 1929, and scouted during the Depression.
p: As a boy in Wheeling he dove into the Ohio River to save a girl who had fallen from a skiff. He found her, but she couldn't be revived; more than 70 years later the memory still brought him to tears.
He liked Worcester so much in his one season there that he made it his home. He bought a New England League team there and won four straight pennants.

In 1935, directing traffic for the state highway department, he was struck by a car and recovered. Elected to the Hall of Fame in 1946: "I thought they weren't going to because everybody had forgotten me."
His father worked as a day laborer, a painter and a repairman on the Wheeling Suspension Bridge, once the longest in the world.
He and his wife, Ellen McGrath, had three children. His greatest disappointment, he told reporters, was that his son Howard never got out of the minors. He died of heart disease in 1953 at 84.

c: A scout came to Danville, Indiana, and found Thompson repairing a neighbor's roof for $2.50. He wouldn't play until the scout paid him the $2.50. He hit two balls into a cornfield, Danville won 9-0, and he was signed on the spot.
When Indianapolis folded in 1885, Detroit's owner kept eight of its players on a steamer in Lake Huron until the deadline for other clubs to claim them had passed.
In his first game Detroit had no uniform big enough for him, and he split his pants sliding into second on a double. Fans loved him from then on.
In 1887 he became the first player with 200 hits in a season, drove in 166 runs, a record until Babe Ruth, and led all hitters in the World Series win over St. Louis.
In 1894 he, Ed Delahanty and Billy Hamilton all hit .400 for the Phillies, the only all-Hall of Fame outfield to do so. He's credited with mastering the one-hop throw from the outfield.
He drove in .923 runs per game for his career, the highest ever, and 61 in August 1894 alone, still the record for a month.
In 1906, at 46, he played a homestand for the Tigers in an outfield with Ty Cobb and Sam Crawford.
The scout who found him on the roof had actually come to look at his older brother Cy, a druggist.
On the steamer Annette: "We were prisoners, but well cared-for prisoners. On the night of the tenth day, at midnight, we were all taken ashore where Watkins met us and signed us to our contracts."
He once hit two bases-loaded triples in a game, a record since tied but never broken.
A sore arm held him to 56 games in 1888, and the Wolverines folded that October.
Philadelphia bought him from Detroit for $5,000 cash.

He planned to jump to the Players' League but stayed with the Phillies after checking the contracts. His salary never went above the league's $2,400 maximum. In 1891 he had surgery to remove "dead bones" from a finger on his left hand, likely old damage from catching bare-handed.
An injury to his left little finger in 1894, which led to a partial amputation, cost him a month. He still hit .407 with 28 triples and a league-leading 147 RBIs.
Manager Bill Watkins: "He was a fine fielder and had a cannon arm and will live in my memory as the greatest natural hitter of all time."
p: His father learned baseball in the Union Army and brought it home to Danville, where the six Thompson boys, all over six feet and 200 pounds, played for the Danville Browns.
In 15 seasons he was never ejected, never in a fight, never suspended. Charlie Bennett: "No one ever quarreled with Sam."
He stayed in Detroit after the Wolverines folded and worked as a deputy U.S. marshal and court bailiff. Each year Bennett threw the season's first pitch at Bennett Park and Thompson caught it.
Detroit's courts and factories stopped for his 1922 funeral, which a Methodist minister and a Catholic priest officiated together for him and his wife.
He was the fifth of 11 children. His father served with the 63rd Indiana Volunteers, guarding Confederate prisoners at Camp Morton.
He married Ida Morasha in 1888; she often traveled with the team, and they had no children. He and Charlie Bennett and their wives appeared several times on evangelist Billy Sunday's "sawdust trail."
In 1922, working as an election official, he collapsed with a heart attack and died at home that day.

c: Home Run Johnson heard he was a wonderful batsman and brought him from Texas to the Philadelphia Giants in 1911. Within weeks he and Cannonball Redding jumped to the Lincoln Giants as the "kid battery."
In 1913 he hit a 485-foot homer off former big-leaguer Doc Scanlan in Elizabethport, New Jersey, said to be the longest ever hit there.
Newspapers called him "the Ty Cobb of colored baseball" and "black baseball's first legitimate home-run slugger." Fans came to see him, so he played almost every one of about 200 games a year.
Hilldale owner Ed Bolden paid him $450 a month and called him "the greatest star and best drawing card we ever had." In 1920 he had three hits off Babe Ruth's touring all-stars.

In Game 8 of the 1924 Colored World Series he drove in a run, then dropped a foul pop with the bases loaded and two outs in the ninth. Frank Duncan got another chance and singled in the tying and winning runs.
He grew up in a tough area and often had to fight.
He once broke three of Oscar Charleston's ribs in an altercation.
The 1913 Lincoln Giants reportedly won 101 of 107 games. In 1916 Nat Strong lured him to the Brooklyn Royal Giants.

Hilldale released him in a salary dump in February 1925 and re-signed him a month later, with Biz Mackey now doing the catching. Hilldale released him for good in July 1926, and he went on to run his own independent team, Santop's Broncos, into the early 1930s.
p: Born Louis Santop Loftin in Fort Worth, he was the oldest of five children of parents who had both been born enslaved.
He served in the Navy in World War I. After baseball he broadcast on Philadelphia's WELK, tended bar, and clerked in the recorder of deeds office at City Hall.
He left his baseball memorabilia to Bill Yancey, who gave it to the Hall of Fame.
When he died in 1942, sportswriter Red Smith took a train to Philadelphia for the funeral "because I had seen him play and knew what he could do."
He married Minnie B. in 1927, at 38. He was a Mason and a Republican committeeman.
He died in an oxygen tent at the Navy hospital in Philadelphia, of an ailment like the one that killed Lou Gehrig. He was elected to the Hall of Fame in 2006.

c: As a boy he was a mascot for Licey, then jumped to rival Escogido as mascot and, in 1923, as a player alongside his brothers. Historian Rob Ruck compared Licey's loss to the Red Sox selling Babe Ruth.
Barnstorming with a "House of David" team in 1931, in fake beards, he was credited with circling the bases in a record 13.25 seconds in Sioux City, Iowa.
His speed earned him the nickname El Gamo Dominicano, "The Dominican Deer." In his late 40s, his Caguas manager Mickey Owen said he "could outrun Jim Rivera and Hank Aaron."
He hit .447 for the New York Cubans in 1943, and .409 in exhibitions against major-league pitching, including 7-for-14 against the Yankees in 1947.
At 47 he beat Ray Dandridge for the 1953 Dominican Summer League batting title, and he played his last season at nearly 50.
In 1961 the stadium in San Pedro de Macorís was renamed Estadio Tetelo Vargas. As a Pirates scout he was credited with signing Julián Javier.

In 1930 he played for the Havana Red Sox, just bought by Syd Pollock, who later signed Hank Aaron for the Indianapolis Clowns. From 1932 to 1934 he played for the Concordia Eagles, sponsored by a son of Venezuelan president Juan Vicente Gómez.
In Puerto Rico he hit .415 for the Guayama Witches, second on the team to Perucho Cepeda, as they won the title. Charlie Dressen, visiting in 1936: "He could fly."
He managed the Dominican Republic at the 1952 Amateur World Series.
p: His father was a shoemaker in Santo Domingo. An uncle called Tetelo started calling the boy "Tete," and soon everyone called him Tetelo.
He married Celia Amaro, a Puerto Rican, in 1927, and settled for life in Guayama, Puerto Rico, though he was revered in the Dominican Republic and Venezuela.
He and Celia had a daughter, Carmen, and a son, Juan Esteban Jr. After she died he married Violeta Incháustegui in Puerto Rico in 1954, and had daughters Ana and Iris.
He died of lung cancer in 1971 at 65 and is buried next to his wife in Guayama.

c: As a Monterrey rookie in 1962 he hit .358 with 105 RBIs and was Rookie of the Year. In 1964 he set the Mexican League home run record with 46.

The Cardinals signed him in 1964 and he hit .300 for Triple-A Jacksonville, but he never played outside Mexico again. He gave different reasons over the years; one writer blamed racism he faced in the U.S.
He turned down offers from the Cardinals, Mets, Padres and Angels, earning the nickname "The Rebel of Chihuahua."
His 484 home runs are the all-time minor-league record. He was walked intentionally 408 times, more than 200 more than anyone else in the Mexican League.
He won 13 batting titles across Mexico's summer and winter leagues and was MVP of the 1974 and 1976 Caribbean Series.

Explanations for why he left the U.S. vary: Total Baseball suggested he liked being a big fish in a small pond, some cited homesickness, and Mexican League writer Bruce Baskin said racism discouraged him.
In 1975 he helped Tampico win the Mexican League title and set a league record with hits in 11 straight at-bats.
He managed Monterrey in 1990 and 1991, going 110–138.
p: Called "The Mexican Babe Ruth," he had his number 21 retired by every pro team in Mexico's summer and winter leagues, and Hermosillo named its stadium for him in 1976.
Most of his records, including the Mexican League season and career home run marks, have since been broken. He died of a heart attack in Monterrey in 1997.

c: When a Puerto Plata team signed him around 1940, nobody there knew him, so fans called him "the pitcher from Guayubín," and the name Guayubín stuck.
He turned down the White Sox in 1948. He didn't speak English, didn't want to work up through the minors, and feared being sent to a segregated Southern town.
In his Colombian debut in 1948 he took a perfect game into the ninth. In the 1951 Dominican summer league he won the pitching Triple Crown.

Dick Stuart told the Pirates, "I'd been hitting against this guy for three years down there and I got two hits off him. Sign this guy!" At 41, in 1960, he became the second-oldest rookie in history, behind Satchel Paige.
As a 43-year-old reliever in 1962 he went 5-1 with a 2.77 ERA, often used as a left-handed specialist, and teamed with Elroy Face.
His 2.11 ERA over 14 seasons with Licey trails only Juan Marichal's in Dominican league history, and the league named its pitching award for him.
In 1944 he went to Caracas with the Dominican team for the Amateur World Series.

After seven straight losses in 1950-51, Aguadilla sold him to San Juan. Once he was thrown out of the stadium and spent a night in jail; he was going to be suspended for the season, but after Licey lobbied and he wrote a public apology, it was cut to six games.
He pitched only 13 innings for the Havana Sugar Kings before going to Mexico, where he went 15-8 for the 1956 champion Red Devils.

Scout Howie Haak persuaded GM Joe L. Brown to gamble on him, but Olivo didn't report to spring training at first. Too late to be eligible for the 1960 World Series, he threw batting practice, and the Pirates gave him $250; Virgil Trucks got $500. At Columbus the International League's writers voted him its most valuable pitcher.
