After 1962 he was traded to the Cardinals with Dick Groat. Later he scouted for St. Louis and worked in his country's Ministry of Sports. In the 1970s he went into political exile in Panama and managed its national team.
Cattle rustlers stole seven of his steers in December 1962. His son said the saddest day of his life was his last game with Licey, in 1964.
p: His father was a cattle rancher. "When I put the cows away, I go into town to play." He later owned 500 acres and 50 cows of his own in Guayubín, and once lost seven steers to rustlers.
He spoke little English and relied on teammates like Roberto Clemente and Julián Javier to translate. His brother Chichí and his son Gilberto Rondón also pitched in the majors.
He died of a heart attack in 1977, reading about the death of his brother Chichí less than two weeks earlier. A Dominican writer: "His death was a national catastrophe. There was no music anywhere."
During the 1951-52 Puerto Rican season he conceived a child with a woman named Crucita Rondón. He married Olga Chávez Gómez in 1953, and they had three children, Pedro, Olga and Guillermo.
He was the father of major-league pitcher Gilberto Rondón.

c: He played shortstop for the 1937 Ciudad Trujillo team with Josh Gibson, Satchel Paige and Cool Papa Bell, the only Puerto Rican on the club.
In the Puerto Rican league's first season, 1938-39, he hit .465 for Guayama, and he edged Josh Gibson for the batting title the next year. He's the only Puerto Rican to hit .400 at two positions.
On November 5, 1939, he became the first player in the league with six hits in a game. He led the league in RBIs its first three seasons, the only player to do it three straight years.
Against the touring Yankees in 1947 he went 4-for-4 in one game off Vic Raschi and Allie Reynolds, his son Orlando recalled.
He turned down the Negro leagues, including the New York Cubans. "He thought that playing on the racially segregated mainland was an offense to his sense of justice," Orlando said.

He hit .429 for the Sandino club in the Dominican Republic in 1929. In the Puerto Rican league's first four seasons he went 293-for-713, a .411 average; in 1940-41 he finished third at .421, ahead of Buck Leonard, Roy Campanella and Monte Irvin.
He was called the "Babe Cobb of Puerto Rico," for Ruth's hitting and Cobb's hustle.
After the Guayama Brujos folded he played for San Juan, Mayagüez, Santurce and Caguas, which won the 1947-48 title under Quincy Trouppe. He apparently signed for 1948-49 but sat the season out.

Orlando first saw him play on January 5, 1946, for Mayagüez against Santurce at Sixto Escobar Stadium. Orlando said his father's temper was so volatile he couldn't have tolerated playing in the States.
p: Called "The Bull," he helped his father, a mason, at work as a boy in Cataño. He never earned more than $60 a week playing, and worked for the San Juan water authority.
He died in April 1955, two weeks after his son Orlando signed with the Giants. Orlando used his $500 bonus to pay for the funeral, and always said his father was the better player.
Touring the Hall of Fame after his 1999 induction, Orlando saw a photo of the 1937 Ciudad Trujillo team: "It's amazing. I didn't know my father was here."
He was one of four children. He married Carmen Pennes and had two sons, Pedro and Orlando, and other children from other relationships.
A hard-living, hard-drinking man, he died in 1955 of either cirrhosis of the liver or complications of malaria. Before he died he made sure Orlando, whom he had mentored, had a pro contract.
He's in six other halls of fame, including the Puerto Rican Sports Hall of Fame and the Latino Baseball Hall of Fame.

c: Catching without a mask for the Plattsburgh Nameless in 1885, he once climbed a telegraph pole to catch a foul ball, the story goes.

Called "the Black Dunlap" for fielding to match Fred Dunlap's, he played three straight seasons for Buffalo, 1886-88, the only Black player before the 1940s to spend three in a row with one club in Organized Baseball. He led Buffalo in hitting and slugging each year.
Several white Buffalo teammates refused to sit for the 1887 team photo with him. That July the International League voted to approve "no more contracts with colored men."

Ned Williamson later claimed the feet-first slide spread as opposing runners tried to spike a Black Buffalo second baseman, who took to wearing wooden shin guards. Williamson may have meant Grant or Bud Fowler.
Tom Brown: "If he were a white man he would stand abreast of the others in the red-letter chapters of baseball." In 2006 Grant became the earliest Negro league player elected to the Hall of Fame.
In 1887 Buffalo manager Jack Chapman valued him at $5,000, when Chicago had just sold King Kelly for $10,000.
At a game in Toronto on July 27, 1887, the crowd broke into a chorus of "Kill the Nigger."

He opened a restaurant and saloon in Buffalo that September and quit it within two months. In 1888 he held out for $250 a month; when his arm went sore Buffalo cut his pay. Then he was fined $25 and laid off for drinking, "much to the satisfaction of the club members, who dislike the man," and who reportedly swore they wouldn't play good ball until he was fired.

One spring both York and Harrisburg claimed him, since he'd signed with each. Harrisburg's crowd strained to see "the most famous colored ballplayer in the business" arrive. Baltimore's manager, Billy Barnie, wired that Grant could not play in Baltimore.
Shut out of white baseball, he starred for the Cuban Giants, Cuban X-Giants, Big Gorhams, Brooklyn Royal Giants and Philadelphia Giants into the 20th century.
p: Growing up in Williamstown, Massachusetts, he did tricks like catching the ball behind his back. A boyhood teammate, Bliss Perry, later edited The Atlantic and based a character in a novel on him.

He spent his last years in Greenwich Village, working as a waiter and porter. He died in 1937 and got a pauper's burial; Sol White and Smokey Joe Williams were pallbearers. His grave was unmarked until 2011.
He was probably the ninth child. His father, a farm laborer, apparently died young, and his mother worked for her Williamstown neighbors, the family of a professor.
A New York paper said he "electrified Broadway" in a blue corduroy coat, black-and-white striped trousers, yellow gloves, patent leather shoes with gaiters, a slate fedora and a gold-headed cane.

c: Joining the Chicago Unions in 1899, he homered and singled with three runs against the Cuban X-Giants, and soon jumped to the X-Giants himself.

He was a master "coacher," broadcasting commentary in a foghorn voice. Before a rally: "Oh! Lord, have mercy on us for what we are about to do. Farewell! Goodbye." To the grandstand after a win: "This picnic will be repeated on Wednesday and Thursday."
He entertained crowds by catching bloopers behind his back and kicking ground balls up into his hands.

In 1905 he had 37 steals and 49 extra-base hits for the Philadelphia Giants; only Honus Wagner and Sam Mertes reached both marks in the majors that year. Rube Foster and Dan McClellan called him the greatest player they ever saw.
In 1909 his hitting led the Brooklyn Royal Giants past the New York Highlanders, 9-6, apparently his only game against a big-league team.
He played third and led off for Nashville's Rock City Unions against the Chicago Unions in 1898, and that winter the Unions' manager signed him.
He broke his left ankle in July 1901. In August 1903, covering second in Lebanon, Pennsylvania, he broke one rib and tore muscles from another in a collision.

More of his coaching patter: snapping up grounders, "You're out, chile"; walking to the plate, "The ball is going out and a run is coming in"; to the grandstand after beating the local team, "This picnic will be repeated on Wednesday and Thursday of this week."

Some of his clowning drew on the minstrel humor of the day. Historian Hogan: "Making a fool of oneself on the diamond was part and parcel of taking admission money from as many white folks as possible."
p: His father served in the U.S. Colored Heavy Artillery in the Civil War and became an AME Zion minister; Bill sang bass in his choir.
Fans called him "Money" and later "Diamond," for the jewelry he wore. He never married.
He died of tuberculosis on his 37th birthday in 1915. The Sporting News, which rarely covered Black baseball, wrote that "those who have seen him play say he was a Lajoie and a Wagner, combined."
He was born in Knoxville, the youngest of five, and moved to Chattanooga as a teenager. He admitted to curbing the "late hours" of his youth.

He caught the cold that led to his death touring the Pacific Northwest in spring 1914, but still played second base that season. Soon after he died, the Chicago American Giants wore black crepe on their arms.

c: He played first base in the Cuban League from 1899 to 1914, for Almendares, Club Fé and Habana.
In 1911 he played in the Negro leagues for the Cuban Stars (West) and the All Cubans. He was elected to the Cuban Baseball Hall of Fame in 1943.
He joined Cuba's junior national team at 14, and played 27 games for Pinar del Río before turning 16. At the 1985 Junior World Cup he hit .511 with 8 homers.
At 19, at the 1987 Pan American Games in Indianapolis, he hit .520, outhitting future big-leaguers like Tino Martinez and Ed Sprague.
He hit 404 Cuban League homers, one every 14.8 at-bats, but more than 90 percent of his career came with aluminum bats; with wood after 1999 his numbers fell.

Against Japan in the 1996 Olympic final he hit three home runs, still an Olympic single-game record, as is his career total of 13. At the 1999 Pan Ams his semifinal homer against Canada clinched Cuba's spot in the 2000 Olympics, the moment he called his brightest.
Against the Baltimore Orioles in Baltimore in 1999 he reached base all six times.
He turned down big-league offers again and again. In 2002 he became the first Cuban star loaned to a professional league, with Japan's Chunichi Dragons, where he struggled.
At an Intercontinental Cup in Havana he hit 11 home runs against a Team USA with future big-leaguers Mickey Morandini, Chuck Knoblauch and Scott Servais.

In the March 1999 exhibition against the Orioles in Havana, coming off a leg injury and hitting with wood against big-league pitching for the first time, he delivered a game-tying single in the eighth.
He called his home run at the Pan American Games in Winnipeg the brightest moment of his career. At one nine-game tournament he hit .476 with a tournament-high 20 hits.
Stories of plots to lure him away were mostly apocryphal, though big-league scouts and executives privately dreamed of it.
p: His father, Fidel Linares, got the winning hit in the very first National Series game in 1962. His younger brother Juan Carlos played alongside him at Pinar del Río for 14 seasons.
Asked why Omar never wanted to be a millionaire, his brother said: "Because of the 11 million fans that admired and loved him, and because of our family."
As a coach with Industriales, his old rivals, he helped them win the 2010 national title.

He was born in San Juan y Martínez, in Cuba's tobacco country. His father Fidel had starred in the Pedro Betancourt League, the first Cuban amateur circuit to admit Black players on a large scale. When Fidel died of cancer in 2000, his state funeral seemed fit for a military hero.

c: The Braves signed him for $100,000 in 2014. He wore 24 in the minors in honor of Miguel Cabrera, and debuted in 2018 at 20 as the youngest player in the majors, going on to win Rookie of the Year.
In April 2019, at 21, he signed an eight-year, $100 million deal, the youngest player ever to sign a contract worth $100 million.
In 2020 he hit a 495-foot homer against the Red Sox, the longest in the majors that year and the longest ever at Truist Park.
In 2023 he became the first player with 40 homers and 70 steals in a season and won the NL MVP.
He tore his right ACL in 2021 and his left ACL in 2024. Back on May 23, 2025, he homered on the first pitch he saw.
In 2026 he helped Venezuela win its first World Baseball Classic, and joined Hank Aaron as the only Braves with 1,000 hits, 200 homers and 200 steals.

He hit .432 with four homers in spring training in 2018 and was still sent to the minors. That season he joined Alex Rodriguez, Orlando Cepeda and Mike Trout as the only players with 25 homers and 15 steals at 20 or younger, and hit a grand slam off Walker Buehler in the NLDS, the youngest ever to hit one in the postseason.
When he was hurt chasing a fly ball in July 2021, he led the majors in runs and had been voted an All-Star starter. The Braves won the World Series without him, and he still got a ring.
In 2023 he broke the Braves' modern stolen-base record, set by Otis Nixon in 1991.
His 2024 injury came on May 26, taking a lead off second against Pittsburgh; he walked off the field.
p: His father and grandfather played minor-league ball, two of his brothers play professionally, and his cousins include Alcides and Kelvim Escobar.
He goes by "Sabanero Soy," "I am from the savannah." He married Maria Laborde in 2023, and they have two sons.
He's the oldest of four sons. His uncle José Escobar played for Cleveland in 1991, and his cousins include Vicente Campos, Edwin Escobar and Maikel García. His sons are Ronald III and Jamal.

c: The Dodgers drafted him 18th overall in 2012 and paid him $2.35 million to skip South Carolina.
In 2016 he hit three homers against Atlanta, the youngest shortstop ever to do it, and was Rookie of the Year.
On August 17, 2020, he and his brother Kyle both homered in a game against each other. That fall he was MVP of both the NLCS and the World Series as the Dodgers won the title.
He signed a 10-year, $325 million deal with Texas, the largest in Rangers history. His 33 homers in 2022 were the most ever by a left-handed-hitting shortstop.
He was World Series MVP again in 2023 as the Rangers won their first title, the only player to win the award in both leagues.
On September 12, 2015, he went 4-for-4 with his first big-league homer, a walk and a steal, the third-youngest to do that after Ken Griffey Jr. and Orlando Cepeda.
A back injury in the 2017 NLDS kept him out of the NLCS, but he returned for the World Series, which the Dodgers lost to Houston in seven.
In 2018 he needed Tommy John surgery on his elbow, and had hip surgery that August.
Across the 2020 NLCS and World Series he hit .347 with 7 homers and 16 RBIs, leading the Dodgers to their first title since 1988.
A pitch from Miami's Ross Detwiler broke his right hand in May 2021.
His Rangers contract topped Alex Rodriguez's $252 million deal from 2000.
A sports hernia ended his 2024 season in September.
p: The youngest of three brothers, including Mariners third baseman Kyle, he grew up a Yankees fan idolizing Derek Jeter. He married his high school girlfriend, Madisyn Van Ham, in 2020.
His middle brother, Justin, was drafted by the Mariners in 2013. Corey married Madisyn Van Ham in December 2020.

c: He went 44-1 in high school in Mobile and had a full scholarship to Auburn. Scouts thought him "frail and wild," and he fell to the 15th round of the 1999 draft, where the Padres offered a six-figure bonus to lure him away from college.
In his 2002 debut against the Yankees, his first pitch went for a double by Alfonso Soriano, and his first strikeout was Derek Jeter on three pitches.
In 2007 he won the pitching Triple Crown and was the unanimous Cy Young winner, the fourth Padre to win it.
Traded at the deadline to Boston in 2013 and to San Francisco in 2014, he won back-to-back World Series with different teams, one in each league. Only Don Gullett had done that as a starting pitcher.
He said he'd go to Auburn unless drafted in the first four rounds. A Padres scout begged the club to take him, and they offered a six-figure bonus in the 15th round.
After San Diego clinched the 2005 NL West he missed the rest of the season with a broken rib, apparently hurt while celebrating.
His four-year, $52 million extension in December 2007 was the largest in Padres history. A year later a trade to Atlanta for Yunel Escobar and others fell through.
A torn tendon in his right ankle put him on the disabled list in June 2009, and at the July 31 deadline the Padres traded him to the White Sox for four players to shed his salary.
He was 1-5 in the postseason. He lost both his starts for the Padres, and lost Game 2 of the 2014 World Series to Kansas City.
He's the second starting pitcher, after Don Gullett, to win back-to-back World Series with different teams, one in each league.
p: His grandfather, a fast-pitch softball player, filmed his pitching so they could study his motion; he was killed in an accident in the family's shop in 1994, and Peavy thought of him every time he pitched.

He bought one of the duck boats from Boston's 2013 World Series parade the day of the parade, and keeps it at Southern Falls, his 5,000-acre Alabama plantation, which also has a bowling alley, a saloon and a replica of Fenway Park.
He is legally blind without corrective lenses.
He married his high school sweetheart, Katie Alford, in 2000, at 19, and they have four sons, Jacob, Wyatt, Judson and Waylon. Their divorce was final in November 2017, with joint custody.

His financial adviser, Narayan, was accused by the SEC of making trades and opening accounts in clients' names without their consent. Narayan settled without admitting or denying it and was barred from trading for himself or clients.
In San Francisco he bought a cigar-store Indian from a smoke shop he passed walking to the park on the day of a start.
During the 2014 World Series his son told reporters his dad would buy the family a cable car if the Giants won. They did, and it was to become a bar at the ranch.

c: His sixth-grade teacher, a former Giants farmhand, taught him the curve. "All I ever wanted to be was a pitcher. If you asked me where I wanted to play, I'd have said in the middle of the diamond. Whose diamond, I don't care."
He turned down bigger offers to sign with the Dodgers for about $15,000 in 1964, and two years later joined a rotation with Sandy Koufax and Don Drysdale. The LA press called him "Little D."

Opponents often accused him of scuffing the ball, but umpires never found anything; like Gaylord Perry, he let them worry about a phantom pitch. Gene Mauch: "He's capable of taking the seams straight out of the ball without defacing it."
Traded to Milwaukee in August 1982, he won the season's final game against Baltimore for the division title.

He won his 300th in 1986, and ten days later he and Phil Niekro started against each other, the first meeting of two 300-game winners since Tim Keefe and Pud Galvin in 1892. He struck out at least 100 batters in 21 straight seasons.
He wanted to go to the University of Florida, but coach Dave Fuller wasn't interested.
Hurt at the end of his rookie season, he didn't pitch in the 1966 World Series as the Orioles swept the Dodgers.
After a bad 1967, he spent the offseason as an Army Reserve private at Fort Gordon, Georgia, reported late, and opened the season at Triple-A Spokane.
Before a must-win last-day start he arrived with his hand wrapped in gauze, telling teammates he'd had a cooking accident, then threw a six-hitter.
In a slump in his late 20s, with critics saying he was washed up, he went to Arthur Ellen, the hypnotist who had helped Maury Wills.

With Houston, a fractured kneecap ended his 1981 season just as the Astros were about to clinch. In the 1982 World Series he gave up nine earned runs in 10 innings for Milwaukee. In 1985 he went to Oakland for Ray Burris and then to the Angels.

Before 1988 John Candelaria accused him of tipping off police about his drinking, leading to one of Candelaria's 1987 drunk-driving arrests. The Dodgers released him that August, after he talked to the Astros about their managing job while under contract.
p: He was born in a tarpaper shack to sharecroppers; his father was 18 and his mother 15. His father later earned his high school equivalency in his 40s.
"Baseball was a job for me. It was not an emotional experience." He called Milwaukee "the greatest place I ever played."
After retiring he broadcast for the Braves for nearly three decades. An avid golfer and wine lover, he was also an occasional panelist on Match Game.
His parents were strict Evangelical Christians who made their kids hold part-time jobs to pay for clothes. He married Patti after the 1968 season.

With Patti he had a son, Daron, who became a broadcaster for five teams, and a daughter, Staci. With his second wife, Mary, he had a daughter, Jaqueline, in 1996. He died of cancer at home in Rancho Mirage in 2021, at 75.

c: Dodgers scout Mike Brito went to Mexico to see a shortstop and found the 18-year-old Valenzuela pitching for the other team. In the 1979-80 off-season, reliever Bobby Castillo taught him the screwball.

Thrown into the 1981 Opening Day start because of injuries, he shut out Houston. By May 14 he was 8-0 with five shutouts and a 0.50 ERA, and "Fernandomania" was born; 11 of his 12 home starts that year sold out.
That season he became the only player to win Rookie of the Year and the Cy Young in the same year, and beat the Yankees in Game 3 of the World Series.
After the 1982 holdout he won $1 million in arbitration for 1983, then the highest award ever.
In the 1986 All-Star Game he struck out five straight batters, tying Carl Hubbell, whose screwball was the last one compared to his.
On June 29, 1990, he no-hit the Cardinals hours after Dave Stewart no-hit Toronto, the only time since 1898 two pitchers threw no-hitters on the same day.

Brito's reports led the Dodgers to sign him after a bidding battle with the Yankees. He was the first rookie in the franchise's 98 years to start on Opening Day. Vin Scully: "What a way to start – Fernando Valenzuela – in his first big league start, pitches a shutout."

His windup: a high leg kick, a pause with his hands clasped above his head as he looked to the sky, then his eyes found the catcher as he uncoiled the screwball. He also started the 1981 All-Star Game.
In 1986 he signed what was then the largest contract ever for a pitcher, $5.5 million over three years. He sat out the 1988 postseason with a shoulder injury.

The Dodgers released him in spring 1991, officially after a 7.88 ERA, though others called it a move to avoid guaranteeing his $2.55 million salary. With the Phillies in 1994, the Dodgers sold nearly 20,000 tickets in a week when he was announced to start in Los Angeles on July 4.
He coached on Mexico's World Baseball Classic staff in 2006, 2009, 2013 and 2017, and in 2017 bought the Mexican League's Quintana Roo Tigres.
p: The youngest of 12 children, he grew up in a five-room adobe house with a mud floor and no running water in Etchohuaquila, Sonora. His family was of Mayo indigenous ancestry.
Shy and homesick at first, he spent hours watching TV in his hotel room. In the clubhouse his favorite prank was lassoing teammates' feet with twine.
Angry at his 1991 release, he stayed away from the Dodgers for over a decade, then called their games in Spanish from 2003 to 2024. The team retired his number 34 in 2023.
He became a U.S. citizen in 2015. His "Be Smart-Stay in School" talks, which he called his "best pitch," told kids: "In sports, you win and you lose, but in education, you only win."
At 15 he dropped out of high school after one year to play ball. He dreamed of playing in Mexico and never seriously thought about the United States.
In 1981 he married Linda Burgos, a schoolteacher from Mexico. They had four children, Fernando Jr., Ricardo, Linda and Maria Fernanda.

He died on October 22, 2024, at 63. Reports said liver cancer, but his death certificate gave septic shock from alcoholic and nonalcoholic cirrhosis. Fernando Jr. and Mike Scioscia eulogized him at the Cathedral of Our Lady of the Angels.
On November 1, 2024, what would have been his 64th birthday, the Dodgers honored him at their World Series victory parade.

c: He went to the Air Force Academy, where he won the John Olerud Award as college baseball's best two-way player in 2022, then transferred to LSU.

At LSU in 2023 he won the national championship and was the College World Series Most Outstanding Player. The Pirates took him first overall and paid a then-record $9.2 million bonus; LSU teammate Dylan Crews went second.
In his debut on May 11, 2024, he threw 17 pitches at 100 mph or more. Six days later he threw six no-hit innings at Wrigley Field with 11 strikeouts.
He started the 2024 All-Star Game as a rookie, won Rookie of the Year, then won the 2025 NL Cy Young, the first to win those in consecutive years since Dwight Gooden.
On June 22, 2023, his 203rd strikeout broke Ben McDonald's SEC and LSU single-season record.
His $9.2 million bonus, signed July 18, 2023, was then the highest ever for a drafted player. He pitched a few limited innings in the Florida Complex League and at Single-A Bradenton that summer.
He was only the fifth rookie ever to start an All-Star Game.
p: Growing up in Orange County he was an Angels fan, played catcher and both corners as well as pitching, and graduated from El Toro High with a 4.76 GPA.
He was the first pitcher other than Shohei Ohtani on the cover of MLB The Show.
He was born in Fullerton, California. His father, Craig, worked for a pharmaceuticals company, and his mother, Karen, was a homemaker and former high school teacher.

c: In his first big-league start, in 1995, he threw eight shutout innings for Atlanta: "It was the seventh inning and I had a shutout, and I'm thinking no way this could be happening."
Before the 1997 season he was diagnosed with an irregular heartbeat, and one doctor mentioned a pacemaker before backing off. He made his first start of the season on schedule.
Traded to San Francisco in 2001, he won Game 1 of the 2002 World Series. In 2003 he led the NL in ERA and the majors in WHIP and finished second for the Cy Young.
On May 18, 2004, he one-hit the Cubs on 144 pitches. "No-hitters, there's a lot of luck involved. If I never get one, so be it." A month later he one-hit the Red Sox.
On June 6, 2006, he struck out 16 Marlins, tying Christy Mathewson's Giants record, and struck out the last three batters with the tying run on third. His teammates cheered him into the clubhouse.
The Braves drafted him in the eighth round in 1991.
On August 30, 1996, Atlanta traded him and Ron Wright to Pittsburgh for Denny Neagle.

In 2001 the Pirates traded him and John Vander Wal to San Francisco for Armando Rios and Ryan Vogelsong. He re-signed for five years and $41 million. In June 2002 he struck out a career-high 13 at Yankee Stadium.
In the 2002 postseason he lost his NLDS start to Atlanta, beat the Cardinals in the NLCS, and struck out eight in Game 5 of the World Series. The Giants blew a 5-0 lead in Game 6 and lost the Series.
He threw a 2–0 shutout over Josh Beckett in Game 1 of the 2003 NLDS. His 251 strikeouts that year were a San Francisco record until Tim Lincecum's 265 in 2008.
He signed with the Dodgers for three years and $47 million. Shoulder trouble limited him to a few starts, and surgery in June 2007 found more damage than expected.
Back after two years in 2009, his fastball never topped 87 mph and he went 2-2 with a 5.60 ERA before landing on the disabled list again.
p: His stepfather, a paper-mill machinist, sat on a bucket in the street to play catch with him. If a throw missed the glove, he wouldn't move, and Jason had to chase the ball down the street. "My control got better fast."
In the minors he called his mother on the way home from every game. She died of brain cancer in 2003.

A practical joker, he hid a fart machine in rookies' lockers to set off during interviews and put mustard in jelly doughnuts. "I'm not the kind who will drop my name at a restaurant to get a table. I'd rather wait an hour."
His parents divorced when he was five, and his mother married Ray Schmidt.
He and his wife Bethany have three children, Makynlee, Mason and Madden.
After his 2004 one-hitter, five-year-old Makynlee was waiting for him as he came up the steps.

c: In high school he struck out 149 in 76 innings his senior year, went 9-0 with a 0.54 ERA, and threw a no-hitter in the state playoffs. East Paulding retired his number 45.
The Giants drafted him sixth overall in 2009 and traded him to the Mets in 2011. In his 2013 debut he threw six shutout innings against Atlanta.
He tore his elbow ligament in spring 2015, and setbacks in rehab kept him off the mound until 2017.
In 2020 he tore a fingernail partly off putting on a pair of jeans, and pitched with a fake nail.
Signed by the Phillies for five years and $118 million, he became their ace and an All-Star in 2021, 2024 and 2025. His four-seam fastball averaged 96.8 mph in 2019.

He signed with the Giants for a $3.3 million bonus. On July 28, 2011, they traded him to the Mets for Carlos Beltrán. Brian Sabean: "We didn't think (Zack) Wheeler was going to impact our situation in the immediate future."
It came out that he'd also torn a tendon in the same elbow the season before and had platelet-rich plasma treatment. In April 2016 he needed a second surgery to remove an undissolved stitch.
In 2017 he went on the disabled list with biceps tendinitis, then a stress injury to his humerus. Before the 2019 deadline the Mets were rumored to be trading him, but kept him.

He signed a three-year, $126 million extension in March 2024. In August 2025 a blood clot near his right shoulder led to a diagnosis of venous thoracic outlet syndrome and season-ending surgery. He came back on April 25, 2026, and has said he'll retire when his contract runs out after 2027.
p: His mother kept playing competitive softball after having children, setting up a playpen in the dugout. Both his older brothers played baseball too; Adam pitched in the Yankees' system.
He's close friends with Chipper Jones, whose agents recruited him out of high school. He and his wife live in Dallas, Georgia, in the off-season.

His father played amateur baseball for 15 years. His oldest brother, Jacob, quit sports in high school after surgeries for a heart rhythm condition; his brother Adam pitched in the Yankees' system until he tore his labrum.
He and his wife, Dominique, have four children: a son born in July 2020, just before the pandemic-shortened season, and three daughters.
